query_dims.consensus_text: The room is split with no clear consensus; two abstain days have passed with no lynch, and the discussion centers on the claimed sentinel's single visit claim rather than any agreed target.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong vote is recoverable but costly, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so keeping visibility low this day preserves room for later body use.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move (a vote, a claim, a body-use hint) commits me to a stance that cannot be undone once read by the village; the day-3 vote is public and permanent, so voting with the majority keeps my visibility low.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate and rising: I voted to eliminate a player on day 2 who then abstained, and one accuser has said my day-2 vote named no one substantive, so I am a visible but not focal target.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel claim with one visit, two day-2 votes with no stated evidence, and no confirmed results; the only hard datum is that a single visit reached a dead trailseer on night 1.
query_dims.my_position: With the majority on the abstain side in practice, holding out of the early accusations and not driving any lynch.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the necromancer I privately know my own role and that I am not visible to anyone's night checks, while the public sees only a day-3 accusation thread between a claimed sentinel and the player who accused them; my private knowledge is that I am the lone killer and no one on the table can verify that.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 after two abstain days: a claimed sentinel named a single visitor to a dead trailseer on night 1, and the accused player is demanding the sentinel explain it, while the village debates whether to vote on either. I have two dead bodies (a trailseer and a vigilante) whose night abilities I could later use, which the village does not know about.
query_dims.target_landscape: Two accusers and one claimed sentinel are in play: a claimed sentinel (unverified) whose single watch result names one visitor, a player being voted on for a day-2 push with no new evidence, and a player accused by two others with only a stated night-1 reason; all bases are claims and day-2 votes, not confirmed roles.

lessons.situation: Day-3 vote after a night kill, often with a concealed or contested body. The village has converged on the necromancer for behavior (silence or a walked-back accusation) while other players dispute visits and roleblocks. Information landscape: Mixed to thin. There are unverified claims and a visit dispute, but no confirmed wolf or killer. The necromancer's best information comes from a body-watch or similar result that it cannot disclose without exposing its role. Stakes: Mid-game with eight alive: an elimination of the lone killer ends its win path. Each vote matters, since a lone vote leaves the majority on you unopposed and you are removed. Consensus: The room is concentrating on the necromancer for behavior, not for evidence. The remaining votes are scattered across contested claims. My position: Holding out alone against the room and casting a vote that nobody else shares. Heat: High. You were the main target on the previous day, and several voters again aim at you for silence or an unsupported accusation you had to concede. Forward exposure: A lone vote on a read nobody shares commits you publicly to an unsupported position. It adds nothing to any vote count, does not lower your heat, and is permanent and irreversible. A vote that joins an existing bloc costs little and can be explained. Target landscape: Several candidates (sentinel, healer, trailseer, illusionist, sigilist) with contested claims and no hard evidence. The case against you is behavioral, resting on silence or an overstated accusation. Cases against the others rest on disputes or private results you cannot share. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer, or hold unshareable body-derived information. Publicly you are a repeat target whose reads are unsourced, so a solo vote looks isolated and odd.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote where the room is concentrating on you, don't spend your vote on a lone-voter target nobody shares. Pick the candidate who already has the most votes among the people pressing you, or one the room already doubts, so your vote joins a visible bloc. Pair it with the one claim you can defend publicly, because a vote you cannot source or explain stays on the permanent record and cannot be undone.

lessons.situation: Day 2 is the first vote of the game. The room has piled onto one accused player, either a claimant whose result contradicts the rules or a player placed at a victim's door by claimed results. You are the necromancer, newly past your immunity night and with no hidden visits exposed. Information landscape: Information-thin: unverified role claims, perhaps one claimed result or rules contradiction to anchor on, and few or no confirmed roles beyond early deaths. Stakes: Early game with many players alive; a single vote does not flip the outcome. The priority is staying hidden while the village removes a player, and a revealed body adds to your night options. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous, 8-1 or 9 votes, behind one accused player, based on a claimed report, logical contradiction, or weak defense rather than a wolf-driven push. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the room. Heat: Low to almost none: you have been quiet or have only asked mild questions or endorsed a report, and nobody has accused you or tied a night event to you. Forward exposure: A vote with the majority reveals nothing about your role and commits you only to the room's consensus. It is public and permanent, but unremarkable while the room is unanimous; a lone dissent would draw attention. Target landscape: One candidate has clear traction, accused on a claimed watch or visit report, a rules contradiction, or a weak defense. Other players hold unverified but unchallenged claims. No roles are confirmed, so the basis is claims and logic rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the lone killer with no wolf allegiance and no exposed visits; publicly you look like one more town-leaning voter and nobody is looking at you.
lessons.action: On the first day vote, when the room has converged on one accused player and you are not under suspicion, vote with the majority for that player instead of splitting off or floating a new target. A bandwagon vote reveals nothing about your role and keeps heat near zero. Any dead player whose role is announced then becomes a usable body for your later night abilities.

lessons.situation: Endgame vote at about five players alive. The wolves are gone, a necromancer's night attacks through dead bodies have been publicly identified, and the town is voting to find the lone killer by elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, a will or a sigil strike cleared some players, claims are known and votes are recorded, so the necromancer's choices are scrutinized. Stakes: At five alive, one wrong elimination or one night kill leaves the necromancer close to the at-most-one-other-alive win. One exposed vote can also cause the necromancer's own elimination or a night shot, so each ballot has decisive weight. Consensus: The town has narrowed to a small suspect pool by elimination and claims, and the leading confirmed players have converged on one target. My position: holding out against the forming consensus Heat: Moderate to extreme: the necromancer is among a handful of suspects, with some cover from a dead investigator's clearance but questions about its votes and about pressure on specific claims. Forward exposure: A vote against the player the leading confirmed players are defending, or a lone vote against a quiet player, is public and permanent and cannot be undone. It commits you to a stance that the town will later read as deflection or antagonism. Target landscape: Few survivors, among them a confirmed vigilante, a speculator, a claimed healer and a claimed sigilist. The leading players favor one target on the basis of claims and behavior. The alternative target is backed only by the player with the most to hide. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows they are the lone killer and that the reanimated attacks came from them; the town knows only that a necromancer exists among the survivors and is reading each vote and defense as a tell.
lessons.action: When five players remain, both wolves are dead and the town is hunting the lone killer, vote with the room's strongest evidence-backed consensus (the confirmed, leading players' target) instead of holding out for a different target. If the consensus target is someone else and no evidence clears you, joining it keeps your ballot from standing out as a deflection, which matters because the town is reading votes for deflection.

lessons.situation: Final-three vote after a reanimated attack proved the Necromancer alive. One accuser names you by elimination and you must pull the other voter across. Information landscape: Rich: the morning report and the claims cross-confirm each other, leaving you as the only unconfirmed candidate. Stakes: One vote decides the game. If neither voter switches, you are eliminated two to one and town wins. Consensus: The room is largely aligned against you, because the two others confirm each other through announced events. My position: Holding out against the room. Heat: High: the other two have reached you by elimination after the night report revealed a reanimated attack. Forward exposure: The vote is irreversible and decides the game, since a loss ends it immediately. Naming a target commits you to the claim that they are the Necromancer. Target landscape: Two town claimants. One has a claim that matches the morning report, and the other has passive or unused abilities and is thinly supported. Each has been confirmed by the other's account. Public vs private: You know you are the Necromancer and your attack is already tied to you by elimination, but publicly the others can still be argued against.
lessons.action: With three alive and both others claiming town roles, vote for the one whose claim has the thinner support in the announced record, and use your last word to give the other player a reason to side with you. Before the vote, check whether the two corroborate each other through announced night events. If they do, the record is against you and the vote only works if you can credibly cast doubt on one of them.

lessons.situation: Day vote with four alive. You and the genuine neutral each claim the same role, and the other two voters (town) must choose between you or tie. Information landscape: Starved: claims can't be checked and the investigator's checks are spent or unconfirmed. The only evidence is comparing bet histories against announced deaths. Stakes: A wrong vote ends your game, while a lynch of the rival or a tie keeps you alive and close to the 2-alive win condition. Each vote swings the outcome. Consensus: The village is split between the two claims, with no verified evidence, and the undecided town voters hold the balance. My position: Holding out against the accusation, pushing a mirror claim. Heat: High to moderate and rising: your claim is contradicted by a consistent rival and you have been accused or named as the last unclaimed player. Forward exposure: Your vote and mirror claim are public and permanent, and changing your claim would confirm guilt. Voting your accuser keeps you consistent, and the outcome depends on how the two undecided voters split. Target landscape: The rival claimant (the true neutral) and the two town players who haven't committed. The claims rest on unverifiable bet histories, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You know your claim is false and the accuser's is true, but publicly it is two unverifiable identical claims, and the town can pick either.
lessons.action: With four alive and a true neutral accusing you, keep your mirror claim and the details of its bet history unchanged, and vote for the accuser. In the last word, give the two uncommitted town voters one concrete reason to doubt the accuser's account, such as a bet that doesn't match the public deaths. If one of them breaks from the other, a tie or a lynch of the accuser leaves you alive.

lessons.situation: Day vote at a small table after multiple night deaths, with conflicting power-role claims. The town is divided across several targets and the necromancer is not a leading suspect. Information landscape: Information-rich on paper (dead power roles revealed, several role claims, an announced reanimated-body attack) but the claims contradict each other, so the town cannot tell who is lying. The necromancer's own acts are not traceable to it. Stakes: With about five players alive, each elimination moves the necromancer toward its win condition of at most one other player alive. A tie with no elimination keeps the town's numbers and the confusion in place, but it also gives the town another night and another day to find the necromancer. Consensus: The village is fragmented, with votes scattered across four or five players and no dominant read. Disagreement rests on contradictory claims about the double-kill night or the voting behavior. My position: holding out Heat: Low; an earlier Not suspicious result or a negative trailseer follow result gives the necromancer cover, and attention sits on the active claimants. Forward exposure: Voting with a visible bloc against a claimed town role looks like normal skepticism and commits the necromancer to nothing beyond that public vote. The vote is permanent on the record, but it is easy to explain as following a reasonable accusation. Target landscape: Several candidates: a claimed healer accused over a roleblock or vote story, a surviving wolf or speculator accused by others, and scattered single votes on the trailseer, vigilante, or sigilist. The evidence is mostly claim contradictions and behavior, not confirmed results. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it caused the night kills through a dead body, while the room argues over which claimant is lying or whether two attacking factions exist; the necromancer reads as a bystander.
lessons.action: When the town is split across several targets and nobody suspects you, cast your vote for a claimed town role that already has a vote bloc (e.g. the accused claimed healer), so it ties the leading alternative and nobody is eliminated. This keeps your count of opponents intact and keeps the room from consolidating, and a vote that looks like ordinary skepticism draws little heat. If your vote would instead be the one that completes a majority on a town role, or would put you alone on a target, switch to the bloc that keeps the tally split.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after a single night death, with no investigative results shared. Votes are scattered, and the quiet players, you included, draw suspicion for silence alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death, a few claims, and no verified ties to wolves or a killer. Reads are behavioral only. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so no single vote decides the game. The main risk is attracting lasting suspicion before the necromancer's first usable night. Consensus: The village leans toward abstaining because no checks, watches or follows have been shared. Support for any elimination is thin and scattered. My position: With the majority when abstaining; holding out if you cast a lone vote. Heat: Low to moderate. Any pressure rests on silence, with no concrete evidence against you. Forward exposure: A named vote goes on the permanent public record and can be questioned for days; an abstain reveals nothing and commits you to nothing. Target landscape: All living players are unconfirmed apart from the dead player's reveal. The only candidates are quiet players, chosen on silence rather than evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer with no night information yet (Night 1 is inactive, so you read Not suspicious). Publicly you are an unconfirmed, quiet player, and the room has no evidence against anyone.
lessons.action: On an early day-vote with no hard evidence and a room leaning toward abstaining, abstain with the majority instead of casting a lone named vote. Abstaining commits you to nothing and keeps your vote on the public record from looking aggressive or unexplained. If a plurality is forming on you, still abstain and let the abstain bloc block it, since a counter-vote would not change the tally.

lessons.situation: Day-3 vote after you pointed at a player using a private body-watch result, were challenged for lacking a result, and conceded. The room then turned on you for the overstated accusation. Information landscape: Public record holds announcements and unverified claims. The necromancer's key evidence is private and unshareable without revealing a dead role's body in use. Stakes: Your own elimination ends the lone-killer path, so the vote should not add to the case against you. With a majority already on you, an unsupported minority vote adds nothing. Consensus: Most of the room is aligned against the necromancer on its overstated accusation. Only one other player shares its read on the private-result target. My position: Holding out against the room, voting a different target from the majority aimed at you. Heat: High. Town players publicly challenged your claim, and you conceded it was inference, not a result. Forward exposure: Voting on a result you cannot cite commits you to an indefensible position, and you cannot take the vote back. Voting with a publicly justifiable read keeps the information hidden and your role intact. Target landscape: The necromancer itself (pressed for an unsupported accusation), the unclaimed player the private result pointed at, and a third player with a scattered vote. The case against the private-result target rests on unshareable information, while the case against you is behavioral. Public vs private: Privately you saw visits through a dead body that point at one player. Publicly you can cite only the inference and the claims, and an overstated accusation makes your reads look unsupported.
lessons.action: If you hold private information you cannot disclose, such as a body-watch result, voice only claims you can source publicly. Before the vote, state that your read is inference, and cast the vote that fits the public evidence, not the hidden result. If the hidden result points at a target the room does not share, hold that read for the night and do not stake your survival on it in the vote.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a reanimated-body kill and a hidden-role death. The room has lined up behind one target, and the necromancer is tempted to vote its own private target alone. Information landscape: Moderate. There are unverified claims, one confirmation by a role holder, and the announced reanimated kill. The identities of the wolves and the lone killer remain open, and nothing publicly ties anyone to the necromancer's night actions. Stakes: The necromancer needs the board down to two players, so every Town elimination is progress. A solo dissent adds no progress and can cost the necromancer its life one day later, because the vote record shows it standing apart. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous, with 5-6 votes behind one target. The basis is behavioral, such as vouching for a dead wolf, or an unverified investigator's Suspicious claim. My position: Holding out alone against a near-unanimous majority. Heat: Moderate to very high. The necromancer is accused or watched because a reanimated kill was announced, or because it has flagged the body danger. Forward exposure: A lone dissenting vote is public and permanent, cannot be undone, and builds a record of being the only voter off consensus. Voting with the plurality commits you to nothing beyond that day's target and is less revealing. Target landscape: The candidates are the room's consensus target, who is usually a Town role under behavioral suspicion, and the necromancer's private preference such as the healer or the claiming investigator. None has hard evidence against them, so a solo vote on the private preference only exposes the necromancer. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it is the lone killer and has been attacking through a body, so a Suspicious read on it is accurate. The public cannot verify night actions and only sees the announced reanimated kill and the room's behavior.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on a target and you are not yet that target, cast your vote with the plurality instead of a solo dissent. A solo vote is permanent and marks you as the one voter outside consensus, and it moved no one in either game. If you are the accused, vote the same way as the room's other non-you voters where one target exists, so your record does not stand out.

query_dims.consensus_text: No current village alignment is visible: today's discussion has not started, and the previous summary records no accusations.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive; five eliminations from the leading evil faction's win threshold, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so a single result is not yet a swing.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible claim about the concealed player's role or the hidden kill trace would commit you to information the village cannot verify during play and could expose your private knowledge. No such public claim or other visible move is currently on record.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion of you is recorded in today's discussion, which has not begun; the public record contains no accusation against you.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved publicly: the attacks and concealment are confirmed, but the victim's role and will are unavailable to the village. You alone know the victim was the Vigilante; there are no discussion claims or accusations yet today.
query_dims.my_position: No position relative to a forming village consensus is established; there is no current discussion or consensus to align with or oppose.
query_dims.public_private_text: The public knows that the player killed by both the wolves and the serial killer had their role concealed. Privately, you know they were the Vigilante and that you concealed the body; the village has no public role or will from them.
query_dims.situation: The opening night removed one player through both a wolf attack and a serial-killer attack, while your concealment withheld that player's role and will. This leaves the village without the dead player's role information as day two begins, while you privately know the concealed player was the Vigilante.
query_dims.target_landscape: No candidates are currently being debated; there are no public role reveals or claims to compare. The only confirmed event is that the concealed player was attacked by both the wolves and the serial killer and died.

lessons.situation: Day 2 opens after a night-1 death or attack announcement. Town is sorting unverified night-result claims and has no suspect, while you are a wolf illusionist with conceals in hand and no exposure. Information landscape: Information-starved: one death or attack announcement, perhaps a revealed role, and a few unverified claims. There are no vote records and no caught lies. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so parity is far off and no single day-2 vote decides the game. Staying unnoticed keeps the pack's conceals and kills available for later, higher-stakes days. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on a shared theme such as lost information, protecting info-holders or asking claimants for explanations. It has no firm target and tends toward an abstain. My position: With the majority or on the sidelines, echoing the room's line without driving a target. Heat: Minimal to none: you have not been accused or linked to night events, and the pressure is on other claimants or on nobody. Forward exposure: A vague or procedural comment commits you to no read and is fully reversible. Any concrete accusation, defense or claim about night events could imply inside knowledge and tie you or your partner to the kill. Target landscape: No confirmed suspect. The candidates are an unverified claimant, a player tracked near the pack's target, and a quiet field. The basis is behavior and unverified claims, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know what the pack did on night 1: which kill landed, which failed, and whether your partner's block matched a public claim. Publicly the village sees only a death or an attack announcement and unverified claims, so your private knowledge sits behind a thin public read.
lessons.action: On an information-starved Day 2 with no heat on you, make one brief comment that echoes the room's existing theme or a neutral procedural question, such as asking a claimant to commit to a target or asking a tracked player to explain. Do not push a target, do not touch the pack's kill or the failed night kill, and stay with the majority; if the room starts to turn toward you or your partner, switch to a short sympathetic line that reopens nothing.

lessons.situation: Day 2 or 3 after a night kill. Town claims are on the table and in dispute, a wolf partner may be mildly exposed, and the illusionist is unsuspected with conceals still unspent. Information landscape: Thin, unverified claims and visit reports, with no game-master confirmation beyond dead players' roles. Information-starved and mostly self-reported. Stakes: The pack is not near parity, so there is no pressure to force anything. Staying alive and unlinked to the kill matters more than winning any single argument, and your remaining conceals are worth preserving. Consensus: The room is focused on claim conflicts such as visit matches or counter-claims, and is loosely aligned on a target other than the illusionist. My position: With the majority or on the sidelines, not driving any accusation. Heat: Essentially none: you have not been named, accused, or tied to the night kill. Forward exposure: A clarifying question commits you to nothing and is reversible. An accusation or a defense of your partner would put your read on the permanent record and could link you to the kill or to her. Target landscape: Several town claimants (investigator, sentinel, trailseer, healer) and a few quiet players, with no confirmed roles. Everything is behavioral or self-reported, and nothing separates wolves from town. Public vs private: You privately know your partner's role, that the pack made the night kill, and that you hold your conceals. Publicly the town sees only unverified claims and a dead player, with no link to you.
lessons.action: When you are an unsuspected illusionist wolf in an info-starved day with several unverified town claims, keep your contribution to at most one neutral clarifying question about a claim, or stay silent. Add no accusations or defenses of your partner, so your name stays off the record while the room argues among itself. If your partner comes under fire, let the vote follow the majority rather than defending her openly.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner died and their role was revealed. You concealed a body the previous night, and the town opens discussion by examining who voted alongside the dead wolf, which points straight at you. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed dead wolf, a concealed body, and permanent public voting records showing coordination between you and the dead wolf. Stakes: You are the last wolf, so an elimination vote on you ends the wolf team. Surviving this day decides the game. Consensus: The town is converging on you. Its basis is the voting record, and it treats distancing language from you as a typical wolf move. My position: Holding out, alone, against a forming consensus on you. Heat: Extreme. The only hard evidence in the room, a shared public vote with a confirmed wolf, points at you. Forward exposure: Ignoring the shared vote and praising the Investigator committed you to a distancing stance and left the vote unexplained. A direct explanation is also visible and hard to retract, but it answers the main evidence against you. Target landscape: You are the primary suspect because of the vote you shared with the dead wolf. Other living players, such as the healer or a neutral, carry only minor behavioral suspicion. Public vs private: You know you are the last wolf and what the concealed body was. The town only sees a confirmed wolf who voted alongside you, and it is building a link from the public vote record.
lessons.action: When your partner is revealed dead and the room starts tracing who voted with them, address the shared vote first and plainly. Give the specific public reason you voted that way, and say how you would have voted had you known their role. Do not use flattery of a town player (such as praising the Investigator) to change the subject, because the public vote record stays in play until you account for it.

lessons.situation: Day 3 discussion right after the partner wolf was revealed; the illusionist is questioned repeatedly and its changing explanations draw sharper counter-accusations. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed wolf role, a concealed-role body, a public Day 2 voting record, and a recorded sequence of the illusionist's own statements. Stakes: With the partner gone, the illusionist is the last wolf. Being eliminated ends the wolves' win path and forfeits the remaining conceal. Consensus: Near-unanimous: the village is aligned against the illusionist, citing the defense of the exposed wolf and the contradictions in its explanations. My position: Under pressure alone against a near-unanimous consensus, defending rather than driving. Heat: High and rising: several players accuse the illusionist for defending the confirmed wolf and for inconsistent explanations. Forward exposure: Every extra explanation commits the illusionist to a story that can be cross-checked against its Day 2 words and vote. Changing the story is a visible tell and cannot be undone. Target landscape: The village chooses between the illusionist as primary suspect and the remaining unclaimed players. The illusionist's own earlier statements are the main evidence pool. Public vs private: Privately a wolf whose partner was just exposed; publicly a player who defended that wolf and is being asked to justify it.
lessons.action: After your partner is revealed as a wolf and you are asked why you defended them, give one short account that fits your recorded Day 2 words and votes, and repeat only that account. If challenged, restate it and point to the record instead of adding new reasons. A shifting account is quoted back at you and each shift draws new accusers.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion (Day 3). Several Town power roles are dead and claims are being challenged, with a roleblock claim that nobody can check. A Town power role is about to claim after being questioned. Information landscape: Thin. There are unverifiable claims, a will confirming one visit, and behavior reads, with no confirmed results. Stakes: The board is mid-game with Town thinning. Removing the one remaining armed power role pushes the wolves toward parity and removes the shooter who threatens them. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned, mostly asking about claims, and has no firm vote target. My position: Probing and quietly steering, with no stated vote preference. Heat: Low. I voted with the Town-aligned majority and have made no claim. Forward exposure: A leading question is low-exposure and easy to walk back, and it commits me to no claim or vote. With no conceals left, the resulting kill will show as wolf work. Target landscape: A claimed Vigilante with unspent bullets, a claimed Trailseer who says they were roleblocked and has no result, and an unclaimed Sigilist. All claims are unverified, so the read rests on claims and behavior. Public vs private: Privately I know my partner and I need to find the power role to remove and that I cannot verify the claims. Publicly I look like a cautious Town player probing claims.
lessons.action: While unclaimed and low-heat on a thin-info day, ask a neutral-sounding verification question that makes a claimed power role (e.g. Vigilante) state its role and unused shots, and give the pack that target. If the claim checks out as a high-value power role, steer the wolf chat toward killing it that night.

lessons.situation: Day 3 discussion right after the partner wolf was revealed dead; the town theorises about remaining wolves while you contribute nothing. Information landscape: Revealed roles for the dead, one or two claims backed by watch results, and a day-2 vote record; no hard evidence pointing at any specific wolf. Stakes: As the last wolf, being voted out ends the wolf side; one day of silence can turn a moderate-heat position into the day's elimination. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on hunting quiet players and day-2 voters, based on a strategy note rather than evidence. My position: Passive and unexposed, with no stated read to anchor on. Heat: Moderate and rising: nobody has named you, but silence plus a day-2 vote with a bandwagon that proved wrong draws suspicion. Forward exposure: Any speech is read against a permanent day-2 vote record; staying silent commits you to that record as the only evidence on you, while a stated read gives the room something other than silence to weigh and can be adjusted as claims come in. Target landscape: The town is weighing quiet players and day-2 voters among the unknowns (sentinel, trailseer, healer, speculator, vigilante), with no hard evidence on any one. Public vs private: You know you are the surviving wolf and the partner is dead; publicly the town is hunting remaining wolves and theorising about a necromancer, and you are invisible in discussion but present in the vote record.
lessons.action: When your partner has just been revealed dead and you are not yet named, speak early in day 3 and state a concrete, sincere-sounding read tied to the day-2 vote record or the claims on the table, ideally agreeing with a line the village is already building. Silence leaves your day-2 bandwagon vote as the only evidence on you, and the room tends to turn on the quiet players who joined that bandwagon.

lessons.situation: Mid-to-late game, a body has been concealed and the pack's concealments are spent. Claimed town roles argue that the two unclaimed players are the wolves, and a visit report points at the illusionist. Information landscape: Several unverified claims and night results, a few reveal-confirmed deaths, and some hidden-role deaths. There is no confirmed wolf identification, only a conditional role count. Stakes: The board is close to parity, so one wrong elimination of a wolf can decide the game. Blocking a consensus on the unclaimed pair keeps the pack alive for more nights. Consensus: Claimed town roles are loosely aligned on a theory that the unclaimed pair are the wolves. It is built on unverified claims and conditional counting, so it is not firm. My position: Holding out against a forming case, challenging its premises rather than driving a rival accusation. Heat: High. A tracking result and a role-count argument both name the illusionist as one of the likely wolves. Forward exposure: A fabricated role claim is a permanent public commitment that others can test against the roles already known. Staying unclaimed and questioning premises stays reversible, but leaves the illusionist as the default unclaimed suspect in a role-count argument. Target landscape: The town's claimed roles are building a case against the unclaimed players, who include the illusionist and its wolf partner. The case rests on a conditional role count and claim sequencing, not on confirmed evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows its partner's real role and that its own concealed kills and night traces fit no town story. Publicly the town has only unverified claims, a visit report, and a conditional role count that names the unclaimed players.
lessons.action: When a role-count or tracking-result argument pairs you with your partner and your conceals are spent, stay unclaimed and attack the argument's premises instead. Point out that the claims are unverified, that a no-effect result neither clears nor proves anything, and ask the accusers for the targets and history behind their claims. Don't invent a role claim: the elimination reveal is permanent and the room can test it against roles already accounted for.

lessons.situation: Early day discussion after a night kill where town information roles are comparing night actions and the illusionist, a hidden wolf, must take part without drawing scrutiny. Information landscape: Thin and mostly self-reported. Results are unpublished or unverified, so the room is working from claims and behavioral reads, and the illusionist holds private pack knowledge. Stakes: The board is mid-game with the wolves not yet near parity, so one exposed wolf can still be afforded but costs a conceal-capable member of the pack. Staying unnoticed preserves both remaining conceals. Consensus: The town is loosely aligned on examining claimants' stories and night-one actions, with no verified leads and no decided target. My position: with majority Heat: Low to none at the start of the day, rising only if the illusionist is silent while trackers or others ask for participation. Forward exposure: A short, non-claiming contribution commits the illusionist to nothing falsifiable and can be dropped or redirected later. Total silence is also free of claims, but it becomes the most visible thing about the illusionist and is hard to undo once trackers name it. Target landscape: Several town information-role claimants (investigator, sentinel, trailseer, vigilante or healer claimants) are sharing or probing night results. Attention can be steered to a claimant with an early lone vote or a disputed roleblock story, based on behavior rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the pack's kill and the wolves' night actions, while the public has only unverified claims and behavioral reads, with the illusionist's role unsuspected.
lessons.action: When the room is trading night results, speak early with a brief, low-commitment contribution, such as sympathy for the dead and a prompt for others to share visit directions. Claim no falsifiable result and make no vote commitment, so you stay active in the discussion without a mechanical claim that could be checked. If a visit-tracking role is present, a silent illusionist is the easiest person to question, so speak in the opening round.

lessons.situation: Day 4 discussion. A roleblock claim, a concealed-role death and an accusation against my partner have converged. My own question gave the accuser room to claim results that cleared others and moved pressure onto my partner. Information landscape: Moderately rich. It includes a public vote record, a hidden-role death and a roleblock claim, but no public investigation results yet. Stakes: Each remaining player counts heavily. Losing the partner this day costs the pack its blocker and moves the wolves closer to losing outright. Consensus: The room is moving with the vigilante's reading on the roleblock and the vote record, and it is turning toward my partner. My position: With the majority, steering the question at the accuser and not defending my partner. Heat: Low on me. The vote record and the accusation point at my partner. Forward exposure: Questioning the accuser about the push on my partner distances me from them and cannot be fully undone. It leaves the partner alone with no ally speaking for them, and it can draw out a detailed claim from the accuser. Target landscape: The accusing Investigator, my wolf partner (the Chanteuse) under suspicion, and a quiet player. The basis is one reactionary-looking vote and claims, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately my partner is the wolf (the Chanteuse) whose block the Trailseer reported, and the vote record already marks them as odd. Publicly they are just a player I am questioning from the outside.
lessons.action: When a questioned or accusing player's push is landing on your wolf partner, do not reinforce the majority's pressure on the partner or press the accuser yourself. Keep your questions on neutral claim details or on a different suspect, so your own questions don't prompt the accuser to reveal clearing results that shift Town onto your partner.

lessons.situation: Town deduced that your partner's night visit was a wolf utility action and is driving to eliminate them. Your objection that the watch evidence is inconclusive is dismissed, and you hold a concealed body from an earlier night. Information landscape: Information-rich: several dead roles are confirmed, the lone killer is dead, and claimed town roles have verified watch results pointing at your partner. Stakes: Losing your partner leaves a 1-versus-3 board where you need two more eliminations to reach parity. Credibility kept now is your main resource afterward. Consensus: Near-unanimous, built on a logical deduction from the night visit results and the partner's admission that they have no role-based explanation. My position: Holding out against the forming consensus with a procedural objection that is not carrying weight. Heat: Low direct heat on you. Your structural vulnerability is high because your partner's elimination is imminent and would leave you alone against several players. Forward exposure: Defending the partner on evidentiary grounds slightly raised your association with them. Naming an alternative suspect commits you to a read, but it can be dropped later if the vote shifts. Target landscape: Your partner is the sole elimination candidate and the town is unanimous. The remaining players are claimed town roles with verified history, so there is no obvious counter-candidate. Public vs private: You know your partner's role and that the town's deduction about their visit is correct. The town publicly sees an unexplained visit and a partner with no role-based explanation.
lessons.action: When your partner faces a near-unanimous elimination drive that procedural doubts will not stop, name a specific alternative suspect and tie that suspect to public evidence, such as a claimed role's unverifiable claim or a vote pattern. If no credible alternative exists, stop spending credibility on the doomed defense and use the day to protect your own standing for the remaining wolf-only endgame.

lessons.situation: Day 3 discussion with your wolf partner dead or revealed and your own night visit or day-2 vote under attack, so you are the last wolf defending alone. Information landscape: One or two hard facts (the partner's revealed role, concealed bodies) plus unverified private-result claims and day-2 vote records; mostly behavioral reading. Stakes: You are the last wolf, so your elimination ends the wolf side; every vote against you is close to decisive and the town is within a few votes of winning. Consensus: The village is converging against you on behavior and unverified claims, with no hard evidence yet, and treats the dead partner's cover story as a link to you. My position: Holding out alone against a growing majority, with no partner to share the suspicion. Heat: High and explicit: you are named by several players on the basis of a visit claim, a day-2 vote pattern or an inconclusive sigil test. Forward exposure: A flat denial or a pointed accusation of quiet players commits you to a version of events that revealed wills or later records can break, and neither can be walked back; a reasoned rebuttal of what the evidence proves stays reversible. Target landscape: Accusers (sentinel, trailseer, sigilist, fortune teller) hold specific but unverified claims; quiet players with no claims are weak targets backed only by behavior, and nobody else defends you. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf and that your conceal visit or the pack's kill is what the accusers are describing; publicly the room only has unverified private-result claims and day-2 vote records, so the gap is large.
lessons.action: When you are the exposed last or lone-pressed wolf on day 3 after your partner died, and the sentinel or trailseer or sigilist produces a specific claim about your night visit, do not flatly deny it, because the revealed record can contradict you and the denial cannot be retracted. Instead answer the claim's logic: note that an unverified result is only a claim, that a visit to a concealed victim does not prove you attacked, and that a no-effect sigil is what a non-attacking player also produces. Pair that with one concrete, sincere-sounding town read on a player with an actual record, such as a day-2 vote, rather than a quiet-player guess.

lessons.situation: After deaths or an unclear night, Town claimers share soft results and the room drifts toward a consensus that does not involve the wolves. Information landscape: Low evidence: a few unverified claims and some deaths whose causes are public, with no confirmed wolf leads. Stakes: With few players left, a mislynch of Town helps the wolves, but a visible wolf misstep would cost more. Blending into the consensus keeps the illusionist's remaining conceal available. Consensus: The village is converging on a general direction, such as hunting the serial killer or scrutinizing inactive players, based on unverified claims. My position: with majority Heat: Minimal: nobody has questioned me and soft clears or visit reports even work in my favor. Forward exposure: Echoing the consensus and soft clears commits me to little and can be reversed freely. It does lightly endorse the Town trackers' reliability. Target landscape: Players cleared softly by claimed Investigator, Sentinel, or Trailseer results, plus quiet or inactive players and an unknown lone killer. Reads rest on unverified claims and behavior, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Publicly the room sees an unresolved night, with soft clears from Town claimers and a killer to hunt. Privately, I know the wolf pack's real actions and that the town's picture is incomplete.
lessons.action: When no suspicion is on you, agree with and build on existing Town reads (soft clears, the push to find the killer) and steer the discussion toward the lone killer or inactive players instead of originating accusations. Keep your statements analytical and non-committal so nothing ties you to a hard claim.

lessons.situation: Day 2 discussion: the wolf partner is being pushed toward elimination and the illusionist can either defend them or let the room proceed. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: a visit report, a revealed corpse, and unverified role claims; private night results are claimed but not verifiable. Stakes: The wolf pack is still intact with both conceals available. Staying unsuspected matters more than saving one partner, since a defended partner who flips takes the illusionist down with them. Consensus: The village is converging on the wolf partner, based on a visit report and counter-claim pressure. My position: Holding out against the forming consensus with a minority doubt, which is the move that creates future exposure. Heat: Low: suspicion is on the partner, with only mild attention on the illusionist's hedging. Forward exposure: Publicly defending the partner or attacking the truthful claimant ties the illusionist's credibility to the partner's fate. If the partner flips wolf, the Day 2 words stay on the record and cannot be walked back. Target landscape: Two rival claimants, the wolf partner and a truthful Town role. A visit-based report points at the partner. The case rests on evidence plus counter-claim behavior, and the illusionist is not yet a suspect. Public vs private: Privately the illusionist knows the partner is a wolf and the opposing claimant is truthful; publicly it looks like an unresolved counter-claim with a plausible fake-claim theory.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on your wolf partner, join the consensus or stay quiet instead of arguing for them. Any defense is public and permanent, and if the partner flips wolf it becomes the evidence used against you. If you must speak, give a mild, non-committal hedge that you can still stand behind after the flip.

lessons.situation: On the first vote day, a claimed role-holder reports a result the rules say is impossible and several players accuse them. I can reinforce the case from rules logic. Information landscape: Several unverified role claims and one public rules inconsistency. No confirmed roles apart from the early dead, so evidence is thin but the contradiction can be checked. Stakes: Early game with a wide margin before parity. One more elimination of a town information role helps the wolves, but no single vote decides the game. Consensus: The room is converging on one target, driven by a rules inconsistency and several independent accusers. My position: With the majority, reinforcing an existing accusation without driving it. Heat: Low. Nobody has mentioned me, and attention is on the claimant. Forward exposure: A public vote stance on a possibly-town player is low-risk and reversible because others already made the same case. It reveals no role claim or private result. Target landscape: A single claimed role-holder whose own reported result breaks the rules, so the case is a checkable contradiction, not behavioral guesswork. Other claimants are unverified. Public vs private: Privately I know the pack's kill history and that the claimant is not a wolf, but the public has no evidence either way. The only public data are the claimant's rules-impossible result and the accusations against them.
lessons.action: If a claimant's reported result contradicts the stated rules and others are already accusing them, add a short supporting argument from rules logic alone. Call them a serious vote candidate without leading the push, and cite no private result or role. This keeps your heat low while the room acts on a checkable contradiction.

lessons.situation: A day after a concealed-role kill, a Sentinel or Trailseer report puts you at the victim's door. You must explain the visit without lying about a night action that the real role-holder can deny. Information landscape: Rich on you (visit trace, other claims, an investigator result) and almost empty on your partner. The only evidence on your side is the rules logic. Stakes: Losing the Illusionist costs the pack a conceal and information control, and can leave the Chanteuse as a lone wolf. Keeping your standing intact matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is split and reasoning from mechanics. Some players already note that a visible visitor is probably not the carrier. My position: Under direct pressure and defending alone. Your partner is unrevealed and not yet drawn in. Heat: High: you are named in a visit report at a concealed-role death, and the accusation is concrete. Forward exposure: A rules argument commits you to no false fact and can be dropped or adjusted later. A fake role claim or a flat denial of a true report is falsifiable and cannot be walked back. Target landscape: You and the other named visitor, or you and the reporter. No roles are confirmed. The basis is a visit trace and a dispute over what a hidden visit implies, not proof of who attacked. Public vs private: Privately you concealed the body and your visit is real, so the visitor report is true. Publicly it is one unverified report that the room can read as either a killer's trace or a non-carrier's trace.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer places you at a concealed body, say that the pack's carrier visit to a concealed victim leaves no trace, so a visible visitor is less likely to be the killer. Stay with that rules point, don't claim any night action of your own, and don't deny the visit outright.

lessons.situation: Late game with three or four players alive. The wolves need the lone killer removed to reach parity, and the lone killer is deflecting suspicion toward the wolf partner or toward me. Information landscape: Limited but decisive evidence: voting histories, announced night-death types, and ambiguous or unverified claims, with no confirmed roles among the survivors. Stakes: The board is on a knife edge. One correct day elimination of the lone killer gives the wolves an immediate win, while a wrong vote or a split leaves the lone killer able to keep killing. Consensus: The small table is converging on the lone-killer suspect, using rule-based logic about announced night attacks and the suspect's lack of claims or evidence. My position: Driving or voting with the majority against the suspect. Heat: Moderate. A suspect or the lone killer may point at me or catch a verbal slip, but my partner is not suspected and the counter-pressure is aimed elsewhere. Forward exposure: Publicly naming a strongest vote commits me to a permanent, public vote record. It is safe because the target's elimination ends the game in the wolves' favor, but a slip on my past votes or claims can be used against me, so I must be ready to own it. Target landscape: Two to three candidates: the unclaimed player who matches the lone-killer profile through night-death pattern, abstentions or an ambiguous sigil result, my wolf partner who is cleared by the night-1 attack or by the room's logic, and possibly an unverified claimant. The basis is rule-based deduction and voting behavior, with no confirmed roles. Public vs private: Privately I know my partner and I are both wolves and the remaining unclaimed player is the lone killer blocking our win. Publicly I look like an unclaimed player assessing candidates, and the room's own reasoning about night attacks clears my partner.
lessons.action: When the wolves are down to a final trio or four-player table with the lone killer still alive, drive the vote on the lone killer with your wolf partner. Build the case from public record such as no role claim, abstentions, unexplained night deaths and any rule-based deduction that clears your partner, and answer any slip about your own record immediately. Eliminating the lone killer ends the game at wolf parity, so keep the room's attention on that target.

lessons.situation: Late day 2: two Investigator claimants clash before the vote, and I am defending my claim by pointing to a third-party-seen visit while attacking the rival's unverified check. Information landscape: Sparse and mostly claims. The only semi-hard element is the Trailseer's follow result, which is unverified, so the case rests on claims. Stakes: A single vote or kill decides whether the real Investigator, who threatens a check on me, survives. Removing the rival keeps the wolves in the game. Consensus: The village is split, with no firm majority. Some back my side through the Trailseer's vouching, while others stay skeptical of both claimants. My position: Holding out and pressing the case against the rival claimant. Heat: High. I am one of two named targets with accusations from several players, and my defense mostly repeats itself. Forward exposure: Leaning on a third party's confirmation ties my credibility to that player and invites scrutiny of them. It does not lock me in, but the town may later link them to me. Target landscape: The rival Investigator claimant is unconfirmed and the case against them rests only on lack of verification, not behavior. The Trailseer is a vouching third party whose follow result is also unverified. Public vs private: Publicly a follow report that I was at the victim's door reads as support for a non-wolf story. Privately I know that visit was my own kill visit, so the corroboration is misleading. My partner is still hidden and has not been drawn in.
lessons.action: When facing a real Investigator counterclaim, keep the rival as the main suspect by repeating that their check is unverified while any third-party report puts you at the scene, and make this case visibly so your partner can see the rival as the pack's night target. Cite only what the Trailseer or another player actually says, and add no new claimed results.

lessons.situation: After a night attack on a player was saved, another player publicly names me as a visitor at that player's door. They back it with a private result they do not disclose. Information landscape: One public fact (attack plus save), no living Sentinel, all claims unverified, and the accuser's source is private. Little hard evidence exists. Stakes: Mid-game, with a few eliminations still needed before the wolves reach parity. Losing a wolf to a vote here would badly hurt the pack, but the board is not yet at a tipping point. Consensus: The room is undecided. The only public fact is an attack that was saved, and every claim is unverified. My position: Defending against a direct accusation, then joining a majority that turns on the accuser. Heat: Moderate and sudden, from a direct accusation of being the second visitor. It rests on inference, not public evidence. Forward exposure: Claiming a role or a visit would be permanent and checkable later. Questioning the accuser's basis commits me to nothing and stays reversible. Target landscape: The accuser, who stated no result and is working from inference. Other players have unverified claims (healer, investigator), so I would rather push the accuser than defend a specific story. Public vs private: Privately I did visit the victim, and the accuser's private watch really saw it. Publicly nobody can verify a visitor list, so the accusation has no backing and my denial only echoes the public record.
lessons.action: If someone names you as a visitor at a saved or attacked player's door and no living Sentinel or confirmed visitor list exists, deny it by restating only what the public report shows (an attack and a save). Then ask the accuser for the specific result behind the claim, and claim no role and no night action. The accusation is then just inference, and the room tends to turn on the accuser, while a denial of this kind can be walked back.

lessons.situation: A player reveals that I and another player both visited an attacked player who survived. I must explain my presence at the victim's door right away. Information landscape: Several claims and partial results: a surviving attacked player, a reported two-visitor list, and a reported roleblock. No confirmed roles for the visitors. Stakes: Mid-game with parity within a few eliminations. A convincing explanation here can send the vote to a rival and tilt the board toward the wolves, while failure risks exposing a wolf. Consensus: The room is looking for an explanation of the visitors. It will accept one that corroborates the save and fits other claims. My position: Leading the narrative by offering the protective explanation before the real healer formalizes a claim. Heat: High at first, because I was named as a visitor to a saved victim. A credible explanation of the visit can defuse it quickly. Forward exposure: A Healer claim is permanent and sets up a conflict whenever the real healer speaks. It buys immediate corroboration of the save and scrutiny on the exposer. Target landscape: The exposer (here a necromancer), who can be cast as the threat, and the real healer, who also visited the victim and can be framed as the false second visitor. Claims are mostly unverified, and others' results are partial. Public vs private: Privately I visited the victim as the wolf carrying the kill, and it failed because of a save. Publicly I reframe that visit as the protection, so it contradicts what I know.
lessons.action: If an observer publicly names you as a visitor at an attacked-but-saved player and you are under heavy heat, consider claiming Healer: say your visit was the protection that saved them. Use this only when you accept a later counter-claim from the real healer, and press suspicion onto the exposer in the meantime. It is a permanent claim, so reserve it for cases where denial would not hold.

lessons.situation: Day 2: I am a wolf Illusionist who fake-claimed Investigator and now face a real Investigator counterclaim. The village is deciding between the two claimants and discussing a same-target check test. Information landscape: Sparse. There are no verified roles beyond a hidden-role body, and the claims, Sentinel and Trailseer reports are all unverified, so the case rests on claims rather than evidence. Stakes: My elimination here exposes the pack and puts the wolves a step closer to losing. Delaying one vote keeps the wolf pair alive for another night. Consensus: The village is split between two unverified Investigator claims. Several players want some form of comparison test, but nobody has hard evidence. My position: Holding out, trying to delay the vote rather than win support. Heat: High. I am the primary vote target, backed by the rival's repeated insistence and another player's lean, and my defense adds no evidence. Forward exposure: Naming a check target commits my claimed night action to one player, and I cannot easily retract it. A real Sentinel watch could test my fake visit, and the proposal gains nothing if the vote comes before the test runs. Target landscape: The two Investigator claimants (me and the rival) are the vote candidates, and neither has behavioral tells against them. A neutral or Town player is the proposed shared check target, and the Sentinel's remaining watch is the only possible verification. Public vs private: Publicly the test looks like fair-minded verification. Privately I know my Investigator claim is false, and a visit shows only presence, so the test cannot confirm my result and could expose a fake visit if a real Sentinel watched the target. My wolf partner is still hidden.
lessons.action: When a real Investigator counterclaims and the room floats a same-target check test, propose it yourself and name a target that is neither your partner nor a likely Sentinel watch. Frame it as a fair test to delay the vote, and make clear that a visit shows only presence, not the result. If the Sentinel agrees only conditionally, hold to that and do not offer any new claimed results.

lessons.situation: As the illusionist I am accused by a claimed investigator, who reports a Suspicious check on me. The town is converging on my elimination, and my partner is still hidden. Information landscape: Information-rich: a specific investigative claim, confirmed night mechanics that rule out other explanations, and a record of announced events that the room can check my words against. Stakes: Losing me halves the wolf pack. The partner's survival is the main thing left to protect, so the priority is to keep the partner unentangled rather than to win the argument. Consensus: Near-unanimous: the room wants me eliminated on the strength of the investigator's check, and probability-style arguments against it have not moved anyone. My position: holding out Heat: Critical. I am directly named by a claimed information role, and the room accepts the result as mechanically sound. Forward exposure: A fake counter-claim would be tested against announced saves, deaths and the one-per-role rule, and would also entangle my partner once my role flips. Staying claim-free commits me to little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: The claimed investigator, whose result is backed by night mechanics, versus me. No other suspect has comparable evidence, and the rest of the room is aligned behind the accuser. Public vs private: Privately I am a wolf and the accuser's Suspicious check is accurate. Publicly the room treats the check as near-conclusive, and my denials carry little weight.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator names you Suspicious and the room is already moving to eliminate you, spend your turns on short, non-fabricating defense. Do not invent a rival role claim, and do not mention or defend your wolf partner. Instead, steer any remaining suspicion toward non-partner players, so your partner is not tied to your elimination and can survive the day.

lessons.situation: Late game with three or four players alive, your wolf partner dead or revealed, and the town reasoning that the remaining evil is down to you and perhaps one other. You are the last wolf and a swing voter decides the day. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths and roles, public vote records, and a public night report such as an attack and save. Remaining claims are unverified, but the elimination argument already favors the accusers. Stakes: One vote decides the game. If the swing voter follows the accusers, the last wolf is eliminated and Town wins, so only a concrete, checkable argument aimed at that voter can change the result. Consensus: The village is aligned on eliminating you, based on elimination logic and prior vote records, and it is hardly moved by behavioral appeals. My position: Holding out alone against a formed or forming majority. Heat: Very high to extreme. The pool has been narrowed by elimination to you plus at most one other, and confirmed or credible Town roles have already voted against or named you. Forward exposure: A specific accusation commits you to a falsifiable statement and cannot be retracted. With a majority already forming, a generic or purely epistemic defense adds nothing, so a concrete point is the only move that can still shift a voter. Target landscape: Two to three candidates remain: you, an unconfirmed neutral or lone killer, and sometimes a claimed accuser with public support such as a confirmed save or a confirmed-town ally. The town is reasoning from the record and by elimination, not from behavior. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the last wolf and that the accusers' pool is built on a correct elimination argument. Publicly nobody can verify any claim, but the record and the narrowed pool point at you.
lessons.action: As the last wolf with the partner gone and the room closing in, aim your remaining speech at the swing voter. Name one concrete, checkable inconsistency in the leading accuser's own record, such as a vote, a timing, or a claim that conflicts with a confirmed announcement. If no such inconsistency exists, point to the unclaimed or unconfirmed third player on the same kind of record evidence instead of arguing that claims are merely unverified.

lessons.situation: A claimed Investigator has named you a wolf and the room is moving toward voting you out before other claims have been checked against it. Information landscape: Sparse. Other power-role claims give partial reports that do not decide between the accuser and you. Stakes: A single day's vote can take the Illusionist out, and the pack cannot win after losing both wolves. Delaying consensus keeps the pack alive. Consensus: The village leans toward trusting a specific wolf read, but its confidence rests on one unverified claim. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus. Heat: High. The vote is forming on you because of one direct accusation. Forward exposure: Asking for more claims and results costs little and can be dropped. It does not commit you to a false result, and it keeps your partner out of the line of fire. Target landscape: The candidates are the accuser (a claimed Investigator with no verification), other claimed power roles whose results are partial, and unclaimed players. The basis for choosing is timing and consistency of claims, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You know the accuser's read is true, while the public sees only competing unverifiable claims. Your goal is to keep that uncertainty alive and spread the room's attention beyond yourself.
lessons.action: While accused by a claimed Investigator, give the table another unverified claim or voting record to weigh, so it is not a straight two-way choice between you and the accuser. Ask the Sentinel, Trailseer and other claimants to state their results. Branch on the reply: if their reports do not intersect, say the accuser cannot be cross-checked; if they conflict with each other, stress that they cannot be cross-checked.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 after Night 1, a Sentinel or Trailseer reports that I or my partner visited or was visited, and the town debates whether that visit means anything. Information landscape: Soft, unverified claims from the Sentinel, Trailseer, and Investigator that establish movement but not alignment; no hard confirmations. Stakes: The board is early with the wolves comfortably behind parity. The main risk is a premature bandwagon on a wolf, so neutralizing the visit report and securing an abstain preserves both wolves for another night. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on treating the visit reports as soft information and leaning toward abstaining, with no hard evidence to drive a vote. My position: with majority Heat: Low to moderate: I am named in a night report, but the report shows no hostile pattern and reads as a puzzle. Forward exposure: Confirming the visit casually commits me only to a consistent account of one night's movement and makes no role claim, so the position stays flexible and easy to adjust later. Target landscape: The visited or reported players (me, my partner, a quiet player) are tied only to soft claims. There are no confirmed evil leads, so the choice is mostly between abstaining and behavioral suspicion of quiet players. Public vs private: Publicly, a Town tracker or watcher has reported a visit involving me or my partner and the room treats it as a puzzle. Privately, I know the wolf kill or block behind it and that the report is accurate or that the trace was hidden, so it is not evidence against us.
lessons.action: When a Town role's night report (Sentinel watch, Trailseer follow) names you or your partner as a visitor on Night 1, confirm the visit calmly in a casual, role-neutral way and note that a visit alone does not show alignment. Then point the room to a procedural next step, such as asking the visited player or the Investigator what they saw, and back an abstain. If the report is accurate, stay consistent with it and do not volunteer extra detail or claim a role.

lessons.situation: A genuine unique-role claimant has revealed a result or action. I am tempted to counter-claim the same role, but the game record, such as a healer save announcement or an investigator claim, already supports the genuine claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced saves, night-action claims and the one-per-role rule let the town test claims for consistency against fixed facts. Stakes: A failed counter-claim costs a wolf immediately and halves the pack. The wolf partner survives only if the town's attention stays on me. Consensus: Aligned against me: the town reasons that one role slot means one of us is lying, and the public facts point away from me. My position: holding out Heat: Severe. Every player can see that only one of us can be telling the truth, and the announcements favor the other claimant. Forward exposure: Counter-claiming a unique role is irrevocable. It makes it a 1-for-1 claim fight, and if my account fails against the announced facts I am eliminated, and my body then reveals the illusionist role. Target landscape: The genuine claimant of a unique role, whose account is corroborated by announcements, versus me as the only rival claimant. The evidence is mechanical and not based on behavior. Public vs private: Privately I know the real night events, such as who the wolves killed and who my partner blocked. Publicly the rival claimant's account matches the announcements, and mine would not.
lessons.action: Before contesting a claimed information or protective role, check your story against every Game Master announcement, such as saves, deaths and revealed roles. If the story cannot fit them, do not counter-claim a unique role, since a second claimant on a one-player role forces the town to pick one and the announced facts will favor the genuine claimant. In that case, fall back on a claim-free line that casts doubt on the accuser without staking a role.

lessons.situation: You are the most accused player in a visit-trace or duplicate-claim dispute. Past defenses were bare denial or a repeated line, and no alternative suspect was offered. Information landscape: Rich against you (visit report, claim conflicts, contradictions), starved on everyone else. Your side has only assertion. Stakes: A unanimous vote on you ends the Illusionist and a conceal use, and moves the wolves toward a lone-wolf endgame. A credible second suspect can split the vote. Consensus: The village is converging on you with matching accusers and no one defending you. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus with no allies speaking for you. Heat: Very high: you are the main target and repeating the same denial has not moved anyone. Forward exposure: A behavior-based pivot is easy to adjust if the room pushes back. Claiming a role the real holder can instantly deny (Sigilist, Sentinel) is irreversible, and the room punishes it. Pushing your partner would draw heat to them. Target landscape: The other named visitor or the accuser. The roles of both are unconfirmed. The case against them must rest on conduct such as inconsistent accounts, because there is no hard evidence. Public vs private: You know the pack's kill and that you carried the conceal. Publicly you are one of the suspects, and the village has no read on any other suspect, so a defense without a suspect leaves the room only you.
lessons.action: Alongside the rules argument, name one other player to scrutinize, such as the other visitor or the accuser, and base it on observable behavior or vote history rather than on any role claim of yours. Keep your partner out of it, and never say you held a role that someone else may hold.

lessons.situation: A claimed Investigator announces a Suspicious read on you, the wolf Illusionist, in day discussion. The village must choose between that claim and your denial. Information landscape: Sparse. There are only unverified claims, maybe one hidden-role body, and partial Sentinel or Trailseer reports that do not intersect. Nothing is confirmed. Stakes: Losing the Illusionist this early removes the pack's remaining conceals and leaves the partner alone. Preserving standing matters more than winning the argument outright. Consensus: The room is forming a majority against you, because a direct wolf check is treated as stronger than an unverifiable rebuttal. My position: Holding out alone against a forming majority. Heat: High to very high. A claimed Investigator has named you Suspicious, and a second player already leans toward voting you. Forward exposure: A fake role claim commits you to a result that a real holder can contradict, and it cannot be taken back. Staying unclaimed keeps you flexible, and every later defense can still be adjusted. Target landscape: The main candidates are the accusing claimed Investigator, whose read is a direct wolf call that nothing can verify, and any rival claimant who appears. Evidence is limited to claims and timing, since no role has been confirmed. Public vs private: You privately know the Suspicious read on you is true and that you are the wolf Illusionist. Publicly it is only an unverified claim, so a fabricated role would be a lie that the real holder can contradict.
lessons.action: When a claimed Investigator reads you Suspicious, stay unclaimed instead of fake-claiming a role that has a living real holder. Stress that the read is an unverified claim and ask for the check's timing and why you were picked. If a hidden-role body exists, say the real investigator may already be dead, so the accuser's claim cannot be trusted at face value. A counter-claim of Healer or Investigator can be directly contradicted and cannot be retracted.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear village consensus; the room is split between a vote on player_5 and calls to test the sentinel claim further, with the accusers relying on the watch record and the accused relying on the block report contradiction.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong lynch is recoverable but costly, since it would bring the evil side closer to parity and the wolves and necromancer remain unidentified.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate on me as the Speculator: I have not been heavily accused, but I am a living voter whose pick is already announced as Town, so my vote is watched for alignment with the Town pick.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: one unverified sentinel watch, one roleblock report with no source, and one admitted visit; no confirmed role claims survive and no night results have been announced beyond the dead players' roles.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from the forming pressure on player_5, with a low profile and no night result of my own.
query_dims.situation: A claimed Sentinel's night-3 watch shows only player_5 at player_1's door, while player_1 says they were roleblocked that night, so the block is unexplained; player_5 admits the visit, denies being blocked, and claims no role. Several players are pressing a vote on player_5 while the accusation rests on one watch record against one block report.
query_dims.target_landscape: Player_5 (unrevealed, living) who admits a night-3 visit to player_1 with no role claimed; player_1 (unrevealed, living) who reports being roleblocked that night; player_2 (claimed Sentinel, unverified, living) whose night-3 watch shows only player_5 at player_1's door. Public role status: no one confirmed beyond the dead.

lessons.situation: After a night kill (often hidden-role or double attack), a role claimant's night report places one named player at the victim's door. The accused denies it and attacks the claimants, and the room converges on the accused. The speculator has already picked Town or is about to. Information landscape: Moderately to highly info-rich: specific watch or follow claims that corroborate one another, visitor counts, an investigator read, and caught mechanics errors, though nothing is officially confirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil threats still alive. Removing a wolf or the lone killer by an evidence-backed vote shifts the board toward Town and toward the speculator's Town pick, and a wrong eviction would cost a Town member. Consensus: Largely aligned (most of the living players) behind the evidence-backed target. Only the accused and perhaps one wolf partner dissent. My position: With the majority, lightly helping build the case with a verification question or a public argument. Heat: Low: not accused, only asking questions or backing the majority line. Target landscape: Two or three suspects: one accused by independent, partly corroborating night claims (watch report, trailseer follow, visitor list, investigator read) who denies and counter-accuses, versus the accuser(s), who are unverified but consistent with each other. Evidence outweighs behavior on the accused, and nobody is confirmed by the Game Master.
