lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. You are the Serial Killer, immune to night attacks, and the wolves are also choosing a kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, votes, deaths or night results exist yet. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and far from parity. One kill gains a single elimination toward being the last one standing but does not decide the game, and a failed or overlapping kill costs little beyond exposing a lone killer. Forward exposure: The kill is irreversible and commits you to nothing publicly. If it overlaps the wolves' victim or is saved, the morning names the serial killer as an attacker. A Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer on you can also see the visit. Target landscape: Nine other players, all unknown, with no claims, votes or behavior to read. Targets differ only by role potential, and a quiet player is as likely as any to hold a check, watch, or bullet.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or reads, kill one quiet, unclaimed player and accept that the pick is blind. The wolves also attack that night, and a kill that lands on the wolves' victim is announced as a double attack that reveals a second killer. Any kill carries the same chance of a watcher having been on that target.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or split day vote. Information roles are claiming and the wolves are also hunting the loudest of them. You must choose a victim without duplicating the pack's kill or walking into a watcher's trace. Information landscape: Moderately thin: a few claims, one or two early bodies, a split or abstain vote, and no hard evidence on any role. You cannot tell who is watching or following whom. Stakes: Mid-game with eight alive, so one wasted or traced kill costs tempo and exposure but does not end the game. Both the wolves and you still need several more deaths. A visit trace can make you the day vote target, and a duplicated kill gives no net body-count gain. Forward exposure: Your kill is an attack and a visit, so a Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer following you will log it. The morning report also names a serial killer attacker if the wolves hit the same player. Neither can be undone once the night resolves. The wolves' illusionist conceal hides only the wolf carrier's visit, never yours. Target landscape: Seven living candidates: claimed Sentinel, Trailseer and Investigator, a claimed Sigilist or Vigilante, and quiet unclaimed players. Claims are unverified, so the choice rests on public role claims and who the wolves most likely want dead, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: On night 2 with about eight alive, kill a living information role (claimed Sentinel, Trailseer or Investigator) that the wolves are least likely to take that night, rather than the loudest one they will obviously hit. A kill on the wolves' probable target wastes your attack, and any victim who is watched or followed puts your name on the visit trace. Prefer a victim whose death removes a watcher or follower, and if the Sentinel and Trailseer are both alive and active, expect a visit to anyone else to be logged.

lessons.situation: After a day-2 vote where nearly everyone abstained but one player voted to eliminate you. You are choosing whether to spend the night kill on that outlier. Information landscape: Moderate to rich: a public voting record isolates the lone accuser, and several power-role claims exist, but nothing hard confirms who the wolves are. Stakes: The kill can remove an active wolf and halve the pack, which shortens your path to a last-standing win. Nobody is at parity yet, so the cost is the day-3 heat the motive link brings, not an immediate loss. Forward exposure: Killing the one voter against you ties the death to a motive and turns their stray vote into evidence for Town. If they were a wolf, the surviving wolf can use that vote to argue you cannot be killed at night. You cannot reverse this after the kill. Target landscape: Seven living candidates: the lone day-2 accuser, claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator or Sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. The accuser is picked on voting behavior alone, not role evidence, and was revealed in these games as a wolf (Chanteuse or Illusionist).
lessons.action: If one player alone voted against you on day 2 while the rest abstained, and no active Sentinel or Trailseer threat is more urgent, you may kill that outlier. They are more likely a wolf or a hostile reader, so you also remove a rival. Pick this target only knowing that the dead player's vote will be used against you on day 3.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and the town is led by a vocal investigator against the lone killer. You are choosing a night target while a healer is probably alive and likely guarding the town's key voice. Information landscape: Information-rich. Wolf flips are confirmed and the investigator's reads are validated. Town's remaining uncertainty is mainly which unverified player is the killer or the neutral. Stakes: A wasted night costs tempo and, via the save, confirms a protective role. The board is small enough that each night kill matters. A failed kill makes your elimination more likely. Forward exposure: The attack is irreversible. A save is announced in the morning, so a failed kill gains nothing and helps the healer confirm their role, narrowing the pool toward you. A kill on a less obvious target keeps the healer's identity unconfirmed. Target landscape: A confirmed or loudly claimed investigator who just helped eliminate the last wolf, an unrevealed healer, an unverified tracker claimant, and quiet town players. The investigator is the obvious protect target. The others are judged on their claims and behavior.
lessons.action: If one prominent confirmed or claimed investigator or other town leader is the obvious protection target, spread your kill to a different live town role instead of repeating the predictable pick. Prefer a role the healer is unlikely to be guarding. A kill into a healer save spends the night and leaves you with fewer unverified players to hide among.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later after a day vote that concentrated suspicion on one player, with a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer active and unblocked. Information landscape: Moderately informative: a public claim by a watcher, a fixed vote record, and some confirmed dead roles. Stakes: A watcher reading your visit leads to a day vote that can eliminate you, ending your game. Avoiding the watched door protects the only win path, since you can be removed only by a vote. Forward exposure: A kill is a visit that a watching Sentinel or a following Trailseer can read, and it cannot be undone after the morning. Killing a focal day target is predictable and invites a watch on that door. Target landscape: The claimed Sentinel, the contested player who just drew votes, and several quiet off-ballot players. Focal targets are the likeliest places for a watcher to be, while quiet players are less likely to be watched.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer has publicly claimed and is still alive, do not kill the player you just voted against or the player the room is focused on, because a watcher on that door sees your visit. Pick an off-ballot quiet player, or the watcher themself if the claim looks credible, so the visit is less likely to be read.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with several claimed Town power roles alive, one of them able to trace night visits. The Healer is dead or fixed on another target, and the wolves are also killing. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich. Public claims, a tracking chain, a held shot, and save announcements are known, but the hidden Healer and the unclaimed roles are unconfirmed. Stakes: A mid-game board where the kill choice shapes who survives to threaten you. Removing the one role that can follow your visit protects your night actions, but each Town death also pushes the wolves toward parity, so the kill should target someone who endangers you. Forward exposure: The kill is a private visit that carries no attribution unless you are watched or followed, but a prominent claimant dying signals an active killer hunting information roles. It cannot be undone, and if the wolves also hit that target the double attack reveals a second killer. Target landscape: Claimed power roles (a Trailseer with a public tracking chain, a Sigilist, a Vigilante holding fire) plus quiet unrevealed players, one of whom may be the Healer. Claimed roles are known only by their own say-so, so the choice rests on behavior and prominence rather than proof.
lessons.action: When a claimed Town information or tracking role (e.g. the Trailseer) is alive and could follow your visits, spend the night's kill on that claimant. If a claimed Healer is known dead or the claimant is not the healer's protected target, the kill lands; if the healer is visibly guarding that claimant, aim at the next most dangerous power role instead.

lessons.situation: Endgame with 3-4 players alive. The serial killer must choose a night victim that determines whether the final daytime vote is winnable. Day votes have shown clear blocs, and a kill can strand the SK against a united pair. Information landscape: Information-rich: public voting records show who sided with and against the SK, some roles are confirmed by reveals, and several claims are on record. Stakes: One kill decides the game. Reaching two alive wins at once, while leaving three alive with an opposing bloc allows a 2-1 vote to eliminate the SK, which cannot be killed at night and can only be removed by a vote. Forward exposure: The kill is irreversible and fixes the final roster. Leaving three alive means a daytime vote decides whether you live, while reaching two alive ends the game immediately. Target landscape: Three or four survivors: a claimed ally who voted with you (vigilante), claimed town role holders (sentinel, investigator), and a wolf pair or wolf plus town voter who have voted against you. Evidence is mainly the public vote record and claims, not verified roles.
lessons.action: When 3-4 players remain, count the day-vote math before choosing your kill: pick the target so the survivors are you plus one other, or at worst you plus a player who is not allied with the other survivor. Avoid kills (or kills overlapping the wolf kill) that leave you outnumbered 2-1 by a pair that has voted together against you. If you can reach exactly two alive this night, take that kill, since it ends the game in your favor.

lessons.situation: The neutral and the wolves are gone. You are the only evil player left among claimed town, and the town is hunting the last non-town player. One of the claimants can track visits. Information landscape: Information-rich. Roles and claims are mostly locked and flips are confirmed, so town can reason by elimination. Any visible visit trace would end the game. Stakes: Only a few players remain and one wrong vote ends you. A visit trace linking you to a corpse is decisive for the town. The night kill must both thin the board and avoid giving proof. Forward exposure: The kill is an irreversible visit. If a living Trailseer follows you, or a Sentinel watches your victim, the visit is seen and can be used as proof against you the next day. Killing the tracker leaves no such witness from that night. Target landscape: A small field of claimed town roles: a healer, a confirmed investigator, a sigilist, and a trailseer. The roles are locked and no cover role is left for you, so the choice rests on who can produce visit evidence.
lessons.action: When only town claimants and you remain and a Trailseer or Sentinel claimant is still alive, make that tracker your night kill. A dead tracker learns nothing from the night, so your visit cannot be followed or watched. If several trackers are claimed, kill the one the room trusts most.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later after a tied or contested day vote. Public claims exist, and an obvious wolf target stands out, such as a claimed investigator or trailseer in a tie. Information landscape: Moderately informative: unverified claims and a public vote record, but no confirmed roles among the living. Stakes: Each night's kill is a scarce progress step toward last-one-standing. A kill that duplicates the wolves' death wastes a night, while a distinct victim yields two deaths and brings the endgame closer. Forward exposure: A double attack on one victim is reported with both attackers, which reveals the extra killer and cannot be undone. The kill is irreversible and gives you no additional elimination. Target landscape: Claimed investigators or trailseers, the contested player from a tied vote, and several quiet players. The wolves' likely target is the publicly visible, accused or information-bearing player, so those candidates risk a wasted kill.
lessons.action: From Night 2 on, choose a victim the wolves are unlikely to hit, such as a quiet player who was not publicly contested, over the player everyone expects to die. A kill that lands on the wolves' obvious target is announced as a joint attack and adds no extra death.

lessons.situation: Late game, around 5 alive with both wolves gone. A tiny voter pool decides whether you are voted out, and a vigilante or sigilist can narrow the suspects to you. Information landscape: Most roles are confirmed by death records and wolf reveals. The only open question is which survivor is the serial killer, so every announced attack narrows suspicion. Stakes: With few players left, each kill and each day vote decides the game. Spending a night on a harmless neutral leaves the sigilist and vigilante alive to expose you. Forward exposure: A kill the same night as a vigilante shot or wolf attack shows several attackers on one victim, and an immune shot report points at you. Once the body is announced you cannot walk it back. Target landscape: Five or so alive: a sigilist, a vigilante with possible bullets, a neutral voting body such as the fortune teller, and a possible healer claimant. The sigilist and vigilante are the real threats to a last-standing win. The neutral is only a vote.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone and only a handful of players remain, kill the player who can most directly stop your last-standing win. That means a vigilante with bullets left or a sigilist, not a side-less neutral that merely adds a vote. If a vigilante is alive, expect a possible same-night shot, which you survive because you cannot be killed at night, and plan for a possible 'immune' report.

lessons.situation: Early-mid game, after a tie or no-elimination day, with several town roles claimed and a healer publicly confirmed. The wolves are also killing each night, and you must pick a night victim among claimed roles. Information landscape: Moderately informative public claims and a save announcement, with partial corroboration and no evidence pointing at you. Hidden roles remain, and you do not know who the healer is unless one claims. Stakes: Several players remain, so each kill moves you toward a final-two win. A confirmed healer can cancel a kill on any night, so removing it early lets later kills land cleanly, though you still face a day vote that could end you. Forward exposure: Killing the claimed healer reveals a threat-removal pattern but leaves no trace pointing at you, and it commits you to no story. The kill cannot be undone, but it removes protection that could blunt every later kill, whoever makes it. Target landscape: Candidates are the self-claimed healer (corroborated by the vigilante and the trailseer's follow), the trusted trailseer, the sentinel, and the sigilist and chanteuse under vote suspicion. The healer is the most openly identified protector, and the choice rests on public claims and corroboration rather than proof.
lessons.action: When a freshly claimed protector (healer) is publicly identified, aim the night kill at that protector rather than at a protected information role. If the save announcement shows a healer is already covering a claimed role, switch to a different target that night instead of repeating the saved one, since a repeat visit can be traced by a follower.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear consensus; the village has abstained on every vote so far and day discussion is about requesting concrete night 1 visit directions from anyone claiming a result, with no shared accusation forming.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game next; a wrong elimination now is recoverable but the agent still has time to observe before committing to a pick, since dying unpicked loses.
query_dims.heat_now: Little suspicion on the agent (player_6, an unpicked speculator who has made no accusations); the agent has not been named in any public accusation.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no verified night result is public, the only public record is the day-2 abstain-majority vote and the one elimination-free day, and the investigator's checks died with them. Claims about night visits are unverified.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from any accusation, with no side pick yet; the village is not forming a consensus the agent needs to join or oppose.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 with the investigator killed on night 2 and no vote yet succeeding. Players are asking whoever claims a night result to give specific visit directions for night 1, while one player states a night 1 roleblock with nothing to share. The agent is an unpicked speculator who must avoid dying unpicked, so its survival and eventual pick depend on the board tilting toward a side.
query_dims.target_landscape: Nine living players, none publicly claimed or confirmed beyond the public abstain record; the only role-revealed death is the investigator (player_9), killed night 2. Candidates for any future vote are all unverified; no one has a public accusation on record except the day-2 vote where player_9 targeted player_8, who is now a claimant of a night 1 roleblock with no verifiable result.

lessons.situation: First day with a vote, after a night-1 death. There are unverified role claims and counter-claims, or no claims at all. The speculator has not yet made its side pick and has no information on any candidate. Information landscape: Information-starved: one dead player with a known role, unverified night-result claims, no confirmed wolf, and no voting history yet. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so one vote does not flip the winning side. A wrongful elimination of a real Town role is costly, and your abstain avoids adding to it. Your win depends only on the later pick. Consensus: The room is split or only loosely aligned. It is either a universal abstain or a near-majority piling onto one player, based on behavior and unverified claims rather than confirmed roles. My position: Holding out by abstaining, either with an abstain bloc or against a bandwagon, without driving any accusation. Heat: Low to none: you have been quiet or only echoed the room's questions, and no one has accused you. Target landscape: Two or more candidates drawing votes, such as a quiet player with no claim, a claimed healer, or rival investigator claimants. Their claims are unverified. The only evidence is a night-1 sentinel or trailseer report or a visit link, and everything else is behavior.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, while your one pick is unused and no candidate has hard evidence against them (only unverified claims, quietness, or a bandwagon), abstain rather than join the pile-on. If a candidate has a concrete contradiction, such as a caught lie or a claim that conflicts with an announced fact, vote for that player instead. If abstaining has been removed after two no-elimination days, vote for the best-supported suspect. Abstaining keeps your heat low, and your win depends on the pick, not on this vote.

lessons.situation: After a night kill (often hidden-role or double attack), a role claimant's night report places one named player at the victim's door. The accused denies it and attacks the claimants, and the room converges on the accused. The speculator has already picked Town or is about to. Information landscape: Moderately to highly info-rich: specific watch or follow claims that corroborate one another, visitor counts, an investigator read, and caught mechanics errors, though nothing is officially confirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil threats still alive. Removing a wolf or the lone killer by an evidence-backed vote shifts the board toward Town and toward the speculator's Town pick, and a wrong eviction would cost a Town member. Consensus: Largely aligned (most of the living players) behind the evidence-backed target. Only the accused and perhaps one wolf partner dissent. My position: With the majority, lightly helping build the case with a verification question or a public argument. Heat: Low: not accused, only asking questions or backing the majority line. Target landscape: Two or three suspects: one accused by independent, partly corroborating night claims (watch report, trailseer follow, visitor list, investigator read) who denies and counter-accuses, versus the accuser(s), who are unverified but consistent with each other. Evidence outweighs behavior on the accused, and nobody is confirmed by the Game Master.
lessons.action: On a day-vote with low heat, vote with the evidence-backed majority on the player whose story is contradicted by independent night reports (a watch claim, a follow match, a visitor count, a counter-claim) rather than on mood. If you have not yet picked, ask for a Trailseer or Sentinel to corroborate before the vote, then vote with the room. Each eviction of a wolf or lone killer moves Town toward winning, which is what your Town pick needs.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a night kill by wolves or the serial killer; the village converges on a single accused player on corroborating night-result claims, and the speculator has the option to join the vote that decides whether the remaining evil is removed. Information landscape: Reasonably information-rich: a wolf is already confirmed dead or revealed, there are corroborating tracking claims and a clean investigator check, and the accused offers only blanket denials. Stakes: With wolves or the lone killer nearly gone, one more correct elimination can end or nearly end the game; the vote is rarely decisive alone but it fixes the board toward a Town win, which is the side the speculator pick favors. Consensus: Largely aligned: a pack of accusers forms on matching tracking and check reports plus the reveals of dead wolves. My position: With the majority, joining the pile-on early or at the last minute rather than holding out. Heat: Low to moderate: no accusation round is aimed at you, though the accused may have counter-accused or voted against you. Target landscape: One accused player named by matching independent tracking or check claims (trailseer, sentinel, investigator); the claims are unverified but agree with each other and with confirmed reveals. The alternative candidates have no case against them; the accused's defense is blanket denial or counter-accusation.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote where several tracking or check reports (trailseer, sentinel, investigator) converge on one accused and confirmed wolves are already known, vote with that convergent group for the accused instead of an unrelated player. Removing a convergent target sharpens the endgame toward Town, which pays off a Town pick; if you still hold your pick, the converging reports are your cue to lock in the side that now looks to be winning.

lessons.situation: The final day vote with three or four players alive. The speculator is the target of the surviving evil players and is voting alone against the player the records implicate. Information landscape: Voting logs, dead-role reveals and announced reanimated-kill reports exist, but no living candidate is confirmed. The evidence has to be read from patterns. Stakes: One more death gives evil parity or the lone-killer win condition, so this vote ends the game. A lost vote also kills the speculator's chance of seeing its pick come true. Consensus: The room has coalesced into a bloc against me, built on my voting history and on mutual cover among the evil players. Town evidence is thin. My position: Holding out alone against a two- or three-vote bloc. Heat: High to extreme. Evil players or a rival claimant are using my past votes or a questionable-player label against me. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed living players, none publicly confirmed as wolf or lone killer. Cases rest on voting records, alignment with dead evil players, and announced body-attack kills, not on revealed roles.
lessons.action: In an endgame vote with three or four players left and a majority leaning on you, vote for the unconfirmed player whose public record ties most directly to evil. Good evidence is a vote alongside a dead wolf, or a body-attack announcement that points to the lone killer. If a rival's case rests only on a single dead player's past vote, vote on the stronger record and not on who is pressuring you, because each vote you add is the only way to reach a tie or majority.

lessons.situation: Day 2 first vote: a claimed power role admitted their reported result looked wrong and the whole table is accusing them, while you have not yet made your side pick. Information landscape: Information-starved: one self-admitted inconsistency and unverified claims; no confirmed roles. Stakes: Early elimination of a Town role weakens Town's information while the serial killer and wolves are still active; a mistaken unanimous vote is hard to reverse and your own pick depends on Town surviving. Consensus: Near-unanimous pile-on against one claimed role based on a single reported inconsistency; the room is driven by claim analysis, not verified facts. My position: With the majority and one of the voices driving it. Heat: Low; you are an unclaimed voice agreeing with the majority. Target landscape: One claimed Sentinel under real pressure after reporting a watch result that omitted their own visit; the other claimant (a trailseer) looks consistent. No competing suspects and no hard evidence beyond the claim's inconsistency.
lessons.action: When the table is piling onto a single claimed role over a stated inconsistency and there is no stronger lead, vote with the consensus only after checking that the inconsistency is a real rules violation rather than a misstatement. If the rule check is unclear, abstain, so you do not help eliminate a likely Town power role while you still hold your pick.

lessons.situation: Late-game day vote at five alive where the vote is split or tied. The speculator's ballot decides whether a useful Town-aligned role survives, and the speculator has already picked a side. Information landscape: Mixed. Some night save announcements and claimed information-role reports exist, but they conflict, and several dead players' roles are hidden. No role is verified. Stakes: At five alive, one elimination can bring evil to parity. A single ballot decides between keeping a protective role alive and handing the wolves or lone killer a free removal. Consensus: Fractured: votes split between two or more targets, with no majority and a tie likely, resting on conflicting claimed visit reports. My position: Holding the swing or deciding ballot, able to join a wagon or drive an alternative target. Heat: Moderate to high: the speculator is accused or voted for by others based on visit reports, though in some cases heat is only low to moderate. Target landscape: Three or four candidates at five alive: a claimed healer with a confirmed save announcement, a claimed trailseer or sentinel, the speculator under accusation, and a quiet unclaimed player. Evidence is claims and visit reconstructions, not confirmed roles.
lessons.action: With about five players alive and the vote split or tied, use your ballot to protect a claimed protective or information role whose behavior and announced results fit. Aim it at the least-evidenced quiet player, since a tie or no elimination keeps the Town-aligned pick alive. If the room is scattered and no role is confirmed, spend it on the most defensible suspect rather than a token vote.

lessons.situation: Endgame of three or four players alive after both wolves are eliminated; the only remaining threat is the lone killer, hidden among the other living players, and your Town pick depends on removing it. Information landscape: Rich by elimination: both wolves revealed, the killer's night kills visible, and claimed trailseer and healer reports consistent with each other and with you. Stakes: The final vote decides the game: eliminating the lone killer ends it as a Town win and pays off the Town pick, while a wrong vote lets the killer reach the at-most-one-other-alive condition. Consensus: Mostly aligned on eliminating the one unverified player, since claims corroborate each other and both wolves are already revealed. My position: With the majority or driving alongside the corroborated claimant, and part of the decisive votes. Heat: Moderate: the suspected killer voted against you, but a matching trailseer result saying you visited no one cleared you. Target landscape: Two or three other living players: claimed information roles whose reports match each other and clear you, and one unclaimed or ability-less player who cast a counter-vote at you. Basis is cross-corroborated claims plus elimination, not just behavior.
lessons.action: When both wolves are confirmed dead and only the lone killer can remain, vote out the one living player whose claim is unverified or who has no corroborated night result, and rely on cross-matching claims such as a trailseer report that agrees with a healer's claim. If you are the one cleared by a corroborated result, join the cleared players against the lone unclaimed or uncorroborated player, because a wrong vote lets the killer reach parity.

lessons.situation: Late game, day vote. Your Town pick is already announced and the Town win needs the last evil player or players removed. A few survivors remain, and one is the remaining wolf or lone killer, often the one who attacked your role or counter-claimed it. Information landscape: Fairly rich by elimination. Dead roles are revealed, some Town results are backed by announced facts, and the suspect pool is narrow. Some of it is still behavioral, such as who pressed whom and how people voted. Stakes: Few players are left, so one wrong elimination could let evil reach parity or hand the game to the lone killer. A correct elimination ends the game and cashes in your pick, so the vote has to land on the true last threat. Consensus: The village is converging on one target through elimination reasoning and shared reads. Most votes are already pointed at the same last unaccounted-for player. My position: With the majority, joining a bloc that is already forming and sometimes helping to start it. Heat: Low to moderate. Your Town pick is announced anonymously, but some players can guess your role from your action pattern or a rival claim. Target landscape: Two or three survivors left unaccounted for after wolves or the lone killer died. The candidates include a counter-claimant or a player pressing on your role, plus quiet players. Roles are confirmed mostly by elimination and sigil or healer reasoning, with voting-bloc behavior as backup.
lessons.action: Once your Town pick is made and announced, vote with the forming majority for the remaining evil player. Use elimination to name them: take the roles already revealed dead, the cleared players, and anyone who counter-claims or presses on your role. Your pick pays off only if Town wins, so keep voting for the last unaccounted-for threat instead of splitting the room.

lessons.situation: A rival counter-claims the Speculator role or publicly ties your pattern of actions to it, and calls your claim late or false. You have to hold your claim while the room decides who the wolf is. Information landscape: Role-uniqueness contradiction plus elimination reasoning from dead roles and Town results. Evidence is moderately rich, although the targeted player's role is not confirmed until the vote. Stakes: Late game with few players left. If the wrong claimant is eliminated, evil can reach parity. Removing the false claimant can end the game. Consensus: The room is mostly backing your claim or already turning on the accuser. The shared basis is the unique-role contradiction and the narrowed suspect pool. My position: With the majority, partly driving it as the original claimant. Heat: Moderate to elevated. A rival claimed your role, or someone linked your actions to the Speculator, and at least one vote has been cast against you. Target landscape: The counter-claimant or the player pressing on your role, versus a few players already cleared by Town results or confirmed by elimination. Evidence is a mix of role uniqueness, elimination logic, and behavior.
lessons.action: If someone counter-claims your Speculator role or ties your behavior to it, keep your claim consistent and point out that there is only one Speculator. Then vote for the counter-claimant or pressurer if the cleared roles and the elimination logic leave them as the remaining evil candidate. This works because the Town pick is already announced and a counter-claimant is forced into being the wolf or a liar.

lessons.situation: Four players alive with one wolf remaining; a dispute between two info claimants over whether a watch counts as a visit, and the room votes out a claimed role over an apparent rules error. Information landscape: Rich in claim histories but poisoned by a rules dispute, so the evidence is contested rather than confirmed. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf left, one wrong elimination of a real Town role gives the wolf parity and ends the game; the vote is decisive. Consensus: Majority formed against the claimed sentinel on a disputed rules argument, with the vigilante holding the decisive bullet. My position: With the majority, joining a vote that was already forming. Heat: Moderate: the claimed vigilante questioned the speculator's lack of a role claim, though attention quickly moved to the dispute between information claimants. Target landscape: Claimed sentinel accused of lying about watching being a visit, versus a claimed trailseer and claimed vigilante pushing the accusation; the case rests on a rules dispute and counter-accusation, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With a wolf still alive and a dispute between claimed info roles, do not just join the majority on a vote over a rules-interpretation quarrel. Check the accusation against the stated rules (for example, a watch is a visit to the target but is not shown in the watcher's own result) and vote for the player whose claim actually conflicts with the rules or other evidence, or hold out if the accusation is only a semantic quarrel.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: With 8 alive and 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, tonight's death does not make the game immediately endable by one more elimination. A correct death bet advances my separate point goal, while a self-bet trades that chance for protection; the faction balance is not on a one-action knife edge.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer were revealed dead, and the Sentinel claim and visitor result are unverified. There is no public attack pattern or confirmed role evidence pointing to tonight's victim; any victim or role prediction is uncertain.
query_dims.situation: After the village abstained on day 2, no one was eliminated and the vote record contains no decisive consensus. At night, the wolves and lone killer can each attack; the public Sentinel claimant may be exposed, but there is no confirmed target. I have 0 points and two self-bets remaining, so the decision is between predicting another player's death and using a self-bet that would make me immune to attacks but earn no points.
query_dims.target_landscape: The exposed player claiming Sentinel is a plausible night target because of the public claim, but that role is unverified. Other living players have no confirmed roles from the public record; there is no clear evidence identifying a likely victim or their role. Betting on myself would prevent an attack on me but score no points that night.

lessons.situation: Midgame with one point scored and one more needed. The wolves and the Necromancer are killing nightly, a double attack on the sentinel and the investigator's death show their focus, and your earlier bet on a non-targeted player missed. Information landscape: Information-richer: revealed illusionist, trailseer record, necromancer vote-out, and a public attack on the sentinel. The killers' next preference is unstated, so the pick is inference from the kill pattern. Stakes: You need one more point to win and each wasted night costs a bet, while both self-bets remain unused. Missed bets on a player nobody is attacking waste nights that cannot be recovered. Target landscape: Six to seven living players: public-activity roles (sentinel, healer) that the wolves or a reanimating killer are visibly pressing, versus a quiet vote-aligned accuser with no sign of being targeted. The basis is public kill patterns and attack reports, not hidden role knowledge.
lessons.action: When you need a point and the previous night's kill pattern shows whom the killers are pressing (the attacked sentinel, the healer, or a role they just struck at), bet on that visible target to die rather than on a quiet accuser nobody is attacking. If your last bet missed, change the pick to follow the killers' current focus instead of repeating it, and keep your self-bets in hand until you have a reason to use them.

lessons.situation: Night betting after the wolf pack has been eliminated. A hidden lone killer (here the Necromancer, attacking through a dead wolf's body) is the only source of night kills, and you still need one or two points. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: wolf identities and many roles are confirmed from lynches and reveals, and role claims are out. Nothing shows who the lone killer is or whom it will target next, so the pick rests on role-value inference. Stakes: The lone killer needs to whittle the town down by attrition. Your win needs only one or two more deaths guessed correctly, so a well-chosen bet can end your game objectively while play continues. Target landscape: Five to seven living players, both wolves already dead. The candidates are claimed power roles (sentinel, trailseer, investigator, sigilist), the hidden lone killer and yourself. The likeliest victim is the loudest, most credible information source, chosen by role-value reasoning rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone or crippled and a lone killer is the only remaining attacker, bet on the most valuable surviving information or power role (e.g. a vocal claimed sentinel) and name that role. A death scores one point even if the role is hidden, and a correct role guess scores two, so the pair can finish your win condition in one night. Keep both self-bets in reserve unless you are one point short and expect the attack to land on you.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game night after a wolf elimination, where multiple killers are active (wolves plus Serial Killer or Necromancer) and exposed claimants are the likelier victims. Earlier bets on a low-profile survivor scored nothing. Information landscape: Starved of confirmed targeting evidence: only public claims, last night's death roles, and killer behavior patterns. The previous bet had no basis beyond having survived. Stakes: Repeated zero-point nights shrink the path to two points. With several killers each night there are often two deaths, so betting on the exposed claimant raises the chance of scoring. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players, including recently claimed information roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, Investigator) who are plausible kill targets for either killer, and low-profile survivors. A pick that survived an earlier night only is weak evidence of a target.
lessons.action: Choose the bet from how the killers have actually behaved: which attacker types have been announced, and whether they hit exposed claimants. Don't bet on a player just because they survived last night. If neither killer has a clear target, bet on the most publicly exposed claimant. If two zero-point nights leave you with few nights left, use a self-bet only if you expect to be attacked.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3, after a vote removed a wolf or resolved a claim conflict. Both the wolves and a lone killer are likely to strike the most threatening public Town claimant. You have 0-1 points, so each night's bet is your main way to score. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: a revealed wolf, claim conflicts and vote records show who threatens the killers. No role is confirmed beyond the reveals, and the healer's protection choice is unknown. Stakes: Scoring two points wins the game for you whatever else happens. Each night's bet is therefore a real chance to progress, and a miss costs only a night, not a use. The Town/wolf balance is not yet critical. Target landscape: Several claimed Town power roles (Investigator, Sentinel, healer, sigilist, trailseer) are alive. One was just validated by a vote or counter-claim win and is the obvious kill target. A healer may be guarding that player. The basis is role-value and behavior reasoning, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack and any lone killer have just lost a member or a public claimant has just been validated, bet on the most visible, freshly validated Town power role (healer, or a claimed Investigator or Sentinel whose report threatens the killers) to die, and name the role if the evidence points to it. Kills tend to aim at that player, so the bet scores if they die; a hidden role still scores, so name the role. If you suspect the healer will guard the obvious target, bet on the next-most-valuable power role the killers could reach instead.

lessons.situation: Early game, night 2. Wolves and a lone killer are probably all hunting, and the town has just produced a visible claimed power role. You must bet on who dies while the healer may protect the most obvious target. Information landscape: Information-starved. There is one revealed death, an unverified claim or two, and little or no vote record. Nothing shows who the killers will pick beyond how visible the claimant is. Stakes: Early game with no imminent parity. The bet is a modest scoring chance, since a miss costs one night's attempt toward the two points. The two self-bets stay in reserve. Target landscape: Seven to nine living players: one or two public power-role claimants (a trailseer, sigilist or sentinel claimant who stands out as a likely kill target), plus quiet unclaimed players with no behavioral signal. The healer is alive and unrevealed. The only evidence is who died on night 1 and who claimed since.
lessons.action: On an early night with both self-bets still held, when killers are active and one publicly claimed investigative role stands out, bet on that claimant to die and name their claimed role only if you would accept losing the second point. Accept that a healer save can turn an accurate prediction into zero, since only a death scores. Do not move your bet to a quiet unclaimed player, because the evidence points at the claimant.

lessons.situation: The night after a failed double attack on a claimed Town role that the healer saved. Both killers have shown interest in that role, and they may pivot or repeat. You have 0 points and unused self-bets. Information landscape: Moderately informed: a saved attack and open claims give real signal about killer priorities, but it is reasoning and not confirmation. You have no cover or confirmed roles. Stakes: You are at 0 points and being voted out before betting would lose you the game, so getting bets placed each night matters. Each unsuccessful night shortens your runway. Target landscape: The previous night's double-attack target was saved by the healer, and the likely next victims are that same player again, another claimed power role such as a sigilist, or the healer. The basis is expected killer behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, place a bet on the likeliest victim instead of holding back, and keep both self-bets in reserve until you are visibly exposed or have been the day's top vote target. If the kill is likely to go onto the same obvious claimant a second time and the healer may repeat the save, pick the second-most-likely target the killers would pivot to, such as a claimed role that bypasses protection.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or abstain day. One claimant of a night-info role is the focal point of the discussion and votes, so the wolves and the lone killer both have reason to kill them. Information landscape: Moderately informative. There is a public role claim and a vote record concentrated on one player, plus evidence from the earlier night that killers are active. Nothing is verified, and the read rests on the claimant's visibility and not on confirmed roles. Stakes: Scoring two points here ends the Fortune Teller's win condition outright. A miss costs nothing but a night, though only a few nights remain to score. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players. One stands out as a visible information threat: a self-declared Trailseer or Sentinel who was roleblocked or took the day's votes. Their role is unverified and rests on their own claim. The rest are quiet, with no comparable profile.
lessons.action: When a player has drawn real visibility, such as a self-declared info-role claim (Trailseer, Sentinel) that has also taken votes or a roleblock, bet on that player to die and name the claimed role. Killers have a motive to remove them, and a correct role is worth two points while a wrong role still scores one for the death.

lessons.situation: The previous night's wolf kill was stopped by a public heal. A wolf was lynched or lost, and a mixed field of wolves and a lone killer remains. You have one point and need one more. Information landscape: Fairly rich: the save was announced, a role was confirmed by a sigil strike, and one wolf's death was revealed. Which player the wolves will pick next is still a guess from motive. Stakes: With six alive and wolves still active, each night's kill brings them closer to parity. A missed bet wastes a night of scoring while you remain on one point, so choose the bet on motive and not on the last victim. Target landscape: Around six living players: a sigilist who has just survived a save, the healer who made the save, a lone killer, and one or more wolves. The healer is the known obstacle and the likelier next kill. The earlier target is a less likely repeat victim, since it was just protected and the wolves have lost a member.
lessons.action: When the wolves have just failed to kill a target through a heal or block, bet on the player who obstructed them, such as the healer, or on whoever their pack most needs gone. Do not re-bet on the previous target who survived. Only a wolf's kill selection can be predicted this way, so the bet on the obstacle is the better read.

lessons.situation: You reached two points by night 3. Reanimated-wolf kills on consecutive nights show an active Necromancer with few suspects left, and a rival Fortune Teller claim is possible. Information landscape: Information-rich on the threat: consecutive reanimated-wolf kills identified a Necromancer, but nobody knows who it is. Targeting rests on behavior and structure, not confirmed roles. Stakes: With two points banked, further bets have no scoring value and a death in the late game removes you from play, so each self-bet buys a night of survival against a lone killer closing in on a win. Target landscape: Remaining Town players plus yourself. Another bet adds nothing once two points are banked, and your own survival is the live variable. The Necromancer has been killing a Town player every night, and your exposure rests on behavioral and structural evidence, not confirmed roles.
lessons.action: Once you have scored your two points and a killer is picking off players nightly, spend a self-bet each night instead of betting on another player, because scoring is already banked and survival is what remains. A self-bet makes an attack on you fail that night, so use it on the nights the killer is most likely to go after you.

lessons.situation: Final-night endgame with an evil killer (wolf or Necromancer) one kill from winning and few or no town night-killing abilities left. The Fortune Teller needs points and can be killed itself. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are announced, spent abilities are known, and the remaining pool is nearly fully identified, so the killer's only plausible victim can be deduced. Stakes: The next kill ends the game, so a wasted bet or an unprotected Fortune Teller means a loss. A correct bet on the forced victim with the role named can score the final two points. A self-bet only buys time and scores nothing. Target landscape: Two or three other living players: a claimed or confirmed town role the sole remaining killer must target (the healer already dead or irrelevant), and an unconfirmed player who is the likely killer, with a Necromancer able to attack through a dead Vigilante body. Reads rest on confirmed deaths and claims, not on behavior.
lessons.action: In a 3-4 player endgame with both self-bets left, first identify which enemy can actually kill tonight. If the only living killer is the one who could attack you and you have no other path to a point, spend a self-bet so an attack on you fails; if your bet target is the one certain victim, bet on them and name their role.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night where the killers' obvious priority target, a verified or claimed investigator, has been publicly shielded or saved by the healer, while other prominent claimants are unprotected. The Fortune Teller must choose a bet to reach two points. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves or the serial killer are dead or confirmed, healer saves are announced, and protection patterns are visible to every player, including the killers. Stakes: Scoring needs two points, and each zero-point night shrinks the remaining nights in which they can be earned. Repeating a bet the healer can block yields no points and pushes the Fortune Teller toward riskier late bets. Target landscape: A claimed investigator or other focal Town player who is openly or recently healer-protected; an unprotected claimed healer or trailseer; and quieter unverified players. The evidence is public announcements of saves and claims, not behavior.
lessons.action: When the obvious high-profile target was publicly healer-protected or saved last night, bet on a different likely victim instead, such as an unprotected prominent claimant (the claimed healer, or a trailseer or sentinel with no cover). If no protector remains alive, bet on the most prominent unprotected Town claimant.

lessons.situation: Night 1, or an opening night with no discussion or only a quiet day. Two or three independent killers may each take someone, and the bet scores if the named player dies by any cause. Information landscape: Completely information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or protection results, and day 1 had no vote. Stakes: Early misses are routine and not decisive, since two points are still reachable later. A blind hit with no role named caps the score at one point instead of two, which is a free loss to avoid. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no claims, votes, behavior or night history. Any pick is a pure guess, and several deaths are possible because there are two or three killers.
lessons.action: When you have no information, still place the bet and always name a role guess. A wrong role costs nothing, since the death still scores one point, and a right role doubles it. If any thin signal exists, such as a power role likely to be a priority kill, use it to pick the target and the role.

lessons.situation: After a day in which the Fortune Teller cast an isolated dissenting vote or otherwise stands out, the remaining killers must choose a victim. The obvious saved target is likely covered again, which makes the exposed Fortune Teller the easy kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: the public voting record and announced saves expose who dissented and who the healer protected, and the killers can read both. Stakes: If the Fortune Teller dies with fewer than two points it loses permanently. A self-bet makes an attack on it fail, so it survives to bet again, though it scores nothing that night. Target landscape: The Fortune Teller's own safety, via a self-bet, versus betting on a re-targeted saved claimant or another Town player. The killers may bypass the healer-protected claimant and hit the visible outlier instead.
lessons.action: When your day-3 vote or behavior marks you as an outlier or likely target, and you are not close to the second point, use one of your two self-bets instead of betting on another player. The attack on you fails that night, so you stay alive to score later.

lessons.situation: Late game: wolves are dead or nearly so, a lone killer (the Necromancer) is still killing each night, and the Fortune Teller needs points or must stay alive long enough to score them. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves' roles are revealed, earlier checks are confirmed, and the killer's attack pattern across several nights is visible. The remaining uncertainty is only which player the killer takes next. Stakes: The game is near its end. One more death can decide the outcome, and the Fortune Teller's own survival and point total matter more than anything else it can do at night. Target landscape: Three or four living players, mostly confirmed or claimed roles such as an Investigator, a claimed Sigilist and a rival Fortune Teller claimant. The likeliest victim is the repeatedly attacked information source, chosen from the kill pattern rather than from confirmed knowledge.
lessons.action: Late in the game, with a lone killer still active and few players alive, bet on the player the killer's pattern most likely hits tonight, such as a repeatedly attacked information source, and name their role for the two-point payout. If you are the visible threat and still have self-bets, spend one that night, because it blocks an attack on you and a death before scoring loses the game.

lessons.situation: Four-player endgame where the wolf must attack a high-threat claimed role while a living healer will probably guard that same player. The Fortune Teller has two self-bets left and one point. Information landscape: Information-rich: sigil mechanics are demonstrated, several dead roles are confirmed, and claims define the remaining pool. The healer's choice cannot be seen. Stakes: One save plus one sigil strike can end the game on the spot with the Fortune Teller short of two points. Choosing a bet that can still score when the obvious kill is saved matters more than matching the most likely attack. Target landscape: The claimed sigilist (the obvious wolf target), an unconfirmed healer claimant likely to guard them, and a quiet surviving wolf. The choice is between the heavily protected obvious victim and the less obvious alternatives, based on claims and prior-night events.
lessons.action: If a living healer can plausibly protect the obvious wolf target, bet on a different player who is likely to die by another cause, such as a player a pending sigil or other attack might strike or an alternate victim the pack might choose. Do not stake the bet on a protected player with an active sigil threat that could eliminate the last wolf and end the game before you score.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer or investigator has publicly accused or outed a player, and both accuser and accused are alive entering the night. The evil faction must decide whether to silence the accuser. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are public claims, a counter-claim dispute, and a visible accusation, but nothing hard confirms the accuser or the accused. Stakes: A correct bet here scores one point toward the two needed. A bet on the accused instead of the accuser yielded zero points when the accuser was killed. Target landscape: An exposer (a claimed trailseer or investigator who caught or outed an evil player), the accused player under suspicion, and other claimants. The basis is public claims and accusations.
lessons.action: When a claimant has publicly accused or exposed a suspected evil player, bet on the exposer as the likely victim, since the wolves are more likely to silence the accuser than to attack their own accused partner. Take that bet only if the exposer is not currently healer-protected.

lessons.situation: Late game with no protective role alive and a single evil killer who must kill the one remaining town power role. The Fortune Teller can predict the casualty and its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: earlier deaths and reveals fix who is alive, who the killer must be, and which role is the logical victim. The claimed role has been corroborated by a visible event. Stakes: The kill decides whether the game ends this night, so the bet is made at the point of highest leverage. Naming the right role can finish the Fortune Teller's win condition alongside the evil side's win. Target landscape: A claimed role whose identity has been established by an earlier reveal (such as a vigilante whose shot exposed the Serial Killer's immunity) and the lone wolf as the only possible killer. The healer is already dead, so nothing can save the victim.
lessons.action: When the killer's victim is forced by elimination, bet on that player to die and name their role, since a correct role scores two points instead of one. Choose the player no remaining protector can cover. Bet only on a death you can explain by who is able to attack, not on a player merely because they are the obvious target.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2-3) after a wolf was voted out or a tie vote. Claims are public, and a Necromancer, wolves or a Serial Killer may strike. The Fortune Teller is not under suspicion and needs two points to win. Information landscape: Moderate public signals: claimed roles, announced attacker types (reanimated attack), prior deaths and vote records. Nothing confirms who the killers will choose. Stakes: The game is not at the brink, but each night is a scoring chance and the Fortune Teller needs two points. A night with several possible killers gives more than one death to land on, so a well-chosen bet is worth making every night. Target landscape: Several living claimants (a Healer who revealed whom they protected, a twice-attacked Investigator, a Sentinel or Trailseer) and contested players from a claim clash or tie vote. Roles are public claims, unverified. Picks rest on behavior and exposure, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, bet on the player the killers are most likely to hit, judged from public exposure: a freshly claimed Healer or information role, a player at the center of a claim clash, or one just named by an announced reanimated attack. Add the role guess only when a public claim makes it a strong inference, since a right role is worth two points and a wrong role still scores one for the death.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is leaning toward eliminating you: three players have stated they would vote for you based on the visit, while another says the visit warrants scrutiny but is not conclusive. The shared basis is the claimed watch result, not independently verified evidence of your action.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five players remain; one elimination from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown. A single vote can flip which faction is winning, and the game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A further defense can reiterate that the claimed watch does not reveal your action, but the visit itself is already on the record and you have no role-based account to offer without inventing one. Redirecting suspicion would risk looking evasive. The imminent public vote is permanent; its outcome cannot be walked back.
query_dims.heat_now: High: three players have accused you and said they would vote for you, citing the claimed visit to the player killed by the Serial Killer. You acknowledged the visit but gave no role-based explanation.
query_dims.information_landscape: Limited and largely behavioral: the public record confirms the Serial Killer’s identity and a wolf attack saved by the Healer, while the visit evidence comes from an unverified Sentinel claim. A player was killed with their role concealed, so their side remains unknown. No public result establishes what your visit was for.
query_dims.my_position: You are the focus of the forming majority and are defending against it; you are not aligned with the likely vote.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Chanteuse, know your living packmate’s identity, and know your own blocks and the pack’s kills. Publicly, your role and packmate remain unrevealed. The claimed Sentinel’s account places you at the player who died to the Serial Killer; the claim does not identify your action, though you know the visit was your block.
query_dims.situation: With five players alive, the day-four vote centers on whether your unexplained visit to the player who died to the Serial Killer is enough to eliminate you. Three players favor your elimination, while the claimed Sentinel’s watch cannot distinguish a block from another action; the Serial Killer’s revealed role explains the other reported visitor but does not clear you.
query_dims.target_landscape: You are the main vote target: a claimed Sentinel reports you visited the player later revealed as the Sigilist, alongside the Serial Killer, but the watch claim does not establish what you did. The claimed Sentinel is supported only by the public wolf-attack save, which confirms an attack and protection, not their role. The leading accusers are identified by behavior, not confirmed roles; the remaining unclaimed player has offered a cautious assessment rather than a clear competing target.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote: a claimed town info role gave a result that breaks the rules, the accused admitted no explanation, and the table piled on. Your wolf partner may be among the accusers. Eliminating the target also removes a town watcher. Information landscape: Thin but concrete: one verifiable rules inconsistency, a few unverified claims, no voting history, and few confirmed roles. Stakes: Early game with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. The outcome is not close, so one vote does not flip the result. The value is in staying invisible while a town information role is removed. Consensus: Near-unanimous (about 8 of 9) and based on a checkable rules inconsistency that the accused conceded, not on tone or pack coordination. My position: With the majority, joining a vote that is already decided. Heat: Low to almost none: you are unclaimed, made few or no accusations, and the attention is entirely on the accused. Forward exposure: A vote with a lopsided majority commits you to nothing and looks like ordinary town behavior. Voting against an accepted target would stand out in the permanent public record with no upside. Target landscape: One candidate, a claimed Sentinel, has a concrete rules contradiction (a watch result that omitted their own visit) and is accused by several players. No other player has comparable evidence against them, so the choice rests on a verifiable inconsistency, not on tone. Public vs private: You privately know the wolf pair (Chanteuse and Illusionist) is alive and that the accused claimant is likely a genuine town role. The public sees only an unverified claim with an impossible result and treats it as grounds to eliminate.
lessons.action: When the room is already converging on a target through a checkable rules contradiction, cast your day vote with the majority and add no distinctive argument. The vote is low-commitment and blends into the pile-on, so a lone vote elsewhere would only draw heat to you.

lessons.situation: A genuine Town claimant (a healer counter-claiming against my partner, or a sentinel accusing me of a visit) is on the ballot at the day vote. Removing them protects the pack or me today, but their role and will will be revealed on death. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are contested role claims, a named visit, confirmed saves, and the public voting record. Nothing is verified until a death reveals the role. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several kills still needed for parity. Removing a healer or sentinel strips Town's protection or visit information and gives the wolves tempo, but a revealed role can expose my own visit history. Consensus: The village is split or leaning against the claimant, based on behavioral skepticism such as delayed disclosure and conflicting claims, not on confirmed facts. My position: With the majority, as one vote in a broad bloc and not the driver. Heat: Ranges from low to severe. Either my partner is under fire in a contested claim, or the claimant is directly accusing me, but the room is skeptical of the claimant. Forward exposure: The vote is permanent and public. If the claimant dies as a confirmed Town role, my vote is tied to the wolf side and any will naming my visit becomes announced fact, so the commitment cannot be undone and can draw night attacks such as a sigil or a vigilante shot. Target landscape: A binary choice between a claimed protective or information role (healer or sentinel) and either my wolf partner or myself. The claimant's role is unverified, and the case against them rests on behavior and timing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Publicly the claimant is an unverified or belated claimant whom the room distrusts. Privately I know the claim is genuine, either because it names my own visit or because my wolf partner is the one faking the role.
lessons.action: When the room is already turning on a claimant who threatens you or your partner (a counter-claimed healer, or a sentinel naming your visit), cast your vote with the broad majority against that claimant. Joining a wide bloc keeps you from standing out as the driver and removes a protective or information role. Expect the revealed role and will to be read out as fact, so take the claimant's most likely true read into account when judging how much heat that reveal will put on you.

lessons.situation: On day 2 a claimed trailseer reported following you to another player's door, a roleblock report on that player corroborated it, and the village is converging on you or on an abstain while you consider voting against the tracker. Information landscape: Starved of announced facts: only unverified claims (a follow report, a roleblock report, a watch claim, possibly your own cover claim), plus a hidden-role death and a confirmed investigator death. Nothing announced identifies you. Stakes: With nine alive and the wolves far from parity, there is no tempo to force a risky vote. Losing the chanteuse, or drawing a sigil or investigator check by standing out, costs the wolves a blocker and leaves the partner alone. Consensus: The room is aligned on either abstaining or eliminating you, based on matching unverified claims about your night movement rather than on any announced fact. My position: Holding out alone against the room, either as the main wagon target or as a solitary voter against an abstain consensus. Heat: High to very high: the tracker's follow report and a target's roleblock report match your real night visit, several players accuse you, and your denial stands alone against a convergent pair of claims. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser is public and permanent, commits you to the story that the report is false, and invites night attention. Voting with the room is reversible and keeps the record neutral; if you are eliminated your role is revealed and your wolf partner comes under suspicion. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed trailseer who named you, players who echoed the roleblock or watch claims (sigilist, vigilante, sentinel), and an abstain option. All are unverified role claims, and the dead so far are an investigator and a concealed body, so nothing hard points at any candidate. Public vs private: You privately know the tracker's report of your visit is true and you blocked or visited that player; publicly it is only an unverified claim that you have denied or covered with a fabricated story.
lessons.action: When a claimed trailseer or other tracker publicly places your night visit on a target, and the room is abstaining or leaning against you, skip the revenge vote and join the room's consensus (abstain or the wagon's target). A solitary vote against your accuser changes no tally, repeats your accusation on the permanent record and marks you as the one player who wants the information role dead.

lessons.situation: Endgame vote at three or four players where a claimed vigilante threatens to eliminate the chanteuse or the wolf partner and a coordinated counter-vote can produce a tie and no elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: most investigative town roles are confirmed dead, roles and past votes are known, and the vigilante's claim and held shot are public. Stakes: The board is near parity, so a single elimination of a wolf could lose the game while a tie with no elimination keeps the wolves alive to reach parity or a winning night. Consensus: The room is split with no majority; the vigilante pushes one wolf while the remaining players are undecided or abstaining, so a tie is reachable. My position: holding out Heat: Ranges from minimal heat on the chanteuse (suspicion on the partner) to high (a claimed vigilante accusing and voting for the chanteuse based on roleblock claims). Forward exposure: Publicly voting an unclaimed or quiet player commits the chanteuse to an adversarial stance against the vigilante's read, but with few players left and no investigative roles alive the exposure is low and the tie can be repeated. Target landscape: Two or three living candidates: a claimed vigilante driving the accusation, and a quiet or unclaimed player with split or no votes and no claims, who is the only viable counter-target; the basis is behavior, not evidence. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows which players are wolves and that the vote target is not evil, while the room is split between the chanteuse or the wolf partner and an unclaimed or quiet player as the last wolf.
lessons.action: In a small endgame vote where a claimed vigilante and others are pushing to eliminate you or your wolf partner, vote for the non-partner player who is least aligned with the vigilante's push so the vote splits into a tie. A tie eliminates no one, so you and your partner survive into the next night; pick the target who is a plausible suspect, not your partner.

lessons.situation: Day vote where the village converges on your wolf partner, who is exposed by a counterclaim or accusation. You must choose between joining the vote against them and defending them. Information landscape: Claims, counterclaims and unverified night reports are present, and some roles may be confirmed by deaths. There are no hard Game Master confirmations of the accused's role, so the room's read rests on deduction. Stakes: The vote outcome is already decided by the majority, so your single vote does not flip the board. What it decides is whether you stay unlinked to the partner on the permanent record, which protects your survival as the remaining wolf. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, around 7 votes or more, on eliminating your partner. The basis is claim contradictions or a claimed check, not confirmed roles. My position: Tempted to hold out to protect the partner, but the correct stance is with the majority. The vote is decided either way. Heat: Low to moderate. Discussion is consumed by the claim collision and you have drawn no accusations. Your own night visits could still surface later. Forward exposure: A vote with the pile-on reads as a normal town vote and links you to nothing. A vote against the majority, for a rival claimant, or an abstain would be public and permanent, and once your partner's role is revealed it would mark you as their ally. Neither vote can be undone. Target landscape: The accused is your wolf partner, claiming a power role (Sentinel, Healer or Investigator) that is contradicted by a counter-claimant or report. The only alternative is a rival claimant who is probably Town. The case rests on claim clashes and visit reports, with nothing confirmed by the Game Master. Public vs private: You privately know the accused or counter-claimed player is your wolf partner, and that their claim or accusation is fabricated cover. Publicly the room reads it as a claim contradiction or a Suspicious check, and no suspicion falls on you.
lessons.action: When a lopsided majority is already set to eliminate your wolf partner and your vote cannot change the result, cast your vote with the majority on the same target. If you hold out, defend the partner, or abstain, the permanent public record ties you to the wolf once their role flips, so don't do any of those. Afterward, plan as the lone wolf rather than relying on the vote to keep you safe.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after your wolf partner died on night 1. You are the lone wolf, and the room mostly leans to abstain while minority blocs name different targets. Information landscape: Starved: a few claimed night results and one slip, with no confirmed roles and no vote history. Stakes: As the lone wolf you have no backup, so one exposure or one night retaliation could end the wolf side; staying low-profile is worth more than a marginal vote. Consensus: Most of the room leans toward abstaining, and a couple of small blocs name different targets. My position: Holding out with a minority bloc against an abstain-leaning room. Heat: Low: no accusations against you, only generic discussion remarks. Forward exposure: A minority vote is public and permanent and ties you to one bloc, so the target and that bloc can see where you stand. You cannot reverse it. Target landscape: Candidates are a claimant who slipped on a night action, another named suspect, or abstaining. Roles are unconfirmed, and the only lead is a behavioral slip. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf with no partner to help, while the town has no read on you.
lessons.action: If your partner is dead or revealed and you are the lone wolf, vote with the majority or abstain instead of joining a small minority bloc on a sigilist or other action-role claimant. A vote that leaves you holding out with a minority marks you to the targeted player, who may act against you that night.

lessons.situation: Late-game day vote where the chanteuse's side is losing. Either a fake-claim counter-claim contest has turned against you, or a credible watch or follow claim has doomed your wolf partner, and the room is converging. Information landscape: Information-rich from the town's view: confirmed roles for the dead, a lone killer possibly already eliminated, and claims corroborated by other claimants. You have nothing verifiable to offer. Stakes: The wolves are within a couple of eliminations of parity, so losing a wolf or exposing the pair is costly. This single vote will not flip the result, so the value is in keeping the wolves' public links minimal. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, with a lopsided majority forming on a claim-based case that looks consistent. There is no strong support for the minority view. My position: Holding out against, or being swept along by, a clear majority. Your vote is not the deciding one. Heat: High. You are either the target of a lost counter-claim with several players already naming you, or you recently pushed against a claimant who has since been corroborated. Forward exposure: Every vote is public and permanent. Matching your partner's vote, or opposing the room's clear pick, ties you to them and cannot be undone once the role is revealed. A vote that diverges costs little because your own vote cannot change a lopsided result. Target landscape: The realistic candidates are your counter-claimant, your exposed partner, and the Sentinel or other accuser. All are judged on claims and corroboration rather than hard proof, and the room has mostly settled on one. Public vs private: You privately know your partner's role and whether your own claim is false. The room is working from claims, counter-claims and past votes, and it sees you as either a liar or a defender of a likely wolf.
lessons.action: If the vote is already lost, because you are the losing side of a counter-claim or your partner is the target of a credible, room-wide case, cast the vote that least links you to your partner. Vote with the room when it is converging on your partner, and when you are the target pick a different name from your partner's. Votes are public and permanent, so a doomed vote that mirrors your partner's ties the two of you together.

lessons.situation: A claiming investigative role (Investigator or Trailseer) has caught my wolf partner with a Suspicious check or a tracked visit to a victim. The village is pushing to eliminate the partner, and the partner is counter-charging the claimant. I must choose between joining the vote on the partner and voting against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich. A living claimant has direct evidence, other claims or mechanics corroborate it, and the votes will become a permanent ledger. Stakes: The board is still early and not at parity, so one vote does not decide the game. The partner is lost either way, and what matters is whether I survive as a low-heat wolf for later days. A solitary or minority vote costs me that standing and gains nothing. Consensus: The village is largely united behind the claimant's result, supported by mechanics or corroborating claims. A counter-wagon would need near-majority support, and in the observed cases it reached 2 to 4 votes against a landslide. My position: holding out Heat: Low. I had stayed neutral in discussion, with no accusations or scrutiny on me, and that standing is what I would lose by backing the partner. Forward exposure: Votes are public and permanent. A vote against the claimant or for the partner's side becomes a visible link to the partner once the partner's role flips as a wolf, and it cannot be undone. A vote with the majority commits me to nothing beyond the consensus. Target landscape: The choice is between my caught wolf partner, who is named by a claiming investigative role's result or movement evidence, and that claimant, whom the partner is accusing of fabrication. The case against the partner rests on evidence and mechanics, while the counter-case rests on behavior and bluster.
