If your own read points at a different suspect and the contradiction is not clear, hold your vote on your own suspect instead of following the room.

lessons.situation: The town must eliminate someone without investigative leads, and the majority is choosing a target on behavioral grounds. Lynching a power role would hand a lone killer (a necromancer) a usable body and an attacker. Information landscape: Behavioral only for the remaining pool. Confirmed facts cover earlier night events, not who is evil now. Stakes: A mistaken lynch of a power role can swing the endgame. A lone killer using a dead Vigilante's body can attack through it and kill more players, including you. Each vote has real weight. Consensus: The majority leans toward the quiet player on inactivity grounds. A minority backs the pushback player. Nobody has verified evidence. My position: With the majority, or about to join it, without an evidence-based reason of your own. Heat: None to low. You have no accusations against you and are aligned with the room. Target landscape: A quiet unconfirmed player suspected only for lack of claims, versus an unconfirmed player who pushed back on town information. Neither has hard evidence against them. Silent players may be power roles.
lessons.action: Vote for the candidate whose case rests on a concrete contradiction or a confirmed fact, such as a claim that conflicts with an announced result. If the cases are only inactivity or a clash of arguments and abstaining is offered, abstain instead of joining a speculative lynch. A silent player may be a Town role holding unused power, such as a vigilante with bullets, and a lynch reveals the role only after it is too late to undo.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six players are alive and the leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity; this night’s protection can preserve a valuable and visibly threatened player, but one protection outcome alone does not make the game immediately endable or flip which faction is winning.
query_dims.information_landscape: Moderately information-starved: public deaths confirm the Investigator, Trailseer, Sigilist, and Serial Killer are gone, and a prior announcement confirms the claimed Sentinel was attacked and saved. The Healer privately knows that their protection caused that save. No public evidence identifies the wolves or establishes the claimant’s role, and current wolf target intent is unknown.
query_dims.situation: With the Serial Killer eliminated and night beginning, the living Healer must choose whom to protect while a claimed Sentinel has already been attacked by the wolves and saved. That prior attack raises the claimant’s apparent exposure, but the save does not verify their claimed role; the remaining players’ likely targets are otherwise unclear.
query_dims.target_landscape: Protection value is highest for the surviving player claiming Sentinel, whose prior wolf attack and healer save make them a publicly exposed, potentially useful town information source; their Sentinel role remains unverified. Other living players have no confirmed role status from the available public record, and their threat levels are behavior-based and uncertain.

lessons.situation: Healer has just revealed the role publicly on day 2 and was vouched for by the player saved, with a lone vote cast against it. Night 2 arrives with the healer now an exposed, claimed role who cannot self-protect, while the serial killer and wolves choose targets. Information landscape: Moderately informed: one self-verified save, a tracker claim consistent with it, and a sentinel watch claim with no visitor. The killers' identities and next targets remain unknown. Stakes: The healer is the town's only protector and cannot be guarded, so its death removes all night protection while both the serial killer and wolves live. Spending the guard on a target nobody attacks wastes the night. Target landscape: Eight other living players: a corroborated Trailseer, a Vigilante vouched for by an earlier save, and unclaimed or quiet slots. There is no evidence of who the killers will pick. Your own public healer claim is the main new fact, and it makes you a visible role who cannot be guarded.
lessons.action: If you have publicly claimed healer or your protection record has been read out or vouched, treat yourself as the likely kill target and pick a guard target whose protection is worth the most if you survive. Since you cannot protect yourself, do not assume your protectee is the one under attack. Weigh the Town asset's actual risk against the chance that the serial killer or wolves go for you, and favor a player the killers have already shown interest in over one with no attack history.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game night after a day in which an information role publicly reported a result or helped drive a wolf elimination. The wolves are active (a chanteuse is blocking, and a wolf kill pattern is aimed at information roles). The healer must choose the one other player to protect. Information landscape: Moderate to rich: public claims from the investigator, sentinel and trailseer, at least one confirmed wolf role from a vote, and roleblock evidence of an active chanteuse. Most role claims are unverified, but some are corroborated by eliminations or matching visits. Stakes: Mid-game with several wolves or killers still alive, so one lost information role noticeably slows the town but does not immediately decide the game. Keeping the verified information source alive preserves remaining checks, and an announced save also confirms the wolves' targeting. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) plus unclaimed players. The investigator with a corroborated check record or a wolf exposure is the top-value target. A sentinel who is repeatedly roleblocked, or any claimant the wolves are already blocking, is a less likely kill target. Unclaimed players are lower threat. The basis is public claims, corroboration and the wolves' visible pattern of attacking information roles.
lessons.action: Protect the publicly claimed, corroborated information role (investigator first, otherwise the sentinel or trailseer) that the town is relying on and that just publicly drove a result or an elimination. The wolves have the clearest reason to remove that player, so a protect there is likely to save them or at least keep the wolves from a free kill. If two such roles are claimed, pick the one whose claim has independent corroboration, such as a confirmed wolf death or a matching visit, over one that is merely loud.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and the serial killer remains among about five players. The healer is the village's only night buffer against parity, and the serial killer may skip the obvious protected target and kill someone else. Information landscape: Information-rich on past events (both wolves confirmed, an Investigator claim is a public reference), but the serial killer's next target is not predictable from evidence. Stakes: With five alive, each unprevented kill brings the serial killer's win condition (at most one other player alive) closer, and the healer is a likely target once the board narrows. A wasted protection on an unattacked player gives the serial killer a free kill. Target landscape: The claimed Investigator, whose check matched a dead wolf and who was protected the previous night, against quieter town members such as the Sigilist and unconfirmed accusers. The serial killer's choice is unreadable because nothing public shows its preference, so any pick is a guess among several candidates.
lessons.action: When the serial killer is the only killer left, or the board is down to four or five players, avoid repeating the same protectee out of habit once the protectee is no longer the obvious target. Weigh which player the serial killer would most want dead, including a quiet role like the Sigilist or Vigilante, and vary protection among those candidates, since a kill that goes through can narrow the board toward the serial killer's win and expose the healer next.

lessons.situation: Early in the game, after a night death and a day without eliminations, the only public information source is a single claimed role, such as a Trailseer. That claimant faces threats from both the wolves and any lone killer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wolves have been caught, no voting records show alignments, and only one unverified claim exists. Stakes: No single kill decides the game yet, but losing the only information source would leave Town blind. The protection may go untriggered, which costs nothing since the healer's protection is never used up. Target landscape: The only publicly declared information-role claimant versus silent, unrevealed players with no distinguishing evidence. The basis is public role status and the claimant's visibility, not behavior or verified evidence.
lessons.action: When no result has been confirmed and the room is quiet, protect the sole publicly declared information-role claimant, as the most likely kill target. Expect that the attack may land elsewhere, and keep the pick tied to who is most visibly valuable rather than switching to guesses about unrevealed players.

lessons.situation: After a day of public information-role claims that ended in an abstain or no-elimination vote, several high-value town claimants are exposed to attack from both the wolves and a lone killer. The healer must choose which one to shield for the night. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple public claims with interlocking visit accounts, prior save announcements and vote records, but none of the alignments are verified. Stakes: With several town roles exposed and two killers active, one unprotected loss of the lead investigator removes the main source of checks. A correct guard keeps town numbers and can expose evil through the public save announcement. Target landscape: Three or two publicly claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) with interlocking but unverified visit accounts; the claimed investigator shares check results and is the main lead, while the others report watches or follows. The healer picks among these on the basis of claim content and threat to evil, not verified roles.
lessons.action: When several public information-role claims are on the board, protect the claimed investigator, the one whose check results most plausibly point at wolves, and keep protecting them on consecutive nights while they stay the likeliest kill target. Do not shift to the claimed sentinel or trailseer just because they are also exposed. Wolves and a lone killer both want the lead investigative claimant, so a repeat guard has the best chance of producing a save.

lessons.situation: Midgame, after the lone killer (necromancer) was voted out and one or two wolves remain. The healer must choose a protection target. The wolves' pack kills have been landing on other players, and the previous save was either untested or just used. Information landscape: Moderate. One elimination validated an information role's read, but the wolves' kill targets stay hidden, some bodies had concealed roles, and the remaining wolves are unconfirmed. Little evidence says who the wolves will hit next. Stakes: With about six players alive and the wolves as the only night killers, each night's kill moves the board toward wolf parity. A correct save cancels the pack's kill for that night. A wasted save costs one of the few nights the town can use to stay ahead. Target landscape: Living candidates are the town info roles (an investigator whose read was validated by an elimination, a trailseer or sentinel with identity information) plus the sigilist and neutrals. None of the wolves is confirmed. The previous night's saved player is the obvious repeat pick, but the wolves rarely re-hit a target once it has been saved. The choice rests on role value and elimination-validated reads, not on behavior.
lessons.action: After the lone killer is voted out and only the wolves remain as night killers, pick your protection target by who the wolves most need dead, such as the confirmed information holder or the player the pack has been unable to read. Do not simply repeat last night's save. A protected player who was not attacked leaves no trace, so a repeat only pays off if the wolves return to that same target.

lessons.situation: After a daytime elimination confirmed a claimed Sentinel or Investigator's result, the surviving wolves and any lone killer are expected to attack that credible information source on the coming night. The healer must choose whom to shield. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced elimination role verified the claimant's result, so their credibility is public and known, and their continued survival is valuable. Stakes: Town leads on numbers, but losing the verified info role would cost the strongest lead-generating source. A save here preserves that edge and denies the evil side a kill, with a strong chance the attack lands on this target. Target landscape: A publicly claimed information role whose result was just confirmed by an announced elimination (caught Serial Killer or wolf), versus other claimed info roles and quiet unrevealed players with no evidence behind them. The choice rests on verified evidence, not on behavior.
lessons.action: When a claimed information role (Sentinel, Investigator, Trailseer) has just produced a result that got a player eliminated, protect that claimant tonight, since the surviving evil factions have the strongest motive to silence them. If two such claimants are both exposed, favor the one whose result was confirmed by an announced elimination role and who still has uses left.

lessons.situation: Late game, after the Chanteuse was voted out. Only one wolf (Illusionist) and possibly a lone killer remain, and the Healer must pick one protectee among a few town players, including a proven information role that the killers have already hit. Information landscape: Moderately to highly informative: dead wolves are confirmed, roles were revealed on death, and one or two information roles have verified track records. There are no leads on the last wolf or the lone killer. Stakes: Few players remain, so one successful kill moves the board toward parity. A save on the most valuable information role denies the killers a kill and preserves the tool that can catch the last killers, but only one player can be covered each night. Target landscape: A small set of living players: a Trailseer or Sentinel with a verified track record (survived attacks, cross-checked by the healer's own visits), a publicly claimed Investigator with spent checks, and quiet unclaimed players such as the Vigilante and Sigilist. Verified information roles outrank quiet slots; the quiet slots offer no evidence to rank them by.
lessons.action: After a wolf is eliminated and the remaining killers are down to one wolf plus the serial killer or a lone wolf, protect the verified information role (e.g. the Trailseer or Sentinel) the killers have already targeted or that the room trusts most. If that role has already been attacked and saved, keep protecting it, because the killers keep returning to it and a save cancels the attack while keeping their intel alive.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after day-vote or sigil results removed a wolf or the serial killer. The remaining killers (a wolf and/or the serial killer or necromancer) are likely to attack the town's most dangerous information source. The healer must pick one other player to cover. Information landscape: Information-rich: eliminated roles are revealed, some claims have been cross-checked by outcomes or by announcements, and one claimant's testimony visibly shifted the vote. The target is still chosen by inference about the killers' motives. Stakes: Few players remain, so each night kill is a large share of town's strength. Losing the main info holder could let the remaining killers reach parity, while a correct save can absorb even a double attack and leave no deaths. Target landscape: Several living claimed or inferred power roles (sentinel, sigilist, investigator, trailseer, vigilante). One of them just publicly drove an elimination or a confirmed strike. Choice rests on that visible impact and on behavior, not on hard verification. The healer cannot cover itself.
lessons.action: On a mid-game night (around night 3) after a wolf or killer has just been exposed, protect the living info role whose testimony or recent action drove that removal (sentinel, trailseer, or confirmed sigilist) rather than a lower-impact claimant. If two info roles are both in play, favor the one most visibly credited with the exposure, since the surviving killers have the most reason to silence them.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or confusing day 2 in which several town information roles (investigator, trailseer, sentinel) claimed publicly; wolves and possibly a lone killer have several visible high-value targets, and you must pick one protectee. Information landscape: Moderately informed: unverified role claims and a day-2 vote record, no confirmed wolf, and the killers' targets unknown. Mostly claim-based reads. Stakes: Mid-game with wolves and a killer still active; losing the investigator costs the town its remaining check, while a save wastes the wolves' kill, so the pick matters but a single miss does not decide the game. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (publicly reported a Not suspicious check, one check left), claimed trailseer, claimed sentinel, and unclaimed sigilist, vigilante and speculator; the choice rests on claimed information value and exposure, not verified evidence.
lessons.action: On night 2 and later, once the day has produced several unverified information-role claims and the town abstained or gave no clear wolf, protect the claimed investigator (the information holder with checks left) rather than a lower-value claimed role. If you were publicly tied to that same protectee, keep protecting them anyway when their check output is still valuable, because the wolves' kill on them is the likeliest high-value attack.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after a save-confirmed attack on a claimed Trailseer. Wolves and the serial killer are both active, and the village is openly discussing whom attackers might pivot to. The healer must choose between repeating the protection or rotating to another power role or unknown. Information landscape: Information-thin about the next target: a prior save is known and an information-role claim is corroborated by one other claimed power role. No investigation results point to the next night's victim. Stakes: Two killer factions are still alive, so each night can cost a power role. Keeping the Trailseer alive preserves the tracker whose follow of the killer can drive a daytime vote. The cost of repeating is that a pivot to another power role goes unprotected. Target landscape: A claimed, partly corroborated information role (Trailseer) that already survived a double attack thanks to your save, versus another claimed power role (Sigilist) and unclaimed quiet slots with no evidence of who gets hit next. The basis is a public claim plus a prior save pattern, not hard proof of the next target.
lessons.action: When a claimed information role (e.g. Trailseer) has been attacked and saved, or has a corroborated claim, keep protecting it on the following nights while no stronger lead points elsewhere. Killers who targeted it once tend to return or are deterred, and a heal that cancels an attack keeps the town's tracker alive to expose the killer. Accept that a night with no announced attack on your protectee is an idle heal, which is the cost of this policy.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, a wolf has been voted out or is revealed, but a lone killer such as the Necromancer is still hidden and could attack anyone. The healer must choose whom to cover among several Town power-role claimants. Information landscape: Partly informative: some roles are confirmed by announced deaths or by confirmed checks and watches. The identity of the hidden killer is unknown and only its attack kind is visible, so the next target is speculative. Stakes: Few players remain, so losing a key Town role or the healer sharply cuts the Town's ability to remove the last killer. Each save matters, but the next target cannot be known. Target landscape: Living claimants: Investigator with confirmed checks, Vigilante holding the last bullet, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist. Their value is ranked by verified results, past attacks on them, and ability left, not by how they talk.
lessons.action: Each night, protect the confirmed-Town player whose ability is the Town's best remaining way to remove the hidden killer, such as the Vigilante with a bullet left or an Investigator with checks left. If one of them was attacked earlier and saved, keep covering them unless a newer attack pattern points elsewhere. Don't spread protection across low-value or unverified claimants just to rotate.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an abstained or low-information day vote and a night-1 death. The healer must choose a protection target with no hard evidence on who the killers will attack. Wolves and a lone killer may both want the same visible information role. Information landscape: Info-starved: one revealed or concealed night-1 death, an abstain vote, at most one unverified claim. Everything else is behavioral. Stakes: Early game with several evil attackers alive. One saved information role can produce the next check or trail result and decide whether town finds the first wolf or killer, but a wrong guess costs only a night of protection. Target landscape: Eight to nine living candidates besides the healer: one or two publicly active information sources (a claimed Investigator with a not-suspicious result, or an open player pushing for information), and the rest silent or unclaimed. Roles are unconfirmed apart from dead-player reveals, so the choice rests on behavior and on who is most useful to town.
lessons.action: On night 2 with no confirmed leads, protect the visible information-providing player the wolves or killer would most want gone: a claimed Investigator with a result, or an active player asking for information. Prefer that over repeating an arbitrary night-1 pick or a silent unclaimed player. A save on such a player preserves the town's information flow.

lessons.situation: Late-mid game after the wolf team has been mostly or fully eliminated via the investigator's checks. The surviving wolf and/or the serial killer remain and need to remove town's key coordinator to survive. The healer has to pick whom to protect that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf flips corroborate the investigator, role reveals clarify claims, and voting records are public, so the town's most valuable player is clear to both town and evil. Stakes: Few players remain, so each night kill moves the board toward parity or the serial killer's win condition. Losing the investigator would remove town's verified information source, while a save denies evil a kill and may cancel multiple simultaneous attacks. Target landscape: The confirmed investigator (role validated by a flipped wolf) is the focal kill target; alternatives are a claimed sentinel/trailseer and several unconfirmed players with no verified roles. The choice rests on verified evidence of who evil most wants dead, not on behavior reads.
lessons.action: When the investigator's findings have been confirmed by a role flip and the evil sides are down to one or two attackers, protect the investigator again, even on consecutive nights. Evil factions (surviving wolf, serial killer) target the town's confirmed information engine, so one protection can absorb several attackers at once. If the investigator is dead or blocked from relevance, shift the protection to the next most publicly validated town leader.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after you publicly claimed Healer and helped push an elimination, either a counterclaiming wolf or a necromancer-led vote. The wolves now have a reason to pick you, and you must still choose someone else to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims and role reveals: an investigator check was validated by an elimination, and a trailseer was partly confirmed. No wolf is fully identified, and a necromancer or reanimated attacker may still be unproven. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. Losing the healer ends all protection, while the wolves and a lone killer can still reach parity. Your own death is probably unavoidable, so your last protection should secure the most useful remaining Town role. Target landscape: Other living players who are not you: a claimed investigator whose read was validated, a claimed trailseer, vigilante and sigilist. Their claims are only partly corroborated and no wolf is confirmed. You are the likely wolf target and cannot be protected by your own action.
lessons.action: When your Healer role is publicly known and you are the likely wolf target, you cannot cover yourself, so protect the most valuable surviving Town player instead. That is usually the investigator or another role whose information is confirmed or corroborated. If your protection pattern is public, switch to the next-most-valuable player, because the protection still stops any other attacker (a necromancer's body, a serial killer) from landing on that player.

lessons.situation: The healer revealed itself after a confirmed save and now faces a likely night kill from the pack or a Necromancer working through a body. The healer must decide whom to protect knowing it cannot cover itself. Information landscape: The healer's claim and the save are on the record. A reanimated-body attack would show a Necromancer is active without naming it. Roles of the remaining players are only partly confirmed. Stakes: The healer is itself a probable victim and nothing it does can prevent that. Its last protections decide whether the remaining Town power roles survive, and one more loss could leave the Town unable to catch up. Target landscape: Candidates are other living Town players, since the healer cannot protect itself. The Investigator, Vigilante and Sentinel are verified or semi-verified, and the other claimants are lower in value and less verified. The healer is the exposed one.
lessons.action: If your Healer role is publicly known and the town just removed a wolf while a killer is still active, assume you are a likely kill target. You cannot protect yourself, so use the night to cover the single most valuable confirmed-Town ally whose death would end the Town's best path to winning. Do not waste the pick on a low-value or unattacked claimant.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after a day elimination or tied vote. The healer must choose which of several claimed town power roles to shield from the remaining killers, who can strike with concealment or through reanimated bodies. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed investigative and tracking results, public morning reports, confirmed eliminations and prior save records, and a known killer attack pattern. Stakes: With few players left and a killer still active, each night kill moves town close to losing its majority, so losing the one remaining active information role can decide the endgame. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed town power roles: a trailseer with active tracking results naming a living suspect, a sentinel whose watches are spent or who was already saved, and a sigilist with a reactive ability; claims are unverified but backed by morning-report facts and are the main evidence.
lessons.action: When several town power-role claimants are alive and an enemy killer is still active, protect the claimant whose live, ongoing output is driving the case (e.g. a trailseer who just tied a living suspect to a victim) in preference to a claimant whose uses are spent or who already got a save. Reason: a night kill on the active information source costs town the most, and two of three observations show the unprotected trailseer being killed with its role concealed. If no claimant has live output, protecting the publicly confirmed sentinel is a sound default.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an early power-role death (sentinel, trailseer, investigator, or fortune teller) and a no-elimination day. Nobody has claimed, and the healer must choose a protectee from behavior alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: one or two revealed night-1 deaths, a unanimous abstain vote, no claims, and no private leads. Reads are purely behavioral. Stakes: Early game with several town power roles still alive. Losing another power role, such as the vigilante or sentinel, to an unprotected kill hurts, but one bad guess does not decide the game. Protection is never used up, so a guess made on a consistent rule costs little each night. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players besides the healer, none with a public role claim. The candidates are a vocal player driving discussion or demanding claims, and several quiet or generic players. The basis is behavior and table presence only, with no checks, results, or hard leads.
lessons.action: On night 2 of an info-starved board with no claims and an all-abstain vote, protect the visible organizer or most active questioner, since the wolves tend to kill players who drive town reasoning. If a quiet player has not drawn attention, do not pick them on a hunch, because the protection was never tested in the observation that did.

lessons.situation: Late game: the lone killer and at least one wolf are dead, one wolf remains, and the Healer is cleared or safe. The remaining wolf must kill to reach parity, so its night target is the most threatening Town player. One wrong protection could cost the game. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced deaths and roles confirm which evil roles are gone, wills or announcements corroborate claims, and a claimed role has said its ability is exhausted. Stakes: With four alive and one wolf left, one unprotected Town death brings the wolves to parity and ends the game. A correct save keeps Town's numbers intact and lets surviving Town power roles finish the wolf the same night or the next day. Target landscape: Three or four living candidates: a publicly claimed power role whose claim was corroborated by announcements, a vocal town leader who drove earlier evil eliminations, and quiet or abstaining players with no verifiable claims. Choice rests on confirmed evidence and on who is still dangerous to the wolf, not on behavior alone.
lessons.action: In the endgame (about four alive) with one wolf left and the lone killer gone, protect the player the wolf most needs to remove: the confirmed, still-active Town power role, or the loudest town leader who drove the earlier evil eliminations. If the leading candidate has publicly said their ability is spent, move the protection to the next-most-threatening active Town voice.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game with no day-1 vote. The healer must protect one other player blind while the wolf pack and possibly a lone killer may attack. The healer itself is sometimes the opening target, so the night-1 pick may be the only protection Town gets. Information landscape: Information-starved: only one day of undirected discussion, with no claims, accusations, deaths or private results to rank targets by. Stakes: Early game with a full table: no single night-1 outcome decides the game. A lucky save gains a body and credibility, while a miss costs nothing. Since information is zero, a cheap blind protection is the right policy. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no claims, no behavior, no votes and no revealed roles. The pick is a blind guess, and wolves, the serial killer and the neutral are all equally possible. The healer cannot protect itself.
lessons.action: On night 1 with no claims, deaths or reads, protect one other player rather than skipping, and choose any quiet, unclaimed player without agonizing over it. Protection is never used up, and a save is announced if the pick is attacked. The visit also leaves a trace a Sentinel or Trailseer may later cross-check.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain before the leading evil faction can win, so this is not a one-result swing and the game cannot end within one more elimination. The target’s removal changes the board, but the supplied parity distance does not make this single decision immediately decisive.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A night attack is not a public commitment to a named target or to your role; the morning report identifies the kind of attacker, while visit evidence could expose a trace. No current evidence links you to the Night 1 death.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the Investigator and Trailseer are confirmed dead, the only living role claim is an unverified Sentinel claim, and the Trailseer’s visit to a player does not identify the attacker. The vote provides behavioral evidence of a three-person push, not role evidence.
query_dims.situation: After a day-two abstention, the game has entered a night with no elimination: three voters targeted a player who said they had no result to share, while most others abstained. Separately, a claimed Sentinel reported that the deceased Trailseer visited another player, but that visit alone does not establish who attacked the Trailseer or implicate the visited player.
query_dims.target_landscape: The leading choice is between the player who drew three elimination votes but gave no confirmed night result, the player visited by the deceased Trailseer according to an unverified Sentinel claim, and other living players with no public role confirmation. The Investigator and Trailseer are system-confirmed dead; the Sentinel claim remains unverified.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later after a day vote that concentrated suspicion on one player, with a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer active and unblocked. Information landscape: Moderately informative: a public claim by a watcher, a fixed vote record, and some confirmed dead roles. Stakes: A watcher reading your visit leads to a day vote that can eliminate you, ending your game. Avoiding the watched door protects the only win path, since you can be removed only by a vote. Forward exposure: A kill is a visit that a watching Sentinel or a following Trailseer can read, and it cannot be undone after the morning. Killing a focal day target is predictable and invites a watch on that door. Target landscape: The claimed Sentinel, the contested player who just drew votes, and several quiet off-ballot players. Focal targets are the likeliest places for a watcher to be, while quiet players are less likely to be watched.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer has publicly claimed and is still alive, do not kill the player you just voted against or the player the room is focused on, because a watcher on that door sees your visit. Pick an off-ballot quiet player, or the watcher themself if the claim looks credible, so the visit is less likely to be read.

lessons.situation: Three players are alive after a daytime elimination, and one night kill by the serial killer brings the count to two. Information landscape: Information-rich: published watch results, a confirmed wolf elimination, and roles largely narrowed down. Stakes: The next kill ends the game, so the SK wins by killing any one of the other two and loses a chance if it fails to kill. Forward exposure: Terminal and irreversible: the kill ends the game immediately, so there is no later exposure to manage. Target landscape: Two other players remain: a claimed town information role (e.g. sentinel) and a quiet player who voted against the SK. Either kill wins; the claimed town role is the safest pick since it is the most likely to hold useful information or protection.
lessons.action: With three alive, you plus two others, and any single kill ending the game, attack whichever other player is alive and can be reached, preferably the one with a role that could otherwise stop you. This reaches the two-alive win condition at once, so no day vote follows.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or split day vote. Information roles are claiming and the wolves are also hunting the loudest of them. You must choose a victim without duplicating the pack's kill or walking into a watcher's trace. Information landscape: Moderately thin: a few claims, one or two early bodies, a split or abstain vote, and no hard evidence on any role. You cannot tell who is watching or following whom. Stakes: Mid-game with eight alive, so one wasted or traced kill costs tempo and exposure but does not end the game. Both the wolves and you still need several more deaths. A visit trace can make you the day vote target, and a duplicated kill gives no net body-count gain. Forward exposure: Your kill is an attack and a visit, so a Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer following you will log it. The morning report also names a serial killer attacker if the wolves hit the same player. Neither can be undone once the night resolves. The wolves' illusionist conceal hides only the wolf carrier's visit, never yours. Target landscape: Seven living candidates: claimed Sentinel, Trailseer and Investigator, a claimed Sigilist or Vigilante, and quiet unclaimed players. Claims are unverified, so the choice rests on public role claims and who the wolves most likely want dead, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: On night 2 with about eight alive, kill a living information role (claimed Sentinel, Trailseer or Investigator) that the wolves are least likely to take that night, rather than the loudest one they will obviously hit. A kill on the wolves' probable target wastes your attack, and any victim who is watched or followed puts your name on the visit trace. Prefer a victim whose death removes a watcher or follower, and if the Sentinel and Trailseer are both alive and active, expect a visit to anyone else to be logged.

lessons.situation: The neutral and the wolves are gone. You are the only evil player left among claimed town, and the town is hunting the last non-town player. One of the claimants can track visits. Information landscape: Information-rich. Roles and claims are mostly locked and flips are confirmed, so town can reason by elimination. Any visible visit trace would end the game. Stakes: Only a few players remain and one wrong vote ends you. A visit trace linking you to a corpse is decisive for the town. The night kill must both thin the board and avoid giving proof. Forward exposure: The kill is an irreversible visit. If a living Trailseer follows you, or a Sentinel watches your victim, the visit is seen and can be used as proof against you the next day. Killing the tracker leaves no such witness from that night. Target landscape: A small field of claimed town roles: a healer, a confirmed investigator, a sigilist, and a trailseer. The roles are locked and no cover role is left for you, so the choice rests on who can produce visit evidence.
lessons.action: When only town claimants and you remain and a Trailseer or Sentinel claimant is still alive, make that tracker your night kill. A dead tracker learns nothing from the night, so your visit cannot be followed or watched. If several trackers are claimed, kill the one the room trusts most.

lessons.situation: Night 3 with the wolves collapsing (one or both revealed or dead). The village is about to treat you as the remaining unexplained killer, while the wolves and others converge on the same prominent target. Information landscape: Info-rich about the wolves (revealed roles, sigil kills, vote records). Thin about you, since no check or watch has confirmed you, but the attack count is public. Stakes: Four eliminations remain before you can finish, so a wasted or duplicated kill costs tempo. A visible duplicated or saved attack turns the day vote toward you once the wolves are gone. Forward exposure: Each announced kill is permanent and adds to the attacker count. A duplicate or saved attack on the same player reveals a second attacker and removes nobody. Once the wolves are gone, the village treats the lone killer as the only unexplained attacker, and the choice cannot be undone. Target landscape: Surviving candidates are the claimed sentinel, trailseer, healer, vigilante, sigilist and a neutral. The sentinel was picked on behavior (accusing or naming you) in both cases where the wolves and a healer covered the same player. No target had hard evidence tying them to you.
lessons.action: On the night the wolves are collapsing, pick a victim the wolves are unlikely to hit, rather than the loudest accuser or the most trusted information role. A quiet player who could still vote you out or punish you later (sigilist, vigilante) fits. If the obvious target is the sentinel or another public figure, assume the wolves and a healer converge there and shift your kill elsewhere.

lessons.situation: After a day-2 vote where nearly everyone abstained but one player voted to eliminate you. You are choosing whether to spend the night kill on that outlier. Information landscape: Moderate to rich: a public voting record isolates the lone accuser, and several power-role claims exist, but nothing hard confirms who the wolves are. Stakes: The kill can remove an active wolf and halve the pack, which shortens your path to a last-standing win. Nobody is at parity yet, so the cost is the day-3 heat the motive link brings, not an immediate loss. Forward exposure: Killing the one voter against you ties the death to a motive and turns their stray vote into evidence for Town. If they were a wolf, the surviving wolf can use that vote to argue you cannot be killed at night. You cannot reverse this after the kill. Target landscape: Seven living candidates: the lone day-2 accuser, claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator or Sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. The accuser is picked on voting behavior alone, not role evidence, and was revealed in these games as a wolf (Chanteuse or Illusionist).
lessons.action: If one player alone voted against you on day 2 while the rest abstained, and no active Sentinel or Trailseer threat is more urgent, you may kill that outlier. They are more likely a wolf or a hostile reader, so you also remove a rival. Pick this target only knowing that the dead player's vote will be used against you on day 3.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. You are the Serial Killer, immune to night attacks, and the wolves are also choosing a kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, votes, deaths or night results exist yet. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and far from parity. One kill gains a single elimination toward being the last one standing but does not decide the game, and a failed or overlapping kill costs little beyond exposing a lone killer. Forward exposure: The kill is irreversible and commits you to nothing publicly. If it overlaps the wolves' victim or is saved, the morning names the serial killer as an attacker. A Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer on you can also see the visit. Target landscape: Nine other players, all unknown, with no claims, votes or behavior to read. Targets differ only by role potential, and a quiet player is as likely as any to hold a check, watch, or bullet.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or reads, kill one quiet, unclaimed player and accept that the pick is blind. The wolves also attack that night, and a kill that lands on the wolves' victim is announced as a double attack that reveals a second killer. Any kill carries the same chance of a watcher having been on that target.

lessons.situation: Endgame with 3-4 players alive. The serial killer must choose a night victim that determines whether the final daytime vote is winnable. Day votes have shown clear blocs, and a kill can strand the SK against a united pair. Information landscape: Information-rich: public voting records show who sided with and against the SK, some roles are confirmed by reveals, and several claims are on record. Stakes: One kill decides the game. Reaching two alive wins at once, while leaving three alive with an opposing bloc allows a 2-1 vote to eliminate the SK, which cannot be killed at night and can only be removed by a vote. Forward exposure: The kill is irreversible and fixes the final roster. Leaving three alive means a daytime vote decides whether you live, while reaching two alive ends the game immediately. Target landscape: Three or four survivors: a claimed ally who voted with you (vigilante), claimed town role holders (sentinel, investigator), and a wolf pair or wolf plus town voter who have voted against you. Evidence is mainly the public vote record and claims, not verified roles.
lessons.action: When 3-4 players remain, count the day-vote math before choosing your kill: pick the target so the survivors are you plus one other, or at worst you plus a player who is not allied with the other survivor. Avoid kills (or kills overlapping the wolf kill) that leave you outnumbered 2-1 by a pair that has voted together against you. If you can reach exactly two alive this night, take that kill, since it ends the game in your favor.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with several claimed Town power roles alive, one of them able to trace night visits. The Healer is dead or fixed on another target, and the wolves are also killing. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich. Public claims, a tracking chain, a held shot, and save announcements are known, but the hidden Healer and the unclaimed roles are unconfirmed. Stakes: A mid-game board where the kill choice shapes who survives to threaten you. Removing the one role that can follow your visit protects your night actions, but each Town death also pushes the wolves toward parity, so the kill should target someone who endangers you. Forward exposure: The kill is a private visit that carries no attribution unless you are watched or followed, but a prominent claimant dying signals an active killer hunting information roles. It cannot be undone, and if the wolves also hit that target the double attack reveals a second killer. Target landscape: Claimed power roles (a Trailseer with a public tracking chain, a Sigilist, a Vigilante holding fire) plus quiet unrevealed players, one of whom may be the Healer. Claimed roles are known only by their own say-so, so the choice rests on behavior and prominence rather than proof.
lessons.action: When a claimed Town information or tracking role (e.g. the Trailseer) is alive and could follow your visits, spend the night's kill on that claimant. If a claimed Healer is known dead or the claimant is not the healer's protected target, the kill lands; if the healer is visibly guarding that claimant, aim at the next most dangerous power role instead.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later after a tied or contested day vote. Public claims exist, and an obvious wolf target stands out, such as a claimed investigator or trailseer in a tie. Information landscape: Moderately informative: unverified claims and a public vote record, but no confirmed roles among the living. Stakes: Each night's kill is a scarce progress step toward last-one-standing. A kill that duplicates the wolves' death wastes a night, while a distinct victim yields two deaths and brings the endgame closer. Forward exposure: A double attack on one victim is reported with both attackers, which reveals the extra killer and cannot be undone. The kill is irreversible and gives you no additional elimination. Target landscape: Claimed investigators or trailseers, the contested player from a tied vote, and several quiet players. The wolves' likely target is the publicly visible, accused or information-bearing player, so those candidates risk a wasted kill.
lessons.action: From Night 2 on, choose a victim the wolves are unlikely to hit, such as a quiet player who was not publicly contested, over the player everyone expects to die. A kill that lands on the wolves' obvious target is announced as a joint attack and adds no extra death.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and the town is led by a vocal investigator against the lone killer. You are choosing a night target while a healer is probably alive and likely guarding the town's key voice. Information landscape: Information-rich. Wolf flips are confirmed and the investigator's reads are validated. Town's remaining uncertainty is mainly which unverified player is the killer or the neutral. Stakes: A wasted night costs tempo and, via the save, confirms a protective role. The board is small enough that each night kill matters. A failed kill makes your elimination more likely. Forward exposure: The attack is irreversible. A save is announced in the morning, so a failed kill gains nothing and helps the healer confirm their role, narrowing the pool toward you. A kill on a less obvious target keeps the healer's identity unconfirmed. Target landscape: A confirmed or loudly claimed investigator who just helped eliminate the last wolf, an unrevealed healer, an unverified tracker claimant, and quiet town players. The investigator is the obvious protect target. The others are judged on their claims and behavior.
lessons.action: If one prominent confirmed or claimed investigator or other town leader is the obvious protection target, spread your kill to a different live town role instead of repeating the predictable pick. Prefer a role the healer is unlikely to be guarding. A kill into a healer save spends the night and leaves you with fewer unverified players to hide among.

lessons.situation: Late game, around 5 alive with both wolves gone. A tiny voter pool decides whether you are voted out, and a vigilante or sigilist can narrow the suspects to you. Information landscape: Most roles are confirmed by death records and wolf reveals. The only open question is which survivor is the serial killer, so every announced attack narrows suspicion. Stakes: With few players left, each kill and each day vote decides the game. Spending a night on a harmless neutral leaves the sigilist and vigilante alive to expose you. Forward exposure: A kill the same night as a vigilante shot or wolf attack shows several attackers on one victim, and an immune shot report points at you. Once the body is announced you cannot walk it back. Target landscape: Five or so alive: a sigilist, a vigilante with possible bullets, a neutral voting body such as the fortune teller, and a possible healer claimant. The sigilist and vigilante are the real threats to a last-standing win. The neutral is only a vote.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone and only a handful of players remain, kill the player who can most directly stop your last-standing win. That means a vigilante with bullets left or a sigilist, not a side-less neutral that merely adds a vote. If a vigilante is alive, expect a possible same-night shot, which you survive because you cannot be killed at night, and plan for a possible 'immune' report.

lessons.situation: Early-mid game, after a tie or no-elimination day, with several town roles claimed and a healer publicly confirmed. The wolves are also killing each night, and you must pick a night victim among claimed roles. Information landscape: Moderately informative public claims and a save announcement, with partial corroboration and no evidence pointing at you. Hidden roles remain, and you do not know who the healer is unless one claims. Stakes: Several players remain, so each kill moves you toward a final-two win. A confirmed healer can cancel a kill on any night, so removing it early lets later kills land cleanly, though you still face a day vote that could end you. Forward exposure: Killing the claimed healer reveals a threat-removal pattern but leaves no trace pointing at you, and it commits you to no story. The kill cannot be undone, but it removes protection that could blunt every later kill, whoever makes it. Target landscape: Candidates are the self-claimed healer (corroborated by the vigilante and the trailseer's follow), the trusted trailseer, the sentinel, and the sigilist and chanteuse under vote suspicion. The healer is the most openly identified protector, and the choice rests on public claims and corroboration rather than proof.
lessons.action: When a freshly claimed protector (healer) is publicly identified, aim the night kill at that protector rather than at a protected information role. If the save announcement shows a healer is already covering a claimed role, switch to a different target that night instead of repeating the saved one, since a repeat visit can be traced by a follower.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win. A wrong lynch is recoverable but costly, and each further mis-elimination moves the wolves and the serial killer closer to parity, so my two checks are a scarce resource that should resolve the most uncertainty before a vote.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved. No confirmed roles beyond the public deaths of the trailseer and speculator and the revealed healer. No claimed results have been tested against a night death. My own two checks are the only private information source on the board, and no other living player has a verified result.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 is approaching with the village just having lynched a Town healer on thin evidence after a blocked role claim that was never named. As the investigator with two checks, I hold the only unspent information tool among the living, and I must decide whether to spend a check on a player the village is currently divided over, or hold both checks until a stronger accusation forms. The concern is that the wolves and serial killer are still active and the village has no reliable reads.
query_dims.target_landscape: Seven players alive: player_3, player_6, player_7, player_8, player_9, player_10, and me. Public roles: player_5 was just eliminated and revealed as the healer, a Town role, so the village is down its protector. The three day-2 accusers of player_5 and the abstainers differ in basis. Player_10 pressed the vote and accused player_5 on the basis of a blocked role claim with no result, and player_5 had accused player_10 in return. No candidate has a verified role; all are unknown and judged from behavior and vote history.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended with a near-universal abstain vote and you stand out as the sole non-abstainer or a revealed investigator. You face a night where you may be hit by a wolf kill and must decide whether to spend a check or hold both. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths or role claims, only the day-2 vote tally showing abstentions and one or two outliers. No hard leads on alignment. Stakes: A night death erases that night's check result and the unspent check with it. Spending a check early gives the best chance of a usable Suspicious result before the wolves cut you down. Holding both checks risks dying with them unused. Target landscape: Nine living players: one vocal player you already voted against, and several quiet players blending into the abstain consensus. None has a confirmed role or any evidence against them. Selection is by behavioral standout or blending.
lessons.action: If you have two checks and are likely to be attacked soon (your role is known, or you stood out by voting alone), spend one now on the most behaviorally anomalous player instead of holding both. A check you never use is worth nothing if you die. Pick the target on a concrete behavioral signal such as an outlier vote or a conspicuous silence, not at random.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an early town-role death and an abstain vote. A key info-role claim, or a result that could steer the next vote, sits unverified, and the investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Mostly information-starved. The only solid information is the investigator's own earlier read, and the other claims are unverified. Stakes: The town needs one trustworthy lead to find the killers. Checking the claimant whose uncorroborated result matters most can turn the best available lead into something the town can act on, without wasting the last check. Target landscape: Eight living players. One player has a claim or result with real consequences for the vote, but no one else can confirm it. The other candidates are silent or unclaimed. Basis is the claim's importance, not evidence against anyone.
lessons.action: If a pivotal claimant, such as a sentinel or trailseer, has an unverified result that the town may act on, use the check on that claimant. A Not suspicious read adds weight to a lead the town would otherwise have to take on faith, and a Suspicious read exposes a false claim. Skip claimants whose visit is already explained by a corroborating watch or follow.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended in near-unanimous abstention or no elimination, with one or two players breaking consensus. The investigator is choosing where to spend a check before a wolf kill or roleblock can stop them. Information landscape: Thin evidence: a night-1 death, perhaps one unverified claim, and a voting record showing only a few non-abstainers. Mostly behavioral reads, with few or no confirmed alignments. Stakes: Wolves are not yet near parity, but the investigator is a prime kill target and may not survive many nights. Each remaining check is scarce, so spending it on the most informative anomaly matters. Target landscape: A handful of living players with no confirmed roles. One or two stand out by breaking the abstain consensus, casting a lone vote, or voting against the investigator. The rest are quiet abstainers with no trail, so the choice rests on voting behavior rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: After a no-elimination Day 2, spend a check on the player whose public behavior stands out, such as the sole proactive voter, a lone dissenter against the room, or a member of a bloc that voted against you. If the result is Suspicious, you have a concrete wolf lead. If it is Not suspicious, you have cleared a likely power-role ally, though that read does not rule out a lone killer.

lessons.situation: Late game after key deaths, with the lone killer or a reanimated attack already surfaced and evil still alive. The investigator holds one final check and must decide whether to spend it on an active contributor or a quiet player. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, wills and claims, there is evidence of night attacks, and an earlier check result exists. The remaining unknowns are a few players, so the check can sort the pool. Stakes: The pool is small enough that one decisive check can expose the last evil role or confirm a strong ally. A wasted check could let parity close before town finds the wolf. Target landscape: A handful of living, mostly unconfirmed players: role claimants with partial support, one unrevealed player, and an active unclaimed player who steers discussion on night abilities or case analysis. The choice rests on behavior, since no hard evidence ties anyone to the evil roles.
lessons.action: With your last check and a shrinking pool of unverified players, check an active, vocal player whose steering of the discussion is still unexplained, in preference to a quiet player or one whose role is already supported. Either result narrows the pool: Suspicious points to a wolf, or to a Necromancer if it attacked that night, and Not suspicious adds a confirmed non-wolf ally.

lessons.situation: After a day-2 vote where nearly everyone abstained, the investigator is publicly known or stands out. They must spend the final check before the wolves likely silence them. A standout player is available to check. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil reads, a concealed or absent role reveal, and a day record of near-universal abstains with one or two outliers. Informational claims exist but none are verified. Stakes: The board is still roughly even, but losing the investigator costs Town its only alignment-check source. One confirmed wolf read could remove half of the wolf pack. A wasted or unreported check leaves Town with only behavioral reads. Target landscape: About eight or nine living players, mostly abstainers with no hard evidence against them. One stands out behaviorally, either by an aggressive outlier vote or by being a silent player others urge scrutiny on. No confirmed evil reads exist yet, so the choice rests on behavior.
lessons.action: With your last check and your role already exposed, check the player whose behavior broke from the room, such as the lone aggressive voter in an all-abstain day or the silent player others are spotlighting. Do it tonight, because you may be killed and an unspent check dies with you. If you survive, the Suspicious or Not suspicious result is hard evidence for the next day.

lessons.situation: Night 2. The illusionist is exposed or dead, the first victim's role is known, and the day-2 vote ended in abstain or a thin consensus. Chanteuse, lone killer and possibly necromancer remain unidentified, and the investigator holds one or two checks. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are one or two own check results, perhaps a claim or two with partial corroboration, and no confirmed wolves besides the dead illusionist. Stakes: The wolf pair is partly broken but the chanteuse and a lone killer are still alive. With few checks left, each one that lands on an unexplained player can decide the next day's vote, while one spent on an already-cleared player is lost value. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players, mostly unclaimed or claimed-unverified. A wolf-read on the illusionist may already be confirmed. No hard evidence on any candidate, so the choice rests on behavior and gaps in the room, such as the quiet player, a lone accuser, or an inconsistent statement.
lessons.action: Spend the check on a living player that no claim, watch or follow has yet explained and who shows a behavioral oddity, such as a quiet or low-profile player, a lone accuser, or someone who slipped in describing their own action. If the unverified pool is large, pick the most anomalous player. A hard Suspicious or Not suspicious on an unexplained player is worth more than re-confirming someone already vouched for.

lessons.situation: After an opening night where several town roles visited or protected the same player and Day 2 ended in abstention, that focal player's alignment is the board's central unknown. Information landscape: Multiple role claims or visit patterns form an activity web around one target, but no alignments are confirmed, so the check can anchor the web. Stakes: Early in the game the town has time but no leads. A check on the hub converts the town's activity into a verified read that can shape later claims and votes. Target landscape: One focal player drawn to by several town-role visits or claimed protections, versus quiet players with no signals. The basis is the converging role activity, not alignment evidence.
lessons.action: When several town roles' claimed visits or protections converge on one player, spend a check on that focal player. If the result is Not suspicious, you have a hub the town can trust, though a lone killer would read the same; if Suspicious, you have exposed a wolf the town was shielding.

lessons.situation: The investigator is publicly exposed or being targeted. One or two players cast opposing votes against the investigator or defended a eliminated wolf, so the investigator has a ready suspect and limited time. Information landscape: Moderately rich: a public voting record, possibly a confirmed dead role, and a visible bloc or lone dissenter. Behavior is readable but no alignment is confirmed. Stakes: The investigator is at risk of dying or being roleblocked, so the last check may be the only one that lands. A Suspicious hit could collapse the wolf pack within a day or two, while a miss leaves the town short of leads. Target landscape: The dissenting voters or the sole counter-voter against the investigator, who show the clearest hostile signal, versus passive abstainers or supporters of the investigator's push. The basis is voting records rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: If the investigator's claim is already public, or the investigator is being pushed, spend the check on the player who actively voted against them or defended a confirmed wolf. A Suspicious result then gives the town a wolf lead and exposes the dissenter's partners, whereas a Not suspicious result clears a wolf-adjacent suspect only of wolf status.

lessons.situation: A focal player has been tied to suspicious activity by other roles' reports or by a counter-claim against you, and the investigator still holds checks to confirm whether they are evil. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead trailseer reveal, a sentinel report, a roleblock claim, and a counter-claimant who made a claim about you that you know is false. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. A confirmed read on the evidence-flagged player settles the main suspect and protects your standing, so the check is worth spending now. Target landscape: One focal player singled out by a sentinel or trailseer report or by a false counter-claim on the investigator, versus quiet players with no evidence against them. The focal player is chosen on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When other night evidence (a trailseer or sentinel report, a counter-claim on you) has narrowed suspicion to one specific player, spend a check on that player to confirm Suspicious or Not suspicious. A Suspicious read on a player already pointed at by independent evidence gives you a verified evil target and corroborates the other power roles.

lessons.situation: A rival investigator claim has appeared. The rival says they checked you and found you Not suspicious, but you know you were never checked by a real investigator. Information landscape: Information-rich: you personally know the rival's claim is false, and trailseer and sentinel reports exist that can corroborate the result. Stakes: Your role is contested and the town may side with the rival and lose its only investigator. Resolving the claim fast with a check is high leverage. Target landscape: The single counter-claimant who falsely says they checked you, versus quiet or unconfirmed players. The counter-claimant is the clear target because you hold direct knowledge of their lie.
lessons.action: If another player counter-claims investigator and says they cleared you, use a check on that counter-claimant at night, since you know their claim about you is false. A Suspicious result gives you hard proof that they are lying and evil, and it stays useful even if another night action removes them first.

query_dims.consensus_text: A tentative lean toward voting for the first accused player is forming, based on their vote against the deceased player and the claimed visit report. The second reported visitor is also being questioned, so alignment is incomplete.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive and it is three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; this decision does not itself determine which faction is winning, though a wrong elimination still costs a scarce day.
query_dims.heat_now: No one has accused you or cited evidence about you; your current suspicion level appears low.
query_dims.information_landscape: The deaths and revealed roles are confirmed, but the Sentinel's visit report is only a claim. Public vote records are factual, yet neither voting for the deceased player nor visiting them establishes an attack. The two original information roles have been revealed dead, leaving the current discussion evidence-poor.
query_dims.my_position: You have passed and have not stated a position; you are not visibly driving or opposing the tentative lean.
query_dims.situation: A claimed Sentinel says two players visited the player killed by the Serial Killer, while the emerging vote focus falls more heavily on one of those visitors because they also voted to eliminate that player. The second visitor points out that both share the visit evidence and vote history, leaving the room to weigh behavioral suspicion against an unverified report.
query_dims.target_landscape: The main vote candidates are the player accused by two speakers and the other player reportedly seen at the same dead player's home. Both are unclaimed by role here; the first also voted to eliminate that dead player, while the second did too. The Sentinel claim and visit report are unverified.

lessons.situation: Few players remain, the town power roles that could clear anyone are dead, and you are the first to publicly narrow the suspects to two. Information landscape: Information-starved on the key question: dead roles are known and one player is confirmed by an announced fact, but nothing separates the last two unknowns. Stakes: Near parity: every vote and night kill is decisive, and a visible lead on a point-short Fortune Teller invites the killer to remove you before you can score the final point. Consensus: The table accepted the narrowing and then debated voting order; the two suspects deflected onto each other with no firm direction. My position: Driving the framing with no personal lead on which suspect is the killer. Heat: Moderate-low: one earlier vote on a dead player is being cited against you, but no real suspicion. Target landscape: Two unaccounted-for players, with the dead roles known and one player confirmed by an announced sigil strike; no claims or checks separate the two, so any lean rests on voting-order behavior only.
lessons.action: When the pool of evil suspects is down to a few players and the town roles that could clear anyone are dead, state your narrowing and name your lead suspect, but deliver it as a shared conclusion alongside the confirmed player rather than leading it alone. If you are one point short of winning, avoid being the visible driver, since a lone-killer or wolf at the table can eliminate you at night.

lessons.situation: Day 4 with most evil already dead. A claimant's reported results look inconsistent with the rules, and you are the main driver of the case against them. Information landscape: Info-rich on mechanics but conflicted on identity. The contradiction is checkable, but the claimant's honesty is in doubt and a real Town role may be misread. Stakes: Few evil players remain, so one wrong elimination can hand the last evil faction parity or remove Town's last investigative role. A visible driver of the vote is also an obvious night-kill target. Consensus: The room is converging on your rule argument, which makes a fast elimination of the claimant likely. My position: Driving the case as the first and most persistent voice. Heat: Moderate. The accused claimant counter-accused you of pushing too eagerly, though the rest of the room backed your argument. Target landscape: The only claimed role on the table, with unclaimed others. The basis for suspicion is a mechanical inconsistency in the claim, not a past check.
lessons.action: When you spot a rule-based contradiction in a claimant's account, state it once, clearly and as a question. Ask what else could explain it, and compare their answer with any counterclaims. Do not repeatedly assign a specific evil role to them, because other players will pile on and the mislynch can cost Town its last investigative role while exposing you to a night kill.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a wolf is revealed dead and further kills were concealed; a lead accuser targets a suspect who defends himself with his vote on the dead wolf. Information landscape: Moderately thin: one confirmed wolf and a voting record, but concealed bodies and otherwise only claims and behavioral inference. Stakes: Midgame with enough players that one vote does not decide the game, but removing a wolf now cuts the wolves' parity threat and the pool of kill sources; the public result may also make me a likelier kill target. Consensus: The room is forming around one suspect, based on the dead wolf's revealed role and voting records rather than hard proof. My position: With the majority, as the second accuser. Heat: Low to moderate: aligned with the lead accuser, nothing exposing said, bets unscored and role undisclosed. Target landscape: A suspect accused of echoing a dead wolf's line who points to his vote on that wolf as proof of innocence, plus quiet players he deflects onto. Only one wolf role is confirmed; the rest is behavioral and voting-record reading.
lessons.action: With a confirmed wolf dead and no night result of your own to share, join the leading accusation against the player whose behavior best fits the dead wolf's. Give a concrete reason, such as a wolf piling onto a doomed partner to blend in, and keep your role and bet history private. If the accusation is led by a player you distrust, state your own independent read instead of echoing it.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer reports tracking an accused player to the door of a night victim whose role was concealed, creating a confrontation over whether the visit is genuine. Information landscape: Mixed: one concealed night death and a single living claimed trailseer's report, with conflicting readings of the mechanics and no corroboration. Stakes: A wrong elimination would cost Town a body and bring the wolves closer to parity, but no single vote decides the game. The fortune teller benefits from a slower, evidence-driven day that keeps it unexposed. Consensus: The room is leaning toward acting on the trailseer's report, but with open doubt about whether the visit was fabricated or genuine and how concealment mechanics affect traces. My position: holding out Heat: Completely cold; participating neutrally with no suspicion directed at me. Target landscape: An accused player said to have visited a dead player whose role was concealed, versus the claimed trailseer making the accusation; evidence is a single uncorroborated claim.
lessons.action: When a high-stakes accusation rests on an unverifiable visit report and you have no heat, urge caution and ask what corroborating evidence exists. Point out how the stated rules (for example, an illusionist's concealment hiding the attacking trace) limit what such a report can prove. This makes you look measured and analytical and keeps you from being drawn into a rushed elimination.

lessons.situation: Late-game day discussion after the wolves are revealed dead; a player's claimed night result is being explained away and the Fortune Teller is asked directly whether a self-bet caused it. Information landscape: Fairly rich: public wolf reveals, a healer save and a sigil death are announced, while the claimed immunity result is still a private claim that my answer can corroborate. Stakes: Few players remain, so one correct vote on the lone killer decides the game; clearing the self-bet explanation lets the town converge on the right target. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on weighing the claimed immunity result; wolves are already confirmed dead, so the debate is about the remaining killer and the unverified claim. My position: With the majority, answering a direct question and removing the main objection. Heat: Moderate and specific: a player floated that I might have bet on myself, making me a possible alternative explanation for the result. Target landscape: A player accused via a claimed night result (e.g. a serial killer said to be immune) versus the credibility of the claimant; the only alternative explanation is the Fortune Teller's own self-bet. Evidence is a private claim plus public deaths and reveals.
lessons.action: When a player directly asks whether your self-bet explains an odd night result (e.g. a claimed immunity), answer plainly and truthfully on whether you self-bet that night; if you didn't, say so and name whom you bet on. This removes the competing explanation, makes the other player's claim the best available evidence, and costs little because a Fortune Teller cannot be blocked and reads Not suspicious.

lessons.situation: Late game with three players left: you and a copycat both claim Fortune Teller, and a single third player's vote decides which of you is eliminated. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified results, only claims, but a detailed bet history against a thin copy creates an asymmetry the voter can check against the public record. Stakes: With three alive, one vote decides the game: eliminating the false claimant can end it in your favor, while losing the vote likely means your death and a loss. Consensus: Split and starved of hard evidence; the outcome depends on one remaining voter judging whose account is more detailed and consistent. My position: Driving the case against the counterclaimant while holding out against their accusation. Heat: High: under a counterclaim, tied in votes, and your claim cannot be independently verified. Target landscape: Two Fortune Teller claimants (you and a false claimant, likely the necromancer) plus one unconfirmed swing voter whose own claim cannot be verified; the false claimant's bets match only public deaths, while your history has specifics that fit the record.
lessons.action: When a rival claims Fortune Teller (or your claim is otherwise disputed) in a late-game room with few players left, state your claim plainly and give your full bet history: which nights, whom you bet on, the role named, which bets scored, and the self-bets. Point out that a copycat's bets match only publicly known deaths while yours include specifics (wrong early bets, self-bets, role names) that fit the public record, and name the copycat as your top suspect so the swing voter has a concrete reason to side with you.

lessons.situation: Day 4, shortly after a wolf flip and a concealed-role kill. One player voted against the consensus on the previous day, and you can ask them to justify it. Information landscape: A confirmed wolf flip, a concealed-role kill, and a public vote record. Few other facts are verified, so most reads rest on behavior. Stakes: The village is mid-game with evil still alive. A cheap question can surface a claim and a counterclaim fight without committing you to an elimination, and it keeps you alive for the later days. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned after a confirmed flip and a recorded vote pattern, and it is receptive to follow-up questions about odd votes. My position: With the majority, steering the question toward the dissenter without leading an accusation. Heat: Low. You have said little publicly and earlier mild skepticism has not been held against you. Target landscape: Survivors with no confirmed roles except what flips have shown. One player was the lone dissenter in the last vote, and all other reads are behavioral.
lessons.action: When a confirmed flip or kill pattern leaves one player as the lone dissenter in the earlier vote, ask them to explain the deviation instead of accusing them. Their answer, whether a claim, a trace, or a dodge, gives the room something to test and moves attention off you. If they give a claim or trace, hold your read until the room has cross-checked it against other claims.

lessons.situation: Day 2 after a night-1 death.
