Conflicting or unverifiable role claims (Investigator, Healer, Trailseer, Sentinel) dominate the discussion, and you are an uncommitted neutral with both self-bets unused. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims, one or two unconfirmed night reports, and a night-1 body, with no caught lies, no votes, and no confirmed wolf identities. Stakes: Early game with many players alive. No single vote or kill decides the game, so staying alive and unexposed to keep betting each night matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: Split or drifting: the room argues over rival claims or abstains, with no hard evidence behind any side. My position: Holding out in the middle or going with the majority, contributing a clarification without driving the vote. Heat: Very low: you have not been named, addressed, or accused, and you have not revealed your role. Target landscape: Two or more rival role claimants (e.g. two Investigators, or two Healers) or one scrutinized claimant, resting on unverified reports and timing. No confirmed wolves, and the night-1 victim's role is either announced or hidden.
lessons.action: When you are an unclaimed, low-heat Fortune Teller on day 2 in an info-starved room of conflicting claims, keep your role hidden and make one short, sincere contribution that shapes the discussion without accusing anyone. Good examples are a procedural point about visit direction, or a note that a hidden-role or dead role means a claim may not be genuine, or a direct question to a player a report ties to a contradiction. This keeps you out of the crossfire while still adding value, since your win depends on night bets rather than on how the vote goes.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so the game can end within one more elimination (the swing flag is set). A wrong lynch or an unprotected kill now would be costly, because the village has very few votes left to correct a mistake.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no living wolf remains to read, and the Necromancer is unrevealed. The only concrete evidence is the Sentinel's two-night watch history and my own private protection and roleblock records; the rest is discussion and voting pattern.
query_dims.situation: The village has just lynched a revealed chanteuse after a dispute over a watch that showed only one visitor, and I, as healer, was roleblocked that same night. The Sentinel's claim and my block report are consistent, so I must decide which living player to protect next night, knowing that a protected player who is attacked survives and that the Necromancer may still be among the living.
query_dims.target_landscape: Four living candidates: a self-declared Sentinel whose claim is unverified but consistent with my own night record, plus three players with no claim (one quieter, two who voted with the majority to lynch the chanteuse). Public role status: the chanteuse was lynched on day 4 and revealed; the vigilante, investigator, sigilist and illusionist are already dead. Evidence is mostly behavioral and vote-based; the only hard datum is the Sentinel's watch, which only I can cross-check against my roleblock.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after a save-confirmed attack on a claimed Trailseer. Wolves and the serial killer are both active, and the village is openly discussing whom attackers might pivot to. The healer must choose between repeating the protection or rotating to another power role or unknown. Information landscape: Information-thin about the next target: a prior save is known and an information-role claim is corroborated by one other claimed power role. No investigation results point to the next night's victim. Stakes: Two killer factions are still alive, so each night can cost a power role. Keeping the Trailseer alive preserves the tracker whose follow of the killer can drive a daytime vote. The cost of repeating is that a pivot to another power role goes unprotected. Target landscape: A claimed, partly corroborated information role (Trailseer) that already survived a double attack thanks to your save, versus another claimed power role (Sigilist) and unclaimed quiet slots with no evidence of who gets hit next. The basis is a public claim plus a prior save pattern, not hard proof of the next target.
lessons.action: When a claimed information role (e.g. Trailseer) has been attacked and saved, or has a corroborated claim, keep protecting it on the following nights while no stronger lead points elsewhere. Killers who targeted it once tend to return or are deterred, and a heal that cancels an attack keeps the town's tracker alive to expose the killer. Accept that a night with no announced attack on your protectee is an idle heal, which is the cost of this policy.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an abstained or low-information day vote and a night-1 death. The healer must choose a protection target with no hard evidence on who the killers will attack. Wolves and a lone killer may both want the same visible information role. Information landscape: Info-starved: one revealed or concealed night-1 death, an abstain vote, at most one unverified claim. Everything else is behavioral. Stakes: Early game with several evil attackers alive. One saved information role can produce the next check or trail result and decide whether town finds the first wolf or killer, but a wrong guess costs only a night of protection. Target landscape: Eight to nine living candidates besides the healer: one or two publicly active information sources (a claimed Investigator with a not-suspicious result, or an open player pushing for information), and the rest silent or unclaimed. Roles are unconfirmed apart from dead-player reveals, so the choice rests on behavior and on who is most useful to town.
lessons.action: On night 2 with no confirmed leads, protect the visible information-providing player the wolves or killer would most want gone: a claimed Investigator with a result, or an active player asking for information. Prefer that over repeating an arbitrary night-1 pick or a silent unclaimed player. A save on such a player preserves the town's information flow.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or confusing day 2 in which several town information roles (investigator, trailseer, sentinel) claimed publicly; wolves and possibly a lone killer have several visible high-value targets, and you must pick one protectee. Information landscape: Moderately informed: unverified role claims and a day-2 vote record, no confirmed wolf, and the killers' targets unknown. Mostly claim-based reads. Stakes: Mid-game with wolves and a killer still active; losing the investigator costs the town its remaining check, while a save wastes the wolves' kill, so the pick matters but a single miss does not decide the game. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (publicly reported a Not suspicious check, one check left), claimed trailseer, claimed sentinel, and unclaimed sigilist, vigilante and speculator; the choice rests on claimed information value and exposure, not verified evidence.
lessons.action: On night 2 and later, once the day has produced several unverified information-role claims and the town abstained or gave no clear wolf, protect the claimed investigator (the information holder with checks left) rather than a lower-value claimed role. If you were publicly tied to that same protectee, keep protecting them anyway when their check output is still valuable, because the wolves' kill on them is the likeliest high-value attack.

lessons.situation: Late game, after the Chanteuse was voted out. Only one wolf (Illusionist) and possibly a lone killer remain, and the Healer must pick one protectee among a few town players, including a proven information role that the killers have already hit. Information landscape: Moderately to highly informative: dead wolves are confirmed, roles were revealed on death, and one or two information roles have verified track records. There are no leads on the last wolf or the lone killer. Stakes: Few players remain, so one successful kill moves the board toward parity. A save on the most valuable information role denies the killers a kill and preserves the tool that can catch the last killers, but only one player can be covered each night. Target landscape: A small set of living players: a Trailseer or Sentinel with a verified track record (survived attacks, cross-checked by the healer's own visits), a publicly claimed Investigator with spent checks, and quiet unclaimed players such as the Vigilante and Sigilist. Verified information roles outrank quiet slots; the quiet slots offer no evidence to rank them by.
lessons.action: After a wolf is eliminated and the remaining killers are down to one wolf plus the serial killer or a lone wolf, protect the verified information role (e.g. the Trailseer or Sentinel) the killers have already targeted or that the room trusts most. If that role has already been attacked and saved, keep protecting it, because the killers keep returning to it and a save cancels the attack while keeping their intel alive.

lessons.situation: After a daytime elimination confirmed a claimed Sentinel or Investigator's result, the surviving wolves and any lone killer are expected to attack that credible information source on the coming night. The healer must choose whom to shield. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced elimination role verified the claimant's result, so their credibility is public and known, and their continued survival is valuable. Stakes: Town leads on numbers, but losing the verified info role would cost the strongest lead-generating source. A save here preserves that edge and denies the evil side a kill, with a strong chance the attack lands on this target. Target landscape: A publicly claimed information role whose result was just confirmed by an announced elimination (caught Serial Killer or wolf), versus other claimed info roles and quiet unrevealed players with no evidence behind them. The choice rests on verified evidence, not on behavior.
lessons.action: When a claimed information role (Sentinel, Investigator, Trailseer) has just produced a result that got a player eliminated, protect that claimant tonight, since the surviving evil factions have the strongest motive to silence them. If two such claimants are both exposed, favor the one whose result was confirmed by an announced elimination role and who still has uses left.

lessons.situation: After a day of public information-role claims that ended in an abstain or no-elimination vote, several high-value town claimants are exposed to attack from both the wolves and a lone killer. The healer must choose which one to shield for the night. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple public claims with interlocking visit accounts, prior save announcements and vote records, but none of the alignments are verified. Stakes: With several town roles exposed and two killers active, one unprotected loss of the lead investigator removes the main source of checks. A correct guard keeps town numbers and can expose evil through the public save announcement. Target landscape: Three or two publicly claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) with interlocking but unverified visit accounts; the claimed investigator shares check results and is the main lead, while the others report watches or follows. The healer picks among these on the basis of claim content and threat to evil, not verified roles.
lessons.action: When several public information-role claims are on the board, protect the claimed investigator, the one whose check results most plausibly point at wolves, and keep protecting them on consecutive nights while they stay the likeliest kill target. Do not shift to the claimed sentinel or trailseer just because they are also exposed. Wolves and a lone killer both want the lead investigative claimant, so a repeat guard has the best chance of producing a save.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after a day elimination or tied vote. The healer must choose which of several claimed town power roles to shield from the remaining killers, who can strike with concealment or through reanimated bodies. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed investigative and tracking results, public morning reports, confirmed eliminations and prior save records, and a known killer attack pattern. Stakes: With few players left and a killer still active, each night kill moves town close to losing its majority, so losing the one remaining active information role can decide the endgame. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed town power roles: a trailseer with active tracking results naming a living suspect, a sentinel whose watches are spent or who was already saved, and a sigilist with a reactive ability; claims are unverified but backed by morning-report facts and are the main evidence.
lessons.action: When several town power-role claimants are alive and an enemy killer is still active, protect the claimant whose live, ongoing output is driving the case (e.g. a trailseer who just tied a living suspect to a victim) in preference to a claimant whose uses are spent or who already got a save. Reason: a night kill on the active information source costs town the most, and two of three observations show the unprotected trailseer being killed with its role concealed. If no claimant has live output, protecting the publicly confirmed sentinel is a sound default.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and the serial killer remains among about five players. The healer is the village's only night buffer against parity, and the serial killer may skip the obvious protected target and kill someone else. Information landscape: Information-rich on past events (both wolves confirmed, an Investigator claim is a public reference), but the serial killer's next target is not predictable from evidence. Stakes: With five alive, each unprevented kill brings the serial killer's win condition (at most one other player alive) closer, and the healer is a likely target once the board narrows. A wasted protection on an unattacked player gives the serial killer a free kill. Target landscape: The claimed Investigator, whose check matched a dead wolf and who was protected the previous night, against quieter town members such as the Sigilist and unconfirmed accusers. The serial killer's choice is unreadable because nothing public shows its preference, so any pick is a guess among several candidates.
lessons.action: When the serial killer is the only killer left, or the board is down to four or five players, avoid repeating the same protectee out of habit once the protectee is no longer the obvious target. Weigh which player the serial killer would most want dead, including a quiet role like the Sigilist or Vigilante, and vary protection among those candidates, since a kill that goes through can narrow the board toward the serial killer's win and expose the healer next.

lessons.situation: Midgame, after the lone killer (necromancer) was voted out and one or two wolves remain. The healer must choose a protection target. The wolves' pack kills have been landing on other players, and the previous save was either untested or just used. Information landscape: Moderate. One elimination validated an information role's read, but the wolves' kill targets stay hidden, some bodies had concealed roles, and the remaining wolves are unconfirmed. Little evidence says who the wolves will hit next. Stakes: With about six players alive and the wolves as the only night killers, each night's kill moves the board toward wolf parity. A correct save cancels the pack's kill for that night. A wasted save costs one of the few nights the town can use to stay ahead. Target landscape: Living candidates are the town info roles (an investigator whose read was validated by an elimination, a trailseer or sentinel with identity information) plus the sigilist and neutrals. None of the wolves is confirmed. The previous night's saved player is the obvious repeat pick, but the wolves rarely re-hit a target once it has been saved. The choice rests on role value and elimination-validated reads, not on behavior.
lessons.action: After the lone killer is voted out and only the wolves remain as night killers, pick your protection target by who the wolves most need dead, such as the confirmed information holder or the player the pack has been unable to read. Do not simply repeat last night's save. A protected player who was not attacked leaves no trace, so a repeat only pays off if the wolves return to that same target.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, a wolf has been voted out or is revealed, but a lone killer such as the Necromancer is still hidden and could attack anyone. The healer must choose whom to cover among several Town power-role claimants. Information landscape: Partly informative: some roles are confirmed by announced deaths or by confirmed checks and watches. The identity of the hidden killer is unknown and only its attack kind is visible, so the next target is speculative. Stakes: Few players remain, so losing a key Town role or the healer sharply cuts the Town's ability to remove the last killer. Each save matters, but the next target cannot be known. Target landscape: Living claimants: Investigator with confirmed checks, Vigilante holding the last bullet, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist. Their value is ranked by verified results, past attacks on them, and ability left, not by how they talk.
lessons.action: Each night, protect the confirmed-Town player whose ability is the Town's best remaining way to remove the hidden killer, such as the Vigilante with a bullet left or an Investigator with checks left. If one of them was attacked earlier and saved, keep covering them unless a newer attack pattern points elsewhere. Don't spread protection across low-value or unverified claimants just to rotate.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an early power-role death (sentinel, trailseer, investigator, or fortune teller) and a no-elimination day. Nobody has claimed, and the healer must choose a protectee from behavior alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: one or two revealed night-1 deaths, a unanimous abstain vote, no claims, and no private leads. Reads are purely behavioral. Stakes: Early game with several town power roles still alive. Losing another power role, such as the vigilante or sentinel, to an unprotected kill hurts, but one bad guess does not decide the game. Protection is never used up, so a guess made on a consistent rule costs little each night. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players besides the healer, none with a public role claim. The candidates are a vocal player driving discussion or demanding claims, and several quiet or generic players. The basis is behavior and table presence only, with no checks, results, or hard leads.
lessons.action: On night 2 of an info-starved board with no claims and an all-abstain vote, protect the visible organizer or most active questioner, since the wolves tend to kill players who drive town reasoning. If a quiet player has not drawn attention, do not pick them on a hunch, because the protection was never tested in the observation that did.

lessons.situation: Early in the game, after a night death and a day without eliminations, the only public information source is a single claimed role, such as a Trailseer. That claimant faces threats from both the wolves and any lone killer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wolves have been caught, no voting records show alignments, and only one unverified claim exists. Stakes: No single kill decides the game yet, but losing the only information source would leave Town blind. The protection may go untriggered, which costs nothing since the healer's protection is never used up. Target landscape: The only publicly declared information-role claimant versus silent, unrevealed players with no distinguishing evidence. The basis is public role status and the claimant's visibility, not behavior or verified evidence.
lessons.action: When no result has been confirmed and the room is quiet, protect the sole publicly declared information-role claimant, as the most likely kill target. Expect that the attack may land elsewhere, and keep the pick tied to who is most visibly valuable rather than switching to guesses about unrevealed players.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after day-vote or sigil results removed a wolf or the serial killer. The remaining killers (a wolf and/or the serial killer or necromancer) are likely to attack the town's most dangerous information source. The healer must pick one other player to cover. Information landscape: Information-rich: eliminated roles are revealed, some claims have been cross-checked by outcomes or by announcements, and one claimant's testimony visibly shifted the vote. The target is still chosen by inference about the killers' motives. Stakes: Few players remain, so each night kill is a large share of town's strength. Losing the main info holder could let the remaining killers reach parity, while a correct save can absorb even a double attack and leave no deaths. Target landscape: Several living claimed or inferred power roles (sentinel, sigilist, investigator, trailseer, vigilante). One of them just publicly drove an elimination or a confirmed strike. Choice rests on that visible impact and on behavior, not on hard verification. The healer cannot cover itself.
lessons.action: On a mid-game night (around night 3) after a wolf or killer has just been exposed, protect the living info role whose testimony or recent action drove that removal (sentinel, trailseer, or confirmed sigilist) rather than a lower-impact claimant. If two info roles are both in play, favor the one most visibly credited with the exposure, since the surviving killers have the most reason to silence them.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game night after a day in which an information role publicly reported a result or helped drive a wolf elimination. The wolves are active (a chanteuse is blocking, and a wolf kill pattern is aimed at information roles). The healer must choose the one other player to protect. Information landscape: Moderate to rich: public claims from the investigator, sentinel and trailseer, at least one confirmed wolf role from a vote, and roleblock evidence of an active chanteuse. Most role claims are unverified, but some are corroborated by eliminations or matching visits. Stakes: Mid-game with several wolves or killers still alive, so one lost information role noticeably slows the town but does not immediately decide the game. Keeping the verified information source alive preserves remaining checks, and an announced save also confirms the wolves' targeting. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) plus unclaimed players. The investigator with a corroborated check record or a wolf exposure is the top-value target. A sentinel who is repeatedly roleblocked, or any claimant the wolves are already blocking, is a less likely kill target. Unclaimed players are lower threat. The basis is public claims, corroboration and the wolves' visible pattern of attacking information roles.
lessons.action: Protect the publicly claimed, corroborated information role (investigator first, otherwise the sentinel or trailseer) that the town is relying on and that just publicly drove a result or an elimination. The wolves have the clearest reason to remove that player, so a protect there is likely to save them or at least keep the wolves from a free kill. If two such roles are claimed, pick the one whose claim has independent corroboration, such as a confirmed wolf death or a matching visit, over one that is merely loud.

lessons.situation: Late-mid game after the wolf team has been mostly or fully eliminated via the investigator's checks. The surviving wolf and/or the serial killer remain and need to remove town's key coordinator to survive. The healer has to pick whom to protect that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf flips corroborate the investigator, role reveals clarify claims, and voting records are public, so the town's most valuable player is clear to both town and evil. Stakes: Few players remain, so each night kill moves the board toward parity or the serial killer's win condition. Losing the investigator would remove town's verified information source, while a save denies evil a kill and may cancel multiple simultaneous attacks. Target landscape: The confirmed investigator (role validated by a flipped wolf) is the focal kill target; alternatives are a claimed sentinel/trailseer and several unconfirmed players with no verified roles. The choice rests on verified evidence of who evil most wants dead, not on behavior reads.
lessons.action: When the investigator's findings have been confirmed by a role flip and the evil sides are down to one or two attackers, protect the investigator again, even on consecutive nights. Evil factions (surviving wolf, serial killer) target the town's confirmed information engine, so one protection can absorb several attackers at once. If the investigator is dead or blocked from relevance, shift the protection to the next most publicly validated town leader.

lessons.situation: Healer has just revealed the role publicly on day 2 and was vouched for by the player saved, with a lone vote cast against it. Night 2 arrives with the healer now an exposed, claimed role who cannot self-protect, while the serial killer and wolves choose targets. Information landscape: Moderately informed: one self-verified save, a tracker claim consistent with it, and a sentinel watch claim with no visitor. The killers' identities and next targets remain unknown. Stakes: The healer is the town's only protector and cannot be guarded, so its death removes all night protection while both the serial killer and wolves live. Spending the guard on a target nobody attacks wastes the night. Target landscape: Eight other living players: a corroborated Trailseer, a Vigilante vouched for by an earlier save, and unclaimed or quiet slots. There is no evidence of who the killers will pick. Your own public healer claim is the main new fact, and it makes you a visible role who cannot be guarded.
lessons.action: If you have publicly claimed healer or your protection record has been read out or vouched, treat yourself as the likely kill target and pick a guard target whose protection is worth the most if you survive. Since you cannot protect yourself, do not assume your protectee is the one under attack. Weigh the Town asset's actual risk against the chance that the serial killer or wolves go for you, and favor a player the killers have already shown interest in over one with no attack history.

lessons.situation: Late game: the lone killer and at least one wolf are dead, one wolf remains, and the Healer is cleared or safe. The remaining wolf must kill to reach parity, so its night target is the most threatening Town player. One wrong protection could cost the game. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced deaths and roles confirm which evil roles are gone, wills or announcements corroborate claims, and a claimed role has said its ability is exhausted. Stakes: With four alive and one wolf left, one unprotected Town death brings the wolves to parity and ends the game. A correct save keeps Town's numbers intact and lets surviving Town power roles finish the wolf the same night or the next day. Target landscape: Three or four living candidates: a publicly claimed power role whose claim was corroborated by announcements, a vocal town leader who drove earlier evil eliminations, and quiet or abstaining players with no verifiable claims. Choice rests on confirmed evidence and on who is still dangerous to the wolf, not on behavior alone.
lessons.action: In the endgame (about four alive) with one wolf left and the lone killer gone, protect the player the wolf most needs to remove: the confirmed, still-active Town power role, or the loudest town leader who drove the earlier evil eliminations. If the leading candidate has publicly said their ability is spent, move the protection to the next-most-threatening active Town voice.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after you publicly claimed Healer and helped push an elimination, either a counterclaiming wolf or a necromancer-led vote. The wolves now have a reason to pick you, and you must still choose someone else to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims and role reveals: an investigator check was validated by an elimination, and a trailseer was partly confirmed. No wolf is fully identified, and a necromancer or reanimated attacker may still be unproven. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. Losing the healer ends all protection, while the wolves and a lone killer can still reach parity. Your own death is probably unavoidable, so your last protection should secure the most useful remaining Town role. Target landscape: Other living players who are not you: a claimed investigator whose read was validated, a claimed trailseer, vigilante and sigilist. Their claims are only partly corroborated and no wolf is confirmed. You are the likely wolf target and cannot be protected by your own action.
lessons.action: When your Healer role is publicly known and you are the likely wolf target, you cannot cover yourself, so protect the most valuable surviving Town player instead. That is usually the investigator or another role whose information is confirmed or corroborated. If your protection pattern is public, switch to the next-most-valuable player, because the protection still stops any other attacker (a necromancer's body, a serial killer) from landing on that player.

lessons.situation: The healer revealed itself after a confirmed save and now faces a likely night kill from the pack or a Necromancer working through a body. The healer must decide whom to protect knowing it cannot cover itself. Information landscape: The healer's claim and the save are on the record. A reanimated-body attack would show a Necromancer is active without naming it. Roles of the remaining players are only partly confirmed. Stakes: The healer is itself a probable victim and nothing it does can prevent that. Its last protections decide whether the remaining Town power roles survive, and one more loss could leave the Town unable to catch up. Target landscape: Candidates are other living Town players, since the healer cannot protect itself. The Investigator, Vigilante and Sentinel are verified or semi-verified, and the other claimants are lower in value and less verified. The healer is the exposed one.
lessons.action: If your Healer role is publicly known and the town just removed a wolf while a killer is still active, assume you are a likely kill target. You cannot protect yourself, so use the night to cover the single most valuable confirmed-Town ally whose death would end the Town's best path to winning. Do not waste the pick on a low-value or unattacked claimant.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game with no day-1 vote. The healer must protect one other player blind while the wolf pack and possibly a lone killer may attack. The healer itself is sometimes the opening target, so the night-1 pick may be the only protection Town gets. Information landscape: Information-starved: only one day of undirected discussion, with no claims, accusations, deaths or private results to rank targets by. Stakes: Early game with a full table: no single night-1 outcome decides the game. A lucky save gains a body and credibility, while a miss costs nothing. Since information is zero, a cheap blind protection is the right policy. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no claims, no behavior, no votes and no revealed roles. The pick is a blind guess, and wolves, the serial killer and the neutral are all equally possible. The healer cannot protect itself.
lessons.action: On night 1 with no claims, deaths or reads, protect one other player rather than skipping, and choose any quiet, unclaimed player without agonizing over it. Protection is never used up, and a save is announced if the pick is attacked. The visit also leaves a trace a Sentinel or Trailseer may later cross-check.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room has no clear consensus on whom to eliminate. Several players are scrutinizing one reported visitor, while others point out that the same vote and claimed visit implicate the second visitor too.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive and it is three eliminations until the leading remaining evil faction can win. The game cannot end within one more elimination, and this decision is not a single-vote-or-kill swing; a wrong elimination is consequential but does not immediately decide the game.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: no one has publicly accused or singled out you, and your Fortune Teller role and missed bets are private.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved about the visitors’ actions: the Sentinel report is an unverified claim, and the public vote record is factual but ambiguous. The dead Investigator, Trailseer, and Sigilist were role-revealed; no public evidence identifies either surviving visitor as an attacker.
query_dims.my_position: Not driving the discussion and not publicly aligned with a clear majority; you have expressed no position.
query_dims.situation: On day 3, a claimed Sentinel reports that two players visited the player killed by the Serial Killer, and both had also voted to eliminate that player. Discussion has focused on whether those shared facts justify scrutiny, but they do not distinguish one visitor from the other or prove either attacked.
query_dims.target_landscape: The main candidates under scrutiny are two players with no public role claims. Both voted to eliminate the player later revealed as the Sigilist, and an unverified Sentinel claim places both at that player’s location the night they died to the Serial Killer; neither fact establishes who attacked.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a hidden lone killer (Necromancer) alive and a claimant whose night report conflicts with the rules; the village must choose between that inconsistency and other unconfirmed players, and I (fortune teller) am among the targets. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: rules-contradicting claims, partial visit confirmations, and a few confirmed deaths; no hard role confirmations on the living candidates. Stakes: Few players remain and a lone killer is still hidden, so each wrong vote can cost Town an information role and bring the killers closer to winning; a correct vote can end the lone killer faction. Consensus: Village is leaning toward one target on the basis of behavior and a rules inconsistency; no confirmed roles among survivors and a lone killer still hidden. My position: With the majority, sometimes driving the argument. Heat: Moderate: one or more votes or a counter-accusation landed on me, but the room did not back it strongly. Target landscape: Claimed info roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) with no confirmed roles; one has a report contradicting the rules, another is a suspect steering suspicion onto unconfirmed players; I am among the scattered vote targets.
lessons.action: When the lone killer is still hidden and a claimant's report contradicts the stated rules (e.g. an omitted own visit, or a 'no visits' result on a night a body was hidden), vote with the accusers on that contradiction rather than drifting onto a lone-vote side. If a vote has already picked up a player who attacked the unconfirmed players or a verified-night-evidence suspect, prefer that suspect over a pure rules-slip claimant, since a slip may be a genuine townie's misreport.

lessons.situation: A necromancer-revealing night (reanimated vigilante shot, sigil strike) is confirmed; the suspect deflects suspicion toward unconfirmed players, and the village is consolidating its vote against the suspect. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed role deaths, announced reanimated attacks, a verified sigil strike, and an investigator's will clearing one living player. Stakes: Removing the lone killer here ends that faction, so one vote shifts which side is winning; joining the majority also takes me out of the line of fire. Consensus: The majority, including cleared town players, is converging on the suspect on the basis of verified night events (reanimated kill, sigil strike) and the suspect's own steering. My position: With the majority. Heat: Moderate: the suspect explicitly called for testing unconfirmed players, which puts scrutiny on me. Target landscape: The suspect steering votes onto unconfirmed players versus the remaining unconfirmed player and a claimed sigilist whose action was verified by the morning report; an investigator's will cleared one living player.
lessons.action: When a suspected killer is publicly pointing scrutiny at the unconfirmed players (including you), cast your vote with the cleared or town-aligned majority on that suspect, so your vote sits on the consensus side and not among the minority votes that land on you. This keeps your standing safe at no cost, since a fortune teller's win depends only on banked bet points and the vote does not score.

lessons.situation: Day vote after a double attack on a Town role that the healer stopped. The village is deciding who is operating a dead role's body, and the Fortune Teller sits low-heat outside the discussion. Information landscape: Moderate: the public double-attack report, some revealed roles and behavioral reads, but nothing directly tying the target to the lone killer. Stakes: The majority can remove the target without your vote. Joining it adds little numerically but keeps you aligned and visible as a participant. Consensus: Four or more players are converging on one suspect from vote history and deflection, with no hard role evidence. My position: Holding out by abstaining while the majority forms without me. Free to join it instead. Heat: Low: quiet, not named, no confirmed alignment but not under direct accusation. Target landscape: A player who voted against the room the day before and pushed deflection, and a player the healer protected. The evidence is behavioral plus the previous night's attack on a Town role.
lessons.action: When your heat is low and a majority is converging on a suspect backed by vote history or the previous night's attack pattern, cast your own vote with it instead of abstaining. A lone killer removed by a visible majority helps Town win, which is the side you share a win with, and your vote on the record keeps you aligned with the room. If the room is split and no case is evidence-backed, vote for the best-supported behavioral candidate.

lessons.situation: Late game (day 5 or 6): a rival claims my same neutral role and we accuse each other. The vote is a close split, and an elimination of me would end my path to scoring points. Information landscape: Starved: incompatible role claims, unverifiable claims from others, and only a single confirmed result; the rest is behavioral reads. Stakes: With about four alive, one vote can eliminate me or a key player; a tie preserves my remaining bets and a wrong elimination could hand the killer or wolves the win. Consensus: The room is split into two camps with no majority; votes tie and no single player is clearly favored. My position: Holding out against one side, aligned with one other player, and helping keep the vote deadlocked. Heat: High: the Investigator and the counterclaimant are voting for me, and my claim and my self-exclusion from the suspect pool were challenged as unsupported. Target landscape: Three or four survivors, none with a verified role: a counterclaimant to my Fortune Teller role, a Sigilist whose claim is unverifiable, and an Investigator whose results are confirmed. One of them is the remaining killer, and the reads rest on claim conflict and voting alignment rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When you are the main target of a late-game day vote with few players alive, vote sincerely for the player whose evidence or claims you find least credible, ideally one who counterclaimed your role or is pushing your elimination. If a deadlock or tie results, that keeps you alive for further bets, so hold your vote steady unless a clearly better read emerges.

lessons.situation: Four players left with a wolf and possibly a lone killer alive; the vote kills the likely last wolf but could leave an armed lone killer behind or end the game before the Fortune Teller scores a second point. Information landscape: Moderately rich: revealed roles, morning reports naming attack types, and earlier votes, but who is the lone killer versus the last wolf remains inferred. Stakes: One elimination could hand Town the game or leave a lone killer free to shoot with no wolf to take the night attack, so the vote changes who wins and whether the Fortune Teller scores. Consensus: Village is converging, often near unanimously, on one target based on claims and morning reports, while a quieter suspect is ignored. My position: With the majority, voting for the consensus target. Heat: Low: not under accusation and had stayed quiet; at most receiving a stray defensive vote from a doomed player. Target landscape: Two or three living candidates; at least one probable last wolf, plus a possible lone killer. Roles are unconfirmed and read from claims, the morning kill reports, and revealed dead roles.
lessons.action: Before voting in a late-game day, count your banked points and which killers remain. If one more point would win it for you and the vote would end the game, or a surviving killer would otherwise have free night kills, weigh whether ending the game now is worth more than staying alive for a night bet. If you are under 2 points and the vote would end the game anyway, a Town win does not give you a win, so favor the vote only if you are sure of the target.

lessons.situation: With one wolf confirmed dead the previous day, the sigilist accuses the player who resisted the tracking claims. You back the accusation and vote, and the target defends himself using that same earlier wolf vote. Information landscape: Moderately informed: one confirmed wolf death and a vote record, but the target's guilt rests on timing and behavior, and other night killers remain unknown. Stakes: Several killers are still alive, so any wrong vote costs town. Your own survival is still at risk at night and you have no points yet. Consensus: The village backs the sigilist's accusation, one wolf is already confirmed dead, and the vote record gives behavioral grounds. My position: Driving alongside the accuser, then with the majority. Heat: Low to moderate: you made an argument against the target, but nobody is accusing you. Target landscape: A suspect who resisted the tracking claims and joined the previous wagon late, versus quiet players the suspect tried to redirect suspicion toward. The basis is behavioral (skepticism, vote timing), with no hard evidence.
lessons.action: When you have no points yet and your heat is low, vote for the behaviorally most suspicious player alongside a credible accuser, and explain your reasoning aloud (for example, that a wolf can bus onto a doomed partner's wagon). A day vote never scores for you, so use it to push town toward removing evil, but do not count on it to advance your own two-point goal.

lessons.situation: Day 5 with four alive after a key town death: each survivor votes against a different player, and I am accused by an ally while a wolf pushes suspicion toward me. Information landscape: Rich: a confirmed sigil strike verified one player as town, two wolf-side deaths are revealed, and the wolf's steering toward me is on record. Stakes: With four alive, removing a wolf shrinks the killer count, but the remaining lone killer may then target me; the vote decides who is left against me. Consensus: Votes are split one-against-one among all four survivors, with no majority forming. My position: Holding out in a split vote, choosing my own target instead of following any bloc. Heat: High: a confirmed-town player suspects me and credits me with starting a wagon, and a wolf is leaning on me. Target landscape: Two or three suspects left: a wolf who has been steering suspicion toward me and another town role, and a lone killer who deflected my name; one confirmed-town ally whose role was shown by a sigil strike. The choice rests on revealed wolf-side deaths and observed accusation patterns.
lessons.action: When a confirmed-town player (such as a sigil-verified Sigilist) exists and the wolves are still being whittled down, vote for the suspect who has been steering suspicion toward you or other town players. Prefer eliminating a wolf-side player that was pushing your name, since that removes a vote against you and reduces the killers' numbers.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day vote with several unconfirmed players left. A wagon is forming on a Town-looking player through argument or suspicion of silence. The fortune teller has no investigative information of its own. Information landscape: Mixed, leaning behavioral. A night death has been confirmed, but the accusations in the vote are only claims and reads. Stakes: Seven players are alive with wolves and a lone killer still in play. A wrong Town lynch costs Town a voice and brings it closer to evil parity. The fortune teller must also survive long enough to score two points. Consensus: The table is split between two candidates and is converging on one by momentum and argument, not on evidence. Confirmed facts exist only about earlier deaths. My position: Not yet committed. You could drive the wagon with an early vote, or follow once the majority is clear. Heat: Low to moderate. You have not been accused, but an early vote would tie your name to the wagon. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed candidates. One is a vocal accuser or critic of a player who looks reliable. Another is a quiet player. The case against each is an argument or inactivity, with no hard role evidence.
lessons.action: When the day's case rests only on arguments or behavior and you have no confirmed lead, wait until other players have voted and the wagon is visible before you cast your vote. Do not be the first vote on an argument-only target, because the first voter gets blamed for the wagon if the target turns out to be Town. Your night bets are what score, and a day vote never does, so keep your heat low.

lessons.situation: A day vote where the village converges on a main suspect while the Fortune Teller, a neutral with no side to defend, is unaligned. Splitting from the room costs safety and gains nothing: the wolves or other killers note any vote against their partner and use it to pick you at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed role results, a visit report at a victim's door and public voting records are all available. None of it is confirmed beyond what the Game Master announced. Stakes: Mid-game board where a single wasted or rogue vote does little to the count, but drawing a night kill before scoring two points ends your win condition. Staying unnoticed matters more than being first to guess right. Consensus: Strong, near-unanimous agreement on one suspect, built on a claimed Sentinel's visit report and the previous day's voting record. My position: Tempted to hold out with an isolated vote or abstain, against the majority. Heat: Little or none: you have spoken minimally and are not on anyone's suspect list. Target landscape: Two or more players named by a claimed Sentinel or by public vote records; one is the clear main suspect of the room. The evidence is public but unverified claims and voting behavior, and you hold no private proof of your own.
lessons.action: When the room has formed an overwhelming consensus on a main suspect backed by public evidence such as a claimed watch or voting records, and you are not under suspicion, vote with the majority on that suspect. An isolated dissenting vote or a pointless abstain marks you as a rogue voter and can make you a night-kill target. You need to stay alive to score your two points.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and a vigilante claims a target was immune to a night attack. Someone asks you whether you self-bet, since a self-bet is the only other source of immunity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed wolf deaths, a public sigil death confirming the sigilist, an immunity claim, and your own denial removing the alternative explanation. Stakes: With the wolves gone, only the lone killer stands between town and a win. A correct vote here can end the game, and a misvote lets the killer keep killing. Consensus: The village is largely aligned (about five of six votes) on one suspect, on the basis of confirmed wolf deaths, a sigil death and a night-immunity claim. My position: With the majority; your public answer helped form it. Heat: Low: nobody is accusing you, and your direct answer about self-betting was accepted. Target landscape: A lone credible target, the claimed night-immune player (serial killer suspect), backed by a vigilante immunity claim, a visitor trace at a concealed death, and a contradicted Trailseer claim. The only other explanation for the immunity is a Fortune Teller self-bet, which you can rule out.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on a suspect and you have low heat, vote with the majority on the best-supported target. If another player asks whether you self-bet, answer plainly and truthfully, because ruling out your own self-bet removes the main alternative explanation for a night-immunity claim and lets the town commit to the serial killer vote.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote with 3-4 players left; a claim conflict (a fake counter-claim of my role, or a conflicting watch claim) decides whether the last killer or wolf survives. Information landscape: Moderately rich: revealed roles of the dead, prior public votes, and my own private knowledge (my bets and self-bet results), but other players' night results remain unverified claims. Stakes: With few players left, a single wrong vote or a no-elimination lets the killers reach their win count; the vote can end the game for Town. Consensus: Village is small and splitting between two claims; the Town-aligned players lean toward the same target on the basis of the revealed deaths and the consistency of claims. My position: Driving the majority or joining it early with a repeated vote. Heat: Moderate: a counter-claimant has accused me of being false, but at least one Town-claiming player has sided with me. Target landscape: Two or three living suspects, no confirmed roles among them: a counter-claimant of my own role whom I know is lying, versus a Town-claiming player whose claims are unverified but consistent with the revealed night deaths. The evidence is private knowledge and revealed dead roles, not behavior alone.
lessons.action: In a small endgame vote (3-4 alive), vote to eliminate the player whose claims your own private knowledge shows to be false (for example a counter-claimant to your Fortune Teller role), and the player whose claim fits the night events and the revealed deaths. Keep voting the same target consistently, because it pulls the other town-aligned voters into a majority and a wrong abstention or split could hand the killers the game.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a night attack. A claimed Investigator brings a Suspicious read on a player who defends by calling the result ambiguous or by claiming Healer against a counterclaim. The village converges on that player, and I am a neutral Fortune Teller who scores by bets on night deaths. Information landscape: Moderately rich: a claimed Investigator read, partly confirmed by an earlier reveal, plus a Healer counterclaim or public attack evidence. Nothing about the target's role is system-confirmed. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several threats alive (wolves plus a lone killer). Each wolf removed delays parity and keeps me alive to place my remaining night bets, so a correct majority vote is high value and one vote rarely decides the outcome. Consensus: Most of the village agrees on the Investigator's target. Support rests on a confirmed earlier read or a coherent Healer counterclaim, with little dissent. My position: With the majority. Heat: Low to moderate: I only made clarifying or skeptical remarks about the evidence and have not been accused or addressed. Target landscape: One accused player flagged Suspicious by a claimed Investigator whose earlier read was confirmed or whose claim is supported by a Healer counterclaim. The accused has no confirmed role and defends only with reasoning (for example that the read could mean the Necromancer), with no competing suspect. The basis is a partly confirmed check plus the accused's weak defense.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote, when a claimed Investigator whose earlier read was confirmed (or who is backed by a Healer counterclaim) names a Suspicious target and the village is converging, vote with that majority. A Suspicious read means a wolf, or a Necromancer on a night it attacked, and either one is a kill you want removed, so a vote on a Suspicious target needs no further proof to be worth casting. Ambiguity in the accused's defense alone is not a reason to hold out.

lessons.situation: First vote day (Day 2) after a night-1 death. The village has only unverified claims (counter-claims, a Sentinel report, a roleblock claim) and must either eliminate a claimant or abstain. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified night claims, one hidden or concealed body, no confirmed roles or voting records. Stakes: Early game with plenty of margin; a single vote is unlikely to decide the game, but a majority-aligned vote keeps the Fortune Teller safe to keep betting and scoring points. Consensus: The room is largely aligned (near-unanimous or a broad abstain) on the basis of unverified claims and claim logic, not confirmed information. My position: With the majority. Heat: Low; no one has accused the Fortune Teller, who has spoken little or only asked a question. Target landscape: Two or more contradictory role claimants (Investigator or Healer counter-claims) or no standout suspect; the first-night victim's role is hidden or revealed; no roles confirmed; the only evidence is unverified claims and behavior.
lessons.action: On the Day 2 vote, with no hard evidence and low heat, vote with the room's emerging majority. If a counter-claim fight has one side backed by a concrete accusation or a claimed watch placing them at a door, vote against that side; if nothing concrete exists, join the abstain or no-elimination majority. Your points come from night bets, so stay low-profile and keep the town's vote from splitting.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame day vote with the wolves mostly or fully gone. The village is hunting the remaining lone killer among a few unconfirmed players, and the Fortune Teller is one of the suspects. Information landscape: Partly information-rich: dead roles, claims and vote records are known. Which unconfirmed player is the lone killer is still speculative. Stakes: A tie or majority on the Fortune Teller costs the player and all remaining self-bets. One vote can decide which suspect the village removes. Consensus: The village is split between two or three targets and heading for a plurality or a tie. No hard evidence settles it. My position: Not yet committed. Free to join the plurality that forms and keep the vote off me. Heat: Moderate to high: a couple of elimination votes are already on the Fortune Teller as an unaccounted-for, unclaimed role. Target landscape: Several unconfirmed players, including a quiet unclaimed player, a late claimer and the Fortune Teller. Cases rest on behavior and vote history, with no hard evidence tying anyone to the lone killer.
lessons.action: When two or more votes are already on you, vote sincerely for the leading behavioral suspect who is not you, so a plurality forms on someone else and you avoid a tie or majority on yourself. Prefer a suspect whose case rests on recorded votes or deflection rather than a pure quiet-player read. You need to survive to keep placing nightly bets, because a day vote never scores.

lessons.situation: First vote of the game (day 2) after one or two night deaths. The Fortune Teller has no private information, since its bets give only points and no reads on roles. Town claimants accuse each other of roleblocking or fabricating, and the vote is the only lever before the next night bet. Information landscape: Starved: unverifiable claims (sentinel watch, trailseer follow, roleblock report), one or two public deaths, and no confirmed roles among the living. Stakes: Early game with many players alive. No single vote decides the game, but an elimination removes a threat, and a wasted split vote lets the wolves and the killer act with no pressure. Consensus: Mixed: sometimes a lopsided pile-on built on cross-matching claims, sometimes a split among abstain and several suspects. Either way it rests on unverified claims. My position: With the majority or in a minority cluster; not driving the vote. Heat: Low. The Fortune Teller has said little or nothing, made no claim, and nobody has accused it. Target landscape: Two or three candidates with no confirmed roles: one accused by several claimed Town roles whose claims cross-match, another who admitted a blocked night and gave no result, and a quiet suspect. The basis is behavior and unverifiable claims, not evidence.
lessons.action: On the first vote with no private evidence, when the room is converging on a suspect backed by multiple independent claims that cross-match, vote with that consensus rather than abstaining or splitting onto a quiet or lone-claim target. If the room is scattered across several weak suspects, vote for the target with the most concrete claim friction instead of a different long shot, so the vote helps produce an elimination.

lessons.situation: The town must eliminate someone without investigative leads, and the majority is choosing a target on behavioral grounds. Lynching a power role would hand a lone killer (a necromancer) a usable body and an attacker. Information landscape: Behavioral only for the remaining pool. Confirmed facts cover earlier night events, not who is evil now. Stakes: A mistaken lynch of a power role can swing the endgame. A lone killer using a dead Vigilante's body can attack through it and kill more players, including you. Each vote has real weight. Consensus: The majority leans toward the quiet player on inactivity grounds. A minority backs the pushback player. Nobody has verified evidence. My position: With the majority, or about to join it, without an evidence-based reason of your own. Heat: None to low. You have no accusations against you and are aligned with the room. Target landscape: A quiet unconfirmed player suspected only for lack of claims, versus an unconfirmed player who pushed back on town information. Neither has hard evidence against them. Silent players may be power roles.
lessons.action: Vote for the candidate whose case rests on a concrete contradiction or a confirmed fact, such as a claim that conflicts with an announced result. If the cases are only inactivity or a clash of arguments and abstaining is offered, abstain instead of joining a speculative lynch. A silent player may be a Town role holding unused power, such as a vigilante with bullets, and a lynch reveals the role only after it is too late to undo.

lessons.situation: A day vote after a night kill or a wolf flip, where one player's explanation of their behavior or role has been contradicted by other claims or reports and a majority is forming against them. Information landscape: Moderately to fairly rich: a confirmed wolf flip, a hidden-role kill, visit reports and rival claims, but nothing confirms the target's role directly. Stakes: Wolves are being removed one at a time, and each correct vote narrows the board toward the lone killer. A wrong vote wastes a day and thins Town, so only a vote backed by revealed facts and contradictions justifies joining the push. Consensus: The room is converging on one suspect, based on a wolf flip, contradicting claims and voting records, and the accusers are mostly players with consistent stories. My position: With the majority, or driving the push alongside it. Heat: Low to moderate: not accused, other players are in the spotlight, and any pressure you drew came from being an active accuser. Target landscape: Several candidates, with one player standing out: either a defender of a flipped wolf who gave shifting excuses, or a player whose claimed role was contradicted by a rival claim and a follow report. No system-confirmed role on the target; the case rests on contradictions and revealed partners, not on a hard result.
lessons.action: When a revealed wolf flip or a contradicted role claim leaves one player with a story that conflicts with independent reports, vote to eliminate that player alongside the majority. If your own read points at a different suspect and the contradiction is not clear, hold your vote on your own suspect instead of following the room.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; this night’s kill or conceal does not make the game end within one more elimination, so the decision is consequential but not immediately decisive.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Concealing the pack victim would be publicly apparent because the morning report would hide their role and omit their will; it would irreversibly spend one of two remaining conceals. Leaving the role revealed could expose whether the Sentinel claim is genuine and, if the victim is Town, make their recorded night information public.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved overall: the village has system-confirmed that the Night 1 wolf victim was the Investigator and the Serial Killer victim was the Trailseer. A claimed Sentinel reported that the Trailseer visited a player, but this does not identify the Trailseer's attacker or verify the claim. No Night 2 private results are available yet, including any result that would identify an immune Serial Killer; no such result has been used or reported.
query_dims.situation: The pack has coordinated a Night 2 kill on a player claiming Sentinel after that player reported a visitor result involving the publicly revealed Trailseer. The claim and result remain unverified, while the claimed role's possible death record could give the village information; the immediate decision is whether to conceal the victim's role and will.
query_dims.target_landscape: The pack's chosen victim is a player claiming Sentinel, whose claim has no public confirmation; the stated basis for targeting them is their potential future visitor information. No competing kill candidate is currently part of the stated pack decision. The victim's actual role is unknown to the village and is not known to you from the information provided.

lessons.situation: The pack is deciding whether to spend the kill and a conceal on the claimed investigator or sentinel, who is the town's information lead, while the healer's likely protection is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: public claims on night-one visits and clearings reveal the town's information lead and its probable guard, and the pack's private knowledge exposes a night-immune player. Stakes: A wasted kill on a protected power role gives the town a free night and keeps its information lead alive. The conceal is refunded, but tempo is lost and the pack is exposed to counterattack, such as from a serial killer. Forward exposure: Authorizing a conceal on a protected target gets no kill, so the charge is refunded. It still commits the pack's kill to a target the town can predict, and a failed attack leaves the claimed power role alive and more trusted. The illusionist's visit to hide the body also shows up to watchers if the attack succeeds. Target landscape: Claimed sentinel or investigator as the obvious priority. Alternatives are unverified quiet players or a known night-immune player (who cannot be killed at night). Evidence is mostly public claims rather than hard reads.
lessons.action: When the most prominent claimed power role (investigator or sentinel) has already been attacked and saved, or a healer claim makes protection of it predictable, steer the pack kill to a different target and hold both conceals. If the town has no healer claim yet, the power role can be killed and concealed, but only if the pack accepts that the healer may be guarding it.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3. The pack has agreed to kill a vocal claimed investigative role, and the serial killer may be attacking the same player. The illusionist must decide whether a conceal is worth spending on this body. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich. Public claims, a tied or abstained day vote, and recorded votes exist, but most roles are unconfirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with parity still a few eliminations away. A wasted conceal costs the pack one of only two uses and gains little, while a well-placed one hides a role the town would otherwise learn. Forward exposure: Spending a conceal is irreversible and uses up a limited ability. On an already-public claim it buys almost no information denial, and the morning report still says an illusionist acted. Target landscape: The pack's candidate is a player who has publicly claimed Trailseer or Sigilist, unverified but already stated. Other candidates are unclaimed players whose roles would be new information if revealed. The pack picked the target on threat and claim rather than confirmed role.
lessons.action: Keep the conceal for a kill whose role the town does not yet know, such as an unclaimed or unverified player, where hiding the role and will denies real information. If the planned victim has already publicly claimed a role and shared results, let the role reveal stand and keep the use for a later night.

lessons.situation: Early night 2. Town power roles have claimed and reported night-1 results that threaten the wolves' cover. The pack agrees to kill one claimant, with the Illusionist deciding whether to spend one of its two conceals on that kill. Information landscape: Information-rich. Public claims and night-1 results are on the table, and day-2 vote records already show wolves voting together. A same-night partner death (sigil strike or Serial Killer) can expose the pack no matter what the Illusionist hides. Stakes: Mid-game with several town power roles alive. Removing a threatening claimant matters, but the conceal charges are scarce. Spending one where the role is already known gains little, and a wolf partner's death or vote record can confirm the pack anyway. Forward exposure: A conceal is irreversible and spends one of two charges. The morning report will say 'Their role is hidden by an illusionist', which confirms an Illusionist is in play. It hides the carrier's visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer, but it cannot hide a wolf partner's death or the voting records. Target landscape: Day-2 kill choices among self-claimed power roles (a claimed Trailseer or Sentinel reporting night-1 visits, a claimed Investigator) versus unrevealed players. The claimed roles are accusations based on claims, not verified results. Their roles are already public, so concealing the body adds little uncertainty.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the victim's role is still unclaimed, or when a living Sentinel or Trailseer could otherwise trace the carrier to the victim's door. If the victim has already publicly claimed their role and no tracker threatens the carrier, kill without concealing and keep both charges for a later night. When the Illusionist itself carries the kill, a conceal leaves no trace at that door, so favor it for that night.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, night 2 or 3. The pack has a failed or contested night behind it and agrees to remove a claimed protector or information role. The carrier makes the kill, perhaps while the Chanteuse blocks another claimant, and the Illusionist decides whether to conceal the body. Information landscape: Moderate information: save announcements, conflicting role claims, and Sentinel or Trailseer reports that are claims only. Nothing about the victim's role is confirmed by the Game Master. Stakes: The board is mid-game, with the pack still a few eliminations from parity and a lone killer possibly alive. Removing the protector or the information source without giving the town a confirmed role widens the pack's lead. A failed kill leaves the wolves exposed to the Healer and the Vigilante. Forward exposure: The conceal is spent only if the victim dies; a save keeps it and leaves nothing hidden. Once spent it cannot be recovered. A hidden body gives the town no role or will, but it also tells them the Illusionist exists and that the pack made the kill. Target landscape: Candidates are publicly claimed power roles: a claimed Healer inferred from a save announcement, a claimed Sentinel whose watch tied a partner to a scene, and a rival Investigator claimant leading an accusation. All are unverified, and the pack picks them on behavior and public logic rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack's agreed kill is a claimed power role (Healer, Investigator or Sentinel) whose confirmed role or will would help the town, spend a conceal on it. The conceal costs nothing if the victim is saved, since the use is kept, so commit even without knowing the Healer's target. When the victim dies, the town cannot verify the claim and the pack loses nothing it needed to hide.

lessons.situation: Your partner carries the kill, or you do, on a role that has already claimed publicly. You have one conceal left and must decide whether to spend it or save it. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims, with several roles claiming results, but nothing verified. Stakes: With no extra conceals after this one, each use should hide something that cannot be inferred from claims. A revealed will carries a limited cost, but spending the last conceal on an already claimed role removes your flexibility for later kills. Forward exposure: Letting the body be revealed publishes the victim's role and any Town will, which may confirm their visit records. This is a one-night choice, and the conceal charge stays available for a later night. Target landscape: A claimed Town power role, such as a Sentinel with a public claim, is the pack's target. Other claimed power roles are active, and the claims are not confirmed.
lessons.action: If you have only one conceal left and the victim's role is already public from a claim, or the victim's will would reveal little, hold the conceal and let the role be announced. Keep it for a later kill of an unclaimed or higher-value role, and use the night's blocks and coordination on other threats.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a thin day with an abstain or tied vote. The wolves, with the chanteuse, have agreed a kill and the illusionist decides whether to hide the victim's role. A partner may have been told the conceals are for a high-impact target. Information landscape: Information-starved: few or no hard leads, a few unverified role claims, no trace results shared, and the wolves unsure where the serial killer or necromancer is acting. Stakes: Early game with several enemies still alive, so no single kill ends it. The two conceals are the pack's scarce tempo tool, and wasting one on a low-value body costs more than a day of town uncertainty gains. Forward exposure: A hidden-role morning report tells the town an illusionist is in the pack, and the use is spent permanently. The hidden role cannot be reversed, and the count of used conceals lets the town track you. Target landscape: The choice is between quiet unclaimed players, whose roles are unknown and chosen for low profile, and a self-claimed info role such as an investigator with a check left. The kill choice rests on role value and behavior, not hard evidence. A conceal on a quiet victim wasted a use on a sentinel nobody had claimed.
lessons.action: On a night-2-style kill, spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a claimed or high-impact info role whose confirmed death or role would help the town, such as an investigator-claimant with a check left. If the victim is a quiet, unclaimed player, keep both uses and let the role be revealed. A spent use is permanent, and the count of hidden-role deaths becomes the town's tool for tracking you.

lessons.situation: The pack is about to kill a claimed investigative player. The illusionist is deciding who carries the kill and whether to spend a conceal, with a hidden Sentinel watch or Sigilist sigil possible. Information landscape: Thin on hidden roles. You do not know whether a Sentinel is watching the door or a sigil is on you, though public Trailseer and Sigilist claims exist. Stakes: Losing the illusionist to a sigil or an exposed trace would cripple the pack's late game and speed a vote against it. Careful carrier choice protects the remaining conceals. Forward exposure: A non-carrier's conceal visit is visible to a Sentinel watching the victim. Carrying the kill yourself leaves no trace at that door but makes you an attacker that night, which a sigil on you would punish. Neither can be undone once the night resolves. Target landscape: The pack's victim is an unconfirmed claimant such as the Trailseer, or a self-claimed Sigilist. The serial killer may hit the same victim, and a Sentinel or Sigilist whose position is unknown may be targeting you or the victim's door.
lessons.action: If you conceal, carry the kill yourself, because then you leave no trace at that door and the carrier's visit is hidden from a Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer following the carrier. If a Sigilist with sigils left is alive or likely, or it is not your turn to carry, let the pack's kill go unconcealed instead of visiting the body as a non-carrier. A non-carrier's visit to hide the body stays visible to a watcher on that door, and a carrier's attack can be punished by a sigil.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later: the pack picks a claimed power role as the kill and the illusionist plans a conceal. A Healer claim or a previous protective visit to that target makes a save plausible, and the illusionist's own visit may be watched. Information landscape: Info-starved to thin: unverified claims, partial night-1 traces and one or two deaths. Hard facts are sparse, and the Healer's protection target is unknown. Stakes: With the pack down to one or two wolves, every visible visit risks heat and every failed kill wastes a night. A saved victim also leaves the illusionist as a known visitor, which can steer the vote toward the pack. Forward exposure: Your visit at the victim's door is irreversible. If the victim is saved, the conceal is kept but nothing is hidden, and the Sentinel or Trailseer sees you as a visitor. Target landscape: Claimed power roles (Investigator, Trailseer, Vigilante) are the obvious kill picks, but a Healer may have protected the same target before. Choosing is mostly a guess among living players, based on threat to the wolves rather than evidence.
lessons.action: When you are the carrier, or the pack's only wolf, and the kill target is a likely protected role (such as a claimed Investigator or Trailseer with a Healer visit onto them), prefer a target the Healer is less likely to guard, or accept that your visit may be seen. A conceal hides the carrier's visit only if the victim dies; if the Healer saves the victim, every visit to them stays visible to a Sentinel watch or a Trailseer follow, so do not rely on it as cover.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, after claims, deaths or votes have created information-bearing town roles. The pack picks a kill, and the illusionist decides whether to conceal the body of a role that matters. Information landscape: Moderately informed: some claims, bodies and records exist but are unverified. Concealing can deny the town role counts and confirmations. Stakes: With fewer players alive, each kill moves the pack closer to parity, and each revealed body feeds town deduction, or a Necromancer's use of the body. Denying role confirmation on a key kill matters more now than on night 1, and unspent conceals are worthless if the illusionist is voted out first. Forward exposure: Irreversible: it spends a use and announces that an illusionist is in play. If you carry the kill and conceal it, you leave no trace at that door. If another wolf carries, your hiding visit can still be seen by a Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Kill candidates are identified by claims or behavior, such as claimed information roles whose role or will would aid the town, rather than by a blind random pick. The pack's reads are partial and unconfirmed.
lessons.action: When the pack targets a town role whose revealed body or record would help the town, such as a claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator or Healer, carry the kill yourself and conceal it. A carrier who conceals leaves no trace at the victim's door, and the town gets neither a role nor a will. If you are not carrying, accept that your own visit stays visible to watchers and followers, and weigh that before spending the conceal.

lessons.situation: Night 1, the pack's first kill, with a conceal on offer and a blind target pick between the illusionist and its wolf partner. Information landscape: No public information at all, only the pack's private chat; nothing is known about anyone's role or night immunity. Stakes: The game is at its start with no pressure on the pack, so the main stake is keeping both conceals for when a role reveal would help the town. Nothing about night 1 forces an early conceal. Forward exposure: A conceal on a victim who survives is kept and shows the town nothing. Holding it back is fully reversible, since both uses stay open for a night when a role reveal would hurt the pack. Target landscape: A single quiet, unclaimed player chosen by default; no claims, reads, votes or deaths. The target's immunity to night kills is unknown, and it could be the lone killer.
lessons.action: With both conceals available and no information on the first-night victim, agree to the pack's kill but hold the conceals for a later night when a power role or a likely-to-die target is the victim. A conceal is only spent if the victim dies, but committing it early to an unscouted quiet player offers no gain, since that target may be night-immune (like a lone killer) and the night-1 kill may fail silently.

lessons.situation: Late game with a tied vote just behind and no conceals left. The pack must stop a claimed Vigilante's remaining shot, and the Illusionist has to judge whether a kill plus a block holds. Information landscape: Info-moderate: the Vigilante claimant said they were blocked and had one bullet left, and the town's other claims are unverified. Stakes: Losing a wolf here leaves a lone wolf against several town players and a vote that can end the game. One failed block or shot can flip which side is ahead. Forward exposure: With no conceals, the victim's role is shown and the carrier's visit can be traced by watchers or followers.
