Backing a kill on a claimed Vigilante commits the pack to that target for the night, and a failed block cannot be taken back. Target landscape: A claimed Vigilante who may have one bullet left, versus a claimed Investigator whose checks are spent. The pack picks the Vigilante on shot threat alone, with no verified evidence.
lessons.action: Before the last conceal is gone, have the pack kill one player and block the other main threat in the same night. Do not rely on a single block to stop a Vigilante who can still shoot, since a block that fails leaves the shot live and can cost the pack a wolf. If both conceals are spent, favor a kill and block pairing that does not leave your partner exposed to a shot.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a close or tied day vote. The wolves are killing a player who drew vote suspicion. Sentinel and Trailseer have been active or have claimed results. Information landscape: Day talk produced a healer claim, a watch result and a follow result, but nothing hard on the wolves. Watchers are plausibly active and you cannot tell which door they chose. Stakes: Mid-early board where being exposed as the illusionist costs the pack a key wolf. The marginal value of hiding an ordinary victim's role is small next to the risk of a logged visit turning suspicion onto you. Forward exposure: If you are not the carrier, your hide-visit is still seen by a watcher on the victim's door, which can lead to a day accusation against you. The conceal cannot be undone and costs a charge, and the pack's kill visit stays hidden either way. Target landscape: The victim is a quiet or lightly suspected player pulled into a day vote, with no confirmed role. A watcher may be on the same door, and the reason to hide is that the reveal could clear them or point at the voters.
lessons.action: With a Sentinel or Trailseer plausibly active and the day having produced watch or follow claims, conceal only when you are the carrier, or when the secrecy of the victim's role clearly outweighs the risk of your hide-visit being logged. Otherwise keep the charge and let the pack's kill resolve unconcealed, because a visit seen at the victim's door can get you accused and eliminated.

lessons.situation: Late game after a tied day vote, you are the last wolf with no conceals left. You must pick a kill among the few remaining town players, who are contesting each other's claims. Information landscape: Info-rich on the town side (a confirmed read on the lone killer, claim conflicts), but the town has not yet worked out your role. Stakes: Two more eliminations bring you to parity. Each night kill decides whether you reach it before the town votes you out. Forward exposure: The kill reveals the victim's role and will, and your carrier visit is visible to any surviving watcher or follower. Because you are the next carrier, a sigil placed on you can strike, and the action cannot be undone. Target landscape: Four living town players (Sigilist, Healer, Investigator, Trailseer) with no hard reads. The Trailseer was chosen because their tracking results threatened your claim, on public behavior rather than evidence.
lessons.action: With no conceals left and you as the carrier, kill the player whose night result most directly threatens your cover, such as a Trailseer or Sentinel who has followed or watched you. Expect the revealed role and will to expose their record, so choose the target whose record does less damage than their living results would.

lessons.situation: Late game, you are the last wolf and lone carrier after your partner died, with one conceal left and trackers or watchers alive. You decide whether to carry and hide the kill. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: some town confirmations exist (an Investigator's read on the lone killer), but the town has no read on you. Stakes: You are the only wolf left, so each kill must also keep you hidden. A trace-free kill gives you a night of cover, but the town is still ahead on numbers. Forward exposure: The morning report announces a hidden-role death, which shows town an illusionist exists and the conceal is spent. Afterward every kill is fully revealed, and the victim's true role (for example a Speculator's pick) may become public and either support or contradict your story. Target landscape: Several unclaimed town and neutral players with no hard reads on you. The victim is chosen from an unclaimed pool by behavior, not evidence, and a tracker who followed you only once is still alive.
lessons.action: As the last wolf with a conceal left, carry the kill yourself and conceal the victim, because an illusionist who carries and conceals leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer. Pick a victim whose role you do not need confirmed, and use the 'no visit' result a follower will report to build a cover story. Spend the conceal on a night when the carrier is you and a tracker or watcher is alive.

lessons.situation: You are the sole surviving wolf after your partner died, choosing the night kill while the healer is known to be active and protecting a publicly attacked player. Information landscape: Information-rich: the game master announced a save on the sentinel, and some town roles are confirmed. The wolves' own stats are known, but the healer's next protection is unknown. Stakes: With one wolf left and a lone killer possibly still alive, each night kill is critical. A wasted kill lets town investigators close in, while one real kill moves the wolves toward parity. Forward exposure: The kill is a lone carry that ties the night's attack to you as the only wolf. Once the target is chosen it is irreversible, and a wasted attack on a healer-covered target gains nothing and removes no town role. Target landscape: Candidates include a claimed sentinel already publicly saved by the healer, a claimed investigator with clears, a confirmed vigilante holding one bullet, and a quiet unverified player. The evidence is public announcements of the saves, not behavior.
lessons.action: As the last wolf, aim the pack kill at a player who was not publicly attacked and saved the previous night, such as a quiet unverified player or a confirmed threat the healer is not visibly guarding. Keep your conceals unspent until a kill is likely to succeed, since a conceal is refunded if the victim survives; if the healer's likely target is unclear, pick the target that was not the previous night's save.

lessons.situation: Late game after the lone killer is gone, with one or two wolves left against a Town that still has an information role able to catch a wolf. The illusionist is choosing whether to commit a limited conceal on tonight's pack kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, claims and watch records are public, and voting records exist. The remaining private results are the main danger to the wolves. Stakes: The board is close to wolf parity, so one surviving investigative result can decide whether a wolf is exposed and voted out. Concealing the right victim's role and will removes that risk, but a charge spent on a harmless victim is wasted. Forward exposure: Concealing signals to the village that an illusionist is active and spends a charge that cannot be recovered. Hiding the body leaves no trace at the victim's door when the illusionist carries the kill. It does not erase the victim's earlier public claims or votes. Target landscape: Living Town investigators and watchers (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and unconfirmed players. Picks rest on who threatens the wolves' cover through private results, rather than on neutral or low-threat players.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a Town role whose private result or will would expose a wolf, such as an Investigator, Sentinel or Trailseer holding a result on you. Otherwise save the charge, since a hidden body does not erase what the victim already said or voted in public. If you carry the kill yourself, the concealed kill leaves no trace at the victim's door, so prefer that route when a watcher or follower is alive.

lessons.situation: Opening night with ten players alive. The wolves must choose a first kill blind and decide whether to commit a conceal charge on the victim. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no roles are confirmed, no discussion has happened, no deaths or claims exist, and the wolves know only their own partner. Stakes: Early game with a large cushion: one kill cannot decide the game. The value is information, since a hidden early victim denies Town a role reveal, and a night-immune target exposes the lone killer at no cost. Forward exposure: Low exposure: a conceal leaves no public trace, a failed attack is never announced, and a kill on a concealed victim leaves no visit for a Sentinel or Trailseer to see. The only commitment is possibly spending one of two conceals on a low-value role, and a failed attack refunds it. Target landscape: Seven unconfirmed non-wolf players with no claims, no public visits and no voting record. The pack picks a quiet player blindly, and the choice rests on no evidence or behavior.
lessons.action: On night one with both conceals unspent and no information, submit a conceal alongside the pack's kill on an unrevealed, quiet target. If the target dies, their role stays hidden and the Illusionist learns it, and if the attack fails because the target is night-immune, the conceal is kept and the pack learns the lone killer.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game, no day-1 vote, no claims. The illusionist and chanteuse agree on a default kill, and the illusionist weighs spending one of two conceals on a victim of unknown role. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, claims, votes or night results. The only knowledge is the pack's private plan. Stakes: The board is early and far from parity, so a single kill is not decisive. The scarce resource is the two conceals, which are worth more on a later high-value body than on a blind first kill. A spent conceal on a neutral or low-value body is wasted, and an unspent one also stays usable by a Necromancer through a revealed body. Forward exposure: Holding costs nothing and is reversible. Spending a conceal is irreversible, announces that an illusionist exists, and leaves your own visit visible to a Sentinel or Trailseer unless you carried the kill yourself. Not carrying also leaves no trace on you. Target landscape: The pack's night-1 victim is an arbitrary quiet player with no claims or behavioral evidence. Nobody knows their role, including the wolves, so the value of hiding it is only speculative.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the kill is an arbitrary pick with no claims or reads, keep both conceals and let the chanteuse carry the kill so you make no visit at the victim's door. Spend a conceal later, on a victim whose revealed role or will would give town real information, such as a claimed investigator, trailseer, sentinel or healer.

lessons.situation: You are the last wolf with unspent conceals facing a daytime vote that may eliminate you, with confirmed town killers still alive. Information landscape: Partly information-rich: town roles are confirmed and your partner is dead, but a lone killer is only hinted at. Whether the healer will cover the target is unknown. Stakes: Dying with unused conceals wastes your remaining power. A successful hidden kill shrinks the town and obscures the evidence needed to eliminate you, while an idle night gains nothing. Forward exposure: A concealed kill still announces the attack and marks a wolf as alive, but the hidden role and hidden carrier trace give town no role or visit evidence. If the victim survives, the conceal is refunded and nothing is hidden, so the exposure is limited. Target landscape: Choose among players not just saved by the healer; the confirmed vigilante and sentinel are the threats worth removing, while quiet unverified players are the cheaper pick. Role status is mostly public.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with conceals in hand and town closing in, use a kill on a target the healer is unlikely to cover and conceal that victim's role. This hides your carrier visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer and denies town the role information, rather than skipping the night and giving up all pressure.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with the pack choosing a kill while the partner Chanteuse blocks a second threat. The Illusionist decides whether the victim is worth a conceal to deny the town role information and trace. Information landscape: Info-moderate: several dead players have public wills, a few living claimants are unverified, and the town's picture of the remaining roles is incomplete. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, and a hidden role plus a missing trace can keep the town from confirming who is left. Late in the game each conceal is scarce and carries real weight. Forward exposure: Using a conceal makes the morning say an illusionist hid the role, so the town learns an illusionist exists, though not who. Each use is permanent and cannot be undone. Once both are spent, every later kill shows its role and the carrier's visit can be traced. Target landscape: Candidates are an unclaimed voter whose role is unknown, a claimed Trailseer whose follow results threaten the pack, and a claimed Vigilante who can be blocked instead of killed. All roles are unverified, and the choice rests on behavior and threat level, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: While conceals remain, put one on a night kill whose victim is an unverified or high-information-value player, or a tracking threat such as a claimed Trailseer. Hiding the role also removes the carrier's visit to that victim from a Sentinel's watch or a Trailseer's follow, and leaves the town unsure which role is gone. Keep the last conceal for the kill where that traceless result matters most.

lessons.situation: Opening night, discussion-only day 1. The wolves must choose a first kill and decide whether the illusionist carries it, and whether to spend a conceal on a victim of unknown value. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or night results, so the target is a blind pick and any Sentinel or Trailseer who happens to be on the victim or carrier is invisible to the pack. Stakes: Early game with the wolves far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The cost that matters is a visit trail from the carrier that a watcher or tracker could use on day 2 or 3, which can get a wolf eliminated and cost the pack a member early. That outweighs keeping both charges in reserve. Forward exposure: Concealing makes the morning report say the role is hidden by an illusionist, which confirms an illusionist exists. It spends one of two charges if the victim dies, and the use cannot be undone. In return it removes the carrier's visit trace from any Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Nine or so living players, none having claimed a role and none read. The pack chooses a quiet, unclaimed target on behavior alone, so the victim's role and any watcher on them are unknown.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the pack picks an unread target and you are the one carrying the kill, spend one conceal on that victim. If the victim dies, your visit leaves no trace for a Sentinel watching them or a Trailseer following you, and if you carried the kill yourself you leave no trace at that door at all. If the victim survives, nothing is hidden and the charge is kept.

lessons.situation: Night after your wolf partner was voted out and revealed. You are the lone wolf and your public vote pattern made you the likely suspect for a Vigilante. Information landscape: Info-rich about your exposure: a revealed wolf confirms your side, and your vote pattern is public and permanent. Stakes: As the lone wolf and prime suspect you can be killed by a Vigilante shot or sigil strike tonight, so passivity loses the game while a kill buys time. Forward exposure: A kill with a conceal leaves no trace at that door but spends your last conceal. Staying home leaves you exposed to a Vigilante shot or a sigil strike, and a sigil on you only strikes if you attack that night. Target landscape: Remaining town are claimed Sentinel, claimed Healer, Vigilante and Sigilist, with roles known only through claims. The Sigilist who pushed the case on your partner is a high-value target.
lessons.action: As the last wolf when your vote record or partner's reveal makes you a prime suspect, use the night to act instead of staying home. Carry the kill on the player most likely to hold a night killing role or to have deduced you (such as a Vigilante or Sigilist), and use a remaining conceal so the victim's role and your carrier visit stay hidden. If you cannot tell who that is, still make the kill rather than pass.

lessons.situation: Repeated wolf attacks on the claimed investigator were repelled by the healer's protection. The remaining wolf must choose between hitting the investigator again and breaking the protection cycle. Information landscape: Information-rich: investigator, healer and sentinel have publicly claimed roles, targets and results, and morning save announcements show the pattern of protection. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity and the protection cycle is the main obstacle. Removing the healer opens the way to the next power-role kill and to winning. Forward exposure: Spending the last conceal leaves zero charges, so later visits to victims are traceable. The kill itself is irreversible. A conceal on a victim who survives is refunded, and a hidden-role morning report only signals that an illusionist is active. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, who survived repeated attacks, versus the claimed healer, who openly took credit for the saves. Both are public claims backed by morning save announcements rather than by behavior alone.
lessons.action: When a claimed healer has been blocking the pack's kills on the claimed investigator or sentinel, aim the pack kill at the claimed healer and spend a conceal on that body. A hidden role denies the town confirmation and the Necromancer a usable body. If the healer is dead, protection stops and the next kill on the power role should land.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with you as the sole surviving wolf. A sigilist with a sigil left has publicly said they will target you, or has already used a sigil to kill your partner. Any kill you make would reach or approach parity, and the sigil strikes anyone who attacks that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, the investigator's record or will clears one living player, and the sigilist's earlier strike or sigil result is public. The sigilist's suspicion of you is explicit. Stakes: One more death reaches or nearly reaches wolf parity, but the sigil can strike you on the same night and end the game for the wolves. A wrong attack loses the game immediately, while holding the kill only postpones the decision to the vote. Forward exposure: Attacking is a visit and an attack. It commits you to a kill that a sigil on you would punish with your own death, and it cannot be undone once the night resolves. Holding the kill reveals nothing and keeps your conceals available. Target landscape: Two or three living players remain: a publicly known or claimed sigilist whose earlier sigil result is confirmed, a player cleared by the investigator who is probably the healer, and possibly one quiet unconfirmed player. Roles come from public evidence and the sigilist's stated intentions, but which target holds an unspent sigil is unknown.
lessons.action: When you are the last evil player and a sigilist has a sigil left and has publicly named or suspected you, hold the kill that night. Your own attack triggers the sigil and the sigil strike still kills you even if the attack succeeds, and a conceal does not help if the healer saves the target. Keep your conceals and let the vote decide, rather than attacking into a possible sigil.

query_dims.consensus_text: No consensus yet on the day 4 target; the room is split between the player_1 line (suspect player_5) and doubt about the Sentinel claim, with no hard evidence either way.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so a single wrong lynch is recoverable but narrows the wolf margin; the game cannot end within one more elimination, leaving room to test the Sentinel claim before committing a vote.
query_dims.heat_now: Low on me as the speculator: I hold no night result and have not been accused; suspicion sits on the trio of player_1, player_5 and the Sentinel claimant.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved beyond one claimed watch result; the day 3 vote record (player_2 and player_8 voted player_1, others voted player_8) and the roleblock on player_1 are the only checkable public facts.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out: passing in the opening round and not driving the vote, since I have no new fact.
query_dims.situation: A Sentinel claimant reported a night 3 watch on player_1 showing only player_5 as a visitor, while the roleblocked player_1 says the visitor was the blocker and player_5 confirms the visit, creating a three-way credibility contest with six players alive and the speculator's pick of Town already made.
query_dims.target_landscape: Two live accusers of each other: player_2 claims Sentinel with a night 3 watch showing only player_5 visiting player_1; player_1 says it was roleblocked and points at player_5; player_5 admits visiting player_1 without claiming a role. Role status of all three is unverified claim-level only; the Sentinel claim is the only public information source.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day with a narrowed suspect pool: you claim Speculator, a wolf (Chanteuse) counter-claims the same unique role, and the contested claim decides the remaining wolf search. Information landscape: Sparse: the Speculator pick is public but its author is hidden; neither claimant can prove anything; only claim order, sigil/vigilante results and elimination logic exist. Stakes: A few players remain and one wrong vote could hand the wolves parity, so winning the contested claim directly decides whether the picked side wins. Consensus: Village is wolf-hunting the last suspects; it leans on claim order and elimination logic since nothing is verifiable. My position: Driving the discussion on claim timing and aligned with a forming majority of role-claiming Town players. Heat: Moderate to high: your claim put you in the suspect pool and a counter-claimant is accusing you of being the wolf behind an alibi role. Target landscape: Two unverifiable Speculator claimants in a small suspect pool; other pool members already cleared by sigil or vigilante accounts; the decision rests on claim timing and logic, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: After your pick is announced and a suspect pool forms, state your Speculator claim yourself, early and plainly, and note that picking is not a visit so you have no night action to account for. If someone counter-claims Speculator, hold the identical claim, point out that your claim came first and theirs came only after the pool narrowed, and ask Town to vote the counter-claimant instead of overcomplicating it.

lessons.situation: Day 3, mid-game. Claimed power roles have corroborated one another and are pushing a lynch on one accused player. The accused may be a lone killer, and the speculator has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Moderately rich but all claims: a claimed watch or check result, healer confirmation, announced death outcomes and a revealed dead wolf, or an unverified Investigator read. The claims interlock but cannot be verified directly. Stakes: With several killers still alive, a correct lynch on Day 3 removes one of the two evil factions Town must clear. A wrong lynch brings evil closer to parity, so a well-reasoned push matters. Consensus: The room is converging on one accused player, mainly on interlocking claimed night results and mechanical reasoning, not on behavior alone. My position: With the majority, adding mechanical or procedural support to the forming consensus instead of staking out a lone read. Heat: Low: you are unaccused and a mostly silent, unexposed player. Any rebuttal from the accused is brief. Target landscape: One accused player under evidence-based pressure from claimed Town roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Healer) whose claims interlock but are unverified. The accused calls it coordinated wolf theater or fabrication. No other candidate has drawn serious attention.
lessons.action: While you still hold your pick on Day 3, add a rules-based argument or a verification test that supports the accusation the room is already converging on, such as pointing out that a missing save announcement fits a night-immune target or proposing that a Sentinel or Trailseer confirm the claim. Keep your own role and intended pick hidden. This helps remove a killer without exposing you, and it lets you pick the side you expect to win later with more information.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day where Town is sorting dueling claims or hunting the last threat, and the Speculator has already picked and is uncontested. Information landscape: Mixed: unverified watch and block claims, concealed-role bodies and a confirmed sigil strike give some structure, but no direct confirmations of the remaining suspects. Stakes: The pick is already locked in, so the Speculator's payoff depends on Town winning; steering the room to testable evidence without drawing heat keeps your vote and the pick alive. Consensus: Village converging on a shared target using testable claims and confirmed results. My position: With the majority, contributing without revealing yourself as the picker. Heat: Low: nobody has accused you and the pick was announced with no name attached. Target landscape: Accused players and claimants with dueling unverified results; sigil strikes, concealed bodies and role claims give structure to test; behavior-based reads for the last threat.
lessons.action: When your pick is already made and you are not under suspicion, join the discussion with a clarifying question or a mechanics-based observation that supports the testable claims, and let the room converge. If the room has no clear lead, ask a claimant to clarify intended targets or results rather than picking a side early.

lessons.situation: A night result (such as a healer save on a claimed role) triggers two competing claims on one unique role. The village debates which claimant is real, and the speculator has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced save or death, wills or night-action claims that can be cross-checked, and mutually exclusive role claims. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. Removing a false claimant (likely a wolf or the necromancer) is valuable, but one vote does not yet decide the game, and the speculator's pick is still pending. Consensus: The room is engaged and roughly aligned on resolving the counterclaim by checking it against the morning report. No fixed vote target has formed yet. My position: with majority Heat: None to low; the speculator is unpressured, often already cleared by a claimed investigator, and attention is on the claimants. Target landscape: Two players in a direct counterclaim over a single-slot role (investigator or healer), with a confirmed public save or death report as the only hard anchor. The claims can be tested against that announcement; the rest is behavioral.
lessons.action: When two players counter-claim the same role and a public morning report (a save or a death) is available, test each claim against that report using only the game rules. Point out which claimant's stated night action explains the announced outcome and which leaves it unexplained, and stay uncommitted on anyone's true role beyond that. This steers the room toward the contradiction, keeps you low-profile with your pick still unspent, and lets the pick wait for the room's outcome.

lessons.situation: A day-2 or day-3 pile-on forms against a claimant who got a rule or result wrong, while the Speculator is unsuspected and holds a pick (made or pending). Information landscape: Mixed but leaning on claims: a few rules-checkable inconsistencies and cross-supporting unverified claims, with no confirmed roles from the Game Master. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. One vote can remove a threat, but it does not yet decide the game. The Speculator's win depends on the pick's side winning, so helping eliminate a likely evil player and staying alive both matter. Consensus: The village is converging on one target, driven by a caught rules mistake and cross-supporting claims, though no role is officially confirmed. My position: With the majority, adding a distinct supporting argument without leading the push. Heat: Very low to low: not named, not accused, and not drawing scrutiny before or after speaking. Target landscape: One accused player whose claim contains a rules-checkable error (a misdescribed role ability or a watch result that cannot fit the rules), possibly with a counter-claimant. Secondary claimants are unverified. The basis is claim contradictions, not behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on a player whose claim has a concrete, rules-checkable contradiction and nobody has pointed at you, join once with one distinct, specific reason tied to that contradiction. Stay with the majority rather than leading, and keep your role and pick to yourself unless the pick is already made and there is no cost to staying quiet.

lessons.situation: Late game with both wolves gone and the speculator's Town pick public; the lone killer is hiding among a few survivors and deflecting suspicion onto the speculator, so the Town win depends on the claimed role-holders voting out the right player. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: revealed dead roles, announced saves and attacks, and a public pick, but the surviving players' roles are only claimed and one check is known not to rule out a serial killer. Stakes: With few players left, one mistaken elimination or a tie-break can hand the lone killer the game, so the speculator's Town pick lives or dies on convincing the swing voters. Consensus: The room is split or forming against the agent, with claimed role-holders unsure whom to trust and no firm consensus on the lone killer. My position: Driving the case against the lone-killer suspect rather than holding out. Heat: Moderate to substantial: the agent is accused for having no claimed night role, and suspects urge the room to scrutinize the agent's past statements. Target landscape: The unclaimed or unconfirmed player who deflects behind a dead player's result or an incomplete check, plus claimed healer, sentinel or investigator whose votes decide the outcome; the case rests on mechanics and records, not only on behavior.
lessons.action: When the pick is Town, the wolves are dead or nearly dead and the lone killer remains, openly own the public Town pick and name the unconfirmed or unclaimed player as the main lone-killer suspect. Support the case with checkable facts, such as an attack through a dead body leaving no visit from the attacker, and push the claimed role-holders (sentinel, investigator, healer) to put their votes on that player; do not rely on asking the suspect to evaluate others.

lessons.situation: After a night death reveals a dead wolf or other evil role, a player misstates the vote record or an evil player tries to use a past vote to vouch for itself. The speculator, who has not yet picked a side, can correct the record and steer the room. Information landscape: Information-rich: public vote tallies, revealed dead roles, a dead wolf's attack trace and an investigator claim with a cleared read. No fresh hard leads on the remaining suspects. Stakes: Mid-game with a few evil players left. A misdirected day vote would waste an elimination and push the board toward evil parity, while an accurate vote can remove a killer or wolf and fix the winning side for the speculator's pick. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned and working from the vote record and a cleared investigator read. It is vulnerable to a misremembered or spun record. My position: With the majority, contributing record-keeping rather than driving an accusation. Heat: Low; the speculator is seen as an attentive, neutral contributor and has not been accused. Its pick is not yet attributed to anyone. Target landscape: A claimed investigator-cleared player, an unverified player with a lone or odd vote, a quiet player, and a surviving wolf or killer. Public roles are partly confirmed by deaths and one check; reads rest on vote records.
lessons.action: When the room misstates the public voting record or leans on a vote as proof of alignment, calmly restate the actual vote history from the record without being combative. Then point the room at the unresolved candidates the record supports, so consensus stays anchored to verified facts rather than a distorted narrative.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, the surviving evil player praises a claimed investigator for voting the dead wolf, and the room debates whether that vote proves town alignment. The speculator challenges the logic and points scrutiny at the praiser. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: one confirmed dead wolf, an investigator claim with a cleared read, and Day 2 voting records tying the surviving suspect to the dead wolf. Stakes: With few players left, a single vote can remove the last wolf or waste the elimination. Raising the distancing point can tip the consensus against the right target before the vote. Consensus: The village is leaning toward the suspected wolf on voting-record links and discussing whether an early vote counts as proof of alignment. My position: With the majority, voicing a skeptical point that supports the forming read. Heat: Low; the speculator abstained earlier and is not under suspicion, though challenging a wolf may draw a defensive counter-vote. Target landscape: A surviving suspected wolf trying to pocket a claimed investigator, the claimed investigator with a cleared read, and a quiet villager under pressure. The suspicion rests on vote links to the dead wolf, not on hard proof.
lessons.action: When a suspected wolf vouches for a claimed role or praises a vote against an already-dead wolf, say aloud that voting a dead packmate can be distancing rather than proof of town alignment. Ask the room to weigh that player's own record, and expect to take some defensive heat for it.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Both wolves, or one wolf and the lone killer, are already dead, and one evil player remains unidentified. The speculator, holding a Town pick, has to steer the surviving cleared players onto that last player instead of itself. Information landscape: Rich by elimination. There are revealed roles for the dead, claims that clear the others, and a track or vote history on the unknown player. Stakes: With so few players left, one wrong vote lets evil reach parity or win. A correct vote ends the game as a Town win and secures the Town pick. Consensus: Cleared town players are largely aligned on narrowing to the remaining unknown. The basis is shared claims and elimination. My position: Driving the discussion together with the cleared town claimants. Heat: Low to moderate. Some deflection is aimed at the speculator, but claims of visits or wills already cover it. Target landscape: Two or three living players: those cleared by role claims, wills, or tracker reports, versus one unverified or quiet player with no claim and no night targets. The basis is elimination plus behavior and vote history, not hard proof.
lessons.action: In a late-game endgame (3-4 alive) where claims and reveals have cleared most players, argue by elimination: name the one unaccounted-for, unclaimed or quiet player as the remaining evil, and cite the specific claims or records that clear everyone else. Put that player on the spot by asking what they did last night and whom they targeted; if they answer vaguely or deflect, press that point and push the room to vote them.

lessons.situation: Early day discussion (day 1 or 2) with the speculator's pick unspent. The village is trading unverified claims and night results, and the speculator is neutral and has not committed to a side. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverified claims, at most one or two revealed bodies, and no vote history or confirmed evil. Stakes: Early game with several eliminations still needed before any evil side can win. The speculator's only loss condition is dying unpicked, so avoiding heat now matters more than pushing a read. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned and still trading claims. Votes are abstain-heavy or tied, and no side is clearly ahead. My position: Holding out or going with the majority, with no stated read and no pick made yet. Heat: Zero to low: nobody has accused or mentioned the speculator, or only a harmless night report about it has come up. Target landscape: No confirmed suspects; the living players are unclaimed or only claim-based, with a few night-result claims (trailseer, sentinel, investigator) and perhaps one or two revealed bodies. Reads rest on claims and behavior, not verified evidence.
lessons.action: While your pick is still unspent and the room has no hard leads, speak only when you are addressed or can restate another player's report accurately, and keep any analysis on the board in general rather than on a named target. Don't announce your role or your leaning. If someone reports a night result about you, confirm it plainly and add nothing contentious, so you stay low-heat while you gather information for the pick.

query_dims.consensus_text: The discussion is aligned around caution: speakers say the claims and matching visit accounts do not establish alignment, and one player favors abstaining. There is no clear elimination consensus.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, so this decision is not immediately decisive; before making your pick, there is time to assess which side is ahead.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion or accusation toward you is recorded; your role as Speculator and your unmade pick are private.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only public night report is a wolf-and-Serial-Killer attack on a player whose role was concealed. The claimed checks and visit observations are unverified; the matching visit accounts corroborate a route but not roles or alignment. No vote record exists.
query_dims.my_position: You have not stated a public position; the room currently leans toward abstaining rather than choosing a target.
query_dims.situation: On day 2, unverified Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claims have produced a matching account of one player visiting another, but the match confirms only the route. The discussion is consequently cautious, with no concrete vote target and a suggestion to abstain.
query_dims.target_landscape: No one is a defined vote target yet. The Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claims are unverified; the Sentinel and Trailseer accounts corroborate a visit route, not roles or alignment. A player claiming Investigator says another player read Not suspicious.

lessons.situation: Day 2 first vote: a claimed power role admitted their reported result looked wrong and the whole table is accusing them, while you have not yet made your side pick. Information landscape: Information-starved: one self-admitted inconsistency and unverified claims; no confirmed roles. Stakes: Early elimination of a Town role weakens Town's information while the serial killer and wolves are still active; a mistaken unanimous vote is hard to reverse and your own pick depends on Town surviving. Consensus: Near-unanimous pile-on against one claimed role based on a single reported inconsistency; the room is driven by claim analysis, not verified facts. My position: With the majority and one of the voices driving it. Heat: Low; you are an unclaimed voice agreeing with the majority. Target landscape: One claimed Sentinel under real pressure after reporting a watch result that omitted their own visit; the other claimant (a trailseer) looks consistent. No competing suspects and no hard evidence beyond the claim's inconsistency.
lessons.action: When the table is piling onto a single claimed role over a stated inconsistency and there is no stronger lead, vote with the consensus only after checking that the inconsistency is a real rules violation rather than a misstatement. If the rule check is unclear, abstain, so you do not help eliminate a likely Town power role while you still hold your pick.

lessons.situation: After a night kill (often hidden-role or double attack), a role claimant's night report places one named player at the victim's door. The accused denies it and attacks the claimants, and the room converges on the accused. The speculator has already picked Town or is about to. Information landscape: Moderately to highly info-rich: specific watch or follow claims that corroborate one another, visitor counts, an investigator read, and caught mechanics errors, though nothing is officially confirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil threats still alive. Removing a wolf or the lone killer by an evidence-backed vote shifts the board toward Town and toward the speculator's Town pick, and a wrong eviction would cost a Town member. Consensus: Largely aligned (most of the living players) behind the evidence-backed target. Only the accused and perhaps one wolf partner dissent. My position: With the majority, lightly helping build the case with a verification question or a public argument. Heat: Low: not accused, only asking questions or backing the majority line. Target landscape: Two or three suspects: one accused by independent, partly corroborating night claims (watch report, trailseer follow, visitor list, investigator read) who denies and counter-accuses, versus the accuser(s), who are unverified but consistent with each other. Evidence outweighs behavior on the accused, and nobody is confirmed by the Game Master.
lessons.action: On a day-vote with low heat, vote with the evidence-backed majority on the player whose story is contradicted by independent night reports (a watch claim, a follow match, a visitor count, a counter-claim) rather than on mood. If you have not yet picked, ask for a Trailseer or Sentinel to corroborate before the vote, then vote with the room. Each eviction of a wolf or lone killer moves Town toward winning, which is what your Town pick needs.

lessons.situation: First day with a vote, after a night-1 death. There are unverified role claims and counter-claims, or no claims at all. The speculator has not yet made its side pick and has no information on any candidate. Information landscape: Information-starved: one dead player with a known role, unverified night-result claims, no confirmed wolf, and no voting history yet. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so one vote does not flip the winning side. A wrongful elimination of a real Town role is costly, and your abstain avoids adding to it. Your win depends only on the later pick. Consensus: The room is split or only loosely aligned. It is either a universal abstain or a near-majority piling onto one player, based on behavior and unverified claims rather than confirmed roles. My position: Holding out by abstaining, either with an abstain bloc or against a bandwagon, without driving any accusation. Heat: Low to none: you have been quiet or only echoed the room's questions, and no one has accused you. Target landscape: Two or more candidates drawing votes, such as a quiet player with no claim, a claimed healer, or rival investigator claimants. Their claims are unverified. The only evidence is a night-1 sentinel or trailseer report or a visit link, and everything else is behavior.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, while your one pick is unused and no candidate has hard evidence against them (only unverified claims, quietness, or a bandwagon), abstain rather than join the pile-on. If a candidate has a concrete contradiction, such as a caught lie or a claim that conflicts with an announced fact, vote for that player instead. If abstaining has been removed after two no-elimination days, vote for the best-supported suspect. Abstaining keeps your heat low, and your win depends on the pick, not on this vote.

lessons.situation: Four players alive with one wolf remaining; a dispute between two info claimants over whether a watch counts as a visit, and the room votes out a claimed role over an apparent rules error. Information landscape: Rich in claim histories but poisoned by a rules dispute, so the evidence is contested rather than confirmed. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf left, one wrong elimination of a real Town role gives the wolf parity and ends the game; the vote is decisive. Consensus: Majority formed against the claimed sentinel on a disputed rules argument, with the vigilante holding the decisive bullet. My position: With the majority, joining a vote that was already forming. Heat: Moderate: the claimed vigilante questioned the speculator's lack of a role claim, though attention quickly moved to the dispute between information claimants. Target landscape: Claimed sentinel accused of lying about watching being a visit, versus a claimed trailseer and claimed vigilante pushing the accusation; the case rests on a rules dispute and counter-accusation, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With a wolf still alive and a dispute between claimed info roles, do not just join the majority on a vote over a rules-interpretation quarrel. Check the accusation against the stated rules (for example, a watch is a visit to the target but is not shown in the watcher's own result) and vote for the player whose claim actually conflicts with the rules or other evidence, or hold out if the accusation is only a semantic quarrel.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a night kill by wolves or the serial killer; the village converges on a single accused player on corroborating night-result claims, and the speculator has the option to join the vote that decides whether the remaining evil is removed. Information landscape: Reasonably information-rich: a wolf is already confirmed dead or revealed, there are corroborating tracking claims and a clean investigator check, and the accused offers only blanket denials. Stakes: With wolves or the lone killer nearly gone, one more correct elimination can end or nearly end the game; the vote is rarely decisive alone but it fixes the board toward a Town win, which is the side the speculator pick favors. Consensus: Largely aligned: a pack of accusers forms on matching tracking and check reports plus the reveals of dead wolves. My position: With the majority, joining the pile-on early or at the last minute rather than holding out. Heat: Low to moderate: no accusation round is aimed at you, though the accused may have counter-accused or voted against you. Target landscape: One accused player named by matching independent tracking or check claims (trailseer, sentinel, investigator); the claims are unverified but agree with each other and with confirmed reveals. The alternative candidates have no case against them; the accused's defense is blanket denial or counter-accusation.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote where several tracking or check reports (trailseer, sentinel, investigator) converge on one accused and confirmed wolves are already known, vote with that convergent group for the accused instead of an unrelated player. Removing a convergent target sharpens the endgame toward Town, which pays off a Town pick; if you still hold your pick, the converging reports are your cue to lock in the side that now looks to be winning.

lessons.situation: Endgame of three or four players alive after both wolves are eliminated; the only remaining threat is the lone killer, hidden among the other living players, and your Town pick depends on removing it. Information landscape: Rich by elimination: both wolves revealed, the killer's night kills visible, and claimed trailseer and healer reports consistent with each other and with you. Stakes: The final vote decides the game: eliminating the lone killer ends it as a Town win and pays off the Town pick, while a wrong vote lets the killer reach the at-most-one-other-alive condition. Consensus: Mostly aligned on eliminating the one unverified player, since claims corroborate each other and both wolves are already revealed. My position: With the majority or driving alongside the corroborated claimant, and part of the decisive votes. Heat: Moderate: the suspected killer voted against you, but a matching trailseer result saying you visited no one cleared you. Target landscape: Two or three other living players: claimed information roles whose reports match each other and clear you, and one unclaimed or ability-less player who cast a counter-vote at you. Basis is cross-corroborated claims plus elimination, not just behavior.
lessons.action: When both wolves are confirmed dead and only the lone killer can remain, vote out the one living player whose claim is unverified or who has no corroborated night result, and rely on cross-matching claims such as a trailseer report that agrees with a healer's claim. If you are the one cleared by a corroborated result, join the cleared players against the lone unclaimed or uncorroborated player, because a wrong vote lets the killer reach parity.

lessons.situation: Late-game day vote at five alive where the vote is split or tied. The speculator's ballot decides whether a useful Town-aligned role survives, and the speculator has already picked a side. Information landscape: Mixed. Some night save announcements and claimed information-role reports exist, but they conflict, and several dead players' roles are hidden. No role is verified. Stakes: At five alive, one elimination can bring evil to parity. A single ballot decides between keeping a protective role alive and handing the wolves or lone killer a free removal. Consensus: Fractured: votes split between two or more targets, with no majority and a tie likely, resting on conflicting claimed visit reports. My position: Holding the swing or deciding ballot, able to join a wagon or drive an alternative target. Heat: Moderate to high: the speculator is accused or voted for by others based on visit reports, though in some cases heat is only low to moderate. Target landscape: Three or four candidates at five alive: a claimed healer with a confirmed save announcement, a claimed trailseer or sentinel, the speculator under accusation, and a quiet unclaimed player. Evidence is claims and visit reconstructions, not confirmed roles.
lessons.action: With about five players alive and the vote split or tied, use your ballot to protect a claimed protective or information role whose behavior and announced results fit. Aim it at the least-evidenced quiet player, since a tie or no elimination keeps the Town-aligned pick alive. If the room is scattered and no role is confirmed, spend it on the most defensible suspect rather than a token vote.

lessons.situation: The final day vote with three or four players alive. The speculator is the target of the surviving evil players and is voting alone against the player the records implicate. Information landscape: Voting logs, dead-role reveals and announced reanimated-kill reports exist, but no living candidate is confirmed. The evidence has to be read from patterns. Stakes: One more death gives evil parity or the lone-killer win condition, so this vote ends the game. A lost vote also kills the speculator's chance of seeing its pick come true. Consensus: The room has coalesced into a bloc against me, built on my voting history and on mutual cover among the evil players. Town evidence is thin. My position: Holding out alone against a two- or three-vote bloc. Heat: High to extreme. Evil players or a rival claimant are using my past votes or a questionable-player label against me. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed living players, none publicly confirmed as wolf or lone killer. Cases rest on voting records, alignment with dead evil players, and announced body-attack kills, not on revealed roles.
lessons.action: In an endgame vote with three or four players left and a majority leaning on you, vote for the unconfirmed player whose public record ties most directly to evil. Good evidence is a vote alongside a dead wolf, or a body-attack announcement that points to the lone killer. If a rival's case rests only on a single dead player's past vote, vote on the stronger record and not on who is pressuring you, because each vote you add is the only way to reach a tie or majority.

lessons.situation: Late game, day vote. Your Town pick is already announced and the Town win needs the last evil player or players removed. A few survivors remain, and one is the remaining wolf or lone killer, often the one who attacked your role or counter-claimed it. Information landscape: Fairly rich by elimination. Dead roles are revealed, some Town results are backed by announced facts, and the suspect pool is narrow. Some of it is still behavioral, such as who pressed whom and how people voted. Stakes: Few players are left, so one wrong elimination could let evil reach parity or hand the game to the lone killer. A correct elimination ends the game and cashes in your pick, so the vote has to land on the true last threat. Consensus: The village is converging on one target through elimination reasoning and shared reads. Most votes are already pointed at the same last unaccounted-for player. My position: With the majority, joining a bloc that is already forming and sometimes helping to start it. Heat: Low to moderate. Your Town pick is announced anonymously, but some players can guess your role from your action pattern or a rival claim. Target landscape: Two or three survivors left unaccounted for after wolves or the lone killer died. The candidates include a counter-claimant or a player pressing on your role, plus quiet players. Roles are confirmed mostly by elimination and sigil or healer reasoning, with voting-bloc behavior as backup.
lessons.action: Once your Town pick is made and announced, vote with the forming majority for the remaining evil player. Use elimination to name them: take the roles already revealed dead, the cleared players, and anyone who counter-claims or presses on your role. Your pick pays off only if Town wins, so keep voting for the last unaccounted-for threat instead of splitting the room.

lessons.situation: A rival counter-claims the Speculator role or publicly ties your pattern of actions to it, and calls your claim late or false. You have to hold your claim while the room decides who the wolf is. Information landscape: Role-uniqueness contradiction plus elimination reasoning from dead roles and Town results. Evidence is moderately rich, although the targeted player's role is not confirmed until the vote. Stakes: Late game with few players left. If the wrong claimant is eliminated, evil can reach parity. Removing the false claimant can end the game. Consensus: The room is mostly backing your claim or already turning on the accuser. The shared basis is the unique-role contradiction and the narrowed suspect pool. My position: With the majority, partly driving it as the original claimant. Heat: Moderate to elevated. A rival claimed your role, or someone linked your actions to the Speculator, and at least one vote has been cast against you. Target landscape: The counter-claimant or the player pressing on your role, versus a few players already cleared by Town results or confirmed by elimination. Evidence is a mix of role uniqueness, elimination logic, and behavior.
lessons.action: If someone counter-claims your Speculator role or ties your behavior to it, keep your claim consistent and point out that there is only one Speculator. Then vote for the counter-claimant or pressurer if the cleared roles and the elimination logic leave them as the remaining evil candidate. This works because the Town pick is already announced and a counter-claimant is forced into being the wolf or a liar.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: With 8 players alive and 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, this night is not immediately decisive: the game cannot end within one more elimination, and a single result does not flip which faction is winning.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Publicly pressing the player who said they were not roleblocked would commit you to treating that inconsistency as meaningful, but it would not reveal your role or private knowledge; the claim remains reversible as an interpretation. Your actual block and pack target are private tonight.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is sparse. Publicly confirmed facts are the wolf killing of the Investigator, the Serial Killer killing of the Trailseer, and the day-two abstention. The Sentinel claim and its visit result are unverified claims. Privately, you know you blocked the player who denied being roleblocked last night; that player’s claimed experience conflicts with your knowledge. The pack has not yet named tonight’s target, and there is no known immune-target attack result.
query_dims.situation: As the Chanteuse and tonight's pack carrier, you face a private coordination decision about a pack kill and a block while the public discussion centers on an unverified Sentinel claim: the claimant says a dead Trailseer visited the player they watched. A player who was roleblocked by you last night says they were not told they were blocked, creating a public inconsistency without establishing that player's role. No night-two results exist yet.
query_dims.target_landscape: The unverified Sentinel claimant is a plausible town night-action target to block, though their claimed watch result is not independently confirmed. The player who denied being roleblocked is another possible block target, but their role and whether they acted are unknown. The pack has not named its kill target; living players are candidates, with no public role confirmation that identifies a preferred target. The night-one wolf kill of the Investigator and Serial Killer kill of the Trailseer are system-confirmed. No attack on a night-immune player has identified the Serial Killer, and no such probe is known to have been used.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a tied day-2 vote with no elimination. The pack kills a scrutinized or quiet player, the illusionist will conceal the body, and the chanteuse must pick which of several active town information roles to cancel. The pack's illusionist is already tied to a visit or is exposed by a claim. Information landscape: Moderately informative but unverified. There are conflicting role claims, a trailseer and sentinel who have reported, and a tied vote. Hard confirmation exists only for any dead roles. The chanteuse does not know every hidden actor, such as a necromancer using a dead body. Stakes: Mid-game with several town information roles alive. One unblocked witness to the illusionist's visit can cost the pack a wolf and bring the pack's win condition much further away, so which witness gets blocked matters more than whether a block happens. Forward exposure: The block is private and can change every night, but a blocked player can say so publicly and name their intended target, which hands town a corroborating signal. An unblocked watcher's report then stands alone. Once the night resolves the choice cannot be undone, so a wrong pick leaves the illusionist's visit open to whoever you left free. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed information roles: a trailseer and a sentinel who reported night-1 results, a claimed healer, and unconfirmed sentinel, sigilist and healer slots. Nobody's claim is verified. The trailseer was the loudest threat to the pack, but the sentinel's watch on the victim was the result that actually exposed the illusionist.
lessons.action: When the pack is killing a victim and the illusionist will visit that body to conceal it, spend the block on the information role most likely to see that visit rather than defaulting to the trailseer. Block the sentinel if it has publicly used a watch and the victim is the kind of player it would watch (a scrutinized or quiet player). Block the trailseer only if it has already followed or named the illusionist. Hiding the body hides only the carrier's visit, so the illusionist's own visit stays visible to a watcher on the victim, or to a follower of the illusionist, unless the illusionist carried the kill itself.

lessons.situation: The pack has already settled its kill target and the chanteuse must choose a block target from the other town information roles, choosing between blocking the victim and blocking a different threat. Information landscape: Information-rich after day-two role claims, with public claims from the investigator, trailseer, and sigilist but no verified results. Stakes: Doubling the block on the kill target wastes the pack's single disruption and leaves another information role free to find a wolf. Spreading disruption keeps town results thin while the kill proceeds. Forward exposure: A block on a second player is a private visit that is only exposed if a Sentinel or Trailseer covers that player. Choosing the wrong player only wastes one night's block, and it can be changed next night. Target landscape: The kill target is the claimed investigator or trailseer. The block candidates are the other claimed information roles (a trailseer, sigilist, or investigator) and the suspected healer. The claims are public but unverified, so the choice rests on behavior.
lessons.action: When the pack kill is already aimed at one claimed role, use the roleblock on a different active threat, such as a claimed trailseer or an unresolved investigator, and not on the kill target. Pick the block target by which result would most expose the wolves. Never double up on the victim, because the kill itself already removes them.

lessons.situation: Midgame after a daytime elimination, with several town power roles publicly claimed. The Trailseer has incriminated a wolf partner or promised an overnight follow, and the Sentinel is confirmed or active. The wolves must choose whom to kill and whom to block. Information landscape: Information-rich: wills of dead roles are revealed, a Trailseer visit chain is public, a Sentinel has been verified, and a Vigilante has claimed. Stakes: The board is still a few eliminations from wolf parity, so a clean night that removes or neutralises the investigative claimants can keep the pack alive, while a wasted block leaves the claimants free to expose a wolf. Forward exposure: A block leaves no public record and the target alone learns they were roleblocked, so the move stays hidden if they die and is only a mild tell if they survive. The block is a visit, so a watcher or follower on you could see it, and it cannot be undone once placed. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed Trailseer, the confirmed or claimed Sentinel, a claimed Vigilante and quiet unconfirmed players. The claims rest on partial verification (a Sentinel catch, a visit chain), not on hard proof.
lessons.action: When town has publicly claimed active investigative roles (Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator) and you are in an information-rich midgame, aim the roleblock at the claimant most likely to act on the pack, and coordinate with your partner so the kill hits the other claimant or a high-threat role. If the kill is going to land on the claimant you would block, block the other active claimant, because a victim who dies makes the block redundant.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an abstain-heavy or one-sided day vote. The pack has chosen its kill, and the chanteuse must pick which town night action to cancel while claimed visit-readers could expose the pack. Information landscape: Moderately informed. There are public claims of visit-based roles, a few confirmed reveals or wills, and no hard evidence against the wolves. Claims are unverified but their roles are plausible. Stakes: Early game with town still numerous and no near parity. One watch or follow report that names a pack member can swing the next day's vote, so removing the visit-readers' information is worth more than a speculative block. Forward exposure: The block is private, but the blocked player is told and may announce a roleblock the next day, which shows that a Chanteuse exists without pointing at you. Blocking is a visit, so a watcher or tracker who is not blocked can still see it. The choice is reversible every night. Target landscape: Claimed Sentinel and Trailseer have public information-role claims backed by visit reports or a dead Sentinel's will. Unclaimed quiet or questioning players are judged on behavior only. The kill target is often the claimed watcher, whom a healer may save.
lessons.action: On night 2, block the claimed Sentinel or Trailseer whose watch or follow could cover the pack's kill or your own visit, and above all a claimed watcher who is the kill target. If both claim, block the one your pack's visits would pass in front of, and change the block target on later nights so you are not a repeated pattern.

lessons.situation: Day claims have exposed Town's information roles. The pack is killing one of them tonight, and you can neutralize a second one so the Town loses its information for the night. Information landscape: Moderately info-rich: public claims and a visible visit pairing, but few verified roles, and you cannot tell which claims are true beyond what the pack knows. Stakes: Town has several power roles in the open. Removing one checker by kill and blanking another in the same night gives a real information advantage, but the value fades if the Town then votes out the lone killer and you. Forward exposure: The blocked player learns they were roleblocked and can cite it by day, confirming a Chanteuse exists. If a Sentinel or Trailseer is on the target, your visit is named. The block is irreversible. Target landscape: Claimed Investigator, Sentinel, Trailseer and Healer, with some cross-confirmation between them. Silent players are the Vigilante, Sigilist and an unknown. Claims are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: On the night the pack kills a Town information role, block the other publicly active information role (claimed Sentinel or Investigator) so it cannot learn anything that night. Prefer a claimed role that is publicly confirmed or likely real, and expect the block to be named by day, so keep it to nights when blanking that role is worth the exposure.

lessons.situation: The wolves need to kill the town's investigative lead, who is likely protected by the healer. A chanteuse with a block available has to choose between blocking the victim, the healer, or another threat. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are partly confirmed by eliminations, a prior morning report verified the healer, and the investigator is publicly claimed or confirmed. Stakes: A failed kill leaves the investigator alive to check a wolf, which can lose the game. A successful block-and-kill removes the town's main source of wolf identification while the pack is thin. Forward exposure: A block on the healer is a private visit that nobody announces. A Sentinel watching or a Trailseer following the healer could still see the chanteuse's visit there. The block cannot be undone once placed, and a wrong guess wastes the night's block. Target landscape: The claimed or confirmed investigator is the kill target. A confirmed or probable healer is the block candidate. The trailseer and sigilist are secondary options. Evidence comes from earlier morning saves and claims, with the rest resting on behavior.
lessons.action: When the pack kill is aimed at the town's key information role (a claimed or confirmed investigator) and a healer may guard them, spend the roleblock on the most likely healer instead of the kill target. If the healer is unknown, block the most probable protector (the player the investigator most plausibly would be shielded by) rather than doubling the block on the victim.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 3) with the pack down to one or two wolves. The healer and other Town power roles have publicly claimed and cross-support each other, and the pack must get its kill through while limiting what Town learns. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: announced saves, mutually supporting role claims and a verified watch. Wolf chat agrees on the kill target, but the chanteuse does not know which power role will act against it. Stakes: With about six players alive and the lone killer gone or dying, each successful kill moves the wolves toward parity. A cancelled kill, or a surviving Investigator, can let the town vote the last wolves out, so the block decides whether the kill sticks. Forward exposure: A block is a visit, and the victim is told 'You were roleblocked'. If they report it, the town learns the chanteuse is alive and can narrow the suspect pool. The block cannot be undone, and repeating it on the same target builds a visible pattern. Target landscape: Several claimed Town power roles are alive: a healer backed by a save or a sentinel's watch, an Investigator, a Trailseer and a Vigilante. Their status rests on claims supported by announced saves and cross-confirming claims, not on hard verification. The healer or the sole living check source is the most valuable block.
lessons.action: When a protector (healer) has publicly claimed and been backed by a save or a watch, block the role most likely to cancel or expose the kill, whether the healer or the lone check source, so the pack's kill on its chosen target lands. If the healer is the pack's own target, block the Investigator or the next most dangerous information role instead and conceal the body.

lessons.situation: Day claims from several town power roles have been cross-verified. The wolves pick a power-role kill, and the chanteuse must choose which one claimed role to block that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: three or four town roles have publicly laid out their night actions, so it is clear who protects, who watches and who follows. The wolves' own visit patterns are exposed to those roles. Stakes: Mid-game with the wolves still outnumbered. A saved or detected kill costs a tempo the pack can't easily regain, while one clean kill plus one neutralized role keeps the pack on pace toward parity. Forward exposure: The block is a private visit that only a watcher or follower could see, so it reveals nothing publicly. It cannot be taken back once placed, and a wrong choice either lets a save go through (zero kills) or leaves a tracker free to see the pack's visits. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, sentinel, trailseer and healer, with night-one visits corroborated across their claims. The kill target is a claimed power role, and the block must pick between the healer, the tracker and the investigator on the basis of who threatens this night's outcome.
lessons.action: When the pack's kill target is a claimed power role and several town roles have publicly corroborated claims, point the block at the role whose action could undo or expose that night's plan. If the kill target was named as visited by a claimed healer, block that healer; if the claimed investigator still holds a check, block the investigator; if a claimed tracker could see the carrier or the illusionist at the victim's door, block that tracker.

lessons.situation: Four players are alive: two wolves, a claimed vigilante, and an unconfirmed player. The wolves need to identify a possible lone killer or neutral before the final votes. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead players' roles and wills are known, leaving one unconfirmed player whose role is unestablished. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity, so the next vote or kill decides the game. Using the block to identify the lone killer lets the wolves unite their votes on the right target instead of guessing. Forward exposure: A block that fails leaves no public trace, and the target does not learn they were tested. It commits only the chanteuse's visit that night. If the block takes, the target is told they were roleblocked, which reveals the wolves' action to them. Target landscape: The claimed vigilante (a killing threat), and an unconfirmed player with no established Town role who could be the lone killer or neutral. The block test is chosen by who remains unverified after dead roles and wills are known.
lessons.action: When a living player has no confirmed Town role and might be the lone killer, aim the roleblock at them while the pack kill goes on a known Town threat such as the claimed vigilante. If you are told the block did not take, that player cannot be blocked, which fits the lone killer or neutral (the rules say both are unblockable), and the pack should treat them as a likely lone killer when it chooses its next targets.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) with the pack's kill already chosen. You must choose whom to block, and the Town's tracking roles (Sentinel, Trailseer) may still be alive and able to see your visit and expose you. Information landscape: Starved or only partly informed: unverified claims, split or abstained votes, and behavioral reads. The one hard clue is your own private block result. Stakes: Mid-game with several Town roles alive, a lone killer still in play, and the pack needing several eliminations. Losing the Chanteuse to a traced visit costs the wolves their only blocker and a partner's cover, so staying unexposed matters more than a speculative block. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit. A Sentinel watching the target sees you, and a Trailseer following you sees where you went. The block cannot be undone, and a blocked player is told they were roleblocked, which confirms a Chanteuse exists. Blocking the watcher or follower removes that trace for the night but is itself a visit. Target landscape: Living Town power roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, claimed Investigator, Healer) plus quiet or vocal players. Roles are mostly unverified claims and behavioral reads, with no hard evidence on who is real. The Sentinel and Trailseer are the ones able to trace your visit.
lessons.action: Before choosing a block target, check which Town information roles (Sentinel, Trailseer) are alive and could register your visit. If one is alive and unblocked, block that watcher or follower first, or pick a target they are unlikely to be watching or following. Treat a 'block did not take' result as proof the target is the lone killer or neutral, and steer later blocks and pack kill suggestions accordingly.

lessons.situation: The wolves carry the kill this night, the Illusionist partner still has a conceal charge, and town has a Sentinel and a Trailseer alive whose results could trace the pack. Information landscape: Information-rich: a lone killer was caught by a Sentinel, a Trailseer reported tracking the partner wolf, and the roles of the claimants are known. Stakes: The Trailseer's claim has already put a wolf at risk of a vote, so removing the claimant and blinding the Sentinel on the same night is a swing for the pack, even though it cannot undo suspicion already placed on the partner. Forward exposure: Carrying the kill makes you the only wolf visiting the victim, but if the Illusionist hides the body the Sentinel and Trailseer see no trace of that visit. The block on the Sentinel is a separate visit that could still show up to a watcher or follower. A hidden role also denies town the role information, though it does not remove suspicion on the wolves. Target landscape: The kill choice is between the claimed Trailseer who points at a wolf partner and the confirmed Sentinel. The block goes on whichever informational role stays alive. Both rest on public claims and verified catches.
lessons.action: When you carry the kill and your Illusionist partner has a conceal charge left, kill the highest-threat claimant and block the one other town role that could watch the victim, such as the known Sentinel. The concealed victim's role and will stay hidden and the carrier's visit goes unseen, so the pack's footprint stays minimal.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later. The town has abstained or voted against wolves, and the chanteuse's role is at risk. An Investigator is publicly or privately identifiable, but the pack is tempted to block a tracker or another visible claim instead. Information landscape: Information-rich with claims, a roleblock admission, and a voting record. The Investigator's identity is plausible but not confirmed. Stakes: A single Suspicious read on the chanteuse can lead to a vote that costs the pack a wolf and its block. Spending the block on the checker protects that tempo. Forward exposure: The block leaves no public trace beyond what the blocked player says, and it makes no visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer would see unless they target you or the investigator. Blocking the investigator reveals only that a roleblocker exists. It can be changed each night. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed or identified Investigator, claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Sigilist, and unclaimed players. The Investigator is the only role whose result directly flags the chanteuse as Suspicious. Trailseer and Sentinel results depend on visits.
lessons.action: If a player has claimed or been shown to hold a check ability, or an Investigator is otherwise identified, make that player your night block rather than a tracker or a behavioral guess. A check reads a wolf as Suspicious, so a free Investigator can mark you, and only a block stops the check.

lessons.situation: Late midgame, with you as the last wolf or the carrier, choosing a kill and a block alone. The previous night's protective activity points to a Healer who would save your target. Information landscape: Fairly informed. A public strike or save is on record, but the Healer's and Investigator's roles are only suspected. No one has accused you yet. Stakes: The pack still needs several eliminations. A saved kill means no one dies and parity does not move, while an unblocked Healer gets to act again the next night. Forward exposure: Blocking the suspected Healer commits your block to a guess about who they are. A wrong guess wastes the block, and the blocked player can still tell the town. An unblocked Healer who saves the target also confirms their own role to the wolves. Target landscape: Six alive, one wolf left. Candidates are a Sigilist with a public strike, an unclaimed suspected Healer, and an Investigator with checks left, and none of their roles are confirmed except the Sigilist's strike. The kill target is the player the Healer most likely protects.
lessons.action: When you must pick both the kill and the block and a Healer is likely, block the suspected Healer on the night you attack a target they have reason to guard. Do not spend the block on an Investigator or other low-value target. A blocked Healer makes no protection, so the kill is more likely to land.
