Stakes: Four alive means one more elimination by vote sets up a night kill that leaves exactly two alive, which is a serial killer win. A fractured vote with no elimination or a wagon on you costs a full cycle and risks your removal. Consensus: The village is split across the three candidates and has no firm majority. Two voters are leaning toward one target on the basis of checks, visit reports, or lack of confirmation. My position: with majority Heat: Moderate to high. Someone voted against you or flagged you as not cleared, and a visit-based or voting-record clue loosely points your way. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and cannot be undone. It aligns you with one other voter and does not reveal your role. It also commits you to the elimination that moves the board toward the final night kill. Target landscape: Three other survivors: an unconfirmed claimant such as a healer, an aggressive accuser such as the speculator, and a claimed investigator or sentinel. Some are backed by evidence, such as a Suspicious check or being named as a victim's visitor, and some only by behavior. Public vs private: You privately know you are the serial killer and that removing any other player by vote sets up the two-alive win. Publicly you are only one of several unconfirmed suspects, and the investigator's note that a serial killer can read Not suspicious is the only thing pointing at you.
lessons.action: With four players left, vote with the plurality forming against a non-you player, joining the most credible accuser or the evidence-backed suspect, so the elimination lands and you are not the focus. Taking the count to three lets your night kill leave two alive, which wins you the game. If the room is split three ways, your vote is the one that makes the plurality decisive, so cast it on the same target as one other voter rather than scattering.

lessons.situation: The first day-2 vote after night-1 deaths. The village is either leadless and abstaining or piling onto a contested claim. You are the unsuspected Serial Killer who needs to survive to keep killing nightly. Information landscape: Information-starved to moderate: a few revealed night-1 dead roles, some unverified claims, and no caught lies or voting history that point to you. Stakes: The board is early, with many players alive and far from the Serial Killer's win threshold. The vote itself is not decisive, so the priority is to stay off the suspect list and alive for the next night kill. Consensus: The village is aligned, either on a unanimous abstain in a leadless day or on a near-unanimous pile-on against a contested claimant. The basis is the room's own discussion, not anything you supplied. My position: With the majority, riding a consensus built without you. Heat: Low to near zero: no one has accused or mentioned you, and you have spoken little or only in support of others. Forward exposure: A vote matching the room commits you to nothing about your role and is indistinguishable from the other votes. Votes are public and permanent, but an abstain can be changed the next day, and joining a shared target is tied to the room, not to you. Target landscape: Around nine or ten living players, with no or only unverified claims. Candidates are a contested claimant or no one, and the basis is behavioral or mechanical speculation rather than hard evidence. You are not among the candidates. Public vs private: You privately know you are the serial killer and caused a night-1 death. Publicly the deaths read as a wolf-side or generic night event, and no one suspects a separate lone killer.
lessons.action: On the first day-2 vote, when you are unsuspected and the room has no lead or has already converged on a target, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain if the room is abstaining, or join the existing pile-on). Don't drive a new accusation or take a lone stance, because a vote identical to the room's carries no tell about your role and keeps your cover for night kills.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a small group alive, where you (the Serial Killer) are on one of two or more competing elimination wagons and your single ballot can create a tie. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed investigator, sentinel, sigilist or healer results, prior vote records and a dead wolf's votes all feed the suspicion, though none are verified. Stakes: Few players remain, so one lynch of you ends the lone killer's game while a tie keeps you alive for another night kill. This vote is decisive. Consensus: The village is split among several wagons with no unified focus, so one vote can decide whether the leading wagon is tied. My position: holding out Heat: High. Several players, including claimed information roles or the surviving wolf, have already voted for or accused you over passivity or suspected night immunity. Forward exposure: A tie-forcing vote on a rival wagon or a lone-voted bystander leaves a visible but low-cost record, since votes are public and permanent. A lone vote on an accuser looks like retaliation and cannot be undone once the vote closes. Target landscape: Two to four competing wagons: yourself, a suspected wolf, and a quiet or lightly voted player. Role claims are partly unverified and the votes are driven by behavior and claimed results rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: The room publicly reads you as a suspect through low activity, a night-immunity deduction or a stray vote. Privately you know you are the serial killer and that your own ballot can decide whether you survive.
lessons.action: When you are an SK on a live elimination wagon, count the votes and cast your ballot so it makes the top counts tie, either by joining a rival wagon or by adding a vote to a lone-voted third player. A tie means no elimination, so the SK survives to kill again; a lone retaliatory vote on an accuser leaves your wagon alone in front.

lessons.situation: A day vote where the room has converged on eliminating a wolf-side player, accused by claimed town roles. The accused counter-accuses or deflects heat onto quiet players, possibly including you. Information landscape: Mostly claims and behavioral reads, with only partial corroboration (such as a sentinel or trailseer claim) and no hard verification until the reveal. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several players alive. Your vote does not decide the outcome, but sitting in the bloc keeps your profile clean while the wolves thin out ahead of your own kills. Consensus: Most of the village is aligned on one wolf-side target, with a five- to six-vote majority built on corroborating claims and behavioral reads. My position: With the majority. Heat: Low to mild. At most one stray mention, for example being called a quiet player, and nobody else picked it up. Forward exposure: A vote with the bloc reveals nothing and keeps your public record identical to the other voters'. The vote is irreversible, but eliminating a wolf you are not allied with is not something you need to undo. Target landscape: The main candidate is a wolf-side player accused by several players on a mix of claims (a sentinel or trailseer claim, or busing logic) and behavior, and denying it. The alternatives are a claimed town role the wolf accused back, or abstaining. No result is confirmed before the elimination. Public vs private: You privately know you are the lone killer and that the targeted player is a rival wolf-side player. Publicly you are just another quiet, unclaimed voter, so the vote costs you nothing.
lessons.action: When a wolf is the target of a majority-backed vote and you are only mildly mentioned or not accused, vote with the majority to eliminate that wolf. Your vote then matches the bloc's and gives the room nothing to pick at, and a wolf removed by a day vote costs you no night kill. Skip abstaining or voting off-bloc, since that is the only way to stand out.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame day vote with about five players alive. The room is converging on an unverified suspect and you, the lone killer, are unsuspected. A deviating vote would stand out. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple revealed roles, a public side pick, and a permanent voting record that later days will be read against. Stakes: With about five alive and a night kill still ahead, your survival matters more than steering this one vote. A stranded outlier vote is the cheapest way to turn a low-heat position into the next day's target. Consensus: The village is forming a majority on one unverified candidate, based on past votes and behavior. The board is information-rich, with several deaths and roles revealed and a public side pick announced. My position: Free to choose between joining the forming majority and holding out alone against it. Heat: Low to negligible. Discussion is focused on other players and no one is accusing you. Forward exposure: Every vote goes on the permanent public ledger and cannot be retracted. A lone vote against a claimed information role marks you as anti-Town if that player is later shown to be Town. Joining the majority commits you to nothing unusual. Target landscape: Two or three unverified candidates, such as an unconfirmed neutral with past-vote suspicion and a claimed information role with disputed results. The room leans toward one of them on behavioral reads, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer, immune to night attacks and removable only by a vote. Publicly you read as an ordinary unconfirmed player with almost no suspicion, and the room is debating other people.
lessons.action: When little or no suspicion is on you and the room is forming a majority against a plausible, unverified player, cast your vote with that majority. Do not cast an isolated vote against a claimed Town role or any other conspicuous target, because votes are public and permanent and a stranded outlier becomes the evidence later used to vote you out.

lessons.situation: After a night death in an information-rich mid-game, the village has locked onto a majority target. As the serial killer with low heat, I am tempted to cast a contrarian vote on a different player, a claimed information role or a quiet suspect, that cannot swing the result. Information landscape: Information-rich. Role reveals from night deaths, public check or follow claims, and the previous day's voting records are all available to be read against my vote. Stakes: Several players remain, so the vote can be fully survived if I stay unremarkable. The majority outcome is unaffected by my ballot, so a dissent gains almost nothing while adding a visible mark that can cost me the final-day vote. Consensus: Strong and decisive. A clear majority is already committed to one target after a night death or a claim chain, and the vote outcome is effectively fixed. My position: Holding out against a forming majority, which is the position this move corrects. Heat: Low. No one is accusing me, and a claimed check or the discussion has deflected suspicion elsewhere. Forward exposure: A vote against a decided majority is public and permanent, and it cannot be retracted. It invites scrutiny the next day, and opponents can cite it as proof I am the killer. A majority-aligned vote commits me to nothing unusual and can be changed later. Target landscape: A consensus suspect (a suspected wolf or a doubted information-role claimant) who is likely to fall regardless, versus a fringe alternative such as a quiet player or an information-role claimant. The consensus basis is behavior and claims; the alternative gives me little concrete evidence to justify a dissent. Public vs private: Privately I am the lone killer who caused the night deaths and reads Not suspicious. Publicly I am treated as low-heat or cleared town, and the room has settled on another target.
lessons.action: When the room has formed a clear majority on a target and your own heat is low, cast your vote with the majority. Hold the lone dissenting vote back for a case where it changes the result. A vote that cannot change the outcome only leaves a permanent outlier record, which opponents cite against you on later days.

lessons.situation: Late-game final vote with three to four players alive and the table pointing at you. Survival depends on whether your vote can combine with another player's vote to deadlock the tally. Information landscape: Rich: most roles are revealed or dead, records have been read out, and claims cross-confirm. The vote history and elimination logic point at you. Stakes: At four alive, losing this vote ends your game. A tie keeps you alive for another night, while a lone dissenting vote gives the town the elimination it wants. Consensus: The room is aligned against you by elimination of other roles, cross-confirmed claims, or a coordinated pair. The other living players are mostly voting as one bloc. My position: Holding out alone or with at most one ally against a majority bloc. Heat: High to critical. You are the last unverified or unrevealed player, or two players are openly coordinating against you, and the vote record is the evidence they are using. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and cannot be reversed. Voting an accuser commits you to open conflict with that player. Voting alone on a neutral or confirmed-looking player adds no pressure and confirms the room's read of you, whereas joining an ally's target can force a tie. Target landscape: The candidates are the lead accuser, the other accusers, and any ally who is also being pushed. Confirmed or cross-confirmed town roles are poor targets. A vote only helps if it matches an ally's vote and leaves the tally level. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving lone killer, immune to night attacks and removable only by a day vote. Publicly, the table has narrowed suspicion onto you by elimination or through coordinated accusations.
lessons.action: When the table is converging on you in a small endgame vote, count the votes before casting yours. If another living player is also under attack or will vote against your accusers, put your vote on the lead accuser they are voting for, so the tally ties and nobody is eliminated. Do not vote for a target nobody else will join, because a lone vote cannot change the result.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single kill or vote ends the game; a concealed victim costs a revealed role the town would otherwise get, but the cost of spending a conceal now is recoverable while two conceals remain for later nights when a more valuable victim may be available.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Using a conceal on tonight's pack victim would hide that victim's role and trace from the town and commit the illusionist's own visit to the body; the role stays hidden until game end and the use cannot be taken back, while holding it preserves the option for a later night.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no night results have been publicly shared, the Investigator died without a public check, and the Fortune Teller died without any bets known to the town; the only firm facts are the two deaths and the abstain vote.
query_dims.situation: Night 2 approaches as the illusionist with two conceals left and the pack's kill still unassigned; the village has just abstained on day 2 with no hard leads, and the wolf partner is actively steering the room. The question is whether tonight's victim is worth a conceal, given that a revealed town role and its record would give the village concrete information.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight living players on the board; no one has claimed a role publicly, and the two dead players are a Fortune Teller and an Investigator whose records were not publicly checked; no candidate has public evidence against them, so any pack target is chosen on behavior alone.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a thin day with an abstain or tied vote. The wolves, with the chanteuse, have agreed a kill and the illusionist decides whether to hide the victim's role. A partner may have been told the conceals are for a high-impact target. Information landscape: Information-starved: few or no hard leads, a few unverified role claims, no trace results shared, and the wolves unsure where the serial killer or necromancer is acting. Stakes: Early game with several enemies still alive, so no single kill ends it. The two conceals are the pack's scarce tempo tool, and wasting one on a low-value body costs more than a day of town uncertainty gains. Forward exposure: A hidden-role morning report tells the town an illusionist is in the pack, and the use is spent permanently. The hidden role cannot be reversed, and the count of used conceals lets the town track you. Target landscape: The choice is between quiet unclaimed players, whose roles are unknown and chosen for low profile, and a self-claimed info role such as an investigator with a check left. The kill choice rests on role value and behavior, not hard evidence. A conceal on a quiet victim wasted a use on a sentinel nobody had claimed.
lessons.action: On a night-2-style kill, spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a claimed or high-impact info role whose confirmed death or role would help the town, such as an investigator-claimant with a check left. If the victim is a quiet, unclaimed player, keep both uses and let the role be revealed. A spent use is permanent, and the count of hidden-role deaths becomes the town's tool for tracking you.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with the pack choosing a kill while the partner Chanteuse blocks a second threat. The Illusionist decides whether the victim is worth a conceal to deny the town role information and trace. Information landscape: Info-moderate: several dead players have public wills, a few living claimants are unverified, and the town's picture of the remaining roles is incomplete. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, and a hidden role plus a missing trace can keep the town from confirming who is left. Late in the game each conceal is scarce and carries real weight. Forward exposure: Using a conceal makes the morning say an illusionist hid the role, so the town learns an illusionist exists, though not who. Each use is permanent and cannot be undone. Once both are spent, every later kill shows its role and the carrier's visit can be traced. Target landscape: Candidates are an unclaimed voter whose role is unknown, a claimed Trailseer whose follow results threaten the pack, and a claimed Vigilante who can be blocked instead of killed. All roles are unverified, and the choice rests on behavior and threat level, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: While conceals remain, put one on a night kill whose victim is an unverified or high-information-value player, or a tracking threat such as a claimed Trailseer. Hiding the role also removes the carrier's visit to that victim from a Sentinel's watch or a Trailseer's follow, and leaves the town unsure which role is gone. Keep the last conceal for the kill where that traceless result matters most.

lessons.situation: Late game after the lone killer is gone, with one or two wolves left against a Town that still has an information role able to catch a wolf. The illusionist is choosing whether to commit a limited conceal on tonight's pack kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, claims and watch records are public, and voting records exist. The remaining private results are the main danger to the wolves. Stakes: The board is close to wolf parity, so one surviving investigative result can decide whether a wolf is exposed and voted out. Concealing the right victim's role and will removes that risk, but a charge spent on a harmless victim is wasted. Forward exposure: Concealing signals to the village that an illusionist is active and spends a charge that cannot be recovered. Hiding the body leaves no trace at the victim's door when the illusionist carries the kill. It does not erase the victim's earlier public claims or votes. Target landscape: Living Town investigators and watchers (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and unconfirmed players. Picks rest on who threatens the wolves' cover through private results, rather than on neutral or low-threat players.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a Town role whose private result or will would expose a wolf, such as an Investigator, Sentinel or Trailseer holding a result on you. Otherwise save the charge, since a hidden body does not erase what the victim already said or voted in public. If you carry the kill yourself, the concealed kill leaves no trace at the victim's door, so prefer that route when a watcher or follower is alive.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game, no day-1 vote, no claims. The illusionist and chanteuse agree on a default kill, and the illusionist weighs spending one of two conceals on a victim of unknown role. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, claims, votes or night results. The only knowledge is the pack's private plan. Stakes: The board is early and far from parity, so a single kill is not decisive. The scarce resource is the two conceals, which are worth more on a later high-value body than on a blind first kill. A spent conceal on a neutral or low-value body is wasted, and an unspent one also stays usable by a Necromancer through a revealed body. Forward exposure: Holding costs nothing and is reversible. Spending a conceal is irreversible, announces that an illusionist exists, and leaves your own visit visible to a Sentinel or Trailseer unless you carried the kill yourself. Not carrying also leaves no trace on you. Target landscape: The pack's night-1 victim is an arbitrary quiet player with no claims or behavioral evidence. Nobody knows their role, including the wolves, so the value of hiding it is only speculative.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the kill is an arbitrary pick with no claims or reads, keep both conceals and let the chanteuse carry the kill so you make no visit at the victim's door. Spend a conceal later, on a victim whose revealed role or will would give town real information, such as a claimed investigator, trailseer, sentinel or healer.

lessons.situation: Early night 2. Town power roles have claimed and reported night-1 results that threaten the wolves' cover. The pack agrees to kill one claimant, with the Illusionist deciding whether to spend one of its two conceals on that kill. Information landscape: Information-rich. Public claims and night-1 results are on the table, and day-2 vote records already show wolves voting together. A same-night partner death (sigil strike or Serial Killer) can expose the pack no matter what the Illusionist hides. Stakes: Mid-game with several town power roles alive. Removing a threatening claimant matters, but the conceal charges are scarce. Spending one where the role is already known gains little, and a wolf partner's death or vote record can confirm the pack anyway. Forward exposure: A conceal is irreversible and spends one of two charges. The morning report will say 'Their role is hidden by an illusionist', which confirms an Illusionist is in play. It hides the carrier's visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer, but it cannot hide a wolf partner's death or the voting records. Target landscape: Day-2 kill choices among self-claimed power roles (a claimed Trailseer or Sentinel reporting night-1 visits, a claimed Investigator) versus unrevealed players. The claimed roles are accusations based on claims, not verified results. Their roles are already public, so concealing the body adds little uncertainty.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the victim's role is still unclaimed, or when a living Sentinel or Trailseer could otherwise trace the carrier to the victim's door. If the victim has already publicly claimed their role and no tracker threatens the carrier, kill without concealing and keep both charges for a later night. When the Illusionist itself carries the kill, a conceal leaves no trace at that door, so favor it for that night.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, after claims, deaths or votes have created information-bearing town roles. The pack picks a kill, and the illusionist decides whether to conceal the body of a role that matters. Information landscape: Moderately informed: some claims, bodies and records exist but are unverified. Concealing can deny the town role counts and confirmations. Stakes: With fewer players alive, each kill moves the pack closer to parity, and each revealed body feeds town deduction, or a Necromancer's use of the body. Denying role confirmation on a key kill matters more now than on night 1, and unspent conceals are worthless if the illusionist is voted out first. Forward exposure: Irreversible: it spends a use and announces that an illusionist is in play. If you carry the kill and conceal it, you leave no trace at that door. If another wolf carries, your hiding visit can still be seen by a Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Kill candidates are identified by claims or behavior, such as claimed information roles whose role or will would aid the town, rather than by a blind random pick. The pack's reads are partial and unconfirmed.
lessons.action: When the pack targets a town role whose revealed body or record would help the town, such as a claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator or Healer, carry the kill yourself and conceal it. A carrier who conceals leaves no trace at the victim's door, and the town gets neither a role nor a will. If you are not carrying, accept that your own visit stays visible to watchers and followers, and weigh that before spending the conceal.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3. The pack has agreed to kill a vocal claimed investigative role, and the serial killer may be attacking the same player. The illusionist must decide whether a conceal is worth spending on this body. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich. Public claims, a tied or abstained day vote, and recorded votes exist, but most roles are unconfirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with parity still a few eliminations away. A wasted conceal costs the pack one of only two uses and gains little, while a well-placed one hides a role the town would otherwise learn. Forward exposure: Spending a conceal is irreversible and uses up a limited ability. On an already-public claim it buys almost no information denial, and the morning report still says an illusionist acted. Target landscape: The pack's candidate is a player who has publicly claimed Trailseer or Sigilist, unverified but already stated. Other candidates are unclaimed players whose roles would be new information if revealed. The pack picked the target on threat and claim rather than confirmed role.
lessons.action: Keep the conceal for a kill whose role the town does not yet know, such as an unclaimed or unverified player, where hiding the role and will denies real information. If the planned victim has already publicly claimed a role and shared results, let the role reveal stand and keep the use for a later night.

lessons.situation: Night 1, the pack's first kill, with a conceal on offer and a blind target pick between the illusionist and its wolf partner. Information landscape: No public information at all, only the pack's private chat; nothing is known about anyone's role or night immunity. Stakes: The game is at its start with no pressure on the pack, so the main stake is keeping both conceals for when a role reveal would help the town. Nothing about night 1 forces an early conceal. Forward exposure: A conceal on a victim who survives is kept and shows the town nothing. Holding it back is fully reversible, since both uses stay open for a night when a role reveal would hurt the pack. Target landscape: A single quiet, unclaimed player chosen by default; no claims, reads, votes or deaths. The target's immunity to night kills is unknown, and it could be the lone killer.
lessons.action: With both conceals available and no information on the first-night victim, agree to the pack's kill but hold the conceals for a later night when a power role or a likely-to-die target is the victim. A conceal is only spent if the victim dies, but committing it early to an unscouted quiet player offers no gain, since that target may be night-immune (like a lone killer) and the night-1 kill may fail silently.

lessons.situation: You are the last wolf with unspent conceals facing a daytime vote that may eliminate you, with confirmed town killers still alive. Information landscape: Partly information-rich: town roles are confirmed and your partner is dead, but a lone killer is only hinted at. Whether the healer will cover the target is unknown. Stakes: Dying with unused conceals wastes your remaining power. A successful hidden kill shrinks the town and obscures the evidence needed to eliminate you, while an idle night gains nothing. Forward exposure: A concealed kill still announces the attack and marks a wolf as alive, but the hidden role and hidden carrier trace give town no role or visit evidence. If the victim survives, the conceal is refunded and nothing is hidden, so the exposure is limited. Target landscape: Choose among players not just saved by the healer; the confirmed vigilante and sentinel are the threats worth removing, while quiet unverified players are the cheaper pick. Role status is mostly public.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with conceals in hand and town closing in, use a kill on a target the healer is unlikely to cover and conceal that victim's role. This hides your carrier visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer and denies town the role information, rather than skipping the night and giving up all pressure.

lessons.situation: The pack is deciding whether to spend the kill and a conceal on the claimed investigator or sentinel, who is the town's information lead, while the healer's likely protection is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: public claims on night-one visits and clearings reveal the town's information lead and its probable guard, and the pack's private knowledge exposes a night-immune player. Stakes: A wasted kill on a protected power role gives the town a free night and keeps its information lead alive. The conceal is refunded, but tempo is lost and the pack is exposed to counterattack, such as from a serial killer. Forward exposure: Authorizing a conceal on a protected target gets no kill, so the charge is refunded. It still commits the pack's kill to a target the town can predict, and a failed attack leaves the claimed power role alive and more trusted. The illusionist's visit to hide the body also shows up to watchers if the attack succeeds. Target landscape: Claimed sentinel or investigator as the obvious priority. Alternatives are unverified quiet players or a known night-immune player (who cannot be killed at night). Evidence is mostly public claims rather than hard reads.
lessons.action: When the most prominent claimed power role (investigator or sentinel) has already been attacked and saved, or a healer claim makes protection of it predictable, steer the pack kill to a different target and hold both conceals. If the town has no healer claim yet, the power role can be killed and concealed, but only if the pack accepts that the healer may be guarding it.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later: the pack picks a claimed power role as the kill and the illusionist plans a conceal. A Healer claim or a previous protective visit to that target makes a save plausible, and the illusionist's own visit may be watched. Information landscape: Info-starved to thin: unverified claims, partial night-1 traces and one or two deaths. Hard facts are sparse, and the Healer's protection target is unknown. Stakes: With the pack down to one or two wolves, every visible visit risks heat and every failed kill wastes a night. A saved victim also leaves the illusionist as a known visitor, which can steer the vote toward the pack. Forward exposure: Your visit at the victim's door is irreversible. If the victim is saved, the conceal is kept but nothing is hidden, and the Sentinel or Trailseer sees you as a visitor. Target landscape: Claimed power roles (Investigator, Trailseer, Vigilante) are the obvious kill picks, but a Healer may have protected the same target before. Choosing is mostly a guess among living players, based on threat to the wolves rather than evidence.
lessons.action: When you are the carrier, or the pack's only wolf, and the kill target is a likely protected role (such as a claimed Investigator or Trailseer with a Healer visit onto them), prefer a target the Healer is less likely to guard, or accept that your visit may be seen. A conceal hides the carrier's visit only if the victim dies; if the Healer saves the victim, every visit to them stays visible to a Sentinel watch or a Trailseer follow, so do not rely on it as cover.

lessons.situation: Your partner carries the kill, or you do, on a role that has already claimed publicly. You have one conceal left and must decide whether to spend it or save it. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims, with several roles claiming results, but nothing verified. Stakes: With no extra conceals after this one, each use should hide something that cannot be inferred from claims. A revealed will carries a limited cost, but spending the last conceal on an already claimed role removes your flexibility for later kills. Forward exposure: Letting the body be revealed publishes the victim's role and any Town will, which may confirm their visit records. This is a one-night choice, and the conceal charge stays available for a later night. Target landscape: A claimed Town power role, such as a Sentinel with a public claim, is the pack's target. Other claimed power roles are active, and the claims are not confirmed.
lessons.action: If you have only one conceal left and the victim's role is already public from a claim, or the victim's will would reveal little, hold the conceal and let the role be announced. Keep it for a later kill of an unclaimed or higher-value role, and use the night's blocks and coordination on other threats.

lessons.situation: Opening night, discussion-only day 1. The wolves must choose a first kill and decide whether the illusionist carries it, and whether to spend a conceal on a victim of unknown value. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or night results, so the target is a blind pick and any Sentinel or Trailseer who happens to be on the victim or carrier is invisible to the pack. Stakes: Early game with the wolves far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The cost that matters is a visit trail from the carrier that a watcher or tracker could use on day 2 or 3, which can get a wolf eliminated and cost the pack a member early. That outweighs keeping both charges in reserve. Forward exposure: Concealing makes the morning report say the role is hidden by an illusionist, which confirms an illusionist exists. It spends one of two charges if the victim dies, and the use cannot be undone. In return it removes the carrier's visit trace from any Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Nine or so living players, none having claimed a role and none read. The pack chooses a quiet, unclaimed target on behavior alone, so the victim's role and any watcher on them are unknown.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the pack picks an unread target and you are the one carrying the kill, spend one conceal on that victim. If the victim dies, your visit leaves no trace for a Sentinel watching them or a Trailseer following you, and if you carried the kill yourself you leave no trace at that door at all. If the victim survives, nothing is hidden and the charge is kept.

lessons.situation: Opening night with ten players alive. The wolves must choose a first kill blind and decide whether to commit a conceal charge on the victim. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no roles are confirmed, no discussion has happened, no deaths or claims exist, and the wolves know only their own partner. Stakes: Early game with a large cushion: one kill cannot decide the game. The value is information, since a hidden early victim denies Town a role reveal, and a night-immune target exposes the lone killer at no cost. Forward exposure: Low exposure: a conceal leaves no public trace, a failed attack is never announced, and a kill on a concealed victim leaves no visit for a Sentinel or Trailseer to see. The only commitment is possibly spending one of two conceals on a low-value role, and a failed attack refunds it. Target landscape: Seven unconfirmed non-wolf players with no claims, no public visits and no voting record. The pack picks a quiet player blindly, and the choice rests on no evidence or behavior.
lessons.action: On night one with both conceals unspent and no information, submit a conceal alongside the pack's kill on an unrevealed, quiet target. If the target dies, their role stays hidden and the Illusionist learns it, and if the attack fails because the target is night-immune, the conceal is kept and the pack learns the lone killer.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, night 2 or 3. The pack has a failed or contested night behind it and agrees to remove a claimed protector or information role. The carrier makes the kill, perhaps while the Chanteuse blocks another claimant, and the Illusionist decides whether to conceal the body. Information landscape: Moderate information: save announcements, conflicting role claims, and Sentinel or Trailseer reports that are claims only. Nothing about the victim's role is confirmed by the Game Master. Stakes: The board is mid-game, with the pack still a few eliminations from parity and a lone killer possibly alive. Removing the protector or the information source without giving the town a confirmed role widens the pack's lead. A failed kill leaves the wolves exposed to the Healer and the Vigilante. Forward exposure: The conceal is spent only if the victim dies; a save keeps it and leaves nothing hidden. Once spent it cannot be recovered. A hidden body gives the town no role or will, but it also tells them the Illusionist exists and that the pack made the kill. Target landscape: Candidates are publicly claimed power roles: a claimed Healer inferred from a save announcement, a claimed Sentinel whose watch tied a partner to a scene, and a rival Investigator claimant leading an accusation. All are unverified, and the pack picks them on behavior and public logic rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack's agreed kill is a claimed power role (Healer, Investigator or Sentinel) whose confirmed role or will would help the town, spend a conceal on it. The conceal costs nothing if the victim is saved, since the use is kept, so commit even without knowing the Healer's target. When the victim dies, the town cannot verify the claim and the pack loses nothing it needed to hide.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a close or tied day vote. The wolves are killing a player who drew vote suspicion. Sentinel and Trailseer have been active or have claimed results. Information landscape: Day talk produced a healer claim, a watch result and a follow result, but nothing hard on the wolves. Watchers are plausibly active and you cannot tell which door they chose. Stakes: Mid-early board where being exposed as the illusionist costs the pack a key wolf. The marginal value of hiding an ordinary victim's role is small next to the risk of a logged visit turning suspicion onto you. Forward exposure: If you are not the carrier, your hide-visit is still seen by a watcher on the victim's door, which can lead to a day accusation against you. The conceal cannot be undone and costs a charge, and the pack's kill visit stays hidden either way. Target landscape: The victim is a quiet or lightly suspected player pulled into a day vote, with no confirmed role. A watcher may be on the same door, and the reason to hide is that the reveal could clear them or point at the voters.
lessons.action: With a Sentinel or Trailseer plausibly active and the day having produced watch or follow claims, conceal only when you are the carrier, or when the secrecy of the victim's role clearly outweighs the risk of your hide-visit being logged. Otherwise keep the charge and let the pack's kill resolve unconcealed, because a visit seen at the victim's door can get you accused and eliminated.

lessons.situation: Late game, you are the last wolf and lone carrier after your partner died, with one conceal left and trackers or watchers alive. You decide whether to carry and hide the kill. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: some town confirmations exist (an Investigator's read on the lone killer), but the town has no read on you. Stakes: You are the only wolf left, so each kill must also keep you hidden. A trace-free kill gives you a night of cover, but the town is still ahead on numbers. Forward exposure: The morning report announces a hidden-role death, which shows town an illusionist exists and the conceal is spent. Afterward every kill is fully revealed, and the victim's true role (for example a Speculator's pick) may become public and either support or contradict your story. Target landscape: Several unclaimed town and neutral players with no hard reads on you. The victim is chosen from an unclaimed pool by behavior, not evidence, and a tracker who followed you only once is still alive.
lessons.action: As the last wolf with a conceal left, carry the kill yourself and conceal the victim, because an illusionist who carries and conceals leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer. Pick a victim whose role you do not need confirmed, and use the 'no visit' result a follower will report to build a cover story. Spend the conceal on a night when the carrier is you and a tracker or watcher is alive.

lessons.situation: Late game with a tied vote just behind and no conceals left. The pack must stop a claimed Vigilante's remaining shot, and the Illusionist has to judge whether a kill plus a block holds. Information landscape: Info-moderate: the Vigilante claimant said they were blocked and had one bullet left, and the town's other claims are unverified. Stakes: Losing a wolf here leaves a lone wolf against several town players and a vote that can end the game. One failed block or shot can flip which side is ahead. Forward exposure: With no conceals, the victim's role is shown and the carrier's visit can be traced by watchers or followers. Backing a kill on a claimed Vigilante commits the pack to that target for the night, and a failed block cannot be taken back. Target landscape: A claimed Vigilante who may have one bullet left, versus a claimed Investigator whose checks are spent. The pack picks the Vigilante on shot threat alone, with no verified evidence.
lessons.action: Before the last conceal is gone, have the pack kill one player and block the other main threat in the same night. Do not rely on a single block to stop a Vigilante who can still shoot, since a block that fails leaves the shot live and can cost the pack a wolf. If both conceals are spent, favor a kill and block pairing that does not leave your partner exposed to a shot.

lessons.situation: The pack is about to kill a claimed investigative player. The illusionist is deciding who carries the kill and whether to spend a conceal, with a hidden Sentinel watch or Sigilist sigil possible. Information landscape: Thin on hidden roles. You do not know whether a Sentinel is watching the door or a sigil is on you, though public Trailseer and Sigilist claims exist. Stakes: Losing the illusionist to a sigil or an exposed trace would cripple the pack's late game and speed a vote against it. Careful carrier choice protects the remaining conceals. Forward exposure: A non-carrier's conceal visit is visible to a Sentinel watching the victim. Carrying the kill yourself leaves no trace at that door but makes you an attacker that night, which a sigil on you would punish. Neither can be undone once the night resolves. Target landscape: The pack's victim is an unconfirmed claimant such as the Trailseer, or a self-claimed Sigilist. The serial killer may hit the same victim, and a Sentinel or Sigilist whose position is unknown may be targeting you or the victim's door.
lessons.action: If you conceal, carry the kill yourself, because then you leave no trace at that door and the carrier's visit is hidden from a Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer following the carrier. If a Sigilist with sigils left is alive or likely, or it is not your turn to carry, let the pack's kill go unconcealed instead of visiting the body as a non-carrier. A non-carrier's visit to hide the body stays visible to a watcher on that door, and a carrier's attack can be punished by a sigil.

lessons.situation: Late game after a tied day vote, you are the last wolf with no conceals left. You must pick a kill among the few remaining town players, who are contesting each other's claims. Information landscape: Info-rich on the town side (a confirmed read on the lone killer, claim conflicts), but the town has not yet worked out your role. Stakes: Two more eliminations bring you to parity. Each night kill decides whether you reach it before the town votes you out. Forward exposure: The kill reveals the victim's role and will, and your carrier visit is visible to any surviving watcher or follower. Because you are the next carrier, a sigil placed on you can strike, and the action cannot be undone. Target landscape: Four living town players (Sigilist, Healer, Investigator, Trailseer) with no hard reads. The Trailseer was chosen because their tracking results threatened your claim, on public behavior rather than evidence.
lessons.action: With no conceals left and you as the carrier, kill the player whose night result most directly threatens your cover, such as a Trailseer or Sentinel who has followed or watched you. Expect the revealed role and will to expose their record, so choose the target whose record does less damage than their living results would.

lessons.situation: You are the sole surviving wolf after your partner died, choosing the night kill while the healer is known to be active and protecting a publicly attacked player. Information landscape: Information-rich: the game master announced a save on the sentinel, and some town roles are confirmed. The wolves' own stats are known, but the healer's next protection is unknown. Stakes: With one wolf left and a lone killer possibly still alive, each night kill is critical. A wasted kill lets town investigators close in, while one real kill moves the wolves toward parity. Forward exposure: The kill is a lone carry that ties the night's attack to you as the only wolf. Once the target is chosen it is irreversible, and a wasted attack on a healer-covered target gains nothing and removes no town role. Target landscape: Candidates include a claimed sentinel already publicly saved by the healer, a claimed investigator with clears, a confirmed vigilante holding one bullet, and a quiet unverified player. The evidence is public announcements of the saves, not behavior.
lessons.action: As the last wolf, aim the pack kill at a player who was not publicly attacked and saved the previous night, such as a quiet unverified player or a confirmed threat the healer is not visibly guarding. Keep your conceals unspent until a kill is likely to succeed, since a conceal is refunded if the victim survives; if the healer's likely target is unclear, pick the target that was not the previous night's save.

lessons.situation: Repeated wolf attacks on the claimed investigator were repelled by the healer's protection. The remaining wolf must choose between hitting the investigator again and breaking the protection cycle. Information landscape: Information-rich: investigator, healer and sentinel have publicly claimed roles, targets and results, and morning save announcements show the pattern of protection. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity and the protection cycle is the main obstacle. Removing the healer opens the way to the next power-role kill and to winning. Forward exposure: Spending the last conceal leaves zero charges, so later visits to victims are traceable. The kill itself is irreversible. A conceal on a victim who survives is refunded, and a hidden-role morning report only signals that an illusionist is active. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, who survived repeated attacks, versus the claimed healer, who openly took credit for the saves. Both are public claims backed by morning save announcements rather than by behavior alone.
lessons.action: When a claimed healer has been blocking the pack's kills on the claimed investigator or sentinel, aim the pack kill at the claimed healer and spend a conceal on that body. A hidden role denies the town confirmation and the Necromancer a usable body. If the healer is dead, protection stops and the next kill on the power role should land.

lessons.situation: Night after your wolf partner was voted out and revealed. You are the lone wolf and your public vote pattern made you the likely suspect for a Vigilante. Information landscape: Info-rich about your exposure: a revealed wolf confirms your side, and your vote pattern is public and permanent. Stakes: As the lone wolf and prime suspect you can be killed by a Vigilante shot or sigil strike tonight, so passivity loses the game while a kill buys time. Forward exposure: A kill with a conceal leaves no trace at that door but spends your last conceal. Staying home leaves you exposed to a Vigilante shot or a sigil strike, and a sigil on you only strikes if you attack that night. Target landscape: Remaining town are claimed Sentinel, claimed Healer, Vigilante and Sigilist, with roles known only through claims. The Sigilist who pushed the case on your partner is a high-value target.
lessons.action: As the last wolf when your vote record or partner's reveal makes you a prime suspect, use the night to act instead of staying home. Carry the kill on the player most likely to hold a night killing role or to have deduced you (such as a Vigilante or Sigilist), and use a remaining conceal so the victim's role and your carrier visit stay hidden. If you cannot tell who that is, still make the kill rather than pass.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with you as the sole surviving wolf. A sigilist with a sigil left has publicly said they will target you, or has already used a sigil to kill your partner. Any kill you make would reach or approach parity, and the sigil strikes anyone who attacks that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, the investigator's record or will clears one living player, and the sigilist's earlier strike or sigil result is public. The sigilist's suspicion of you is explicit. Stakes: One more death reaches or nearly reaches wolf parity, but the sigil can strike you on the same night and end the game for the wolves. A wrong attack loses the game immediately, while holding the kill only postpones the decision to the vote. Forward exposure: Attacking is a visit and an attack. It commits you to a kill that a sigil on you would punish with your own death, and it cannot be undone once the night resolves. Holding the kill reveals nothing and keeps your conceals available. Target landscape: Two or three living players remain: a publicly known or claimed sigilist whose earlier sigil result is confirmed, a player cleared by the investigator who is probably the healer, and possibly one quiet unconfirmed player. Roles come from public evidence and the sigilist's stated intentions, but which target holds an unspent sigil is unknown.
lessons.action: When you are the last evil player and a sigilist has a sigil left and has publicly named or suspected you, hold the kill that night. Your own attack triggers the sigil and the sigil strike still kills you even if the attack succeeds, and a conceal does not help if the healer saves the target. Keep your conceals and let the vote decide, rather than attacking into a possible sigil.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination can end the game, so the pick is not forced this turn, but a speculator that dies unpicked loses outright, so the pick must be made before a death becomes likely.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved. One night-kill record (player_9 investigator, night 2), one lynch record (vigilante, night 1 roleblock, night 2 held fire), public day-2 abstain vote and day-3 vote split, and unverified visit-direction requests with no result claims yet made publicly.
query_dims.situation: As the unpicked speculator, you face the day-3 aftermath: the town just lynched a vigilante, the discussion is now asking who received night results and who visited whom, and the village has no confirmed wolf. Dying without a pick loses, so the open question is whether the board is trending toward Town, the Wolves, or a lone killer strong enough to make a pick worthwhile now.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight players alive; the decision is whether and when the speculator makes its one irreversible side pick, which must be chosen among Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or itself. Public role status: the day-3 vote eliminated a player revealed as a vigilante (claimed night-1 roleblock, held fire night 2); player_9 was revealed as an investigator killed night 2. Evidence basis: only the vote record and the claims about night 1; no confirmed wolf identity and no confirmed lone killer identity.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game (nights 2-3) with the speculator alive and unpicked. One wolf has been voted out or a Town save has been announced, but the lone killer and at least one wolf are still hidden. Killers are active every night. Information landscape: Mixed. Some announced facts exist (a revealed wolf death, an announced save, dead power roles), but most night results are unverified claims. The strength of the evil factions is inferred from counts and trend, with no confirmation of the lone killer. Stakes: The board is not at the brink, but each night a hidden killer or wolf can remove the speculator before it picks, and that is a guaranteed loss. The pick is permanent, so a Town pick pays off only if Town survives the lone killer, and Town did lose to a hidden Necromancer or the wolves in some games. Picking by night 2-3 locks in the likeliest winner while the speculator is still alive. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town has the most living members and often a revealed wolf death or verified saves. The wolf pack and lone killer are mostly hidden, and the self pick only wins by being the last player standing. The read rests on public counts and trend more than on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Once Town has a confirmed evil kill or a clear numbers lead (for example a wolf revealed dead and Town power roles still alive), spend your one pick on Town that night. If no side looks clearly ahead, still pick by night 2 or 3, because dying unpicked is an automatic loss and Town is the default side with the most players.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after one or two evil eliminations (Chanteuse, Illusionist, or Serial Killer). Town looks ahead and the Speculator must decide whether to lock in its single pick now or wait. Information landscape: Mostly information-rich: role reveals for dead evil players and a validated Sentinel watch. Some gaps remain: one wolf or the lone killer may be hidden behind a cleared read, and the claimed Investigator and Healer are unverified. Stakes: Town holds a clear numerical majority, but one remaining killer, or a double-kill night, could strip key roles and reverse the lead. The pick is permanent and the Speculator has no other ability, so timing matters more than the margin shown. Target landscape: Town, the wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town looks dominant after the Serial Killer and one or two wolves were eliminated. Evidence is mixed: a confirmed Sentinel result and role reveals for the dead, but the remaining evil's identity is only inferred from behavior or from unverified Investigator claims.
lessons.action: Pick Town only once both the wolves and the lone killer are confirmed dead or identified and Town's investigative and protective core is still alive. If a hidden killer is still unaccounted for, or a likely double-kill night is coming, delay the pick one more night, because a Speculator that dies before picking loses.

lessons.situation: Night 1 (or early night 2) of a ten-player game, with the Speculator's single irreversible pick unspent and nothing established yet. Delaying risks an unannounced night kill by the wolves or the serial killer, which would make the Speculator lose automatically. Information landscape: Information-starved: day 1 was discussion only with no vote, no deaths, no verified claims, and no check results. Any read would be behavioral at best. Stakes: The board is far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The Speculator's own survival to the pick is the main risk: dying unpicked is a guaranteed personal loss, while an early Town pick costs little and keeps the win tied to the largest side. Target landscape: Four sides: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or self. No deaths, claims, or votes exist, so the choice rests on prior side sizes: Town has six roles, wolves two, the lone killer one, and a pick of self wins only as last one standing.
lessons.action: On the first night where you still hold your pick and nothing has been confirmed, lock in your pick right away instead of waiting. Choose Town, the largest side (six Town roles against two wolves, one lone killer and you), since a Speculator that dies unpicked loses and any night attack can remove you before you act. If a night-2 report has already confirmed the wolves are dead or clearly outnumbered, pick Town immediately.

lessons.situation: A morning after a visible Town success (a lone killer or wolf voted out, or the claimed Investigator saved by the Healer) tempts the Speculator to commit to Town at once. Wolves remain hidden, and Town can still fracture through mis-votes, friendly fire or losing its Healer. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of eliminated players are confirmed and the Investigator's checks are on record. What is missing is the identity of the surviving evil players and whether Town can keep up its voting discipline. Stakes: Town leads comfortably, so an early pick gains little extra. The pick is permanent and announced. Both games showed Town collapsing after the pick through mis-eliminations and the loss of its Healer, which let the wolves win and left the Speculator with a loss. Waiting costs nothing while the Speculator is safe, and the risk is dying unpicked. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or Self. Town leads on numbers, with a living Investigator and Healer. One evil faction is already confirmed dead, but one or two wolves, or a lone killer, are still hidden. The Self pick is unrealistic. Confirmed kills and checks are the evidence; Town's cohesion is only a behavioral read.
lessons.action: When Town looks dominant only because one evil side was just removed, but a wolf or lone killer is still hidden or alive, keep the one pick unspent for another night while the Speculator is not under suspicion. Lock in Town once the remaining evil is down to one hidden wolf with Town's key roles intact. If the Speculator becomes a likely target, pick the leading side right away, because dying unpicked is a loss.

lessons.situation: Midgame, day 3 or later. One evil faction member has just been voted out with a confirmed role, and Town is clearly ahead of what remains. The speculator has not picked and is alive and unexposed. It faces a choice between waiting for more information and locking in a side now. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: a system-confirmed role reveal from the elimination, dead roles revealed, and public vote records showing the village voting together. One or two evil players remain unconfirmed. Stakes: Town's lead over the remaining evil is real but not unbeatable. Evil kills each night, and the speculator is an ordinary kill target. Dying unpicked is a guaranteed loss, so each night of delay costs more than the extra information is worth. Target landscape: Four options: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or itself. By now at least one evil faction is eliminated and revealed (a wolf or the lone killer). Town still has a numerical majority over the remaining evil, and the evidence is public reveals and vote records rather than behavior. A self-pick is almost impossible to win.
lessons.action: Once a night arrives in which a lone killer or wolf has been voted out and revealed and the roles left show Town holding a clear majority edge over the remaining evil, spend your single pick that night on Town instead of waiting. The pick is not a visit and cannot be blocked. If you die before picking you lose, and a pick made first still counts after you die.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive, and the leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this night is consequential but not a single-action swing.
query_dims.forward_exposure: The public abstention is permanent and commits no daytime target. The coordinated night actions are private: blocking a target or carrying out the kill would not publicly reveal the actor, but the block is spent for the night and a successful kill cannot be reversed.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is limited and mostly claims: the Investigator claimant reports a Not suspicious check, the Sentinel claimant reports a visitor, and a follower’s account matches that route. These details do not verify the claimed roles or alignments. Publicly, the concealed victim was attacked by both wolves and the serial killer, but their role and side remain unknown. The Chanteuse privately knows the prior block did not affect its target; there is no night-immune-target result identifying the serial killer.
query_dims.situation: After a no-elimination day, the Chanteuse is coordinating a split night action with a living wolf partner: cancel the claimed Investigator’s possible check while the Chanteuse carries the pack kill against the claimed Sentinel. The two public information-role claims remain unverified, and the village abstained despite one vote against the player read as Not suspicious by the claimant.
query_dims.target_landscape: The pack’s current coordination favors blocking the unverified Investigator claimant, whose remaining checks are unknown, while the Chanteuse carries the kill against the unverified Sentinel claimant. The Investigator and Sentinel claims have no public confirmation; the visit accounts corroborate a route, not roles or alignment. The living partner supports this split. No attack on a night-immune player has identified the lone killer; the prior attack on the concealed victim resulted in a death, so that test was not used.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a tied day-2 vote with no elimination. The pack kills a scrutinized or quiet player, the illusionist will conceal the body, and the chanteuse must pick which of several active town information roles to cancel. The pack's illusionist is already tied to a visit or is exposed by a claim. Information landscape: Moderately informative but unverified. There are conflicting role claims, a trailseer and sentinel who have reported, and a tied vote. Hard confirmation exists only for any dead roles. The chanteuse does not know every hidden actor, such as a necromancer using a dead body. Stakes: Mid-game with several town information roles alive. One unblocked witness to the illusionist's visit can cost the pack a wolf and bring the pack's win condition much further away, so which witness gets blocked matters more than whether a block happens. Forward exposure: The block is private and can change every night, but a blocked player can say so publicly and name their intended target, which hands town a corroborating signal. An unblocked watcher's report then stands alone. Once the night resolves the choice cannot be undone, so a wrong pick leaves the illusionist's visit open to whoever you left free. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed information roles: a trailseer and a sentinel who reported night-1 results, a claimed healer, and unconfirmed sentinel, sigilist and healer slots. Nobody's claim is verified. The trailseer was the loudest threat to the pack, but the sentinel's watch on the victim was the result that actually exposed the illusionist.
lessons.action: When the pack is killing a victim and the illusionist will visit that body to conceal it, spend the block on the information role most likely to see that visit rather than defaulting to the trailseer. Block the sentinel if it has publicly used a watch and the victim is the kind of player it would watch (a scrutinized or quiet player). Block the trailseer only if it has already followed or named the illusionist. Hiding the body hides only the carrier's visit, so the illusionist's own visit stays visible to a watcher on the victim, or to a follower of the illusionist, unless the illusionist carried the kill itself.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an abstain-heavy or one-sided day vote. The pack has chosen its kill, and the chanteuse must pick which town night action to cancel while claimed visit-readers could expose the pack. Information landscape: Moderately informed. There are public claims of visit-based roles, a few confirmed reveals or wills, and no hard evidence against the wolves. Claims are unverified but their roles are plausible. Stakes: Early game with town still numerous and no near parity. One watch or follow report that names a pack member can swing the next day's vote, so removing the visit-readers' information is worth more than a speculative block. Forward exposure: The block is private, but the blocked player is told and may announce a roleblock the next day, which shows that a Chanteuse exists without pointing at you. Blocking is a visit, so a watcher or tracker who is not blocked can still see it. The choice is reversible every night. Target landscape: Claimed Sentinel and Trailseer have public information-role claims backed by visit reports or a dead Sentinel's will. Unclaimed quiet or questioning players are judged on behavior only. The kill target is often the claimed watcher, whom a healer may save.
lessons.action: On night 2, block the claimed Sentinel or Trailseer whose watch or follow could cover the pack's kill or your own visit, and above all a claimed watcher who is the kill target. If both claim, block the one your pack's visits would pass in front of, and change the block target on later nights so you are not a repeated pattern.

lessons.situation: The wolves need to kill the town's investigative lead, who is likely protected by the healer. A chanteuse with a block available has to choose between blocking the victim, the healer, or another threat. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles are partly confirmed by eliminations, a prior morning report verified the healer, and the investigator is publicly claimed or confirmed. Stakes: A failed kill leaves the investigator alive to check a wolf, which can lose the game. A successful block-and-kill removes the town's main source of wolf identification while the pack is thin. Forward exposure: A block on the healer is a private visit that nobody announces. A Sentinel watching or a Trailseer following the healer could still see the chanteuse's visit there. The block cannot be undone once placed, and a wrong guess wastes the night's block. Target landscape: The claimed or confirmed investigator is the kill target. A confirmed or probable healer is the block candidate. The trailseer and sigilist are secondary options. Evidence comes from earlier morning saves and claims, with the rest resting on behavior.
lessons.action: When the pack kill is aimed at the town's key information role (a claimed or confirmed investigator) and a healer may guard them, spend the roleblock on the most likely healer instead of the kill target. If the healer is unknown, block the most probable protector (the player the investigator most plausibly would be shielded by) rather than doubling the block on the victim.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later. The town has abstained or voted against wolves, and the chanteuse's role is at risk. An Investigator is publicly or privately identifiable, but the pack is tempted to block a tracker or another visible claim instead. Information landscape: Information-rich with claims, a roleblock admission, and a voting record. The Investigator's identity is plausible but not confirmed. Stakes: A single Suspicious read on the chanteuse can lead to a vote that costs the pack a wolf and its block. Spending the block on the checker protects that tempo. Forward exposure: The block leaves no public trace beyond what the blocked player says, and it makes no visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer would see unless they target you or the investigator. Blocking the investigator reveals only that a roleblocker exists. It can be changed each night. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed or identified Investigator, claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Sigilist, and unclaimed players. The Investigator is the only role whose result directly flags the chanteuse as Suspicious. Trailseer and Sentinel results depend on visits.
lessons.action: If a player has claimed or been shown to hold a check ability, or an Investigator is otherwise identified, make that player your night block rather than a tracker or a behavioral guess. A check reads a wolf as Suspicious, so a free Investigator can mark you, and only a block stops the check.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 3) with the pack down to one or two wolves. The healer and other Town power roles have publicly claimed and cross-support each other, and the pack must get its kill through while limiting what Town learns. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: announced saves, mutually supporting role claims and a verified watch. Wolf chat agrees on the kill target, but the chanteuse does not know which power role will act against it. Stakes: With about six players alive and the lone killer gone or dying, each successful kill moves the wolves toward parity. A cancelled kill, or a surviving Investigator, can let the town vote the last wolves out, so the block decides whether the kill sticks. Forward exposure: A block is a visit, and the victim is told 'You were roleblocked'. If they report it, the town learns the chanteuse is alive and can narrow the suspect pool. The block cannot be undone, and repeating it on the same target builds a visible pattern. Target landscape: Several claimed Town power roles are alive: a healer backed by a save or a sentinel's watch, an Investigator, a Trailseer and a Vigilante. Their status rests on claims supported by announced saves and cross-confirming claims, not on hard verification. The healer or the sole living check source is the most valuable block.
lessons.action: When a protector (healer) has publicly claimed and been backed by a save or a watch, block the role most likely to cancel or expose the kill, whether the healer or the lone check source, so the pack's kill on its chosen target lands. If the healer is the pack's own target, block the Investigator or the next most dangerous information role instead and conceal the body.

lessons.situation: Early-mid game (night 2) with the wolves carrying a kill and the chanteuse picking a block. A lone killer is active or suspected, and claims or deaths from the first night have made the board partly readable. Information landscape: Info-starved: a night-1 death, a few unverified claims, and possibly one immunity reveal. Nobody has identified the healer or investigator. Stakes: Four players must still be removed before the wolves reach parity, and the lone killer is also still alive. One wasted block or one saved kill costs tempo but is not decisive. A chanteuse who dies early leaves the partner alone with Town's investigator and healer free to act. Forward exposure: A block is a private visit and leaves no public trace. The blocked player is told they were roleblocked and could report it, and the target can change each night. A wasted block is invisible to the town, but it forfeits the night's one chance to protect the kill. Target landscape: Living candidates are mostly unconfirmed. A few have claimed roles, and one may be pinned as the serial killer or necromancer through an immunity or Suspicious read, and so cannot be blocked. The healer and investigator are usually unidentified. Choices rest on reasoning about who threatens the kill, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Choose the block only from players it can take on, meaning Town roles and your wolf partner, and skip anyone the immunity reveal or the rules mark as the lone killer or a neutral. Among those, block the role whose action would most directly undo or expose tonight's pack kill, such as the healer if you can narrow them down, or otherwise the investigator or a claimed protective or tracking role. Do not spend the block on a speculative threat like a sigil that matters only if it lands on the carrier.

lessons.situation: The pack has already settled its kill target and the chanteuse must choose a block target from the other town information roles, choosing between blocking the victim and blocking a different threat. Information landscape: Information-rich after day-two role claims, with public claims from the investigator, trailseer, and sigilist but no verified results. Stakes: Doubling the block on the kill target wastes the pack's single disruption and leaves another information role free to find a wolf. Spreading disruption keeps town results thin while the kill proceeds. Forward exposure: A block on a second player is a private visit that is only exposed if a Sentinel or Trailseer covers that player. Choosing the wrong player only wastes one night's block, and it can be changed next night. Target landscape: The kill target is the claimed investigator or trailseer. The block candidates are the other claimed information roles (a trailseer, sigilist, or investigator) and the suspected healer. The claims are public but unverified, so the choice rests on behavior.
lessons.action: When the pack kill is already aimed at one claimed role, use the roleblock on a different active threat, such as a claimed trailseer or an unresolved investigator, and not on the kill target. Pick the block target by which result would most expose the wolves. Never double up on the victim, because the kill itself already removes them.

lessons.situation: Four players are alive: two wolves, a claimed vigilante, and an unconfirmed player. The wolves need to identify a possible lone killer or neutral before the final votes. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead players' roles and wills are known, leaving one unconfirmed player whose role is unestablished. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity, so the next vote or kill decides the game. Using the block to identify the lone killer lets the wolves unite their votes on the right target instead of guessing. Forward exposure: A block that fails leaves no public trace, and the target does not learn they were tested. It commits only the chanteuse's visit that night. If the block takes, the target is told they were roleblocked, which reveals the wolves' action to them. Target landscape: The claimed vigilante (a killing threat), and an unconfirmed player with no established Town role who could be the lone killer or neutral. The block test is chosen by who remains unverified after dead roles and wills are known.
lessons.action: When a living player has no confirmed Town role and might be the lone killer, aim the roleblock at them while the pack kill goes on a known Town threat such as the claimed vigilante. If you are told the block did not take, that player cannot be blocked, which fits the lone killer or neutral (the rules say both are unblockable), and the pack should treat them as a likely lone killer when it chooses its next targets.

lessons.situation: Day claims have exposed Town's information roles. The pack is killing one of them tonight, and you can neutralize a second one so the Town loses its information for the night. Information landscape: Moderately info-rich: public claims and a visible visit pairing, but few verified roles, and you cannot tell which claims are true beyond what the pack knows. Stakes: Town has several power roles in the open. Removing one checker by kill and blanking another in the same night gives a real information advantage, but the value fades if the Town then votes out the lone killer and you. Forward exposure: The blocked player learns they were roleblocked and can cite it by day, confirming a Chanteuse exists. If a Sentinel or Trailseer is on the target, your visit is named. The block is irreversible. Target landscape: Claimed Investigator, Sentinel, Trailseer and Healer, with some cross-confirmation between them. Silent players are the Vigilante, Sigilist and an unknown. Claims are mostly unverified.
lessons.action: On the night the pack kills a Town information role, block the other publicly active information role (claimed Sentinel or Investigator) so it cannot learn anything that night. Prefer a claimed role that is publicly confirmed or likely real, and expect the block to be named by day, so keep it to nights when blanking that role is worth the exposure.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) with the pack's kill already chosen. You must choose whom to block, and the Town's tracking roles (Sentinel, Trailseer) may still be alive and able to see your visit and expose you. Information landscape: Starved or only partly informed: unverified claims, split or abstained votes, and behavioral reads. The one hard clue is your own private block result. Stakes: Mid-game with several Town roles alive, a lone killer still in play, and the pack needing several eliminations. Losing the Chanteuse to a traced visit costs the wolves their only blocker and a partner's cover, so staying unexposed matters more than a speculative block. Forward exposure: Blocking is a visit. A Sentinel watching the target sees you, and a Trailseer following you sees where you went. The block cannot be undone, and a blocked player is told they were roleblocked, which confirms a Chanteuse exists. Blocking the watcher or follower removes that trace for the night but is itself a visit. Target landscape: Living Town power roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, claimed Investigator, Healer) plus quiet or vocal players. Roles are mostly unverified claims and behavioral reads, with no hard evidence on who is real. The Sentinel and Trailseer are the ones able to trace your visit.
lessons.action: Before choosing a block target, check which Town information roles (Sentinel, Trailseer) are alive and could register your visit. If one is alive and unblocked, block that watcher or follower first, or pick a target they are unlikely to be watching or following.
