Target landscape: Eight or so living players, none with confirmed alignment or visit trails. They are vocal accusers and quiet players, and any pick rests on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: With both sigils left and no hard leads, place one sigil each night on the player most plausibly carrying a night attack (a suspected wolf or killer), and keep the second in reserve. A sigil only strikes a target that attacks that night, so placing one early at least makes a visit that can punish a kill. Holding both risks dying with them unused.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with one wolf or lone killer still active among five or six living players, and the sigilist is a likely kill target. Information landscape: Information-rich on dead evil roles, cleared players and voting records, but the last attacker is identified only by behavior and elimination. Stakes: Each night costs a player and the board is close to parity, so a sigil that strikes the last killer can win the game outright, and one held until death is wasted. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a secret visit that spends the charge whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. A no-effect result means the target did not attack, which fits a non-killer or an attacker who held back, and it does not clear them. Target landscape: A few living unverified candidates, with the others cleared by the investigator or sentinel. The best suspect is picked from behavior, such as an isolated vote against a confirmed role or a quiet profile, because no hard proof exists.
lessons.action: When few players remain (about 5-6) and one killer is left, place a sigil each night on the most probable unverified killer, chosen from voting record and investigator or sentinel clearances, rather than holding both sigils. If that player attacks, the sigil strikes them, so you convert a read into a kill. With one sigil left, spend it on your best read, since an unspent sigil does nothing if you are killed first.

lessons.situation: The sigilist took several elimination votes by day and now faces a night where it is a likely target, with both sigils still unspent. Dying unspent wastes the role's whole contribution. Information landscape: Info-starved: Day 2 votes and an unverified Sentinel claim, with no confirmed evil identities. Stakes: The sigilist is a likely kill target with two sigils at stake. Unused sigils vanish with its death, while one used on a probable attacker could remove a killer. Forward exposure: A sigil is a visit that watchers may see and it spends one of two charges, leaving one in reserve. Holding both keeps full flexibility but risks dying with them unused. Target landscape: Several players who voted against you (a claimed Sentinel and unexplained voters) alongside quiet abstainers. The basis is voting behavior only, with no confirmed roles.
lessons.action: If you were heavily voted yesterday, place a sigil on the most likely attacker among your accusers instead of passing with both sigils unspent. A sigil on a likely wolf or killer punishes a night attack by them only if it resolves, and unspent sigils are worth nothing if you die overnight. Do not count on it to prevent your own death.

lessons.situation: Late game (night 3) after one evil was voted out. At least one wolf is believed to still be alive and attacking every night. You have not yet used either sigil and have already counter-claimed the sigilist role publicly. Information landscape: Mixed: in one case rich (revealed roles, visitor lists, an investigator's clearing read), in the other thin, with unverified claims and only the fact that attacks were happening each night. Either way the sigil depends on predicting who will attack. Stakes: A few players remain and a wolf is still killing each night. Removing the last wolf with a sigil strike can end the game or leave only the serial killer for a day vote. Holding both sigils unused wastes the one tool that punishes a night attacker. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a visit and spends it whether or not it triggers. A strike is announced publicly as a sigil death, which exposes you as the sigilist, but your role was already claimed publicly, so little extra exposure. It cannot be undone once placed, though a second sigil remains. Target landscape: A few living candidates, including a contested healer claimant versus a player cleared Not suspicious by the investigator, or an unresolved field of vigilante, trailseer, illusionist, speculator, sentinel and serial killer. The best-supported target is the one public deduction marks as an evil attacker; where the evidence is thin, the pick rests on a guess about who attacks.
lessons.action: On a night when only one or two attackers likely remain (a lone wolf, or a wolf plus a killer) and you hold both sigils, place a sigil on the player you most suspect of attacking, rather than keeping both. A sigil strikes only if the target attacks, so choose the likeliest attacker from public reads: a wolf cleared of nothing, a contested claimant, or whoever the room's math points to. If you place the sigil and it does not strike, you still have one left for the next night.

lessons.situation: Mid-game with a killer still active at night. One suspect has been tracked to a victim or looks like the attacker, and the day vote has not resolved them. The sigilist can punish an attack but cannot know who will attack. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: trailseer or sentinel traces and public night outcomes exist, but nothing shows who will carry the attack tonight. Stakes: Killers are still active and each night costs a town player. A sigil that strikes a real attacker could remove one. With only two charges, each wasted use cuts the remaining chances. Forward exposure: A placed sigil is spent whether or not it triggers and leaves one charge. The placement is a visit that a watcher or follower may see. A null result is private to you and cannot be undone. Target landscape: A prime suspect tied by hard evidence to a victim's door or to repeated kills, versus quieter unvetted players and confirmed or likely town. Evidence-backed suspects outrank behavior-only reads, but a wolf suspect may not carry the kill that night.
lessons.action: Place the sigil on the prime suspect whose evidence (a trailseer follow, a sentinel watch, or a repeated visit pattern) ties them to night killing. Prefer a suspected lone killer, who attacks every night, over a wolf, since only the rotating carrier attacks. If you target a wolf, aim at the one likely to carry the kill that night. The sigil only strikes a target who attacks, and a healer can still stop the strike.

lessons.situation: Night with a night-immune lone killer possibly still alive. The sigilist has one sigil left and a vote-pressured suspect it believes is the Serial Killer. Information landscape: Moderately thin. There is a public record of votes and confirmed roles for several dead players, but no verified read on the killers. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity, so spending the last sigil on a target that cannot be struck is a costly miss. The sigilist then has no night action left. Forward exposure: A sigil placed on a suspected Serial Killer reveals nothing publicly and is spent. A no-effect result matches both a target who did not attack and an attacker protected by night immunity. Reporting that result by day exposes the sigilist. Target landscape: Two or three suspects narrowed by structural clues, such as who was or was not attacked. One suspect may be a night-immune Serial Killer, and the evidence is behavioral and structural.
lessons.action: Before spending a sigil, list the attackers still possible, such as the wolf carrier, an active lone killer or a possible shooter. Aim the sigil at the suspect who is most likely to attack that night and is not night-immune. If the narrowed suspect may be the Serial Killer, a no-effect result is ambiguous and a strike cannot happen, so choose a different target or hold the sigil.

lessons.situation: Late game with most roles mapped by deaths, reveals and claims; one evil attacker (wolf or lone killer) is still hidden among very few unverified players, and the sigilist holds its last sigil. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed dead roles, investigator clears, healer confirmation and visit tracking leave one plausible attacker. Stakes: Few players remain and the next night kill could tip parity or end the game, so one well-aimed sigil can either strike the last attacker and win or confirm immunity evidence that wins the next day vote. Forward exposure: Spends the last sigil irreversibly and leaves no further night tool, so later progress depends on daytime deduction; the placement is a visit but is hidden from the town. Target landscape: One unverified candidate (claimed vigilante or unvetted player) remains against confirmed healer, investigator, trailseer or cleared players; the pick is based on elimination of confirmed roles, not on behavior alone.
lessons.action: When one sigil remains and deduction through confirmed roles and clears leaves a single unverified killer candidate, place the sigil on that candidate. If they attack that night the sigil strikes them (resolved after their attack), so a strike ends the threat. If it has no effect, that is consistent with them not attacking or with night immunity, so weigh it against later visit evidence rather than as a clear.

lessons.situation: After a vote where one player broke consensus, the sigilist considers committing its last sigil on that behavioral outlier. That player may be a wolf whose role is blocking, not attacking, that night, or may not attack at all. Information landscape: Mostly information-starved: one unverified investigator claim cleared a player, and the only kill was concealed by an illusionist. No visit evidence points to who carries the attack. Stakes: Wolves and a lone killer are both still alive, so the last sigil is Town's only reactive deterrent. Wasting it on a non-attacker leaves no deterrent for the rest of the game. Forward exposure: Spending the final sigil is irreversible and leaves the role with no remaining power. The action itself stays private unless the sigilist discloses it. Target landscape: The loud outlier voter who broke an abstain consensus, an unverified investigator claimant, and quiet abstainers. The choice among them rests on voting behavior, not on evidence.
lessons.action: With one sigil left, place it on a player a concrete lead marks as a probable attacker, such as a Suspicious result or a visit trail. Absent such a lead, keep the last charge. A mere behavioral outlier may be a non-attacker such as the Chanteuse, who blocks instead of killing, and the sigil is then spent for nothing.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) after a day with no clear lead. You have publicly claimed Sigilist and hold one sigil. A loud Town power role has survived a double attack because of a healer save, so the wolves and the killer are expected to pivot to other power roles, you among them. Information landscape: Info-starved. There is a death or two and a save, but nothing identifies who the wolves or the killer are, so there is no attacker signal. Stakes: The board is still contested, but a power-role death moves wolves and killer closer to parity. If you die with the sigil unplaced, Town loses both its power role and any chance of a sigil strike. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a visit and cannot be undone, and it spends the sigil whether or not the target attacks. Your role and your remaining sigil count are already known, so the move adds little new exposure, and holding the sigil does not stop the pack from targeting you. Target landscape: Candidates are the healer-protected Trailseer who keeps getting attacked, the healer, and quiet or unclaimed players. No evidence points to a specific attacker, so any pick rests on behavior and voting reads. The pack was expected to pivot away from the protected target toward other power roles, including you.
lessons.action: When your role is already public, you are a likely kill target, and you are info-starved, place your remaining sigil on the most plausible attacker instead of holding it. Pick the player whose votes or behavior fit an attacker best, and avoid the healer-protected player the pack keeps hitting, since a victim who is attacked is not the one the sigil punishes. An unplaced sigil is worth nothing if you die that night, while a placed one strikes any wolf carrier or killer who attacks the target.

lessons.situation: A mid-game night with about seven players alive. Wolves and a lone killer are still active, nobody has identified tonight's attacker, and you are tempted to spend a sigil on a thinly justified pick. Information landscape: Information-starved about night attackers. Claims are contested, and roles are partly hidden because of body-attacks or concealments. You have only behavioral reads and no confirmed attacker identity or carrier order. Stakes: Evil is not yet close to parity, so there is time to wait. Each sigil is a scarce one-shot kill threat against an attacker, and wasting one on a non-attacker lowers your endgame deterrent for no gain. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a visit that is publicly invisible unless a Trailseer or Sentinel covers you, but it spends the sigil permanently and cannot be undone. A 'no effect' result is ambiguous, so it commits you without confirming anything. Holding the sigil reveals nothing and keeps the option open. A Chanteuse block means no sigil is placed and none is spent. Target landscape: Several unconfirmed players remain: an unclaimed quiet player, a neutral such as the Fortune Teller, and Town claimants with contested results. Roles are unrevealed and the pick rests on behavior rather than evidence. Neutral betting players and most Town roles never attack, so a sigil on them is wasted.
lessons.action: Place a sigil only when you can name a target likely to attack that night, such as a suspected wolf whose turn as carrier is due in seat order, or a player you strongly believe is the lone killer. If you only have a vague behavioral hunch, or your pool is neutrals and Town-claimers, keep the sigil. A sigil is spent when placed, whether or not it triggers, and a 'no effect' result cannot tell a non-attacker from a protected attacker.

lessons.situation: Night 1 (or any early night) with the sigilist holding two sigils and no information about who will attack. Blind placements in this regime hit a non-attacker, a target that night immunity protects, or a victim killed by another player. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day vote on Day 1, no claims, no night reports, no confirmed roles. Any target is a pure guess. Stakes: Early game with all players alive, so no single night decides the game. The two sigils are the sigilist's only offense. Spending one blind halves it for no return, while holding keeps full strength for when evidence appears. Forward exposure: Holding is not a visit and leaves no trace for a Sentinel or Trailseer. It commits nothing, and both sigils stay available. Placing a sigil is a visit that can be seen, and the spent charge cannot be recovered. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes, deaths or behavioral history. Nothing separates a likely attacker (wolf carrier, lone killer, Vigilante) from non-attackers such as the Healer or Trailseer, so any pick is a coin flip.
lessons.action: On an opening night with no deaths, claims, votes or results, keep both sigils and place nothing. A sigil is spent on placement and only matters if the target attacks that night. A blind guess among nine unknowns mostly returns only 'no effect', which is also what a target who did not attack looks like.

lessons.situation: An attacked and saved player had two known visitors, and the choice is which one might be the attacker. Visiting a victim is ambiguous because a protector looks the same as an attacker. Information landscape: Information-rich on who visited, but ambiguous on intent. A dead role revealed the door traffic, and the claims conflict. Stakes: A sigil placed on the genuine healer exhausts the sigilist and builds misdirected suspicion against a key protector. Wolves stay free to attack. Forward exposure: Holding keeps the sigil fully in reserve and leaves no visit trace. Placing it on a protector spends the last charge irreversibly, and the miss looks the same as a non-attacker. Target landscape: Two visitors at a saved victim's door, one a plausible healer and one possibly a malicious visitor posing as a protector, with quiet players unvetted. Evidence is the door traffic and competing claims, with no confirmed attacker.
lessons.action: When the unresolved suspects are players whose visit may be protective, such as a possible healer at a saved victim's door, keep the remaining sigil instead of placing it on them. Hold it until a suspect with attack-consistent behavior emerges, because a sigil on a protector is wasted and cannot stop the wolves.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a 10-player game; the Sigilist must decide between a speculative sigil placement and keeping both charges, with no discussion or vote having occurred yet. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no public statements, deaths, role claims, votes, or night results exist. Stakes: Early game with full board; no single night decides the game, but only two sigils exist for the whole game. Wasting one on a blind guess has a high cost and almost no expected payoff. Forward exposure: Holding makes no visit and leaves no trace, and it commits nothing; both sigils stay available. Placing one would be an irreversible, secret visit with a spent charge that could be seen by a Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none claimed, no voting record and no behavior to read. Nothing separates the wolves, the lone killer or a Vigilante from ordinary Town, so any target would be a pure guess.
lessons.action: On opening night with no claims, votes, or night results, keep both sigils instead of placing one on a random guess. A sigil only matters if its target attacks that night, so a blind placement on one of nine players is a low-odds spend of half your lifetime charges; hold them until a death, a result, or voting behavior points to a likely attacker.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single kill or vote can end the game this night; a wasted attack costs little now, but each lost body or wrongly revealed attack raises the risk that the town identifies the necromancer before the wolf count can reach parity.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move tonight (a reanimated kill or shot through the dead Investigator-adjacent bodies, or a claim) would reveal to the village that the Necromancer is active, and a kill through a body is announced as 'killed by a reanimated' kind, so the attacker's identity-type becomes public; a kill through the dead Vigilante or Investigator body is irreversible once announced.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only public facts are the day 2 abstain vote, the day 3 lynch of the vigilante, the night 1 roleblock on player_8 and the night 2 hold-fire, and player_9's death as investigator. No living player has verified a night result, so every visit-direction claim is unverified.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 ended with the town lynching the self-described vigilante player_8 after player_8 had accused player_1 in the vote; no role claims have been made by any living player. Tonight you, a necromancer with no kill yet, hold two usable bodies, the dead vigilante and the dead investigator. Any attack you make through a body reads Suspicious to an investigator that night, and no role result is public yet beyond the day 2 killed investigator.
query_dims.target_landscape: Seven living candidates besides yourself: player_1, player_2, player_3, player_4, player_5, player_6, player_10. None has a public role claim with confirmation. player_1 and player_2 are on record as the mutual accusers from the day 3 vote (player_2 voted to eliminate player_1), and player_3 has been pressing for visit-direction line-ups. Only dead bodies usable: player_8 (vigilante, shot-capable, a night 2 hold-fire with a night 1 roleblock) and player_9 (investigator, check ability that reads Suspicious on attack nights).

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 3-4) after the wolves' Illusionist died and its role was announced, with the Necromancer unsuspected. The Necromancer can attack through the body at no visible cost to itself, while the town believes the evil is finished or narrowed. Information landscape: Info-rich: dead roles are announced and the town's investigative roles and records are partly known. Nobody has a read on the Necromancer. Stakes: Few players remain, so each kill moves the Necromancer much closer to the at-most-one-other-alive win, and removing the Vigilante or Investigator takes away the town's main ways to stop it. A wasted night costs tempo while the town still has threats. Forward exposure: The morning names a 'reanimated wolf' attack, which publicly confirms a Necromancer is active; this cannot be undone. The kill hides the victim's role and the attacker's identity, and the sigil cannot punish an attack made through a body. If the Investigator is dead or dying that night, no Suspicious read can follow from it. Target landscape: Revealed bodies include the Illusionist, plus other dead roles. Living candidates are the Vigilante (could kill the Necromancer), the Investigator (could read it Suspicious), the Sentinel, the Trailseer and the Sigilist. The Vigilante's and Investigator's threat comes from their role mechanics, not from behavior; the Sentinel's influence on votes is behavioral evidence only.
lessons.action: When a dead wolf's Illusionist body has its role announced and conceals remain, attack through it and aim at the living player who can most threaten you: the Vigilante, who can shoot you, or the Investigator, who would read you Suspicious on an attack night. If that threat is already dying to the wolves or is dead, take the strongest remaining information role instead. The concealed role and the 'reanimated wolf' wording give the town a Necromancer's presence but no suspect.

lessons.situation: A wolf (Illusionist) was voted out and is now the necromancer's body. Town still has the Healer, and surviving information roles are cross-verifying each other, while one wolf may remain. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Illusionist's flip validated certain claims and visit chains exist. The Healer's coverage is unknown, which makes the attack target a guess. Stakes: Each kill moves the necromancer closer to the 'at most one other alive' condition, but a failed or visible kill reveals a Necromancer and draws a vote. A kill that removes a verifier and conceals its role gives the most value per exposure. Forward exposure: The morning report will name a reanimated wolf attack, so the town learns a Necromancer is active and an investigator check on you that night reads Suspicious. This cannot be undone. A hidden-role kill withholds the victim's role, and the Necromancer learns it. Target landscape: The dead Illusionist is the usable body. Candidates are the claimed Sentinel, claimed Trailseer, claimed Investigator, and quiet unconfirmed players. Public claims have been partly validated by the Illusionist's flip, but healer coverage is unknown.
lessons.action: When a dead Illusionist's body is available, attack a key town information role (claimed Sentinel, Trailseer or Investigator) or an unconfirmed player through it, so the victim's role is hidden if they die and the town cannot cross-check it. Prefer a target the Healer is unlikely to be covering (not the most-claimed or most-visible role that the Healer would protect), and check the Illusionist still has conceals left, since the hidden role depends on them.

lessons.situation: A town role or wolf has just died with an announced role, giving the necromancer a usable offensive body while town information roles are alive and coordinating the hunt. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced flips and wills, claimed sentinel and trailseer results, confirmed visits, and a public record of earlier night events. Stakes: The board is a few kills from the end of the game. Each town information role removed speeds the collapse toward two survivors, while a failed attack on a protected target gives town a verified pair that will vote me out. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is announced by the body's kind (reanimated vigilante, wolf, or sigil), so town learns a necromancer is active, though not who. I also read Suspicious to any Investigator check that night. The kill cannot be undone, but the dead player's name rather than mine is what a watcher or follower sees at the door. Target landscape: Claimed or confirmed sentinel, trailseer, investigator, and a claimed healer, plus a spent sigilist, an unconfirmed remaining wolf, and quiet unconfirmed players. Town roles are known from claims and flips; the wolf is known only by behavior.
lessons.action: When a freshly dead role with an announced attack body (vigilante, or a wolf's illusionist) is available and the board is crowded with confirmed town information roles, attack through that body at the night's highest-value information or coordination role, such as a sentinel or trailseer that has not been shown to be protected. If a healer is alive and has already been seen protecting that role, shift the target to a different information role, since a save shows the healer is working and ties town together.

lessons.situation: Mid-to-late game with three or four players alive; the town already knows a Necromancer exists from an earlier 'reanimated' report, and a further attack would not yet end the game. Information landscape: Info-rich on roles and votes but with no hard evidence about who the Necromancer is. The town deduces your identity from the attack reports and the vote splits. Stakes: An extra announced attack that does not win the game moved the room to a three-player vote where two others could remove you; the kill achieved nothing a vote could not undo. Forward exposure: Each announced reanimated kill confirms a Necromancer exists, and repeated attacks through the same body narrow the pool to the few unknowns. A second announcement makes you the obvious suspect and cannot be reversed, whereas a non-attacking use leaves no announcement. Target landscape: Three other living players, all unconfirmed claims or behavioral reads: a vocal accuser (Fortune Teller), a Sigilist, and a Vigilante or Investigator. None is a verified evil, and some (a Fortune Teller who has already scored two points) gain you nothing if killed.
lessons.action: When four players remain and the kill would not reach your win threshold, use a night action that does not announce a reanimated attack (such as a block or an information-gathering ability through a dead body) rather than a second announced attack, unless the target removes the vote threat. Keep the town from learning that a Necromancer is alive and from narrowing the suspects down to you.

lessons.situation: Night 4 with both wolves dead and you as the lone killer. About four or five players are alive and the town has just lynched a wolf. You must choose whether to attack through a reusable dead-wolf body and whom to hit. Information landscape: Moderately info-rich: both wolves are revealed, several role claims are public, and the Investigator's checks are known to be spent, so your Suspicious reading cannot be exploited. Stakes: Each kill moves you toward the win condition of at most one other player alive. Removing the player who can trace your visits keeps you hidden while the board shrinks. Forward exposure: The attack is announced as made by a reanimated wolf, so the town learns a Necromancer exists, and you read Suspicious to the Investigator that night. With the checks spent, no check can exploit that. The victim's role is hidden if they die, and the announcement itself cannot be undone. Target landscape: Public claimants: a Trailseer who followed the Chanteuse to you, an Investigator with an on-record Not-suspicious read of you, and a counterclaiming Sigilist. They are ranked by how likely each is to reveal your visits, based on their claims and on evidence rather than on behavior alone.
lessons.action: When you are the lone killer with the wolves dead or nearly dead, the Investigator's checks are spent or known, and a usable Illusionist body is available, attack through it against the public claimant most likely to expose your visits (such as a Trailseer who has followed you). If the Investigator still has checks left, switch to a passive use of a dead body instead.

lessons.situation: Night 3 is your first usable-body night. Town and the wolves are fighting publicly, the Investigator or another info role is active, and no one suspects the necromancer. Information landscape: Moderately rich. A revealed body with its record exists and some public accusations and claims are out, but there is no direct evidence on the necromancer. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. You are far from the at-most-one-other-alive win, so staying unseen while Town and the wolves trade kills matters more than rushing a kill, and there is no swing this night. Forward exposure: A passive check or follow through a body is not an attack, so it leaves no morning trace and you read Not suspicious to the Investigator. It commits you to nothing and is fully reversible, whereas an attack through a body would announce a reanimated killer and read Suspicious. Target landscape: Usable bodies are few: a revealed Investigator or Trailseer, while wolf-kill victims with concealed roles cannot be used. Living targets are the publicly contested wolf suspect and the active Town info roles, with mostly unverified claims.
lessons.action: On night 3, when you have only one or two usable bodies and no attack is needed to win the night, use a passive info body (Investigator, Trailseer or Sentinel) on the most contested or highest-threat living player instead of attacking. If the result confirms a public claim, keep staying quiet; if it contradicts one, keep the result as private leverage for a later night.

lessons.situation: A wolf chanteuse has been eliminated and revealed, giving the necromancer a usable block body from night two onward. The necromancer is under suspicion after a tied or contested vote and must decide whom to roleblock. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of dead players are confirmed, vote splits are public, and several claims (healer save, investigator results) are on record. The living players' roles remain unverified claims. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive, so a single block rarely flips the game, but the necromancer is being voted against and a wasted night or a visible trace costs tempo it cannot spare. Forward exposure: A block through the dead chanteuse's body shows the dead wolf's name at the door of any watching Sentinel, telling the town a Necromancer is active though not who. It is irreversible once seen, and a block on a player who cannot act yields no gain for that exposure. Target landscape: Living players include a claimed healer, claimed sigilist, claimed investigator with checks reportedly spent, and quiet villagers. Their claims are unverified, and only the chanteuse's role is system-confirmed. Choice rests on remaining ability uses and on who accused the necromancer, not on pure behavior.
lessons.action: When the only usable body is a dead chanteuse, aim the block at a player whose action can still matter that night (a Town role with uses left, or one publicly suspected of protecting a likely wolf target) rather than one whose resources are publicly exhausted. If a Sentinel could be watching your target, treat the dead wolf's name at the door as a visible trace and prefer a target where that trace points suspicion at others.

lessons.situation: A revealed will or confirmed visit trace implicates a specific player as a wolf, and a dead vigilante's body is available to the necromancer. Information landscape: Information-rich but indirect: a sentinel's will names a visitor to the night 1 casualty, and no wolf is confirmed by a flip. Stakes: Two wolves plus a lone killer remain, so removing one wolf lowers the chance of the wolves reaching parity before I reach the final two. A mistaken shot only costs a night and a town power role. Forward exposure: The morning will announce a reanimated vigilante shot, which tells town a necromancer exists but gives no identity. I will read Suspicious to any Investigator check that night. Killing a wolf cannot be reversed, and a miss on a non-wolf spends the night and angers town. Target landscape: The player named in a dead sentinel's will as visiting the first victim, versus town power roles and unrevealed players. The lead is a will-based visit trace rather than a confirmed role.
lessons.action: When a dead player's will or a visit trace points at a suspected wolf and the vigilante body is available, shoot that suspect through the reanimated vigilante, accepting the risk that a wrong read wastes the night. This removes a wolf and cuts the pressure of wolf parity, while the dead body's name, not mine, appears in any watch or follow result.

lessons.situation: Night 2, your first night able to act. Town and wolves are both intact, you may already have drawn day-2 votes, and no usable body exists to act through. Information landscape: Info-starved: one or two revealed roles, partial and unverified claims, and no hard leads on the quiet players. Stakes: Early game with most players alive, so no single night decides the outcome. Staying alive and unexposed matters more than forcing a low-value action, and you cannot yet win by attrition. Forward exposure: Staying put commits you to nothing, leaves no trace, and is fully reversible because the bodies remain usable on later nights. Any attack through a body would be announced as a reanimated kill and show the town a necromancer exists. Target landscape: Only one or two dead bodies with revealed roles, none with a usable attack or block. Living players are mostly unverified claimants plus quiet unknowns, and you hold no read on who the wolves are.
lessons.action: On your first acting night, if the only revealed bodies give no attack, block, heal or other useful ability (e.g. a fortune teller), stay put. You make no visit and no attack, so you read Not suspicious and the same bodies stay available later. If a dead wolf, vigilante or information role appears on a later night, reassess then.

lessons.situation: Night 4 with about six players alive, one wolf left, and you are an unrevealed lone killer. The town still has a voting majority and the wolves are already killing for you. Information landscape: Rich on town roles but incomplete on wolf identities, and nobody else knows your threat status. Stakes: The town could still outvote a revealed Necromancer. Staying hidden while the wolves thin the town sets up the late kills needed to win. Forward exposure: A passive check through a body is fully reversible and leaves no announcement or Suspicious reading. An attack would announce a reanimated killer and give a live Investigator a Suspicious result on that night. Holding back commits you to nothing and keeps the option to strike later. Target landscape: Remaining targets are the Fortune Teller and the Sigilist, plus the last wolf. The usable bodies are a dead Investigator and a wolf. The Fortune Teller has been accurate with reads and bets, so a Not-suspicious check clears it only partially, since many roles read Not suspicious.
lessons.action: If the town still holds a voting majority and a live Investigator could read you Suspicious, hold the attack and use a dead Investigator's body to check a surviving player, which leaves you Not suspicious. Resume killing once the pack is gone or the town is down to the last few players, so the final kills land when the town cannot respond.

lessons.situation: Five players are alive and you have a usable attacking body, such as a dead Vigilante's. A confirmed Investigator with an unspent check is still alive. Any attack you make this night will read you as Suspicious to that check. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Investigator is confirmed by an earlier wolf flip, and the other claims and visit results are public. Dead roles are revealed, so the usable bodies are known. Stakes: With five alive, one wrong step lets the Investigator's check expose you and you are voted out the next day. Dealing with the Investigator, or not reading Suspicious, matters more than picking off a lesser target. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is announced in the morning by the body's kind (for example a reanimated vigilante), which tells the town a Necromancer struck. It also makes you read Suspicious on that night. A block through a Chanteuse body leaves no announcement and no Suspicious reading. Target landscape: The confirmed Investigator with an unspent check, the other claimed investigative roles such as a Trailseer, an unverified claimant, and an unclaimed player. The Investigator's status is confirmed by a prior flip, so it is the one evidence-backed threat to you. The others are claims or behavior reads.
lessons.action: If a confirmed Investigator with an unspent check is alive, either remove them or keep them from checking you. Use a dead Chanteuse's body to block the Investigator, or attack the Investigator directly, since a player killed at night learns nothing from it. If you can do neither, take a non-attacking action or stay put so you read Not suspicious, rather than attacking a secondary target.

lessons.situation: Necromancy has just unlocked, an investigator is alive and likely to check, the town has abstained or has few leads, and the necromancer is currently unsuspected. A free attack is available but would immediately mark the necromancer as the lone killer. Information landscape: Information-starved: little public evidence, with wolves and town both searching. The investigator's targeting is unknown. Stakes: Being outed this early is costly: the necromancer can be removed by a daytime vote or, from night 2, by a night attack. Many players remain, so patience costs little, while an early announced kill invited the vote that eliminated the necromancer. Forward exposure: Any attack through a body is announced by the body's kind and reads Suspicious to an investigator that night, so it cannot be hidden afterward. A non-attacking night reads Not suspicious and leaves no announcement. Target landscape: Available bodies include a dead Vigilante (free shot) or dead wolves, with all living players unconfirmed. Attacking a wolf with a Vigilante body removes a threat but reveals a Necromancer to the town and the investigator.
lessons.action: If you are not yet under suspicion and no check or vote is aimed at you, hold the attack and use a non-attacking body ability (follow, watch, check) on the night you fear an investigator may look at you. Attack through a body only when the victim is unlikely to be protected and the gain outweighs the Suspicious read and reanimation headline.

lessons.situation: Late game, about four players alive, with a Necromancer attack available through a dead Illusionist or another wolf body. One kill now decides who is in the final three and how the last vote splits. Information landscape: Mostly inferred roles with some hard history (a confirmed healer save, public pick or claims, repeated roleblocks). The town has seen only reanimated strikes and has not confirmed the Necromancer's identity. Stakes: Two eliminations from the Necromancer win condition (at most one other player alive). The next kill decides whether the final three-player vote is 2-1 for you or 2-1 against you. A wrong target choice gives the town a guaranteed vote on the final day. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is announced as a reanimated strike, so the town learns a Necromancer is alive, though not who. Hiding the victim's role denies the town a reveal and cannot be undone. It commits you to winning the final three-player vote. Target landscape: Three or four living others: an established town pair (claimed healer and sentinel, one protected or repeatedly blocked), a neutral speculator, and possibly a wolf ally. Roles are mostly inferred, apart from confirmed saves and public claims. Pick the target by who would form a voting bloc against you, not by who is the easiest kill.
lessons.action: With four alive and a body that lets you attack (a dead Illusionist), spend the kill on a member of the town pair or the last visit-reading role, so the final three leaves you with a wolf or neutral who may side with you. If a confirmed pair (for example healer and sentinel) would remain, kill one of them rather than the lone neutral. Use the concealing body while it still has conceals left.

lessons.situation: Night with exactly three players alive (you and two others), all wolves dead or irrelevant, and a revealed dead wolf or Vigilante body available for an attack. One kill reaches the necromancer win condition. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are revealed, the remaining roles are confirmed or their abilities exhausted, and only your own identity is hidden. Stealth no longer has value. Stakes: One successful kill wins the game outright; if it is skipped or fails, the next day's vote will likely eliminate you since two players can outvote one. This is the highest-leverage night of the game. Forward exposure: The attack is visible (a 'reanimated' kill announcement), but it triggers the win condition at once, so no day or vote remains in which the exposure could be used against you. It cannot be undone, but it does not need to be. Target landscape: Two remaining players, both non-evil and both mortal. Typically a neutral Fortune Teller and a Sigilist with spent sigils, or the Investigator. Either kill ends the game; the choice only matters if a counter-action or protection could stop the attack.
lessons.action: At final three (you plus two others) with a usable dead attacker body (a wolf's or the Vigilante's), attack either remaining player that night. The kill leaves at most one other player alive and ends the game before any vote can expose the reanimated-attack report. Pick the target who could otherwise protect or retaliate, and if neither can, pick the one most likely to sway the vote.

lessons.situation: Late game, all wolves dead, you are the sole evil role facing a known armed Vigilante and a known Healer. A choice between attacking through the Illusionist's body and blocking through the Chanteuse's body. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves are dead and revealed, the Vigilante is verified by its kill, and the Healer's role is public. The protection target is easy to predict. Stakes: A failed attack leaves you facing a live Vigilante; here the Vigilante's counter-shot killed the necromancer the same night. Two more kills are needed to win, so a wasted or blocked strike costs the game. Forward exposure: An attack through a body announces 'reanimated' and identifies a Necromancer to the town, and it cannot be undone. A block through a dead Chanteuse leaves no such public announcement, so it keeps your identity hidden while removing the protector. Target landscape: Four alive: a confirmed Vigilante with a bullet left, a claimed Healer likely to guard the obvious kill target, and a third player. Dead Illusionist and Chanteuse bodies are both usable. The Healer's identity is publicly known, so the kill target is predictable.
lessons.action: With four players left and a mortal guarded or armed threat alive (a confirmed Vigilante with a bullet, or a Healer free to protect), use a dead Chanteuse's body to block that Healer or the gun instead of attacking into the expected protection. Attack only when the most likely protector is neutralized, since a failed attack announces a reanimated strike and exposes you to a counter-shot.

lessons.situation: Late game, about six players alive, the wolves nearly gone. A claimed Vigilante with a bullet left is alive, and your day votes or abstains may have drawn attention. You hold several announced dead bodies, including a Chanteuse's, but you are choosing whether to act or stay put. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Vigilante's claim and remaining-bullet count are public, dead roles are revealed, and the vote record is permanent. Your own night actions stay hidden. Stakes: One Vigilante shot at you ends your game outright, and you cannot be protected from it. Staying put does nothing to stop the shot, so neutralising the shooter this night is the highest-value use of the night. Forward exposure: Blocking through the Chanteuse's body leaves no necromancer trace. A Sentinel or Trailseer would see the dead Chanteuse's name at the door, and the morning report announces nothing. It commits you to nothing publicly and can be repeated on later nights, so it is easy to reverse. Target landscape: The public Vigilante claimant with one bullet left is the main threat. Usable announced bodies are a Chanteuse (block), an Illusionist (attack), and Investigator, Sigilist or Sentinel bodies. The threat is evidence-based, since a public claim plus a spent-or-unspent bullet count is on record.
lessons.action: If a living player has publicly claimed a Vigilante with a bullet left and a dead Chanteuse's role was announced, act through that body and block the claimed Vigilante. A blocked player does nothing and makes no visit, so the shot cannot land, and blocking is not an attack, so you do not read Suspicious. If no Chanteuse body is usable, take the next-best step against the Vigilante, such as a body attack on the claimant, instead of idling.

lessons.situation: First night of necromancy (night 2 onward), the day-2 vote ended without a useful elimination or on a town-side vote, and the only usable body is a dead investigative role. The necromancer has no kill-capable body yet and wants intel while staying hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: few deaths, unverified role claims, and no public record of who the lone killer or neutral is. Only behavioral reads are available. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so there is no need to force a kill. Spending the first night on safe information costs nothing and builds a picture of the healer, the protected targets and visit traffic for later strikes. Forward exposure: A non-attacking use of an investigative body produces no morning announcement. Any watcher or follower sees the dead player's name, not yours, and an investigator reads you Not suspicious because you did not attack. Fully reversible: nothing is committed, and you can switch to attacking later. Target landscape: One or two announced investigative bodies (dead Sentinel or Trailseer), and nine or so living players with no confirmed roles. Candidates are the claimed investigator, a suspected shooter or healer, and quiet players. Choice rests on behavioral reads and expected traffic rather than evidence.
lessons.action: On the first night a body is usable, if the only body is a non-attacking investigative role (Sentinel, Trailseer, Investigator), use it to watch, follow or check the most likely focal player (for example the likely healer target, or a claimed power role) rather than staying put. Those actions announce nothing, leave only the dead player's name at the door, and read Not suspicious to an investigator on a night with no attack, so you gain information at no exposure cost and can repeat it each night.

lessons.situation: Your first acting night, with several revealed bodies available, including both a sigilist and an information role. Wolves are still active and you must choose which body and target to use. Information landscape: Info-starved for you: few revealed bodies, no attacks yet made through a body, and no read on who carries the wolves' kill. Stakes: Mid-early game with eight alive. A wasted ability night costs tempo toward the two-left-alive condition, while a useful read could direct later attacks without exposing you. Forward exposure: An information-body action is private and unannounced, so it exposes nothing and keeps your options open. A sigil is spent when placed and is wasted if the target does not attack that night. A sigil on a non-attacker such as a watcher gives no information and no kill. Target landscape: Usable bodies are a revealed sigilist (places a sigil) and a revealed investigator (gives a read on a living player). Living candidates include a publicly active sentinel and other claimants, with no confirmed wolf or killer.
lessons.action: When a dead Investigator, Sentinel or Trailseer body with a revealed role is available on a night you act, use it on a plausible living player to gather a read rather than spending a sigil on a player who probably won't attack. Information roles are quiet: they produce no announcement and leave you Not suspicious on nights you don't attack. If you do use a sigilist body, place the sigil on a player likely to attack that night, since a sigil only strikes a target who attacks.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: With 9 players alive and 5 eliminations until the leading evil faction could win at worst for the town, a single result cannot end the game or flip which faction is winning; the concealed body’s unknown side means this is the closest possible parity estimate.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved for alignment: there are no publicly confirmed roles or revealed wills, and the concealed night-1 victim’s role remains unknown. Available evidence consists of unverified role and result claims, your private finding that your target visited no one, and the public vote record; the corroborated visit route does not establish alignment.
query_dims.situation: The day-2 vote ended in an abstention with no elimination: nearly everyone abstained, while one player voted to eliminate the player whom an unverified Investigator claim had cleared as Not suspicious. The Investigator’s claimed result, your private trail result on a different player, and an unverified Sentinel account provide limited, non-alignment evidence as the next trail decision approaches.
query_dims.target_landscape: The unresolved candidates are the player with a claimed Not-suspicious result and the player they checked, plus the player who alone voted to eliminate that checked player. The Investigator and Sentinel claims remain unverified; your own follow confirms only that the watched player visited no one, not anyone’s alignment.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a night-1 death and an all-abstain day-2 vote. Nobody has claimed a night result, and the Trailseer must choose whom to follow with only discussion tone to go on. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death, a unanimous abstain, a few cautious statements, no night claims and no cross-checkable roles. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive and no eliminations yet from votes. One follow can give the town its first concrete lead, but a misread visit could point at an innocent, so the result needs corroboration. Target landscape: Living players with the most public presence in the day-2 discussion, none with a confirmed role or hard evidence against them. Picks rest on behavior (who urged caution or steered the room), not on evidence. A follow only shows where the target went, not why.
lessons.action: On a night 2 with no claims, no hard leads and an all-abstain day, follow a vocal, influential player whose day talk steered the room, rather than a quiet player or a past victim. If the follow shows a visit, treat it as one data point that names a possible partner or victim, not as proof, and weigh the visited player's own record before acting on it.

lessons.situation: After a day elimination validated an investigative claim, the Trailseer chooses between auditing that claimant and chasing unknown suspects. The claimant may be a target for the wolves or the Chanteuse's block. Information landscape: Information-rich. There is a confirmed wolf flip from the Investigator's check, public claims, and a Sentinel watch that reported no visitors. Stakes: The remaining evil, a wolf and the lone killer, is still unknown. The Investigator's survival and credibility drive the village's votes, so verifying that they acted gives some value, but the follow adds no direct information on the remaining evil. Target landscape: A claimed Investigator whose check was validated by an elimination, versus a claimed Sentinel with a quiet watch result or unconfirmed quiet players. The choice rests on the value of verifying a key Town role.
lessons.action: When the Investigator's claim has just produced a confirmed result and the room trusts it, follow that Investigator to see whether they visited someone. If they visited no one, that matches a roleblock or a skipped check, but it is not proof of role. If they visited a player, you confirm they acted and learn who they checked.

lessons.situation: After a tied or no-result day 2, you are a claimed Trailseer with an unverified or contested result. Your night 1 or 2 follow was blocked, or your target is publicly known, and a Chanteuse may be blocking you on a predictable pattern. Information landscape: Information-starved: your own private follow result, a few unverified claims, and a split vote record. No confirmed wolf identity. Stakes: Each night of lost trail information costs the town its only movement data while the wolves keep carrying kills. A wasted follow, or your death, removes your role from the board. Target landscape: Several living players: the previously followed or publicly accused suspect, plus quiet unclaimed players, a claimed Investigator or Sigilist, and neutrals. All have little or no trail data, and the suspect was chosen on behavior rather than evidence.
lessons.action: If you were roleblocked last night, or you have publicly named your intended follow target, pick a different living player to follow tonight, ideally one you have not mentioned. A repeat on a publicly known target is easy for the Chanteuse to predict, and in this cluster those repeats were blocked and yielded no result.

lessons.situation: The lone killer's kills come through a dead role's ability. The trailseer followed a quiet, unclaimed player and saw no visits, then treated the empty result as clearing them. Information landscape: Information-rich on role deaths, but the killer is unidentified, and an empty follow result is weak evidence because the killer's attack may be made through a body rather than its own visit. Stakes: With the wolves gone, the town can afford very few more mistakes. Treating one 'visited no one' as a clearance can steer the vote away from the killer and expose the trailseer's own standing, so the follow should narrow the field without being counted as proof of innocence. Target landscape: Both wolves dead; living players are a claimed sentinel, an unconfirmed healer, a neutral speculator, and a quiet unclaimed player. None is proven, and the choice rests on behavior and elimination of roles.
lessons.action: When the lone killer may be attacking through a dead player's body, as in a 'reanimated' morning report, follow the most suspicious survivor but record a 'visited no one' result as inconclusive. Keep the suspect on the list and choose the next night's follow from the remaining candidates, since a Necromancer's attack through a body would not appear as its own visit.

lessons.situation: One or two nights in, a killer's victim has been found. Town's checks and watches are unverified. A Sentinel may be watching the same door, and you must decide whose outgoing movements to trail. Information landscape: Some evidence exists: a revealed night-1 victim, public vote and claim history, and visible activity from one claimed role. No hard confirmation of any killer's identity. Stakes: Town still has room to find the killers, but each night without usable, corroborated information lets the wolves and the lone killer close in. A result that another role's report can corroborate is worth more than a lone claim. Target landscape: A self-claimed, visibly active Town role (such as a Sigilist) who is a likely kill target, versus unclaimed or unverified players and a publicly accused suspect. The choice rests on predicting which player the killers will go after, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Follow an exposed, likely-to-be-attacked player, such as a claimed Sigilist or Investigator who is active and already drawing attention, instead of the loudest suspect. You learn whom that player visited, and your own visit to their door can be recorded by a Sentinel watching them. That gives the town an independent cross-check on your claim.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after a Day 3 vote removed a wolf or the necromancer. Another evil player is still hidden, and the trailseer must pick one follow target with no direct lead. Information landscape: Moderate and patchy. A few roles are revealed by deaths, but nothing hard points at the remaining wolf or killer. The trailseer's own follow result is the only direct evidence about who moves at night. Stakes: The board is mid-to-late game with few players alive, so each night kill and each vote matters a lot. A follow that yields only a no-visit result wastes one of the few remaining information nights. Target landscape: Four to six living candidates after a wolf or lone killer was voted out: claimed sigilist, investigator, vigilante or sentinel, plus quiet unclaimed players. No role is confirmed beyond unverified claims, and suspicion rests on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On the night after a key elimination, follow a player who claims an acting night role (sigilist, investigator, vigilante, sentinel) or has a concrete public case against them, not a silent bystander. A named visit can be cross-checked against that night's deaths, saves and claims, and a claimed role that visits no one is checkable too. A 'visited no one' result only means no visit was seen: the follow shows only where they went, and a concealed pack kill leaves no trace on the carrier.

lessons.situation: Early game after a no-elimination or low-information Day 2, with several investigative claims out. The Trailseer must pick whom to follow on a night when wolves are likely to kill an exposed claimant. Information landscape: Mostly information-starved. There are claims and behavioral reads such as one lone vote or one silent player, but no hard evidence tying anyone to wolves or the lone killer. Stakes: Mid-game with several wolves and a lone killer still alive. Wasting a follow on an already-plausible Town claimant costs a night of tracking, while a follow that catches a killer's visit can turn the next vote. Target landscape: Unvetted suspects (a silent player with a lone vote, an aggressive voter against you) versus claimed investigative roles (Investigator, Sentinel) whose claims are unverified; choice rests on behavior, with no confirmed evil flips.
lessons.action: On Night 2, follow the quiet or hostile player who has drawn a lone vote or suspicion but has not been checked, rather than a claimed Town investigative role. If they visit a player who then dies or is attacked, that is a direct lead for the next vote; if they visit no one, they stay unresolved and you pick a different unchecked suspect the next night.

lessons.situation: Midgame night with the wolf pack mostly or fully eliminated and a lone killer (necromancer or serial killer) still hidden among the unconfirmed players. The Trailseer chooses whom to follow. Information landscape: Information-rich about dead wolves and validated Town roles, but information-starved about the identity of the remaining lone killer. Only behavioral reads exist for unconfirmed players. Stakes: The lone killer is still active and each night costs a life. A wasted follow on a cleared role leaves Town with no evidence for the next vote, so every follow must test an unconfirmed player. Target landscape: Unconfirmed, non-claiming players (quiet healer-type, abstaining neutral-type, unclaimed villagers) versus already-validated Town roles (confirmed investigator, sentinel, vigilante). Evidence for the unconfirmed is behavioral only; the validated roles are already cleared by cross-checks.
lessons.action: When the wolves are largely dead and a lone killer (likely the necromancer) is still unidentified, follow an unconfirmed, non-claiming player whose behavior is quiet or unexplained, not a role already validated as Town. A follow shows only whom they visited, so a visit onto a night-death victim or a dead body's door points at the hidden killer, while a protective or empty visit narrows the pool by elimination.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2-3) after one or two wolf-side deaths or a necromancer sighting, with a visit-count or claim conflict among town power roles and no hard visit data except what the Trailseer can generate. Information landscape: Rich in public facts (role reveals, vote records, a confirmed check) but poor on who the remaining killers are; a trail is one of the few independent hard visit signals, though it shows only the target's outbound visits. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one accurate visit datum can steer the next day's vote, but a trail used to push out a genuine town role costs real information, so the follow should test the claim rather than prove guilt. Target landscape: Claimed town power roles (Sentinel, Healer, Investigator) with unverifiable night claims, plus quiet players; the claimed Sentinel's trail is cheap to check against their own watch report, while the others rest on behavior and counterclaims.
lessons.action: Follow the claimed power role whose night action is publicly disputed or unverified (e.g. a claimed Sentinel or Healer in a count conflict), and record exactly whom they went to or that they went to no one. Report it as a one-way fact ("they went to X"), and if the trail contradicts their own result list, treat that as a hard inconsistency, but if it fits their claim, say it fits without calling it proof.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with the wolves gone or nearly gone and a lone killer (Serial Killer) still hidden. The Trailseer must pick whom to follow among the remaining unexplained suspects to either implicate or clear them. Information landscape: Information-rich on identities, since most roles are revealed or deduced, but the last killer's identity is unresolved. A follow gives a hard visit trace (whom the target visited, or that they visited no one) that can settle the last unknown. Stakes: With few players left and a killer striking every night, one more night kill brings the killer or wolves close to winning. A correct follow can identify the killer for the next vote, so the pick of target is decisive for the Town win. Target landscape: Few unexplained survivors (2-3) remain after wolves and most roles are revealed or cleared. They are not role-confirmed, and the choice rests on behavior such as being quiet, deflecting, or being night-immune, plus elimination logic. One of them is the hidden lone killer.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone or identified and one lone killer is still unrevealed, follow the unexplained survivor you most suspect of being the killer, choosing between the few remaining candidates. If they visited you on a night you were attacked, or visited another victim, that is direct contact evidence to bring forward. If they visited no one, that argues against them being the Serial Killer, so move your next follow to the other unexplained candidate.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a Town-side loss or a wolf exposure, the Trailseer chooses whom to follow. The wolves are likely to kill the key information role, and the actives hide among the vocal players. Information landscape: Only revealed deaths, claims and votes are confirmed. No trail or watch reports have been shared publicly, so cross-matching visits is the main way to create hard evidence. Stakes: Town is a few eliminations from wolf parity and cannot afford more blind votes. A visit trail that survives a death or confirms a night role can decide the next vote or shot. Target landscape: A surviving claimed Investigator (counter-claimant just exposed as a wolf) or a vocal accuser who drove a mis-elimination, versus quiet unconfirmed players; choices rest on behavior and claim status, with no prior tracking evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, follow the player most likely to be acting at night, not a quiet bystander. That means a surviving claimed information role the wolves will want dead (so their last visit is recorded even if they die), or, when nothing is confirmed, a vocal accuser who pushed a wagon on a revealed Town role. Report the exact visit direction ("X went to Y") so it can be matched against other night results such as a Sentinel watch or a roleblock claim.

lessons.situation: A prior follow gave a null result, and a wolf or the serial killer is still hidden. The trailseer decides whether to re-follow the same suspect or switch. Information landscape: Starved on the hidden evil players. The earlier no-visit result neither cleared nor implicated anyone, because inactivity, a held-back ability, a block and a concealed kill all look the same to a follower. Stakes: With a wolf and a killer both still alive, each night adds a victim. A second follow that learns nothing new costs tempo that Town cannot easily spare. Target landscape: Remaining uncertain players, including one already followed with a no-visit result, plus claimants and quiet players not yet followed. All are judged on behavior and claims, with no confirmed roles among them.
lessons.action: When last night's follow produced only a 'visited no one' or otherwise uninformative result, move the follow to a different, untested player. Pick one whose night behavior could contradict their stated role or tie them to a night death, a save or the surviving wolf's kill. Repeating the same follow rarely adds anything, while a new target widens what you can cross-check.

lessons.situation: Trailseer has publicly claimed and shared Night 1 results, then drew a hostile vote on Day 2. Wolves can see the claim and may kill or block the Trailseer on Night 2. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich. There are public claims, a vote record, and concealed or revealed bodies, but none of it gives a verified link to wolves. Stakes: As a publicly claimed tracker under suspicion, you are a likely wolf target, so a night spent re-following the same suspect may yield nothing if you are blocked or killed. Choosing the follow target with more information value matters. Target landscape: The suspect who voted against you and was already followed on Night 1, versus other quiet players or an unverified claimant. The vote against you is behavioral evidence, not proof of wolf alignment.
lessons.action: If you are exposed after claiming, follow a suspect chosen by evidence, not just the player who voted against you. Prefer a different unchecked suspect or a player linked to a likely kill target, since the Chanteuse can block you and the wolves can kill you that night. Hold the same suspect only if no better candidate exists.

lessons.situation: Night 1 with all ten alive, no day-1 vote, no claims and no deaths. The trailseer must choose its first follow blind. Possible outcomes are a visit to the wolves' victim, a visit to some other player, no visit, a roleblock, or being killed before getting a result. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no night results, no voting record. The follow itself is the only evidence source, and one night's movement of one player shows where they went, not their role. Stakes: Early game with a full board and no pressure to act. One follow cannot flip the game, but a visit to the night's victim can give the town an early concrete lead on a wolf. Because every pick is a blind guess, the value is in collecting a trail, not in being right about a role. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, deaths or behavioral tells. The pick is effectively arbitrary, so choose a quiet player who has not drawn attention and who is not you.
lessons.action: On night 1 with no claims or deaths, follow one quiet, unclaimed player and treat the follow as a probe. If they visited someone who is then attacked or killed that night, that player is a strong carrier lead. If they visited no one, treat it as weak, non-clearing information, since a follow shows only where a player went and a concealed kill can leave no trace.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game with no discussion history. The Trailseer must pick a follow target blind while wolves, a lone killer and possibly a roleblocker are active, and the Trailseer may be blocked or killed that night. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: only the role list and your own role knowledge. No claims, results or votes exist. Stakes: Early game with every faction at full strength. No single night here decides the game, so a blind follow is cheap, and the main value is getting a first visit trace to compare against later events. Target landscape: All nine other players are equally unknown: no claims, no votes, no deaths and no behavior. The pick rests on no evidence, so any name is as good as another.
lessons.action: On a blind first night, follow one other player rather than holding back, since the follow costs nothing and any visit it reveals is a lead. A null result or a block says little, so keep the target-to-visited pairing exact for later cross-checking and choose later targets from claims and morning outcomes.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) with several unrevealed evil roles (a wolf pair and/or a lone killer) alive. The trailseer must pick whose movements to follow. Roleblocks and night kills have been landing on the trailseer when it acts predictably. Information landscape: Thin: a few confirmed wills or lynch results, one tied or split vote, no verified findings. The trailseer's own results are sparse (no-visit result, blocks) and speculative behavioral reads dominate. Stakes: Town is only a couple of eliminations from wolf parity, and the trailseer is one of few remaining information sources. A wasted follow, caused by being blocked or by following a target who is unlikely to reveal anything, can cost the town its last chance to find evil. Target landscape: Several living players with no confirmed roles, plus possibly a vocal claimed power role (e.g. vigilante) who has challenged you. Choice rests on day chatter and vote patterns, not hard evidence. Following a quiet, unscrutinized player yielded the one decisive lead; following the loud claimant produced nothing.
lessons.action: Each night, follow a player who has not been confirmed or strongly suspected but whose day behavior or votes you want pinned down, and prefer a target who is not a loud accuser of you. If your result shows the target visiting a night victim or another suspicious stop, treat that as a lead to act on; if you were blocked and got nothing, do not read it as evidence about the target.

lessons.situation: The Trailseer is a repeated target of night attacks (survived because protected), perhaps after being roleblocked on an earlier night, and needs to find the attacker among the few suspects. Information landscape: Moderately rich: an eliminated wolf, a double attack pattern, and earlier clears narrow the field. The follow supplies a visit trace that can be cross-checked against the Healer's claimed protection. Stakes: Mid-late board with a killer actively targeting you. Identifying the killer now prevents further losses, and your survival depends on the Healer's protection continuing. Target landscape: A handful of suspects, with some cleared-ish or role-claimed (Healer, Vigilante, replacement roles). The remaining quiet, deflecting, night-immune-looking player is the prime suspect, judged on behavior rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When you have been attacked repeatedly or protected and the lone killer is among a short list of suspects, follow the suspect whose behavior fits a night-immune killer. If they visited you on a night you were attacked, they are the killer or your protector, and the Healer's claim can separate the two. This turns the attacks on you into evidence.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six alive with two eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, and the game cannot end within one more elimination, so a single misplaced sigil costs one of two remaining sigils without ending the game but narrowing the margin for error; a wasted sigil leaves the sigilist with one strike for the rest of the game.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Placing a sigil is a visible-in-outcome act: if it strikes, the struck player is revealed as an attacker, and a sigil with no effect narrows the target to a non-attacker; the sigil itself is spent on placement whether or not it triggers, so the choice is irreversible.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no living player has verified a night result, the sentinel and investigator and fortune teller and healer are dead, and the only public data are the sentinel's will (watched player_9, saw no one) and the healer's will (protected player_4 and player_6, no attacks announced) plus one unverified trailseer chain.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 ended with the healer lynched, and the village is now split between a trailseer claim and players who deny it, with the carrier of the wolves' kill unknown. The sigilist must predict which living player will attack tonight, since a sigil placed on a player who does not attack is wasted, and a sigil on a carrier or on a vigilante who shoots strikes them.
query_dims.target_landscape: Six players alive: the sigilist's own seat plus five others (player_2, player_3, player_6, player_8, player_9). Public roles are unclaimed except a trailseer claim by player_3 with a night chain that has not been verified; the vigilante has not yet revealed. Evidence is behavioral and vote-based, with the trailseer chain the only concrete trail and it places the now-lynched healer, not any living player, at the sentinel.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with one wolf or lone killer still active among five or six living players, and the sigilist is a likely kill target. Information landscape: Information-rich on dead evil roles, cleared players and voting records, but the last attacker is identified only by behavior and elimination. Stakes: Each night costs a player and the board is close to parity, so a sigil that strikes the last killer can win the game outright, and one held until death is wasted. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a secret visit that spends the charge whether or not it triggers, so it cannot be undone. A no-effect result means the target did not attack, which fits a non-killer or an attacker who held back, and it does not clear them. Target landscape: A few living unverified candidates, with the others cleared by the investigator or sentinel. The best suspect is picked from behavior, such as an isolated vote against a confirmed role or a quiet profile, because no hard proof exists.
lessons.action: When few players remain (about 5-6) and one killer is left, place a sigil each night on the most probable unverified killer, chosen from voting record and investigator or sentinel clearances, rather than holding both sigils. If that player attacks, the sigil strikes them, so you convert a read into a kill. With one sigil left, spend it on your best read, since an unspent sigil does nothing if you are killed first.

lessons.situation: One or both wolves may already be dead. A killer keeps targeting a known town player, and the sigilist is tempted to put the sigil on that expected victim to counter the next attack. Information landscape: Role information is public, such as confirmed investigator results and verified healer saves. There is still no trace pointing at the remaining killer. Stakes: The remaining killer can keep striking, but the town is not on the brink. Preserving limited sigils for an identified attacker matters more than acting every night. Forward exposure: Holding commits you to nothing and reveals nothing. You keep both charges and can place one on any later night. Target landscape: The remaining candidates are likely victims, such as a claimed investigator who survived an attack or was healer-protected, or unvetted players with no attack evidence. None has been tied to a kill.
lessons.action: If no living suspect has evidence of attacking and the only candidates are likely victims or confirmed-Town players such as a protected investigator, keep your sigils that night. Wait for a suspect with an attack pattern. A sigil on a player who does not attack does nothing, and a likely victim is the one player who will not attack.

lessons.situation: Late game (night 3) after one evil was voted out. At least one wolf is believed to still be alive and attacking every night. You have not yet used either sigil and have already counter-claimed the sigilist role publicly. Information landscape: Mixed: in one case rich (revealed roles, visitor lists, an investigator's clearing read), in the other thin, with unverified claims and only the fact that attacks were happening each night. Either way the sigil depends on predicting who will attack. Stakes: A few players remain and a wolf is still killing each night. Removing the last wolf with a sigil strike can end the game or leave only the serial killer for a day vote. Holding both sigils unused wastes the one tool that punishes a night attacker. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a visit and spends it whether or not it triggers. A strike is announced publicly as a sigil death, which exposes you as the sigilist, but your role was already claimed publicly, so little extra exposure. It cannot be undone once placed, though a second sigil remains. Target landscape: A few living candidates, including a contested healer claimant versus a player cleared Not suspicious by the investigator, or an unresolved field of vigilante, trailseer, illusionist, speculator, sentinel and serial killer. The best-supported target is the one public deduction marks as an evil attacker; where the evidence is thin, the pick rests on a guess about who attacks.
lessons.action: On a night when only one or two attackers likely remain (a lone wolf, or a wolf plus a killer) and you hold both sigils, place a sigil on the player you most suspect of attacking, rather than keeping both. A sigil strikes only if the target attacks, so choose the likeliest attacker from public reads: a wolf cleared of nothing, a contested claimant, or whoever the room's math points to. If you place the sigil and it does not strike, you still have one left for the next night.

lessons.situation: Late game with most roles mapped by deaths, reveals and claims; one evil attacker (wolf or lone killer) is still hidden among very few unverified players, and the sigilist holds its last sigil.
