Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed dead roles, investigator clears, healer confirmation and visit tracking leave one plausible attacker. Stakes: Few players remain and the next night kill could tip parity or end the game, so one well-aimed sigil can either strike the last attacker and win or confirm immunity evidence that wins the next day vote. Forward exposure: Spends the last sigil irreversibly and leaves no further night tool, so later progress depends on daytime deduction; the placement is a visit but is hidden from the town. Target landscape: One unverified candidate (claimed vigilante or unvetted player) remains against confirmed healer, investigator, trailseer or cleared players; the pick is based on elimination of confirmed roles, not on behavior alone.
lessons.action: When one sigil remains and deduction through confirmed roles and clears leaves a single unverified killer candidate, place the sigil on that candidate. If they attack that night the sigil strikes them (resolved after their attack), so a strike ends the threat. If it has no effect, that is consistent with them not attacking or with night immunity, so weigh it against later visit evidence rather than as a clear.

lessons.situation: Night after a mis-elimination or an unproductive day. The investigator is dead or silent and no visit trails exist. The sigilist must choose between a blind ward and conserving charges while the wolves or a lone killer may target it next. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified results, and no night visits are corroborated. Only voting behavior and speech are available. Stakes: The board is still mid-game but narrowing, and the sigilist is itself a possible kill target. Unused charges die with it, so a deterrent held back forever delivers nothing to Town. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a private visit that a Sentinel or Trailseer could trace. It is irreversible once spent, but it leaves one charge in reserve and does not reveal the sigilist's role. Target landscape: Eight or so living players, none with confirmed alignment or visit trails. They are vocal accusers and quiet players, and any pick rests on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: With both sigils left and no hard leads, place one sigil each night on the player most plausibly carrying a night attack (a suspected wolf or killer), and keep the second in reserve. A sigil only strikes a target that attacks that night, so placing one early at least makes a visit that can punish a kill. Holding both risks dying with them unused.

lessons.situation: Mid-game with a killer still active at night. One suspect has been tracked to a victim or looks like the attacker, and the day vote has not resolved them. The sigilist can punish an attack but cannot know who will attack. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: trailseer or sentinel traces and public night outcomes exist, but nothing shows who will carry the attack tonight. Stakes: Killers are still active and each night costs a town player. A sigil that strikes a real attacker could remove one. With only two charges, each wasted use cuts the remaining chances. Forward exposure: A placed sigil is spent whether or not it triggers and leaves one charge. The placement is a visit that a watcher or follower may see. A null result is private to you and cannot be undone. Target landscape: A prime suspect tied by hard evidence to a victim's door or to repeated kills, versus quieter unvetted players and confirmed or likely town. Evidence-backed suspects outrank behavior-only reads, but a wolf suspect may not carry the kill that night.
lessons.action: Place the sigil on the prime suspect whose evidence (a trailseer follow, a sentinel watch, or a repeated visit pattern) ties them to night killing. Prefer a suspected lone killer, who attacks every night, over a wolf, since only the rotating carrier attacks. If you target a wolf, aim at the one likely to carry the kill that night. The sigil only strikes a target who attacks, and a healer can still stop the strike.

lessons.situation: The sigilist took several elimination votes by day and now faces a night where it is a likely target, with both sigils still unspent. Dying unspent wastes the role's whole contribution. Information landscape: Info-starved: Day 2 votes and an unverified Sentinel claim, with no confirmed evil identities. Stakes: The sigilist is a likely kill target with two sigils at stake. Unused sigils vanish with its death, while one used on a probable attacker could remove a killer. Forward exposure: A sigil is a visit that watchers may see and it spends one of two charges, leaving one in reserve. Holding both keeps full flexibility but risks dying with them unused. Target landscape: Several players who voted against you (a claimed Sentinel and unexplained voters) alongside quiet abstainers. The basis is voting behavior only, with no confirmed roles.
lessons.action: If you were heavily voted yesterday, place a sigil on the most likely attacker among your accusers instead of passing with both sigils unspent. A sigil on a likely wolf or killer punishes a night attack by them only if it resolves, and unspent sigils are worth nothing if you die overnight. Do not count on it to prevent your own death.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) after a day with no clear lead. You have publicly claimed Sigilist and hold one sigil. A loud Town power role has survived a double attack because of a healer save, so the wolves and the killer are expected to pivot to other power roles, you among them. Information landscape: Info-starved. There is a death or two and a save, but nothing identifies who the wolves or the killer are, so there is no attacker signal. Stakes: The board is still contested, but a power-role death moves wolves and killer closer to parity. If you die with the sigil unplaced, Town loses both its power role and any chance of a sigil strike. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a visit and cannot be undone, and it spends the sigil whether or not the target attacks. Your role and your remaining sigil count are already known, so the move adds little new exposure, and holding the sigil does not stop the pack from targeting you. Target landscape: Candidates are the healer-protected Trailseer who keeps getting attacked, the healer, and quiet or unclaimed players. No evidence points to a specific attacker, so any pick rests on behavior and voting reads. The pack was expected to pivot away from the protected target toward other power roles, including you.
lessons.action: When your role is already public, you are a likely kill target, and you are info-starved, place your remaining sigil on the most plausible attacker instead of holding it. Pick the player whose votes or behavior fit an attacker best, and avoid the healer-protected player the pack keeps hitting, since a victim who is attacked is not the one the sigil punishes. An unplaced sigil is worth nothing if you die that night, while a placed one strikes any wolf carrier or killer who attacks the target.

lessons.situation: After a vote where one player broke consensus, the sigilist considers committing its last sigil on that behavioral outlier. That player may be a wolf whose role is blocking, not attacking, that night, or may not attack at all. Information landscape: Mostly information-starved: one unverified investigator claim cleared a player, and the only kill was concealed by an illusionist. No visit evidence points to who carries the attack. Stakes: Wolves and a lone killer are both still alive, so the last sigil is Town's only reactive deterrent. Wasting it on a non-attacker leaves no deterrent for the rest of the game. Forward exposure: Spending the final sigil is irreversible and leaves the role with no remaining power. The action itself stays private unless the sigilist discloses it. Target landscape: The loud outlier voter who broke an abstain consensus, an unverified investigator claimant, and quiet abstainers. The choice among them rests on voting behavior, not on evidence.
lessons.action: With one sigil left, place it on a player a concrete lead marks as a probable attacker, such as a Suspicious result or a visit trail. Absent such a lead, keep the last charge. A mere behavioral outlier may be a non-attacker such as the Chanteuse, who blocks instead of killing, and the sigil is then spent for nothing.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a 10-player game; the Sigilist must decide between a speculative sigil placement and keeping both charges, with no discussion or vote having occurred yet. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no public statements, deaths, role claims, votes, or night results exist. Stakes: Early game with full board; no single night decides the game, but only two sigils exist for the whole game. Wasting one on a blind guess has a high cost and almost no expected payoff. Forward exposure: Holding makes no visit and leaves no trace, and it commits nothing; both sigils stay available. Placing one would be an irreversible, secret visit with a spent charge that could be seen by a Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none claimed, no voting record and no behavior to read. Nothing separates the wolves, the lone killer or a Vigilante from ordinary Town, so any target would be a pure guess.
lessons.action: On opening night with no claims, votes, or night results, keep both sigils instead of placing one on a random guess. A sigil only matters if its target attacks that night, so a blind placement on one of nine players is a low-odds spend of half your lifetime charges; hold them until a death, a result, or voting behavior points to a likely attacker.

lessons.situation: Night with a night-immune lone killer possibly still alive. The sigilist has one sigil left and a vote-pressured suspect it believes is the Serial Killer. Information landscape: Moderately thin. There is a public record of votes and confirmed roles for several dead players, but no verified read on the killers. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity, so spending the last sigil on a target that cannot be struck is a costly miss. The sigilist then has no night action left. Forward exposure: A sigil placed on a suspected Serial Killer reveals nothing publicly and is spent. A no-effect result matches both a target who did not attack and an attacker protected by night immunity. Reporting that result by day exposes the sigilist. Target landscape: Two or three suspects narrowed by structural clues, such as who was or was not attacked. One suspect may be a night-immune Serial Killer, and the evidence is behavioral and structural.
lessons.action: Before spending a sigil, list the attackers still possible, such as the wolf carrier, an active lone killer or a possible shooter. Aim the sigil at the suspect who is most likely to attack that night and is not night-immune. If the narrowed suspect may be the Serial Killer, a no-effect result is ambiguous and a strike cannot happen, so choose a different target or hold the sigil.

lessons.situation: A mid-game night with about seven players alive. Wolves and a lone killer are still active, nobody has identified tonight's attacker, and you are tempted to spend a sigil on a thinly justified pick. Information landscape: Information-starved about night attackers. Claims are contested, and roles are partly hidden because of body-attacks or concealments. You have only behavioral reads and no confirmed attacker identity or carrier order. Stakes: Evil is not yet close to parity, so there is time to wait. Each sigil is a scarce one-shot kill threat against an attacker, and wasting one on a non-attacker lowers your endgame deterrent for no gain. Forward exposure: Placing a sigil is a visit that is publicly invisible unless a Trailseer or Sentinel covers you, but it spends the sigil permanently and cannot be undone. A 'no effect' result is ambiguous, so it commits you without confirming anything. Holding the sigil reveals nothing and keeps the option open. A Chanteuse block means no sigil is placed and none is spent. Target landscape: Several unconfirmed players remain: an unclaimed quiet player, a neutral such as the Fortune Teller, and Town claimants with contested results. Roles are unrevealed and the pick rests on behavior rather than evidence. Neutral betting players and most Town roles never attack, so a sigil on them is wasted.
lessons.action: Place a sigil only when you can name a target likely to attack that night, such as a suspected wolf whose turn as carrier is due in seat order, or a player you strongly believe is the lone killer. If you only have a vague behavioral hunch, or your pool is neutrals and Town-claimers, keep the sigil. A sigil is spent when placed, whether or not it triggers, and a 'no effect' result cannot tell a non-attacker from a protected attacker.

lessons.situation: Night 1 (or any early night) with the sigilist holding two sigils and no information about who will attack. Blind placements in this regime hit a non-attacker, a target that night immunity protects, or a victim killed by another player. Information landscape: Information-starved: no day vote on Day 1, no claims, no night reports, no confirmed roles. Any target is a pure guess. Stakes: Early game with all players alive, so no single night decides the game. The two sigils are the sigilist's only offense. Spending one blind halves it for no return, while holding keeps full strength for when evidence appears. Forward exposure: Holding is not a visit and leaves no trace for a Sentinel or Trailseer. It commits nothing, and both sigils stay available. Placing a sigil is a visit that can be seen, and the spent charge cannot be recovered. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none with claims, votes, deaths or behavioral history. Nothing separates a likely attacker (wolf carrier, lone killer, Vigilante) from non-attackers such as the Healer or Trailseer, so any pick is a coin flip.
lessons.action: On an opening night with no deaths, claims, votes or results, keep both sigils and place nothing. A sigil is spent on placement and only matters if the target attacks that night. A blind guess among nine unknowns mostly returns only 'no effect', which is also what a target who did not attack looks like.

lessons.situation: An attacked and saved player had two known visitors, and the choice is which one might be the attacker. Visiting a victim is ambiguous because a protector looks the same as an attacker. Information landscape: Information-rich on who visited, but ambiguous on intent. A dead role revealed the door traffic, and the claims conflict. Stakes: A sigil placed on the genuine healer exhausts the sigilist and builds misdirected suspicion against a key protector. Wolves stay free to attack. Forward exposure: Holding keeps the sigil fully in reserve and leaves no visit trace. Placing it on a protector spends the last charge irreversibly, and the miss looks the same as a non-attacker. Target landscape: Two visitors at a saved victim's door, one a plausible healer and one possibly a malicious visitor posing as a protector, with quiet players unvetted. Evidence is the door traffic and competing claims, with no confirmed attacker.
lessons.action: When the unresolved suspects are players whose visit may be protective, such as a possible healer at a saved victim's door, keep the remaining sigil instead of placing it on them. Hold it until a suspect with attack-consistent behavior emerges, because a sigil on a protector is wasted and cannot stop the wolves.

query_dims.consensus_text: There is no clear village consensus or coordinated accusation. The speakers so far agree that the Trailseer visiting the watched player does not identify who attacked the Trailseer, and they are seeking more information.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; this decision cannot end the game within one more elimination, so the immediate stakes are not a one-result swing.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Saying the Trailseer’s visit is consistent with a follow action, and asking why the Sentinel chose that target, would reinforce a public interpretation already voiced without revealing your role or night knowledge. It is readily reversible as discussion, though a later shift to accusing the watched player could look inconsistent.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: the Sentinel asked why you were watched, but no one has accused you or cited evidence against you.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is limited: two Town roles were publicly revealed dead, but neither death report supplies a visitor trace. The only claimed Night 1 result is the Sentinel’s watch showing the Trailseer visited the watched player; no independent result corroborates it, and no one has presented a verified lead identifying the killer.
query_dims.my_position: Not driving a consensus; your stated interpretation is aligned with the cautious public reading, while the room has no clear direction.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know the pack killed the player revealed as the Investigator. Publicly, both the Investigator and Trailseer were revealed among the Night 1 dead, and the Sentinel claim says the Trailseer visited the player they watched; the room has not connected that visit to the attack.
query_dims.situation: After Night 1 killed the publicly revealed Investigator and Trailseer, an unverified Sentinel claim that the Trailseer visited the watched player prompted questions about whether that visit implicates the watched player. The Trailseer’s role makes following a plausible explanation, and the discussion has not produced a concrete accusation or vote direction.
query_dims.target_landscape: No elimination candidates have emerged. The watched player is not publicly implicated by the visit alone; the Sentinel is an unverified claimant, and the Trailseer’s revealed role makes a follow action a plausible explanation. No evidence currently distinguishes other living players as vote targets.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote: I am the primary target after an accuser's check or watch result, backed by a second claimant. My own counterclaim or deflection has attracted no followers. Information landscape: Starved to moderate: conflicting or unverified role claims, a concealed or ambiguous body, and a visit report that implicates me. No role reveals confirm either side. Stakes: My single vote cannot change an 8-1 outcome, so its value lies in the signal it sends and in not tying myself to a doomed counterclaim. Losing a wolf this early also removes a voter and a conceal that the pack cannot replace. Consensus: Lopsided against me, resting on a corroborating claim from a second player and a weak defense from me. My position: Holding out alone against the forming consensus. Heat: Very high: several players named me, I was the most accused, and I gave a last word. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser is public and permanent, ties me to my counterclaim and reads as self-protective. If I am eliminated, my role reveal confirms the accuser and makes them trusted for later days. Target landscape: Candidates are the accuser (a claimed investigator or sentinel with partial corroboration) and myself. Neither can be verified by a role reveal yet, so the room weighs the claims and my defense. Public vs private: I privately know the accuser's read on me is true, or that the visit evidence against me is accurate. Publicly the village sees a corroborated accusation against me and an unresolved counter-claim from me, with no confirmed roles.
lessons.action: When the room is lopsided against you on corroborated evidence, check whether any accuser's claim has real traction before you vote. If the room is clearly locked on you, put your vote on a second-tier suspect the room already doubts, not the accuser who named you. That pairs your vote with other doubt, avoids another lone self-protective vote, and keeps your last word credible if it reads as a sincere read.

lessons.situation: A Town information role has publicly tied you to a night kill, and a second player backs the claim. Your partner is alive but is distancing from you, and you are the favorite to be eliminated today. Information landscape: Moderately rich: a specific result naming you, corroborating claims and a prior vote record. All of it is unverified, but it fits together. Stakes: Losing you leaves one wolf with several eliminations still to go before parity. Your vote cannot rescue you, so its only use is to hit the most dangerous accurser and keep the surviving wolf alive. Consensus: The village is aligned against you on a consistent claim and its corroboration, and it has little other evidence to weigh. My position: Holding out alone with a counter-vote while the room piles onto you. Heat: High. You are the named suspect and the primary target of the day, with several players accusing you from the start. Forward exposure: Your vote and denial go on the public record and cannot be retracted. If the accuser is read as truthful and you die, your role is revealed and your partner is left to survive alone. Target landscape: The candidates are the accuser and the player who corroborates them. Neither has a confirmed role, and the case rests on a specific claim plus consistent backing rather than on behavior alone. Public vs private: You privately know the accusation against you is true, for example the watch result that names you at a victim's door. Publicly it is only an unverified claim, though corroborating claims and a roleblock story make it look consistent.
lessons.action: When the vote is converging on you and your single vote cannot change the count, spend it on the accuser whose claim or case against you is most credible. That is the Town player most likely to hold accurate information, and removing them helps your partner survive. Keep denying the specific claim instead of switching to a new target, so your partner can still look like an independent Town voter.

lessons.situation: A day 2 vote in which two players claim investigator, your wolf partner is one of them (a fake claim) and was placed at a night scene by a watch. The village must choose between them. Information landscape: Moderate: one watch result and one follow result were shared, but both investigator claims are unverified and the key check result was never given. Stakes: The vote decides whether the town keeps its checker or the pack's partner is exposed. Eight players are alive and parity is about three eliminations away, so removing the real checker materially helps the wolves. Consensus: A clear majority is forming against the claimed investigator on the basis of claim contradiction and your partner's push. My position: With the majority, not driving. Heat: Low: you have barely spoken, are not named in the accusations, and stand outside the two-way fight. Forward exposure: A vote for the claimed investigator matches your partner's push and the room's lean, so it exposes little. Voting to save your partner would tie you to a player the visit evidence already places at the scene; the vote is public and permanent either way. Target landscape: Two candidates in a role-claim contradiction: a claimed investigator with no verifiable result, and your partner, who gave a counter-claim and was placed at a night scene by a watch. Neither role is confirmed; the basis is claim contradiction and a visit report. Public vs private: Privately you know your partner is a wolf and the investigator claimant is probably the real role; publicly the room sees only a contradiction between two role claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other checker is contested and your partner has pushed against them, join the majority vote to eliminate that player, provided your partner is not the one the room is leaning toward. This removes a role that threatens the pack, while a vote with the room and your partner's push keeps your heat low; if the majority is instead forming on your partner, avoid defending them loudly and keep your vote on the room's lead alternative.

lessons.situation: Day vote after an investigator names you Suspicious or counterclaims against you. The village forces an elimination between you and the investigator, and the vote is lopsided against you. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game master-confirmed healer save, night-one logic that excludes other Suspicious roles, and cross-referenced night actions all support the investigator. Stakes: Losing a wolf here halves the pack's voting power and leaves a dead body for the necromancer to use if the role is revealed. A partner dragged down by a shared vote would cost the pack its last wolf. Consensus: The village is strongly aligned against you, about 7 votes to 2 or 3, because the investigator's claim is verified or consistent with mechanics and the game master's announcements. My position: Holding out or driving against the room's consensus, with at most your wolf partner voting alongside. Heat: Extreme to critical. You are named Suspicious or countered by an investigator claimant, the trailseer may be piling on, and an elimination vote on you is imminent. Forward exposure: Voting against the investigator who accused you commits you to the losing side of a public, permanent record. If you flip wolf, everyone who voted alongside you is exposed, and the vote cannot be undone. Target landscape: The claimed investigator, either uncontested or in a counterclaim duel with you, versus other living players with no hard evidence against them. The investigator's claim is backed by cross-checked night logic, while any alternative target rests on behavior alone. Public vs private: Privately you know the investigator's result or counterclaim is true or false, and that the pack is exposed. Publicly the room is still trying to decide who is authentic and is leaning heavily toward eliminating you.
lessons.action: When the room is clearly lined up against you and an investigator claim is driving it, treat the vote as likely lost. Do not give your partner a visible reason to copy you: cast your vote on a different plausible suspect, or on the claimant only if the room is split. Votes are public and permanent, so a lone-wolf vote on the accuser links your partner to you if you flip wolf.

lessons.situation: Day vote, with the village converging on your wolf partner (the chanteuse) after tracking, watch or role claims linked her to suspicious visits. You must choose between joining the wagon, abstaining, or voting on someone else. Information landscape: Claim-heavy and unverified. Only the morning kill announcements are confirmed, and no roles have been revealed by vote yet. Stakes: The wolf side is still alive but about to drop to a single wolf, so your survival and cover now carry the pack. Your vote does not change the outcome. It only decides whether you look like a villager or a partner of the dead wolf when the next day's suspicion begins. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous against your partner, on claim-based evidence such as a follow report, a block claim or a watch claim. Nothing has been confirmed by announcement. My position: With the overwhelming majority. Your vote adds to a wagon that would succeed without it. Heat: Low. You have only voiced mild skepticism or been questioned peripherally, and have not defended the partner by name. Forward exposure: The vote is public and permanent and cannot be undone. Voting with the wagon on your partner looks like ordinary town behavior and stays cover if she is revealed as a wolf. Abstaining or voting a different target looks like distancing or defending, and is read against you once her role is shown. Target landscape: The main candidate is your wolf partner, whose role is unrevealed, accused by several players on unverified claims (a follow report, a block claim, a watch claim, or a contested role claim). The alternatives are the claimants who accuse her, who may be real Town roles. The basis is behavioral and claim-based, with nothing confirmed by announcement. Public vs private: You privately know the accused player is your wolf partner and that the claims against her are accurate or at least dangerous. Publicly she is only an accused player facing several accusers backed by unverified claims, and nobody knows her role.
lessons.action: When a near-unanimous wagon is already closing on your wolf partner and your vote can't change the result, cast your vote with the majority on her. Your public record then reads as an ordinary villager and gives you a defense line for the next day, so a vote elsewhere doesn't mark you as her ally. Hold that line and avoid any earlier defense or pushback that could be tied to her.

lessons.situation: With the serial killer dead, the town unites behind an accusation of the illusionist, who has one conceal left. The surviving wolf partner can still vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed serial killer elimination, a dead trailseer's recorded tracking result and a claimed sigilist's reported test. These facts make the accusation hard to rebut. Stakes: Losing a wolf here halves the pack and leaves the survivor needing two more eliminations to reach parity. Because the town's votes are already locked, only a pooled counter-vote could change the result. Consensus: Near-unanimous among the non-wolves, resting on one dead player's recorded result and the serial killer's removal. It is firm and unlikely to move. My position: holding out Heat: Critical. Four or more town votes are locked on you from a standing accusation, while your partner has low heat. Forward exposure: A vote is public and permanent. Joining the partner's target signals a wolf-side counter-wagon but commits both wolves to the same name. Scattering votes reveals isolation and gains nothing. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed sigilist, whom the partner already voted for, and unpressured bystanders. The sigilist's reported test is unverified, so any case against them rests on behavior and has no hard evidence. Public vs private: Town is united on the illusionist because of a dead player's lingering tracking report. Privately the illusionist knows the accusation is true, and the partner is unsuspected and free to coordinate.
lessons.action: If you are the locked-in vote target and your wolf partner is alive, put your vote on the same counter-target the partner is already voting for, such as a claimed role with a thin case. Do not scatter a lone vote onto an unpressured player. Pooled wolf votes can create a tie or a doubt, while a scattered vote shows isolation and adds no pressure.

lessons.situation: First vote day after a night-1 death, with only unverified claims and no leads on any evil faction. Information landscape: Information-starved: self-reported results only, no confirmed roles, no voting history. Stakes: Early game with a wide margin before wolf parity. A wasted or mis-targeted vote gains little, while staying hidden preserves the pack's flexibility. Consensus: The table is quiet and leaning toward abstaining, with no accusations and no evidence-based lead. My position: With the majority, joining the abstain. Heat: Very low: nobody has accused you and you have only made generic comments. Forward exposure: A named vote would be permanent on the record and tie you to a mis-elimination with no evidence behind it. An abstain commits you to nothing and keeps all options open. Target landscape: No strong candidates. Claims are unverified, no roles are confirmed, and any target would be a behavioral guess. Public vs private: You privately know the wolf pack, your own kill and any conceal you used. Publicly the table has only unverified self-reports or a bare death announcement, with no accusations against wolves.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, when no one has accused anyone and no role is confirmed, abstain with the table rather than naming an evidence-free target. If the room is already abstaining, your abstain is invisible, commits you to no read, and keeps both wolves unremarked for another night.

lessons.situation: Day-2 vote where a claimed information role gave a result impossible under the rules and the room is piling on. Information landscape: Information-rich on one point: a rules-checkable contradiction. Otherwise little is known. Stakes: The elimination is likely to land on a Town role regardless of your vote, which favors the pack. Staying aligned keeps your heat low. Consensus: The village is aligned on the contradicted claimant, with several players spelling out the case. My position: With the majority, among the voices building the case. Heat: Low: you have made rules-based comments, not accusations of others, and nobody suspects you. Forward exposure: Voting with a unanimous or near-unanimous room is low-commitment and reveals nothing about wolf identity. Dissenting would make you stand out. Target landscape: One claimant with a self-admitted contradiction of the rules, versus other claimants with no public contradictions. The basis is evidence, not behavior. Public vs private: You privately know the pack and the hidden-role kill, but nothing about whether the accused lied or erred. Publicly the room has an evidence-backed case that fits your interests.
lessons.action: When the room converges on a player with a rules-verifiable contradiction in their claim, vote with the majority, ideally after pointing out why the defense fails. If the target is a Town information role, this also removes it for the pack without exposing you.

lessons.situation: You are the last wolf after your partner was exposed and removed, and the village is convinced you were the partner's ally based on voting patterns. Information landscape: Thin. The only hard facts are the partner's reveal as a wolf and the concealed night kills, so the village argues about who voted for whom. Stakes: You are the last wolf, so your elimination ends the wolf side's chances. A single vote cannot change a lopsided count, so the vote is only worth casting where it removes a likely Town power role. Consensus: The village is aligned on you, based on voting-record links to your dead partner and not on hard evidence. My position: Holding out alone, the single voter against the lead accuser while everyone else piles onto you. Heat: High. You are the primary target of several accusers, who link your earlier vote to your dead partner. Forward exposure: Your vote and your accusation of the quiet players go on the public record and cannot be reversed. If you are eliminated, your role is revealed and the wolf side is gone. Target landscape: The candidates are your main accuser plus several quiet or accusing players. None has a confirmed role, since only your dead partner was revealed, so the case against you rests on behavioral links to your partner. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf, with your partner already dead and revealed. Publicly you are a player whose earlier vote and pushback drew suspicion, and your voting record is the main evidence against you.
lessons.action: As the last wolf under accusation, cast your vote on the main accuser who pushed the case, not an abstention, and use your last word to point at a quiet player. Pick the accuser who looks most likely to be a Town power role, since you need real Town eliminations to get anywhere near parity. If the room is already four or more against you, treat the vote as the best way to remove a dangerous Town player.

lessons.situation: Day vote with four players alive: you are the last wolf (partner dead or revealed, no conceals left), a necromancer is alive, and the table is converging on you. Information landscape: Role eliminations are known and the necromancer's presence is confirmed by reanimated kills or sigil strikes, but nothing hard separates you from the necromancer. Stakes: With four alive and a lone killer in play, your elimination ends the wolf team and hands the necromancer your body. Removing the necromancer is the wolves' only path to a win. Consensus: The village is aligned against you as the remaining wolf, based on eliminated roles and voting behaviour, with no hard evidence against the other suspect. My position: Holding out alone on a different target from the room. Heat: Critical. The other survivors have publicly narrowed the pool to you and one other player, and two or three of them are voting for you. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and commits you to a named target. If you are eliminated, your role is revealed and your body becomes usable by the necromancer, so the vote cannot be walked back. Target landscape: Three candidates: a confirmed sigilist, a neutral (fortune teller) claimant, and the unconfirmed necromancer. Evidence is a sentinel killed by a reanimated vigilante or a sigil strike, plus voting behaviour. No role among the three is confirmed to be the necromancer. Public vs private: You know you are the last wolf and that a necromancer is acting, while the table believes the pool is you and one other unconfirmed player, and the other voters are converging on you.
lessons.action: As the last wolf in a four-player vote with a necromancer still alive, put your vote on the player you judge most likely to be the necromancer. Use the reanimated-kill evidence and the voting records. Only that elimination can ever let the wolves win, and it also stops the necromancer from using your body after you die; if you can win over one other voter, a 2-2 tie spares you.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after the wolf partner was revealed or killed. You are the last wolf and the most accused player, and the room is hunting the Day 2 bandwagon participants. The lone killer is still alive. Information landscape: Rich: the partner's role is revealed, the Day 2 public voting record exists, and night reports from Town roles corroborate the story against you. Stakes: With the partner gone and the room converging on you, your elimination is likely and would end the wolf side. A lone isolated vote cannot change the count, so it should at least seed a credible alternative suspect instead of confirming your guilt. Consensus: The village is nearly unified against you, with a large majority converging on your Day 2 voting and defense pattern now that your partner's role is confirmed. My position: Holding out alone against a lopsided consensus, casting a counter-vote. Heat: Very high: several players have accused you, citing your Day 2 defense or vote of the partner who has since been revealed. Your explanations have shifted, and you are the most accused player. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and irreversible, and if you are eliminated your role is revealed. A spiteful or isolated counter-vote confirms that you are reacting defensively and commits you to a target nobody else shares. A vote with a record-based reason at least gives the room a second suspect. Target landscape: The living candidates are active Town claimants or unconfirmed players, plus possibly a neutral or the lone killer. None has hard evidence against them. The choice rests on voting-record behavior, and the loudest accuser is the most obvious but weakest retaliation target. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf and that your Day 2 stance was wolf coordination. The room has read it as wolf behavior from the voting record and your partner's reveal, so the public read about you is largely correct.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf, your partner is revealed, and the room is lined up on you, vote for the living player whom the public record gives the best second-suspect case, such as a Day 2 bandwagon voter or an inconsistent claimant. Give a short reason drawn from that record. Do not retaliate on your loudest accuser or on the one player not piling on you, because the vote is public, permanent and reads as defensive.

lessons.situation: An early day vote (day 1 or 2) in which the village has only unverified role claims and partial night reports. The room is split between a lead target and abstaining, and no wolf is identified. You are the hidden illusionist wolf with your partner alive and unrevealed. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable role claims, a follow or watch report, no caught lies and no confirmed wolf. Stakes: Early game with many players alive and parity far off. No single vote decides the game, so the priority is staying unlinked and unsuspected while the pack keeps its kill plan. Consensus: The room is split or tied between a plurality target and an abstain bloc, with no hard evidence on anyone. My position: With the majority or a plurality, not driving the push. Heat: Low: you have spoken little, asked a question or defended a visit, and no one is accusing you. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and ties you to a side of the table. A vote with the majority or on an unlinked target reveals nothing about your role and carries little commitment, but it cannot be reversed that day. Target landscape: Candidates are an unclaimed quiet player, a claimed power role whose claim is corroborated or contested, and abstain. The basis is claim contradictions and behavior, not hard evidence; your partner and the pack's next kill target are not among your options. Public vs private: Privately you know the wolf pair, the pack's intended kill, and sometimes who is immune or a real power role; publicly there are only unverified claims and no wolf is identified.
lessons.action: When you are an illusionist wolf with low heat and no wolf identified, cast your day vote with the room's existing plurality on a player who is not your partner or your pack's next kill target. If the room is split and you hold a private fact such as who must be the immune Serial Killer, vote on that player instead, so your vote stays unlinked from the pack's plan and still passes as an ordinary Town vote.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote where your wolf partner casts an aggressive vote against a quiet player or splits the room, and you must decide between backing them and blending into the majority. Information landscape: Information-starved. The only evidence is unverified claims from investigative roles, with no confirmed flips. Stakes: Your partner's exposure can cascade onto you through the permanent vote record. The vote is not a swing because the village can abstain, so staying distant protects the pack's second wolf. Consensus: The room mostly abstains and has little hard information. A few claimants are pushing separate soft reads. My position: Tempted to join your partner's minority and hold out against the abstain majority. Heat: Low. A claimed sentinel or investigator result gave you temporary credibility, and your partner is the one attracting scrutiny. Forward exposure: Joining your partner's vote permanently pairs your public record with theirs. If they die and flip as a wolf, the town will review Day 2 votes and can pair the two minority votes, which makes the link undeniable. Target landscape: The options are to abstain with the majority, to join the partner's vote on a quiet player, or to vote for a player the town has accused. The partner-pushed target has no public evidence against them, only the partner's behavioral push. Public vs private: You know the co-voter is your wolf partner pushing a mislynch. The village only sees an unexplained minority push during a consensus abstain.
lessons.action: When your partner has already cast a rogue vote against a quiet player or toward a split, vote with the abstain majority, or with the broad majority on a target the town has independently pushed, rather than joining your partner's minority. Your votes should look independent of your partner's, so that if your partner dies and flips as a wolf, no paired wolf vote exists for the town to trace to you.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day vote (day 4-5) with few players left. You are a high-heat unclaimed wolf, the vote is tied between you and another suspect, and Town claimants are pushing reads that include you. Information landscape: Claims are unverified and no hard result clears or convicts anyone. Role-count deduction and voting behavior drive the reads, so the evidence is thin and speculative. Stakes: A few more eliminations let the wolves reach parity, so one vote decides whether the pack keeps its numbers. A tie costs the pack nothing and buys a night for the kill, while a lost vote leaves the wolves a man down, close to losing. Consensus: The room is fractured: Town claimants back one another's reads, the votes split into ties, and no single target has a clear majority. My position: Holding out against the bloc that is pressing on you. Heat: High: two or more players voted or named you, and an uncleared result or role-count reasoning marks you as one of the last unclaimed suspects. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent. Voting a Town claimant commits you to a counter-read that cannot be retracted, and voting your partner trades away a wolf. A tie only delays the elimination, and it leaves your exposure and your pair's pattern on the record. Target landscape: Candidates are you, your unclaimed partner, and Town claimants (investigator, vigilante, trailseer, sigilist). All claims are unverified, so the choice rests on role-count logic and behavior, not on hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know you are a wolf (and often that a Town claim is true or that the pack's remaining threat is a specific role). Publicly your claim status is unverified, and role-count reasoning or an uncleared result has put you among the likeliest wolves.
lessons.action: When you are one of the top two suspects and the room is split, cast your vote on the strongest rival suspect, preferably an unverified Town claimant who is not your partner, so the vote stays tied with you and nobody is eliminated. Treat the tie as only one bought day, and do not vote for your own partner just to stay alive.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single night or vote ends the game; a wrong bet costs one point's progress toward two, and a self-bet spent without a real threat wastes one of the two remaining uses that protect the scoring path.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: one night death, no checks, no watches, no follows, no public claims verified by the game master. Only the fortune teller's private point record (1 of 2) and its own bet history are known.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 ended with the town abstaining after a split vote, and the discussion is now centered on whether visit claims must state direction. The fortune teller has a night bet to place on the likeliest victim with no role-revealing evidence, and must decide whether to spend one of two self-bets on a night where an attack on itself may or may not be probable.
query_dims.target_landscape: Nine players alive; the fortune teller's own night bet and self-bet choices range over all living players. Public roles: only player_2 (trailseer) is confirmed dead; no living player has a public role confirmation. Claims are unverified: nobody has announced a checked or watched result, and the day-2 vote split (abstain plurality, two players each accused by one voter) gives no hard evidence on any target.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night where the killers' obvious priority target, a verified or claimed investigator, has been publicly shielded or saved by the healer, while other prominent claimants are unprotected. The Fortune Teller must choose a bet to reach two points. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves or the serial killer are dead or confirmed, healer saves are announced, and protection patterns are visible to every player, including the killers. Stakes: Scoring needs two points, and each zero-point night shrinks the remaining nights in which they can be earned. Repeating a bet the healer can block yields no points and pushes the Fortune Teller toward riskier late bets. Target landscape: A claimed investigator or other focal Town player who is openly or recently healer-protected; an unprotected claimed healer or trailseer; and quieter unverified players. The evidence is public announcements of saves and claims, not behavior.
lessons.action: When the obvious high-profile target was publicly healer-protected or saved last night, bet on a different likely victim instead, such as an unprotected prominent claimant (the claimed healer, or a trailseer or sentinel with no cover). If no protector remains alive, bet on the most prominent unprotected Town claimant.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or abstain day. One claimant of a night-info role is the focal point of the discussion and votes, so the wolves and the lone killer both have reason to kill them. Information landscape: Moderately informative. There is a public role claim and a vote record concentrated on one player, plus evidence from the earlier night that killers are active. Nothing is verified, and the read rests on the claimant's visibility and not on confirmed roles. Stakes: Scoring two points here ends the Fortune Teller's win condition outright. A miss costs nothing but a night, though only a few nights remain to score. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players. One stands out as a visible information threat: a self-declared Trailseer or Sentinel who was roleblocked or took the day's votes. Their role is unverified and rests on their own claim. The rest are quiet, with no comparable profile.
lessons.action: When a player has drawn real visibility, such as a self-declared info-role claim (Trailseer, Sentinel) that has also taken votes or a roleblock, bet on that player to die and name the claimed role. Killers have a motive to remove them, and a correct role is worth two points while a wrong role still scores one for the death.

lessons.situation: After a day in which the Fortune Teller cast an isolated dissenting vote or otherwise stands out, the remaining killers must choose a victim. The obvious saved target is likely covered again, which makes the exposed Fortune Teller the easy kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: the public voting record and announced saves expose who dissented and who the healer protected, and the killers can read both. Stakes: If the Fortune Teller dies with fewer than two points it loses permanently. A self-bet makes an attack on it fail, so it survives to bet again, though it scores nothing that night. Target landscape: The Fortune Teller's own safety, via a self-bet, versus betting on a re-targeted saved claimant or another Town player. The killers may bypass the healer-protected claimant and hit the visible outlier instead.
lessons.action: When your day-3 vote or behavior marks you as an outlier or likely target, and you are not close to the second point, use one of your two self-bets instead of betting on another player. The attack on you fails that night, so you stay alive to score later.

lessons.situation: Final-night endgame with an evil killer (wolf or Necromancer) one kill from winning and few or no town night-killing abilities left. The Fortune Teller needs points and can be killed itself. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are announced, spent abilities are known, and the remaining pool is nearly fully identified, so the killer's only plausible victim can be deduced. Stakes: The next kill ends the game, so a wasted bet or an unprotected Fortune Teller means a loss. A correct bet on the forced victim with the role named can score the final two points. A self-bet only buys time and scores nothing. Target landscape: Two or three other living players: a claimed or confirmed town role the sole remaining killer must target (the healer already dead or irrelevant), and an unconfirmed player who is the likely killer, with a Necromancer able to attack through a dead Vigilante body. Reads rest on confirmed deaths and claims, not on behavior.
lessons.action: In a 3-4 player endgame with both self-bets left, first identify which enemy can actually kill tonight. If the only living killer is the one who could attack you and you have no other path to a point, spend a self-bet so an attack on you fails; if your bet target is the one certain victim, bet on them and name their role.

lessons.situation: Late game with no protective role alive and a single evil killer who must kill the one remaining town power role. The Fortune Teller can predict the casualty and its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: earlier deaths and reveals fix who is alive, who the killer must be, and which role is the logical victim. The claimed role has been corroborated by a visible event. Stakes: The kill decides whether the game ends this night, so the bet is made at the point of highest leverage. Naming the right role can finish the Fortune Teller's win condition alongside the evil side's win. Target landscape: A claimed role whose identity has been established by an earlier reveal (such as a vigilante whose shot exposed the Serial Killer's immunity) and the lone wolf as the only possible killer. The healer is already dead, so nothing can save the victim.
lessons.action: When the killer's victim is forced by elimination, bet on that player to die and name their role, since a correct role scores two points instead of one. Choose the player no remaining protector can cover. Bet only on a death you can explain by who is able to attack, not on a player merely because they are the obvious target.

lessons.situation: Four-player endgame where the wolf must attack a high-threat claimed role while a living healer will probably guard that same player. The Fortune Teller has two self-bets left and one point. Information landscape: Information-rich: sigil mechanics are demonstrated, several dead roles are confirmed, and claims define the remaining pool. The healer's choice cannot be seen. Stakes: One save plus one sigil strike can end the game on the spot with the Fortune Teller short of two points. Choosing a bet that can still score when the obvious kill is saved matters more than matching the most likely attack. Target landscape: The claimed sigilist (the obvious wolf target), an unconfirmed healer claimant likely to guard them, and a quiet surviving wolf. The choice is between the heavily protected obvious victim and the less obvious alternatives, based on claims and prior-night events.
lessons.action: If a living healer can plausibly protect the obvious wolf target, bet on a different player who is likely to die by another cause, such as a player a pending sigil or other attack might strike or an alternate victim the pack might choose. Do not stake the bet on a protected player with an active sigil threat that could eliminate the last wolf and end the game before you score.

lessons.situation: The night after a failed double attack on a claimed Town role that the healer saved. Both killers have shown interest in that role, and they may pivot or repeat. You have 0 points and unused self-bets. Information landscape: Moderately informed: a saved attack and open claims give real signal about killer priorities, but it is reasoning and not confirmation. You have no cover or confirmed roles. Stakes: You are at 0 points and being voted out before betting would lose you the game, so getting bets placed each night matters. Each unsuccessful night shortens your runway. Target landscape: The previous night's double-attack target was saved by the healer, and the likely next victims are that same player again, another claimed power role such as a sigilist, or the healer. The basis is expected killer behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, place a bet on the likeliest victim instead of holding back, and keep both self-bets in reserve until you are visibly exposed or have been the day's top vote target. If the kill is likely to go onto the same obvious claimant a second time and the healer may repeat the save, pick the second-most-likely target the killers would pivot to, such as a claimed role that bypasses protection.

lessons.situation: You reached two points by night 3. Reanimated-wolf kills on consecutive nights show an active Necromancer with few suspects left, and a rival Fortune Teller claim is possible. Information landscape: Information-rich on the threat: consecutive reanimated-wolf kills identified a Necromancer, but nobody knows who it is. Targeting rests on behavior and structure, not confirmed roles. Stakes: With two points banked, further bets have no scoring value and a death in the late game removes you from play, so each self-bet buys a night of survival against a lone killer closing in on a win. Target landscape: Remaining Town players plus yourself. Another bet adds nothing once two points are banked, and your own survival is the live variable. The Necromancer has been killing a Town player every night, and your exposure rests on behavioral and structural evidence, not confirmed roles.
lessons.action: Once you have scored your two points and a killer is picking off players nightly, spend a self-bet each night instead of betting on another player, because scoring is already banked and survival is what remains. A self-bet makes an attack on you fail that night, so use it on the nights the killer is most likely to go after you.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2-3) after a wolf was voted out or a tie vote. Claims are public, and a Necromancer, wolves or a Serial Killer may strike. The Fortune Teller is not under suspicion and needs two points to win. Information landscape: Moderate public signals: claimed roles, announced attacker types (reanimated attack), prior deaths and vote records. Nothing confirms who the killers will choose. Stakes: The game is not at the brink, but each night is a scoring chance and the Fortune Teller needs two points. A night with several possible killers gives more than one death to land on, so a well-chosen bet is worth making every night. Target landscape: Several living claimants (a Healer who revealed whom they protected, a twice-attacked Investigator, a Sentinel or Trailseer) and contested players from a claim clash or tie vote. Roles are public claims, unverified. Picks rest on behavior and exposure, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, bet on the player the killers are most likely to hit, judged from public exposure: a freshly claimed Healer or information role, a player at the center of a claim clash, or one just named by an announced reanimated attack. Add the role guess only when a public claim makes it a strong inference, since a right role is worth two points and a wrong role still scores one for the death.

lessons.situation: Late game: wolves are dead or nearly so, a lone killer (the Necromancer) is still killing each night, and the Fortune Teller needs points or must stay alive long enough to score them. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves' roles are revealed, earlier checks are confirmed, and the killer's attack pattern across several nights is visible. The remaining uncertainty is only which player the killer takes next. Stakes: The game is near its end. One more death can decide the outcome, and the Fortune Teller's own survival and point total matter more than anything else it can do at night. Target landscape: Three or four living players, mostly confirmed or claimed roles such as an Investigator, a claimed Sigilist and a rival Fortune Teller claimant. The likeliest victim is the repeatedly attacked information source, chosen from the kill pattern rather than from confirmed knowledge.
lessons.action: Late in the game, with a lone killer still active and few players alive, bet on the player the killer's pattern most likely hits tonight, such as a repeatedly attacked information source, and name their role for the two-point payout. If you are the visible threat and still have self-bets, spend one that night, because it blocks an attack on you and a death before scoring loses the game.

lessons.situation: Early game, night 2. Wolves and a lone killer are probably all hunting, and the town has just produced a visible claimed power role. You must bet on who dies while the healer may protect the most obvious target. Information landscape: Information-starved. There is one revealed death, an unverified claim or two, and little or no vote record. Nothing shows who the killers will pick beyond how visible the claimant is. Stakes: Early game with no imminent parity. The bet is a modest scoring chance, since a miss costs one night's attempt toward the two points. The two self-bets stay in reserve. Target landscape: Seven to nine living players: one or two public power-role claimants (a trailseer, sigilist or sentinel claimant who stands out as a likely kill target), plus quiet unclaimed players with no behavioral signal. The healer is alive and unrevealed. The only evidence is who died on night 1 and who claimed since.
lessons.action: On an early night with both self-bets still held, when killers are active and one publicly claimed investigative role stands out, bet on that claimant to die and name their claimed role only if you would accept losing the second point. Accept that a healer save can turn an accurate prediction into zero, since only a death scores. Do not move your bet to a quiet unclaimed player, because the evidence points at the claimant.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game night after a wolf elimination, where multiple killers are active (wolves plus Serial Killer or Necromancer) and exposed claimants are the likelier victims. Earlier bets on a low-profile survivor scored nothing. Information landscape: Starved of confirmed targeting evidence: only public claims, last night's death roles, and killer behavior patterns. The previous bet had no basis beyond having survived. Stakes: Repeated zero-point nights shrink the path to two points. With several killers each night there are often two deaths, so betting on the exposed claimant raises the chance of scoring. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players, including recently claimed information roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, Investigator) who are plausible kill targets for either killer, and low-profile survivors. A pick that survived an earlier night only is weak evidence of a target.
lessons.action: Choose the bet from how the killers have actually behaved: which attacker types have been announced, and whether they hit exposed claimants. Don't bet on a player just because they survived last night. If neither killer has a clear target, bet on the most publicly exposed claimant. If two zero-point nights leave you with few nights left, use a self-bet only if you expect to be attacked.

lessons.situation: Midgame with one point scored and one more needed. The wolves and the Necromancer are killing nightly, a double attack on the sentinel and the investigator's death show their focus, and your earlier bet on a non-targeted player missed. Information landscape: Information-richer: revealed illusionist, trailseer record, necromancer vote-out, and a public attack on the sentinel. The killers' next preference is unstated, so the pick is inference from the kill pattern. Stakes: You need one more point to win and each wasted night costs a bet, while both self-bets remain unused. Missed bets on a player nobody is attacking waste nights that cannot be recovered. Target landscape: Six to seven living players: public-activity roles (sentinel, healer) that the wolves or a reanimating killer are visibly pressing, versus a quiet vote-aligned accuser with no sign of being targeted. The basis is public kill patterns and attack reports, not hidden role knowledge.
lessons.action: When you need a point and the previous night's kill pattern shows whom the killers are pressing (the attacked sentinel, the healer, or a role they just struck at), bet on that visible target to die rather than on a quiet accuser nobody is attacking. If your last bet missed, change the pick to follow the killers' current focus instead of repeating it, and keep your self-bets in hand until you have a reason to use them.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer or investigator has publicly accused or outed a player, and both accuser and accused are alive entering the night. The evil faction must decide whether to silence the accuser. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are public claims, a counter-claim dispute, and a visible accusation, but nothing hard confirms the accuser or the accused. Stakes: A correct bet here scores one point toward the two needed. A bet on the accused instead of the accuser yielded zero points when the accuser was killed. Target landscape: An exposer (a claimed trailseer or investigator who caught or outed an evil player), the accused player under suspicion, and other claimants. The basis is public claims and accusations.
lessons.action: When a claimant has publicly accused or exposed a suspected evil player, bet on the exposer as the likely victim, since the wolves are more likely to silence the accuser than to attack their own accused partner. Take that bet only if the exposer is not currently healer-protected.

lessons.situation: Night betting after the wolf pack has been eliminated. A hidden lone killer (here the Necromancer, attacking through a dead wolf's body) is the only source of night kills, and you still need one or two points. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: wolf identities and many roles are confirmed from lynches and reveals, and role claims are out. Nothing shows who the lone killer is or whom it will target next, so the pick rests on role-value inference. Stakes: The lone killer needs to whittle the town down by attrition. Your win needs only one or two more deaths guessed correctly, so a well-chosen bet can end your game objectively while play continues. Target landscape: Five to seven living players, both wolves already dead. The candidates are claimed power roles (sentinel, trailseer, investigator, sigilist), the hidden lone killer and yourself. The likeliest victim is the loudest, most credible information source, chosen by role-value reasoning rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone or crippled and a lone killer is the only remaining attacker, bet on the most valuable surviving information or power role (e.g. a vocal claimed sentinel) and name that role. A death scores one point even if the role is hidden, and a correct role guess scores two, so the pair can finish your win condition in one night. Keep both self-bets in reserve unless you are one point short and expect the attack to land on you.

lessons.situation: Night 1, or an opening night with no discussion or only a quiet day. Two or three independent killers may each take someone, and the bet scores if the named player dies by any cause. Information landscape: Completely information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or protection results, and day 1 had no vote. Stakes: Early misses are routine and not decisive, since two points are still reachable later. A blind hit with no role named caps the score at one point instead of two, which is a free loss to avoid. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no claims, votes, behavior or night history. Any pick is a pure guess, and several deaths are possible because there are two or three killers.
lessons.action: When you have no information, still place the bet and always name a role guess. A wrong role costs nothing, since the death still scores one point, and a right role doubles it. If any thin signal exists, such as a power role likely to be a priority kill, use it to pick the target and the role.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3, after a vote removed a wolf or resolved a claim conflict. Both the wolves and a lone killer are likely to strike the most threatening public Town claimant. You have 0-1 points, so each night's bet is your main way to score. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: a revealed wolf, claim conflicts and vote records show who threatens the killers. No role is confirmed beyond the reveals, and the healer's protection choice is unknown. Stakes: Scoring two points wins the game for you whatever else happens. Each night's bet is therefore a real chance to progress, and a miss costs only a night, not a use. The Town/wolf balance is not yet critical. Target landscape: Several claimed Town power roles (Investigator, Sentinel, healer, sigilist, trailseer) are alive. One was just validated by a vote or counter-claim win and is the obvious kill target. A healer may be guarding that player. The basis is role-value and behavior reasoning, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack and any lone killer have just lost a member or a public claimant has just been validated, bet on the most visible, freshly validated Town power role (healer, or a claimed Investigator or Sentinel whose report threatens the killers) to die, and name the role if the evidence points to it. Kills tend to aim at that player, so the bet scores if they die; a hidden role still scores, so name the role. If you suspect the healer will guard the obvious target, bet on the next-most-valuable power role the killers could reach instead.

lessons.situation: The previous night's wolf kill was stopped by a public heal. A wolf was lynched or lost, and a mixed field of wolves and a lone killer remains. You have one point and need one more. Information landscape: Fairly rich: the save was announced, a role was confirmed by a sigil strike, and one wolf's death was revealed. Which player the wolves will pick next is still a guess from motive. Stakes: With six alive and wolves still active, each night's kill brings them closer to parity. A missed bet wastes a night of scoring while you remain on one point, so choose the bet on motive and not on the last victim. Target landscape: Around six living players: a sigilist who has just survived a save, the healer who made the save, a lone killer, and one or more wolves. The healer is the known obstacle and the likelier next kill. The earlier target is a less likely repeat victim, since it was just protected and the wolves have lost a member.
lessons.action: When the wolves have just failed to kill a target through a heal or block, bet on the player who obstructed them, such as the healer, or on whoever their pack most needs gone. Do not re-bet on the previous target who survived. Only a wolf's kill selection can be predicted this way, so the bet on the obstacle is the better read.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the necromancer wins at two alive or fewer, so the next elimination brings the board to four alive and any further elimination makes the win close. A wrong lynch on a town player is recoverable but costly, while the necromancer's own survival is what decides the final count.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible night kill or shot is public in the morning and reveals that a body was used; using the Illusionist body is the only route whose role stays hidden, and that route spends a conceal and the Necromancer's presence is still shown as a reanimated attack. Staying put reveals nothing but leaves the pressure on the table.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only public traces are two conflicting claims (a sentinel watch and a trailseer follow that disagree on who visited whom), a healer save on night 4, and votes. No role among the living is verified; the Speculator has picked Town publicly, so the wolf-side has no living wolves and the lone killer is the only evil threat left.
query_dims.situation: Day 5 ended in a tie between two accused survivors after a vote in which the two sides split: one bloc is pushing player_1 while another is pushing player_6, and the day 4 save on a claimed sentinel was attributed by public accusation to the same pair. The necromancer must choose which dead body to act through at night, and any attack reads Suspicious to an investigator, which is a dead role, so only the reanimated kind shows in the morning.
query_dims.target_landscape: Surviving players are player_1, player_2, player_6, player_10 (and self as necromancer). Player_10 claims trailseer, player_2 claims sentinel, both unverified. Player_1 and player_6 are both tied in today's vote and each has been accused of being the healer or the attacker; neither has a confirmed role. Dead bodies available: investigator, vigilante, Illusionist, sigilist, chanteuse, with the illusionist body carrying two conceals.

lessons.situation: A wolf chanteuse has been eliminated and revealed, giving the necromancer a usable block body from night two onward. The necromancer is under suspicion after a tied or contested vote and must decide whom to roleblock. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of dead players are confirmed, vote splits are public, and several claims (healer save, investigator results) are on record. The living players' roles remain unverified claims. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive, so a single block rarely flips the game, but the necromancer is being voted against and a wasted night or a visible trace costs tempo it cannot spare. Forward exposure: A block through the dead chanteuse's body shows the dead wolf's name at the door of any watching Sentinel, telling the town a Necromancer is active though not who. It is irreversible once seen, and a block on a player who cannot act yields no gain for that exposure. Target landscape: Living players include a claimed healer, claimed sigilist, claimed investigator with checks reportedly spent, and quiet villagers. Their claims are unverified, and only the chanteuse's role is system-confirmed. Choice rests on remaining ability uses and on who accused the necromancer, not on pure behavior.
lessons.action: When the only usable body is a dead chanteuse, aim the block at a player whose action can still matter that night (a Town role with uses left, or one publicly suspected of protecting a likely wolf target) rather than one whose resources are publicly exhausted. If a Sentinel could be watching your target, treat the dead wolf's name at the door as a visible trace and prefer a target where that trace points suspicion at others.

lessons.situation: A wolf (Illusionist) was voted out and is now the necromancer's body. Town still has the Healer, and surviving information roles are cross-verifying each other, while one wolf may remain. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Illusionist's flip validated certain claims and visit chains exist. The Healer's coverage is unknown, which makes the attack target a guess. Stakes: Each kill moves the necromancer closer to the 'at most one other alive' condition, but a failed or visible kill reveals a Necromancer and draws a vote. A kill that removes a verifier and conceals its role gives the most value per exposure. Forward exposure: The morning report will name a reanimated wolf attack, so the town learns a Necromancer is active and an investigator check on you that night reads Suspicious. This cannot be undone. A hidden-role kill withholds the victim's role, and the Necromancer learns it. Target landscape: The dead Illusionist is the usable body. Candidates are the claimed Sentinel, claimed Trailseer, claimed Investigator, and quiet unconfirmed players. Public claims have been partly validated by the Illusionist's flip, but healer coverage is unknown.
lessons.action: When a dead Illusionist's body is available, attack a key town information role (claimed Sentinel, Trailseer or Investigator) or an unconfirmed player through it, so the victim's role is hidden if they die and the town cannot cross-check it. Prefer a target the Healer is unlikely to be covering (not the most-claimed or most-visible role that the Healer would protect), and check the Illusionist still has conceals left, since the hidden role depends on them.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 3-4) after the wolves' Illusionist died and its role was announced, with the Necromancer unsuspected. The Necromancer can attack through the body at no visible cost to itself, while the town believes the evil is finished or narrowed. Information landscape: Info-rich: dead roles are announced and the town's investigative roles and records are partly known. Nobody has a read on the Necromancer. Stakes: Few players remain, so each kill moves the Necromancer much closer to the at-most-one-other-alive win, and removing the Vigilante or Investigator takes away the town's main ways to stop it. A wasted night costs tempo while the town still has threats. Forward exposure: The morning names a 'reanimated wolf' attack, which publicly confirms a Necromancer is active; this cannot be undone. The kill hides the victim's role and the attacker's identity, and the sigil cannot punish an attack made through a body. If the Investigator is dead or dying that night, no Suspicious read can follow from it. Target landscape: Revealed bodies include the Illusionist, plus other dead roles. Living candidates are the Vigilante (could kill the Necromancer), the Investigator (could read it Suspicious), the Sentinel, the Trailseer and the Sigilist. The Vigilante's and Investigator's threat comes from their role mechanics, not from behavior; the Sentinel's influence on votes is behavioral evidence only.
lessons.action: When a dead wolf's Illusionist body has its role announced and conceals remain, attack through it and aim at the living player who can most threaten you: the Vigilante, who can shoot you, or the Investigator, who would read you Suspicious on an attack night. If that threat is already dying to the wolves or is dead, take the strongest remaining information role instead. The concealed role and the 'reanimated wolf' wording give the town a Necromancer's presence but no suspect.

lessons.situation: Mid-to-late game with three or four players alive; the town already knows a Necromancer exists from an earlier 'reanimated' report, and a further attack would not yet end the game. Information landscape: Info-rich on roles and votes but with no hard evidence about who the Necromancer is. The town deduces your identity from the attack reports and the vote splits. Stakes: An extra announced attack that does not win the game moved the room to a three-player vote where two others could remove you; the kill achieved nothing a vote could not undo. Forward exposure: Each announced reanimated kill confirms a Necromancer exists, and repeated attacks through the same body narrow the pool to the few unknowns. A second announcement makes you the obvious suspect and cannot be reversed, whereas a non-attacking use leaves no announcement. Target landscape: Three other living players, all unconfirmed claims or behavioral reads: a vocal accuser (Fortune Teller), a Sigilist, and a Vigilante or Investigator. None is a verified evil, and some (a Fortune Teller who has already scored two points) gain you nothing if killed.
lessons.action: When four players remain and the kill would not reach your win threshold, use a night action that does not announce a reanimated attack (such as a block or an information-gathering ability through a dead body) rather than a second announced attack, unless the target removes the vote threat. Keep the town from learning that a Necromancer is alive and from narrowing the suspects down to you.
