Stakes: Losing your partner now leaves a single wolf against a near-parity board, so one more elimination decides the game. Keeping your partner alive is worth a small amount of heat. Consensus: The village is converging fast on your partner, based on earlier tracking evidence and a fresh sigil or block result. My position: Holding out silently while the majority forms against your partner. Heat: Zero to low: nobody has brought you up or examined your earlier positions. Forward exposure: A brief, evidence-based doubt is easy to walk back and commits you to little. Heavy defense of your partner links you to them and is hard to undo. Target landscape: The main candidate is your partner, who has carryover suspicion from earlier tracking evidence. Other candidates are the Sigilist with a charge left and the roleblocked Sentinel, all claimed and unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know your partner is the last other wolf and you know why the night's events happened, for example that your block caused the Sentinel's failed watch. Publicly the village sees only an announced result and a suspect with carryover suspicion, and nobody is looking at you.
lessons.action: When the room converges on your partner and you are unscrutinized, offer at least one alternative suspect or a doubt about the evidence against your partner. Base it on real inconsistencies, such as a claimed result that can't be verified, and keep it short and low-heat. Don't stay completely silent, since silence lets the town unite on your partner and leaves you alone.

lessons.situation: After night deaths, claimed information roles present early results and urge suspicion on silent players while the chanteuse has said nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed by the moderator, and living claimed information roles are publicly reporting night results. Stakes: The pack still has room before parity, but a wolf voted out now removes a killer and the chanteuse's block. Staying off the lurker list matters more than winning any argument. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned behind the claimed information roles' reports and a shared plan to press non-participants. My position: Holding out by staying silent, which is the position drawing the pressure. Heat: Moderate and rising, because the leaders have agreed to scrutinize players who stay silent after morning claims. Forward exposure: A short, non-committal contribution is cheap and reversible and commits to no role claim. Total silence is already public record once the room agrees to interrogate lurkers, and it invites a vote. Target landscape: Claimed investigator and claimed sentinel leading the discussion, the player they have cleared, and other uncommitted town members. The basis is mostly claimed night results plus behavior such as lurking. Public vs private: Publicly the room treats claimed information roles as leaders and flags silent players as suspect. Privately the chanteuse knows its partner's real status and what the pack did overnight, and cannot afford to be the quiet one.
lessons.action: When claimed information roles are reporting results and asking quiet players to engage, speak early with one concrete, town-sounding contribution. For example, ask a claimed role a specific question about its result, or give a short read on an uncommitted player who is not your partner. If your partner is under attack, keep the comment general and do not name or defend them.

lessons.situation: After a night death, a claimed info role lays out a visit chain implicating another player. I appear only incidentally in that chain, and an evasive player asks me to share my information. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role's revealed will, a claimed multi-night Trailseer record, and other claims that are not yet verified. Stakes: Pack is within a couple of eliminations of parity. Letting the town spend its vote on the accused player, rather than on me or my partner, keeps the wolf bloc intact. Consensus: The room is aligned on testing the claimed visit chain and gathering around the player it implicates, with little attention on me. My position: With the majority, letting the accusation play out. Heat: Low: I was mentioned in passing, and the questioner's prompt did not frame me as an attacker. Forward exposure: Making no claim commits me to nothing and cannot be counter-claimed, and I can still claim later if pressure rises. The risk is that continued silence reads as evasive if another player keeps pressing me. Target landscape: The claimed info role, the player that role accuses, and any unproven claimant such as a Vigilante. The basis is claimed visit records and behavior, not confirmed results. Public vs private: Privately I am a wolf using night blocks, while publicly I read as an unaligned townie who was merely visited or mentioned.
lessons.action: When a player asks you to state your results and you are only a minor name in a claimed info role's visit chain, decline to counter-claim and instead call for the info roles to present testable, cross-checkable results. Let the room's attention settle on the player the visit chain actually accuses.

lessons.situation: Day 3, after a night attack that was saved or that killed a role. An accusation or mechanical theory is aimed at your wolf partner or at a claimant, and you can steer the room by probing the evidence behind it. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are a few claimed night results and one public fact, such as a save or a death, but no verified visitor lists, and the reads are speculative. Stakes: The pack is a few eliminations from parity, so keeping both wolves alive and unsuspected through this vote matters. One misdirected vote can shift the count, but this day does not by itself decide the game. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned and drifting toward whoever has the weakest evidence. No firm consensus exists yet, and the reads rest on inference rather than verified results. My position: With the majority, nudging it by questioning the evidence rather than leading an accusation. Heat: Low. No one has linked you to the night's visits or the roleblock, and your questions read as neutral. Forward exposure: Asking for evidence is a low-commitment, reversible move. Endorsing a specific claim or mechanism, such as a sentinel's watch, commits you to it and is hard to undo once the town trusts that claim. Target landscape: The candidates are the accuser, the accused packmate, and unverified role claimants. No hard evidence exists, so the basis is inference and behavior, and the only new fact is a night result that confirms a wolf attack. Public vs private: You privately know the pack's actions, so the accusation may be accurate in substance, but publicly it is an unverified inference. Asking for the evidence behind it exposes the gap without revealing what you know.
lessons.action: When a day-3 accusation lands on your wolf partner or on a hard-to-verify claim, ask in neutral evidence-seeking terms what separate result backs it, and add mechanical points only where the rules clearly support them. Posing as an arbiter of evidence keeps your heat low, and the accuser has to retract or the room moves to a different target.

lessons.situation: On day 2 after a concealed night kill, several unverifiable night-result claims are in play, including a claim of being roleblocked, and the chanteuse is not under suspicion. Information landscape: Starved: only unverified night-result claims, one hidden-role body, and a roleblock claim that implies a chanteuse exists. Stakes: Nothing forces a move today. Staying hidden protects the pack's blocker and the pack's room to act at night. Consensus: No clear consensus. Attention is on the claimants and on their disputes with each other. My position: Outside the discussion, not driving anything and not attracting attention. Heat: Low: no one has named you, and the roleblock claim attaches to no particular player. Forward exposure: Each new statement is a checkable commitment that others can later compare with your votes. Brevity commits you to nothing and can be changed later. Target landscape: The room has no confirmed roles, only unverified claims from the investigator, sigilist, trailseer and sentinel. Reads are behavioral and no one has been singled out. Public vs private: You know you blocked a player and that your partner may have hidden a body. Publicly the town sees only a roleblock claim that implies a chanteuse exists, not who it is.
lessons.action: When no one has named you and a roleblock claim exists but points at no one, keep your discussion turns brief and generic and make no claim about roleblocks, visits or night results. Anything you say can be cross-checked later, and saying nothing keeps the heat on the claimants.

lessons.situation: Final three at Day 5-6: you are the last wolf, the lone killer is alive, and one other player is Town or neutral. The elimination vote is the last decision, and only removing the lone killer wins it for the wolves. Information landscape: Mostly revealed roles for the dead, public night-kill reports, and the vote history. Nothing is confirmed about the two survivors, so reads rest on elimination logic and behavior. Stakes: One vote decides the game. Removing the lone killer gives the wolves an immediate win at one wolf against one other player. Removing the Town player lets the lone killer win with one other player left. Consensus: The room is split two against one, with the other two accusing each other. The deciding voter is undecided and weighing logic and voting records. My position: Swing voter who can drive the outcome by persuading the undecided player; staying passive hands the framing to the lone killer. Heat: Low to moderate. Others call you quiet or background, or the lone killer tries to frame you with role-count math, but no one has made a decisive case against you. Forward exposure: Naming a target in speech commits your vote and sets the third player's choice. The day ends in an immediate vote with no later discussion, so a wrong pick cannot be undone. Staying silent leaves the room to the lone killer's framing. Target landscape: Two candidates, the third Town-aligned or neutral player and the lone killer, with neither role confirmed. The basis is deduction from dead roles, the trail of reanimated kills or night results, and past votes, with little direct evidence. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the last wolf, and one of the other two is the lone killer; you may or may not know which. Publicly the two others accuse each other and you are the swing voter, with little hard evidence beyond role-count deduction and voting history.
lessons.action: As the last wolf in a three-player endgame with a lone killer still alive, speak early and state a concrete case against whichever player is more likely the lone killer. Build it from role-count elimination, the reanimated-kill or visit trail, and voting records, then ask the third player to commit to that vote. Removing the lone killer leaves you level with the last other player, which ends the game for the wolves, whereas voting out the Town player lets the lone killer reach its own win count.

lessons.situation: A player claims a visit-watching role and says they saw you at a night victim's door. The village doubts the accuser for waiting to speak. Information landscape: Information-starved. Two prior night deaths, no confirmed living roles, and a sudden unverified visit claim. Stakes: The mid-game board leaves little margin. A confirmed visit report on you would likely get you voted out or targeted at night, which costs the wolves their blocker. Consensus: The village is skeptical of the accuser's late disclosure and leaning toward voting them out, without hard evidence either way. My position: driving Heat: High. A direct claim names you at the murder scene, partly dampened by distrust of the accuser's timing. Forward exposure: Driving the accuser's elimination risks the system confirming their role and will, which would permanently validate the visit claim against you. Keeping a low profile leaves room to shift later. Target landscape: The accuser, who claims a visit-seeing role and gives a delayed report, versus you, who are named at the kill scene. The basis is an unverified claim plus distrust of timing, with no confirmed living roles. Public vs private: You privately know the accuser's visit report is true because you carried the pack kill to that victim. Publicly the town distrusts the accuser's delayed reveal and has no confirmed roles.
lessons.action: If a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer names you at a night victim and the claim is accurate, keep your skepticism about the claimant's timing low-key and let the room carry any pressure instead of driving their elimination. Make no role or night-action claim. If the room starts voting the accuser out, stay in the background, because eliminating a true investigator reveals their role and will, which would confirm their visit report against you.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a night in which the Sentinel and Trailseer report your visit to a player who was blocked, or who sat next to a dead player. The room asks you to explain. Information landscape: Moderate. There are confirmed visits and a dead player or a block claim, but your role is not confirmed and no checks have been shared. Stakes: The board is mid-game, with several eliminations still needed before the wolves can reach parity. Being voted out as a revealed chanteuse costs the pack its blocker and exposes your partner, so avoiding a collision that gets you eliminated matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is converging on you as the one to explain. The basis is the confirmed visit and a victim or reporter saying they were blocked or killed. There is no verified role to anchor on. My position: Holding out against the room's demand, defending under pressure. Heat: High. You are singled out by name as a visitor, with a watch- or follow-confirmed visit and no explanation, and others are demanding one. Forward exposure: A fake role claim commits you to a role whose real holder can counter-claim at once, and a single death can expose it. If you are revealed as a wolf, your partner is put at risk too. A claim cannot be retracted. Withholding a role and attacking the evidence's meaning stays reversible. Target landscape: The choice is between a fake role claim, silence, or reframing the visit. The only hard evidence is the confirmed visit. Every role claim is unverified, and the room judges on timing and demeanor. Public vs private: Privately you are the chanteuse who made the visit, and you know the visit was a block. Publicly, a Sentinel or Trailseer report puts your name on the visit, so you are the only player with an unexplained visit.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer report puts your visit on record, don't invent a role the real holder can contradict. Say that a visit shows only that you went there, never why. Then redirect the room to every other visitor and to the reporters' exact wording, and ask what else the reports show. If an unclaimed role's holder is still alive, any claim to that role invites an instant counter-claim, so claim a role only when the holder is already revealed dead or no counter-claim could come.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion in which several claims conflict and a night-mechanics dispute is open, and the chanteuse wants to question another player's statement without exposing itself. Information landscape: Mostly claim-based with a few confirmed roles from deaths. Visit and check results are self-reported and unverifiable. Stakes: Board is mid-game with several unconfirmed roles and a lone killer still alive. One careless slip showing wolf-side knowledge could cost the last wolf, but a clean question costs little. Consensus: The village is split among unverified claims and a disputed visit story. There is no firm consensus, and the last vote produced little or nothing. My position: Holding out and probing, not driving any elimination. Heat: Low to moderate. The chanteuse has stayed quiet and has no accusation or claim against it, but a pointed question draws attention. Forward exposure: A pointed mechanical question can show you know night details that a plain villager would not be tracking, and it invites scrutiny of how you know. It is moderately reversible if you concede quickly when the rule is explained. Target landscape: Several living players with no confirmed roles, judged on claims and claimed results rather than hard evidence. The probe targets a claimant whose statement looks inconsistent. Public vs private: The chanteuse privately knows whom it blocked and what nobody could have seen. Publicly the town has only unverified claims and reads the chanteuse as a quiet, curious player.
lessons.action: When heat is low and you want to probe a claim, build the question only from facts already public: announced deaths, stated claims, and the rules of how checks and watches work. Do not cite who was blocked or who could have watched whom, because only a wolf, the blocker or the blocked player would track that. If the answer cuts against your premise, drop the line at once.

lessons.situation: Day discussion with you as the primary target of a near-unanimous push. You are a lone defender, and your hidden partner is tempted to speak up for you. Information landscape: Evidence is thin and claim-based, with one or two unverified claims or an ambiguous result. No role is confirmed for you or your partner, so alignment and defenses are read as signals. Stakes: The wolves are still far from parity. Losing the partner as well as yourself would leave the pack with no kill and no voice, so protecting the partner's cover is worth more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is close to unanimous against you, anchored on a claimed night result and a counter-claim test rather than on behavior. My position: Holding out alone against the majority. Heat: Maximum. Several players have accused you and the room is lining up to vote you out, mostly on the strength of a claimed result. Forward exposure: Having the partner defend you ties the partner's reputation to yours, and that link cannot be undone once the room sees it. Distancing costs little, and it is reversible because you can still argue your own case. Target landscape: The village is choosing between you and a claimed counter-role or a Suspicious-result claimant. Neither side has a confirmed role, so the basis is a claimed result and argument rather than behavior. Your partner is a bystander who may become collateral damage. Public vs private: Privately you know your partner is a wolf and that you are in trouble. Publicly the town has no confirmed role for either of you, but it reads a defender of the accused as a possible partner.
lessons.action: If you are the accused and your living wolf partner is not yet linked to you, say nothing that asks the partner to vouch for you, and let the partner vote and speak with the room's majority. If the partner defends you anyway, answer in your own voice and do not return the favour, because a defender gets tied to the accused and pulled down the next day.

lessons.situation: Three players are left and you are accused as the wolf, either by the lone killer using role-count math or by a Town role such as a claimed vigilante or sigilist. The third player is the swing and is weighing you against the other suspect. Information landscape: Info-rich in places: claimed night results, previous-day votes and confirmed deaths allow narrow role-count deduction. Nothing about the survivors is confirmed. Stakes: If the deciding player votes you out, the wolves lose. If the vote splits or lands on the other suspect, you survive and can win that day or at night. Consensus: The room is split and undecided. The deciding player is torn between you and the other player. My position: Driving the discussion to deflect suspicion and shape the deciding player's vote. Heat: High to critical from a direct accusation or a claimed block, but the deciding player is still undecided. Forward exposure: A firm counter-accusation commits you to the vote and to a pro-Town framing that your voting record must support. It is irreversible because the vote follows immediately. Target landscape: The accuser, who may be the lone killer or a claimed Town role, against the quieter third player. Both are judged on behavior, voting history and role-count logic rather than confirmed roles. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the wolf who blocked people, while publicly you must appear as a pro-Town player making an unverified deduction. A claimed roleblock victim or a lone killer may be accusing you.
lessons.action: If the lone killer or the Town player accuses you of being the wolf, rebut with their own logic. Show that the role-count points the other way, that a roleblock claim does not identify who did the blocking, and that your past votes opposed the real killer. Then steer the undecided player toward the other suspect, whose passive or inconsistent record you can point to.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion: you are the main suspect over a coincidence, and you answer your accusers by repeatedly pointing at another player's unverified claim instead of engaging the accusation. Information landscape: Several unverified private claims and one real but non-decisive tension. There are no confirmed roles or caught lies, so the argument rests on claim consistency and timing. Stakes: The board is mid-game with the wolves still needing a few eliminations. Being voted out here costs the pack its blocker and tempo, so surviving the vote matters more than landing a counter-accusation. Consensus: The village is converging on you around a coincidence, such as a block or visit timing that looks suspicious. The claimed tension on someone else is not strong enough to move anyone. My position: Holding out against the consensus and trying to redirect it, with no allies speaking up. Heat: High: multiple accusers are on you, and your repeated deflection reads as a defense with no new content. Forward exposure: A repeated line against another player's claim is easy to repeat but hard to retract. It commits you to that claim being false, and it can look like you know who carried the kill. A single, public-fact-based doubt is cheap to walk back. Target landscape: Only one claimed role is a plausible alternative target, and the room treats its claim with only mild skepticism. Everyone else is aligned on you, and the basis is claim timing and coincidence rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know a claim's inconsistency or truth from the wolf side, such as who carried the kill, but the table only sees unverified claims. Pushing a point that depends on private knowledge risks looking pre-informed.
lessons.action: When several players are accusing you, answer the accusation itself with at least one new, concrete point each turn, such as why your read or action is consistent with public facts. Raise any doubt about another player's claim once, using only publicly checkable tension, and do not repeat the same pivot or lean on what you privately know as a wolf. If your turn adds nothing new, stay brief.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator announces a Suspicious result on the chanteuse's wolf partner, and the village is converging on eliminating them. Information landscape: Information-rich: a specific claimed investigator result plus public deduction about what the result implies. Stakes: Losing the partner is costly, but a visible link to them risks the chanteuse too, and the investigator may still have checks left. Protecting the chanteuse's standing keeps the pack alive. Consensus: The village is strongly aligned against the accused, backed by a claimed hard check and rules-based reasoning. My position: Holding out, softly braking momentum for the partner. Heat: Low at the moment, because scrutiny sits entirely on the accused. It would rise if the chanteuse is seen defending them. Forward exposure: Questioning the investigator or pleading for restraint publicly associates the chanteuse with the accused. If the accused is revealed as a wolf, that association becomes a trail that cannot be undone. Target landscape: The claimed investigator versus the accused partner. The room weighs a hard night result and rules-based deduction against the accused's behavioral defense. Other uncommitted players are available as alternative targets. Public vs private: Publicly the accused partner looks guilty on a result the room finds mechanically plausible. Privately the chanteuse knows the result is accurate and that any defense of the partner ties the chanteuse to them.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator's result on your partner is credible and the room is moving against them, do not argue for them or praise their defense. Join the evidence-based consensus or stay neutral, and steer any questions toward a different uncommitted player. This keeps a collusion link from forming that an investigator could cite when choosing whom to check.

lessons.situation: A claimed investigator, who earlier made a conflicting claim, publicly names you Suspicious on a day-discussion turn, and other claimants are already dismantling their credibility. Information landscape: Rich in claims but unverified: an accusation against you, a proven contradictory claim, and no confirmed roles beyond a hidden body. Stakes: Mid-game, with several players still alive. Losing the Chanteuse to a vote now would weaken the wolves, but the room is not pushing in that direction, so keeping a low profile is enough. Consensus: The village is converging on the accuser because of their inconsistent claims and the pushback from other power-role claimants. My position: With the majority, not driving it. Heat: Moderate and rising, from a public Suspicious accusation whose source is already discredited. Forward exposure: A loud defense would link your name to the accusation and invite scrutiny of your block. Silence or minimal agreement keeps your options open, but you cannot take back a total silence once the vote is over. Target landscape: The accuser is the only live suspect, with a self-contradicting claim and a Suspicious call on you. The other players are unclaimed and not accusatory. The case against the accuser rests on their claim contradictions, not on confirmed roles. Public vs private: You know the Suspicious read on you is true, but publicly it comes from a self-contradicting claimant, so it reads as a desperate bluff.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator names you Suspicious but the room is already turning on them for contradictory claims, add one short point agreeing that their shifting claims are the problem, and make no personal defense. Keep your vote with the majority so you stay inside the consensus and don't tie yourself to the check on you or to your night block.

lessons.situation: Day discussion where the town's attention is on a conflict between two other players, and the chanteuse has so far raised only a side point that did not affect the vote. Information landscape: Contested claims and a disputed visit-count story, with only partial corroboration from a follow result. There are almost no role confirmations from deaths. Stakes: Votes are approaching with no confirmed roles, so shaping which claimer is doubted matters more than commenting on bystanders. A side remark moves nothing. Consensus: The village is focused on one live conflict between two claimers and has not settled on a target. My position: On the edge of the main debate, with the chance to move into it. Heat: Low. The chanteuse has no accusation or role claim against it. Forward exposure: Taking a side commits you to a read that can be checked later. It is more exposed than a side remark but is reversible if new claims shift the picture. Target landscape: The disputants, such as a sentinel and a healer-claimer, have no confirmed roles, and other claimants such as a vigilante sit on the sidelines. The basis is claim consistency, not hard evidence. Public vs private: The chanteuse privately knows which claims about being blocked are true, for example that its own block hit the vigilante. Publicly those are only unverified words, and the chanteuse can lean on the public contradictions without confirming anything.
lessons.action: When two other players are in a live dispute that will shape the vote, give a clear read on which side's account fits the public claims better, instead of raising a side topic. Anchor it in a concrete inconsistency, such as whether a protection visit could coexist with a roleblock. This pushes suspicion onto town players without tying you to any private knowledge.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner has made a false role claim against a genuine claimant. A public night report supports the genuine claimant, so the village is united on eliminating the partner. Information landscape: Information-rich. An announced night result directly validates one of two competing claims. Stakes: A mid-game wolf loss is not decisive by itself. Staying unlinked keeps the surviving wolf side alive and your night blocks available. Consensus: Overwhelming, evidence-based agreement that the false claimant is lying and should go. My position: with majority Heat: None. No one has questioned or suspected you. Forward exposure: Defending the partner would permanently tie you to a wolf once their role is revealed on elimination, and could not be undone. Endorsing the claim-sorting process commits you to nothing false and is fully reversible. Target landscape: The false claimant (your partner) versus the genuine role claimant whose claim matches an announced night outcome. The evidence is a public report that validates one claim, not behavior. Public vs private: You privately know the counter-claimant is your wolf partner running a fabricated claim. Publicly the town is sorting claims by which one fits an announced night result, and nobody links you to the partner.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is exposed by a contradicted claim and the village is converging on eliminating them, stay with the majority and add only neutral procedural input on sorting the conflicting claims. Do not defend, vouch for, or question the vote against the partner. Defending a caught wolf would tie you to them once their role is revealed, while staying neutral commits you to no false fact.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion in which a claimed investigative role (such as the Trailseer) ties you or your pair to a visit or wolf pairing. You must respond without a verified role to hide behind. Information landscape: Mostly claims with at most one hard trail result. Dead roles may be hidden, and the rest of the evidence is unverified. It is thin enough that attacking the logic of the accusation can work. Stakes: With few players left, one wrongly-aimed vote on you could cost the pack its carrier and blocker. Surviving the day with a tie or split keeps blocks and kills going. Consensus: The room is split. It leans on the accuser's claimed result but cannot verify it, and no role has been confirmed beyond the dead. My position: Holding out alone against a pairing or trail accusation. Heat: High: a claimed Trailseer has named you, either as a wolf pair or as a visitor at a specific door, and you are one of few unclaimed players. Forward exposure: Staying unclaimed commits you to nothing and can be revised later. A fake role claim is irreversible, and a live holder of that role, possibly hidden, can contradict it at any moment. Target landscape: Candidates are you and your partner (unclaimed, named by the accuser), plus the claimed Trailseer, Vigilante, Sigilist and Investigator. All claims are unverified, and the case against you is role-count elimination or a single trail result, not confirmed fact. Public vs private: Privately you know the accusation is accurate or that the visit was yours, and you know your real role. Publicly it is only an unverifiable claim or a conditional resting on unconfirmed roles, and nobody can check your role.
lessons.action: When a Trailseer or other accuser puts you at a door or pairs you with your partner, stay unclaimed. Say you have no night result to share, and show that the accusation rests on unverified claims or a hidden role. Then point the room at a concrete, checkable detail on another claimed player, such as a bullet history. Don't commit to a specific Town role that a live holder can counterclaim.

lessons.situation: The chanteuse pushed an accusation using a night event that was never publicly announced, and a town player is asking how they could know it. Information landscape: Evidence-rich: multiple role claims and night reports are public, so any discrepancy between a statement and the announced record is quickly noticed. Stakes: As a lone or near-lone wolf, one exposed slip can turn the vote against the chanteuse and end the game. Defusing it quickly keeps the wolf alive into the endgame. Consensus: The room is not yet aligned and is willing to accept a plausible mistake. Votes are likely to split. My position: holding out Heat: Moderate and sudden. A credible town player is challenging the factual basis of the chanteuse's statement. Forward exposure: Retracting is fully reversible and costs only a little credibility. Defending the unannounced detail would commit the chanteuse to an explanation that cannot be verified and would invite a wolf-knowledge accusation. Target landscape: The room is debating a suspected serial killer, a quiet player, and a claimed vigilante, with the healer and investigator seen as cleared. The challenger (healer) is a credible town voice. Public vs private: The chanteuse privately knows an event, such as a failed pack attack on an immune target, that was never publicly announced. The town sees only that the chanteuse referenced something nobody could have known.
lessons.action: If another player questions how you knew a night event that was never announced, immediately concede it as a confusion or mistake and withdraw the point instead of defending it. Move the discussion back to publicly announced facts so the slip is not examined further.

lessons.situation: A claimed Sentinel or Trailseer reports a visit chain that includes me alongside another player at a night death or at the dead info role's house. The room must decide which visitor to suspect. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed visit reports, a confirmed killer's kill or the dead role's reveal, and public vote records, though none of it verifies my own night action. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. One wrong vote on me costs the pack its blocker, but a vote on the other visitor keeps the wolf bloc intact and moves it toward parity. Consensus: The room is information-rich and tends to follow the claimed info role's visit chain. It converges on whichever named player explains themselves worst. My position: Driving the scrutiny toward the rival suspect early, or going with the majority once it forms. Heat: Moderate to high when a claimed info role names me at a death scene or in a visit chain. Low when I am only mentioned in passing and not framed as an attacker. Forward exposure: Admitting the visit while offering no cover story avoids a falsifiable fake claim, so it is reversible. But it leaves my visit unexplained, so scrutiny returns if the rival suspect flips as town or is cleared. Target landscape: Me and one or two other named visitors, all unconfirmed. The case is a visit report from a claimed role plus vote history, so it rests on thin evidence and each suspect's behavior. Public vs private: Privately I know my visit was a Chanteuse block (or other wolf action) and that the pack is behind the night's events; publicly the town only sees a visit record placing me at a door and a possible fellow suspect.
lessons.action: When a claiming Sentinel or Trailseer names you among a victim's visitors, acknowledge the visit and shared vote history without inventing a fake night action, then redirect the room to the other named visitor's weakest, most evasive reasoning. If no other visitor is named, say nothing more about your own visit and press other claimed information roles to give testable results.

lessons.situation: Two investigator claims conflict, and you hold the false one. The only evidence is a third party's confirmation that your visit happened. Information landscape: Info-starved on roles, with a single hard fact (the visit confirmation) that supports neither claimed role over the other. Stakes: The vote can remove the real investigator, a key town information source, but a failed bluff would expose the Chanteuse. One shift in the room decides which claim dies. Consensus: The room is split between two conflicting claims and is leaning on timing and behavior reads rather than substance. My position: Driving the argument against the counter-claimant, then likely ending with the majority. Heat: Moderate to high. You are accused by the counter-claimant and others, but the confirmed visit gives you partial cover. Forward exposure: Repeating the visit as proof commits you to one story, and you cannot retract it without confessing a wolf role. The town can still weigh it against the counter-claim, so the position is only partly reversible. Target landscape: The two accused are you and the counter-claimant, with no revealed roles for either. The accusations rest on timing and behavior, and only the visit confirmation is external evidence. Public vs private: You know your claim is false and the counter-claimant's is true, but publicly the two claims look symmetric except for the confirmed visit on your side.
lessons.action: If you have already fake-claimed investigator and a real investigator counter-claims, keep pointing to the one hard external fact in your favor, such as a sentinel or trailseer confirming your visit. Press the counter-claimant on why they spoke up only after your visit became public, and give no check results beyond the minimum. If the room starts to weigh the two claims evenly, hold your line rather than adding new details that could be checked.

lessons.situation: Your wolf partner is accused by a claimed watch or tracking result that the table finds credible, and you must decide how loudly to defend or distance yourself. Information landscape: Several private-claim results, with no public verification because key roles are concealed. It is a claims-and-timing argument. Stakes: The pack is down to a thin margin, and losing the partner leaves you alone against the vote. Staying out of the partner's defender list protects your own survival even if the partner is lost. Consensus: The room is lining up behind the claimant and the partner's removal, based on claim credibility and a corroborating story rather than verified facts. My position: Holding out with a soft, non-committal objection, not driving anything. Heat: Moderate and rising: you were not an initial suspect, but skepticism toward the claimant can get you flagged as an accuser alongside your partner. Forward exposure: Vouching hard for the partner ties you to a likely wolf if the claim holds up. Attacking the claimant makes you the one who pushed against a claim that turns out true. A single mild call for more evidence is cheap and reversible. Target landscape: The choice is between siding with a claimed role whose result is unverified but backed by another claimant, and defending the accused partner. No roles are confirmed on either side, so credibility of claims, not evidence, decides it. Public vs private: You privately know the claimed watch or tracking result is accurate and implicates your partner, but publicly it is an unverified claim you could frame as shaky.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is under heavy accusation from a claim you know to be true, speak at most once and keep it short and general, such as asking for more than one unverified claim before a lynch. Do not vouch hard for the partner, and do not name or hammer the claimant, because a direct jab draws a reply and makes you an accuser in the record. You stay out of the defender list, and a mild statement can be dropped later without cost.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a credible claimant names you Suspicious, with your partner dead or gone and a Necromancer attack plausible. A defense of 'it could be a Necromancer' has not moved the room. Information landscape: There is one confirmed prior result and a public reanimated-wolf report, but the current Suspicious result cannot separate a wolf from an attacking Necromancer. Stakes: If you are voted out as the last wolf, the wolves lose their win condition, so the discussion must move at least some votes. A defense that only buys time and moves nobody is not enough. Consensus: The room is nearly unanimous against you. The claimant admits the result is ambiguous, yet the others follow the push anyway. My position: Holding out as the target and arguing against the consensus. Heat: High. A claimant with a confirmed earlier result named you Suspicious, and others joined the push. Forward exposure: Naming a rival commits you to that accusation and exposes you if the rival's role is later confirmed as Town. You can drop it, but you lose credibility. Staying unclaimed keeps your options open but leaves you nothing to counter-claim with. Target landscape: The accused is you, backed by a credible claimant whose earlier result was confirmed. The alternatives are a Necromancer hypothesis and the accusers who push the vote, who are judged on behavior and incentive rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are a wolf and the accusing result is accurate. Publicly it is only an ambiguous Suspicious result that also fits an attacking Necromancer.
lessons.action: When an accuser's result or claim is ambiguous and you are the target, spend the discussion on a concrete rival suspect and a specific question for the claimant, rather than only saying your result fits another role. Pick the loudest pusher who gains from your elimination, such as a player whose own role is at stake, and ask the town to weigh their incentive. If the room still stays locked on you, keep the argument short and do not rely on staying unclaimed or on the ambiguity alone.

lessons.situation: A claimant explains a night result as caused by a roleblock (your own block) and another player calls the claim unreliable. Information landscape: Sparse: unverified claims about roleblocks, a concealed or unconfirmed body, and no hard evidence. Stakes: Moderately tight board: a small slip that links you to a block could expose the pack, so any comment must stay short and reversible. Consensus: A single accuser has questioned the claim, with no firm majority yet and the discussion moving on to other reports. My position: Interjecting with a mild counterpoint, neither driving nor holding out. Heat: Low: you have not been accused or targeted. Forward exposure: Vouching for the roleblock explanation implicitly ties you to knowledge of blocks. It is a mild, visible commitment that you can walk back by calling it neutral rules logic. Target landscape: One claimed town role under doubt, whose claim is partly explained by your own block. The decision is whether to soften the doubt or stay silent, and the basis is rule logic rather than behavior or evidence. Public vs private: Privately you know you blocked the claimant, so their blocked claim is true, while publicly it is only a disputed claim, and defending it too firmly would make you look too well informed.
lessons.action: If a claim that you know is true because of your own block (for example 'I was roleblocked') is being doubted, you may offer it only as general rules logic: a roleblock can explain a missed action, so it is a weakness rather than a contradiction. Phrase it as neutral reasoning and never say you placed the block. Keep it to one comment and drop the point if anyone asks how you know.

lessons.situation: On day 2 a claimed visit report (sentinel or trailseer) puts you at the door of a player who says they were roleblocked or who counter-claims, and you must answer for the visit. Information landscape: Unverified claims that happen to fit together, with no Game Master confirmation beyond the night deaths. Roleblocks are private, so neither side can prove its story. Stakes: Losing the blocker on day 2 weakens the pack and strands your partner without a defender. The board is not yet near parity, so you have time to survive the day rather than win it outright. Consensus: The room is converging on you because independent-looking claims (a visit list plus a roleblock report) match. Nothing has been confirmed by an announcement or a will. My position: Holding out alone against a forming majority. Heat: High and rising: two or three players have accused you and your only defender is your partner, speaking softly. Forward exposure: A flat denial or fake role claim commits you to a falsehood the matching reports can expose, and it cannot be retracted. Repeating the same line ties you tighter to it. Questions about the accusers' reports commit you to nothing checkable and can be changed. Target landscape: The room is choosing between you and the accusers or the counter-claimant, such as the blocked player, a claimed sentinel or a claimed trailseer. All of them are unconfirmed claims. The case against you rests on how well the reports fit together, not on proof. Public vs private: You know you blocked someone and that the visit report is true. Publicly it is only a claim, but it lines up with a blocked player's claim and looks corroborated.
lessons.action: When a claimed watcher or follower lists your visit and a blocked player says they were roleblocked, make each turn a new, specific challenge to the weakest part of an accuser's report, such as a detail that does not fit another claim. A visit list shows only where you went, so keep your own statements general and avoid a flat denial or a counter-role claim that a blocked player can contradict. Get your partner to voice doubt about the accuser before the room commits.

lessons.situation: A fake role claim made to cover a confirmed visit has just been counter-claimed by the real holder, and the room is weighing two claimants. Information landscape: Moderate. Two claims, confirmed visits, and no hard role confirmation for either claimant. Stakes: A vote on this standoff can remove you, a wolf, or the real role holder. Losing the vote exposes the pack and leaves your partner alone. Consensus: The room treats the collision as a standoff in which you are the likelier liar. It is waiting for evidence and leans on timing and demeanor. My position: Holding out alone, defending a contested claim. Heat: High. You hold a claim that has been contested, and the visit is on record. Forward exposure: Pressing the counter-claimant on timing alone makes you look like the likelier liar, and you cannot take back a claim already made. Moving the room to other evidence keeps the standoff open without adding any new claim or result. Target landscape: Two claimants to the same role, both unverified. The Sentinel or Trailseer confirmed only your visit, not your role. The room is weighing timing and demeanor. Public vs private: Privately you know your claim is fake. Publicly there are two claimants to the same role and no verified record for either, so the room is judging on demeanor.
lessons.action: If a real holder counter-claims the role you took, stop attacking their timing, since that read reads as opportunistic. Reduce the standoff to a few specific, checkable points, such as which other players the reports put at the door and what the counter-claimant can show. Then ask the room to hold the vote until the Sentinel, Trailseer or other reporters add more.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is split between players pressing for specific visit directions and players abstaining; there is no forming majority on any target.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill ends the game; a silent stance is cheap now but any misstep compounds over the coming days.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible claim or night action would commit me to a public role or result that the village can check against the visit record, and a claim cannot be taken back once the room has read it.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: I have a quiet, abstaining record on day 2 with no accusations pointed at me in the summary.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: only the day-2 abstain vote and a night-one roleblock claim by one player; no verified night results exist yet.
query_dims.my_position: With the abstaining majority, holding out of any accusation.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the Necromancer I privately know I have not yet acted and hold no results, while the public sees only a quiet player who has not claimed anything; the gap is that the village is trading night-visit claims I cannot contribute to.
query_dims.situation: Day 3 after a night-two kill of the investigator, with the room asking for night-one visit directions to line up results while I, the necromancer, hold no result and have no reason to speak.
query_dims.target_landscape: The village is discussing who claims night results; no one is yet on record with a verified role, so every claimant is unverified and I cannot yet tell which claims are real.

lessons.situation: Day-3 vote after a night kill, often with a concealed or contested body. The village has converged on the necromancer for behavior (silence or a walked-back accusation) while other players dispute visits and roleblocks. Information landscape: Mixed to thin. There are unverified claims and a visit dispute, but no confirmed wolf or killer. The necromancer's best information comes from a body-watch or similar result that it cannot disclose without exposing its role. Stakes: Mid-game with eight alive: an elimination of the lone killer ends its win path. Each vote matters, since a lone vote leaves the majority on you unopposed and you are removed. Consensus: The room is concentrating on the necromancer for behavior, not for evidence. The remaining votes are scattered across contested claims. My position: Holding out alone against the room and casting a vote that nobody else shares. Heat: High. You were the main target on the previous day, and several voters again aim at you for silence or an unsupported accusation you had to concede. Forward exposure: A lone vote on a read nobody shares commits you publicly to an unsupported position. It adds nothing to any vote count, does not lower your heat, and is permanent and irreversible. A vote that joins an existing bloc costs little and can be explained. Target landscape: Several candidates (sentinel, healer, trailseer, illusionist, sigilist) with contested claims and no hard evidence. The case against you is behavioral, resting on silence or an overstated accusation. Cases against the others rest on disputes or private results you cannot share. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer, or hold unshareable body-derived information. Publicly you are a repeat target whose reads are unsourced, so a solo vote looks isolated and odd.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote where the room is concentrating on you, don't spend your vote on a lone-voter target nobody shares. Pick the candidate who already has the most votes among the people pressing you, or one the room already doubts, so your vote joins a visible bloc. Pair it with the one claim you can defend publicly, because a vote you cannot source or explain stays on the permanent record and cannot be undone.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after a single night death, with no investigative results shared. Votes are scattered, and the quiet players, you included, draw suspicion for silence alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death, a few claims, and no verified ties to wolves or a killer. Reads are behavioral only. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so no single vote decides the game. The main risk is attracting lasting suspicion before the necromancer's first usable night. Consensus: The village leans toward abstaining because no checks, watches or follows have been shared. Support for any elimination is thin and scattered. My position: With the majority when abstaining; holding out if you cast a lone vote. Heat: Low to moderate. Any pressure rests on silence, with no concrete evidence against you. Forward exposure: A named vote goes on the permanent public record and can be questioned for days; an abstain reveals nothing and commits you to nothing. Target landscape: All living players are unconfirmed apart from the dead player's reveal. The only candidates are quiet players, chosen on silence rather than evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer with no night information yet (Night 1 is inactive, so you read Not suspicious). Publicly you are an unconfirmed, quiet player, and the room has no evidence against anyone.
lessons.action: On an early day-vote with no hard evidence and a room leaning toward abstaining, abstain with the majority instead of casting a lone named vote. Abstaining commits you to nothing and keeps your vote on the public record from looking aggressive or unexplained. If a plurality is forming on you, still abstain and let the abstain bloc block it, since a counter-vote would not change the tally.

lessons.situation: Day vote at a small table after multiple night deaths, with conflicting power-role claims. The town is divided across several targets and the necromancer is not a leading suspect. Information landscape: Information-rich on paper (dead power roles revealed, several role claims, an announced reanimated-body attack) but the claims contradict each other, so the town cannot tell who is lying. The necromancer's own acts are not traceable to it. Stakes: With about five players alive, each elimination moves the necromancer toward its win condition of at most one other player alive. A tie with no elimination keeps the town's numbers and the confusion in place, but it also gives the town another night and another day to find the necromancer. Consensus: The village is fragmented, with votes scattered across four or five players and no dominant read. Disagreement rests on contradictory claims about the double-kill night or the voting behavior. My position: holding out Heat: Low; an earlier Not suspicious result or a negative trailseer follow result gives the necromancer cover, and attention sits on the active claimants. Forward exposure: Voting with a visible bloc against a claimed town role looks like normal skepticism and commits the necromancer to nothing beyond that public vote. The vote is permanent on the record, but it is easy to explain as following a reasonable accusation. Target landscape: Several candidates: a claimed healer accused over a roleblock or vote story, a surviving wolf or speculator accused by others, and scattered single votes on the trailseer, vigilante, or sigilist. The evidence is mostly claim contradictions and behavior, not confirmed results. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it caused the night kills through a dead body, while the room argues over which claimant is lying or whether two attacking factions exist; the necromancer reads as a bystander.
lessons.action: When the town is split across several targets and nobody suspects you, cast your vote for a claimed town role that already has a vote bloc (e.g. the accused claimed healer), so it ties the leading alternative and nobody is eliminated. This keeps your count of opponents intact and keeps the room from consolidating, and a vote that looks like ordinary skepticism draws little heat. If your vote would instead be the one that completes a majority on a town role, or would put you alone on a target, switch to the bloc that keeps the tally split.

lessons.situation: Day 2 is the first vote of the game. The room has piled onto one accused player, either a claimant whose result contradicts the rules or a player placed at a victim's door by claimed results. You are the necromancer, newly past your immunity night and with no hidden visits exposed. Information landscape: Information-thin: unverified role claims, perhaps one claimed result or rules contradiction to anchor on, and few or no confirmed roles beyond early deaths. Stakes: Early game with many players alive; a single vote does not flip the outcome. The priority is staying hidden while the village removes a player, and a revealed body adds to your night options. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous, 8-1 or 9 votes, behind one accused player, based on a claimed report, logical contradiction, or weak defense rather than a wolf-driven push. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the room. Heat: Low to almost none: you have been quiet or have only asked mild questions or endorsed a report, and nobody has accused you or tied a night event to you. Forward exposure: A vote with the majority reveals nothing about your role and commits you only to the room's consensus. It is public and permanent, but unremarkable while the room is unanimous; a lone dissent would draw attention. Target landscape: One candidate has clear traction, accused on a claimed watch or visit report, a rules contradiction, or a weak defense. Other players hold unverified but unchallenged claims. No roles are confirmed, so the basis is claims and logic rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the lone killer with no wolf allegiance and no exposed visits; publicly you look like one more town-leaning voter and nobody is looking at you.
lessons.action: On the first day vote, when the room has converged on one accused player and you are not under suspicion, vote with the majority for that player instead of splitting off or floating a new target. A bandwagon vote reveals nothing about your role and keeps heat near zero. Any dead player whose role is announced then becomes a usable body for your later night abilities.

lessons.situation: Final-three vote after a reanimated attack proved the Necromancer alive. One accuser names you by elimination and you must pull the other voter across. Information landscape: Rich: the morning report and the claims cross-confirm each other, leaving you as the only unconfirmed candidate. Stakes: One vote decides the game. If neither voter switches, you are eliminated two to one and town wins. Consensus: The room is largely aligned against you, because the two others confirm each other through announced events. My position: Holding out against the room. Heat: High: the other two have reached you by elimination after the night report revealed a reanimated attack. Forward exposure: The vote is irreversible and decides the game, since a loss ends it immediately. Naming a target commits you to the claim that they are the Necromancer. Target landscape: Two town claimants. One has a claim that matches the morning report, and the other has passive or unused abilities and is thinly supported. Each has been confirmed by the other's account. Public vs private: You know you are the Necromancer and your attack is already tied to you by elimination, but publicly the others can still be argued against.
lessons.action: With three alive and both others claiming town roles, vote for the one whose claim has the thinner support in the announced record, and use your last word to give the other player a reason to side with you. Before the vote, check whether the two corroborate each other through announced night events. If they do, the record is against you and the vote only works if you can credibly cast doubt on one of them.

lessons.situation: Endgame vote at about five players alive. The wolves are gone, a necromancer's night attacks through dead bodies have been publicly identified, and the town is voting to find the lone killer by elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, a will or a sigil strike cleared some players, claims are known and votes are recorded, so the necromancer's choices are scrutinized. Stakes: At five alive, one wrong elimination or one night kill leaves the necromancer close to the at-most-one-other-alive win. One exposed vote can also cause the necromancer's own elimination or a night shot, so each ballot has decisive weight. Consensus: The town has narrowed to a small suspect pool by elimination and claims, and the leading confirmed players have converged on one target. My position: holding out against the forming consensus Heat: Moderate to extreme: the necromancer is among a handful of suspects, with some cover from a dead investigator's clearance but questions about its votes and about pressure on specific claims. Forward exposure: A vote against the player the leading confirmed players are defending, or a lone vote against a quiet player, is public and permanent and cannot be undone. It commits you to a stance that the town will later read as deflection or antagonism. Target landscape: Few survivors, among them a confirmed vigilante, a speculator, a claimed healer and a claimed sigilist. The leading players favor one target on the basis of claims and behavior. The alternative target is backed only by the player with the most to hide. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows they are the lone killer and that the reanimated attacks came from them; the town knows only that a necromancer exists among the survivors and is reading each vote and defense as a tell.
lessons.action: When five players remain, both wolves are dead and the town is hunting the lone killer, vote with the room's strongest evidence-backed consensus (the confirmed, leading players' target) instead of holding out for a different target. If the consensus target is someone else and no evidence clears you, joining it keeps your ballot from standing out as a deflection, which matters because the town is reading votes for deflection.

lessons.situation: Day-3 vote after you pointed at a player using a private body-watch result, were challenged for lacking a result, and conceded. The room then turned on you for the overstated accusation. Information landscape: Public record holds announcements and unverified claims. The necromancer's key evidence is private and unshareable without revealing a dead role's body in use. Stakes: Your own elimination ends the lone-killer path, so the vote should not add to the case against you. With a majority already on you, an unsupported minority vote adds nothing. Consensus: Most of the room is aligned against the necromancer on its overstated accusation. Only one other player shares its read on the private-result target. My position: Holding out against the room, voting a different target from the majority aimed at you. Heat: High. Town players publicly challenged your claim, and you conceded it was inference, not a result. Forward exposure: Voting on a result you cannot cite commits you to an indefensible position, and you cannot take the vote back. Voting with a publicly justifiable read keeps the information hidden and your role intact. Target landscape: The necromancer itself (pressed for an unsupported accusation), the unclaimed player the private result pointed at, and a third player with a scattered vote. The case against the private-result target rests on unshareable information, while the case against you is behavioral. Public vs private: Privately you saw visits through a dead body that point at one player. Publicly you can cite only the inference and the claims, and an overstated accusation makes your reads look unsupported.
lessons.action: If you hold private information you cannot disclose, such as a body-watch result, voice only claims you can source publicly. Before the vote, state that your read is inference, and cast the vote that fits the public evidence, not the hidden result. If the hidden result points at a target the room does not share, hold that read for the night and do not stake your survival on it in the vote.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a reanimated-body kill and a hidden-role death. The room has lined up behind one target, and the necromancer is tempted to vote its own private target alone. Information landscape: Moderate. There are unverified claims, one confirmation by a role holder, and the announced reanimated kill. The identities of the wolves and the lone killer remain open, and nothing publicly ties anyone to the necromancer's night actions. Stakes: The necromancer needs the board down to two players, so every Town elimination is progress. A solo dissent adds no progress and can cost the necromancer its life one day later, because the vote record shows it standing apart. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous, with 5-6 votes behind one target. The basis is behavioral, such as vouching for a dead wolf, or an unverified investigator's Suspicious claim. My position: Holding out alone against a near-unanimous majority. Heat: Moderate to very high. The necromancer is accused or watched because a reanimated kill was announced, or because it has flagged the body danger. Forward exposure: A lone dissenting vote is public and permanent, cannot be undone, and builds a record of being the only voter off consensus. Voting with the plurality commits you to nothing beyond that day's target and is less revealing. Target landscape: The candidates are the room's consensus target, who is usually a Town role under behavioral suspicion, and the necromancer's private preference such as the healer or the claiming investigator. None has hard evidence against them, so a solo vote on the private preference only exposes the necromancer. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it is the lone killer and has been attacking through a body, so a Suspicious read on it is accurate. The public cannot verify night actions and only sees the announced reanimated kill and the room's behavior.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on a target and you are not yet that target, cast your vote with the plurality instead of a solo dissent. A solo vote is permanent and marks you as the one voter outside consensus, and it moved no one in either game. If you are the accused, vote the same way as the room's other non-you voters where one target exists, so your record does not stand out.

lessons.situation: Day vote with four alive. You and the genuine neutral each claim the same role, and the other two voters (town) must choose between you or tie. Information landscape: Starved: claims can't be checked and the investigator's checks are spent or unconfirmed. The only evidence is comparing bet histories against announced deaths. Stakes: A wrong vote ends your game, while a lynch of the rival or a tie keeps you alive and close to the 2-alive win condition. Each vote swings the outcome. Consensus: The village is split between the two claims, with no verified evidence, and the undecided town voters hold the balance. My position: Holding out against the accusation, pushing a mirror claim. Heat: High to moderate and rising: your claim is contradicted by a consistent rival and you have been accused or named as the last unclaimed player. Forward exposure: Your vote and mirror claim are public and permanent, and changing your claim would confirm guilt. Voting your accuser keeps you consistent, and the outcome depends on how the two undecided voters split. Target landscape: The rival claimant (the true neutral) and the two town players who haven't committed. The claims rest on unverifiable bet histories, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You know your claim is false and the accuser's is true, but publicly it is two unverifiable identical claims, and the town can pick either.
lessons.action: With four alive and a true neutral accusing you, keep your mirror claim and the details of its bet history unchanged, and vote for the accuser. In the last word, give the two uncommitted town voters one concrete reason to doubt the accuser's account, such as a bet that doesn't match the public deaths. If one of them breaks from the other, a tie or a lynch of the accuser leaves you alive.

query_dims.consensus_text: No consensus yet on day 2; the room is information-starved with no accusations recorded and players are still settling into discussion.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine alive with five eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single vote or kill can end the game, so early day-2 errors are recoverable but each wrong elimination pushes the wolves closer to parity.
query_dims.heat_now: Low. As the fortune teller I have a private record of one correct bet on the night-1 death, but nothing public links me to any role, so suspicion on me is minimal.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: one public death with a revealed role and no will, no claims, no checks or watches reported publicly.
query_dims.my_position: Holding back with the room, blending in as a neutral player while avoiding early claims.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 opens with no vote history and a quiet room after a night-1 wolf kill of a trailseer, which removed a town information source. The fortune teller is alive with two self-bets remaining and must decide how to speak without drawing wolf attention.
query_dims.target_landscape: Nine living players with no public claims or accusations yet; no one has been voted on since day 1 has no vote. The only public death is a trailseer killed by the wolves on night 1, with no will read out and no evidence pointing at any specific player.

lessons.situation: Day 2 after a night-1 death. Conflicting or unverifiable role claims (Investigator, Healer, Trailseer, Sentinel) dominate the discussion, and you are an uncommitted neutral with both self-bets unused. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims, one or two unconfirmed night reports, and a night-1 body, with no caught lies, no votes, and no confirmed wolf identities. Stakes: Early game with many players alive. No single vote or kill decides the game, so staying alive and unexposed to keep betting each night matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: Split or drifting: the room argues over rival claims or abstains, with no hard evidence behind any side. My position: Holding out in the middle or going with the majority, contributing a clarification without driving the vote. Heat: Very low: you have not been named, addressed, or accused, and you have not revealed your role. Target landscape: Two or more rival role claimants (e.g. two Investigators, or two Healers) or one scrutinized claimant, resting on unverified reports and timing. No confirmed wolves, and the night-1 victim's role is either announced or hidden.
lessons.action: When you are an unclaimed, low-heat Fortune Teller on day 2 in an info-starved room of conflicting claims, keep your role hidden and make one short, sincere contribution that shapes the discussion without accusing anyone. Good examples are a procedural point about visit direction, or a note that a hidden-role or dead role means a claim may not be genuine, or a direct question to a player a report ties to a contradiction. This keeps you out of the crossfire while still adding value, since your win depends on night bets rather than on how the vote goes.

lessons.situation: Late-game day discussion after the wolves are revealed dead; a player's claimed night result is being explained away and the Fortune Teller is asked directly whether a self-bet caused it. Information landscape: Fairly rich: public wolf reveals, a healer save and a sigil death are announced, while the claimed immunity result is still a private claim that my answer can corroborate. Stakes: Few players remain, so one correct vote on the lone killer decides the game; clearing the self-bet explanation lets the town converge on the right target. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on weighing the claimed immunity result; wolves are already confirmed dead, so the debate is about the remaining killer and the unverified claim. My position: With the majority, answering a direct question and removing the main objection. Heat: Moderate and specific: a player floated that I might have bet on myself, making me a possible alternative explanation for the result. Target landscape: A player accused via a claimed night result (e.g. a serial killer said to be immune) versus the credibility of the claimant; the only alternative explanation is the Fortune Teller's own self-bet. Evidence is a private claim plus public deaths and reveals.
lessons.action: When a player directly asks whether your self-bet explains an odd night result (e.g. a claimed immunity), answer plainly and truthfully on whether you self-bet that night; if you didn't, say so and name whom you bet on. This removes the competing explanation, makes the other player's claim the best available evidence, and costs little because a Fortune Teller cannot be blocked and reads Not suspicious.

lessons.situation: Day 4, shortly after a wolf flip and a concealed-role kill. One player voted against the consensus on the previous day, and you can ask them to justify it. Information landscape: A confirmed wolf flip, a concealed-role kill, and a public vote record. Few other facts are verified, so most reads rest on behavior. Stakes: The village is mid-game with evil still alive. A cheap question can surface a claim and a counterclaim fight without committing you to an elimination, and it keeps you alive for the later days. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned after a confirmed flip and a recorded vote pattern, and it is receptive to follow-up questions about odd votes. My position: With the majority, steering the question toward the dissenter without leading an accusation. Heat: Low. You have said little publicly and earlier mild skepticism has not been held against you. Target landscape: Survivors with no confirmed roles except what flips have shown. One player was the lone dissenter in the last vote, and all other reads are behavioral.
lessons.action: When a confirmed flip or kill pattern leaves one player as the lone dissenter in the earlier vote, ask them to explain the deviation instead of accusing them. Their answer, whether a claim, a trace, or a dodge, gives the room something to test and moves attention off you. If they give a claim or trace, hold your read until the room has cross-checked it against other claims.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer reports tracking an accused player to the door of a night victim whose role was concealed, creating a confrontation over whether the visit is genuine. Information landscape: Mixed: one concealed night death and a single living claimed trailseer's report, with conflicting readings of the mechanics and no corroboration. Stakes: A wrong elimination would cost Town a body and bring the wolves closer to parity, but no single vote decides the game. The fortune teller benefits from a slower, evidence-driven day that keeps it unexposed. Consensus: The room is leaning toward acting on the trailseer's report, but with open doubt about whether the visit was fabricated or genuine and how concealment mechanics affect traces. My position: holding out Heat: Completely cold; participating neutrally with no suspicion directed at me. Target landscape: An accused player said to have visited a dead player whose role was concealed, versus the claimed trailseer making the accusation; evidence is a single uncorroborated claim.
lessons.action: When a high-stakes accusation rests on an unverifiable visit report and you have no heat, urge caution and ask what corroborating evidence exists. Point out how the stated rules (for example, an illusionist's concealment hiding the attacking trace) limit what such a report can prove. This makes you look measured and analytical and keeps you from being drawn into a rushed elimination.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a wolf is revealed dead and further kills were concealed; a lead accuser targets a suspect who defends himself with his vote on the dead wolf. Information landscape: Moderately thin: one confirmed wolf and a voting record, but concealed bodies and otherwise only claims and behavioral inference. Stakes: Midgame with enough players that one vote does not decide the game, but removing a wolf now cuts the wolves' parity threat and the pool of kill sources; the public result may also make me a likelier kill target. Consensus: The room is forming around one suspect, based on the dead wolf's revealed role and voting records rather than hard proof. My position: With the majority, as the second accuser. Heat: Low to moderate: aligned with the lead accuser, nothing exposing said, bets unscored and role undisclosed. Target landscape: A suspect accused of echoing a dead wolf's line who points to his vote on that wolf as proof of innocence, plus quiet players he deflects onto. Only one wolf role is confirmed; the rest is behavioral and voting-record reading.
lessons.action: With a confirmed wolf dead and no night result of your own to share, join the leading accusation against the player whose behavior best fits the dead wolf's. Give a concrete reason, such as a wolf piling onto a doomed partner to blend in, and keep your role and bet history private. If the accusation is led by a player you distrust, state your own independent read instead of echoing it.

lessons.situation: Late game with three players left: you and a copycat both claim Fortune Teller, and a single third player's vote decides which of you is eliminated. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified results, only claims, but a detailed bet history against a thin copy creates an asymmetry the voter can check against the public record. Stakes: With three alive, one vote decides the game: eliminating the false claimant can end it in your favor, while losing the vote likely means your death and a loss. Consensus: Split and starved of hard evidence; the outcome depends on one remaining voter judging whose account is more detailed and consistent. My position: Driving the case against the counterclaimant while holding out against their accusation. Heat: High: under a counterclaim, tied in votes, and your claim cannot be independently verified. Target landscape: Two Fortune Teller claimants (you and a false claimant, likely the necromancer) plus one unconfirmed swing voter whose own claim cannot be verified; the false claimant's bets match only public deaths, while your history has specifics that fit the record.
lessons.action: When a rival claims Fortune Teller (or your claim is otherwise disputed) in a late-game room with few players left, state your claim plainly and give your full bet history: which nights, whom you bet on, the role named, which bets scored, and the self-bets. Point out that a copycat's bets match only publicly known deaths while yours include specifics (wrong early bets, self-bets, role names) that fit the public record, and name the copycat as your top suspect so the swing voter has a concrete reason to side with you.

lessons.situation: Few players remain, the town power roles that could clear anyone are dead, and you are the first to publicly narrow the suspects to two.
