Information landscape: Information-starved on the key question: dead roles are known and one player is confirmed by an announced fact, but nothing separates the last two unknowns. Stakes: Near parity: every vote and night kill is decisive, and a visible lead on a point-short Fortune Teller invites the killer to remove you before you can score the final point. Consensus: The table accepted the narrowing and then debated voting order; the two suspects deflected onto each other with no firm direction. My position: Driving the framing with no personal lead on which suspect is the killer. Heat: Moderate-low: one earlier vote on a dead player is being cited against you, but no real suspicion. Target landscape: Two unaccounted-for players, with the dead roles known and one player confirmed by an announced sigil strike; no claims or checks separate the two, so any lean rests on voting-order behavior only.
lessons.action: When the pool of evil suspects is down to a few players and the town roles that could clear anyone are dead, state your narrowing and name your lead suspect, but deliver it as a shared conclusion alongside the confirmed player rather than leading it alone. If you are one point short of winning, avoid being the visible driver, since a lone-killer or wolf at the table can eliminate you at night.

lessons.situation: Day 4 with most evil already dead. A claimant's reported results look inconsistent with the rules, and you are the main driver of the case against them. Information landscape: Info-rich on mechanics but conflicted on identity. The contradiction is checkable, but the claimant's honesty is in doubt and a real Town role may be misread. Stakes: Few evil players remain, so one wrong elimination can hand the last evil faction parity or remove Town's last investigative role. A visible driver of the vote is also an obvious night-kill target. Consensus: The room is converging on your rule argument, which makes a fast elimination of the claimant likely. My position: Driving the case as the first and most persistent voice. Heat: Moderate. The accused claimant counter-accused you of pushing too eagerly, though the rest of the room backed your argument. Target landscape: The only claimed role on the table, with unclaimed others. The basis for suspicion is a mechanical inconsistency in the claim, not a past check.
lessons.action: When you spot a rule-based contradiction in a claimant's account, state it once, clearly and as a question. Ask what else could explain it, and compare their answer with any counterclaims. Do not repeatedly assign a specific evil role to them, because other players will pile on and the mislynch can cost Town its last investigative role while exposing you to a night kill.

query_dims.consensus_text: The village is split and mostly stalled: two abstain days, a day 2 vote spread across several names, and no majority forming on a target, with the room asking for concrete claims rather than lynch pushes.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a single wrong lynch is recoverable at this distance but each mistaken elimination brings the wolves closer, so the board can absorb a few more errors before the margin narrows.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible block or claim I make would reveal my role or tie me to a night result I cannot prove; abstaining and pressing player_4's unexplained day 2 vote keeps exposure low and remains reversible.
query_dims.heat_now: Moderate: player_4 and player_7 have accused me of being the visitor to the dead trailseer on night 1, and player_5-pressure is circulating, but no concrete evidence beyond player_4's claim ties to me.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: only one public claim (sentinel watch on a dead trailseer showing one visitor), no corroboration, two abstain days, and the dead player's role was revealed but no will was read out for a wolf victim-equivalent.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out: I am abstaining against lynch pressure while the room debates player_4's sentinel claim, not with any forming majority.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately I am the chanteuse, a wolf, and my wolf partner is believed to be the illusionist, still alive and unrevealed; publicly I claim no role, and the village reads the day 2 vote and the night 1 sentinel claim by player_4 as the main lead, with no one knowing my role.
query_dims.situation: After a sentinel claim by one player that names the accused as the only visitor to a night 1 victim, the accused is being pressed by two others to justify a day 2 vote, and the day 2 vote record is what the room is arguing over, with a day 2 lynch that failed to happen.
query_dims.target_landscape: Two live candidates dominate: player_4, who publicly claims sentinel and whose night 1 watch claim is untestable beyond the single visit, and player_10, a day 2 vote target of player_3 that has since been dropped; player_4's claim is single-source and rests on a visit that is partly shaped by my own night 1 visit to player_2.

lessons.situation: On day 2 a claimed trailseer reported following you to another player's door, a roleblock report on that player corroborated it, and the village is converging on you or on an abstain while you consider voting against the tracker. Information landscape: Starved of announced facts: only unverified claims (a follow report, a roleblock report, a watch claim, possibly your own cover claim), plus a hidden-role death and a confirmed investigator death. Nothing announced identifies you. Stakes: With nine alive and the wolves far from parity, there is no tempo to force a risky vote. Losing the chanteuse, or drawing a sigil or investigator check by standing out, costs the wolves a blocker and leaves the partner alone. Consensus: The room is aligned on either abstaining or eliminating you, based on matching unverified claims about your night movement rather than on any announced fact. My position: Holding out alone against the room, either as the main wagon target or as a solitary voter against an abstain consensus. Heat: High to very high: the tracker's follow report and a target's roleblock report match your real night visit, several players accuse you, and your denial stands alone against a convergent pair of claims. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser is public and permanent, commits you to the story that the report is false, and invites night attention. Voting with the room is reversible and keeps the record neutral; if you are eliminated your role is revealed and your wolf partner comes under suspicion. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed trailseer who named you, players who echoed the roleblock or watch claims (sigilist, vigilante, sentinel), and an abstain option. All are unverified role claims, and the dead so far are an investigator and a concealed body, so nothing hard points at any candidate. Public vs private: You privately know the tracker's report of your visit is true and you blocked or visited that player; publicly it is only an unverified claim that you have denied or covered with a fabricated story.
lessons.action: When a claimed trailseer or other tracker publicly places your night visit on a target, and the room is abstaining or leaning against you, skip the revenge vote and join the room's consensus (abstain or the wagon's target). A solitary vote against your accuser changes no tally, repeats your accusation on the permanent record and marks you as the one player who wants the information role dead.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after your wolf partner died on night 1. You are the lone wolf, and the room mostly leans to abstain while minority blocs name different targets. Information landscape: Starved: a few claimed night results and one slip, with no confirmed roles and no vote history. Stakes: As the lone wolf you have no backup, so one exposure or one night retaliation could end the wolf side; staying low-profile is worth more than a marginal vote. Consensus: Most of the room leans toward abstaining, and a couple of small blocs name different targets. My position: Holding out with a minority bloc against an abstain-leaning room. Heat: Low: no accusations against you, only generic discussion remarks. Forward exposure: A minority vote is public and permanent and ties you to one bloc, so the target and that bloc can see where you stand. You cannot reverse it. Target landscape: Candidates are a claimant who slipped on a night action, another named suspect, or abstaining. Roles are unconfirmed, and the only lead is a behavioral slip. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf with no partner to help, while the town has no read on you.
lessons.action: If your partner is dead or revealed and you are the lone wolf, vote with the majority or abstain instead of joining a small minority bloc on a sigilist or other action-role claimant. A vote that leaves you holding out with a minority marks you to the targeted player, who may act against you that night.

lessons.situation: Late-game day vote where the chanteuse's side is losing. Either a fake-claim counter-claim contest has turned against you, or a credible watch or follow claim has doomed your wolf partner, and the room is converging. Information landscape: Information-rich from the town's view: confirmed roles for the dead, a lone killer possibly already eliminated, and claims corroborated by other claimants. You have nothing verifiable to offer. Stakes: The wolves are within a couple of eliminations of parity, so losing a wolf or exposing the pair is costly. This single vote will not flip the result, so the value is in keeping the wolves' public links minimal. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, with a lopsided majority forming on a claim-based case that looks consistent. There is no strong support for the minority view. My position: Holding out against, or being swept along by, a clear majority. Your vote is not the deciding one. Heat: High. You are either the target of a lost counter-claim with several players already naming you, or you recently pushed against a claimant who has since been corroborated. Forward exposure: Every vote is public and permanent. Matching your partner's vote, or opposing the room's clear pick, ties you to them and cannot be undone once the role is revealed. A vote that diverges costs little because your own vote cannot change a lopsided result. Target landscape: The realistic candidates are your counter-claimant, your exposed partner, and the Sentinel or other accuser. All are judged on claims and corroboration rather than hard proof, and the room has mostly settled on one. Public vs private: You privately know your partner's role and whether your own claim is false. The room is working from claims, counter-claims and past votes, and it sees you as either a liar or a defender of a likely wolf.
lessons.action: If the vote is already lost, because you are the losing side of a counter-claim or your partner is the target of a credible, room-wide case, cast the vote that least links you to your partner. Vote with the room when it is converging on your partner, and when you are the target pick a different name from your partner's. Votes are public and permanent, so a doomed vote that mirrors your partner's ties the two of you together.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote: a claimed town info role gave a result that breaks the rules, the accused admitted no explanation, and the table piled on. Your wolf partner may be among the accusers. Eliminating the target also removes a town watcher. Information landscape: Thin but concrete: one verifiable rules inconsistency, a few unverified claims, no voting history, and few confirmed roles. Stakes: Early game with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. The outcome is not close, so one vote does not flip the result. The value is in staying invisible while a town information role is removed. Consensus: Near-unanimous (about 8 of 9) and based on a checkable rules inconsistency that the accused conceded, not on tone or pack coordination. My position: With the majority, joining a vote that is already decided. Heat: Low to almost none: you are unclaimed, made few or no accusations, and the attention is entirely on the accused. Forward exposure: A vote with a lopsided majority commits you to nothing and looks like ordinary town behavior. Voting against an accepted target would stand out in the permanent public record with no upside. Target landscape: One candidate, a claimed Sentinel, has a concrete rules contradiction (a watch result that omitted their own visit) and is accused by several players. No other player has comparable evidence against them, so the choice rests on a verifiable inconsistency, not on tone. Public vs private: You privately know the wolf pair (Chanteuse and Illusionist) is alive and that the accused claimant is likely a genuine town role. The public sees only an unverified claim with an impossible result and treats it as grounds to eliminate.
lessons.action: When the room is already converging on a target through a checkable rules contradiction, cast your day vote with the majority and add no distinctive argument. The vote is low-commitment and blends into the pile-on, so a lone vote elsewhere would only draw heat to you.

lessons.situation: Day 2 is the first vote of the game. Information is thin, with a night-1 death or a few unverified claims, and the village is split between piling on a target and abstaining. Information landscape: Starved: unverified claims, perhaps one revealed death, no confirmed roles and no vote history. Stakes: Early game with many players alive; no single vote decides the game, so staying unnoticed matters more than pushing an elimination. Consensus: The room is split or undecided between several targets and abstaining, with no evidence-based convergence. My position: With the majority or a plurality bloc, not driving. Heat: Low: you have not been accused and have only spoken mildly or generically. Forward exposure: A named vote is public and permanent and can later be read as wolf coordination if your partner is exposed. An abstain or a vote with the plurality commits you to little and carries low risk. Target landscape: Candidates are quiet players, unverified claimants, and abstaining. No roles are confirmed, so any named target is a behavior-based guess. Public vs private: You privately know both wolves and the pack's night plan, while the public has only unverified night-1 claims, one death at most, and behavioral reads, so nothing points at you.
lessons.action: On the first day-2 vote, when no roles are confirmed and you have low heat, cast your vote with the room's existing plurality, which is often abstain or a split. Keep your vote consistent with your partner's but do not drive the accusation. Voting with the room adds no new suspicion, and an unforced named vote is permanent record you cannot undo.

lessons.situation: Day vote where the village converges on your wolf partner, who is exposed by a counterclaim or accusation. You must choose between joining the vote against them and defending them. Information landscape: Claims, counterclaims and unverified night reports are present, and some roles may be confirmed by deaths. There are no hard Game Master confirmations of the accused's role, so the room's read rests on deduction. Stakes: The vote outcome is already decided by the majority, so your single vote does not flip the board. What it decides is whether you stay unlinked to the partner on the permanent record, which protects your survival as the remaining wolf. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, around 7 votes or more, on eliminating your partner. The basis is claim contradictions or a claimed check, not confirmed roles. My position: Tempted to hold out to protect the partner, but the correct stance is with the majority. The vote is decided either way. Heat: Low to moderate. Discussion is consumed by the claim collision and you have drawn no accusations. Your own night visits could still surface later. Forward exposure: A vote with the pile-on reads as a normal town vote and links you to nothing. A vote against the majority, for a rival claimant, or an abstain would be public and permanent, and once your partner's role is revealed it would mark you as their ally. Neither vote can be undone. Target landscape: The accused is your wolf partner, claiming a power role (Sentinel, Healer or Investigator) that is contradicted by a counter-claimant or report. The only alternative is a rival claimant who is probably Town. The case rests on claim clashes and visit reports, with nothing confirmed by the Game Master. Public vs private: You privately know the accused or counter-claimed player is your wolf partner, and that their claim or accusation is fabricated cover. Publicly the room reads it as a claim contradiction or a Suspicious check, and no suspicion falls on you.
lessons.action: When a lopsided majority is already set to eliminate your wolf partner and your vote cannot change the result, cast your vote with the majority on the same target. If you hold out, defend the partner, or abstain, the permanent public record ties you to the wolf once their role flips, so don't do any of those. Afterward, plan as the lone wolf rather than relying on the vote to keep you safe.

lessons.situation: A genuine Town claimant (a healer counter-claiming against my partner, or a sentinel accusing me of a visit) is on the ballot at the day vote. Removing them protects the pack or me today, but their role and will will be revealed on death. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are contested role claims, a named visit, confirmed saves, and the public voting record. Nothing is verified until a death reveals the role. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several kills still needed for parity. Removing a healer or sentinel strips Town's protection or visit information and gives the wolves tempo, but a revealed role can expose my own visit history. Consensus: The village is split or leaning against the claimant, based on behavioral skepticism such as delayed disclosure and conflicting claims, not on confirmed facts. My position: With the majority, as one vote in a broad bloc and not the driver. Heat: Ranges from low to severe. Either my partner is under fire in a contested claim, or the claimant is directly accusing me, but the room is skeptical of the claimant. Forward exposure: The vote is permanent and public. If the claimant dies as a confirmed Town role, my vote is tied to the wolf side and any will naming my visit becomes announced fact, so the commitment cannot be undone and can draw night attacks such as a sigil or a vigilante shot. Target landscape: A binary choice between a claimed protective or information role (healer or sentinel) and either my wolf partner or myself. The claimant's role is unverified, and the case against them rests on behavior and timing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Publicly the claimant is an unverified or belated claimant whom the room distrusts. Privately I know the claim is genuine, either because it names my own visit or because my wolf partner is the one faking the role.
lessons.action: When the room is already turning on a claimant who threatens you or your partner (a counter-claimed healer, or a sentinel naming your visit), cast your vote with the broad majority against that claimant. Joining a wide bloc keeps you from standing out as the driver and removes a protective or information role. Expect the revealed role and will to be read out as fact, so take the claimant's most likely true read into account when judging how much heat that reveal will put on you.

lessons.situation: A day vote on an early day with a forming majority, either abstain-heavy or piled on one suspect, where the chanteuse has no real evidence-based target and a lone vote would only mark them as the outlier. Information landscape: Starved: unverified power-role claims, a few roleblock complaints and no confirmed roles or voting history to anchor a read. Stakes: Many players are still alive and no single vote decides the game. Wolf survival depends on staying unnoticed, so the vote is worth little compared with the cost of a record that gets used against you. Consensus: The village is fairly aligned, either piling onto one behavior-based suspect or abstaining in bulk, with little hard evidence behind it. My position: Free to choose between joining the majority and standing alone; joining the majority keeps you unremarkable. Heat: Low to moderate: nobody is accusing you, but an off-consensus vote would create heat immediately. Forward exposure: A vote is public and permanent. An outlier vote on a quiet or claimed player creates a record that can be quoted back and cannot be undone, whereas a vote with the room commits you to little and is easy to explain. Target landscape: Candidates are mostly unrevealed players: a room-favored suspect chosen on behavior or quietness, claimed power roles with unverifiable results, and quiet players with no evidence against them. There is no confirmed wolf, so any off-consensus pick rests on thin or no evidence. Public vs private: You privately know the pack, your own blocks and the real roles of some players, but publicly you are an unremarkable, unclaimed player whom nobody is accusing, and the room is thin on evidence and leaning toward one target or toward abstaining.
lessons.action: When the room is converging or abstaining and you have no evidence-backed target, cast your vote with the majority, or abstain if abstaining is offered, rather than being the lone off-consensus voter. If you are forced to name someone, pick the room's leading target or one your wolf partner also backs, so your permanent record has no outlier vote that can later be quoted as reactionary deflection.

lessons.situation: A claiming investigative role (Investigator or Trailseer) has caught my wolf partner with a Suspicious check or a tracked visit to a victim. The village is pushing to eliminate the partner, and the partner is counter-charging the claimant. I must choose between joining the vote on the partner and voting against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich. A living claimant has direct evidence, other claims or mechanics corroborate it, and the votes will become a permanent ledger. Stakes: The board is still early and not at parity, so one vote does not decide the game. The partner is lost either way, and what matters is whether I survive as a low-heat wolf for later days. A solitary or minority vote costs me that standing and gains nothing. Consensus: The village is largely united behind the claimant's result, supported by mechanics or corroborating claims. A counter-wagon would need near-majority support, and in the observed cases it reached 2 to 4 votes against a landslide. My position: holding out Heat: Low. I had stayed neutral in discussion, with no accusations or scrutiny on me, and that standing is what I would lose by backing the partner. Forward exposure: Votes are public and permanent. A vote against the claimant or for the partner's side becomes a visible link to the partner once the partner's role flips as a wolf, and it cannot be undone. A vote with the majority commits me to nothing beyond the consensus. Target landscape: The choice is between my caught wolf partner, who is named by a claiming investigative role's result or movement evidence, and that claimant, whom the partner is accusing of fabrication. The case against the partner rests on evidence and mechanics, while the counter-case rests on behavior and bluster. Public vs private: I privately know my partner is a wolf and the claimant's result is probably genuine. The room is converging on that read, and my only open choice is whether to be seen defending the partner.
lessons.action: When a credible, info-rich claim has the room converging on your wolf partner and your own heat is low, vote with the majority against the partner instead of voting against the claimant. If the counter-wagon cannot reach a majority, your vote on the public record only ties you to the partner, so keep your standing for the later days.

lessons.situation: Endgame vote at three or four players where a claimed vigilante threatens to eliminate the chanteuse or the wolf partner and a coordinated counter-vote can produce a tie and no elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: most investigative town roles are confirmed dead, roles and past votes are known, and the vigilante's claim and held shot are public. Stakes: The board is near parity, so a single elimination of a wolf could lose the game while a tie with no elimination keeps the wolves alive to reach parity or a winning night. Consensus: The room is split with no majority; the vigilante pushes one wolf while the remaining players are undecided or abstaining, so a tie is reachable. My position: holding out Heat: Ranges from minimal heat on the chanteuse (suspicion on the partner) to high (a claimed vigilante accusing and voting for the chanteuse based on roleblock claims). Forward exposure: Publicly voting an unclaimed or quiet player commits the chanteuse to an adversarial stance against the vigilante's read, but with few players left and no investigative roles alive the exposure is low and the tie can be repeated. Target landscape: Two or three living candidates: a claimed vigilante driving the accusation, and a quiet or unclaimed player with split or no votes and no claims, who is the only viable counter-target; the basis is behavior, not evidence. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows which players are wolves and that the vote target is not evil, while the room is split between the chanteuse or the wolf partner and an unclaimed or quiet player as the last wolf.
lessons.action: In a small endgame vote where a claimed vigilante and others are pushing to eliminate you or your wolf partner, vote for the non-partner player who is least aligned with the vigilante's push so the vote splits into a tie. A tie eliminates no one, so you and your partner survive into the next night; pick the target who is a plausible suspect, not your partner.

lessons.situation: Endgame with 3-4 players alive, I am the sole surviving wolf, and the day vote is a terminal step toward parity. The lone killer or a town or neutral player is the target, and the town is pressuring me on my voting record. Information landscape: Information-rich: claims, announced roles from dead players, wills, and a public voting record narrow the suspects down to a few players. Stakes: One elimination from a night kill that reaches parity. This vote decides whether I go into the night with the lone killer gone and equal numbers, or lose on the spot. Consensus: The room is split but active. One or two town voices want a decisive elimination, and a plurality can form around a target I can also support. My position: driving or with majority; I join the likeliest plurality so my vote decides the result and the votes against me stay short. Heat: Moderate to high; a claimed Sentinel, a Speculator or the Serial Killer pointed at me from voting history or role counts, but they lacked the numbers for a majority. Forward exposure: The vote is public, permanent and irreversible. If it fails to form a plurality and the vote lands on me, the wolves lose at once, so line up a majority with a willing voter before committing. Target landscape: Two to three living non-wolf players, among them the lone killer (claimed or unclaimed) and town utility roles; the choice rests on role counts, claims, and voting records rather than hard proof. Public vs private: Privately I know I am the last wolf and that the wolf win needs the lone killer gone and parity reached; the table sees only an unverified choice between suspects with no sure wolf among them.
lessons.action: As the last living wolf in a 3-4 player endgame, vote to eliminate any non-wolf player, joining whichever other voter can make a plurality. If the lone killer is still alive, prioritize it because the wolves cannot win while it lives; otherwise remove a town or neutral player to reach parity. Count the votes first so your own name cannot take the plurality, since losing the last wolf ends the game.

lessons.situation: A split day vote where the Town claimants disagree, and a no-elimination tie would keep a rival killer alive to thin Town overnight. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims (investigator, sentinel, healer) but with no confirmed evil targets and an unconfirmed Night 1 event. Stakes: Town can't afford another night of attrition, so a tie that keeps a killer alive favors the evil side. This only pays if your own elimination isn't within reach of the vote. Consensus: Town is split across several wagons with no agreement on who is evil, and there are rival claims from the investigator, sentinel and healer. My position: Driving a minority wagon, aiming for a tie, not a majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A claimed vigilante has voted for you and a claimed healer is questioning your narrative. Forward exposure: A vote on a contested suspect commits you to a push a claimed healer has already questioned, and you take heat if the target flips Town. The vote is visible and permanent, but a tie costs little because nobody is eliminated. Target landscape: A suspected killer voted by a claimed investigator, a quiet unaligned player voted by a claimed healer and the suspect, and you voted by a claimed vigilante. The reads rest on claims and unconfirmed night results, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know a suspect has night immunity or a role that helps your side. Publicly that is unconfirmed, so Town doubts the push against them.
lessons.action: If you are not the main target and a killer or other threat still threatens Town, vote for a plausible suspect who is already contested so the votes split into a tie. A tie means no elimination and gives the threat another night to cut Town's power roles. If your own heat is high and a vigilante-type is voting you, skip this and consolidate onto the leading wagon instead.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is substantially aligned against you: multiple players favor your elimination because your claimed protection account does not explain the save, while recognizing that the report does not identify who protected the saved player. This is an evidence-limited consensus based on competing claims and the public save, not verified role information.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive; four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town; this vote is consequential but not immediately decisive.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible defense or vote in the coming elimination would commit you publicly amid a conflict where you are the leading accused player. Further specific claims about night actions could be challenged against the public record; your stated protection of a different player does not explain the confirmed save. Your remaining concealment is private and is not itself exposed by a daytime statement.
query_dims.heat_now: High and direct: four players accused you, and the moderator named you as the most accused player for the last word. The basis is the conflict between the two Healer claims and your stated protection of someone other than the player publicly confirmed saved.
query_dims.information_landscape: Moderate but incomplete: public facts include the save, the revealed Sentinel and their will, and the concealed first victim; claims include both Healer accounts, the Investigator's check and roleblock, and the Trailseer's follow result. The save confirms protection but not the protector, and the Night 1 concealment withholds a role and will. You privately know the concealed victim was the Vigilante and know your own wolf identity and pack history.
query_dims.my_position: You are the accused holdout: your public account maintains that you protected a different player, while the forming majority favors eliminating you. You have not publicly claimed knowledge that resolves the Healer dispute.
query_dims.public_private_text: Concealment is central to the gap: the village knows a player was killed on Night 1 and their role concealed, and the Night 2 victim was revealed as the Sentinel. Privately, you know the concealed player was the Vigilante and that the surviving behavioral ally is a wolf partner; no partner has been revealed. You know your own Healer claim is false. Publicly, the village is weighing your unsupported Healer claim against the other Healer claimant and the confirmed save of the claimed Investigator.
query_dims.situation: With the day 3 vote approaching, two players claim Healer after a public report confirms that the claimed Investigator was saved from a Serial Killer attack. You are the accused claimant, and your stated protection target differs from the saved player; several others treat the competing claimant's account as a better fit. The first wolf victim's role remains concealed, while the second wolf victim was publicly revealed as the Sentinel.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate choice is between you, a player claiming Healer whose Night 2 account does not explain the save, and the other player claiming Healer whose account of protecting the saved player fits it but does not prove their role. The claimed Investigator was saved from the Serial Killer and says they were roleblocked; their Night 1 Not suspicious check on a player does not rule out that player being the Serial Killer. The concealed Night 1 victim's role remains publicly unknown.

lessons.situation: A Town information role has publicly tied you to a night kill, and a second player backs the claim. Your partner is alive but is distancing from you, and you are the favorite to be eliminated today. Information landscape: Moderately rich: a specific result naming you, corroborating claims and a prior vote record. All of it is unverified, but it fits together. Stakes: Losing you leaves one wolf with several eliminations still to go before parity. Your vote cannot rescue you, so its only use is to hit the most dangerous accurser and keep the surviving wolf alive. Consensus: The village is aligned against you on a consistent claim and its corroboration, and it has little other evidence to weigh. My position: Holding out alone with a counter-vote while the room piles onto you. Heat: High. You are the named suspect and the primary target of the day, with several players accusing you from the start. Forward exposure: Your vote and denial go on the public record and cannot be retracted. If the accuser is read as truthful and you die, your role is revealed and your partner is left to survive alone. Target landscape: The candidates are the accuser and the player who corroborates them. Neither has a confirmed role, and the case rests on a specific claim plus consistent backing rather than on behavior alone. Public vs private: You privately know the accusation against you is true, for example the watch result that names you at a victim's door. Publicly it is only an unverified claim, though corroborating claims and a roleblock story make it look consistent.
lessons.action: When the vote is converging on you and your single vote cannot change the count, spend it on the accuser whose claim or case against you is most credible. That is the Town player most likely to hold accurate information, and removing them helps your partner survive. Keep denying the specific claim instead of switching to a new target, so your partner can still look like an independent Town voter.

lessons.situation: A day 2 vote in which two players claim investigator, your wolf partner is one of them (a fake claim) and was placed at a night scene by a watch. The village must choose between them. Information landscape: Moderate: one watch result and one follow result were shared, but both investigator claims are unverified and the key check result was never given. Stakes: The vote decides whether the town keeps its checker or the pack's partner is exposed. Eight players are alive and parity is about three eliminations away, so removing the real checker materially helps the wolves. Consensus: A clear majority is forming against the claimed investigator on the basis of claim contradiction and your partner's push. My position: With the majority, not driving. Heat: Low: you have barely spoken, are not named in the accusations, and stand outside the two-way fight. Forward exposure: A vote for the claimed investigator matches your partner's push and the room's lean, so it exposes little. Voting to save your partner would tie you to a player the visit evidence already places at the scene; the vote is public and permanent either way. Target landscape: Two candidates in a role-claim contradiction: a claimed investigator with no verifiable result, and your partner, who gave a counter-claim and was placed at a night scene by a watch. Neither role is confirmed; the basis is claim contradiction and a visit report. Public vs private: Privately you know your partner is a wolf and the investigator claimant is probably the real role; publicly the room sees only a contradiction between two role claims.
lessons.action: When a claimed investigator or other checker is contested and your partner has pushed against them, join the majority vote to eliminate that player, provided your partner is not the one the room is leaning toward. This removes a role that threatens the pack, while a vote with the room and your partner's push keeps your heat low; if the majority is instead forming on your partner, avoid defending them loudly and keep your vote on the room's lead alternative.

lessons.situation: With the serial killer dead, the town unites behind an accusation of the illusionist, who has one conceal left. The surviving wolf partner can still vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: a confirmed serial killer elimination, a dead trailseer's recorded tracking result and a claimed sigilist's reported test. These facts make the accusation hard to rebut. Stakes: Losing a wolf here halves the pack and leaves the survivor needing two more eliminations to reach parity. Because the town's votes are already locked, only a pooled counter-vote could change the result. Consensus: Near-unanimous among the non-wolves, resting on one dead player's recorded result and the serial killer's removal. It is firm and unlikely to move. My position: holding out Heat: Critical. Four or more town votes are locked on you from a standing accusation, while your partner has low heat. Forward exposure: A vote is public and permanent. Joining the partner's target signals a wolf-side counter-wagon but commits both wolves to the same name. Scattering votes reveals isolation and gains nothing. Target landscape: The candidates are the claimed sigilist, whom the partner already voted for, and unpressured bystanders. The sigilist's reported test is unverified, so any case against them rests on behavior and has no hard evidence. Public vs private: Town is united on the illusionist because of a dead player's lingering tracking report. Privately the illusionist knows the accusation is true, and the partner is unsuspected and free to coordinate.
lessons.action: If you are the locked-in vote target and your wolf partner is alive, put your vote on the same counter-target the partner is already voting for, such as a claimed role with a thin case. Do not scatter a lone vote onto an unpressured player. Pooled wolf votes can create a tie or a doubt, while a scattered vote shows isolation and adds no pressure.

lessons.situation: You are the last wolf after your partner was exposed and removed, and the village is convinced you were the partner's ally based on voting patterns. Information landscape: Thin. The only hard facts are the partner's reveal as a wolf and the concealed night kills, so the village argues about who voted for whom. Stakes: You are the last wolf, so your elimination ends the wolf side's chances. A single vote cannot change a lopsided count, so the vote is only worth casting where it removes a likely Town power role. Consensus: The village is aligned on you, based on voting-record links to your dead partner and not on hard evidence. My position: Holding out alone, the single voter against the lead accuser while everyone else piles onto you. Heat: High. You are the primary target of several accusers, who link your earlier vote to your dead partner. Forward exposure: Your vote and your accusation of the quiet players go on the public record and cannot be reversed. If you are eliminated, your role is revealed and the wolf side is gone. Target landscape: The candidates are your main accuser plus several quiet or accusing players. None has a confirmed role, since only your dead partner was revealed, so the case against you rests on behavioral links to your partner. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf, with your partner already dead and revealed. Publicly you are a player whose earlier vote and pushback drew suspicion, and your voting record is the main evidence against you.
lessons.action: As the last wolf under accusation, cast your vote on the main accuser who pushed the case, not an abstention, and use your last word to point at a quiet player. Pick the accuser who looks most likely to be a Town power role, since you need real Town eliminations to get anywhere near parity. If the room is already four or more against you, treat the vote as the best way to remove a dangerous Town player.

lessons.situation: Day vote after an investigator names you Suspicious or counterclaims against you. The village forces an elimination between you and the investigator, and the vote is lopsided against you. Information landscape: Information-rich: a game master-confirmed healer save, night-one logic that excludes other Suspicious roles, and cross-referenced night actions all support the investigator. Stakes: Losing a wolf here halves the pack's voting power and leaves a dead body for the necromancer to use if the role is revealed. A partner dragged down by a shared vote would cost the pack its last wolf. Consensus: The village is strongly aligned against you, about 7 votes to 2 or 3, because the investigator's claim is verified or consistent with mechanics and the game master's announcements. My position: Holding out or driving against the room's consensus, with at most your wolf partner voting alongside. Heat: Extreme to critical. You are named Suspicious or countered by an investigator claimant, the trailseer may be piling on, and an elimination vote on you is imminent. Forward exposure: Voting against the investigator who accused you commits you to the losing side of a public, permanent record. If you flip wolf, everyone who voted alongside you is exposed, and the vote cannot be undone. Target landscape: The claimed investigator, either uncontested or in a counterclaim duel with you, versus other living players with no hard evidence against them. The investigator's claim is backed by cross-checked night logic, while any alternative target rests on behavior alone. Public vs private: Privately you know the investigator's result or counterclaim is true or false, and that the pack is exposed. Publicly the room is still trying to decide who is authentic and is leaning heavily toward eliminating you.
lessons.action: When the room is clearly lined up against you and an investigator claim is driving it, treat the vote as likely lost. Do not give your partner a visible reason to copy you: cast your vote on a different plausible suspect, or on the claimant only if the room is split. Votes are public and permanent, so a lone-wolf vote on the accuser links your partner to you if you flip wolf.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote: I am the primary target after an accuser's check or watch result, backed by a second claimant. My own counterclaim or deflection has attracted no followers. Information landscape: Starved to moderate: conflicting or unverified role claims, a concealed or ambiguous body, and a visit report that implicates me. No role reveals confirm either side. Stakes: My single vote cannot change an 8-1 outcome, so its value lies in the signal it sends and in not tying myself to a doomed counterclaim. Losing a wolf this early also removes a voter and a conceal that the pack cannot replace. Consensus: Lopsided against me, resting on a corroborating claim from a second player and a weak defense from me. My position: Holding out alone against the forming consensus. Heat: Very high: several players named me, I was the most accused, and I gave a last word. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser is public and permanent, ties me to my counterclaim and reads as self-protective. If I am eliminated, my role reveal confirms the accuser and makes them trusted for later days. Target landscape: Candidates are the accuser (a claimed investigator or sentinel with partial corroboration) and myself. Neither can be verified by a role reveal yet, so the room weighs the claims and my defense. Public vs private: I privately know the accuser's read on me is true, or that the visit evidence against me is accurate. Publicly the village sees a corroborated accusation against me and an unresolved counter-claim from me, with no confirmed roles.
lessons.action: When the room is lopsided against you on corroborated evidence, check whether any accuser's claim has real traction before you vote. If the room is clearly locked on you, put your vote on a second-tier suspect the room already doubts, not the accuser who named you. That pairs your vote with other doubt, avoids another lone self-protective vote, and keeps your last word credible if it reads as a sincere read.

lessons.situation: Day vote, with the village converging on your wolf partner (the chanteuse) after tracking, watch or role claims linked her to suspicious visits. You must choose between joining the wagon, abstaining, or voting on someone else. Information landscape: Claim-heavy and unverified. Only the morning kill announcements are confirmed, and no roles have been revealed by vote yet. Stakes: The wolf side is still alive but about to drop to a single wolf, so your survival and cover now carry the pack. Your vote does not change the outcome. It only decides whether you look like a villager or a partner of the dead wolf when the next day's suspicion begins. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous against your partner, on claim-based evidence such as a follow report, a block claim or a watch claim. Nothing has been confirmed by announcement. My position: With the overwhelming majority. Your vote adds to a wagon that would succeed without it. Heat: Low. You have only voiced mild skepticism or been questioned peripherally, and have not defended the partner by name. Forward exposure: The vote is public and permanent and cannot be undone. Voting with the wagon on your partner looks like ordinary town behavior and stays cover if she is revealed as a wolf. Abstaining or voting a different target looks like distancing or defending, and is read against you once her role is shown. Target landscape: The main candidate is your wolf partner, whose role is unrevealed, accused by several players on unverified claims (a follow report, a block claim, a watch claim, or a contested role claim). The alternatives are the claimants who accuse her, who may be real Town roles. The basis is behavioral and claim-based, with nothing confirmed by announcement. Public vs private: You privately know the accused player is your wolf partner and that the claims against her are accurate or at least dangerous. Publicly she is only an accused player facing several accusers backed by unverified claims, and nobody knows her role.
lessons.action: When a near-unanimous wagon is already closing on your wolf partner and your vote can't change the result, cast your vote with the majority on her. Your public record then reads as an ordinary villager and gives you a defense line for the next day, so a vote elsewhere doesn't mark you as her ally. Hold that line and avoid any earlier defense or pushback that could be tied to her.

lessons.situation: Day vote with four players alive: you are the last wolf (partner dead or revealed, no conceals left), a necromancer is alive, and the table is converging on you. Information landscape: Role eliminations are known and the necromancer's presence is confirmed by reanimated kills or sigil strikes, but nothing hard separates you from the necromancer. Stakes: With four alive and a lone killer in play, your elimination ends the wolf team and hands the necromancer your body. Removing the necromancer is the wolves' only path to a win. Consensus: The village is aligned against you as the remaining wolf, based on eliminated roles and voting behaviour, with no hard evidence against the other suspect. My position: Holding out alone on a different target from the room. Heat: Critical. The other survivors have publicly narrowed the pool to you and one other player, and two or three of them are voting for you. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and commits you to a named target. If you are eliminated, your role is revealed and your body becomes usable by the necromancer, so the vote cannot be walked back. Target landscape: Three candidates: a confirmed sigilist, a neutral (fortune teller) claimant, and the unconfirmed necromancer. Evidence is a sentinel killed by a reanimated vigilante or a sigil strike, plus voting behaviour. No role among the three is confirmed to be the necromancer. Public vs private: You know you are the last wolf and that a necromancer is acting, while the table believes the pool is you and one other unconfirmed player, and the other voters are converging on you.
lessons.action: As the last wolf in a four-player vote with a necromancer still alive, put your vote on the player you judge most likely to be the necromancer. Use the reanimated-kill evidence and the voting records. Only that elimination can ever let the wolves win, and it also stops the necromancer from using your body after you die; if you can win over one other voter, a 2-2 tie spares you.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after the wolf partner was revealed or killed. You are the last wolf and the most accused player, and the room is hunting the Day 2 bandwagon participants. The lone killer is still alive. Information landscape: Rich: the partner's role is revealed, the Day 2 public voting record exists, and night reports from Town roles corroborate the story against you. Stakes: With the partner gone and the room converging on you, your elimination is likely and would end the wolf side. A lone isolated vote cannot change the count, so it should at least seed a credible alternative suspect instead of confirming your guilt. Consensus: The village is nearly unified against you, with a large majority converging on your Day 2 voting and defense pattern now that your partner's role is confirmed. My position: Holding out alone against a lopsided consensus, casting a counter-vote. Heat: Very high: several players have accused you, citing your Day 2 defense or vote of the partner who has since been revealed. Your explanations have shifted, and you are the most accused player. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and irreversible, and if you are eliminated your role is revealed. A spiteful or isolated counter-vote confirms that you are reacting defensively and commits you to a target nobody else shares. A vote with a record-based reason at least gives the room a second suspect. Target landscape: The living candidates are active Town claimants or unconfirmed players, plus possibly a neutral or the lone killer. None has hard evidence against them. The choice rests on voting-record behavior, and the loudest accuser is the most obvious but weakest retaliation target. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf and that your Day 2 stance was wolf coordination. The room has read it as wolf behavior from the voting record and your partner's reveal, so the public read about you is largely correct.
lessons.action: When you are the last wolf, your partner is revealed, and the room is lined up on you, vote for the living player whom the public record gives the best second-suspect case, such as a Day 2 bandwagon voter or an inconsistent claimant. Give a short reason drawn from that record. Do not retaliate on your loudest accuser or on the one player not piling on you, because the vote is public, permanent and reads as defensive.

lessons.situation: Day-2 vote where a claimed information role gave a result impossible under the rules and the room is piling on. Information landscape: Information-rich on one point: a rules-checkable contradiction. Otherwise little is known. Stakes: The elimination is likely to land on a Town role regardless of your vote, which favors the pack. Staying aligned keeps your heat low. Consensus: The village is aligned on the contradicted claimant, with several players spelling out the case. My position: With the majority, among the voices building the case. Heat: Low: you have made rules-based comments, not accusations of others, and nobody suspects you. Forward exposure: Voting with a unanimous or near-unanimous room is low-commitment and reveals nothing about wolf identity. Dissenting would make you stand out. Target landscape: One claimant with a self-admitted contradiction of the rules, versus other claimants with no public contradictions. The basis is evidence, not behavior. Public vs private: You privately know the pack and the hidden-role kill, but nothing about whether the accused lied or erred. Publicly the room has an evidence-backed case that fits your interests.
lessons.action: When the room converges on a player with a rules-verifiable contradiction in their claim, vote with the majority, ideally after pointing out why the defense fails. If the target is a Town information role, this also removes it for the pack without exposing you.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day vote (day 4-5) with few players left. You are a high-heat unclaimed wolf, the vote is tied between you and another suspect, and Town claimants are pushing reads that include you. Information landscape: Claims are unverified and no hard result clears or convicts anyone. Role-count deduction and voting behavior drive the reads, so the evidence is thin and speculative. Stakes: A few more eliminations let the wolves reach parity, so one vote decides whether the pack keeps its numbers. A tie costs the pack nothing and buys a night for the kill, while a lost vote leaves the wolves a man down, close to losing. Consensus: The room is fractured: Town claimants back one another's reads, the votes split into ties, and no single target has a clear majority. My position: Holding out against the bloc that is pressing on you. Heat: High: two or more players voted or named you, and an uncleared result or role-count reasoning marks you as one of the last unclaimed suspects. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent. Voting a Town claimant commits you to a counter-read that cannot be retracted, and voting your partner trades away a wolf. A tie only delays the elimination, and it leaves your exposure and your pair's pattern on the record. Target landscape: Candidates are you, your unclaimed partner, and Town claimants (investigator, vigilante, trailseer, sigilist). All claims are unverified, so the choice rests on role-count logic and behavior, not on hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know you are a wolf (and often that a Town claim is true or that the pack's remaining threat is a specific role). Publicly your claim status is unverified, and role-count reasoning or an uncleared result has put you among the likeliest wolves.
lessons.action: When you are one of the top two suspects and the room is split, cast your vote on the strongest rival suspect, preferably an unverified Town claimant who is not your partner, so the vote stays tied with you and nobody is eliminated. Treat the tie as only one bought day, and do not vote for your own partner just to stay alive.

lessons.situation: An early day vote (day 1 or 2) in which the village has only unverified role claims and partial night reports. The room is split between a lead target and abstaining, and no wolf is identified. You are the hidden illusionist wolf with your partner alive and unrevealed. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverifiable role claims, a follow or watch report, no caught lies and no confirmed wolf. Stakes: Early game with many players alive and parity far off. No single vote decides the game, so the priority is staying unlinked and unsuspected while the pack keeps its kill plan. Consensus: The room is split or tied between a plurality target and an abstain bloc, with no hard evidence on anyone. My position: With the majority or a plurality, not driving the push. Heat: Low: you have spoken little, asked a question or defended a visit, and no one is accusing you. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and ties you to a side of the table. A vote with the majority or on an unlinked target reveals nothing about your role and carries little commitment, but it cannot be reversed that day. Target landscape: Candidates are an unclaimed quiet player, a claimed power role whose claim is corroborated or contested, and abstain. The basis is claim contradictions and behavior, not hard evidence; your partner and the pack's next kill target are not among your options. Public vs private: Privately you know the wolf pair, the pack's intended kill, and sometimes who is immune or a real power role; publicly there are only unverified claims and no wolf is identified.
lessons.action: When you are an illusionist wolf with low heat and no wolf identified, cast your day vote with the room's existing plurality on a player who is not your partner or your pack's next kill target. If the room is split and you hold a private fact such as who must be the immune Serial Killer, vote on that player instead, so your vote stays unlinked from the pack's plan and still passes as an ordinary Town vote.

lessons.situation: First vote day after a night-1 death, with only unverified claims and no leads on any evil faction. Information landscape: Information-starved: self-reported results only, no confirmed roles, no voting history. Stakes: Early game with a wide margin before wolf parity. A wasted or mis-targeted vote gains little, while staying hidden preserves the pack's flexibility. Consensus: The table is quiet and leaning toward abstaining, with no accusations and no evidence-based lead. My position: With the majority, joining the abstain. Heat: Very low: nobody has accused you and you have only made generic comments. Forward exposure: A named vote would be permanent on the record and tie you to a mis-elimination with no evidence behind it. An abstain commits you to nothing and keeps all options open. Target landscape: No strong candidates. Claims are unverified, no roles are confirmed, and any target would be a behavioral guess. Public vs private: You privately know the wolf pack, your own kill and any conceal you used. Publicly the table has only unverified self-reports or a bare death announcement, with no accusations against wolves.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, when no one has accused anyone and no role is confirmed, abstain with the table rather than naming an evidence-free target. If the room is already abstaining, your abstain is invisible, commits you to no read, and keeps both wolves unremarked for another night.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote where your wolf partner casts an aggressive vote against a quiet player or splits the room, and you must decide between backing them and blending into the majority. Information landscape: Information-starved. The only evidence is unverified claims from investigative roles, with no confirmed flips. Stakes: Your partner's exposure can cascade onto you through the permanent vote record. The vote is not a swing because the village can abstain, so staying distant protects the pack's second wolf. Consensus: The room mostly abstains and has little hard information. A few claimants are pushing separate soft reads. My position: Tempted to join your partner's minority and hold out against the abstain majority. Heat: Low. A claimed sentinel or investigator result gave you temporary credibility, and your partner is the one attracting scrutiny. Forward exposure: Joining your partner's vote permanently pairs your public record with theirs. If they die and flip as a wolf, the town will review Day 2 votes and can pair the two minority votes, which makes the link undeniable. Target landscape: The options are to abstain with the majority, to join the partner's vote on a quiet player, or to vote for a player the town has accused. The partner-pushed target has no public evidence against them, only the partner's behavioral push. Public vs private: You know the co-voter is your wolf partner pushing a mislynch. The village only sees an unexplained minority push during a consensus abstain.
lessons.action: When your partner has already cast a rogue vote against a quiet player or toward a split, vote with the abstain majority, or with the broad majority on a target the town has independently pushed, rather than joining your partner's minority. Your votes should look independent of your partner's, so that if your partner dies and flips as a wolf, no paired wolf vote exists for the town to trace to you.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear consensus on which side is ahead or who should be eliminated. On day 2, nearly everyone abstained, with one vote against you.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive, and it is 4 eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, so this decision is consequential but not immediately decisive.
query_dims.heat_now: Low or unclear: one player voted to eliminate you on day 2, while the rest abstained; no current-day accusations have been made.
query_dims.information_landscape: Limited and partly unverified: one concealed death leaves that player's role unknown; a revealed Sentinel's night-one record is public fact; the Investigator and Trailseer claims and the Not suspicious result are unverified. The save confirms an attack on the claimant, not their role.
query_dims.my_position: No stated position on which side is ahead; your day-2 abstention matched the overwhelming vote outcome.
query_dims.situation: Before making your one-time side pick, you are weighing an information-starved board: the first-night victim's role is concealed, a player claiming Investigator reported a Not suspicious check, and the publicly confirmed Sentinel's record supports a claimed Trailseer's account of a visit route. The second-night report confirms a serial-killer attack was saved and a Sentinel was killed by the wolves, but does not establish which side is closest to winning.
query_dims.target_landscape: The private pick is among Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or self; the concealed first-night victim's side remains unknown, and no side has been eliminated or confirmed as ahead.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day where Town is sorting dueling claims or hunting the last threat, and the Speculator has already picked and is uncontested. Information landscape: Mixed: unverified watch and block claims, concealed-role bodies and a confirmed sigil strike give some structure, but no direct confirmations of the remaining suspects. Stakes: The pick is already locked in, so the Speculator's payoff depends on Town winning; steering the room to testable evidence without drawing heat keeps your vote and the pick alive. Consensus: Village converging on a shared target using testable claims and confirmed results. My position: With the majority, contributing without revealing yourself as the picker. Heat: Low: nobody has accused you and the pick was announced with no name attached. Target landscape: Accused players and claimants with dueling unverified results; sigil strikes, concealed bodies and role claims give structure to test; behavior-based reads for the last threat.
lessons.action: When your pick is already made and you are not under suspicion, join the discussion with a clarifying question or a mechanics-based observation that supports the testable claims, and let the room converge. If the room has no clear lead, ask a claimant to clarify intended targets or results rather than picking a side early.

lessons.situation: Late game with both wolves gone and the speculator's Town pick public; the lone killer is hiding among a few survivors and deflecting suspicion onto the speculator, so the Town win depends on the claimed role-holders voting out the right player. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: revealed dead roles, announced saves and attacks, and a public pick, but the surviving players' roles are only claimed and one check is known not to rule out a serial killer. Stakes: With few players left, one mistaken elimination or a tie-break can hand the lone killer the game, so the speculator's Town pick lives or dies on convincing the swing voters. Consensus: The room is split or forming against the agent, with claimed role-holders unsure whom to trust and no firm consensus on the lone killer. My position: Driving the case against the lone-killer suspect rather than holding out. Heat: Moderate to substantial: the agent is accused for having no claimed night role, and suspects urge the room to scrutinize the agent's past statements. Target landscape: The unclaimed or unconfirmed player who deflects behind a dead player's result or an incomplete check, plus claimed healer, sentinel or investigator whose votes decide the outcome; the case rests on mechanics and records, not only on behavior.
lessons.action: When the pick is Town, the wolves are dead or nearly dead and the lone killer remains, openly own the public Town pick and name the unconfirmed or unclaimed player as the main lone-killer suspect. Support the case with checkable facts, such as an attack through a dead body leaving no visit from the attacker, and push the claimed role-holders (sentinel, investigator, healer) to put their votes on that player; do not rely on asking the suspect to evaluate others.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day with a narrowed suspect pool: you claim Speculator, a wolf (Chanteuse) counter-claims the same unique role, and the contested claim decides the remaining wolf search. Information landscape: Sparse: the Speculator pick is public but its author is hidden; neither claimant can prove anything; only claim order, sigil/vigilante results and elimination logic exist. Stakes: A few players remain and one wrong vote could hand the wolves parity, so winning the contested claim directly decides whether the picked side wins. Consensus: Village is wolf-hunting the last suspects; it leans on claim order and elimination logic since nothing is verifiable. My position: Driving the discussion on claim timing and aligned with a forming majority of role-claiming Town players. Heat: Moderate to high: your claim put you in the suspect pool and a counter-claimant is accusing you of being the wolf behind an alibi role. Target landscape: Two unverifiable Speculator claimants in a small suspect pool; other pool members already cleared by sigil or vigilante accounts; the decision rests on claim timing and logic, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: After your pick is announced and a suspect pool forms, state your Speculator claim yourself, early and plainly, and note that picking is not a visit so you have no night action to account for. If someone counter-claims Speculator, hold the identical claim, point out that your claim came first and theirs came only after the pool narrowed, and ask Town to vote the counter-claimant instead of overcomplicating it.

lessons.situation: After a wolf's death, the surviving evil player praises a claimed investigator for voting the dead wolf, and the room debates whether that vote proves town alignment. The speculator challenges the logic and points scrutiny at the praiser. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: one confirmed dead wolf, an investigator claim with a cleared read, and Day 2 voting records tying the surviving suspect to the dead wolf. Stakes: With few players left, a single vote can remove the last wolf or waste the elimination. Raising the distancing point can tip the consensus against the right target before the vote. Consensus: The village is leaning toward the suspected wolf on voting-record links and discussing whether an early vote counts as proof of alignment. My position: With the majority, voicing a skeptical point that supports the forming read. Heat: Low; the speculator abstained earlier and is not under suspicion, though challenging a wolf may draw a defensive counter-vote. Target landscape: A surviving suspected wolf trying to pocket a claimed investigator, the claimed investigator with a cleared read, and a quiet villager under pressure. The suspicion rests on vote links to the dead wolf, not on hard proof.
lessons.action: When a suspected wolf vouches for a claimed role or praises a vote against an already-dead wolf, say aloud that voting a dead packmate can be distancing rather than proof of town alignment. Ask the room to weigh that player's own record, and expect to take some defensive heat for it.

lessons.situation: Final three or four players. Both wolves, or one wolf and the lone killer, are already dead, and one evil player remains unidentified. The speculator, holding a Town pick, has to steer the surviving cleared players onto that last player instead of itself. Information landscape: Rich by elimination. There are revealed roles for the dead, claims that clear the others, and a track or vote history on the unknown player. Stakes: With so few players left, one wrong vote lets evil reach parity or win. A correct vote ends the game as a Town win and secures the Town pick. Consensus: Cleared town players are largely aligned on narrowing to the remaining unknown. The basis is shared claims and elimination. My position: Driving the discussion together with the cleared town claimants. Heat: Low to moderate. Some deflection is aimed at the speculator, but claims of visits or wills already cover it. Target landscape: Two or three living players: those cleared by role claims, wills, or tracker reports, versus one unverified or quiet player with no claim and no night targets. The basis is elimination plus behavior and vote history, not hard proof.
lessons.action: In a late-game endgame (3-4 alive) where claims and reveals have cleared most players, argue by elimination: name the one unaccounted-for, unclaimed or quiet player as the remaining evil, and cite the specific claims or records that clear everyone else. Put that player on the spot by asking what they did last night and whom they targeted; if they answer vaguely or deflect, press that point and push the room to vote them.

lessons.situation: Day 3, mid-game. Claimed power roles have corroborated one another and are pushing a lynch on one accused player. The accused may be a lone killer, and the speculator has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Moderately rich but all claims: a claimed watch or check result, healer confirmation, announced death outcomes and a revealed dead wolf, or an unverified Investigator read. The claims interlock but cannot be verified directly. Stakes: With several killers still alive, a correct lynch on Day 3 removes one of the two evil factions Town must clear. A wrong lynch brings evil closer to parity, so a well-reasoned push matters. Consensus: The room is converging on one accused player, mainly on interlocking claimed night results and mechanical reasoning, not on behavior alone. My position: With the majority, adding mechanical or procedural support to the forming consensus instead of staking out a lone read. Heat: Low: you are unaccused and a mostly silent, unexposed player. Any rebuttal from the accused is brief. Target landscape: One accused player under evidence-based pressure from claimed Town roles (Investigator, Sentinel, Healer) whose claims interlock but are unverified. The accused calls it coordinated wolf theater or fabrication. No other candidate has drawn serious attention.
lessons.action: While you still hold your pick on Day 3, add a rules-based argument or a verification test that supports the accusation the room is already converging on, such as pointing out that a missing save announcement fits a night-immune target or proposing that a Sentinel or Trailseer confirm the claim. Keep your own role and intended pick hidden. This helps remove a killer without exposing you, and it lets you pick the side you expect to win later with more information.

lessons.situation: A night result (such as a healer save on a claimed role) triggers two competing claims on one unique role. The village debates which claimant is real, and the speculator has not yet picked a side. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced save or death, wills or night-action claims that can be cross-checked, and mutually exclusive role claims. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. Removing a false claimant (likely a wolf or the necromancer) is valuable, but one vote does not yet decide the game, and the speculator's pick is still pending. Consensus: The room is engaged and roughly aligned on resolving the counterclaim by checking it against the morning report. No fixed vote target has formed yet. My position: with majority Heat: None to low; the speculator is unpressured, often already cleared by a claimed investigator, and attention is on the claimants. Target landscape: Two players in a direct counterclaim over a single-slot role (investigator or healer), with a confirmed public save or death report as the only hard anchor. The claims can be tested against that announcement; the rest is behavioral.
lessons.action: When two players counter-claim the same role and a public morning report (a save or a death) is available, test each claim against that report using only the game rules. Point out which claimant's stated night action explains the announced outcome and which leaves it unexplained, and stay uncommitted on anyone's true role beyond that. This steers the room toward the contradiction, keeps you low-profile with your pick still unspent, and lets the pick wait for the room's outcome.

lessons.situation: After a night death reveals a dead wolf or other evil role, a player misstates the vote record or an evil player tries to use a past vote to vouch for itself. The speculator, who has not yet picked a side, can correct the record and steer the room. Information landscape: Information-rich: public vote tallies, revealed dead roles, a dead wolf's attack trace and an investigator claim with a cleared read. No fresh hard leads on the remaining suspects. Stakes: Mid-game with a few evil players left. A misdirected day vote would waste an elimination and push the board toward evil parity, while an accurate vote can remove a killer or wolf and fix the winning side for the speculator's pick. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned and working from the vote record and a cleared investigator read. It is vulnerable to a misremembered or spun record. My position: With the majority, contributing record-keeping rather than driving an accusation. Heat: Low; the speculator is seen as an attentive, neutral contributor and has not been accused. Its pick is not yet attributed to anyone. Target landscape: A claimed investigator-cleared player, an unverified player with a lone or odd vote, a quiet player, and a surviving wolf or killer. Public roles are partly confirmed by deaths and one check; reads rest on vote records.
lessons.action: When the room misstates the public voting record or leans on a vote as proof of alignment, calmly restate the actual vote history from the record without being combative. Then point the room at the unresolved candidates the record supports, so consensus stays anchored to verified facts rather than a distorted narrative.

lessons.situation: A day-2 or day-3 pile-on forms against a claimant who got a rule or result wrong, while the Speculator is unsuspected and holds a pick (made or pending). Information landscape: Mixed but leaning on claims: a few rules-checkable inconsistencies and cross-supporting unverified claims, with no confirmed roles from the Game Master. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. One vote can remove a threat, but it does not yet decide the game. The Speculator's win depends on the pick's side winning, so helping eliminate a likely evil player and staying alive both matter. Consensus: The village is converging on one target, driven by a caught rules mistake and cross-supporting claims, though no role is officially confirmed. My position: With the majority, adding a distinct supporting argument without leading the push. Heat: Very low to low: not named, not accused, and not drawing scrutiny before or after speaking. Target landscape: One accused player whose claim contains a rules-checkable error (a misdescribed role ability or a watch result that cannot fit the rules), possibly with a counter-claimant. Secondary claimants are unverified. The basis is claim contradictions, not behavior alone.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on a player whose claim has a concrete, rules-checkable contradiction and nobody has pointed at you, join once with one distinct, specific reason tied to that contradiction. Stay with the majority rather than leading, and keep your role and pick to yourself unless the pick is already made and there is no cost to staying quiet.

lessons.situation: Early day discussion (day 1 or 2) with the speculator's pick unspent. The village is trading unverified claims and night results, and the speculator is neutral and has not committed to a side. Information landscape: Information-starved: a few unverified claims, at most one or two revealed bodies, and no vote history or confirmed evil. Stakes: Early game with several eliminations still needed before any evil side can win. The speculator's only loss condition is dying unpicked, so avoiding heat now matters more than pushing a read. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned and still trading claims. Votes are abstain-heavy or tied, and no side is clearly ahead. My position: Holding out or going with the majority, with no stated read and no pick made yet. Heat: Zero to low: nobody has accused or mentioned the speculator, or only a harmless night report about it has come up. Target landscape: No confirmed suspects; the living players are unclaimed or only claim-based, with a few night-result claims (trailseer, sentinel, investigator) and perhaps one or two revealed bodies. Reads rest on claims and behavior, not verified evidence.
lessons.action: While your pick is still unspent and the room has no hard leads, speak only when you are addressed or can restate another player's report accurately, and keep any analysis on the board in general rather than on a named target.
