Don't announce your role or your leaning. If someone reports a night result about you, confirm it plainly and add nothing contentious, so you stay low-heat while you gather information for the pick.

query_dims.consensus_text: The village has no settled consensus; the last vote eliminated a claimed healer and the remaining players are split on who is lying.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four alive with the game able to end on the next elimination: at worst for the town, a single kill or vote could end the game, so each night decision carries a direct chance of ending the game.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible accusation or vote you make commits you to a public stance that is hard to retract; staying silent keeps your heat low but leaves the village's accusation pattern to form without you.
query_dims.heat_now: Low on you personally: no one has named you, and the accusations on day 3 were directed at the dead trailseer and the voted-out healer.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only public records are the dead players' past night results and the day discussion; no living player has verifiable night information.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from any forming consensus, with no committed accusation.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the serial killer, you privately know you killed the fortune teller, sentinel and trailseer, while the village only knows a claimed trailseer was stabbed and a claimed vigilante (player_8) is alive; the public read is that the remaining players are still searching for the killer.
query_dims.situation: Four players remain after a day-3 lynch and a night-3 kill; the village has lost its healer, trailseer and sentinel and is now debating a claimed vigilante's accusations with no living information role confirmed. You, the lone killer, face the choice of which accuser to target next while keeping your public read clean.
query_dims.target_landscape: Four living players: the claimed vigilante who has been accusing others, one quiet player, and two others with no public role claims; the only public role evidence is the accusation record and the trailseer's claimed chain, which you know is accurate about its night 1 and 2 visits.

lessons.situation: Late game (day 4-5) with the wolves already eliminated and 3-4 players alive. The town's surviving claims corroborate each other and the village is pointing at you as the only unexplained player. Information landscape: Information-rich for the town: revealed roles, cross-supporting claims and public vote records leave only one open slot. The serial killer has no evidence to offer in its own defense. Stakes: Every vote is decisive: being eliminated ends your win outright. With 4 alive you need two more deaths to win, so surviving the day by splitting or stalling the vote matters more than clearing your name. Consensus: The village is converging on one answer by elimination, since roles are revealed and the surviving claims support each other. The only unresolved name is yours. My position: Holding out alone against a forming majority, with at most one other player as a secondary target. Heat: High and rising: you are named or implied as the last unaccounted-for player, with no claim or counter-argument to deflect it. Forward exposure: Accusing the other unexplained player is a visible, committed vote target, but it needs no role claim and can be redirected as new reads arrive. Staying vague or silent commits you to nothing and gives the room nothing to doubt, so the elimination logic stands unopposed. Target landscape: The 2-3 other survivors, most with partial credentials: a trailseer or healer claim that cross-supports the other, a speculator cleared only by someone's follow report, or an unclaimed player. The basis is claims and elimination, not verified evidence, and you are the only one with no backing. Public vs private: Privately you are the Serial Killer and know you are not a wolf. Publicly you are simply the player the others have not yet explained, and the town reasons by elimination from the revealed roles and mutually supporting claims.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone and you are one of the last 3-4 players, don't answer the room's elimination logic with a vague echo or an ambiguity argument. Name the one other unexplained player and build a concrete case on the gap in their story: their cleared status rests on a single unverifiable claim, or two claims vouch only for each other, and nothing is verified unless the Game Master announced it. Then push for a split vote on that player, since with 4 alive a 2-2 split means no elimination.

lessons.situation: Late in day 3 discussion, the sentinel, healer and investigator claims all point at me as the night-immune Serial Killer. My attempts to call those claims fabricated have been rebutted one after another. Information landscape: Information-rich and one-sided: a confirmed wolf death, a watch result matched by the healer, no save announced, an investigator clear, and no live evidence supporting my denials. Stakes: If the vote lands on me, my solo win condition ends and only the town and the wolves are left to contest the game. This discussion is probably my last chance to move even one vote, and a failed denial adds no information and only tightens the case. Consensus: Near-unanimous and evidence-based: claims cross-confirm, a wolf is confirmed dead, and my survival without a save announcement is read as night immunity. Alternative theories offered so far were rebutted on the spot. My position: Holding out alone against everyone. Heat: Maximal. Seven or eight of the nine living players have named me, the vote is imminent, and the case is built on interlocking claims and mechanical deduction rather than mood. Forward exposure: Each further denial of a true result, or a theory of coordinated fabrication, commits me to a story the record can test and cannot be retracted. A single redirect toward a living suspect costs little and can be dropped, but only if it fits the confirmed facts. Target landscape: The accusers' claims (investigator, sentinel, healer) interlock and each confirms the others. Their case rests on mechanics, such as surviving an attack with no save announced, plus vote records. Any other living player I could point at has little evidence against them, so a redirect has to rest on their votes or claim consistency. Public vs private: Privately I know the watch, the protect and the clear describe me accurately. Publicly the room has already deduced I am the Serial Killer, and my own denials only added contradictions.
lessons.action: When interlocking claims make your night immunity deducible and the room is converging on you, stop contesting each claim one by one. Spend your remaining speech on a single narrow case that doesn't contradict anything already confirmed, steering suspicion toward a living player whose claim or votes are weakest, and ask the village to weigh the wolves still alive before using the vote on you. If no living candidate has a checkable weakness, make no further claims that the record can contradict.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, after wolf-side deaths and reveals, the town debates claims such as a suspicious check, sentinel or trailseer results, or a neutral's pick. Attention is on wolves and on each other, with nothing pointing at the serial killer. Information landscape: Moderate and information-rich about wolves: revealed roles, claimed check or watch results, announcements, and vote records. Nothing in it points to a lone killer. Stakes: Several eliminations remain before the serial killer can win, so the move is about staying unsuspected while the village thins out the wolves. A needless endorsement or accusation now costs more than staying quiet. Consensus: The village is fairly aligned on hunting wolves, based on a revealed wolf death, role claims, and vote records. No one is considering a third evil faction. My position: With the majority, echoing rather than driving. Heat: Low to none. You have spoken little, sided with the room, and no one has named you or raised the possibility of a lone killer. Forward exposure: Echoing the room's wolf-focused line costs nothing and can be reversed. Endorsing a role claim or naming a new threat commits you to a read that is hard to walk back and may expose a lone-killer hypothesis. You have not yet been asked for your role. Target landscape: The live candidates are wolf-side or suspect players already under discussion: a self-explained non-visiting neutral, a questioning wolf, and claimed investigative roles. The evidence against them is mostly claims and vote records, not hard proof, and you are not among them. Public vs private: Privately you know you are a lone killer that no one suspects, and the wolves are your rivals. Publicly the village believes the only remaining threats are wolves, so you sit inside the town-looking majority.
lessons.action: When the room is busy hunting wolves and no one suspects a lone killer, speak briefly in line with the majority and add sincere, behavior- or vote-record-based observations that keep the wolf-vs-town fight going. Avoid vouching for any role claim as true beyond saying it is mechanically consistent, so you do not help a confirmed town bloc form that later closes in on you. If someone asks for your role or reads, answer vaguely, in line with the room, instead of volunteering a new threat theory.

lessons.situation: Early day after night-one deaths, with the village lacking leads. A player is evasive about their role or night action, or a vocal player prompts others for results, so the room is forming around whoever looks least forthcoming. Information landscape: Information-starved: only night deaths and perhaps a dead town player's will are known, with no confirmed investigative checks or tracked visit chains presented yet. Stakes: The board is early and far from parity, so no single vote or kill decides the game. Staying low-heat preserves the serial killer's nightly kills while the town spends its day votes on its own members. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on getting claims and results out, and on pressuring whoever withholds information; there is no hard evidence behind any lead. My position: with_majority Heat: None; no accusations, investigative reports, or visit records point at the serial killer. Forward exposure: Echoing standard town scumhunting demands commits the serial killer only to an orthodox, low-profile stance, with no fake claim and no counter-claim risk. It is fully reversible and can be dropped if the room's focus turns toward the serial killer. Target landscape: Evasive or silent players who refuse to claim a role or night result, a vocal player pressing for claims with no information, and not-yet-heard investigative roles such as the trailseer or vigilante. The basis is behavior only, since no verified investigative evidence exists. Public vs private: Privately knows which night deaths were its own kills and that it is not a suspect; publicly it appears as an ordinary townsperson trying to sort role claims, while the village does not know a serial killer is operating.
lessons.action: When early deaths leave the room hunting for leads and no heat is on you, speak as an ordinary town member and echo the room's demand that evasive or vague players state their role and night action. If a vocal player pushes for claims without offering information, ask them to say whether they hold any, so the room's scrutiny lands on claimants and evasive players instead of on you.

lessons.situation: Day 3-5 with 3-4 players alive. You are asked to account for your role, and the town can test any claim against announced deaths, revealed roles, and the other claimants' statements. Information landscape: Fairly rich: many roles are revealed or dead, and the announced night reports constrain which role stories are credible. There is little room to bluff. Stakes: At 3 alive one more death gets you to the win condition, and one vote against you ends your game. A claim that fails the record check loses immediately. Consensus: The room has framed the vote as a choice between two or three players and is checking each claim against what has been announced. My position: Holding out against the forming consensus and under direct pressure to account for your role. Heat: High: you are named as one of the last suspects, and a late claim will draw an immediate challenge. Forward exposure: A role claim is checkable against announced events and other claims and is nearly impossible to retract. A role-less or already-disproved claim leaves you with no fallback story once challenged. Target landscape: The other survivors and their claims, with revealed roles (dead town and wolves) known to everyone. The open question is which unrevealed or unclaimed role you could plausibly hold. The basis is mostly timing and announced facts, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the Serial Killer with no town ability to report. Publicly any claim is judged against the announced deaths, revealed roles and other players' claims, and a role already dead or already claimed by someone else will not hold.
lessons.action: If you must give a role story to escape elimination by exclusion, first check the public record and claim only a role that is not already revealed as dead and not already claimed by a living player. Also pick a role whose claimed results cannot be contradicted by announced night reports or by another player's confirmed account. Skip claiming no ability at all, which fits only a villager or the killer, and skip a role the record already disproves.

lessons.situation: On Day 2, after a night kill, a sentinel or trailseer publicly says they saw me visit the dead player. The vote is coming, and there is a second candidate with visit evidence against them. Information landscape: Information-rich: night victims' roles are announced, and one or two claimed visit reports connect specific players to those victims. All of it is claims, none verified by the Game Master. Stakes: A vote-out ends my game at once, as the lone killer is removed only by a day vote. The board is still wide enough that surviving a few more days is worth far more than winning this argument. Consensus: The room is converging on me because the visit report is concrete and no one has offered a competing explanation. Players are amplifying the contradiction. My position: holding out against a forming consensus Heat: Very high. A claimed hard mechanical report names me at the victim's door, and I am the likely vote target. Forward exposure: Pointing at a competing lead commits me to a specific accusation, but I can drop it and shift to another suspect if the room rejects it. It does not tie me to any role claim, so I keep my options open. Target landscape: Two or more players are tied to night victims by claimed visit reports. I am the clearest one, and the others have only a single sighting or trace each. All of it rests on claimed night results, not on verified roles. Public vs private: Privately I carried out the kill and made the visit; publicly a single report places me at the victim's door while at least one other player has comparable visit evidence against them.
lessons.action: When a sentinel or trailseer report puts you at a victim's door on Day 2, reframe a visit as not proof of the kill, since several roles visit. Then redirect the room's attention to any other player with comparable visit evidence, such as someone seen at a different victim, and push a vote on that player. Aim to split the vote or reach a tie so you survive the day, and keep your account to a few simple points that cannot be checked against another living player.

lessons.situation: On the day after a night result, a claimed Vigilante or Sentinel reveals a mechanical result (my immunity to their shot, or my visit to a freshly killed player). I am the lone or leading suspect and a daytime vote is coming. Information landscape: Information-rich. There are claimed role results, announced deaths and public vote records that tie me to the night's events, and little ambiguity is left for behavioral reads to resolve. Stakes: A daytime vote is the only way the Serial Killer can be removed. With few players left, one lost vote ends my solo win path, so this discussion decides the game. Consensus: The village is converging against me on a mechanical report, and the town roles and any wolf are happy to remove the lone killer. Nobody is defending me. My position: Holding out alone as the main accused, opposed by nearly the whole room. Heat: Maximum. I am named directly through a night result, accusers are pressing me to justify my visit or survival, and the room has no other suspect with comparable evidence. Forward exposure: A bare denial or an admission of 'no reason' cannot be walked back and leaves a single unanswered mechanical fact, so the vote is effectively decided. A fake role claim commits me to a story the room can test, but it gives the town an alternative reading to weigh and can be dropped later. Target landscape: The main candidates are me and any other player placed at the same scene, or the claimed power role whose report I would have to discredit. The case against me rests on a hard night result, while the case for the alternative is only behavioral. The room will pick the one with the mechanical link unless I give them a competing explanation. Public vs private: Privately I know the accuser's mechanical result is true (I made the visit or I was shot at and survived because of night immunity). Publicly the room treats it as a verified result and is waiting for any explanation from me.
lessons.action: When a claimed Sentinel or Vigilante puts hard evidence on you (you were seen at a victim's door, or you survived a shot), give a concrete, believable benign account instead of calling it fabricated or conceding you have no reason. For example, claim a visiting Town role such as Healer, Trailseer or Investigator, say whom you went to and why, and point at the other visitor or accuser as the likelier killer. If another player has already claimed that role, pick a different role claim or stay vague about your own night and attack the other visitor's lack of an explanation.

lessons.situation: A three-way dispute covers your account, a rival visitor's contradicted sigil story, and the reliability of the Sentinel's list. You can use another player's counterclaim to push the vote onto the rival. Information landscape: Several conflicting private claims, none confirmed, with a partly corrected visitor list. A counterclaim against the rival is the clearest piece of evidence. Stakes: One vote swings the day. Moving it onto the rival keeps you alive for the next night's kill, though it won't protect you if a later shot or result exposes you. Consensus: Divided between suspecting you, the rival, and the Sentinel's list. Another player's counterclaim against the rival is pulling attention off you. My position: Holding out and steering attention toward the competing suspect. Heat: High but shared with the rival visitor, since another player is also disputing their story. Forward exposure: Pointing at a contradiction that already exists is low-commitment and reversible, because you rely on someone else's statement and not your own claim. It does fix your vote on that rival, so keep your own account minimal. Target landscape: The rival visitor who claimed a sigil placement is the best alternative target. The basis is a direct contradiction from a claimed Sigilist, which is behavioral and claim-based, not confirmed. Public vs private: You know you are the killer. Publicly, the rival visitor's story has been contradicted by a claimed role-holder, which gives you a real discrepancy to point at.
lessons.action: Spend your speech on the other named visitor's checkable inconsistency, such as a sigil story the real Sigilist contradicts, and name it as the stronger lead. Then ask who can confirm their account. This moves the vote to a rival whose story has already been disputed by another player.

lessons.situation: I am under heavy pressure as a visitor or caught liar, and I try to redirect the room to a rival claim conflict, such as two Healer claimants, to avoid a sure elimination. Information landscape: Rich: a caught mechanics error, a counter-claimed role, and a visitor list leave one proven liar in the room, me, while the claim conflict is unproven. Stakes: A unanimous vote on me ends my run, so any redirect has to land before the room fixes on the proven liar. Raising it after the lie is caught did not move anyone. Consensus: Near-unanimous on removing the proven liar, with the claim conflict seen as secondary. My position: Holding out alone against a lopsided consensus. Heat: Very high where a caught false claim is already on record, with many accusers. Moderate if I am only a named visitor. Forward exposure: Pushing a 1v1 between two claimants reads as siding against whoever the town trusts less. If I am already the proven liar, it looks like a diversion, and the town can turn it around because removing a proven liar is a safe vote. Target landscape: Two rival Healer claimants (one real, one a wolf) are unresolved and rest only on claims. I am a visitor with a caught lie, which is concrete evidence. The town prefers the concrete target. Public vs private: Privately I know I attacked the victim. Publicly the visitor list and any caught error point at me, while the claim conflict elsewhere is a real, checkable contradiction.
lessons.action: If you are named in a visitor list but not yet caught in a lie, put forward the real unresolved conflict, such as two Healer claimants where one must be a wolf. Do it before you commit to any false claim, and tie it to the visitor pool: a watch shows who came, not why. Treat it as a way to widen the suspect pool, and keep it going only if others pick it up.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the next vote or kill cannot end the game, so a mistaken lynch is recoverable but each lost town member narrows the margin, and the unresolved abstain pattern means no information is being produced yet.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no public claims, no announced checks or watches, no verified night results; only the public death roles and the abstain tally exist.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 opened with no role claims after two night kills and an unanimous abstain vote; players are pressing each other to state night results, and the Trailseer holds a private follow of one living player whose visit could be cross-checked against tomorrow's morning report.
query_dims.target_landscape: Seven-to-eight living players with no public role claims; the only confirmed facts are the two night deaths (a fortune teller and an investigator, roles revealed) and an abstain-everywhere day 2 vote. No candidate has a public role status or verified evidence; every suspect is judged on behavior in discussion alone.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a night-1 death and an all-abstain day-2 vote. Nobody has claimed a night result, and the Trailseer must choose whom to follow with only discussion tone to go on. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death, a unanimous abstain, a few cautious statements, no night claims and no cross-checkable roles. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive and no eliminations yet from votes. One follow can give the town its first concrete lead, but a misread visit could point at an innocent, so the result needs corroboration. Target landscape: Living players with the most public presence in the day-2 discussion, none with a confirmed role or hard evidence against them. Picks rest on behavior (who urged caution or steered the room), not on evidence. A follow only shows where the target went, not why.
lessons.action: On a night 2 with no claims, no hard leads and an all-abstain day, follow a vocal, influential player whose day talk steered the room, rather than a quiet player or a past victim. If the follow shows a visit, treat it as one data point that names a possible partner or victim, not as proof, and weigh the visited player's own record before acting on it.

lessons.situation: After a tied or no-result day 2, you are a claimed Trailseer with an unverified or contested result. Your night 1 or 2 follow was blocked, or your target is publicly known, and a Chanteuse may be blocking you on a predictable pattern. Information landscape: Information-starved: your own private follow result, a few unverified claims, and a split vote record. No confirmed wolf identity. Stakes: Each night of lost trail information costs the town its only movement data while the wolves keep carrying kills. A wasted follow, or your death, removes your role from the board. Target landscape: Several living players: the previously followed or publicly accused suspect, plus quiet unclaimed players, a claimed Investigator or Sigilist, and neutrals. All have little or no trail data, and the suspect was chosen on behavior rather than evidence.
lessons.action: If you were roleblocked last night, or you have publicly named your intended follow target, pick a different living player to follow tonight, ideally one you have not mentioned. A repeat on a publicly known target is easy for the Chanteuse to predict, and in this cluster those repeats were blocked and yielded no result.

lessons.situation: Early game after a no-elimination or low-information Day 2, with several investigative claims out. The Trailseer must pick whom to follow on a night when wolves are likely to kill an exposed claimant. Information landscape: Mostly information-starved. There are claims and behavioral reads such as one lone vote or one silent player, but no hard evidence tying anyone to wolves or the lone killer. Stakes: Mid-game with several wolves and a lone killer still alive. Wasting a follow on an already-plausible Town claimant costs a night of tracking, while a follow that catches a killer's visit can turn the next vote. Target landscape: Unvetted suspects (a silent player with a lone vote, an aggressive voter against you) versus claimed investigative roles (Investigator, Sentinel) whose claims are unverified; choice rests on behavior, with no confirmed evil flips.
lessons.action: On Night 2, follow the quiet or hostile player who has drawn a lone vote or suspicion but has not been checked, rather than a claimed Town investigative role. If they visit a player who then dies or is attacked, that is a direct lead for the next vote; if they visit no one, they stay unresolved and you pick a different unchecked suspect the next night.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after a Day 3 vote removed a wolf or the necromancer. Another evil player is still hidden, and the trailseer must pick one follow target with no direct lead. Information landscape: Moderate and patchy. A few roles are revealed by deaths, but nothing hard points at the remaining wolf or killer. The trailseer's own follow result is the only direct evidence about who moves at night. Stakes: The board is mid-to-late game with few players alive, so each night kill and each vote matters a lot. A follow that yields only a no-visit result wastes one of the few remaining information nights. Target landscape: Four to six living candidates after a wolf or lone killer was voted out: claimed sigilist, investigator, vigilante or sentinel, plus quiet unclaimed players. No role is confirmed beyond unverified claims, and suspicion rests on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On the night after a key elimination, follow a player who claims an acting night role (sigilist, investigator, vigilante, sentinel) or has a concrete public case against them, not a silent bystander. A named visit can be cross-checked against that night's deaths, saves and claims, and a claimed role that visits no one is checkable too. A 'visited no one' result only means no visit was seen: the follow shows only where they went, and a concealed pack kill leaves no trace on the carrier.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2-3) after one or two wolf-side deaths or a necromancer sighting, with a visit-count or claim conflict among town power roles and no hard visit data except what the Trailseer can generate. Information landscape: Rich in public facts (role reveals, vote records, a confirmed check) but poor on who the remaining killers are; a trail is one of the few independent hard visit signals, though it shows only the target's outbound visits. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one accurate visit datum can steer the next day's vote, but a trail used to push out a genuine town role costs real information, so the follow should test the claim rather than prove guilt. Target landscape: Claimed town power roles (Sentinel, Healer, Investigator) with unverifiable night claims, plus quiet players; the claimed Sentinel's trail is cheap to check against their own watch report, while the others rest on behavior and counterclaims.
lessons.action: Follow the claimed power role whose night action is publicly disputed or unverified (e.g. a claimed Sentinel or Healer in a count conflict), and record exactly whom they went to or that they went to no one. Report it as a one-way fact ("they went to X"), and if the trail contradicts their own result list, treat that as a hard inconsistency, but if it fits their claim, say it fits without calling it proof.

lessons.situation: One or two nights in, a killer's victim has been found. Town's checks and watches are unverified. A Sentinel may be watching the same door, and you must decide whose outgoing movements to trail. Information landscape: Some evidence exists: a revealed night-1 victim, public vote and claim history, and visible activity from one claimed role. No hard confirmation of any killer's identity. Stakes: Town still has room to find the killers, but each night without usable, corroborated information lets the wolves and the lone killer close in. A result that another role's report can corroborate is worth more than a lone claim. Target landscape: A self-claimed, visibly active Town role (such as a Sigilist) who is a likely kill target, versus unclaimed or unverified players and a publicly accused suspect. The choice rests on predicting which player the killers will go after, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Follow an exposed, likely-to-be-attacked player, such as a claimed Sigilist or Investigator who is active and already drawing attention, instead of the loudest suspect. You learn whom that player visited, and your own visit to their door can be recorded by a Sentinel watching them. That gives the town an independent cross-check on your claim.

lessons.situation: Midgame night with the wolf pack mostly or fully eliminated and a lone killer (necromancer or serial killer) still hidden among the unconfirmed players. The Trailseer chooses whom to follow. Information landscape: Information-rich about dead wolves and validated Town roles, but information-starved about the identity of the remaining lone killer. Only behavioral reads exist for unconfirmed players. Stakes: The lone killer is still active and each night costs a life. A wasted follow on a cleared role leaves Town with no evidence for the next vote, so every follow must test an unconfirmed player. Target landscape: Unconfirmed, non-claiming players (quiet healer-type, abstaining neutral-type, unclaimed villagers) versus already-validated Town roles (confirmed investigator, sentinel, vigilante). Evidence for the unconfirmed is behavioral only; the validated roles are already cleared by cross-checks.
lessons.action: When the wolves are largely dead and a lone killer (likely the necromancer) is still unidentified, follow an unconfirmed, non-claiming player whose behavior is quiet or unexplained, not a role already validated as Town. A follow shows only whom they visited, so a visit onto a night-death victim or a dead body's door points at the hidden killer, while a protective or empty visit narrows the pool by elimination.

lessons.situation: The lone killer's kills come through a dead role's ability. The trailseer followed a quiet, unclaimed player and saw no visits, then treated the empty result as clearing them. Information landscape: Information-rich on role deaths, but the killer is unidentified, and an empty follow result is weak evidence because the killer's attack may be made through a body rather than its own visit. Stakes: With the wolves gone, the town can afford very few more mistakes. Treating one 'visited no one' as a clearance can steer the vote away from the killer and expose the trailseer's own standing, so the follow should narrow the field without being counted as proof of innocence. Target landscape: Both wolves dead; living players are a claimed sentinel, an unconfirmed healer, a neutral speculator, and a quiet unclaimed player. None is proven, and the choice rests on behavior and elimination of roles.
lessons.action: When the lone killer may be attacking through a dead player's body, as in a 'reanimated' morning report, follow the most suspicious survivor but record a 'visited no one' result as inconclusive. Keep the suspect on the list and choose the next night's follow from the remaining candidates, since a Necromancer's attack through a body would not appear as its own visit.

lessons.situation: Night 1 with all ten alive, no day-1 vote, no claims and no deaths. The trailseer must choose its first follow blind. Possible outcomes are a visit to the wolves' victim, a visit to some other player, no visit, a roleblock, or being killed before getting a result. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no night results, no voting record. The follow itself is the only evidence source, and one night's movement of one player shows where they went, not their role. Stakes: Early game with a full board and no pressure to act. One follow cannot flip the game, but a visit to the night's victim can give the town an early concrete lead on a wolf. Because every pick is a blind guess, the value is in collecting a trail, not in being right about a role. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, deaths or behavioral tells. The pick is effectively arbitrary, so choose a quiet player who has not drawn attention and who is not you.
lessons.action: On night 1 with no claims or deaths, follow one quiet, unclaimed player and treat the follow as a probe. If they visited someone who is then attacked or killed that night, that player is a strong carrier lead. If they visited no one, treat it as weak, non-clearing information, since a follow shows only where a player went and a concealed kill can leave no trace.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with the wolves gone or nearly gone and a lone killer (Serial Killer) still hidden. The Trailseer must pick whom to follow among the remaining unexplained suspects to either implicate or clear them. Information landscape: Information-rich on identities, since most roles are revealed or deduced, but the last killer's identity is unresolved. A follow gives a hard visit trace (whom the target visited, or that they visited no one) that can settle the last unknown. Stakes: With few players left and a killer striking every night, one more night kill brings the killer or wolves close to winning. A correct follow can identify the killer for the next vote, so the pick of target is decisive for the Town win. Target landscape: Few unexplained survivors (2-3) remain after wolves and most roles are revealed or cleared. They are not role-confirmed, and the choice rests on behavior such as being quiet, deflecting, or being night-immune, plus elimination logic. One of them is the hidden lone killer.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone or identified and one lone killer is still unrevealed, follow the unexplained survivor you most suspect of being the killer, choosing between the few remaining candidates. If they visited you on a night you were attacked, or visited another victim, that is direct contact evidence to bring forward. If they visited no one, that argues against them being the Serial Killer, so move your next follow to the other unexplained candidate.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a Town-side loss or a wolf exposure, the Trailseer chooses whom to follow. The wolves are likely to kill the key information role, and the actives hide among the vocal players. Information landscape: Only revealed deaths, claims and votes are confirmed. No trail or watch reports have been shared publicly, so cross-matching visits is the main way to create hard evidence. Stakes: Town is a few eliminations from wolf parity and cannot afford more blind votes. A visit trail that survives a death or confirms a night role can decide the next vote or shot. Target landscape: A surviving claimed Investigator (counter-claimant just exposed as a wolf) or a vocal accuser who drove a mis-elimination, versus quiet unconfirmed players; choices rest on behavior and claim status, with no prior tracking evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, follow the player most likely to be acting at night, not a quiet bystander. That means a surviving claimed information role the wolves will want dead (so their last visit is recorded even if they die), or, when nothing is confirmed, a vocal accuser who pushed a wagon on a revealed Town role. Report the exact visit direction ("X went to Y") so it can be matched against other night results such as a Sentinel watch or a roleblock claim.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game with no discussion history. The Trailseer must pick a follow target blind while wolves, a lone killer and possibly a roleblocker are active, and the Trailseer may be blocked or killed that night. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: only the role list and your own role knowledge. No claims, results or votes exist. Stakes: Early game with every faction at full strength. No single night here decides the game, so a blind follow is cheap, and the main value is getting a first visit trace to compare against later events. Target landscape: All nine other players are equally unknown: no claims, no votes, no deaths and no behavior. The pick rests on no evidence, so any name is as good as another.
lessons.action: On a blind first night, follow one other player rather than holding back, since the follow costs nothing and any visit it reveals is a lead. A null result or a block says little, so keep the target-to-visited pairing exact for later cross-checking and choose later targets from claims and morning outcomes.

lessons.situation: Trailseer has publicly claimed and shared Night 1 results, then drew a hostile vote on Day 2. Wolves can see the claim and may kill or block the Trailseer on Night 2. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich. There are public claims, a vote record, and concealed or revealed bodies, but none of it gives a verified link to wolves. Stakes: As a publicly claimed tracker under suspicion, you are a likely wolf target, so a night spent re-following the same suspect may yield nothing if you are blocked or killed. Choosing the follow target with more information value matters. Target landscape: The suspect who voted against you and was already followed on Night 1, versus other quiet players or an unverified claimant. The vote against you is behavioral evidence, not proof of wolf alignment.
lessons.action: If you are exposed after claiming, follow a suspect chosen by evidence, not just the player who voted against you. Prefer a different unchecked suspect or a player linked to a likely kill target, since the Chanteuse can block you and the wolves can kill you that night. Hold the same suspect only if no better candidate exists.

lessons.situation: After a day elimination validated an investigative claim, the Trailseer chooses between auditing that claimant and chasing unknown suspects. The claimant may be a target for the wolves or the Chanteuse's block. Information landscape: Information-rich. There is a confirmed wolf flip from the Investigator's check, public claims, and a Sentinel watch that reported no visitors. Stakes: The remaining evil, a wolf and the lone killer, is still unknown. The Investigator's survival and credibility drive the village's votes, so verifying that they acted gives some value, but the follow adds no direct information on the remaining evil. Target landscape: A claimed Investigator whose check was validated by an elimination, versus a claimed Sentinel with a quiet watch result or unconfirmed quiet players. The choice rests on the value of verifying a key Town role.
lessons.action: When the Investigator's claim has just produced a confirmed result and the room trusts it, follow that Investigator to see whether they visited someone. If they visited no one, that matches a roleblock or a skipped check, but it is not proof of role. If they visited a player, you confirm they acted and learn who they checked.

lessons.situation: A prior follow gave a null result, and a wolf or the serial killer is still hidden. The trailseer decides whether to re-follow the same suspect or switch. Information landscape: Starved on the hidden evil players. The earlier no-visit result neither cleared nor implicated anyone, because inactivity, a held-back ability, a block and a concealed kill all look the same to a follower. Stakes: With a wolf and a killer both still alive, each night adds a victim. A second follow that learns nothing new costs tempo that Town cannot easily spare. Target landscape: Remaining uncertain players, including one already followed with a no-visit result, plus claimants and quiet players not yet followed. All are judged on behavior and claims, with no confirmed roles among them.
lessons.action: When last night's follow produced only a 'visited no one' or otherwise uninformative result, move the follow to a different, untested player. Pick one whose night behavior could contradict their stated role or tie them to a night death, a save or the surviving wolf's kill. Repeating the same follow rarely adds anything, while a new target widens what you can cross-check.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) with several unrevealed evil roles (a wolf pair and/or a lone killer) alive. The trailseer must pick whose movements to follow. Roleblocks and night kills have been landing on the trailseer when it acts predictably. Information landscape: Thin: a few confirmed wills or lynch results, one tied or split vote, no verified findings. The trailseer's own results are sparse (no-visit result, blocks) and speculative behavioral reads dominate. Stakes: Town is only a couple of eliminations from wolf parity, and the trailseer is one of few remaining information sources. A wasted follow, caused by being blocked or by following a target who is unlikely to reveal anything, can cost the town its last chance to find evil. Target landscape: Several living players with no confirmed roles, plus possibly a vocal claimed power role (e.g. vigilante) who has challenged you. Choice rests on day chatter and vote patterns, not hard evidence. Following a quiet, unscrutinized player yielded the one decisive lead; following the loud claimant produced nothing.
lessons.action: Each night, follow a player who has not been confirmed or strongly suspected but whose day behavior or votes you want pinned down, and prefer a target who is not a loud accuser of you. If your result shows the target visiting a night victim or another suspicious stop, treat that as a lead to act on; if you were blocked and got nothing, do not read it as evidence about the target.

lessons.situation: The Trailseer is a repeated target of night attacks (survived because protected), perhaps after being roleblocked on an earlier night, and needs to find the attacker among the few suspects. Information landscape: Moderately rich: an eliminated wolf, a double attack pattern, and earlier clears narrow the field. The follow supplies a visit trace that can be cross-checked against the Healer's claimed protection. Stakes: Mid-late board with a killer actively targeting you. Identifying the killer now prevents further losses, and your survival depends on the Healer's protection continuing. Target landscape: A handful of suspects, with some cleared-ish or role-claimed (Healer, Vigilante, replacement roles). The remaining quiet, deflecting, night-immune-looking player is the prime suspect, judged on behavior rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When you have been attacked repeatedly or protected and the lone killer is among a short list of suspects, follow the suspect whose behavior fits a night-immune killer. If they visited you on a night you were attacked, they are the killer or your protector, and the Healer's claim can separate the two. This turns the attacks on you into evidence.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Six players are alive and the leading remaining evil faction is two eliminations from parity; one night result alone cannot end the game or flip the winning position, though it reduces the room for error.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved for predicting tonight's victim: public deaths confirm the Investigator, Trailseer, Sigilist, and Serial Killer are gone, and a healer save was announced on the claimed Sentinel on the previous night. There is no public evidence identifying the remaining wolves or establishing who will be attacked tonight.
query_dims.situation: After the Serial Killer was eliminated on day 3, six players remain, including you. The lone killer is gone, but the wolves' night attack remains a threat; no living player's role is publicly confirmed, and a claimed Sentinel is unverified. You must settle a death prediction against the option of spending a self-bet for protection.
query_dims.target_landscape: Tonight's bet can name any living player other than you, or use one of your two remaining self-bets to prevent an attack on you at the cost of scoring no points. The claimed Sentinel is unverified; the other living players have no publicly confirmed roles. There is little evidence to distinguish likely victims or predict their roles.

lessons.situation: Night betting after the wolf pack has been eliminated. A hidden lone killer (here the Necromancer, attacking through a dead wolf's body) is the only source of night kills, and you still need one or two points. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: wolf identities and many roles are confirmed from lynches and reveals, and role claims are out. Nothing shows who the lone killer is or whom it will target next, so the pick rests on role-value inference. Stakes: The lone killer needs to whittle the town down by attrition. Your win needs only one or two more deaths guessed correctly, so a well-chosen bet can end your game objectively while play continues. Target landscape: Five to seven living players, both wolves already dead. The candidates are claimed power roles (sentinel, trailseer, investigator, sigilist), the hidden lone killer and yourself. The likeliest victim is the loudest, most credible information source, chosen by role-value reasoning rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone or crippled and a lone killer is the only remaining attacker, bet on the most valuable surviving information or power role (e.g. a vocal claimed sentinel) and name that role. A death scores one point even if the role is hidden, and a correct role guess scores two, so the pair can finish your win condition in one night. Keep both self-bets in reserve unless you are one point short and expect the attack to land on you.

lessons.situation: The previous night's wolf kill was stopped by a public heal. A wolf was lynched or lost, and a mixed field of wolves and a lone killer remains. You have one point and need one more. Information landscape: Fairly rich: the save was announced, a role was confirmed by a sigil strike, and one wolf's death was revealed. Which player the wolves will pick next is still a guess from motive. Stakes: With six alive and wolves still active, each night's kill brings them closer to parity. A missed bet wastes a night of scoring while you remain on one point, so choose the bet on motive and not on the last victim. Target landscape: Around six living players: a sigilist who has just survived a save, the healer who made the save, a lone killer, and one or more wolves. The healer is the known obstacle and the likelier next kill. The earlier target is a less likely repeat victim, since it was just protected and the wolves have lost a member.
lessons.action: When the wolves have just failed to kill a target through a heal or block, bet on the player who obstructed them, such as the healer, or on whoever their pack most needs gone. Do not re-bet on the previous target who survived. Only a wolf's kill selection can be predicted this way, so the bet on the obstacle is the better read.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game night after a wolf elimination, where multiple killers are active (wolves plus Serial Killer or Necromancer) and exposed claimants are the likelier victims. Earlier bets on a low-profile survivor scored nothing. Information landscape: Starved of confirmed targeting evidence: only public claims, last night's death roles, and killer behavior patterns. The previous bet had no basis beyond having survived. Stakes: Repeated zero-point nights shrink the path to two points. With several killers each night there are often two deaths, so betting on the exposed claimant raises the chance of scoring. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players, including recently claimed information roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, Investigator) who are plausible kill targets for either killer, and low-profile survivors. A pick that survived an earlier night only is weak evidence of a target.
lessons.action: Choose the bet from how the killers have actually behaved: which attacker types have been announced, and whether they hit exposed claimants. Don't bet on a player just because they survived last night. If neither killer has a clear target, bet on the most publicly exposed claimant. If two zero-point nights leave you with few nights left, use a self-bet only if you expect to be attacked.

lessons.situation: Midgame with one point scored and one more needed. The wolves and the Necromancer are killing nightly, a double attack on the sentinel and the investigator's death show their focus, and your earlier bet on a non-targeted player missed. Information landscape: Information-richer: revealed illusionist, trailseer record, necromancer vote-out, and a public attack on the sentinel. The killers' next preference is unstated, so the pick is inference from the kill pattern. Stakes: You need one more point to win and each wasted night costs a bet, while both self-bets remain unused. Missed bets on a player nobody is attacking waste nights that cannot be recovered. Target landscape: Six to seven living players: public-activity roles (sentinel, healer) that the wolves or a reanimating killer are visibly pressing, versus a quiet vote-aligned accuser with no sign of being targeted. The basis is public kill patterns and attack reports, not hidden role knowledge.
lessons.action: When you need a point and the previous night's kill pattern shows whom the killers are pressing (the attacked sentinel, the healer, or a role they just struck at), bet on that visible target to die rather than on a quiet accuser nobody is attacking. If your last bet missed, change the pick to follow the killers' current focus instead of repeating it, and keep your self-bets in hand until you have a reason to use them.

lessons.situation: You reached two points by night 3. Reanimated-wolf kills on consecutive nights show an active Necromancer with few suspects left, and a rival Fortune Teller claim is possible. Information landscape: Information-rich on the threat: consecutive reanimated-wolf kills identified a Necromancer, but nobody knows who it is. Targeting rests on behavior and structure, not confirmed roles. Stakes: With two points banked, further bets have no scoring value and a death in the late game removes you from play, so each self-bet buys a night of survival against a lone killer closing in on a win. Target landscape: Remaining Town players plus yourself. Another bet adds nothing once two points are banked, and your own survival is the live variable. The Necromancer has been killing a Town player every night, and your exposure rests on behavioral and structural evidence, not confirmed roles.
lessons.action: Once you have scored your two points and a killer is picking off players nightly, spend a self-bet each night instead of betting on another player, because scoring is already banked and survival is what remains. A self-bet makes an attack on you fail that night, so use it on the nights the killer is most likely to go after you.

lessons.situation: Early game, night 2. Wolves and a lone killer are probably all hunting, and the town has just produced a visible claimed power role. You must bet on who dies while the healer may protect the most obvious target. Information landscape: Information-starved. There is one revealed death, an unverified claim or two, and little or no vote record. Nothing shows who the killers will pick beyond how visible the claimant is. Stakes: Early game with no imminent parity. The bet is a modest scoring chance, since a miss costs one night's attempt toward the two points. The two self-bets stay in reserve. Target landscape: Seven to nine living players: one or two public power-role claimants (a trailseer, sigilist or sentinel claimant who stands out as a likely kill target), plus quiet unclaimed players with no behavioral signal. The healer is alive and unrevealed. The only evidence is who died on night 1 and who claimed since.
lessons.action: On an early night with both self-bets still held, when killers are active and one publicly claimed investigative role stands out, bet on that claimant to die and name their claimed role only if you would accept losing the second point. Accept that a healer save can turn an accurate prediction into zero, since only a death scores. Do not move your bet to a quiet unclaimed player, because the evidence points at the claimant.

lessons.situation: The night after a failed double attack on a claimed Town role that the healer saved. Both killers have shown interest in that role, and they may pivot or repeat. You have 0 points and unused self-bets. Information landscape: Moderately informed: a saved attack and open claims give real signal about killer priorities, but it is reasoning and not confirmation. You have no cover or confirmed roles. Stakes: You are at 0 points and being voted out before betting would lose you the game, so getting bets placed each night matters. Each unsuccessful night shortens your runway. Target landscape: The previous night's double-attack target was saved by the healer, and the likely next victims are that same player again, another claimed power role such as a sigilist, or the healer. The basis is expected killer behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, place a bet on the likeliest victim instead of holding back, and keep both self-bets in reserve until you are visibly exposed or have been the day's top vote target. If the kill is likely to go onto the same obvious claimant a second time and the healer may repeat the save, pick the second-most-likely target the killers would pivot to, such as a claimed role that bypasses protection.

lessons.situation: Late game: wolves are dead or nearly so, a lone killer (the Necromancer) is still killing each night, and the Fortune Teller needs points or must stay alive long enough to score them. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves' roles are revealed, earlier checks are confirmed, and the killer's attack pattern across several nights is visible. The remaining uncertainty is only which player the killer takes next. Stakes: The game is near its end. One more death can decide the outcome, and the Fortune Teller's own survival and point total matter more than anything else it can do at night. Target landscape: Three or four living players, mostly confirmed or claimed roles such as an Investigator, a claimed Sigilist and a rival Fortune Teller claimant. The likeliest victim is the repeatedly attacked information source, chosen from the kill pattern rather than from confirmed knowledge.
lessons.action: Late in the game, with a lone killer still active and few players alive, bet on the player the killer's pattern most likely hits tonight, such as a repeatedly attacked information source, and name their role for the two-point payout. If you are the visible threat and still have self-bets, spend one that night, because it blocks an attack on you and a death before scoring loses the game.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or abstain day. One claimant of a night-info role is the focal point of the discussion and votes, so the wolves and the lone killer both have reason to kill them. Information landscape: Moderately informative. There is a public role claim and a vote record concentrated on one player, plus evidence from the earlier night that killers are active. Nothing is verified, and the read rests on the claimant's visibility and not on confirmed roles. Stakes: Scoring two points here ends the Fortune Teller's win condition outright. A miss costs nothing but a night, though only a few nights remain to score. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players. One stands out as a visible information threat: a self-declared Trailseer or Sentinel who was roleblocked or took the day's votes. Their role is unverified and rests on their own claim. The rest are quiet, with no comparable profile.
lessons.action: When a player has drawn real visibility, such as a self-declared info-role claim (Trailseer, Sentinel) that has also taken votes or a roleblock, bet on that player to die and name the claimed role. Killers have a motive to remove them, and a correct role is worth two points while a wrong role still scores one for the death.

lessons.situation: Final-night endgame with an evil killer (wolf or Necromancer) one kill from winning and few or no town night-killing abilities left. The Fortune Teller needs points and can be killed itself. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are announced, spent abilities are known, and the remaining pool is nearly fully identified, so the killer's only plausible victim can be deduced. Stakes: The next kill ends the game, so a wasted bet or an unprotected Fortune Teller means a loss. A correct bet on the forced victim with the role named can score the final two points. A self-bet only buys time and scores nothing. Target landscape: Two or three other living players: a claimed or confirmed town role the sole remaining killer must target (the healer already dead or irrelevant), and an unconfirmed player who is the likely killer, with a Necromancer able to attack through a dead Vigilante body. Reads rest on confirmed deaths and claims, not on behavior.
lessons.action: In a 3-4 player endgame with both self-bets left, first identify which enemy can actually kill tonight. If the only living killer is the one who could attack you and you have no other path to a point, spend a self-bet so an attack on you fails; if your bet target is the one certain victim, bet on them and name their role.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3, after a vote removed a wolf or resolved a claim conflict. Both the wolves and a lone killer are likely to strike the most threatening public Town claimant. You have 0-1 points, so each night's bet is your main way to score. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: a revealed wolf, claim conflicts and vote records show who threatens the killers. No role is confirmed beyond the reveals, and the healer's protection choice is unknown. Stakes: Scoring two points wins the game for you whatever else happens. Each night's bet is therefore a real chance to progress, and a miss costs only a night, not a use. The Town/wolf balance is not yet critical. Target landscape: Several claimed Town power roles (Investigator, Sentinel, healer, sigilist, trailseer) are alive. One was just validated by a vote or counter-claim win and is the obvious kill target. A healer may be guarding that player. The basis is role-value and behavior reasoning, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack and any lone killer have just lost a member or a public claimant has just been validated, bet on the most visible, freshly validated Town power role (healer, or a claimed Investigator or Sentinel whose report threatens the killers) to die, and name the role if the evidence points to it. Kills tend to aim at that player, so the bet scores if they die; a hidden role still scores, so name the role. If you suspect the healer will guard the obvious target, bet on the next-most-valuable power role the killers could reach instead.

lessons.situation: Four-player endgame where the wolf must attack a high-threat claimed role while a living healer will probably guard that same player. The Fortune Teller has two self-bets left and one point. Information landscape: Information-rich: sigil mechanics are demonstrated, several dead roles are confirmed, and claims define the remaining pool. The healer's choice cannot be seen. Stakes: One save plus one sigil strike can end the game on the spot with the Fortune Teller short of two points. Choosing a bet that can still score when the obvious kill is saved matters more than matching the most likely attack. Target landscape: The claimed sigilist (the obvious wolf target), an unconfirmed healer claimant likely to guard them, and a quiet surviving wolf. The choice is between the heavily protected obvious victim and the less obvious alternatives, based on claims and prior-night events.
lessons.action: If a living healer can plausibly protect the obvious wolf target, bet on a different player who is likely to die by another cause, such as a player a pending sigil or other attack might strike or an alternate victim the pack might choose. Do not stake the bet on a protected player with an active sigil threat that could eliminate the last wolf and end the game before you score.

lessons.situation: Late game with no protective role alive and a single evil killer who must kill the one remaining town power role. The Fortune Teller can predict the casualty and its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: earlier deaths and reveals fix who is alive, who the killer must be, and which role is the logical victim. The claimed role has been corroborated by a visible event. Stakes: The kill decides whether the game ends this night, so the bet is made at the point of highest leverage. Naming the right role can finish the Fortune Teller's win condition alongside the evil side's win. Target landscape: A claimed role whose identity has been established by an earlier reveal (such as a vigilante whose shot exposed the Serial Killer's immunity) and the lone wolf as the only possible killer. The healer is already dead, so nothing can save the victim.
lessons.action: When the killer's victim is forced by elimination, bet on that player to die and name their role, since a correct role scores two points instead of one. Choose the player no remaining protector can cover. Bet only on a death you can explain by who is able to attack, not on a player merely because they are the obvious target.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night where the killers' obvious priority target, a verified or claimed investigator, has been publicly shielded or saved by the healer, while other prominent claimants are unprotected. The Fortune Teller must choose a bet to reach two points. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves or the serial killer are dead or confirmed, healer saves are announced, and protection patterns are visible to every player, including the killers. Stakes: Scoring needs two points, and each zero-point night shrinks the remaining nights in which they can be earned. Repeating a bet the healer can block yields no points and pushes the Fortune Teller toward riskier late bets. Target landscape: A claimed investigator or other focal Town player who is openly or recently healer-protected; an unprotected claimed healer or trailseer; and quieter unverified players. The evidence is public announcements of saves and claims, not behavior.
lessons.action: When the obvious high-profile target was publicly healer-protected or saved last night, bet on a different likely victim instead, such as an unprotected prominent claimant (the claimed healer, or a trailseer or sentinel with no cover). If no protector remains alive, bet on the most prominent unprotected Town claimant.

lessons.situation: After a day in which the Fortune Teller cast an isolated dissenting vote or otherwise stands out, the remaining killers must choose a victim. The obvious saved target is likely covered again, which makes the exposed Fortune Teller the easy kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: the public voting record and announced saves expose who dissented and who the healer protected, and the killers can read both. Stakes: If the Fortune Teller dies with fewer than two points it loses permanently. A self-bet makes an attack on it fail, so it survives to bet again, though it scores nothing that night. Target landscape: The Fortune Teller's own safety, via a self-bet, versus betting on a re-targeted saved claimant or another Town player. The killers may bypass the healer-protected claimant and hit the visible outlier instead.
lessons.action: When your day-3 vote or behavior marks you as an outlier or likely target, and you are not close to the second point, use one of your two self-bets instead of betting on another player. The attack on you fails that night, so you stay alive to score later.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2-3) after a wolf was voted out or a tie vote. Claims are public, and a Necromancer, wolves or a Serial Killer may strike. The Fortune Teller is not under suspicion and needs two points to win. Information landscape: Moderate public signals: claimed roles, announced attacker types (reanimated attack), prior deaths and vote records. Nothing confirms who the killers will choose. Stakes: The game is not at the brink, but each night is a scoring chance and the Fortune Teller needs two points. A night with several possible killers gives more than one death to land on, so a well-chosen bet is worth making every night. Target landscape: Several living claimants (a Healer who revealed whom they protected, a twice-attacked Investigator, a Sentinel or Trailseer) and contested players from a claim clash or tie vote. Roles are public claims, unverified. Picks rest on behavior and exposure, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, bet on the player the killers are most likely to hit, judged from public exposure: a freshly claimed Healer or information role, a player at the center of a claim clash, or one just named by an announced reanimated attack. Add the role guess only when a public claim makes it a strong inference, since a right role is worth two points and a wrong role still scores one for the death.

lessons.situation: Night 1, or an opening night with no discussion or only a quiet day. Two or three independent killers may each take someone, and the bet scores if the named player dies by any cause. Information landscape: Completely information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or protection results, and day 1 had no vote. Stakes: Early misses are routine and not decisive, since two points are still reachable later. A blind hit with no role named caps the score at one point instead of two, which is a free loss to avoid. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no claims, votes, behavior or night history. Any pick is a pure guess, and several deaths are possible because there are two or three killers.
lessons.action: When you have no information, still place the bet and always name a role guess. A wrong role costs nothing, since the death still scores one point, and a right role doubles it. If any thin signal exists, such as a power role likely to be a priority kill, use it to pick the target and the role.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer or investigator has publicly accused or outed a player, and both accuser and accused are alive entering the night. The evil faction must decide whether to silence the accuser. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are public claims, a counter-claim dispute, and a visible accusation, but nothing hard confirms the accuser or the accused. Stakes: A correct bet here scores one point toward the two needed. A bet on the accused instead of the accuser yielded zero points when the accuser was killed. Target landscape: An exposer (a claimed trailseer or investigator who caught or outed an evil player), the accused player under suspicion, and other claimants. The basis is public claims and accusations.
lessons.action: When a claimant has publicly accused or exposed a suspected evil player, bet on the exposer as the likely victim, since the wolves are more likely to silence the accuser than to attack their own accused partner. Take that bet only if the exposer is not currently healer-protected.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; the next single elimination does not end the game, so a misdirected block or kill is recoverable but each wasted night brings the wolves closer to parity.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible move tonight (a claim, a block declared, or a vote) would commit the chanteuse's standing in a village where the healer was just lynched and no claim has yet been tested; a public block cannot be retracted once the blocked player reports it.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no public result has been announced except the day 1 kill and the day 2 lynch. The only private information is the chanteuse's own block record and the pack's kill. No town claim has been checked against a death, so every candidate block target is unverified.
query_dims.situation: Night 2 for a chanteuse who blocked the healer on night 1 and whose pack has agreed on a quiet town player as the kill. The healer was lynched on day 2 after being blocked on night 1 and refusing to name their role, and the village is still waiting for a claimed sentinel or investigator result to test against tonight's deaths. The carrier rotates to a partner wolf, who has set the kill, so this night's block must be chosen to avoid the pack's victim while removing the most dangerous town night action.
query_dims.target_landscape: Town players alive: the quiet player the pack has settled on as the kill (no public role claim, no pushed read), the player who has been pressing for claimed results, and the player who has been voting with the majority. None of these has a verified public role; all judgments rest on behavior and vote pattern, not evidence.

lessons.situation: Early-mid game (night 2) with the wolves carrying a kill and the chanteuse picking a block. A lone killer is active or suspected, and claims or deaths from the first night have made the board partly readable. Information landscape: Info-starved: a night-1 death, a few unverified claims, and possibly one immunity reveal. Nobody has identified the healer or investigator. Stakes: Four players must still be removed before the wolves reach parity, and the lone killer is also still alive. One wasted block or one saved kill costs tempo but is not decisive. A chanteuse who dies early leaves the partner alone with Town's investigator and healer free to act. Forward exposure: A block is a private visit and leaves no public trace. The blocked player is told they were roleblocked and could report it, and the target can change each night. A wasted block is invisible to the town, but it forfeits the night's one chance to protect the kill. Target landscape: Living candidates are mostly unconfirmed. A few have claimed roles, and one may be pinned as the serial killer or necromancer through an immunity or Suspicious read, and so cannot be blocked. The healer and investigator are usually unidentified. Choices rest on reasoning about who threatens the kill, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Choose the block only from players it can take on, meaning Town roles and your wolf partner, and skip anyone the immunity reveal or the rules mark as the lone killer or a neutral. Among those, block the role whose action would most directly undo or expose tonight's pack kill, such as the healer if you can narrow them down, or otherwise the investigator or a claimed protective or tracking role. Do not spend the block on a speculative threat like a sigil that matters only if it lands on the carrier.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a tied day-2 vote with no elimination. The pack kills a scrutinized or quiet player, the illusionist will conceal the body, and the chanteuse must pick which of several active town information roles to cancel. The pack's illusionist is already tied to a visit or is exposed by a claim. Information landscape: Moderately informative but unverified. There are conflicting role claims, a trailseer and sentinel who have reported, and a tied vote. Hard confirmation exists only for any dead roles. The chanteuse does not know every hidden actor, such as a necromancer using a dead body. Stakes: Mid-game with several town information roles alive. One unblocked witness to the illusionist's visit can cost the pack a wolf and bring the pack's win condition much further away, so which witness gets blocked matters more than whether a block happens. Forward exposure: The block is private and can change every night, but a blocked player can say so publicly and name their intended target, which hands town a corroborating signal. An unblocked watcher's report then stands alone. Once the night resolves the choice cannot be undone, so a wrong pick leaves the illusionist's visit open to whoever you left free. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed information roles: a trailseer and a sentinel who reported night-1 results, a claimed healer, and unconfirmed sentinel, sigilist and healer slots. Nobody's claim is verified. The trailseer was the loudest threat to the pack, but the sentinel's watch on the victim was the result that actually exposed the illusionist.
lessons.action: When the pack is killing a victim and the illusionist will visit that body to conceal it, spend the block on the information role most likely to see that visit rather than defaulting to the trailseer. Block the sentinel if it has publicly used a watch and the victim is the kind of player it would watch (a scrutinized or quiet player). Block the trailseer only if it has already followed or named the illusionist. Hiding the body hides only the carrier's visit, so the illusionist's own visit stays visible to a watcher on the victim, or to a follower of the illusionist, unless the illusionist carried the kill itself.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 3) with the pack down to one or two wolves. The healer and other Town power roles have publicly claimed and cross-support each other, and the pack must get its kill through while limiting what Town learns. Information landscape: Information-rich on the public side: announced saves, mutually supporting role claims and a verified watch. Wolf chat agrees on the kill target, but the chanteuse does not know which power role will act against it. Stakes: With about six players alive and the lone killer gone or dying, each successful kill moves the wolves toward parity. A cancelled kill, or a surviving Investigator, can let the town vote the last wolves out, so the block decides whether the kill sticks. Forward exposure: A block is a visit, and the victim is told 'You were roleblocked'. If they report it, the town learns the chanteuse is alive and can narrow the suspect pool. The block cannot be undone, and repeating it on the same target builds a visible pattern. Target landscape: Several claimed Town power roles are alive: a healer backed by a save or a sentinel's watch, an Investigator, a Trailseer and a Vigilante. Their status rests on claims supported by announced saves and cross-confirming claims, not on hard verification. The healer or the sole living check source is the most valuable block.
lessons.action: When a protector (healer) has publicly claimed and been backed by a save or a watch, block the role most likely to cancel or expose the kill, whether the healer or the lone check source, so the pack's kill on its chosen target lands. If the healer is the pack's own target, block the Investigator or the next most dangerous information role instead and conceal the body.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with the pack's kill already agreed, often on a player who accused the illusionist or is a likely power role. The chanteuse must choose whom to block. The danger is wasting the block on the victim while a town role acts on the carrier, as when an unblocked sigilist killed the illusionist who carried the attack. Information landscape: Moderately informed: a day-2 clash, a tied or split vote, one or two claimed roles and a dead sentinel or fortune teller. The investigator and healer are unidentified. Night results are hidden, so the town's actions can only be guessed from claims. Stakes: The board is mid-game with a lone killer still alive, so a single mistimed block can cost a wolf. Losing the illusionist or chanteuse leaves the pack unable to reach parity. Each night's block is the pack's main protection for the carrier. Forward exposure: A blocked player is told they were roleblocked, so the target learns the wolves feared their action that night. That fact is permanent and can be tied to the pack. The block cannot be undone once placed, and a redundant block wastes the night's only utility. Target landscape: Candidates are the pack's victim, who is already doomed and gains nothing from a block, and the living town power roles (sigilist, trailseer, sentinel, investigator). Public role status is thin, with a few claims and one confirmed power role. The block choice rests on what each role could do to the carrier, not on behavior.
lessons.action: Spend the block on the living town role most able to expose or punish the carrier that night, such as the sigilist, trailseer or sentinel, not on the player the pack is already killing. If the illusionist carries the kill, block the sigilist when one is plausibly alive, because a sigil strikes an attacker. Otherwise block the trailseer or sentinel when the pack's visit would otherwise be seen.

lessons.situation: The pack has already settled its kill target and the chanteuse must choose a block target from the other town information roles, choosing between blocking the victim and blocking a different threat. Information landscape: Information-rich after day-two role claims, with public claims from the investigator, trailseer, and sigilist but no verified results. Stakes: Doubling the block on the kill target wastes the pack's single disruption and leaves another information role free to find a wolf. Spreading disruption keeps town results thin while the kill proceeds.
