query_dims.public_private_text: You know privately that your pack killed the revealed Investigator and that your block on the questioned player succeeded. Publicly, the confirmed night deaths were the Investigator killed by wolves and the Trailseer killed by the Serial Killer. The Sentinel’s unverified account says the dead Trailseer visited another player; the public discussion treats that as compatible with a follow action, not proof of guilt.
query_dims.situation: On day 2, after the wolves’ night kill revealed an Investigator and the Serial Killer’s attack revealed a Trailseer, the Sentinel claimant reported that the dead Trailseer visited a living player. The group regards this as consistent with a follow action rather than incriminating evidence, while a separate question about whether another player’s action resolved has produced no confirmed result.
query_dims.target_landscape: No specific elimination target has emerged. The dead Investigator and Trailseer are system-confirmed Town roles; the living players’ roles are otherwise unknown or, for the Sentinel claimant, unverified. The only concrete visitor evidence is the Sentinel claimant’s account, which fits the Trailseer’s possible follow action and does not establish wrongdoing by the visited player.

lessons.situation: On day 2 a claimed trailseer reported following you to another player's door, a roleblock report on that player corroborated it, and the village is converging on you or on an abstain while you consider voting against the tracker. Information landscape: Starved of announced facts: only unverified claims (a follow report, a roleblock report, a watch claim, possibly your own cover claim), plus a hidden-role death and a confirmed investigator death. Nothing announced identifies you. Stakes: With nine alive and the wolves far from parity, there is no tempo to force a risky vote. Losing the chanteuse, or drawing a sigil or investigator check by standing out, costs the wolves a blocker and leaves the partner alone. Consensus: The room is aligned on either abstaining or eliminating you, based on matching unverified claims about your night movement rather than on any announced fact. My position: Holding out alone against the room, either as the main wagon target or as a solitary voter against an abstain consensus. Heat: High to very high: the tracker's follow report and a target's roleblock report match your real night visit, several players accuse you, and your denial stands alone against a convergent pair of claims. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser is public and permanent, commits you to the story that the report is false, and invites night attention. Voting with the room is reversible and keeps the record neutral; if you are eliminated your role is revealed and your wolf partner comes under suspicion. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed trailseer who named you, players who echoed the roleblock or watch claims (sigilist, vigilante, sentinel), and an abstain option. All are unverified role claims, and the dead so far are an investigator and a concealed body, so nothing hard points at any candidate. Public vs private: You privately know the tracker's report of your visit is true and you blocked or visited that player; publicly it is only an unverified claim that you have denied or covered with a fabricated story.
lessons.action: When a claimed trailseer or other tracker publicly places your night visit on a target, and the room is abstaining or leaning against you, skip the revenge vote and join the room's consensus (abstain or the wagon's target). A solitary vote against your accuser changes no tally, repeats your accusation on the permanent record and marks you as the one player who wants the information role dead.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote: a claimed town info role gave a result that breaks the rules, the accused admitted no explanation, and the table piled on. Your wolf partner may be among the accusers. Eliminating the target also removes a town watcher. Information landscape: Thin but concrete: one verifiable rules inconsistency, a few unverified claims, no voting history, and few confirmed roles. Stakes: Early game with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. The outcome is not close, so one vote does not flip the result. The value is in staying invisible while a town information role is removed. Consensus: Near-unanimous (about 8 of 9) and based on a checkable rules inconsistency that the accused conceded, not on tone or pack coordination. My position: With the majority, joining a vote that is already decided. Heat: Low to almost none: you are unclaimed, made few or no accusations, and the attention is entirely on the accused. Forward exposure: A vote with a lopsided majority commits you to nothing and looks like ordinary town behavior. Voting against an accepted target would stand out in the permanent public record with no upside. Target landscape: One candidate, a claimed Sentinel, has a concrete rules contradiction (a watch result that omitted their own visit) and is accused by several players. No other player has comparable evidence against them, so the choice rests on a verifiable inconsistency, not on tone. Public vs private: You privately know the wolf pair (Chanteuse and Illusionist) is alive and that the accused claimant is likely a genuine town role. The public sees only an unverified claim with an impossible result and treats it as grounds to eliminate.
lessons.action: When the room is already converging on a target through a checkable rules contradiction, cast your day vote with the majority and add no distinctive argument. The vote is low-commitment and blends into the pile-on, so a lone vote elsewhere would only draw heat to you.

lessons.situation: A genuine Town claimant (a healer counter-claiming against my partner, or a sentinel accusing me of a visit) is on the ballot at the day vote. Removing them protects the pack or me today, but their role and will will be revealed on death. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are contested role claims, a named visit, confirmed saves, and the public voting record. Nothing is verified until a death reveals the role. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several kills still needed for parity. Removing a healer or sentinel strips Town's protection or visit information and gives the wolves tempo, but a revealed role can expose my own visit history. Consensus: The village is split or leaning against the claimant, based on behavioral skepticism such as delayed disclosure and conflicting claims, not on confirmed facts. My position: With the majority, as one vote in a broad bloc and not the driver. Heat: Ranges from low to severe. Either my partner is under fire in a contested claim, or the claimant is directly accusing me, but the room is skeptical of the claimant. Forward exposure: The vote is permanent and public. If the claimant dies as a confirmed Town role, my vote is tied to the wolf side and any will naming my visit becomes announced fact, so the commitment cannot be undone and can draw night attacks such as a sigil or a vigilante shot. Target landscape: A binary choice between a claimed protective or information role (healer or sentinel) and either my wolf partner or myself. The claimant's role is unverified, and the case against them rests on behavior and timing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Publicly the claimant is an unverified or belated claimant whom the room distrusts. Privately I know the claim is genuine, either because it names my own visit or because my wolf partner is the one faking the role.
lessons.action: When the room is already turning on a claimant who threatens you or your partner (a counter-claimed healer, or a sentinel naming your visit), cast your vote with the broad majority against that claimant. Joining a wide bloc keeps you from standing out as the driver and removes a protective or information role. Expect the revealed role and will to be read out as fact, so take the claimant's most likely true read into account when judging how much heat that reveal will put on you.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after your wolf partner died on night 1. You are the lone wolf, and the room mostly leans to abstain while minority blocs name different targets. Information landscape: Starved: a few claimed night results and one slip, with no confirmed roles and no vote history. Stakes: As the lone wolf you have no backup, so one exposure or one night retaliation could end the wolf side; staying low-profile is worth more than a marginal vote. Consensus: Most of the room leans toward abstaining, and a couple of small blocs name different targets. My position: Holding out with a minority bloc against an abstain-leaning room. Heat: Low: no accusations against you, only generic discussion remarks. Forward exposure: A minority vote is public and permanent and ties you to one bloc, so the target and that bloc can see where you stand. You cannot reverse it. Target landscape: Candidates are a claimant who slipped on a night action, another named suspect, or abstaining. Roles are unconfirmed, and the only lead is a behavioral slip. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf with no partner to help, while the town has no read on you.
lessons.action: If your partner is dead or revealed and you are the lone wolf, vote with the majority or abstain instead of joining a small minority bloc on a sigilist or other action-role claimant. A vote that leaves you holding out with a minority marks you to the targeted player, who may act against you that night.

lessons.situation: A claiming investigative role (Investigator or Trailseer) has caught my wolf partner with a Suspicious check or a tracked visit to a victim. The village is pushing to eliminate the partner, and the partner is counter-charging the claimant. I must choose between joining the vote on the partner and voting against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich. A living claimant has direct evidence, other claims or mechanics corroborate it, and the votes will become a permanent ledger. Stakes: The board is still early and not at parity, so one vote does not decide the game. The partner is lost either way, and what matters is whether I survive as a low-heat wolf for later days. A solitary or minority vote costs me that standing and gains nothing. Consensus: The village is largely united behind the claimant's result, supported by mechanics or corroborating claims. A counter-wagon would need near-majority support, and in the observed cases it reached 2 to 4 votes against a landslide. My position: holding out Heat: Low. I had stayed neutral in discussion, with no accusations or scrutiny on me, and that standing is what I would lose by backing the partner. Forward exposure: Votes are public and permanent. A vote against the claimant or for the partner's side becomes a visible link to the partner once the partner's role flips as a wolf, and it cannot be undone. A vote with the majority commits me to nothing beyond the consensus. Target landscape: The choice is between my caught wolf partner, who is named by a claiming investigative role's result or movement evidence, and that claimant, whom the partner is accusing of fabrication. The case against the partner rests on evidence and mechanics, while the counter-case rests on behavior and bluster. Public vs private: I privately know my partner is a wolf and the claimant's result is probably genuine. The room is converging on that read, and my only open choice is whether to be seen defending the partner.
lessons.action: When a credible, info-rich claim has the room converging on your wolf partner and your own heat is low, vote with the majority against the partner instead of voting against the claimant. If the counter-wagon cannot reach a majority, your vote on the public record only ties you to the partner, so keep your standing for the later days.

lessons.situation: Day 2 is the first vote of the game. Information is thin, with a night-1 death or a few unverified claims, and the village is split between piling on a target and abstaining. Information landscape: Starved: unverified claims, perhaps one revealed death, no confirmed roles and no vote history. Stakes: Early game with many players alive; no single vote decides the game, so staying unnoticed matters more than pushing an elimination. Consensus: The room is split or undecided between several targets and abstaining, with no evidence-based convergence. My position: With the majority or a plurality bloc, not driving. Heat: Low: you have not been accused and have only spoken mildly or generically. Forward exposure: A named vote is public and permanent and can later be read as wolf coordination if your partner is exposed. An abstain or a vote with the plurality commits you to little and carries low risk. Target landscape: Candidates are quiet players, unverified claimants, and abstaining. No roles are confirmed, so any named target is a behavior-based guess. Public vs private: You privately know both wolves and the pack's night plan, while the public has only unverified night-1 claims, one death at most, and behavioral reads, so nothing points at you.
lessons.action: On the first day-2 vote, when no roles are confirmed and you have low heat, cast your vote with the room's existing plurality, which is often abstain or a split. Keep your vote consistent with your partner's but do not drive the accusation. Voting with the room adds no new suspicion, and an unforced named vote is permanent record you cannot undo.

lessons.situation: Late-game day vote where the chanteuse's side is losing. Either a fake-claim counter-claim contest has turned against you, or a credible watch or follow claim has doomed your wolf partner, and the room is converging. Information landscape: Information-rich from the town's view: confirmed roles for the dead, a lone killer possibly already eliminated, and claims corroborated by other claimants. You have nothing verifiable to offer. Stakes: The wolves are within a couple of eliminations of parity, so losing a wolf or exposing the pair is costly. This single vote will not flip the result, so the value is in keeping the wolves' public links minimal. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, with a lopsided majority forming on a claim-based case that looks consistent. There is no strong support for the minority view. My position: Holding out against, or being swept along by, a clear majority. Your vote is not the deciding one. Heat: High. You are either the target of a lost counter-claim with several players already naming you, or you recently pushed against a claimant who has since been corroborated. Forward exposure: Every vote is public and permanent. Matching your partner's vote, or opposing the room's clear pick, ties you to them and cannot be undone once the role is revealed. A vote that diverges costs little because your own vote cannot change a lopsided result. Target landscape: The realistic candidates are your counter-claimant, your exposed partner, and the Sentinel or other accuser. All are judged on claims and corroboration rather than hard proof, and the room has mostly settled on one. Public vs private: You privately know your partner's role and whether your own claim is false. The room is working from claims, counter-claims and past votes, and it sees you as either a liar or a defender of a likely wolf.
lessons.action: If the vote is already lost, because you are the losing side of a counter-claim or your partner is the target of a credible, room-wide case, cast the vote that least links you to your partner. Vote with the room when it is converging on your partner, and when you are the target pick a different name from your partner's. Votes are public and permanent, so a doomed vote that mirrors your partner's ties the two of you together.

lessons.situation: Endgame vote at three or four players where a claimed vigilante threatens to eliminate the chanteuse or the wolf partner and a coordinated counter-vote can produce a tie and no elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: most investigative town roles are confirmed dead, roles and past votes are known, and the vigilante's claim and held shot are public. Stakes: The board is near parity, so a single elimination of a wolf could lose the game while a tie with no elimination keeps the wolves alive to reach parity or a winning night. Consensus: The room is split with no majority; the vigilante pushes one wolf while the remaining players are undecided or abstaining, so a tie is reachable. My position: holding out Heat: Ranges from minimal heat on the chanteuse (suspicion on the partner) to high (a claimed vigilante accusing and voting for the chanteuse based on roleblock claims). Forward exposure: Publicly voting an unclaimed or quiet player commits the chanteuse to an adversarial stance against the vigilante's read, but with few players left and no investigative roles alive the exposure is low and the tie can be repeated. Target landscape: Two or three living candidates: a claimed vigilante driving the accusation, and a quiet or unclaimed player with split or no votes and no claims, who is the only viable counter-target; the basis is behavior, not evidence. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows which players are wolves and that the vote target is not evil, while the room is split between the chanteuse or the wolf partner and an unclaimed or quiet player as the last wolf.
lessons.action: In a small endgame vote where a claimed vigilante and others are pushing to eliminate you or your wolf partner, vote for the non-partner player who is least aligned with the vigilante's push so the vote splits into a tie. A tie eliminates no one, so you and your partner survive into the next night; pick the target who is a plausible suspect, not your partner.

lessons.situation: Day vote where the village converges on your wolf partner, who is exposed by a counterclaim or accusation. You must choose between joining the vote against them and defending them. Information landscape: Claims, counterclaims and unverified night reports are present, and some roles may be confirmed by deaths. There are no hard Game Master confirmations of the accused's role, so the room's read rests on deduction. Stakes: The vote outcome is already decided by the majority, so your single vote does not flip the board. What it decides is whether you stay unlinked to the partner on the permanent record, which protects your survival as the remaining wolf. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, around 7 votes or more, on eliminating your partner. The basis is claim contradictions or a claimed check, not confirmed roles. My position: Tempted to hold out to protect the partner, but the correct stance is with the majority. The vote is decided either way. Heat: Low to moderate. Discussion is consumed by the claim collision and you have drawn no accusations. Your own night visits could still surface later. Forward exposure: A vote with the pile-on reads as a normal town vote and links you to nothing. A vote against the majority, for a rival claimant, or an abstain would be public and permanent, and once your partner's role is revealed it would mark you as their ally. Neither vote can be undone. Target landscape: The accused is your wolf partner, claiming a power role (Sentinel, Healer or Investigator) that is contradicted by a counter-claimant or report. The only alternative is a rival claimant who is probably Town. The case rests on claim clashes and visit reports, with nothing confirmed by the Game Master. Public vs private: You privately know the accused or counter-claimed player is your wolf partner, and that their claim or accusation is fabricated cover. Publicly the room reads it as a claim contradiction or a Suspicious check, and no suspicion falls on you.
lessons.action: When a lopsided majority is already set to eliminate your wolf partner and your vote cannot change the result, cast your vote with the majority on the same target. If you hold out, defend the partner, or abstain, the permanent public record ties you to the wolf once their role flips, so don't do any of those. Afterward, plan as the lone wolf rather than relying on the vote to keep you safe.

lessons.situation: A day vote on an early day with a forming majority, either abstain-heavy or piled on one suspect, where the chanteuse has no real evidence-based target and a lone vote would only mark them as the outlier. Information landscape: Starved: unverified power-role claims, a few roleblock complaints and no confirmed roles or voting history to anchor a read. Stakes: Many players are still alive and no single vote decides the game. Wolf survival depends on staying unnoticed, so the vote is worth little compared with the cost of a record that gets used against you. Consensus: The village is fairly aligned, either piling onto one behavior-based suspect or abstaining in bulk, with little hard evidence behind it. My position: Free to choose between joining the majority and standing alone; joining the majority keeps you unremarkable. Heat: Low to moderate: nobody is accusing you, but an off-consensus vote would create heat immediately. Forward exposure: A vote is public and permanent. An outlier vote on a quiet or claimed player creates a record that can be quoted back and cannot be undone, whereas a vote with the room commits you to little and is easy to explain. Target landscape: Candidates are mostly unrevealed players: a room-favored suspect chosen on behavior or quietness, claimed power roles with unverifiable results, and quiet players with no evidence against them. There is no confirmed wolf, so any off-consensus pick rests on thin or no evidence. Public vs private: You privately know the pack, your own blocks and the real roles of some players, but publicly you are an unremarkable, unclaimed player whom nobody is accusing, and the room is thin on evidence and leaning toward one target or toward abstaining.
lessons.action: When the room is converging or abstaining and you have no evidence-backed target, cast your vote with the majority, or abstain if abstaining is offered, rather than being the lone off-consensus voter. If you are forced to name someone, pick the room's leading target or one your wolf partner also backs, so your permanent record has no outlier vote that can later be quoted as reactionary deflection.

lessons.situation: Endgame with 3-4 players alive, I am the sole surviving wolf, and the day vote is a terminal step toward parity. The lone killer or a town or neutral player is the target, and the town is pressuring me on my voting record. Information landscape: Information-rich: claims, announced roles from dead players, wills, and a public voting record narrow the suspects down to a few players. Stakes: One elimination from a night kill that reaches parity. This vote decides whether I go into the night with the lone killer gone and equal numbers, or lose on the spot. Consensus: The room is split but active. One or two town voices want a decisive elimination, and a plurality can form around a target I can also support. My position: driving or with majority; I join the likeliest plurality so my vote decides the result and the votes against me stay short. Heat: Moderate to high; a claimed Sentinel, a Speculator or the Serial Killer pointed at me from voting history or role counts, but they lacked the numbers for a majority. Forward exposure: The vote is public, permanent and irreversible. If it fails to form a plurality and the vote lands on me, the wolves lose at once, so line up a majority with a willing voter before committing. Target landscape: Two to three living non-wolf players, among them the lone killer (claimed or unclaimed) and town utility roles; the choice rests on role counts, claims, and voting records rather than hard proof. Public vs private: Privately I know I am the last wolf and that the wolf win needs the lone killer gone and parity reached; the table sees only an unverified choice between suspects with no sure wolf among them.
lessons.action: As the last living wolf in a 3-4 player endgame, vote to eliminate any non-wolf player, joining whichever other voter can make a plurality. If the lone killer is still alive, prioritize it because the wolves cannot win while it lives; otherwise remove a town or neutral player to reach parity. Count the votes first so your own name cannot take the plurality, since losing the last wolf ends the game.

lessons.situation: A split day vote where the Town claimants disagree, and a no-elimination tie would keep a rival killer alive to thin Town overnight. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims (investigator, sentinel, healer) but with no confirmed evil targets and an unconfirmed Night 1 event. Stakes: Town can't afford another night of attrition, so a tie that keeps a killer alive favors the evil side. This only pays if your own elimination isn't within reach of the vote. Consensus: Town is split across several wagons with no agreement on who is evil, and there are rival claims from the investigator, sentinel and healer. My position: Driving a minority wagon, aiming for a tie, not a majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A claimed vigilante has voted for you and a claimed healer is questioning your narrative. Forward exposure: A vote on a contested suspect commits you to a push a claimed healer has already questioned, and you take heat if the target flips Town. The vote is visible and permanent, but a tie costs little because nobody is eliminated. Target landscape: A suspected killer voted by a claimed investigator, a quiet unaligned player voted by a claimed healer and the suspect, and you voted by a claimed vigilante. The reads rest on claims and unconfirmed night results, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know a suspect has night immunity or a role that helps your side. Publicly that is unconfirmed, so Town doubts the push against them.
lessons.action: If you are not the main target and a killer or other threat still threatens Town, vote for a plausible suspect who is already contested so the votes split into a tie. A tie means no elimination and gives the threat another night to cut Town's power roles. If your own heat is high and a vigilante-type is voting you, skip this and consolidate onto the leading wagon instead.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear direction. The discussion treats the claimed Sentinel's result cautiously and is seeking additional information; no vote target has been established.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and the leading evil faction needs four eliminations to reach parity; a single vote or kill cannot end the game, though an unsupported elimination could still cost the village a scarce player.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: no one has accused or singled you out in the discussion.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved, with two public Night 1 deaths and revealed roles, but no wills or private results publicly verified. The Sentinel claim is unverified, and its reported visit is compatible with the Trailseer's role.
query_dims.my_position: Not driving and not visibly aligned with a forming majority; you have not stated a position in the discussion.
query_dims.situation: On the first voting day, a claimed Sentinel reported that the player revealed as Trailseer visited the watched player on Night 1. The room recognizes this could be the Trailseer's ordinary follow action, so the result neither implicates the watched player nor identifies who killed the Trailseer; no competing concrete lead has surfaced.
query_dims.target_landscape: No elimination candidate has emerged. The living player claiming Sentinel is unverified; their account that the revealed Trailseer visited the watched player is consistent with that role's follow action, but does not identify an attacker.

lessons.situation: First vote day (Day 2) after a night-1 death. The village has only unverified claims (counter-claims, a Sentinel report, a roleblock claim) and must either eliminate a claimant or abstain. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified night claims, one hidden or concealed body, no confirmed roles or voting records. Stakes: Early game with plenty of margin; a single vote is unlikely to decide the game, but a majority-aligned vote keeps the Fortune Teller safe to keep betting and scoring points. Consensus: The room is largely aligned (near-unanimous or a broad abstain) on the basis of unverified claims and claim logic, not confirmed information. My position: With the majority. Heat: Low; no one has accused the Fortune Teller, who has spoken little or only asked a question. Target landscape: Two or more contradictory role claimants (Investigator or Healer counter-claims) or no standout suspect; the first-night victim's role is hidden or revealed; no roles confirmed; the only evidence is unverified claims and behavior.
lessons.action: On the Day 2 vote, with no hard evidence and low heat, vote with the room's emerging majority. If a counter-claim fight has one side backed by a concrete accusation or a claimed watch placing them at a door, vote against that side; if nothing concrete exists, join the abstain or no-elimination majority. Your points come from night bets, so stay low-profile and keep the town's vote from splitting.

lessons.situation: First vote of the game (day 2) after one or two night deaths. The Fortune Teller has no private information, since its bets give only points and no reads on roles. Town claimants accuse each other of roleblocking or fabricating, and the vote is the only lever before the next night bet. Information landscape: Starved: unverifiable claims (sentinel watch, trailseer follow, roleblock report), one or two public deaths, and no confirmed roles among the living. Stakes: Early game with many players alive. No single vote decides the game, but an elimination removes a threat, and a wasted split vote lets the wolves and the killer act with no pressure. Consensus: Mixed: sometimes a lopsided pile-on built on cross-matching claims, sometimes a split among abstain and several suspects. Either way it rests on unverified claims. My position: With the majority or in a minority cluster; not driving the vote. Heat: Low. The Fortune Teller has said little or nothing, made no claim, and nobody has accused it. Target landscape: Two or three candidates with no confirmed roles: one accused by several claimed Town roles whose claims cross-match, another who admitted a blocked night and gave no result, and a quiet suspect. The basis is behavior and unverifiable claims, not evidence.
lessons.action: On the first vote with no private evidence, when the room is converging on a suspect backed by multiple independent claims that cross-match, vote with that consensus rather than abstaining or splitting onto a quiet or lone-claim target. If the room is scattered across several weak suspects, vote for the target with the most concrete claim friction instead of a different long shot, so the vote helps produce an elimination.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a hidden lone killer (Necromancer) alive and a claimant whose night report conflicts with the rules; the village must choose between that inconsistency and other unconfirmed players, and I (fortune teller) am among the targets. Information landscape: Mostly behavioral: rules-contradicting claims, partial visit confirmations, and a few confirmed deaths; no hard role confirmations on the living candidates. Stakes: Few players remain and a lone killer is still hidden, so each wrong vote can cost Town an information role and bring the killers closer to winning; a correct vote can end the lone killer faction. Consensus: Village is leaning toward one target on the basis of behavior and a rules inconsistency; no confirmed roles among survivors and a lone killer still hidden. My position: With the majority, sometimes driving the argument. Heat: Moderate: one or more votes or a counter-accusation landed on me, but the room did not back it strongly. Target landscape: Claimed info roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist) with no confirmed roles; one has a report contradicting the rules, another is a suspect steering suspicion onto unconfirmed players; I am among the scattered vote targets.
lessons.action: When the lone killer is still hidden and a claimant's report contradicts the stated rules (e.g. an omitted own visit, or a 'no visits' result on a night a body was hidden), vote with the accusers on that contradiction rather than drifting onto a lone-vote side. If a vote has already picked up a player who attacked the unconfirmed players or a verified-night-evidence suspect, prefer that suspect over a pure rules-slip claimant, since a slip may be a genuine townie's misreport.

lessons.situation: A necromancer-revealing night (reanimated vigilante shot, sigil strike) is confirmed; the suspect deflects suspicion toward unconfirmed players, and the village is consolidating its vote against the suspect. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed role deaths, announced reanimated attacks, a verified sigil strike, and an investigator's will clearing one living player. Stakes: Removing the lone killer here ends that faction, so one vote shifts which side is winning; joining the majority also takes me out of the line of fire. Consensus: The majority, including cleared town players, is converging on the suspect on the basis of verified night events (reanimated kill, sigil strike) and the suspect's own steering. My position: With the majority. Heat: Moderate: the suspect explicitly called for testing unconfirmed players, which puts scrutiny on me. Target landscape: The suspect steering votes onto unconfirmed players versus the remaining unconfirmed player and a claimed sigilist whose action was verified by the morning report; an investigator's will cleared one living player.
lessons.action: When a suspected killer is publicly pointing scrutiny at the unconfirmed players (including you), cast your vote with the cleared or town-aligned majority on that suspect, so your vote sits on the consensus side and not among the minority votes that land on you. This keeps your standing safe at no cost, since a fortune teller's win depends only on banked bet points and the vote does not score.

lessons.situation: A day vote where the village converges on a main suspect while the Fortune Teller, a neutral with no side to defend, is unaligned. Splitting from the room costs safety and gains nothing: the wolves or other killers note any vote against their partner and use it to pick you at night. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed role results, a visit report at a victim's door and public voting records are all available. None of it is confirmed beyond what the Game Master announced. Stakes: Mid-game board where a single wasted or rogue vote does little to the count, but drawing a night kill before scoring two points ends your win condition. Staying unnoticed matters more than being first to guess right. Consensus: Strong, near-unanimous agreement on one suspect, built on a claimed Sentinel's visit report and the previous day's voting record. My position: Tempted to hold out with an isolated vote or abstain, against the majority. Heat: Little or none: you have spoken minimally and are not on anyone's suspect list. Target landscape: Two or more players named by a claimed Sentinel or by public vote records; one is the clear main suspect of the room. The evidence is public but unverified claims and voting behavior, and you hold no private proof of your own.
lessons.action: When the room has formed an overwhelming consensus on a main suspect backed by public evidence such as a claimed watch or voting records, and you are not under suspicion, vote with the majority on that suspect. An isolated dissenting vote or a pointless abstain marks you as a rogue voter and can make you a night-kill target. You need to stay alive to score your two points.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and a vigilante claims a target was immune to a night attack. Someone asks you whether you self-bet, since a self-bet is the only other source of immunity. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed wolf deaths, a public sigil death confirming the sigilist, an immunity claim, and your own denial removing the alternative explanation. Stakes: With the wolves gone, only the lone killer stands between town and a win. A correct vote here can end the game, and a misvote lets the killer keep killing. Consensus: The village is largely aligned (about five of six votes) on one suspect, on the basis of confirmed wolf deaths, a sigil death and a night-immunity claim. My position: With the majority; your public answer helped form it. Heat: Low: nobody is accusing you, and your direct answer about self-betting was accepted. Target landscape: A lone credible target, the claimed night-immune player (serial killer suspect), backed by a vigilante immunity claim, a visitor trace at a concealed death, and a contradicted Trailseer claim. The only other explanation for the immunity is a Fortune Teller self-bet, which you can rule out.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on a suspect and you have low heat, vote with the majority on the best-supported target. If another player asks whether you self-bet, answer plainly and truthfully, because ruling out your own self-bet removes the main alternative explanation for a night-immunity claim and lets the town commit to the serial killer vote.

lessons.situation: Four players left with a wolf and possibly a lone killer alive; the vote kills the likely last wolf but could leave an armed lone killer behind or end the game before the Fortune Teller scores a second point. Information landscape: Moderately rich: revealed roles, morning reports naming attack types, and earlier votes, but who is the lone killer versus the last wolf remains inferred. Stakes: One elimination could hand Town the game or leave a lone killer free to shoot with no wolf to take the night attack, so the vote changes who wins and whether the Fortune Teller scores. Consensus: Village is converging, often near unanimously, on one target based on claims and morning reports, while a quieter suspect is ignored. My position: With the majority, voting for the consensus target. Heat: Low: not under accusation and had stayed quiet; at most receiving a stray defensive vote from a doomed player. Target landscape: Two or three living candidates; at least one probable last wolf, plus a possible lone killer. Roles are unconfirmed and read from claims, the morning kill reports, and revealed dead roles.
lessons.action: Before voting in a late-game day, count your banked points and which killers remain. If one more point would win it for you and the vote would end the game, or a surviving killer would otherwise have free night kills, weigh whether ending the game now is worth more than staying alive for a night bet. If you are under 2 points and the vote would end the game anyway, a Town win does not give you a win, so favor the vote only if you are sure of the target.

lessons.situation: With one wolf confirmed dead the previous day, the sigilist accuses the player who resisted the tracking claims. You back the accusation and vote, and the target defends himself using that same earlier wolf vote. Information landscape: Moderately informed: one confirmed wolf death and a vote record, but the target's guilt rests on timing and behavior, and other night killers remain unknown. Stakes: Several killers are still alive, so any wrong vote costs town. Your own survival is still at risk at night and you have no points yet. Consensus: The village backs the sigilist's accusation, one wolf is already confirmed dead, and the vote record gives behavioral grounds. My position: Driving alongside the accuser, then with the majority. Heat: Low to moderate: you made an argument against the target, but nobody is accusing you. Target landscape: A suspect who resisted the tracking claims and joined the previous wagon late, versus quiet players the suspect tried to redirect suspicion toward. The basis is behavioral (skepticism, vote timing), with no hard evidence.
lessons.action: When you have no points yet and your heat is low, vote for the behaviorally most suspicious player alongside a credible accuser, and explain your reasoning aloud (for example, that a wolf can bus onto a doomed partner's wagon). A day vote never scores for you, so use it to push town toward removing evil, but do not count on it to advance your own two-point goal.

lessons.situation: Late game (day 5 or 6): a rival claims my same neutral role and we accuse each other. The vote is a close split, and an elimination of me would end my path to scoring points. Information landscape: Starved: incompatible role claims, unverifiable claims from others, and only a single confirmed result; the rest is behavioral reads. Stakes: With about four alive, one vote can eliminate me or a key player; a tie preserves my remaining bets and a wrong elimination could hand the killer or wolves the win. Consensus: The room is split into two camps with no majority; votes tie and no single player is clearly favored. My position: Holding out against one side, aligned with one other player, and helping keep the vote deadlocked. Heat: High: the Investigator and the counterclaimant are voting for me, and my claim and my self-exclusion from the suspect pool were challenged as unsupported. Target landscape: Three or four survivors, none with a verified role: a counterclaimant to my Fortune Teller role, a Sigilist whose claim is unverifiable, and an Investigator whose results are confirmed. One of them is the remaining killer, and the reads rest on claim conflict and voting alignment rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When you are the main target of a late-game day vote with few players alive, vote sincerely for the player whose evidence or claims you find least credible, ideally one who counterclaimed your role or is pushing your elimination. If a deadlock or tie results, that keeps you alive for further bets, so hold your vote steady unless a clearly better read emerges.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a night attack. A claimed Investigator brings a Suspicious read on a player who defends by calling the result ambiguous or by claiming Healer against a counterclaim. The village converges on that player, and I am a neutral Fortune Teller who scores by bets on night deaths. Information landscape: Moderately rich: a claimed Investigator read, partly confirmed by an earlier reveal, plus a Healer counterclaim or public attack evidence. Nothing about the target's role is system-confirmed. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several threats alive (wolves plus a lone killer). Each wolf removed delays parity and keeps me alive to place my remaining night bets, so a correct majority vote is high value and one vote rarely decides the outcome. Consensus: Most of the village agrees on the Investigator's target. Support rests on a confirmed earlier read or a coherent Healer counterclaim, with little dissent. My position: With the majority. Heat: Low to moderate: I only made clarifying or skeptical remarks about the evidence and have not been accused or addressed. Target landscape: One accused player flagged Suspicious by a claimed Investigator whose earlier read was confirmed or whose claim is supported by a Healer counterclaim. The accused has no confirmed role and defends only with reasoning (for example that the read could mean the Necromancer), with no competing suspect. The basis is a partly confirmed check plus the accused's weak defense.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote, when a claimed Investigator whose earlier read was confirmed (or who is backed by a Healer counterclaim) names a Suspicious target and the village is converging, vote with that majority. A Suspicious read means a wolf, or a Necromancer on a night it attacked, and either one is a kill you want removed, so a vote on a Suspicious target needs no further proof to be worth casting. Ambiguity in the accused's defense alone is not a reason to hold out.

lessons.situation: Day vote after a double attack on a Town role that the healer stopped. The village is deciding who is operating a dead role's body, and the Fortune Teller sits low-heat outside the discussion. Information landscape: Moderate: the public double-attack report, some revealed roles and behavioral reads, but nothing directly tying the target to the lone killer. Stakes: The majority can remove the target without your vote. Joining it adds little numerically but keeps you aligned and visible as a participant. Consensus: Four or more players are converging on one suspect from vote history and deflection, with no hard role evidence. My position: Holding out by abstaining while the majority forms without me. Free to join it instead. Heat: Low: quiet, not named, no confirmed alignment but not under direct accusation. Target landscape: A player who voted against the room the day before and pushed deflection, and a player the healer protected. The evidence is behavioral plus the previous night's attack on a Town role.
lessons.action: When your heat is low and a majority is converging on a suspect backed by vote history or the previous night's attack pattern, cast your own vote with it instead of abstaining. A lone killer removed by a visible majority helps Town win, which is the side you share a win with, and your vote on the record keeps you aligned with the room. If the room is split and no case is evidence-backed, vote for the best-supported behavioral candidate.

lessons.situation: Day 5 with four alive after a key town death: each survivor votes against a different player, and I am accused by an ally while a wolf pushes suspicion toward me. Information landscape: Rich: a confirmed sigil strike verified one player as town, two wolf-side deaths are revealed, and the wolf's steering toward me is on record. Stakes: With four alive, removing a wolf shrinks the killer count, but the remaining lone killer may then target me; the vote decides who is left against me. Consensus: Votes are split one-against-one among all four survivors, with no majority forming. My position: Holding out in a split vote, choosing my own target instead of following any bloc. Heat: High: a confirmed-town player suspects me and credits me with starting a wagon, and a wolf is leaning on me. Target landscape: Two or three suspects left: a wolf who has been steering suspicion toward me and another town role, and a lone killer who deflected my name; one confirmed-town ally whose role was shown by a sigil strike. The choice rests on revealed wolf-side deaths and observed accusation patterns.
lessons.action: When a confirmed-town player (such as a sigil-verified Sigilist) exists and the wolves are still being whittled down, vote for the suspect who has been steering suspicion toward you or other town players. Prefer eliminating a wolf-side player that was pushing your name, since that removes a vote against you and reduces the killers' numbers.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day vote with several unconfirmed players left. A wagon is forming on a Town-looking player through argument or suspicion of silence. The fortune teller has no investigative information of its own. Information landscape: Mixed, leaning behavioral. A night death has been confirmed, but the accusations in the vote are only claims and reads. Stakes: Seven players are alive with wolves and a lone killer still in play. A wrong Town lynch costs Town a voice and brings it closer to evil parity. The fortune teller must also survive long enough to score two points. Consensus: The table is split between two candidates and is converging on one by momentum and argument, not on evidence. Confirmed facts exist only about earlier deaths. My position: Not yet committed. You could drive the wagon with an early vote, or follow once the majority is clear. Heat: Low to moderate. You have not been accused, but an early vote would tie your name to the wagon. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed candidates. One is a vocal accuser or critic of a player who looks reliable. Another is a quiet player. The case against each is an argument or inactivity, with no hard role evidence.
lessons.action: When the day's case rests only on arguments or behavior and you have no confirmed lead, wait until other players have voted and the wagon is visible before you cast your vote. Do not be the first vote on an argument-only target, because the first voter gets blamed for the wagon if the target turns out to be Town. Your night bets are what score, and a day vote never does, so keep your heat low.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame day vote with the wolves mostly or fully gone. The village is hunting the remaining lone killer among a few unconfirmed players, and the Fortune Teller is one of the suspects. Information landscape: Partly information-rich: dead roles, claims and vote records are known. Which unconfirmed player is the lone killer is still speculative. Stakes: A tie or majority on the Fortune Teller costs the player and all remaining self-bets. One vote can decide which suspect the village removes. Consensus: The village is split between two or three targets and heading for a plurality or a tie. No hard evidence settles it. My position: Not yet committed. Free to join the plurality that forms and keep the vote off me. Heat: Moderate to high: a couple of elimination votes are already on the Fortune Teller as an unaccounted-for, unclaimed role. Target landscape: Several unconfirmed players, including a quiet unclaimed player, a late claimer and the Fortune Teller. Cases rest on behavior and vote history, with no hard evidence tying anyone to the lone killer.
lessons.action: When two or more votes are already on you, vote sincerely for the leading behavioral suspect who is not you, so a plurality forms on someone else and you avoid a tie or majority on yourself. Prefer a suspect whose case rests on recorded votes or deflection rather than a pure quiet-player read. You need to survive to keep placing nightly bets, because a day vote never scores.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote with 3-4 players left; a claim conflict (a fake counter-claim of my role, or a conflicting watch claim) decides whether the last killer or wolf survives. Information landscape: Moderately rich: revealed roles of the dead, prior public votes, and my own private knowledge (my bets and self-bet results), but other players' night results remain unverified claims. Stakes: With few players left, a single wrong vote or a no-elimination lets the killers reach their win count; the vote can end the game for Town. Consensus: Village is small and splitting between two claims; the Town-aligned players lean toward the same target on the basis of the revealed deaths and the consistency of claims. My position: Driving the majority or joining it early with a repeated vote. Heat: Moderate: a counter-claimant has accused me of being false, but at least one Town-claiming player has sided with me. Target landscape: Two or three living suspects, no confirmed roles among them: a counter-claimant of my own role whom I know is lying, versus a Town-claiming player whose claims are unverified but consistent with the revealed night deaths. The evidence is private knowledge and revealed dead roles, not behavior alone.
lessons.action: In a small endgame vote (3-4 alive), vote to eliminate the player whose claims your own private knowledge shows to be false (for example a counter-claimant to your Fortune Teller role), and the player whose claim fits the night events and the revealed deaths. Keep voting the same target consistently, because it pulls the other town-aligned voters into a majority and a wrong abstention or split could hand the killers the game.

lessons.situation: A day vote after a night kill or a wolf flip, where one player's explanation of their behavior or role has been contradicted by other claims or reports and a majority is forming against them. Information landscape: Moderately to fairly rich: a confirmed wolf flip, a hidden-role kill, visit reports and rival claims, but nothing confirms the target's role directly. Stakes: Wolves are being removed one at a time, and each correct vote narrows the board toward the lone killer. A wrong vote wastes a day and thins Town, so only a vote backed by revealed facts and contradictions justifies joining the push. Consensus: The room is converging on one suspect, based on a wolf flip, contradicting claims and voting records, and the accusers are mostly players with consistent stories. My position: With the majority, or driving the push alongside it. Heat: Low to moderate: not accused, other players are in the spotlight, and any pressure you drew came from being an active accuser. Target landscape: Several candidates, with one player standing out: either a defender of a flipped wolf who gave shifting excuses, or a player whose claimed role was contradicted by a rival claim and a follow report. No system-confirmed role on the target; the case rests on contradictions and revealed partners, not on a hard result.
lessons.action: When a revealed wolf flip or a contradicted role claim leaves one player with a story that conflicts with independent reports, vote to eliminate that player alongside the majority. If your own read points at a different suspect and the contradiction is not clear, hold your vote on your own suspect instead of following the room.

lessons.situation: The town must eliminate someone without investigative leads, and the majority is choosing a target on behavioral grounds. Lynching a power role would hand a lone killer (a necromancer) a usable body and an attacker. Information landscape: Behavioral only for the remaining pool. Confirmed facts cover earlier night events, not who is evil now. Stakes: A mistaken lynch of a power role can swing the endgame. A lone killer using a dead Vigilante's body can attack through it and kill more players, including you. Each vote has real weight. Consensus: The majority leans toward the quiet player on inactivity grounds. A minority backs the pushback player. Nobody has verified evidence. My position: With the majority, or about to join it, without an evidence-based reason of your own. Heat: None to low. You have no accusations against you and are aligned with the room. Target landscape: A quiet unconfirmed player suspected only for lack of claims, versus an unconfirmed player who pushed back on town information. Neither has hard evidence against them. Silent players may be power roles.
lessons.action: Vote for the candidate whose case rests on a concrete contradiction or a confirmed fact, such as a claim that conflicts with an announced result. If the cases are only inactivity or a clash of arguments and abstaining is offered, abstain instead of joining a speculative lynch. A silent player may be a Town role holding unused power, such as a vigilante with bullets, and a lynch reveals the role only after it is too late to undo.

query_dims.consensus_text: No village consensus has formed; the room is fragmented after the sentinel lynch, with the sigilist claim being the only fresh public statement and no shared target emerging.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; no single elimination ends the game, so a wrong lynch is recoverable but each mistake shortens the margin toward a wolf or necromancer win.
query_dims.heat_now: Low on me: I have made no claims and have no accusations aimed at me; my only public exposure is the night bets which have scored once and missed twice.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only tested reports are the dead sentinel's night 1 watch, now unverifiable, and the sigilist's unverified claim; no living player has a confirmed result to share.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out, with no stated position against any forming consensus and making no claim.
query_dims.situation: Day 4 with five players alive after a sentinel lynch and two night kills of town-side roles. A player claiming sigilist says their sigil struck the chanteuse last night and is holding the last sigil for a clear attacker, while the wolves' remaining members are still hidden and no vote has been held since the day 3 lynch.
query_dims.target_landscape: Five living players: player_3, player_8, player_9 (claims sigilist, sigil placed on a dead chanteuse), player_10, and me (fortune teller, unrevealed). Public role status: dead are trailseer, vigilante, sentinel, chanteuse, investigator; no living player has a verified role except the sigilist claim, which is unconfirmed by any announcement and only a single claim. Evidence basis is mostly day-2 vote history and the dead sentinel's night 1 claim, which is now dead-end.

lessons.situation: Day 2 after a night-1 death. Conflicting or unverifiable role claims (Investigator, Healer, Trailseer, Sentinel) dominate the discussion, and you are an uncommitted neutral with both self-bets unused. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims, one or two unconfirmed night reports, and a night-1 body, with no caught lies, no votes, and no confirmed wolf identities. Stakes: Early game with many players alive. No single vote or kill decides the game, so staying alive and unexposed to keep betting each night matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: Split or drifting: the room argues over rival claims or abstains, with no hard evidence behind any side. My position: Holding out in the middle or going with the majority, contributing a clarification without driving the vote. Heat: Very low: you have not been named, addressed, or accused, and you have not revealed your role. Target landscape: Two or more rival role claimants (e.g. two Investigators, or two Healers) or one scrutinized claimant, resting on unverified reports and timing. No confirmed wolves, and the night-1 victim's role is either announced or hidden.
lessons.action: When you are an unclaimed, low-heat Fortune Teller on day 2 in an info-starved room of conflicting claims, keep your role hidden and make one short, sincere contribution that shapes the discussion without accusing anyone. Good examples are a procedural point about visit direction, or a note that a hidden-role or dead role means a claim may not be genuine, or a direct question to a player a report ties to a contradiction. This keeps you out of the crossfire while still adding value, since your win depends on night bets rather than on how the vote goes.

lessons.situation: Late-game day discussion after the wolves are revealed dead; a player's claimed night result is being explained away and the Fortune Teller is asked directly whether a self-bet caused it. Information landscape: Fairly rich: public wolf reveals, a healer save and a sigil death are announced, while the claimed immunity result is still a private claim that my answer can corroborate. Stakes: Few players remain, so one correct vote on the lone killer decides the game; clearing the self-bet explanation lets the town converge on the right target. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on weighing the claimed immunity result; wolves are already confirmed dead, so the debate is about the remaining killer and the unverified claim. My position: With the majority, answering a direct question and removing the main objection. Heat: Moderate and specific: a player floated that I might have bet on myself, making me a possible alternative explanation for the result. Target landscape: A player accused via a claimed night result (e.g. a serial killer said to be immune) versus the credibility of the claimant; the only alternative explanation is the Fortune Teller's own self-bet. Evidence is a private claim plus public deaths and reveals.
lessons.action: When a player directly asks whether your self-bet explains an odd night result (e.g. a claimed immunity), answer plainly and truthfully on whether you self-bet that night; if you didn't, say so and name whom you bet on. This removes the competing explanation, makes the other player's claim the best available evidence, and costs little because a Fortune Teller cannot be blocked and reads Not suspicious.

lessons.situation: Day 4 with most evil already dead. A claimant's reported results look inconsistent with the rules, and you are the main driver of the case against them. Information landscape: Info-rich on mechanics but conflicted on identity. The contradiction is checkable, but the claimant's honesty is in doubt and a real Town role may be misread. Stakes: Few evil players remain, so one wrong elimination can hand the last evil faction parity or remove Town's last investigative role. A visible driver of the vote is also an obvious night-kill target. Consensus: The room is converging on your rule argument, which makes a fast elimination of the claimant likely. My position: Driving the case as the first and most persistent voice. Heat: Moderate. The accused claimant counter-accused you of pushing too eagerly, though the rest of the room backed your argument. Target landscape: The only claimed role on the table, with unclaimed others. The basis for suspicion is a mechanical inconsistency in the claim, not a past check.
lessons.action: When you spot a rule-based contradiction in a claimant's account, state it once, clearly and as a question. Ask what else could explain it, and compare their answer with any counterclaims. Do not repeatedly assign a specific evil role to them, because other players will pile on and the mislynch can cost Town its last investigative role while exposing you to a night kill.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer reports tracking an accused player to the door of a night victim whose role was concealed, creating a confrontation over whether the visit is genuine. Information landscape: Mixed: one concealed night death and a single living claimed trailseer's report, with conflicting readings of the mechanics and no corroboration. Stakes: A wrong elimination would cost Town a body and bring the wolves closer to parity, but no single vote decides the game. The fortune teller benefits from a slower, evidence-driven day that keeps it unexposed. Consensus: The room is leaning toward acting on the trailseer's report, but with open doubt about whether the visit was fabricated or genuine and how concealment mechanics affect traces. My position: holding out Heat: Completely cold; participating neutrally with no suspicion directed at me. Target landscape: An accused player said to have visited a dead player whose role was concealed, versus the claimed trailseer making the accusation; evidence is a single uncorroborated claim.
lessons.action: When a high-stakes accusation rests on an unverifiable visit report and you have no heat, urge caution and ask what corroborating evidence exists. Point out how the stated rules (for example, an illusionist's concealment hiding the attacking trace) limit what such a report can prove. This makes you look measured and analytical and keeps you from being drawn into a rushed elimination.

lessons.situation: Day 4, shortly after a wolf flip and a concealed-role kill. One player voted against the consensus on the previous day, and you can ask them to justify it. Information landscape: A confirmed wolf flip, a concealed-role kill, and a public vote record. Few other facts are verified, so most reads rest on behavior. Stakes: The village is mid-game with evil still alive. A cheap question can surface a claim and a counterclaim fight without committing you to an elimination, and it keeps you alive for the later days. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned after a confirmed flip and a recorded vote pattern, and it is receptive to follow-up questions about odd votes. My position: With the majority, steering the question toward the dissenter without leading an accusation. Heat: Low. You have said little publicly and earlier mild skepticism has not been held against you. Target landscape: Survivors with no confirmed roles except what flips have shown. One player was the lone dissenter in the last vote, and all other reads are behavioral.
lessons.action: When a confirmed flip or kill pattern leaves one player as the lone dissenter in the earlier vote, ask them to explain the deviation instead of accusing them. Their answer, whether a claim, a trace, or a dodge, gives the room something to test and moves attention off you. If they give a claim or trace, hold your read until the room has cross-checked it against other claims.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a wolf is revealed dead and further kills were concealed; a lead accuser targets a suspect who defends himself with his vote on the dead wolf. Information landscape: Moderately thin: one confirmed wolf and a voting record, but concealed bodies and otherwise only claims and behavioral inference. Stakes: Midgame with enough players that one vote does not decide the game, but removing a wolf now cuts the wolves' parity threat and the pool of kill sources; the public result may also make me a likelier kill target. Consensus: The room is forming around one suspect, based on the dead wolf's revealed role and voting records rather than hard proof. My position: With the majority, as the second accuser. Heat: Low to moderate: aligned with the lead accuser, nothing exposing said, bets unscored and role undisclosed. Target landscape: A suspect accused of echoing a dead wolf's line who points to his vote on that wolf as proof of innocence, plus quiet players he deflects onto. Only one wolf role is confirmed; the rest is behavioral and voting-record reading.
lessons.action: With a confirmed wolf dead and no night result of your own to share, join the leading accusation against the player whose behavior best fits the dead wolf's. Give a concrete reason, such as a wolf piling onto a doomed partner to blend in, and keep your role and bet history private. If the accusation is led by a player you distrust, state your own independent read instead of echoing it.

lessons.situation: Late game with three players left: you and a copycat both claim Fortune Teller, and a single third player's vote decides which of you is eliminated. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified results, only claims, but a detailed bet history against a thin copy creates an asymmetry the voter can check against the public record. Stakes: With three alive, one vote decides the game: eliminating the false claimant can end it in your favor, while losing the vote likely means your death and a loss. Consensus: Split and starved of hard evidence; the outcome depends on one remaining voter judging whose account is more detailed and consistent. My position: Driving the case against the counterclaimant while holding out against their accusation. Heat: High: under a counterclaim, tied in votes, and your claim cannot be independently verified. Target landscape: Two Fortune Teller claimants (you and a false claimant, likely the necromancer) plus one unconfirmed swing voter whose own claim cannot be verified; the false claimant's bets match only public deaths, while your history has specifics that fit the record.
lessons.action: When a rival claims Fortune Teller (or your claim is otherwise disputed) in a late-game room with few players left, state your claim plainly and give your full bet history: which nights, whom you bet on, the role named, which bets scored, and the self-bets. Point out that a copycat's bets match only publicly known deaths while yours include specifics (wrong early bets, self-bets, role names) that fit the public record, and name the copycat as your top suspect so the swing voter has a concrete reason to side with you.

lessons.situation: Few players remain, the town power roles that could clear anyone are dead, and you are the first to publicly narrow the suspects to two. Information landscape: Information-starved on the key question: dead roles are known and one player is confirmed by an announced fact, but nothing separates the last two unknowns. Stakes: Near parity: every vote and night kill is decisive, and a visible lead on a point-short Fortune Teller invites the killer to remove you before you can score the final point. Consensus: The table accepted the narrowing and then debated voting order; the two suspects deflected onto each other with no firm direction. My position: Driving the framing with no personal lead on which suspect is the killer. Heat: Moderate-low: one earlier vote on a dead player is being cited against you, but no real suspicion. Target landscape: Two unaccounted-for players, with the dead roles known and one player confirmed by an announced sigil strike; no claims or checks separate the two, so any lean rests on voting-order behavior only.
lessons.action: When the pool of evil suspects is down to a few players and the town roles that could clear anyone are dead, state your narrowing and name your lead suspect, but deliver it as a shared conclusion alongside the confirmed player rather than leading it alone. If you are one point short of winning, avoid being the visible driver, since a lone-killer or wolf at the table can eliminate you at night.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four players remain, and the leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single death or vote can sharply change the winning position; concealing a victim could also withhold a role and will that might help the village identify the remaining wolf.
query_dims.forward_exposure: The pack's victim and any resulting death or save will be publicly reported. Using the remaining conceal would hide a dead victim's role and Town will, but would reveal that an illusionist conceal was used; it is irreversible once the body is concealed. No attack on a night-immune player has identified the Serial Killer through my private results; the Serial Killer was instead publicly eliminated on day 3.
query_dims.information_landscape: The board has substantial confirmed history: the Investigator and Trailseer died night 1, the claimed Sentinel's watched visits are unverified private-result claims, a wolf attack on that claimant was publicly saved night 2, and the Serial Killer and Chanteuse were publicly revealed on elimination. The night 3 victim's role and will remain hidden from everyone but me. There is no result from an attack on an immune player identifying the Serial Killer; that killer's elimination is public. The remaining candidates' roles and the purpose of their actions are largely unknown, so the present target choice is information-starved.
query_dims.situation: After the Chanteuse was eliminated and revealed as a wolf, I am the sole surviving wolf among four players, with the Serial Killer already eliminated. I must choose a night victim and whether to spend my final conceal; a successful kill leaves three alive, making the next elimination especially consequential. The previous concealed victim's role remains unknown to the village, though I privately learned they were the Fortune Teller.
query_dims.target_landscape: The living candidates are the player claiming Sentinel, whose two claimed watches are spent; the player who voted with the majority to eliminate the Chanteuse; and the player who also voted to eliminate the Chanteuse and was saved from the wolves on night 2. Their roles are otherwise unconfirmed. A death could reveal a Town role and will, while concealing it would deny the village that information. The Chanteuse is dead, so there is no living wolf partner to coordinate with; I am tonight's carrier.

lessons.situation: You are the last wolf with unspent conceals facing a daytime vote that may eliminate you, with confirmed town killers still alive. Information landscape: Partly information-rich: town roles are confirmed and your partner is dead, but a lone killer is only hinted at. Whether the healer will cover the target is unknown. Stakes: Dying with unused conceals wastes your remaining power. A successful hidden kill shrinks the town and obscures the evidence needed to eliminate you, while an idle night gains nothing. Forward exposure: A concealed kill still announces the attack and marks a wolf as alive, but the hidden role and hidden carrier trace give town no role or visit evidence. If the victim survives, the conceal is refunded and nothing is hidden, so the exposure is limited. Target landscape: Choose among players not just saved by the healer; the confirmed vigilante and sentinel are the threats worth removing, while quiet unverified players are the cheaper pick. Role status is mostly public.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with conceals in hand and town closing in, use a kill on a target the healer is unlikely to cover and conceal that victim's role. This hides your carrier visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer and denies town the role information, rather than skipping the night and giving up all pressure.

lessons.situation: Late game after the lone killer is gone, with one or two wolves left against a Town that still has an information role able to catch a wolf. The illusionist is choosing whether to commit a limited conceal on tonight's pack kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, claims and watch records are public, and voting records exist. The remaining private results are the main danger to the wolves. Stakes: The board is close to wolf parity, so one surviving investigative result can decide whether a wolf is exposed and voted out. Concealing the right victim's role and will removes that risk, but a charge spent on a harmless victim is wasted. Forward exposure: Concealing signals to the village that an illusionist is active and spends a charge that cannot be recovered. Hiding the body leaves no trace at the victim's door when the illusionist carries the kill. It does not erase the victim's earlier public claims or votes. Target landscape: Living Town investigators and watchers (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and unconfirmed players. Picks rest on who threatens the wolves' cover through private results, rather than on neutral or low-threat players.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a Town role whose private result or will would expose a wolf, such as an Investigator, Sentinel or Trailseer holding a result on you. Otherwise save the charge, since a hidden body does not erase what the victim already said or voted in public. If you carry the kill yourself, the concealed kill leaves no trace at the victim's door, so prefer that route when a watcher or follower is alive.

lessons.situation: You are the sole surviving wolf after your partner died, choosing the night kill while the healer is known to be active and protecting a publicly attacked player. Information landscape: Information-rich: the game master announced a save on the sentinel, and some town roles are confirmed. The wolves' own stats are known, but the healer's next protection is unknown. Stakes: With one wolf left and a lone killer possibly still alive, each night kill is critical. A wasted kill lets town investigators close in, while one real kill moves the wolves toward parity. Forward exposure: The kill is a lone carry that ties the night's attack to you as the only wolf. Once the target is chosen it is irreversible, and a wasted attack on a healer-covered target gains nothing and removes no town role. Target landscape: Candidates include a claimed sentinel already publicly saved by the healer, a claimed investigator with clears, a confirmed vigilante holding one bullet, and a quiet unverified player. The evidence is public announcements of the saves, not behavior.
lessons.action: As the last wolf, aim the pack kill at a player who was not publicly attacked and saved the previous night, such as a quiet unverified player or a confirmed threat the healer is not visibly guarding. Keep your conceals unspent until a kill is likely to succeed, since a conceal is refunded if the victim survives; if the healer's likely target is unclear, pick the target that was not the previous night's save.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a thin day with an abstain or tied vote. The wolves, with the chanteuse, have agreed a kill and the illusionist decides whether to hide the victim's role. A partner may have been told the conceals are for a high-impact target. Information landscape: Information-starved: few or no hard leads, a few unverified role claims, no trace results shared, and the wolves unsure where the serial killer or necromancer is acting. Stakes: Early game with several enemies still alive, so no single kill ends it. The two conceals are the pack's scarce tempo tool, and wasting one on a low-value body costs more than a day of town uncertainty gains. Forward exposure: A hidden-role morning report tells the town an illusionist is in the pack, and the use is spent permanently. The hidden role cannot be reversed, and the count of used conceals lets the town track you. Target landscape: The choice is between quiet unclaimed players, whose roles are unknown and chosen for low profile, and a self-claimed info role such as an investigator with a check left. The kill choice rests on role value and behavior, not hard evidence. A conceal on a quiet victim wasted a use on a sentinel nobody had claimed.
lessons.action: On a night-2-style kill, spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a claimed or high-impact info role whose confirmed death or role would help the town, such as an investigator-claimant with a check left. If the victim is a quiet, unclaimed player, keep both uses and let the role be revealed. A spent use is permanent, and the count of hidden-role deaths becomes the town's tool for tracking you.

lessons.situation: Late game after a tied day vote, you are the last wolf with no conceals left. You must pick a kill among the few remaining town players, who are contesting each other's claims. Information landscape: Info-rich on the town side (a confirmed read on the lone killer, claim conflicts), but the town has not yet worked out your role. Stakes: Two more eliminations bring you to parity. Each night kill decides whether you reach it before the town votes you out. Forward exposure: The kill reveals the victim's role and will, and your carrier visit is visible to any surviving watcher or follower. Because you are the next carrier, a sigil placed on you can strike, and the action cannot be undone. Target landscape: Four living town players (Sigilist, Healer, Investigator, Trailseer) with no hard reads. The Trailseer was chosen because their tracking results threatened your claim, on public behavior rather than evidence.
lessons.action: With no conceals left and you as the carrier, kill the player whose night result most directly threatens your cover, such as a Trailseer or Sentinel who has followed or watched you. Expect the revealed role and will to expose their record, so choose the target whose record does less damage than their living results would.

lessons.situation: Late game, you are the last wolf and lone carrier after your partner died, with one conceal left and trackers or watchers alive. You decide whether to carry and hide the kill.
