Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: some town confirmations exist (an Investigator's read on the lone killer), but the town has no read on you. Stakes: You are the only wolf left, so each kill must also keep you hidden. A trace-free kill gives you a night of cover, but the town is still ahead on numbers. Forward exposure: The morning report announces a hidden-role death, which shows town an illusionist exists and the conceal is spent. Afterward every kill is fully revealed, and the victim's true role (for example a Speculator's pick) may become public and either support or contradict your story. Target landscape: Several unclaimed town and neutral players with no hard reads on you. The victim is chosen from an unclaimed pool by behavior, not evidence, and a tracker who followed you only once is still alive.
lessons.action: As the last wolf with a conceal left, carry the kill yourself and conceal the victim, because an illusionist who carries and conceals leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer. Pick a victim whose role you do not need confirmed, and use the 'no visit' result a follower will report to build a cover story. Spend the conceal on a night when the carrier is you and a tracker or watcher is alive.

lessons.situation: Early night 2. Town power roles have claimed and reported night-1 results that threaten the wolves' cover. The pack agrees to kill one claimant, with the Illusionist deciding whether to spend one of its two conceals on that kill. Information landscape: Information-rich. Public claims and night-1 results are on the table, and day-2 vote records already show wolves voting together. A same-night partner death (sigil strike or Serial Killer) can expose the pack no matter what the Illusionist hides. Stakes: Mid-game with several town power roles alive. Removing a threatening claimant matters, but the conceal charges are scarce. Spending one where the role is already known gains little, and a wolf partner's death or vote record can confirm the pack anyway. Forward exposure: A conceal is irreversible and spends one of two charges. The morning report will say 'Their role is hidden by an illusionist', which confirms an Illusionist is in play. It hides the carrier's visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer, but it cannot hide a wolf partner's death or the voting records. Target landscape: Day-2 kill choices among self-claimed power roles (a claimed Trailseer or Sentinel reporting night-1 visits, a claimed Investigator) versus unrevealed players. The claimed roles are accusations based on claims, not verified results. Their roles are already public, so concealing the body adds little uncertainty.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the victim's role is still unclaimed, or when a living Sentinel or Trailseer could otherwise trace the carrier to the victim's door. If the victim has already publicly claimed their role and no tracker threatens the carrier, kill without concealing and keep both charges for a later night. When the Illusionist itself carries the kill, a conceal leaves no trace at that door, so favor it for that night.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later: the pack picks a claimed power role as the kill and the illusionist plans a conceal. A Healer claim or a previous protective visit to that target makes a save plausible, and the illusionist's own visit may be watched. Information landscape: Info-starved to thin: unverified claims, partial night-1 traces and one or two deaths. Hard facts are sparse, and the Healer's protection target is unknown. Stakes: With the pack down to one or two wolves, every visible visit risks heat and every failed kill wastes a night. A saved victim also leaves the illusionist as a known visitor, which can steer the vote toward the pack. Forward exposure: Your visit at the victim's door is irreversible. If the victim is saved, the conceal is kept but nothing is hidden, and the Sentinel or Trailseer sees you as a visitor. Target landscape: Claimed power roles (Investigator, Trailseer, Vigilante) are the obvious kill picks, but a Healer may have protected the same target before. Choosing is mostly a guess among living players, based on threat to the wolves rather than evidence.
lessons.action: When you are the carrier, or the pack's only wolf, and the kill target is a likely protected role (such as a claimed Investigator or Trailseer with a Healer visit onto them), prefer a target the Healer is less likely to guard, or accept that your visit may be seen. A conceal hides the carrier's visit only if the victim dies; if the Healer saves the victim, every visit to them stays visible to a Sentinel watch or a Trailseer follow, so do not rely on it as cover.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3. The pack has agreed to kill a vocal claimed investigative role, and the serial killer may be attacking the same player. The illusionist must decide whether a conceal is worth spending on this body. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich. Public claims, a tied or abstained day vote, and recorded votes exist, but most roles are unconfirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with parity still a few eliminations away. A wasted conceal costs the pack one of only two uses and gains little, while a well-placed one hides a role the town would otherwise learn. Forward exposure: Spending a conceal is irreversible and uses up a limited ability. On an already-public claim it buys almost no information denial, and the morning report still says an illusionist acted. Target landscape: The pack's candidate is a player who has publicly claimed Trailseer or Sigilist, unverified but already stated. Other candidates are unclaimed players whose roles would be new information if revealed. The pack picked the target on threat and claim rather than confirmed role.
lessons.action: Keep the conceal for a kill whose role the town does not yet know, such as an unclaimed or unverified player, where hiding the role and will denies real information. If the planned victim has already publicly claimed a role and shared results, let the role reveal stand and keep the use for a later night.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, after claims, deaths or votes have created information-bearing town roles. The pack picks a kill, and the illusionist decides whether to conceal the body of a role that matters. Information landscape: Moderately informed: some claims, bodies and records exist but are unverified. Concealing can deny the town role counts and confirmations. Stakes: With fewer players alive, each kill moves the pack closer to parity, and each revealed body feeds town deduction, or a Necromancer's use of the body. Denying role confirmation on a key kill matters more now than on night 1, and unspent conceals are worthless if the illusionist is voted out first. Forward exposure: Irreversible: it spends a use and announces that an illusionist is in play. If you carry the kill and conceal it, you leave no trace at that door. If another wolf carries, your hiding visit can still be seen by a Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Kill candidates are identified by claims or behavior, such as claimed information roles whose role or will would aid the town, rather than by a blind random pick. The pack's reads are partial and unconfirmed.
lessons.action: When the pack targets a town role whose revealed body or record would help the town, such as a claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator or Healer, carry the kill yourself and conceal it. A carrier who conceals leaves no trace at the victim's door, and the town gets neither a role nor a will. If you are not carrying, accept that your own visit stays visible to watchers and followers, and weigh that before spending the conceal.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with the pack choosing a kill while the partner Chanteuse blocks a second threat. The Illusionist decides whether the victim is worth a conceal to deny the town role information and trace. Information landscape: Info-moderate: several dead players have public wills, a few living claimants are unverified, and the town's picture of the remaining roles is incomplete. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, and a hidden role plus a missing trace can keep the town from confirming who is left. Late in the game each conceal is scarce and carries real weight. Forward exposure: Using a conceal makes the morning say an illusionist hid the role, so the town learns an illusionist exists, though not who. Each use is permanent and cannot be undone. Once both are spent, every later kill shows its role and the carrier's visit can be traced. Target landscape: Candidates are an unclaimed voter whose role is unknown, a claimed Trailseer whose follow results threaten the pack, and a claimed Vigilante who can be blocked instead of killed. All roles are unverified, and the choice rests on behavior and threat level, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: While conceals remain, put one on a night kill whose victim is an unverified or high-information-value player, or a tracking threat such as a claimed Trailseer. Hiding the role also removes the carrier's visit to that victim from a Sentinel's watch or a Trailseer's follow, and leaves the town unsure which role is gone. Keep the last conceal for the kill where that traceless result matters most.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, night 2 or 3. The pack has a failed or contested night behind it and agrees to remove a claimed protector or information role. The carrier makes the kill, perhaps while the Chanteuse blocks another claimant, and the Illusionist decides whether to conceal the body. Information landscape: Moderate information: save announcements, conflicting role claims, and Sentinel or Trailseer reports that are claims only. Nothing about the victim's role is confirmed by the Game Master. Stakes: The board is mid-game, with the pack still a few eliminations from parity and a lone killer possibly alive. Removing the protector or the information source without giving the town a confirmed role widens the pack's lead. A failed kill leaves the wolves exposed to the Healer and the Vigilante. Forward exposure: The conceal is spent only if the victim dies; a save keeps it and leaves nothing hidden. Once spent it cannot be recovered. A hidden body gives the town no role or will, but it also tells them the Illusionist exists and that the pack made the kill. Target landscape: Candidates are publicly claimed power roles: a claimed Healer inferred from a save announcement, a claimed Sentinel whose watch tied a partner to a scene, and a rival Investigator claimant leading an accusation. All are unverified, and the pack picks them on behavior and public logic rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack's agreed kill is a claimed power role (Healer, Investigator or Sentinel) whose confirmed role or will would help the town, spend a conceal on it. The conceal costs nothing if the victim is saved, since the use is kept, so commit even without knowing the Healer's target. When the victim dies, the town cannot verify the claim and the pack loses nothing it needed to hide.

lessons.situation: Your partner carries the kill, or you do, on a role that has already claimed publicly. You have one conceal left and must decide whether to spend it or save it. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims, with several roles claiming results, but nothing verified. Stakes: With no extra conceals after this one, each use should hide something that cannot be inferred from claims. A revealed will carries a limited cost, but spending the last conceal on an already claimed role removes your flexibility for later kills. Forward exposure: Letting the body be revealed publishes the victim's role and any Town will, which may confirm their visit records. This is a one-night choice, and the conceal charge stays available for a later night. Target landscape: A claimed Town power role, such as a Sentinel with a public claim, is the pack's target. Other claimed power roles are active, and the claims are not confirmed.
lessons.action: If you have only one conceal left and the victim's role is already public from a claim, or the victim's will would reveal little, hold the conceal and let the role be announced. Keep it for a later kill of an unclaimed or higher-value role, and use the night's blocks and coordination on other threats.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a close or tied day vote. The wolves are killing a player who drew vote suspicion. Sentinel and Trailseer have been active or have claimed results. Information landscape: Day talk produced a healer claim, a watch result and a follow result, but nothing hard on the wolves. Watchers are plausibly active and you cannot tell which door they chose. Stakes: Mid-early board where being exposed as the illusionist costs the pack a key wolf. The marginal value of hiding an ordinary victim's role is small next to the risk of a logged visit turning suspicion onto you. Forward exposure: If you are not the carrier, your hide-visit is still seen by a watcher on the victim's door, which can lead to a day accusation against you. The conceal cannot be undone and costs a charge, and the pack's kill visit stays hidden either way. Target landscape: The victim is a quiet or lightly suspected player pulled into a day vote, with no confirmed role. A watcher may be on the same door, and the reason to hide is that the reveal could clear them or point at the voters.
lessons.action: With a Sentinel or Trailseer plausibly active and the day having produced watch or follow claims, conceal only when you are the carrier, or when the secrecy of the victim's role clearly outweighs the risk of your hide-visit being logged. Otherwise keep the charge and let the pack's kill resolve unconcealed, because a visit seen at the victim's door can get you accused and eliminated.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game, no day-1 vote, no claims. The illusionist and chanteuse agree on a default kill, and the illusionist weighs spending one of two conceals on a victim of unknown role. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, claims, votes or night results. The only knowledge is the pack's private plan. Stakes: The board is early and far from parity, so a single kill is not decisive. The scarce resource is the two conceals, which are worth more on a later high-value body than on a blind first kill. A spent conceal on a neutral or low-value body is wasted, and an unspent one also stays usable by a Necromancer through a revealed body. Forward exposure: Holding costs nothing and is reversible. Spending a conceal is irreversible, announces that an illusionist exists, and leaves your own visit visible to a Sentinel or Trailseer unless you carried the kill yourself. Not carrying also leaves no trace on you. Target landscape: The pack's night-1 victim is an arbitrary quiet player with no claims or behavioral evidence. Nobody knows their role, including the wolves, so the value of hiding it is only speculative.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the kill is an arbitrary pick with no claims or reads, keep both conceals and let the chanteuse carry the kill so you make no visit at the victim's door. Spend a conceal later, on a victim whose revealed role or will would give town real information, such as a claimed investigator, trailseer, sentinel or healer.

lessons.situation: Late game with a tied vote just behind and no conceals left. The pack must stop a claimed Vigilante's remaining shot, and the Illusionist has to judge whether a kill plus a block holds. Information landscape: Info-moderate: the Vigilante claimant said they were blocked and had one bullet left, and the town's other claims are unverified. Stakes: Losing a wolf here leaves a lone wolf against several town players and a vote that can end the game. One failed block or shot can flip which side is ahead. Forward exposure: With no conceals, the victim's role is shown and the carrier's visit can be traced by watchers or followers. Backing a kill on a claimed Vigilante commits the pack to that target for the night, and a failed block cannot be taken back. Target landscape: A claimed Vigilante who may have one bullet left, versus a claimed Investigator whose checks are spent. The pack picks the Vigilante on shot threat alone, with no verified evidence.
lessons.action: Before the last conceal is gone, have the pack kill one player and block the other main threat in the same night. Do not rely on a single block to stop a Vigilante who can still shoot, since a block that fails leaves the shot live and can cost the pack a wolf. If both conceals are spent, favor a kill and block pairing that does not leave your partner exposed to a shot.

lessons.situation: Opening night with ten players alive. The wolves must choose a first kill blind and decide whether to commit a conceal charge on the victim. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no roles are confirmed, no discussion has happened, no deaths or claims exist, and the wolves know only their own partner. Stakes: Early game with a large cushion: one kill cannot decide the game. The value is information, since a hidden early victim denies Town a role reveal, and a night-immune target exposes the lone killer at no cost. Forward exposure: Low exposure: a conceal leaves no public trace, a failed attack is never announced, and a kill on a concealed victim leaves no visit for a Sentinel or Trailseer to see. The only commitment is possibly spending one of two conceals on a low-value role, and a failed attack refunds it. Target landscape: Seven unconfirmed non-wolf players with no claims, no public visits and no voting record. The pack picks a quiet player blindly, and the choice rests on no evidence or behavior.
lessons.action: On night one with both conceals unspent and no information, submit a conceal alongside the pack's kill on an unrevealed, quiet target. If the target dies, their role stays hidden and the Illusionist learns it, and if the attack fails because the target is night-immune, the conceal is kept and the pack learns the lone killer.

lessons.situation: The pack is deciding whether to spend the kill and a conceal on the claimed investigator or sentinel, who is the town's information lead, while the healer's likely protection is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: public claims on night-one visits and clearings reveal the town's information lead and its probable guard, and the pack's private knowledge exposes a night-immune player. Stakes: A wasted kill on a protected power role gives the town a free night and keeps its information lead alive. The conceal is refunded, but tempo is lost and the pack is exposed to counterattack, such as from a serial killer. Forward exposure: Authorizing a conceal on a protected target gets no kill, so the charge is refunded. It still commits the pack's kill to a target the town can predict, and a failed attack leaves the claimed power role alive and more trusted. The illusionist's visit to hide the body also shows up to watchers if the attack succeeds. Target landscape: Claimed sentinel or investigator as the obvious priority. Alternatives are unverified quiet players or a known night-immune player (who cannot be killed at night). Evidence is mostly public claims rather than hard reads.
lessons.action: When the most prominent claimed power role (investigator or sentinel) has already been attacked and saved, or a healer claim makes protection of it predictable, steer the pack kill to a different target and hold both conceals. If the town has no healer claim yet, the power role can be killed and concealed, but only if the pack accepts that the healer may be guarding it.

lessons.situation: Opening night, discussion-only day 1. The wolves must choose a first kill and decide whether the illusionist carries it, and whether to spend a conceal on a victim of unknown value. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or night results, so the target is a blind pick and any Sentinel or Trailseer who happens to be on the victim or carrier is invisible to the pack. Stakes: Early game with the wolves far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The cost that matters is a visit trail from the carrier that a watcher or tracker could use on day 2 or 3, which can get a wolf eliminated and cost the pack a member early. That outweighs keeping both charges in reserve. Forward exposure: Concealing makes the morning report say the role is hidden by an illusionist, which confirms an illusionist exists. It spends one of two charges if the victim dies, and the use cannot be undone. In return it removes the carrier's visit trace from any Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Nine or so living players, none having claimed a role and none read. The pack chooses a quiet, unclaimed target on behavior alone, so the victim's role and any watcher on them are unknown.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the pack picks an unread target and you are the one carrying the kill, spend one conceal on that victim. If the victim dies, your visit leaves no trace for a Sentinel watching them or a Trailseer following you, and if you carried the kill yourself you leave no trace at that door at all. If the victim survives, nothing is hidden and the charge is kept.

lessons.situation: Night 1, the pack's first kill, with a conceal on offer and a blind target pick between the illusionist and its wolf partner. Information landscape: No public information at all, only the pack's private chat; nothing is known about anyone's role or night immunity. Stakes: The game is at its start with no pressure on the pack, so the main stake is keeping both conceals for when a role reveal would help the town. Nothing about night 1 forces an early conceal. Forward exposure: A conceal on a victim who survives is kept and shows the town nothing. Holding it back is fully reversible, since both uses stay open for a night when a role reveal would hurt the pack. Target landscape: A single quiet, unclaimed player chosen by default; no claims, reads, votes or deaths. The target's immunity to night kills is unknown, and it could be the lone killer.
lessons.action: With both conceals available and no information on the first-night victim, agree to the pack's kill but hold the conceals for a later night when a power role or a likely-to-die target is the victim. A conceal is only spent if the victim dies, but committing it early to an unscouted quiet player offers no gain, since that target may be night-immune (like a lone killer) and the night-1 kill may fail silently.

lessons.situation: Night after your wolf partner was voted out and revealed. You are the lone wolf and your public vote pattern made you the likely suspect for a Vigilante. Information landscape: Info-rich about your exposure: a revealed wolf confirms your side, and your vote pattern is public and permanent. Stakes: As the lone wolf and prime suspect you can be killed by a Vigilante shot or sigil strike tonight, so passivity loses the game while a kill buys time. Forward exposure: A kill with a conceal leaves no trace at that door but spends your last conceal. Staying home leaves you exposed to a Vigilante shot or a sigil strike, and a sigil on you only strikes if you attack that night. Target landscape: Remaining town are claimed Sentinel, claimed Healer, Vigilante and Sigilist, with roles known only through claims. The Sigilist who pushed the case on your partner is a high-value target.
lessons.action: As the last wolf when your vote record or partner's reveal makes you a prime suspect, use the night to act instead of staying home. Carry the kill on the player most likely to hold a night killing role or to have deduced you (such as a Vigilante or Sigilist), and use a remaining conceal so the victim's role and your carrier visit stay hidden. If you cannot tell who that is, still make the kill rather than pass.

lessons.situation: Repeated wolf attacks on the claimed investigator were repelled by the healer's protection. The remaining wolf must choose between hitting the investigator again and breaking the protection cycle. Information landscape: Information-rich: investigator, healer and sentinel have publicly claimed roles, targets and results, and morning save announcements show the pattern of protection. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity and the protection cycle is the main obstacle. Removing the healer opens the way to the next power-role kill and to winning. Forward exposure: Spending the last conceal leaves zero charges, so later visits to victims are traceable. The kill itself is irreversible. A conceal on a victim who survives is refunded, and a hidden-role morning report only signals that an illusionist is active. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, who survived repeated attacks, versus the claimed healer, who openly took credit for the saves. Both are public claims backed by morning save announcements rather than by behavior alone.
lessons.action: When a claimed healer has been blocking the pack's kills on the claimed investigator or sentinel, aim the pack kill at the claimed healer and spend a conceal on that body. A hidden role denies the town confirmation and the Necromancer a usable body. If the healer is dead, protection stops and the next kill on the power role should land.

lessons.situation: The pack is about to kill a claimed investigative player. The illusionist is deciding who carries the kill and whether to spend a conceal, with a hidden Sentinel watch or Sigilist sigil possible. Information landscape: Thin on hidden roles. You do not know whether a Sentinel is watching the door or a sigil is on you, though public Trailseer and Sigilist claims exist. Stakes: Losing the illusionist to a sigil or an exposed trace would cripple the pack's late game and speed a vote against it. Careful carrier choice protects the remaining conceals. Forward exposure: A non-carrier's conceal visit is visible to a Sentinel watching the victim. Carrying the kill yourself leaves no trace at that door but makes you an attacker that night, which a sigil on you would punish. Neither can be undone once the night resolves. Target landscape: The pack's victim is an unconfirmed claimant such as the Trailseer, or a self-claimed Sigilist. The serial killer may hit the same victim, and a Sentinel or Sigilist whose position is unknown may be targeting you or the victim's door.
lessons.action: If you conceal, carry the kill yourself, because then you leave no trace at that door and the carrier's visit is hidden from a Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer following the carrier. If a Sigilist with sigils left is alive or likely, or it is not your turn to carry, let the pack's kill go unconcealed instead of visiting the body as a non-carrier. A non-carrier's visit to hide the body stays visible to a watcher on that door, and a carrier's attack can be punished by a sigil.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with you as the sole surviving wolf. A sigilist with a sigil left has publicly said they will target you, or has already used a sigil to kill your partner. Any kill you make would reach or approach parity, and the sigil strikes anyone who attacks that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, the investigator's record or will clears one living player, and the sigilist's earlier strike or sigil result is public. The sigilist's suspicion of you is explicit. Stakes: One more death reaches or nearly reaches wolf parity, but the sigil can strike you on the same night and end the game for the wolves. A wrong attack loses the game immediately, while holding the kill only postpones the decision to the vote. Forward exposure: Attacking is a visit and an attack. It commits you to a kill that a sigil on you would punish with your own death, and it cannot be undone once the night resolves. Holding the kill reveals nothing and keeps your conceals available. Target landscape: Two or three living players remain: a publicly known or claimed sigilist whose earlier sigil result is confirmed, a player cleared by the investigator who is probably the healer, and possibly one quiet unconfirmed player. Roles come from public evidence and the sigilist's stated intentions, but which target holds an unspent sigil is unknown.
lessons.action: When you are the last evil player and a sigilist has a sigil left and has publicly named or suspected you, hold the kill that night. Your own attack triggers the sigil and the sigil strike still kills you even if the attack succeeds, and a conceal does not help if the healer saves the target. Keep your conceals and let the vote decide, rather than attacking into a possible sigil.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive; the leading evil faction is 5 eliminations from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown. At worst for the town, the game can end within one more elimination, so a single death may decide whether the board remains playable; the effect of any particular target’s removal on the endgame is unclear without their role.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A night kill is not publicly attributed to its killer, but the victim and that the attack came from the Serial Killer are announced if the target can be killed at night. The death is irreversible; no particular endgame advantage is established without knowing the target’s role or faction.
query_dims.information_landscape: The Illusionist’s elimination and the Night 2 Sentinel record are system-confirmed. The public save confirms an attack on the claimed Investigator and that the Healer protected them, but not who protected them. The Healer, Investigator, and Trailseer claims are not role-confirmed; the Night 1 concealed death leaves that player’s role and faction unknown. The Serial Killer privately knows their own attacks and that the Night 2 target survived because of a healer save. Information is limited and asymmetric.
query_dims.situation: After the village eliminated a player revealed as the Illusionist, the surviving Serial Killer faces a concealed-role board and a night-kill choice among seven living players. Public discussion has centered on conflicting Healer claims: one claimant’s protection account fits the announced save, while the other says they protected someone else. The other role claims and private night results remain unverified.
query_dims.target_landscape: The living candidates include a claimed Healer whose account fits the public save but whose role is unverified, a claimed Investigator with an unverified Not suspicious result, a claimed Trailseer with an unverified follow result, and other living players with no publicly established roles. The recently eliminated Illusionist’s revealed role confirms one wolf is gone, but the side of the player whose role was concealed on Night 1 remains unknown.

lessons.situation: Three players are alive after a daytime elimination, and one night kill by the serial killer brings the count to two. Information landscape: Information-rich: published watch results, a confirmed wolf elimination, and roles largely narrowed down. Stakes: The next kill ends the game, so the SK wins by killing any one of the other two and loses a chance if it fails to kill. Forward exposure: Terminal and irreversible: the kill ends the game immediately, so there is no later exposure to manage. Target landscape: Two other players remain: a claimed town information role (e.g. sentinel) and a quiet player who voted against the SK. Either kill wins; the claimed town role is the safest pick since it is the most likely to hold useful information or protection.
lessons.action: With three alive, you plus two others, and any single kill ending the game, attack whichever other player is alive and can be reached, preferably the one with a role that could otherwise stop you. This reaches the two-alive win condition at once, so no day vote follows.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with several claimed Town power roles alive, one of them able to trace night visits. The Healer is dead or fixed on another target, and the wolves are also killing. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich. Public claims, a tracking chain, a held shot, and save announcements are known, but the hidden Healer and the unclaimed roles are unconfirmed. Stakes: A mid-game board where the kill choice shapes who survives to threaten you. Removing the one role that can follow your visit protects your night actions, but each Town death also pushes the wolves toward parity, so the kill should target someone who endangers you. Forward exposure: The kill is a private visit that carries no attribution unless you are watched or followed, but a prominent claimant dying signals an active killer hunting information roles. It cannot be undone, and if the wolves also hit that target the double attack reveals a second killer. Target landscape: Claimed power roles (a Trailseer with a public tracking chain, a Sigilist, a Vigilante holding fire) plus quiet unrevealed players, one of whom may be the Healer. Claimed roles are known only by their own say-so, so the choice rests on behavior and prominence rather than proof.
lessons.action: When a claimed Town information or tracking role (e.g. the Trailseer) is alive and could follow your visits, spend the night's kill on that claimant. If a claimed Healer is known dead or the claimant is not the healer's protected target, the kill lands; if the healer is visibly guarding that claimant, aim at the next most dangerous power role instead.

lessons.situation: Early-mid game, after a tie or no-elimination day, with several town roles claimed and a healer publicly confirmed. The wolves are also killing each night, and you must pick a night victim among claimed roles. Information landscape: Moderately informative public claims and a save announcement, with partial corroboration and no evidence pointing at you. Hidden roles remain, and you do not know who the healer is unless one claims. Stakes: Several players remain, so each kill moves you toward a final-two win. A confirmed healer can cancel a kill on any night, so removing it early lets later kills land cleanly, though you still face a day vote that could end you. Forward exposure: Killing the claimed healer reveals a threat-removal pattern but leaves no trace pointing at you, and it commits you to no story. The kill cannot be undone, but it removes protection that could blunt every later kill, whoever makes it. Target landscape: Candidates are the self-claimed healer (corroborated by the vigilante and the trailseer's follow), the trusted trailseer, the sentinel, and the sigilist and chanteuse under vote suspicion. The healer is the most openly identified protector, and the choice rests on public claims and corroboration rather than proof.
lessons.action: When a freshly claimed protector (healer) is publicly identified, aim the night kill at that protector rather than at a protected information role. If the save announcement shows a healer is already covering a claimed role, switch to a different target that night instead of repeating the saved one, since a repeat visit can be traced by a follower.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and the town is led by a vocal investigator against the lone killer. You are choosing a night target while a healer is probably alive and likely guarding the town's key voice. Information landscape: Information-rich. Wolf flips are confirmed and the investigator's reads are validated. Town's remaining uncertainty is mainly which unverified player is the killer or the neutral. Stakes: A wasted night costs tempo and, via the save, confirms a protective role. The board is small enough that each night kill matters. A failed kill makes your elimination more likely. Forward exposure: The attack is irreversible. A save is announced in the morning, so a failed kill gains nothing and helps the healer confirm their role, narrowing the pool toward you. A kill on a less obvious target keeps the healer's identity unconfirmed. Target landscape: A confirmed or loudly claimed investigator who just helped eliminate the last wolf, an unrevealed healer, an unverified tracker claimant, and quiet town players. The investigator is the obvious protect target. The others are judged on their claims and behavior.
lessons.action: If one prominent confirmed or claimed investigator or other town leader is the obvious protection target, spread your kill to a different live town role instead of repeating the predictable pick. Prefer a role the healer is unlikely to be guarding. A kill into a healer save spends the night and leaves you with fewer unverified players to hide among.

lessons.situation: Night 3 with the wolves collapsing (one or both revealed or dead). The village is about to treat you as the remaining unexplained killer, while the wolves and others converge on the same prominent target. Information landscape: Info-rich about the wolves (revealed roles, sigil kills, vote records). Thin about you, since no check or watch has confirmed you, but the attack count is public. Stakes: Four eliminations remain before you can finish, so a wasted or duplicated kill costs tempo. A visible duplicated or saved attack turns the day vote toward you once the wolves are gone. Forward exposure: Each announced kill is permanent and adds to the attacker count. A duplicate or saved attack on the same player reveals a second attacker and removes nobody. Once the wolves are gone, the village treats the lone killer as the only unexplained attacker, and the choice cannot be undone. Target landscape: Surviving candidates are the claimed sentinel, trailseer, healer, vigilante, sigilist and a neutral. The sentinel was picked on behavior (accusing or naming you) in both cases where the wolves and a healer covered the same player. No target had hard evidence tying them to you.
lessons.action: On the night the wolves are collapsing, pick a victim the wolves are unlikely to hit, rather than the loudest accuser or the most trusted information role. A quiet player who could still vote you out or punish you later (sigilist, vigilante) fits. If the obvious target is the sentinel or another public figure, assume the wolves and a healer converge there and shift your kill elsewhere.

lessons.situation: Endgame with 3-4 players alive. The serial killer must choose a night victim that determines whether the final daytime vote is winnable. Day votes have shown clear blocs, and a kill can strand the SK against a united pair. Information landscape: Information-rich: public voting records show who sided with and against the SK, some roles are confirmed by reveals, and several claims are on record. Stakes: One kill decides the game. Reaching two alive wins at once, while leaving three alive with an opposing bloc allows a 2-1 vote to eliminate the SK, which cannot be killed at night and can only be removed by a vote. Forward exposure: The kill is irreversible and fixes the final roster. Leaving three alive means a daytime vote decides whether you live, while reaching two alive ends the game immediately. Target landscape: Three or four survivors: a claimed ally who voted with you (vigilante), claimed town role holders (sentinel, investigator), and a wolf pair or wolf plus town voter who have voted against you. Evidence is mainly the public vote record and claims, not verified roles.
lessons.action: When 3-4 players remain, count the day-vote math before choosing your kill: pick the target so the survivors are you plus one other, or at worst you plus a player who is not allied with the other survivor. Avoid kills (or kills overlapping the wolf kill) that leave you outnumbered 2-1 by a pair that has voted together against you. If you can reach exactly two alive this night, take that kill, since it ends the game in your favor.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game after a discussion-only Day 1. You are the Serial Killer, immune to night attacks, and the wolves are also choosing a kill. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, votes, deaths or night results exist yet. Stakes: Early game with all ten alive and far from parity. One kill gains a single elimination toward being the last one standing but does not decide the game, and a failed or overlapping kill costs little beyond exposing a lone killer. Forward exposure: The kill is irreversible and commits you to nothing publicly. If it overlaps the wolves' victim or is saved, the morning names the serial killer as an attacker. A Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer on you can also see the visit. Target landscape: Nine other players, all unknown, with no claims, votes or behavior to read. Targets differ only by role potential, and a quiet player is as likely as any to hold a check, watch, or bullet.
lessons.action: On Night 1, with no claims or reads, kill one quiet, unclaimed player and accept that the pick is blind. The wolves also attack that night, and a kill that lands on the wolves' victim is announced as a double attack that reveals a second killer. Any kill carries the same chance of a watcher having been on that target.

lessons.situation: The neutral and the wolves are gone. You are the only evil player left among claimed town, and the town is hunting the last non-town player. One of the claimants can track visits. Information landscape: Information-rich. Roles and claims are mostly locked and flips are confirmed, so town can reason by elimination. Any visible visit trace would end the game. Stakes: Only a few players remain and one wrong vote ends you. A visit trace linking you to a corpse is decisive for the town. The night kill must both thin the board and avoid giving proof. Forward exposure: The kill is an irreversible visit. If a living Trailseer follows you, or a Sentinel watches your victim, the visit is seen and can be used as proof against you the next day. Killing the tracker leaves no such witness from that night. Target landscape: A small field of claimed town roles: a healer, a confirmed investigator, a sigilist, and a trailseer. The roles are locked and no cover role is left for you, so the choice rests on who can produce visit evidence.
lessons.action: When only town claimants and you remain and a Trailseer or Sentinel claimant is still alive, make that tracker your night kill. A dead tracker learns nothing from the night, so your visit cannot be followed or watched. If several trackers are claimed, kill the one the room trusts most.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or split day vote. Information roles are claiming and the wolves are also hunting the loudest of them. You must choose a victim without duplicating the pack's kill or walking into a watcher's trace. Information landscape: Moderately thin: a few claims, one or two early bodies, a split or abstain vote, and no hard evidence on any role. You cannot tell who is watching or following whom. Stakes: Mid-game with eight alive, so one wasted or traced kill costs tempo and exposure but does not end the game. Both the wolves and you still need several more deaths. A visit trace can make you the day vote target, and a duplicated kill gives no net body-count gain. Forward exposure: Your kill is an attack and a visit, so a Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer following you will log it. The morning report also names a serial killer attacker if the wolves hit the same player. Neither can be undone once the night resolves. The wolves' illusionist conceal hides only the wolf carrier's visit, never yours. Target landscape: Seven living candidates: claimed Sentinel, Trailseer and Investigator, a claimed Sigilist or Vigilante, and quiet unclaimed players. Claims are unverified, so the choice rests on public role claims and who the wolves most likely want dead, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: On night 2 with about eight alive, kill a living information role (claimed Sentinel, Trailseer or Investigator) that the wolves are least likely to take that night, rather than the loudest one they will obviously hit. A kill on the wolves' probable target wastes your attack, and any victim who is watched or followed puts your name on the visit trace. Prefer a victim whose death removes a watcher or follower, and if the Sentinel and Trailseer are both alive and active, expect a visit to anyone else to be logged.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later after a day vote that concentrated suspicion on one player, with a claimed Sentinel or Trailseer active and unblocked. Information landscape: Moderately informative: a public claim by a watcher, a fixed vote record, and some confirmed dead roles. Stakes: A watcher reading your visit leads to a day vote that can eliminate you, ending your game. Avoiding the watched door protects the only win path, since you can be removed only by a vote. Forward exposure: A kill is a visit that a watching Sentinel or a following Trailseer can read, and it cannot be undone after the morning. Killing a focal day target is predictable and invites a watch on that door. Target landscape: The claimed Sentinel, the contested player who just drew votes, and several quiet off-ballot players. Focal targets are the likeliest places for a watcher to be, while quiet players are less likely to be watched.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer has publicly claimed and is still alive, do not kill the player you just voted against or the player the room is focused on, because a watcher on that door sees your visit. Pick an off-ballot quiet player, or the watcher themself if the claim looks credible, so the visit is less likely to be read.

lessons.situation: Late game, around 5 alive with both wolves gone. A tiny voter pool decides whether you are voted out, and a vigilante or sigilist can narrow the suspects to you. Information landscape: Most roles are confirmed by death records and wolf reveals. The only open question is which survivor is the serial killer, so every announced attack narrows suspicion. Stakes: With few players left, each kill and each day vote decides the game. Spending a night on a harmless neutral leaves the sigilist and vigilante alive to expose you. Forward exposure: A kill the same night as a vigilante shot or wolf attack shows several attackers on one victim, and an immune shot report points at you. Once the body is announced you cannot walk it back. Target landscape: Five or so alive: a sigilist, a vigilante with possible bullets, a neutral voting body such as the fortune teller, and a possible healer claimant. The sigilist and vigilante are the real threats to a last-standing win. The neutral is only a vote.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone and only a handful of players remain, kill the player who can most directly stop your last-standing win. That means a vigilante with bullets left or a sigilist, not a side-less neutral that merely adds a vote. If a vigilante is alive, expect a possible same-night shot, which you survive because you cannot be killed at night, and plan for a possible 'immune' report.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later after a tied or contested day vote. Public claims exist, and an obvious wolf target stands out, such as a claimed investigator or trailseer in a tie. Information landscape: Moderately informative: unverified claims and a public vote record, but no confirmed roles among the living. Stakes: Each night's kill is a scarce progress step toward last-one-standing. A kill that duplicates the wolves' death wastes a night, while a distinct victim yields two deaths and brings the endgame closer. Forward exposure: A double attack on one victim is reported with both attackers, which reveals the extra killer and cannot be undone. The kill is irreversible and gives you no additional elimination. Target landscape: Claimed investigators or trailseers, the contested player from a tied vote, and several quiet players. The wolves' likely target is the publicly visible, accused or information-bearing player, so those candidates risk a wasted kill.
lessons.action: From Night 2 on, choose a victim the wolves are unlikely to hit, such as a quiet player who was not publicly contested, over the player everyone expects to die. A kill that lands on the wolves' obvious target is announced as a joint attack and adds no extra death.

lessons.situation: After a day-2 vote where nearly everyone abstained but one player voted to eliminate you. You are choosing whether to spend the night kill on that outlier. Information landscape: Moderate to rich: a public voting record isolates the lone accuser, and several power-role claims exist, but nothing hard confirms who the wolves are. Stakes: The kill can remove an active wolf and halve the pack, which shortens your path to a last-standing win. Nobody is at parity yet, so the cost is the day-3 heat the motive link brings, not an immediate loss. Forward exposure: Killing the one voter against you ties the death to a motive and turns their stray vote into evidence for Town. If they were a wolf, the surviving wolf can use that vote to argue you cannot be killed at night. You cannot reverse this after the kill. Target landscape: Seven living candidates: the lone day-2 accuser, claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator or Sigilist, and quiet unclaimed players. The accuser is picked on voting behavior alone, not role evidence, and was revealed in these games as a wolf (Chanteuse or Illusionist).
lessons.action: If one player alone voted against you on day 2 while the rest abstained, and no active Sentinel or Trailseer threat is more urgent, you may kill that outlier. They are more likely a wolf or a hostile reader, so you also remove a rival. Pick this target only knowing that the dead player's vote will be used against you on day 3.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is substantially aligned against you: all three other living players have accused you or stated they are voting for you. The stated case combines the Suspicious result with the unresolved contradiction between the Healer claims; absence of a public save does not resolve that contradiction.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four players are alive, and the leading evil faction is two eliminations from winning at worst for the town, because a concealed body’s side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this vote is a swing decision with potentially immediate endgame consequences.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Maintaining the Healer claim commits you to a role claim that conflicts with another player’s account of protecting the same target on night two. That commitment is already public and cannot be withdrawn without a credibility cost; further explanation could add claims that are difficult to verify.
query_dims.heat_now: High: three of the other living players have accused you and said they are voting for you. Their stated basis is the claimed investigator’s Suspicious result and the incompatible Healer claims; no public event directly confirms either Healer account.
query_dims.information_landscape: There is some discriminating public history: the investigator claimant’s earlier Suspicious result matched a revealed Illusionist, and the Trailseer’s revealed will establishes what the followed player visited, not who visited them. The current Suspicious check and both Healer accounts remain private claims, with no public save or other direct confirmation; evidence is mixed rather than conclusive.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out against the forming consensus: you maintain the Healer claim while acknowledging that the check is evidence against you and that the competing protection claims cannot both be true.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Necromancer and know the night actions you made through dead players’ bodies. Publicly, you have claimed Healer; the village has no confirmation of that claim. The public read includes a Suspicious check from a claimant whose earlier Suspicious result was corroborated by an eliminated player’s revealed role.
query_dims.situation: A player claiming Investigator, whose earlier Suspicious finding was corroborated when the accused was revealed as an Illusionist, now reports a Suspicious check on the claimed Healer. The claimed Healer and another player both say they protected the same target on night two; no save was announced, and the revealed Trailseer’s follow only showed that the target visited no one. The other living players are aligned in accusing the claimed Healer.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate vote centers on the claimed Healer with the Suspicious result versus the player making the competing Healer claim. The investigator’s earlier result was strongly supported by a revealed role; the current result is a private claim. Neither Healer claim is publicly confirmed, and the fourth living player has claimed Sigilist without public verification.

lessons.situation: Day vote with four alive. You and the genuine neutral each claim the same role, and the other two voters (town) must choose between you or tie. Information landscape: Starved: claims can't be checked and the investigator's checks are spent or unconfirmed. The only evidence is comparing bet histories against announced deaths. Stakes: A wrong vote ends your game, while a lynch of the rival or a tie keeps you alive and close to the 2-alive win condition. Each vote swings the outcome. Consensus: The village is split between the two claims, with no verified evidence, and the undecided town voters hold the balance. My position: Holding out against the accusation, pushing a mirror claim. Heat: High to moderate and rising: your claim is contradicted by a consistent rival and you have been accused or named as the last unclaimed player. Forward exposure: Your vote and mirror claim are public and permanent, and changing your claim would confirm guilt. Voting your accuser keeps you consistent, and the outcome depends on how the two undecided voters split. Target landscape: The rival claimant (the true neutral) and the two town players who haven't committed. The claims rest on unverifiable bet histories, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You know your claim is false and the accuser's is true, but publicly it is two unverifiable identical claims, and the town can pick either.
lessons.action: With four alive and a true neutral accusing you, keep your mirror claim and the details of its bet history unchanged, and vote for the accuser. In the last word, give the two uncommitted town voters one concrete reason to doubt the accuser's account, such as a bet that doesn't match the public deaths. If one of them breaks from the other, a tie or a lynch of the accuser leaves you alive.

lessons.situation: Final-three vote after a reanimated attack proved the Necromancer alive. One accuser names you by elimination and you must pull the other voter across. Information landscape: Rich: the morning report and the claims cross-confirm each other, leaving you as the only unconfirmed candidate. Stakes: One vote decides the game. If neither voter switches, you are eliminated two to one and town wins. Consensus: The room is largely aligned against you, because the two others confirm each other through announced events. My position: Holding out against the room. Heat: High: the other two have reached you by elimination after the night report revealed a reanimated attack. Forward exposure: The vote is irreversible and decides the game, since a loss ends it immediately. Naming a target commits you to the claim that they are the Necromancer. Target landscape: Two town claimants. One has a claim that matches the morning report, and the other has passive or unused abilities and is thinly supported. Each has been confirmed by the other's account. Public vs private: You know you are the Necromancer and your attack is already tied to you by elimination, but publicly the others can still be argued against.
lessons.action: With three alive and both others claiming town roles, vote for the one whose claim has the thinner support in the announced record, and use your last word to give the other player a reason to side with you. Before the vote, check whether the two corroborate each other through announced night events. If they do, the record is against you and the vote only works if you can credibly cast doubt on one of them.

lessons.situation: Day-3 vote after you pointed at a player using a private body-watch result, were challenged for lacking a result, and conceded. The room then turned on you for the overstated accusation. Information landscape: Public record holds announcements and unverified claims. The necromancer's key evidence is private and unshareable without revealing a dead role's body in use. Stakes: Your own elimination ends the lone-killer path, so the vote should not add to the case against you. With a majority already on you, an unsupported minority vote adds nothing. Consensus: Most of the room is aligned against the necromancer on its overstated accusation. Only one other player shares its read on the private-result target. My position: Holding out against the room, voting a different target from the majority aimed at you. Heat: High. Town players publicly challenged your claim, and you conceded it was inference, not a result. Forward exposure: Voting on a result you cannot cite commits you to an indefensible position, and you cannot take the vote back. Voting with a publicly justifiable read keeps the information hidden and your role intact. Target landscape: The necromancer itself (pressed for an unsupported accusation), the unclaimed player the private result pointed at, and a third player with a scattered vote. The case against the private-result target rests on unshareable information, while the case against you is behavioral. Public vs private: Privately you saw visits through a dead body that point at one player. Publicly you can cite only the inference and the claims, and an overstated accusation makes your reads look unsupported.
lessons.action: If you hold private information you cannot disclose, such as a body-watch result, voice only claims you can source publicly. Before the vote, state that your read is inference, and cast the vote that fits the public evidence, not the hidden result. If the hidden result points at a target the room does not share, hold that read for the night and do not stake your survival on it in the vote.

lessons.situation: Endgame vote at about five players alive. The wolves are gone, a necromancer's night attacks through dead bodies have been publicly identified, and the town is voting to find the lone killer by elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed, a will or a sigil strike cleared some players, claims are known and votes are recorded, so the necromancer's choices are scrutinized. Stakes: At five alive, one wrong elimination or one night kill leaves the necromancer close to the at-most-one-other-alive win. One exposed vote can also cause the necromancer's own elimination or a night shot, so each ballot has decisive weight. Consensus: The town has narrowed to a small suspect pool by elimination and claims, and the leading confirmed players have converged on one target. My position: holding out against the forming consensus Heat: Moderate to extreme: the necromancer is among a handful of suspects, with some cover from a dead investigator's clearance but questions about its votes and about pressure on specific claims. Forward exposure: A vote against the player the leading confirmed players are defending, or a lone vote against a quiet player, is public and permanent and cannot be undone. It commits you to a stance that the town will later read as deflection or antagonism. Target landscape: Few survivors, among them a confirmed vigilante, a speculator, a claimed healer and a claimed sigilist. The leading players favor one target on the basis of claims and behavior. The alternative target is backed only by the player with the most to hide. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows they are the lone killer and that the reanimated attacks came from them; the town knows only that a necromancer exists among the survivors and is reading each vote and defense as a tell.
lessons.action: When five players remain, both wolves are dead and the town is hunting the lone killer, vote with the room's strongest evidence-backed consensus (the confirmed, leading players' target) instead of holding out for a different target. If the consensus target is someone else and no evidence clears you, joining it keeps your ballot from standing out as a deflection, which matters because the town is reading votes for deflection.

lessons.situation: Day vote at a small table after multiple night deaths, with conflicting power-role claims. The town is divided across several targets and the necromancer is not a leading suspect. Information landscape: Information-rich on paper (dead power roles revealed, several role claims, an announced reanimated-body attack) but the claims contradict each other, so the town cannot tell who is lying. The necromancer's own acts are not traceable to it. Stakes: With about five players alive, each elimination moves the necromancer toward its win condition of at most one other player alive. A tie with no elimination keeps the town's numbers and the confusion in place, but it also gives the town another night and another day to find the necromancer. Consensus: The village is fragmented, with votes scattered across four or five players and no dominant read. Disagreement rests on contradictory claims about the double-kill night or the voting behavior. My position: holding out Heat: Low; an earlier Not suspicious result or a negative trailseer follow result gives the necromancer cover, and attention sits on the active claimants. Forward exposure: Voting with a visible bloc against a claimed town role looks like normal skepticism and commits the necromancer to nothing beyond that public vote. The vote is permanent on the record, but it is easy to explain as following a reasonable accusation. Target landscape: Several candidates: a claimed healer accused over a roleblock or vote story, a surviving wolf or speculator accused by others, and scattered single votes on the trailseer, vigilante, or sigilist. The evidence is mostly claim contradictions and behavior, not confirmed results. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it caused the night kills through a dead body, while the room argues over which claimant is lying or whether two attacking factions exist; the necromancer reads as a bystander.
lessons.action: When the town is split across several targets and nobody suspects you, cast your vote for a claimed town role that already has a vote bloc (e.g. the accused claimed healer), so it ties the leading alternative and nobody is eliminated. This keeps your count of opponents intact and keeps the room from consolidating, and a vote that looks like ordinary skepticism draws little heat. If your vote would instead be the one that completes a majority on a town role, or would put you alone on a target, switch to the bloc that keeps the tally split.

lessons.situation: Day-3 vote after a night kill, often with a concealed or contested body. The village has converged on the necromancer for behavior (silence or a walked-back accusation) while other players dispute visits and roleblocks. Information landscape: Mixed to thin. There are unverified claims and a visit dispute, but no confirmed wolf or killer. The necromancer's best information comes from a body-watch or similar result that it cannot disclose without exposing its role. Stakes: Mid-game with eight alive: an elimination of the lone killer ends its win path. Each vote matters, since a lone vote leaves the majority on you unopposed and you are removed. Consensus: The room is concentrating on the necromancer for behavior, not for evidence. The remaining votes are scattered across contested claims. My position: Holding out alone against the room and casting a vote that nobody else shares. Heat: High. You were the main target on the previous day, and several voters again aim at you for silence or an unsupported accusation you had to concede. Forward exposure: A lone vote on a read nobody shares commits you publicly to an unsupported position. It adds nothing to any vote count, does not lower your heat, and is permanent and irreversible. A vote that joins an existing bloc costs little and can be explained. Target landscape: Several candidates (sentinel, healer, trailseer, illusionist, sigilist) with contested claims and no hard evidence. The case against you is behavioral, resting on silence or an overstated accusation. Cases against the others rest on disputes or private results you cannot share. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer, or hold unshareable body-derived information. Publicly you are a repeat target whose reads are unsourced, so a solo vote looks isolated and odd.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote where the room is concentrating on you, don't spend your vote on a lone-voter target nobody shares. Pick the candidate who already has the most votes among the people pressing you, or one the room already doubts, so your vote joins a visible bloc. Pair it with the one claim you can defend publicly, because a vote you cannot source or explain stays on the permanent record and cannot be undone.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a reanimated-body kill and a hidden-role death. The room has lined up behind one target, and the necromancer is tempted to vote its own private target alone. Information landscape: Moderate. There are unverified claims, one confirmation by a role holder, and the announced reanimated kill. The identities of the wolves and the lone killer remain open, and nothing publicly ties anyone to the necromancer's night actions. Stakes: The necromancer needs the board down to two players, so every Town elimination is progress. A solo dissent adds no progress and can cost the necromancer its life one day later, because the vote record shows it standing apart. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous, with 5-6 votes behind one target. The basis is behavioral, such as vouching for a dead wolf, or an unverified investigator's Suspicious claim. My position: Holding out alone against a near-unanimous majority. Heat: Moderate to very high. The necromancer is accused or watched because a reanimated kill was announced, or because it has flagged the body danger. Forward exposure: A lone dissenting vote is public and permanent, cannot be undone, and builds a record of being the only voter off consensus. Voting with the plurality commits you to nothing beyond that day's target and is less revealing. Target landscape: The candidates are the room's consensus target, who is usually a Town role under behavioral suspicion, and the necromancer's private preference such as the healer or the claiming investigator. None has hard evidence against them, so a solo vote on the private preference only exposes the necromancer. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it is the lone killer and has been attacking through a body, so a Suspicious read on it is accurate. The public cannot verify night actions and only sees the announced reanimated kill and the room's behavior.
lessons.action: When the room is converging on a target and you are not yet that target, cast your vote with the plurality instead of a solo dissent. A solo vote is permanent and marks you as the one voter outside consensus, and it moved no one in either game. If you are the accused, vote the same way as the room's other non-you voters where one target exists, so your record does not stand out.

lessons.situation: Day 2 is the first vote of the game. The room has piled onto one accused player, either a claimant whose result contradicts the rules or a player placed at a victim's door by claimed results. You are the necromancer, newly past your immunity night and with no hidden visits exposed. Information landscape: Information-thin: unverified role claims, perhaps one claimed result or rules contradiction to anchor on, and few or no confirmed roles beyond early deaths. Stakes: Early game with many players alive; a single vote does not flip the outcome. The priority is staying hidden while the village removes a player, and a revealed body adds to your night options. Consensus: The village is nearly unanimous, 8-1 or 9 votes, behind one accused player, based on a claimed report, logical contradiction, or weak defense rather than a wolf-driven push. My position: With the majority, voting alongside the room. Heat: Low to almost none: you have been quiet or have only asked mild questions or endorsed a report, and nobody has accused you or tied a night event to you. Forward exposure: A vote with the majority reveals nothing about your role and commits you only to the room's consensus. It is public and permanent, but unremarkable while the room is unanimous; a lone dissent would draw attention. Target landscape: One candidate has clear traction, accused on a claimed watch or visit report, a rules contradiction, or a weak defense. Other players hold unverified but unchallenged claims. No roles are confirmed, so the basis is claims and logic rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the lone killer with no wolf allegiance and no exposed visits; publicly you look like one more town-leaning voter and nobody is looking at you.
lessons.action: On the first day vote, when the room has converged on one accused player and you are not under suspicion, vote with the majority for that player instead of splitting off or floating a new target. A bandwagon vote reveals nothing about your role and keeps heat near zero. Any dead player whose role is announced then becomes a usable body for your later night abilities.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after a single night death, with no investigative results shared. Votes are scattered, and the quiet players, you included, draw suspicion for silence alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death, a few claims, and no verified ties to wolves or a killer. Reads are behavioral only. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so no single vote decides the game. The main risk is attracting lasting suspicion before the necromancer's first usable night. Consensus: The village leans toward abstaining because no checks, watches or follows have been shared. Support for any elimination is thin and scattered. My position: With the majority when abstaining; holding out if you cast a lone vote. Heat: Low to moderate. Any pressure rests on silence, with no concrete evidence against you. Forward exposure: A named vote goes on the permanent public record and can be questioned for days; an abstain reveals nothing and commits you to nothing. Target landscape: All living players are unconfirmed apart from the dead player's reveal. The only candidates are quiet players, chosen on silence rather than evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer with no night information yet (Night 1 is inactive, so you read Not suspicious). Publicly you are an unconfirmed, quiet player, and the room has no evidence against anyone.
lessons.action: On an early day-vote with no hard evidence and a room leaning toward abstaining, abstain with the majority instead of casting a lone named vote. Abstaining commits you to nothing and keeps your vote on the public record from looking aggressive or unexplained. If a plurality is forming on you, still abstain and let the abstain bloc block it, since a counter-vote would not change the tally.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear village consensus. One player weakly favors the agent based on the unexplained Day 2 vote; that player has withdrawn the vote as a strong argument. Others are probing the claimed Investigator’s blocked actions, without converging on a target.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five players remain; the leading evil faction is 3 eliminations from parity, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination in the worst case for the town, so this vote is a swing decision with potentially immediate game-ending consequences.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: the agent is the tentative target of a weak vote preference because the revealed Trailseer voted for the agent on Day 2. No one has presented independent evidence against the agent, and the claimed Investigator’s result, if true, is Not suspicious.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved. Confirmed facts include the dead Sentinel’s and Trailseer’s roles and wills, the former Illusionist’s revealed role, the healer save on the claimed Investigator, and the public vote records. The Investigator claim and its results are not independently verified; the body concealed on Night 1 remains unknown, and there is no confirmed current alignment result.
query_dims.my_position: Under mild pressure but not a settled majority target; the agent has not advanced a competing elimination case in today’s discussion.
query_dims.situation: With five alive, the village is trying to choose an elimination despite little actionable information: a claimed Investigator reports two consecutive roleblocks and one earlier Not-suspicious result on the agent, while the only stated case against the agent is the revealed Trailseer’s unexplained Day 2 vote. The former Illusionist was eliminated, but a wolf and possibly the lone killer remain.
query_dims.target_landscape: The live elimination discussion centers weakly on the player who favored eliminating the agent on Day 2, based only on that vote; the claimed Investigator says that player read Not suspicious, which rules out wolf suspicion if true but does not exclude the lone killer. The claimed Investigator’s two blocked checks are unverified. No other clear candidate is established.

lessons.situation: Day 2 first vote: a claimed power role admitted their reported result looked wrong and the whole table is accusing them, while you have not yet made your side pick. Information landscape: Information-starved: one self-admitted inconsistency and unverified claims; no confirmed roles. Stakes: Early elimination of a Town role weakens Town's information while the serial killer and wolves are still active; a mistaken unanimous vote is hard to reverse and your own pick depends on Town surviving. Consensus: Near-unanimous pile-on against one claimed role based on a single reported inconsistency; the room is driven by claim analysis, not verified facts. My position: With the majority and one of the voices driving it. Heat: Low; you are an unclaimed voice agreeing with the majority. Target landscape: One claimed Sentinel under real pressure after reporting a watch result that omitted their own visit; the other claimant (a trailseer) looks consistent. No competing suspects and no hard evidence beyond the claim's inconsistency.
lessons.action: When the table is piling onto a single claimed role over a stated inconsistency and there is no stronger lead, vote with the consensus only after checking that the inconsistency is a real rules violation rather than a misstatement. If the rule check is unclear, abstain, so you do not help eliminate a likely Town power role while you still hold your pick.

lessons.situation: Endgame of three or four players alive after both wolves are eliminated; the only remaining threat is the lone killer, hidden among the other living players, and your Town pick depends on removing it. Information landscape: Rich by elimination: both wolves revealed, the killer's night kills visible, and claimed trailseer and healer reports consistent with each other and with you. Stakes: The final vote decides the game: eliminating the lone killer ends it as a Town win and pays off the Town pick, while a wrong vote lets the killer reach the at-most-one-other-alive condition. Consensus: Mostly aligned on eliminating the one unverified player, since claims corroborate each other and both wolves are already revealed. My position: With the majority or driving alongside the corroborated claimant, and part of the decisive votes. Heat: Moderate: the suspected killer voted against you, but a matching trailseer result saying you visited no one cleared you. Target landscape: Two or three other living players: claimed information roles whose reports match each other and clear you, and one unclaimed or ability-less player who cast a counter-vote at you. Basis is cross-corroborated claims plus elimination, not just behavior.
lessons.action: When both wolves are confirmed dead and only the lone killer can remain, vote out the one living player whose claim is unverified or who has no corroborated night result, and rely on cross-matching claims such as a trailseer report that agrees with a healer's claim. If you are the one cleared by a corroborated result, join the cleared players against the lone unclaimed or uncorroborated player, because a wrong vote lets the killer reach parity.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote after a night kill by wolves or the serial killer; the village converges on a single accused player on corroborating night-result claims, and the speculator has the option to join the vote that decides whether the remaining evil is removed. Information landscape: Reasonably information-rich: a wolf is already confirmed dead or revealed, there are corroborating tracking claims and a clean investigator check, and the accused offers only blanket denials. Stakes: With wolves or the lone killer nearly gone, one more correct elimination can end or nearly end the game; the vote is rarely decisive alone but it fixes the board toward a Town win, which is the side the speculator pick favors. Consensus: Largely aligned: a pack of accusers forms on matching tracking and check reports plus the reveals of dead wolves. My position: With the majority, joining the pile-on early or at the last minute rather than holding out. Heat: Low to moderate: no accusation round is aimed at you, though the accused may have counter-accused or voted against you. Target landscape: One accused player named by matching independent tracking or check claims (trailseer, sentinel, investigator); the claims are unverified but agree with each other and with confirmed reveals. The alternative candidates have no case against them; the accused's defense is blanket denial or counter-accusation.
lessons.action: On a day-3 vote where several tracking or check reports (trailseer, sentinel, investigator) converge on one accused and confirmed wolves are already known, vote with that convergent group for the accused instead of an unrelated player. Removing a convergent target sharpens the endgame toward Town, which pays off a Town pick; if you still hold your pick, the converging reports are your cue to lock in the side that now looks to be winning.

lessons.situation: Late game, day vote. Your Town pick is already announced and the Town win needs the last evil player or players removed. A few survivors remain, and one is the remaining wolf or lone killer, often the one who attacked your role or counter-claimed it. Information landscape: Fairly rich by elimination. Dead roles are revealed, some Town results are backed by announced facts, and the suspect pool is narrow. Some of it is still behavioral, such as who pressed whom and how people voted. Stakes: Few players are left, so one wrong elimination could let evil reach parity or hand the game to the lone killer.
