A correct elimination ends the game and cashes in your pick, so the vote has to land on the true last threat. Consensus: The village is converging on one target through elimination reasoning and shared reads. Most votes are already pointed at the same last unaccounted-for player. My position: With the majority, joining a bloc that is already forming and sometimes helping to start it. Heat: Low to moderate. Your Town pick is announced anonymously, but some players can guess your role from your action pattern or a rival claim. Target landscape: Two or three survivors left unaccounted for after wolves or the lone killer died. The candidates include a counter-claimant or a player pressing on your role, plus quiet players. Roles are confirmed mostly by elimination and sigil or healer reasoning, with voting-bloc behavior as backup.
lessons.action: Once your Town pick is made and announced, vote with the forming majority for the remaining evil player. Use elimination to name them: take the roles already revealed dead, the cleared players, and anyone who counter-claims or presses on your role. Your pick pays off only if Town wins, so keep voting for the last unaccounted-for threat instead of splitting the room.

lessons.situation: After a night kill (often hidden-role or double attack), a role claimant's night report places one named player at the victim's door. The accused denies it and attacks the claimants, and the room converges on the accused. The speculator has already picked Town or is about to. Information landscape: Moderately to highly info-rich: specific watch or follow claims that corroborate one another, visitor counts, an investigator read, and caught mechanics errors, though nothing is officially confirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil threats still alive. Removing a wolf or the lone killer by an evidence-backed vote shifts the board toward Town and toward the speculator's Town pick, and a wrong eviction would cost a Town member. Consensus: Largely aligned (most of the living players) behind the evidence-backed target. Only the accused and perhaps one wolf partner dissent. My position: With the majority, lightly helping build the case with a verification question or a public argument. Heat: Low: not accused, only asking questions or backing the majority line. Target landscape: Two or three suspects: one accused by independent, partly corroborating night claims (watch report, trailseer follow, visitor list, investigator read) who denies and counter-accuses, versus the accuser(s), who are unverified but consistent with each other. Evidence outweighs behavior on the accused, and nobody is confirmed by the Game Master.
lessons.action: On a day-vote with low heat, vote with the evidence-backed majority on the player whose story is contradicted by independent night reports (a watch claim, a follow match, a visitor count, a counter-claim) rather than on mood. If you have not yet picked, ask for a Trailseer or Sentinel to corroborate before the vote, then vote with the room. Each eviction of a wolf or lone killer moves Town toward winning, which is what your Town pick needs.

lessons.situation: Late-game day vote at five alive where the vote is split or tied. The speculator's ballot decides whether a useful Town-aligned role survives, and the speculator has already picked a side. Information landscape: Mixed. Some night save announcements and claimed information-role reports exist, but they conflict, and several dead players' roles are hidden. No role is verified. Stakes: At five alive, one elimination can bring evil to parity. A single ballot decides between keeping a protective role alive and handing the wolves or lone killer a free removal. Consensus: Fractured: votes split between two or more targets, with no majority and a tie likely, resting on conflicting claimed visit reports. My position: Holding the swing or deciding ballot, able to join a wagon or drive an alternative target. Heat: Moderate to high: the speculator is accused or voted for by others based on visit reports, though in some cases heat is only low to moderate. Target landscape: Three or four candidates at five alive: a claimed healer with a confirmed save announcement, a claimed trailseer or sentinel, the speculator under accusation, and a quiet unclaimed player. Evidence is claims and visit reconstructions, not confirmed roles.
lessons.action: With about five players alive and the vote split or tied, use your ballot to protect a claimed protective or information role whose behavior and announced results fit. Aim it at the least-evidenced quiet player, since a tie or no elimination keeps the Town-aligned pick alive. If the room is scattered and no role is confirmed, spend it on the most defensible suspect rather than a token vote.

lessons.situation: The final day vote with three or four players alive. The speculator is the target of the surviving evil players and is voting alone against the player the records implicate. Information landscape: Voting logs, dead-role reveals and announced reanimated-kill reports exist, but no living candidate is confirmed. The evidence has to be read from patterns. Stakes: One more death gives evil parity or the lone-killer win condition, so this vote ends the game. A lost vote also kills the speculator's chance of seeing its pick come true. Consensus: The room has coalesced into a bloc against me, built on my voting history and on mutual cover among the evil players. Town evidence is thin. My position: Holding out alone against a two- or three-vote bloc. Heat: High to extreme. Evil players or a rival claimant are using my past votes or a questionable-player label against me. Target landscape: Two or three unconfirmed living players, none publicly confirmed as wolf or lone killer. Cases rest on voting records, alignment with dead evil players, and announced body-attack kills, not on revealed roles.
lessons.action: In an endgame vote with three or four players left and a majority leaning on you, vote for the unconfirmed player whose public record ties most directly to evil. Good evidence is a vote alongside a dead wolf, or a body-attack announcement that points to the lone killer. If a rival's case rests only on a single dead player's past vote, vote on the stronger record and not on who is pressuring you, because each vote you add is the only way to reach a tie or majority.

lessons.situation: Four players alive with one wolf remaining; a dispute between two info claimants over whether a watch counts as a visit, and the room votes out a claimed role over an apparent rules error. Information landscape: Rich in claim histories but poisoned by a rules dispute, so the evidence is contested rather than confirmed. Stakes: At four alive with a wolf left, one wrong elimination of a real Town role gives the wolf parity and ends the game; the vote is decisive. Consensus: Majority formed against the claimed sentinel on a disputed rules argument, with the vigilante holding the decisive bullet. My position: With the majority, joining a vote that was already forming. Heat: Moderate: the claimed vigilante questioned the speculator's lack of a role claim, though attention quickly moved to the dispute between information claimants. Target landscape: Claimed sentinel accused of lying about watching being a visit, versus a claimed trailseer and claimed vigilante pushing the accusation; the case rests on a rules dispute and counter-accusation, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With a wolf still alive and a dispute between claimed info roles, do not just join the majority on a vote over a rules-interpretation quarrel. Check the accusation against the stated rules (for example, a watch is a visit to the target but is not shown in the watcher's own result) and vote for the player whose claim actually conflicts with the rules or other evidence, or hold out if the accusation is only a semantic quarrel.

lessons.situation: First day with a vote, after a night-1 death. There are unverified role claims and counter-claims, or no claims at all. The speculator has not yet made its side pick and has no information on any candidate. Information landscape: Information-starved: one dead player with a known role, unverified night-result claims, no confirmed wolf, and no voting history yet. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so one vote does not flip the winning side. A wrongful elimination of a real Town role is costly, and your abstain avoids adding to it. Your win depends only on the later pick. Consensus: The room is split or only loosely aligned. It is either a universal abstain or a near-majority piling onto one player, based on behavior and unverified claims rather than confirmed roles. My position: Holding out by abstaining, either with an abstain bloc or against a bandwagon, without driving any accusation. Heat: Low to none: you have been quiet or only echoed the room's questions, and no one has accused you. Target landscape: Two or more candidates drawing votes, such as a quiet player with no claim, a claimed healer, or rival investigator claimants. Their claims are unverified. The only evidence is a night-1 sentinel or trailseer report or a visit link, and everything else is behavior.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, while your one pick is unused and no candidate has hard evidence against them (only unverified claims, quietness, or a bandwagon), abstain rather than join the pile-on. If a candidate has a concrete contradiction, such as a caught lie or a claim that conflicts with an announced fact, vote for that player instead. If abstaining has been removed after two no-elimination days, vote for the best-supported suspect. Abstaining keeps your heat low, and your win depends on the pick, not on this vote.

lessons.situation: A rival counter-claims the Speculator role or publicly ties your pattern of actions to it, and calls your claim late or false. You have to hold your claim while the room decides who the wolf is. Information landscape: Role-uniqueness contradiction plus elimination reasoning from dead roles and Town results. Evidence is moderately rich, although the targeted player's role is not confirmed until the vote. Stakes: Late game with few players left. If the wrong claimant is eliminated, evil can reach parity. Removing the false claimant can end the game. Consensus: The room is mostly backing your claim or already turning on the accuser. The shared basis is the unique-role contradiction and the narrowed suspect pool. My position: With the majority, partly driving it as the original claimant. Heat: Moderate to elevated. A rival claimed your role, or someone linked your actions to the Speculator, and at least one vote has been cast against you. Target landscape: The counter-claimant or the player pressing on your role, versus a few players already cleared by Town results or confirmed by elimination. Evidence is a mix of role uniqueness, elimination logic, and behavior.
lessons.action: If someone counter-claims your Speculator role or ties your behavior to it, keep your claim consistent and point out that there is only one Speculator. Then vote for the counter-claimant or pressurer if the cleared roles and the elimination logic leave them as the remaining evil candidate. This works because the Town pick is already announced and a counter-claimant is forced into being the wolf or a liar.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive. The leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town, because the concealed body’s side is unknown; nevertheless, the board can end within one more elimination at worst for the town. The pick’s end-of-game effect is unclear until the winning side is known; choosing now locks in that side, while dying unpicked loses.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information is mixed but incomplete: the Illusionist’s elimination is system-confirmed, and the public record confirms a Serial Killer attack was stopped by a healer save. The first night’s victim remains role-concealed; remaining role claims and night accounts are not independently verified, and there is no public evidence establishing the current count or identity of the surviving evil roles.
query_dims.situation: After the village unanimously eliminated a player revealed as the Illusionist, the board has fewer known wolves but still includes an unresolved concealed death and an unverified claim to be the Investigator. You face the one-time choice of which side you expect to win while the surviving evil balance and the concealed player’s side remain uncertain; choosing a side only helps if that side wins, while delaying risks dying before picking.
query_dims.target_landscape: Your one-time pick is still unspent; the candidates are Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or yourself. The eliminated player was revealed as an Illusionist, but the other concealed night-death’s side remains unknown, and no public evidence identifies the surviving members of any side. The pick is announced without revealing who made it; dying before choosing means you lose.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after one or two evil eliminations (Chanteuse, Illusionist, or Serial Killer). Town looks ahead and the Speculator must decide whether to lock in its single pick now or wait. Information landscape: Mostly information-rich: role reveals for dead evil players and a validated Sentinel watch. Some gaps remain: one wolf or the lone killer may be hidden behind a cleared read, and the claimed Investigator and Healer are unverified. Stakes: Town holds a clear numerical majority, but one remaining killer, or a double-kill night, could strip key roles and reverse the lead. The pick is permanent and the Speculator has no other ability, so timing matters more than the margin shown. Target landscape: Town, the wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town looks dominant after the Serial Killer and one or two wolves were eliminated. Evidence is mixed: a confirmed Sentinel result and role reveals for the dead, but the remaining evil's identity is only inferred from behavior or from unverified Investigator claims.
lessons.action: Pick Town only once both the wolves and the lone killer are confirmed dead or identified and Town's investigative and protective core is still alive. If a hidden killer is still unaccounted for, or a likely double-kill night is coming, delay the pick one more night, because a Speculator that dies before picking loses.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game (nights 2-3) with the speculator alive and unpicked. One wolf has been voted out or a Town save has been announced, but the lone killer and at least one wolf are still hidden. Killers are active every night. Information landscape: Mixed. Some announced facts exist (a revealed wolf death, an announced save, dead power roles), but most night results are unverified claims. The strength of the evil factions is inferred from counts and trend, with no confirmation of the lone killer. Stakes: The board is not at the brink, but each night a hidden killer or wolf can remove the speculator before it picks, and that is a guaranteed loss. The pick is permanent, so a Town pick pays off only if Town survives the lone killer, and Town did lose to a hidden Necromancer or the wolves in some games. Picking by night 2-3 locks in the likeliest winner while the speculator is still alive. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town has the most living members and often a revealed wolf death or verified saves. The wolf pack and lone killer are mostly hidden, and the self pick only wins by being the last player standing. The read rests on public counts and trend more than on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Once Town has a confirmed evil kill or a clear numbers lead (for example a wolf revealed dead and Town power roles still alive), spend your one pick on Town that night. If no side looks clearly ahead, still pick by night 2 or 3, because dying unpicked is an automatic loss and Town is the default side with the most players.

lessons.situation: A morning after a visible Town success (a lone killer or wolf voted out, or the claimed Investigator saved by the Healer) tempts the Speculator to commit to Town at once. Wolves remain hidden, and Town can still fracture through mis-votes, friendly fire or losing its Healer. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of eliminated players are confirmed and the Investigator's checks are on record. What is missing is the identity of the surviving evil players and whether Town can keep up its voting discipline. Stakes: Town leads comfortably, so an early pick gains little extra. The pick is permanent and announced. Both games showed Town collapsing after the pick through mis-eliminations and the loss of its Healer, which let the wolves win and left the Speculator with a loss. Waiting costs nothing while the Speculator is safe, and the risk is dying unpicked. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or Self. Town leads on numbers, with a living Investigator and Healer. One evil faction is already confirmed dead, but one or two wolves, or a lone killer, are still hidden. The Self pick is unrealistic. Confirmed kills and checks are the evidence; Town's cohesion is only a behavioral read.
lessons.action: When Town looks dominant only because one evil side was just removed, but a wolf or lone killer is still hidden or alive, keep the one pick unspent for another night while the Speculator is not under suspicion. Lock in Town once the remaining evil is down to one hidden wolf with Town's key roles intact. If the Speculator becomes a likely target, pick the leading side right away, because dying unpicked is a loss.

lessons.situation: Night 1 (or early night 2) of a ten-player game, with the Speculator's single irreversible pick unspent and nothing established yet. Delaying risks an unannounced night kill by the wolves or the serial killer, which would make the Speculator lose automatically. Information landscape: Information-starved: day 1 was discussion only with no vote, no deaths, no verified claims, and no check results. Any read would be behavioral at best. Stakes: The board is far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The Speculator's own survival to the pick is the main risk: dying unpicked is a guaranteed personal loss, while an early Town pick costs little and keeps the win tied to the largest side. Target landscape: Four sides: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or self. No deaths, claims, or votes exist, so the choice rests on prior side sizes: Town has six roles, wolves two, the lone killer one, and a pick of self wins only as last one standing.
lessons.action: On the first night where you still hold your pick and nothing has been confirmed, lock in your pick right away instead of waiting. Choose Town, the largest side (six Town roles against two wolves, one lone killer and you), since a Speculator that dies unpicked loses and any night attack can remove you before you act. If a night-2 report has already confirmed the wolves are dead or clearly outnumbered, pick Town immediately.

lessons.situation: Midgame, day 3 or later. One evil faction member has just been voted out with a confirmed role, and Town is clearly ahead of what remains. The speculator has not picked and is alive and unexposed. It faces a choice between waiting for more information and locking in a side now. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: a system-confirmed role reveal from the elimination, dead roles revealed, and public vote records showing the village voting together. One or two evil players remain unconfirmed. Stakes: Town's lead over the remaining evil is real but not unbeatable. Evil kills each night, and the speculator is an ordinary kill target. Dying unpicked is a guaranteed loss, so each night of delay costs more than the extra information is worth. Target landscape: Four options: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or itself. By now at least one evil faction is eliminated and revealed (a wolf or the lone killer). Town still has a numerical majority over the remaining evil, and the evidence is public reveals and vote records rather than behavior. A self-pick is almost impossible to win.
lessons.action: Once a night arrives in which a lone killer or wolf has been voted out and revealed and the roles left show Town holding a clear majority edge over the remaining evil, spend your single pick that night on Town instead of waiting. The pick is not a visit and cannot be blocked. If you die before picking you lose, and a pick made first still counts after you die.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Ten alive and six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single vote or kill can end the game now; the board is far from any decisive result. The cost of waiting is that a Speculator dying unpicked loses outright, so the pick has to be made before a night kill or lynch removes the option, while still early enough that the board is not yet clear.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no night results have been announced, no deaths, no role claims that are verified, and only one public vote record (an abstain majority with one accusation). Private knowledge is limited to my own speculator status and an unset pick.
query_dims.situation: As the unpicked Speculator, I face the open question of when to commit to a side. The village abstained on day 2 with one lone accusation (player_9 against player_8) and no claims yet. The board is information-starved, and the day 2 vote suggests the living players are not converging on any target. Dying unpicked would be a loss for me, so the timing of my single pick is the live decision, with the board still too unclear to tell which side is trending.
query_dims.target_landscape: Day 2 with no eliminations yet; the only public vote so far was an abstain-heavy round in which one player (player_9) voted to eliminate player_8 alone and everyone else abstained. Candidates are all nine other living players, none with a public role claim or public evidence; the sole public signal is player_9's lone accusation of player_8, which rests on no shown evidence. As the Speculator with no pick yet, I have no role-based information to weigh them against.

lessons.situation: Midgame, day 3 or later. One evil faction member has just been voted out with a confirmed role, and Town is clearly ahead of what remains. The speculator has not picked and is alive and unexposed. It faces a choice between waiting for more information and locking in a side now. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: a system-confirmed role reveal from the elimination, dead roles revealed, and public vote records showing the village voting together. One or two evil players remain unconfirmed. Stakes: Town's lead over the remaining evil is real but not unbeatable. Evil kills each night, and the speculator is an ordinary kill target. Dying unpicked is a guaranteed loss, so each night of delay costs more than the extra information is worth. Target landscape: Four options: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or itself. By now at least one evil faction is eliminated and revealed (a wolf or the lone killer). Town still has a numerical majority over the remaining evil, and the evidence is public reveals and vote records rather than behavior. A self-pick is almost impossible to win.
lessons.action: Once a night arrives in which a lone killer or wolf has been voted out and revealed and the roles left show Town holding a clear majority edge over the remaining evil, spend your single pick that night on Town instead of waiting. The pick is not a visit and cannot be blocked. If you die before picking you lose, and a pick made first still counts after you die.

lessons.situation: A morning after a visible Town success (a lone killer or wolf voted out, or the claimed Investigator saved by the Healer) tempts the Speculator to commit to Town at once. Wolves remain hidden, and Town can still fracture through mis-votes, friendly fire or losing its Healer. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of eliminated players are confirmed and the Investigator's checks are on record. What is missing is the identity of the surviving evil players and whether Town can keep up its voting discipline. Stakes: Town leads comfortably, so an early pick gains little extra. The pick is permanent and announced. Both games showed Town collapsing after the pick through mis-eliminations and the loss of its Healer, which let the wolves win and left the Speculator with a loss. Waiting costs nothing while the Speculator is safe, and the risk is dying unpicked. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or Self. Town leads on numbers, with a living Investigator and Healer. One evil faction is already confirmed dead, but one or two wolves, or a lone killer, are still hidden. The Self pick is unrealistic. Confirmed kills and checks are the evidence; Town's cohesion is only a behavioral read.
lessons.action: When Town looks dominant only because one evil side was just removed, but a wolf or lone killer is still hidden or alive, keep the one pick unspent for another night while the Speculator is not under suspicion. Lock in Town once the remaining evil is down to one hidden wolf with Town's key roles intact. If the Speculator becomes a likely target, pick the leading side right away, because dying unpicked is a loss.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after one or two evil eliminations (Chanteuse, Illusionist, or Serial Killer). Town looks ahead and the Speculator must decide whether to lock in its single pick now or wait. Information landscape: Mostly information-rich: role reveals for dead evil players and a validated Sentinel watch. Some gaps remain: one wolf or the lone killer may be hidden behind a cleared read, and the claimed Investigator and Healer are unverified. Stakes: Town holds a clear numerical majority, but one remaining killer, or a double-kill night, could strip key roles and reverse the lead. The pick is permanent and the Speculator has no other ability, so timing matters more than the margin shown. Target landscape: Town, the wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town looks dominant after the Serial Killer and one or two wolves were eliminated. Evidence is mixed: a confirmed Sentinel result and role reveals for the dead, but the remaining evil's identity is only inferred from behavior or from unverified Investigator claims.
lessons.action: Pick Town only once both the wolves and the lone killer are confirmed dead or identified and Town's investigative and protective core is still alive. If a hidden killer is still unaccounted for, or a likely double-kill night is coming, delay the pick one more night, because a Speculator that dies before picking loses.

lessons.situation: Night 1 (or early night 2) of a ten-player game, with the Speculator's single irreversible pick unspent and nothing established yet. Delaying risks an unannounced night kill by the wolves or the serial killer, which would make the Speculator lose automatically. Information landscape: Information-starved: day 1 was discussion only with no vote, no deaths, no verified claims, and no check results. Any read would be behavioral at best. Stakes: The board is far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The Speculator's own survival to the pick is the main risk: dying unpicked is a guaranteed personal loss, while an early Town pick costs little and keeps the win tied to the largest side. Target landscape: Four sides: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or self. No deaths, claims, or votes exist, so the choice rests on prior side sizes: Town has six roles, wolves two, the lone killer one, and a pick of self wins only as last one standing.
lessons.action: On the first night where you still hold your pick and nothing has been confirmed, lock in your pick right away instead of waiting. Choose Town, the largest side (six Town roles against two wolves, one lone killer and you), since a Speculator that dies unpicked loses and any night attack can remove you before you act. If a night-2 report has already confirmed the wolves are dead or clearly outnumbered, pick Town immediately.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game (nights 2-3) with the speculator alive and unpicked. One wolf has been voted out or a Town save has been announced, but the lone killer and at least one wolf are still hidden. Killers are active every night. Information landscape: Mixed. Some announced facts exist (a revealed wolf death, an announced save, dead power roles), but most night results are unverified claims. The strength of the evil factions is inferred from counts and trend, with no confirmation of the lone killer. Stakes: The board is not at the brink, but each night a hidden killer or wolf can remove the speculator before it picks, and that is a guaranteed loss. The pick is permanent, so a Town pick pays off only if Town survives the lone killer, and Town did lose to a hidden Necromancer or the wolves in some games. Picking by night 2-3 locks in the likeliest winner while the speculator is still alive. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town has the most living members and often a revealed wolf death or verified saves. The wolf pack and lone killer are mostly hidden, and the self pick only wins by being the last player standing. The read rests on public counts and trend more than on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Once Town has a confirmed evil kill or a clear numbers lead (for example a wolf revealed dead and Town power roles still alive), spend your one pick on Town that night. If no side looks clearly ahead, still pick by night 2 or 3, because dying unpicked is an automatic loss and Town is the default side with the most players.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is unsettled and fragmented, with no shared read; discussion is centered on demanding that player_5 name a role, and no coalition has formed.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; a wrong vote is recoverable but costly, and no single vote or kill can end the game this day.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any visible claim about my night or any push against another player commits me to a checkable account; a Sentinel or Trailseer naming me would turn the visit into a public test, and a denial would be hard to reverse.
query_dims.heat_now: Low to moderate: player_5 has drawn several pointed demands and a light low-confidence vote lean from player_10, but I have not been named by anyone with a result.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no verified night results, no revealed Town wills beyond role reveals, and only claims about blocks and unnamed roles.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from any forming consensus, since none exists yet; I am engaging with checkable points to avoid being the passive default vote.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the serial killer, I privately know I killed player_2 on night 1, while the public record shows only that a speculator was stabbed by the serial killer; the village now knows the killer is alive and unnamed, and I have publicly said nothing about my own night, which is the gap I must keep hidden.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 after a night in which a speculator was killed by the serial killer and a trailseer died to the wolves, with a blocked player_5 refusing to name their role while several players press for a vote on that basis.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight alive, all unclaimed on the public record except player_5 who says a night role was blocked without naming it; the accusations so far rest on behavior and unverified blocked-role claims rather than any result.

lessons.situation: First vote of the game after a night-1 death. There are only unverified claims (Trailseer follow, roleblock, Investigator check) and no confirmed roles. The village wants a target but has no hard leads, and you are an unaccused, quiet Serial Killer. Information landscape: Starved: unverifiable claims, one or two corroborations at most, and behavioral reads only. The only confirmed roles are the dead. Stakes: Early in the game with many players alive, no single vote decides the outcome. The priority is to stay unsuspected while the wolves and town thin each other, and to reach the late game with the night kills intact. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around one claim-fight target or split between a target and abstain, with no hard evidence behind either. My position: With the plurality or the abstain bloc, not driving the push. Heat: Low to very low: no accusations, results or contradictions against you, though a stray vote or two may land on you. Forward exposure: A vote with the plurality or an abstain with the room is public and permanent, but it reveals nothing about your role and is cheap to walk back later. A lone outlier vote would be hard to explain and would invite attention. Target landscape: Candidates are a contested claimant (claimed Trailseer or accused wolf-side player), an unclaimed quiet player, or abstain. Every basis is behavioral or an unverified claim, with no confirmed roles besides the dead. Public vs private: You privately know you are the Serial Killer and that you caused the night-1 death. Publicly it is only an unexplained death with unverified claims and no confirmed roles, and nobody has singled you out.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, when you are an unaccused Serial Killer and the room is info-starved, cast your vote for the same target as the largest bloc, preferring a target the wolves or claim-fight evidence already point at. If the room is heading toward an abstain tie, abstain with it rather than splitting off alone; a visible outlier vote gains nothing and invites scrutiny. This keeps you looking like an ordinary town voter while the town and wolves fight each other.

lessons.situation: The first day-2 vote after night-1 deaths. The village is either leadless and abstaining or piling onto a contested claim. You are the unsuspected Serial Killer who needs to survive to keep killing nightly. Information landscape: Information-starved to moderate: a few revealed night-1 dead roles, some unverified claims, and no caught lies or voting history that point to you. Stakes: The board is early, with many players alive and far from the Serial Killer's win threshold. The vote itself is not decisive, so the priority is to stay off the suspect list and alive for the next night kill. Consensus: The village is aligned, either on a unanimous abstain in a leadless day or on a near-unanimous pile-on against a contested claimant. The basis is the room's own discussion, not anything you supplied. My position: With the majority, riding a consensus built without you. Heat: Low to near zero: no one has accused or mentioned you, and you have spoken little or only in support of others. Forward exposure: A vote matching the room commits you to nothing about your role and is indistinguishable from the other votes. Votes are public and permanent, but an abstain can be changed the next day, and joining a shared target is tied to the room, not to you. Target landscape: Around nine or ten living players, with no or only unverified claims. Candidates are a contested claimant or no one, and the basis is behavioral or mechanical speculation rather than hard evidence. You are not among the candidates. Public vs private: You privately know you are the serial killer and caused a night-1 death. Publicly the deaths read as a wolf-side or generic night event, and no one suspects a separate lone killer.
lessons.action: On the first day-2 vote, when you are unsuspected and the room has no lead or has already converged on a target, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain if the room is abstaining, or join the existing pile-on). Don't drive a new accusation or take a lone stance, because a vote identical to the room's carries no tell about your role and keeps your cover for night kills.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote with four players alive, wolves dead or nearly dead, and the serial killer among the survivors. A vote can end with a tie or a counter-wagon on you if it fractures. A decisive elimination reduces the living count to three. Information landscape: Information-rich. Roles are confirmed in the graveyard, full voting histories are on record, and night-visit claims or check results are in play. Stakes: Four alive means one more elimination by vote sets up a night kill that leaves exactly two alive, which is a serial killer win. A fractured vote with no elimination or a wagon on you costs a full cycle and risks your removal. Consensus: The village is split across the three candidates and has no firm majority. Two voters are leaning toward one target on the basis of checks, visit reports, or lack of confirmation. My position: with majority Heat: Moderate to high. Someone voted against you or flagged you as not cleared, and a visit-based or voting-record clue loosely points your way. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and cannot be undone. It aligns you with one other voter and does not reveal your role. It also commits you to the elimination that moves the board toward the final night kill. Target landscape: Three other survivors: an unconfirmed claimant such as a healer, an aggressive accuser such as the speculator, and a claimed investigator or sentinel. Some are backed by evidence, such as a Suspicious check or being named as a victim's visitor, and some only by behavior. Public vs private: You privately know you are the serial killer and that removing any other player by vote sets up the two-alive win. Publicly you are only one of several unconfirmed suspects, and the investigator's note that a serial killer can read Not suspicious is the only thing pointing at you.
lessons.action: With four players left, vote with the plurality forming against a non-you player, joining the most credible accuser or the evidence-backed suspect, so the elimination lands and you are not the focus. Taking the count to three lets your night kill leave two alive, which wins you the game. If the room is split three ways, your vote is the one that makes the plurality decisive, so cast it on the same target as one other voter rather than scattering.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a small group alive, where you (the Serial Killer) are on one of two or more competing elimination wagons and your single ballot can create a tie. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed investigator, sentinel, sigilist or healer results, prior vote records and a dead wolf's votes all feed the suspicion, though none are verified. Stakes: Few players remain, so one lynch of you ends the lone killer's game while a tie keeps you alive for another night kill. This vote is decisive. Consensus: The village is split among several wagons with no unified focus, so one vote can decide whether the leading wagon is tied. My position: holding out Heat: High. Several players, including claimed information roles or the surviving wolf, have already voted for or accused you over passivity or suspected night immunity. Forward exposure: A tie-forcing vote on a rival wagon or a lone-voted bystander leaves a visible but low-cost record, since votes are public and permanent. A lone vote on an accuser looks like retaliation and cannot be undone once the vote closes. Target landscape: Two to four competing wagons: yourself, a suspected wolf, and a quiet or lightly voted player. Role claims are partly unverified and the votes are driven by behavior and claimed results rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: The room publicly reads you as a suspect through low activity, a night-immunity deduction or a stray vote. Privately you know you are the serial killer and that your own ballot can decide whether you survive.
lessons.action: When you are an SK on a live elimination wagon, count the votes and cast your ballot so it makes the top counts tie, either by joining a rival wagon or by adding a vote to a lone-voted third player. A tie means no elimination, so the SK survives to kill again; a lone retaliatory vote on an accuser leaves your wagon alone in front.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame day vote with about five players alive. The room is converging on an unverified suspect and you, the lone killer, are unsuspected. A deviating vote would stand out. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple revealed roles, a public side pick, and a permanent voting record that later days will be read against. Stakes: With about five alive and a night kill still ahead, your survival matters more than steering this one vote. A stranded outlier vote is the cheapest way to turn a low-heat position into the next day's target. Consensus: The village is forming a majority on one unverified candidate, based on past votes and behavior. The board is information-rich, with several deaths and roles revealed and a public side pick announced. My position: Free to choose between joining the forming majority and holding out alone against it. Heat: Low to negligible. Discussion is focused on other players and no one is accusing you. Forward exposure: Every vote goes on the permanent public ledger and cannot be retracted. A lone vote against a claimed information role marks you as anti-Town if that player is later shown to be Town. Joining the majority commits you to nothing unusual. Target landscape: Two or three unverified candidates, such as an unconfirmed neutral with past-vote suspicion and a claimed information role with disputed results. The room leans toward one of them on behavioral reads, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer, immune to night attacks and removable only by a vote. Publicly you read as an ordinary unconfirmed player with almost no suspicion, and the room is debating other people.
lessons.action: When little or no suspicion is on you and the room is forming a majority against a plausible, unverified player, cast your vote with that majority. Do not cast an isolated vote against a claimed Town role or any other conspicuous target, because votes are public and permanent and a stranded outlier becomes the evidence later used to vote you out.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote where the town has deduced that you are the serial killer, or are night-immune, from visitor lists and claim contradictions. You are the unanimous target and must choose a vote: abstain, join the vote on yourself, or name someone else. Information landscape: Information-rich. A visitor list, a follow result, a check result, a counter-claim, and your own mechanics slip all point at you, and your rebuttals have been refuted. Stakes: Your elimination ends the lone killer's win chance, and your single vote cannot prevent it. The only remaining lever is removing a threat or leaving a record that muddies the remaining town's reads. A solo vote is not decisive in either direction. Consensus: The village is almost unanimously aligned on eliminating you. The basis is a coherent chain of evidence, such as the sentinel visitor list, the lack of a save announcement, or a failed role claim. My position: Holding out alone against a lopsided majority on you. Heat: Maximum. Seven or eight players are publicly accusing you on mechanical evidence that your counter-arguments did not refute. Forward exposure: The vote is public and permanent, and cannot be reversed once cast. A vote on a claimed role links you to the line that the claim is fake. With the majority settled it cannot change the result, so the main cost is the record it leaves. Target landscape: You are the near-certain elimination target. The alternatives are the claimants who built the case against you, such as an investigator, sentinel, healer, or counter-claimed role, and a suspected wolf. Their status rests on unverified claims and a few private reads, with no confirmed roles. Public vs private: Privately you know your night-immunity or failed claim has been correctly deduced. Publicly the town has converged on you through visitor lists, a missing save announcement, a counter-claim, or a mechanics error, and your counter-theories have been refuted.
lessons.action: When a near-unanimous majority has already locked onto you and your single vote cannot change the tally, still cast it, and spend it on the living player whose survival most threatens a lone-killer win, such as the information role vouching against you or a wolf. If the room is not yet locked and a swing is possible, first try to split the room before using the vote this way.

lessons.situation: Late-game final vote with three to four players alive and the table pointing at you. Survival depends on whether your vote can combine with another player's vote to deadlock the tally. Information landscape: Rich: most roles are revealed or dead, records have been read out, and claims cross-confirm. The vote history and elimination logic point at you. Stakes: At four alive, losing this vote ends your game. A tie keeps you alive for another night, while a lone dissenting vote gives the town the elimination it wants. Consensus: The room is aligned against you by elimination of other roles, cross-confirmed claims, or a coordinated pair. The other living players are mostly voting as one bloc. My position: Holding out alone or with at most one ally against a majority bloc. Heat: High to critical. You are the last unverified or unrevealed player, or two players are openly coordinating against you, and the vote record is the evidence they are using. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and cannot be reversed. Voting an accuser commits you to open conflict with that player. Voting alone on a neutral or confirmed-looking player adds no pressure and confirms the room's read of you, whereas joining an ally's target can force a tie. Target landscape: The candidates are the lead accuser, the other accusers, and any ally who is also being pushed. Confirmed or cross-confirmed town roles are poor targets. A vote only helps if it matches an ally's vote and leaves the tally level. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving lone killer, immune to night attacks and removable only by a day vote. Publicly, the table has narrowed suspicion onto you by elimination or through coordinated accusations.
lessons.action: When the table is converging on you in a small endgame vote, count the votes before casting yours. If another living player is also under attack or will vote against your accusers, put your vote on the lead accuser they are voting for, so the tally ties and nobody is eliminated. Do not vote for a target nobody else will join, because a lone vote cannot change the result.

lessons.situation: A day vote where the room has converged on eliminating a wolf-side player, accused by claimed town roles. The accused counter-accuses or deflects heat onto quiet players, possibly including you. Information landscape: Mostly claims and behavioral reads, with only partial corroboration (such as a sentinel or trailseer claim) and no hard verification until the reveal. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several players alive. Your vote does not decide the outcome, but sitting in the bloc keeps your profile clean while the wolves thin out ahead of your own kills. Consensus: Most of the village is aligned on one wolf-side target, with a five- to six-vote majority built on corroborating claims and behavioral reads. My position: With the majority. Heat: Low to mild. At most one stray mention, for example being called a quiet player, and nobody else picked it up. Forward exposure: A vote with the bloc reveals nothing and keeps your public record identical to the other voters'. The vote is irreversible, but eliminating a wolf you are not allied with is not something you need to undo. Target landscape: The main candidate is a wolf-side player accused by several players on a mix of claims (a sentinel or trailseer claim, or busing logic) and behavior, and denying it. The alternatives are a claimed town role the wolf accused back, or abstaining. No result is confirmed before the elimination. Public vs private: You privately know you are the lone killer and that the targeted player is a rival wolf-side player. Publicly you are just another quiet, unclaimed voter, so the vote costs you nothing.
lessons.action: When a wolf is the target of a majority-backed vote and you are only mildly mentioned or not accused, vote with the majority to eliminate that wolf. Your vote then matches the bloc's and gives the room nothing to pick at, and a wolf removed by a day vote costs you no night kill. Skip abstaining or voting off-bloc, since that is the only way to stand out.

lessons.situation: After a night death in an information-rich mid-game, the village has locked onto a majority target. As the serial killer with low heat, I am tempted to cast a contrarian vote on a different player, a claimed information role or a quiet suspect, that cannot swing the result. Information landscape: Information-rich. Role reveals from night deaths, public check or follow claims, and the previous day's voting records are all available to be read against my vote. Stakes: Several players remain, so the vote can be fully survived if I stay unremarkable. The majority outcome is unaffected by my ballot, so a dissent gains almost nothing while adding a visible mark that can cost me the final-day vote. Consensus: Strong and decisive. A clear majority is already committed to one target after a night death or a claim chain, and the vote outcome is effectively fixed. My position: Holding out against a forming majority, which is the position this move corrects. Heat: Low. No one is accusing me, and a claimed check or the discussion has deflected suspicion elsewhere. Forward exposure: A vote against a decided majority is public and permanent, and it cannot be retracted. It invites scrutiny the next day, and opponents can cite it as proof I am the killer. A majority-aligned vote commits me to nothing unusual and can be changed later. Target landscape: A consensus suspect (a suspected wolf or a doubted information-role claimant) who is likely to fall regardless, versus a fringe alternative such as a quiet player or an information-role claimant. The consensus basis is behavior and claims; the alternative gives me little concrete evidence to justify a dissent. Public vs private: Privately I am the lone killer who caused the night deaths and reads Not suspicious. Publicly I am treated as low-heat or cleared town, and the room has settled on another target.
lessons.action: When the room has formed a clear majority on a target and your own heat is low, cast your vote with the majority. Hold the lone dissenting vote back for a case where it changes the result. A vote that cannot change the outcome only leaves a permanent outlier record, which opponents cite against you on later days.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Ten alive with six eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, so no single night or vote can end the game; the board is far from decisive, which means a watch spent early is recoverable but each of my two watches is a finite resource that cannot be reloaded.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no night results, no claims, no recorded discussion. The only public data is the day 2 vote record and the day 1 quiet night. Any watch is the first real evidence on the board.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 ended in an abstain: the village voted to abstain with one lone accusation against a single player that nobody joined, and no claims or discussion have been recorded. As the Sentinel, I hold both watches unspent and must decide whether to spend one tonight on a player who is a likely victim or a suspect, knowing that a watch shows who visited that player and never reveals my own visit.
query_dims.target_landscape: Nine living players with no public role claims and no night results yet; the only public action so far is one vote from a player against another on day 2 that drew no support, and the village abstained. Everyone's role status is unverified, so candidates rest on no evidence beyond silence and one lone accusation.

lessons.situation: After a day of mostly abstentions, the sentinel is deciding whether to spend its final watch on a suspect, either someone who voted against it or the only visitor seen at the first victim, rather than on a likely victim. Information landscape: Public information is thin because of the abstain consensus, with only a few outlier votes and one or two old visit reports. The sentinel's private visit data is old and has not been refreshed by any recent watch. Stakes: The sentinel has one watch left, so the choice is final. A wasted or blocked watch leaves it with no information power and little credibility. A watch that catches the night's visitor could confirm an evil player the town can vote on, so the pick has to be a door someone is likely to visit. Target landscape: Living players with no confirmed roles: a vote-based suspect (lone accuser or outlier voter), a player seen visiting the first victim, and likely kill targets such as vocal or claimed power roles. Reads rest on voting behavior and one earlier visit, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: With one watch left, put it on the player the killers are most likely to attack tonight, such as a vocal or claimed power role or someone who has been guessing correctly, instead of on a suspect picked from votes or early visits. A watch only shows who came to the watched player, so a suspect's door shows nothing unless someone targets them. If no likely victim stands out, keep the watch and act when one does.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended in abstain or a mis-elimination with no deaths or only one. Evil killers are still active, and you have one watch left to use on someone. Information landscape: Mixed, mostly thin. There are a few public claims, a Day 2 vote record and possibly one early death, but no verified wolf or killer. Night interactions are unseen. Stakes: Several evil factions are alive and the town has no leads on them. A visitor trace from your last watch could be the main evidence for eliminating a killer or wolf over the next two days. Wasting it leaves the town with no watcher coverage. Target landscape: A contested player who drew Day 2 votes or a roleblock question and has no verified role, a high-profile claimed Town role (Investigator or Trailseer), and quiet players who abstained. Everything is judged from vote records and behavior, not from checks.
lessons.action: With your last watch, watch the player the day left most exposed to a night visit: someone who drew several votes, whose claim or roleblock story is doubted, or who is a likely kill or block target. The visitor list can then catch the killer, a wolf carrier or the chanteuse, and it tests the watched player's own account of the night. Prefer this to a quiet player or a suspect no one is likely to visit, since an unvisited door shows nothing.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a day-2 vote or abstain, usually with the chanteuse revealed or dead. The sentinel is a known information role, may be blocked or killed, and has one watch left. Only one of the observed cases (the one where the watch was aimed at a claim-linked suspect) turned the watch into usable town information. Information landscape: Moderately informed. There are a few claims (tracker, block, investigator or vigilante) and one's own night-1 watch record, but the remaining wolf, the lone killer and the neutral are unconfirmed. Evidence is thin and mostly behavioral. Stakes: Town still has slack but is losing information roles each night. A watch that confirms a claimed shooter's visit lets Town trust that player's remaining bullets. A watch that is blocked, concealed or aimed at nothing leaves the sentinel with no further visit data. Target landscape: About eight living players. One or two have a public record (e.g. caught visiting a door on night 1, or carrying a contested claim) and may be a claimed actor's next target. The rest are quiet players with only behavioral reads. The likely kill victim is a poor watch target if the illusionist can still conceal the body.
lessons.action: On night 2 with your last watch, put it on a door where the result can corroborate or refute a specific public claim. Good doors are a player a claimed shooter or visitor is expected to target, or a suspect who already has a public record. If no door is testable, a blind watch on a quiet player gains little, so keep the watch rather than spend it on pure behavior.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an early death or two and a vote that was tied, abstained, or produced no lead. The sentinel has one watch left and must pick whose door to stand at. Information landscape: Information-starved: few revealed roles, no verified wolf identity, and only behavioral pressure points such as vote totals or who drives the discussion. Stakes: Mid-game with the wolves still at full strength. A visitor name from the last watch may be the only hard lead, and spending it well can unlock a wolf elimination the next day. The cost is losing your watches and becoming a visible kill target. Target landscape: Roughly 7-8 living players with no confirmed roles beyond the early dead. Candidates are the loudest discussion-driver or a quiet player who drew votes. They are chosen on behavior as likely next wolf kill targets, not on evidence.
lessons.action: On night 2 with your last watch and no hard leads, watch the player the wolves are most likely to attack next, such as the most vocal question-driver or a quiet player drawing votes, rather than holding the watch or watching yourself. If a visitor appears, you have a concrete lead on who went to that door. If none appears, it may point to a night-immune target or a different kill choice.

lessons.situation: Night 1 with no deaths, claims, or votes. The sentinel must decide whether to spend one of two watches blind or hold both. Its own role is a plausible wolf kill target, and an enemy roleblocker may be active. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no night history, public claims, deaths, or voting records. Any watch is a speculative guess, but a watch can still reveal visitors that no other source gives. Stakes: The board is early and far from parity, so spending one watch is cheap and keeps one in reserve. A watch that sees visitors gives Town its first hard night fact, such as the wolf carrier or other active roles. Dying or being blocked on Night 1 wastes the use, which is a risk this policy accepts. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unconfirmed after a discussion-only Day 1. There is no evidence, so the pick rests on guessing which door wolves or active night roles will visit.
lessons.action: On a blind opening night, spend one of the two watches rather than holding both, and put it on a player who looks like an appealing wolf kill or active night-role door (not a player who looks inert). A kill victim's door shows the carrier's visit, and other active roles' visits also show, unless the body is concealed or the watch is blocked. Keep the second watch for a later night when a death, claim or lead gives a target.

lessons.situation: After a key information role was voted out, the town cannot identify the necromancer or wolves. The sentinel is the last watcher, was just double-attacked and saved only by the healer, and is an obvious chanteuse block target. Information landscape: Information-starved: only a reanimated-attack signature and a revealed record, with no confirmed suspect. Reads on who pushed votes are behavioral and weak. Stakes: Moderate pressure: the sentinel has been a direct target, and a blocked watch loses both information and the use. Spending a limited watch on weak behavior reads risks yielding nothing at an important point. Target landscape: One unconfirmed killer suspect chosen on voting behavior with weak evidence, versus likely victims such as other power roles or oneself, whose door a wolf or killer must visit to attack.
lessons.action: If you have a watch left and the town has no hard lead on the remaining killer or wolves, first consider who is likely to be attacked rather than a behavior-only suspect. If you do watch a suspect, expect the chanteuse to block you, since a blocked watch is wasted and shows nothing, so prefer the watch on the likely victim.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended without an elimination after rival investigator claims. A night-1 death with a revealed role, with a necromancer able to use the body, leaves the sentinel deciding whether to spend a watch on the most contested suspect. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: a revealed night-1 death, a trailseer follow placing a suspect at the victim's door, conflicting claims, and no confirmed wolf. Stakes: Mid-game with enough town alive to absorb a miss, but a lone killer is likely active. A watch on the focal suspect can expose a body-attack that is otherwise invisible. Target landscape: A contested suspect placed at the night-1 victim's door by a trailseer follow, who clashes with a rival investigator claimant; alternatives are the other claimant, a quiet player, or the likely next victim. No role is confirmed, so the basis is a tracked visit plus behavior.
lessons.action: When a contested suspect exists (a tracked visit at a victim's door plus a rival claim) and you still hold watches, spend a watch on that suspect rather than holding it, and keep your choice of door private. The visitor list can reveal who is acting on them, including a dead player's name at the door that exposes a necromancer working a body.

lessons.situation: Late game after the lone killer (necromancer) was voted out. The wolf pack, including a chanteuse, is the only remaining threat and needs kills, so the healer and power roles are the obvious next targets. The sentinel has one watch left. Information landscape: Information-rich about the dead roles and the healer's protective pattern, but thin on living wolf identities. No confirmed wolf besides a dead one, so behavioral reads are speculative and the visitor list at a likely victim's door is the best available hard evidence. Stakes: The wolves are a few eliminations from parity, and one correct wolf identification can end the game. A wasted last watch removes the sentinel's only source of hard evidence, so it should go where a visitor would directly incriminate. Target landscape: Likely wolf kill targets (the healer and remaining town power roles, publicly alive and valuable) versus behavior-only suspects with no evidence; the choice is between a victim-side watch that yields visitor names and a suspect-side watch that rests on weak reads.
lessons.action: With one watch left and only the wolf pack still threatening, spend it on the most likely wolf kill target, such as the healer or another power role the pack needs gone, rather than on a behavior-only suspect. A visitor seen at that door is a concrete, reportable lead on a wolf, and if no one visited, you keep the information that the pack went elsewhere.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, night 3 or later. One or more evil killers (wolf pack plus a serial killer or necromancer) are still active, and town's key information asset is the obvious kill target. The Sentinel has to decide where to spend its last watch, or whether to keep it. Information landscape: Moderate to rich. Some roles are confirmed by flips or reveals and an earlier investigator result is known. The remaining killer's identity is unknown, and claims about night results are unverified. Stakes: Town can still afford to lose a role, but each lost information role makes the wolf and lone-killer hunt harder. This is the Sentinel's last watch, so a wasted one leaves town with no door-watching for the rest of the game. Target landscape: The most validated or claimed information-role player (investigator or trailseer, already attacked or clearly threatening to wolves), versus an unconfirmed claimant (e.g. sigilist), a soft-cleared quiet player, and a roleblocked healer. Reads on who is the likely kill target rest on behavior and claim strength, since no wolf is hard-identified.
lessons.action: With your last watch at night 3 or later, put it on the living player the killers are most likely to attack, usually the validated investigator or trailseer-type information source. Do not spend it on a soft-cleared or low-threat player. A watch there can show who came to the door, which can name an attacker or confirm others' claimed visits, while a watch on a safe player will probably return nothing.

lessons.situation: The chanteuse blocks the sentinel night after night while the wolves keep targeting the investigator. The sentinel keeps picking a watch door anyway and learns nothing, only discovering the block the next morning. Information landscape: Info-starved for the sentinel: no watch result since night 1, and the town's picture rests on the investigator's checks alone. Stakes: Mid-to-late game with the wolves steadily trimming town. Each night the sentinel is blocked produces no information while two watches remain unspent. Target landscape: The investigator (the likely wolf target after being attacked and saved) and a partly cleared sigilist claimant, among seven to eight alive. No one else has hard evidence against them.
lessons.action: After you've been roleblocked on consecutive nights and the wolves keep going after the same target, change your pattern. Hold your watch for a night, or put it on a different door than the one you'd normally expect traffic at, so your remaining watches aren't spent into repeated blocks. Do not keep choosing the same predictable doors every night while the block pattern persists.

lessons.situation: The sentinel committed its last watch to a named door in front of the room, to run a visit test between two rival investigator claimants. The chanteuse blocked the sentinel that night, so the test never happened. Information landscape: Info-starved on the target itself: only a claim conflict and a concealed first-night victim. No visit evidence justified the specific door beyond the experiment. Stakes: With one watch left, a blocked night wastes the sentinel's last chance at a result. The town's resolution of the claim conflict hangs on that one result. Target landscape: The fortune teller as a publicly proposed shared target for a visit test between two rival investigator claimants. There was no suspicion on them, so it was an arbitrary neutral pick with no evidence behind it.
lessons.action: Choose your watch door from your own private reasoning and don't tie it to a target the room has publicly named, because a chanteuse can block a sentinel whose door was announced in advance. If you can't tell whether you're being targeted, pick the door by where visits are most likely rather than where you announced.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is leaning toward eliminating you: the claimed Sigilist and unclaimed player openly support that vote, and the Investigator has framed you as a likely target. The Healer claim dispute and absence of an explicit Investigator vote leave the alignment short of confirmed unanimity.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: With four alive, it is two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so this vote is a swing decision with an immediate endgame risk.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Maintaining the Healer claim and directing attention toward the unclaimed player commits you to a public identity and accusation that are difficult to retract. Revealing your Necromancer role or the concealed victim’s role would expose private information and your earlier attacks; the current Healer claim has not disclosed that information.
query_dims.heat_now: High: the claimed Investigator reports a Suspicious read on you, and the claimed Sigilist and unclaimed player are explicitly voting for you. The Investigator has credibility from the earlier read that matched the revealed Illusionist.
query_dims.information_landscape: There is substantial public mechanical evidence: the Illusionist and Vigilante were revealed, the Trailseer’s will was read, and two deaths were announced as reanimated attacks. The concealed night-2 victim’s role is unavailable publicly. Current role and result claims, including the competing protection accounts and the new Suspicious read, are not independently verified; the earlier Investigator claim has strong support from the Illusionist reveal.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out against the forming vote against you; you maintain the Healer claim and point to the unclaimed player’s account as a competing issue.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Necromancer: you attacked through the revealed Illusionist’s body on night 2, killing the player whose role was concealed, and through the revealed Vigilante’s body on night 3, killing the Trailseer. Publicly, the village knows those deaths were made by reanimated abilities, but the night-2 victim’s role remains concealed. The claimed Investigator’s Suspicious read on you and the competing Healer claims are public claims, not verified role facts.
query_dims.situation: At four alive, a claimed Investigator’s Suspicious result puts the Healer claimant under strong elimination pressure, while a second player disputes the Healer’s account of a night-2 protection. The conflict is especially consequential because two prior deaths were publicly attributed to reanimated attacks, but the private identity of the Necromancer and the concealed night-2 victim’s role remain unknown to the village.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate vote landscape centers on you, whom a claimed Investigator says read Suspicious and who claims Healer; the Investigator claimant, whose earlier Suspicious result against the revealed Illusionist has strong public support; a player claiming Sigilist without public confirmation; and an unclaimed player who says they protected the Investigator on night 2. The claimed Healer’s night-2 protection claim conflicts with that last account, but neither protection claim has public confirmation.

lessons.situation: Late game with three or four alive after a public reanimated attack. The Necromancer pool has been narrowed to a few players, I am one of them, and I must either claim a cover role or accuse the other suspect before the vote. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: announced night attack types, revealed roles, public vote records and a narrowed suspect pool. The remaining evidence is unverified claims. Stakes: With three alive, one vote or one night kill decides the game. If the vote lands on me, Town wins at once; if it lands elsewhere, I am a night kill from winning. Consensus: The room is converging against me. The other suspects' accounts fit the announced night events, and a ballot of two or three players can tie or flip on a single vote. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus and trying to turn the swing voter. Heat: High. I was named the Necromancer by elimination or by a rival claimant, and a public reanimated attack points at whoever has been channeling it. Forward exposure: A fabricated role claim or a flat counter-accusation commits me to a story that the public night record or the real role holder can test. It cannot be withdrawn without confessing, and with three alive the next vote is final. Target landscape: Two or three living suspects, including me. Their roles are claimed but unverified, and the basis is claims plus the public reanimated-attack report, which fits whoever is suspected. Public vs private: I know I am the Necromancer and that my reanimated attack is already public. Publicly I am one of two or three suspects, and my accusers' claims fit the announced night events.
lessons.action: When the Necromancer pool has shrunk to about three and you are named, anchor your defense only in announced facts such as morning reports, public votes and revealed roles. Pick a cover story that no living player can contradict from a private record. If a living player's own record already fits the facts better than your story, shift to showing that their account explains the announced night events no better than yours does. Do not invent a detailed record, such as bets, that a real holder can contradict.

lessons.situation: Late game with about five players alive. A body-assisted attack has been announced and the town is hunting the lone killer among the few unconfirmed players, while you are one of them. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced role reveals, a will clearing a player, a reanimated-attack announcement, and permanent public votes give the town a lot to cross-check. Stakes: With five alive, one wrongly directed or lost day vote can end your game. Being named the necromancer this round is likely fatal, so avoiding contradictions matters more than pushing a theory. Consensus: The village is converging on a small set of unconfirmed players using announced facts, and it is ready to punish evasive or inconsistent framing. My position: holding out Heat: High. The announced reanimated attack proves a necromancer is alive, so scrutiny falls on every unconfirmed player, and your unexplained votes draw questions. Forward exposure: Claiming to be outside the suspect pool commits you to a facade that cross-examination of your votes can break, and you cannot take it back once challenged. Staying inside the pool and giving consistent reasons commits you to little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: A few unconfirmed players (you, a surviving wolf or neutral, and others) next to cleared or confirmed players such as a healer cleared by an investigator's will. The only hard evidence is announced facts and wills, and the rest is voting-record behavior. Public vs private: You privately know you used a dead wolf's or vigilante's body to attack, while the room knows only that a necromancer is alive and is narrowing down the unconfirmed players.
lessons.action: When a reanimated attack has been announced and you sit in a small unconfirmed pool, put yourself in that pool openly and answer questions about your voting record with reasons that match the public record. Then argue from announced facts such as wills, saves and kill types, and name the other unconfirmed players as candidates alongside yourself instead of presenting yourself as a neutral judge outside the pool.

lessons.situation: A claimed Investigator publicly accuses or reads you as Suspicious, around a night where a hidden-role death or a reanimated kill hints at a Necromancer. The village debates how to verify the claim while you are the only one contesting it. Information landscape: Thin hard evidence: an unverified Investigator claim with at most a half-confirmed earlier check, one hidden-role death, and no Trailseer or Sentinel corroboration. Stakes: Being voted out ends the necromancer's only win path, which is to be last standing. This day's vote is therefore existential, and heat must come down before it. Consensus: The village is converging on the claimant's read, and its only open question is how to verify it. The basis is the claim plus any partial confirmation, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out alone against the consensus. Heat: High and rising. A Suspicious read from a plausible Investigator, a public announcement that a Necromancer struck, and your own pushback have put you at the center. Forward exposure: Resisting or denying locks you into an all-in 'fake claim' story that collapses if the claimant is corroborated, and it cannot be taken back. Endorsing verification commits you to little, and you can still shift your stance later. Target landscape: The candidates are the Investigator claimant, who has partial corroboration and no role contest, and you, the accused. No other player is a clear alternative suspect, and Trailseer or Sentinel confirmers are unclaimed or may be dead under a hidden role. Public vs private: You privately know the Investigator's read on you is accurate, or that no one can truly confirm or refute it. Publicly the village sees an unverified claimant versus an accused player and is searching for a way to test it.
lessons.action: When a claimed Investigator names you and the village is looking for a way to verify it, endorse the verification and don't fight it. Offer a cooperative test, such as asking the claimant for the full check history and asking any Trailseer or Sentinel to speak up, and press the village to put its vote on a rival suspect if the evidence stays thin. A flat denial or repeated pushback only reads as fear of proof and leaves you alone against the room.

lessons.situation: Endgame with about four alive and the wolves dead or nearly dead. The town reasons by elimination that you are the Necromancer, and a rival claimant is pushing a vote on you. Information landscape: Info-starved: no hard evidence, role claims cannot be verified, and the discussion rests on elimination logic and vote records. Stakes: With four alive, one wrong vote or kill decides the game. If you survive the vote, your next night kill leaves three alive and brings you close to winning. Consensus: Undecided and fragile: the town knows a lone killer is still alive, but has no evidence separating the remaining players. My position: Holding out against an accusation, countering it rather than driving a wagon. Heat: High: you are the leading suspect through role elimination and the only player without a trusted claim. Forward exposure: A false claim commits you to a consistent fabricated history that can be compared against the real claimant's, and it can only be sustained until the vote closes. It is hard to retract once made. Target landscape: Three or four remaining players: the accuser (a claimant of a neutral role), one other uncommitted claimant, and a possible leftover wolf. Roles are judged on claim-versus-claim and vote tone, not on hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the Necromancer and the accuser's claim may even be true, but publicly it is one unverifiable claim against another, with no hard evidence either way.
lessons.action: When wolves are mostly dead and you are named Necromancer by elimination in a four-player endgame, counter-accuse the accuser and hold a stable story: if the accuser is a claimed neutral, counterclaim that role with a bet or result history that does not line up with deaths the town already knows. Aim to split the remaining voters rather than win every vote, because a split or a wasted vote keeps you alive for your night attack.

lessons.situation: With the wolves gone and few players left, a confirmed vigilante is leading the hunt for the lone necromancer and the town is choosing between claimed role players. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves eliminated, a confirmed vigilante kill announced, spent-sigil claims and repeated roleblock claims. A confirmed shooter still holds a bullet. Stakes: A confirmed vigilante with a bullet can kill you at night if you look like the necromancer, so any extra heat can end the game. Consensus: The town is moving toward one elimination on claim-based reasoning, and it is explicitly treating anyone who attacks the protective claimants as suspect.
