lessons.situation: A player reveals that I and another player both visited an attacked player who survived. I must explain my presence at the victim's door right away. Information landscape: Several claims and partial results: a surviving attacked player, a reported two-visitor list, and a reported roleblock. No confirmed roles for the visitors. Stakes: Mid-game with parity within a few eliminations. A convincing explanation here can send the vote to a rival and tilt the board toward the wolves, while failure risks exposing a wolf. Consensus: The room is looking for an explanation of the visitors. It will accept one that corroborates the save and fits other claims. My position: Leading the narrative by offering the protective explanation before the real healer formalizes a claim. Heat: High at first, because I was named as a visitor to a saved victim. A credible explanation of the visit can defuse it quickly. Forward exposure: A Healer claim is permanent and sets up a conflict whenever the real healer speaks. It buys immediate corroboration of the save and scrutiny on the exposer. Target landscape: The exposer (here a necromancer), who can be cast as the threat, and the real healer, who also visited the victim and can be framed as the false second visitor. Claims are mostly unverified, and others' results are partial. Public vs private: Privately I visited the victim as the wolf carrying the kill, and it failed because of a save. Publicly I reframe that visit as the protection, so it contradicts what I know.
lessons.action: If an observer publicly names you as a visitor at an attacked-but-saved player and you are under heavy heat, consider claiming Healer: say your visit was the protection that saved them. Use this only when you accept a later counter-claim from the real healer, and press suspicion onto the exposer in the meantime. It is a permanent claim, so reserve it for cases where denial would not hold.

lessons.situation: Late game with three or four players alive, your wolf partner dead or revealed, and the town reasoning that the remaining evil is down to you and perhaps one other. You are the last wolf and a swing voter decides the day. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed deaths and roles, public vote records, and a public night report such as an attack and save. Remaining claims are unverified, but the elimination argument already favors the accusers. Stakes: One vote decides the game. If the swing voter follows the accusers, the last wolf is eliminated and Town wins, so only a concrete, checkable argument aimed at that voter can change the result. Consensus: The village is aligned on eliminating you, based on elimination logic and prior vote records, and it is hardly moved by behavioral appeals. My position: Holding out alone against a formed or forming majority. Heat: Very high to extreme. The pool has been narrowed by elimination to you plus at most one other, and confirmed or credible Town roles have already voted against or named you. Forward exposure: A specific accusation commits you to a falsifiable statement and cannot be retracted. With a majority already forming, a generic or purely epistemic defense adds nothing, so a concrete point is the only move that can still shift a voter. Target landscape: Two to three candidates remain: you, an unconfirmed neutral or lone killer, and sometimes a claimed accuser with public support such as a confirmed save or a confirmed-town ally. The town is reasoning from the record and by elimination, not from behavior. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the last wolf and that the accusers' pool is built on a correct elimination argument. Publicly nobody can verify any claim, but the record and the narrowed pool point at you.
lessons.action: As the last wolf with the partner gone and the room closing in, aim your remaining speech at the swing voter. Name one concrete, checkable inconsistency in the leading accuser's own record, such as a vote, a timing, or a claim that conflicts with a confirmed announcement. If no such inconsistency exists, point to the unclaimed or unconfirmed third player on the same kind of record evidence instead of arguing that claims are merely unverified.

lessons.situation: A day after a concealed-role kill, a Sentinel or Trailseer report puts you at the victim's door. You must explain the visit without lying about a night action that the real role-holder can deny. Information landscape: Rich on you (visit trace, other claims, an investigator result) and almost empty on your partner. The only evidence on your side is the rules logic. Stakes: Losing the Illusionist costs the pack a conceal and information control, and can leave the Chanteuse as a lone wolf. Keeping your standing intact matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The room is split and reasoning from mechanics. Some players already note that a visible visitor is probably not the carrier. My position: Under direct pressure and defending alone. Your partner is unrevealed and not yet drawn in. Heat: High: you are named in a visit report at a concealed-role death, and the accusation is concrete. Forward exposure: A rules argument commits you to no false fact and can be dropped or adjusted later. A fake role claim or a flat denial of a true report is falsifiable and cannot be walked back. Target landscape: You and the other named visitor, or you and the reporter. No roles are confirmed. The basis is a visit trace and a dispute over what a hidden visit implies, not proof of who attacked. Public vs private: Privately you concealed the body and your visit is real, so the visitor report is true. Publicly it is one unverified report that the room can read as either a killer's trace or a non-carrier's trace.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer places you at a concealed body, say that the pack's carrier visit to a concealed victim leaves no trace, so a visible visitor is less likely to be the killer. Stay with that rules point, don't claim any night action of your own, and don't deny the visit outright.

lessons.situation: On Day 2 after Night 1, a Sentinel or Trailseer reports that I or my partner visited or was visited, and the town debates whether that visit means anything. Information landscape: Soft, unverified claims from the Sentinel, Trailseer, and Investigator that establish movement but not alignment; no hard confirmations. Stakes: The board is early with the wolves comfortably behind parity. The main risk is a premature bandwagon on a wolf, so neutralizing the visit report and securing an abstain preserves both wolves for another night. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on treating the visit reports as soft information and leaning toward abstaining, with no hard evidence to drive a vote. My position: with majority Heat: Low to moderate: I am named in a night report, but the report shows no hostile pattern and reads as a puzzle. Forward exposure: Confirming the visit casually commits me only to a consistent account of one night's movement and makes no role claim, so the position stays flexible and easy to adjust later. Target landscape: The visited or reported players (me, my partner, a quiet player) are tied only to soft claims. There are no confirmed evil leads, so the choice is mostly between abstaining and behavioral suspicion of quiet players. Public vs private: Publicly, a Town tracker or watcher has reported a visit involving me or my partner and the room treats it as a puzzle. Privately, I know the wolf kill or block behind it and that the report is accurate or that the trace was hidden, so it is not evidence against us.
lessons.action: When a Town role's night report (Sentinel watch, Trailseer follow) names you or your partner as a visitor on Night 1, confirm the visit calmly in a casual, role-neutral way and note that a visit alone does not show alignment. Then point the room to a procedural next step, such as asking the visited player or the Investigator what they saw, and back an abstain. If the report is accurate, stay consistent with it and do not volunteer extra detail or claim a role.

lessons.situation: A genuine unique-role claimant has revealed a result or action. I am tempted to counter-claim the same role, but the game record, such as a healer save announcement or an investigator claim, already supports the genuine claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced saves, night-action claims and the one-per-role rule let the town test claims for consistency against fixed facts. Stakes: A failed counter-claim costs a wolf immediately and halves the pack. The wolf partner survives only if the town's attention stays on me. Consensus: Aligned against me: the town reasons that one role slot means one of us is lying, and the public facts point away from me. My position: holding out Heat: Severe. Every player can see that only one of us can be telling the truth, and the announcements favor the other claimant. Forward exposure: Counter-claiming a unique role is irrevocable. It makes it a 1-for-1 claim fight, and if my account fails against the announced facts I am eliminated, and my body then reveals the illusionist role. Target landscape: The genuine claimant of a unique role, whose account is corroborated by announcements, versus me as the only rival claimant. The evidence is mechanical and not based on behavior. Public vs private: Privately I know the real night events, such as who the wolves killed and who my partner blocked. Publicly the rival claimant's account matches the announcements, and mine would not.
lessons.action: Before contesting a claimed information or protective role, check your story against every Game Master announcement, such as saves, deaths and revealed roles. If the story cannot fit them, do not counter-claim a unique role, since a second claimant on a one-player role forces the town to pick one and the announced facts will favor the genuine claimant. In that case, fall back on a claim-free line that casts doubt on the accuser without staking a role.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the remaining evil faction can win, and the game can end within one more elimination; a wrong lynch now leaves the village one loss from a wolf-side outcome, so the next vote is high-cost.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no living player has a firm night result to share. Public evidence is limited to the night 3 record (a player struck by a sigil and killed by a reanimated vigilante, the investigator's day 2 check) and the claims of the living players, which are unverified.
query_dims.situation: Four players remain alive after the day 4 vote eliminated a player revealed as the necromancer. The village is weighing a sigilist claim that is consistent with the night 3 record, while two unclaimed players are being pressed for what they did, and the remaining evil roles are believed to be the illusionist and fortune teller, both still hidden.
query_dims.target_landscape: Three living players: player_1 (abstained both days, no claimed role, no night result), player_9 (claims sigilist, sigil placed on a player who was struck down on night 3, consistent with the record), and player_10 (claims no result, voted to abstain today, pressed others to explain their votes). Public role status: no living player has a confirmed role; player_9's sigil claim is claimed with partial public support, while player_1 and player_10 are unclaimed.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, a wolf has been voted out or is revealed, but a lone killer such as the Necromancer is still hidden and could attack anyone. The healer must choose whom to cover among several Town power-role claimants. Information landscape: Partly informative: some roles are confirmed by announced deaths or by confirmed checks and watches. The identity of the hidden killer is unknown and only its attack kind is visible, so the next target is speculative. Stakes: Few players remain, so losing a key Town role or the healer sharply cuts the Town's ability to remove the last killer. Each save matters, but the next target cannot be known. Target landscape: Living claimants: Investigator with confirmed checks, Vigilante holding the last bullet, Sentinel, Trailseer, Sigilist. Their value is ranked by verified results, past attacks on them, and ability left, not by how they talk.
lessons.action: Each night, protect the confirmed-Town player whose ability is the Town's best remaining way to remove the hidden killer, such as the Vigilante with a bullet left or an Investigator with checks left. If one of them was attacked earlier and saved, keep covering them unless a newer attack pattern points elsewhere. Don't spread protection across low-value or unverified claimants just to rotate.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after a day elimination or tied vote. The healer must choose which of several claimed town power roles to shield from the remaining killers, who can strike with concealment or through reanimated bodies. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed investigative and tracking results, public morning reports, confirmed eliminations and prior save records, and a known killer attack pattern. Stakes: With few players left and a killer still active, each night kill moves town close to losing its majority, so losing the one remaining active information role can decide the endgame. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed town power roles: a trailseer with active tracking results naming a living suspect, a sentinel whose watches are spent or who was already saved, and a sigilist with a reactive ability; claims are unverified but backed by morning-report facts and are the main evidence.
lessons.action: When several town power-role claimants are alive and an enemy killer is still active, protect the claimant whose live, ongoing output is driving the case (e.g. a trailseer who just tied a living suspect to a victim) in preference to a claimant whose uses are spent or who already got a save. Reason: a night kill on the active information source costs town the most, and two of three observations show the unprotected trailseer being killed with its role concealed. If no claimant has live output, protecting the publicly confirmed sentinel is a sound default.

lessons.situation: Late game, after the Chanteuse was voted out. Only one wolf (Illusionist) and possibly a lone killer remain, and the Healer must pick one protectee among a few town players, including a proven information role that the killers have already hit. Information landscape: Moderately to highly informative: dead wolves are confirmed, roles were revealed on death, and one or two information roles have verified track records. There are no leads on the last wolf or the lone killer. Stakes: Few players remain, so one successful kill moves the board toward parity. A save on the most valuable information role denies the killers a kill and preserves the tool that can catch the last killers, but only one player can be covered each night. Target landscape: A small set of living players: a Trailseer or Sentinel with a verified track record (survived attacks, cross-checked by the healer's own visits), a publicly claimed Investigator with spent checks, and quiet unclaimed players such as the Vigilante and Sigilist. Verified information roles outrank quiet slots; the quiet slots offer no evidence to rank them by.
lessons.action: After a wolf is eliminated and the remaining killers are down to one wolf plus the serial killer or a lone wolf, protect the verified information role (e.g. the Trailseer or Sentinel) the killers have already targeted or that the room trusts most. If that role has already been attacked and saved, keep protecting it, because the killers keep returning to it and a save cancels the attack while keeping their intel alive.

lessons.situation: Healer has just revealed the role publicly on day 2 and was vouched for by the player saved, with a lone vote cast against it. Night 2 arrives with the healer now an exposed, claimed role who cannot self-protect, while the serial killer and wolves choose targets. Information landscape: Moderately informed: one self-verified save, a tracker claim consistent with it, and a sentinel watch claim with no visitor. The killers' identities and next targets remain unknown. Stakes: The healer is the town's only protector and cannot be guarded, so its death removes all night protection while both the serial killer and wolves live. Spending the guard on a target nobody attacks wastes the night. Target landscape: Eight other living players: a corroborated Trailseer, a Vigilante vouched for by an earlier save, and unclaimed or quiet slots. There is no evidence of who the killers will pick. Your own public healer claim is the main new fact, and it makes you a visible role who cannot be guarded.
lessons.action: If you have publicly claimed healer or your protection record has been read out or vouched, treat yourself as the likely kill target and pick a guard target whose protection is worth the most if you survive. Since you cannot protect yourself, do not assume your protectee is the one under attack. Weigh the Town asset's actual risk against the chance that the serial killer or wolves go for you, and favor a player the killers have already shown interest in over one with no attack history.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after day-vote or sigil results removed a wolf or the serial killer. The remaining killers (a wolf and/or the serial killer or necromancer) are likely to attack the town's most dangerous information source. The healer must pick one other player to cover. Information landscape: Information-rich: eliminated roles are revealed, some claims have been cross-checked by outcomes or by announcements, and one claimant's testimony visibly shifted the vote. The target is still chosen by inference about the killers' motives. Stakes: Few players remain, so each night kill is a large share of town's strength. Losing the main info holder could let the remaining killers reach parity, while a correct save can absorb even a double attack and leave no deaths. Target landscape: Several living claimed or inferred power roles (sentinel, sigilist, investigator, trailseer, vigilante). One of them just publicly drove an elimination or a confirmed strike. Choice rests on that visible impact and on behavior, not on hard verification. The healer cannot cover itself.
lessons.action: On a mid-game night (around night 3) after a wolf or killer has just been exposed, protect the living info role whose testimony or recent action drove that removal (sentinel, trailseer, or confirmed sigilist) rather than a lower-impact claimant. If two info roles are both in play, favor the one most visibly credited with the exposure, since the surviving killers have the most reason to silence them.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or confusing day 2 in which several town information roles (investigator, trailseer, sentinel) claimed publicly; wolves and possibly a lone killer have several visible high-value targets, and you must pick one protectee. Information landscape: Moderately informed: unverified role claims and a day-2 vote record, no confirmed wolf, and the killers' targets unknown. Mostly claim-based reads. Stakes: Mid-game with wolves and a killer still active; losing the investigator costs the town its remaining check, while a save wastes the wolves' kill, so the pick matters but a single miss does not decide the game. Target landscape: Claimed investigator (publicly reported a Not suspicious check, one check left), claimed trailseer, claimed sentinel, and unclaimed sigilist, vigilante and speculator; the choice rests on claimed information value and exposure, not verified evidence.
lessons.action: On night 2 and later, once the day has produced several unverified information-role claims and the town abstained or gave no clear wolf, protect the claimed investigator (the information holder with checks left) rather than a lower-value claimed role. If you were publicly tied to that same protectee, keep protecting them anyway when their check output is still valuable, because the wolves' kill on them is the likeliest high-value attack.

lessons.situation: Late game: the lone killer and at least one wolf are dead, one wolf remains, and the Healer is cleared or safe. The remaining wolf must kill to reach parity, so its night target is the most threatening Town player. One wrong protection could cost the game. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced deaths and roles confirm which evil roles are gone, wills or announcements corroborate claims, and a claimed role has said its ability is exhausted. Stakes: With four alive and one wolf left, one unprotected Town death brings the wolves to parity and ends the game. A correct save keeps Town's numbers intact and lets surviving Town power roles finish the wolf the same night or the next day. Target landscape: Three or four living candidates: a publicly claimed power role whose claim was corroborated by announcements, a vocal town leader who drove earlier evil eliminations, and quiet or abstaining players with no verifiable claims. Choice rests on confirmed evidence and on who is still dangerous to the wolf, not on behavior alone.
lessons.action: In the endgame (about four alive) with one wolf left and the lone killer gone, protect the player the wolf most needs to remove: the confirmed, still-active Town power role, or the loudest town leader who drove the earlier evil eliminations. If the leading candidate has publicly said their ability is spent, move the protection to the next-most-threatening active Town voice.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are dead and the serial killer remains among about five players. The healer is the village's only night buffer against parity, and the serial killer may skip the obvious protected target and kill someone else. Information landscape: Information-rich on past events (both wolves confirmed, an Investigator claim is a public reference), but the serial killer's next target is not predictable from evidence. Stakes: With five alive, each unprevented kill brings the serial killer's win condition (at most one other player alive) closer, and the healer is a likely target once the board narrows. A wasted protection on an unattacked player gives the serial killer a free kill. Target landscape: The claimed Investigator, whose check matched a dead wolf and who was protected the previous night, against quieter town members such as the Sigilist and unconfirmed accusers. The serial killer's choice is unreadable because nothing public shows its preference, so any pick is a guess among several candidates.
lessons.action: When the serial killer is the only killer left, or the board is down to four or five players, avoid repeating the same protectee out of habit once the protectee is no longer the obvious target. Weigh which player the serial killer would most want dead, including a quiet role like the Sigilist or Vigilante, and vary protection among those candidates, since a kill that goes through can narrow the board toward the serial killer's win and expose the healer next.

lessons.situation: After a day of public information-role claims that ended in an abstain or no-elimination vote, several high-value town claimants are exposed to attack from both the wolves and a lone killer. The healer must choose which one to shield for the night. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple public claims with interlocking visit accounts, prior save announcements and vote records, but none of the alignments are verified. Stakes: With several town roles exposed and two killers active, one unprotected loss of the lead investigator removes the main source of checks. A correct guard keeps town numbers and can expose evil through the public save announcement. Target landscape: Three or two publicly claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) with interlocking but unverified visit accounts; the claimed investigator shares check results and is the main lead, while the others report watches or follows. The healer picks among these on the basis of claim content and threat to evil, not verified roles.
lessons.action: When several public information-role claims are on the board, protect the claimed investigator, the one whose check results most plausibly point at wolves, and keep protecting them on consecutive nights while they stay the likeliest kill target. Do not shift to the claimed sentinel or trailseer just because they are also exposed. Wolves and a lone killer both want the lead investigative claimant, so a repeat guard has the best chance of producing a save.

lessons.situation: After a daytime elimination confirmed a claimed Sentinel or Investigator's result, the surviving wolves and any lone killer are expected to attack that credible information source on the coming night. The healer must choose whom to shield. Information landscape: Information-rich: an announced elimination role verified the claimant's result, so their credibility is public and known, and their continued survival is valuable. Stakes: Town leads on numbers, but losing the verified info role would cost the strongest lead-generating source. A save here preserves that edge and denies the evil side a kill, with a strong chance the attack lands on this target. Target landscape: A publicly claimed information role whose result was just confirmed by an announced elimination (caught Serial Killer or wolf), versus other claimed info roles and quiet unrevealed players with no evidence behind them. The choice rests on verified evidence, not on behavior.
lessons.action: When a claimed information role (Sentinel, Investigator, Trailseer) has just produced a result that got a player eliminated, protect that claimant tonight, since the surviving evil factions have the strongest motive to silence them. If two such claimants are both exposed, favor the one whose result was confirmed by an announced elimination role and who still has uses left.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night after a save-confirmed attack on a claimed Trailseer. Wolves and the serial killer are both active, and the village is openly discussing whom attackers might pivot to. The healer must choose between repeating the protection or rotating to another power role or unknown. Information landscape: Information-thin about the next target: a prior save is known and an information-role claim is corroborated by one other claimed power role. No investigation results point to the next night's victim. Stakes: Two killer factions are still alive, so each night can cost a power role. Keeping the Trailseer alive preserves the tracker whose follow of the killer can drive a daytime vote. The cost of repeating is that a pivot to another power role goes unprotected. Target landscape: A claimed, partly corroborated information role (Trailseer) that already survived a double attack thanks to your save, versus another claimed power role (Sigilist) and unclaimed quiet slots with no evidence of who gets hit next. The basis is a public claim plus a prior save pattern, not hard proof of the next target.
lessons.action: When a claimed information role (e.g. Trailseer) has been attacked and saved, or has a corroborated claim, keep protecting it on the following nights while no stronger lead points elsewhere. Killers who targeted it once tend to return or are deterred, and a heal that cancels an attack keeps the town's tracker alive to expose the killer. Accept that a night with no announced attack on your protectee is an idle heal, which is the cost of this policy.

lessons.situation: Late-mid game after the wolf team has been mostly or fully eliminated via the investigator's checks. The surviving wolf and/or the serial killer remain and need to remove town's key coordinator to survive. The healer has to pick whom to protect that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolf flips corroborate the investigator, role reveals clarify claims, and voting records are public, so the town's most valuable player is clear to both town and evil. Stakes: Few players remain, so each night kill moves the board toward parity or the serial killer's win condition. Losing the investigator would remove town's verified information source, while a save denies evil a kill and may cancel multiple simultaneous attacks. Target landscape: The confirmed investigator (role validated by a flipped wolf) is the focal kill target; alternatives are a claimed sentinel/trailseer and several unconfirmed players with no verified roles. The choice rests on verified evidence of who evil most wants dead, not on behavior reads.
lessons.action: When the investigator's findings have been confirmed by a role flip and the evil sides are down to one or two attackers, protect the investigator again, even on consecutive nights. Evil factions (surviving wolf, serial killer) target the town's confirmed information engine, so one protection can absorb several attackers at once. If the investigator is dead or blocked from relevance, shift the protection to the next most publicly validated town leader.

lessons.situation: Early in the game, after a night death and a day without eliminations, the only public information source is a single claimed role, such as a Trailseer. That claimant faces threats from both the wolves and any lone killer. Information landscape: Information-starved: no wolves have been caught, no voting records show alignments, and only one unverified claim exists. Stakes: No single kill decides the game yet, but losing the only information source would leave Town blind. The protection may go untriggered, which costs nothing since the healer's protection is never used up. Target landscape: The only publicly declared information-role claimant versus silent, unrevealed players with no distinguishing evidence. The basis is public role status and the claimant's visibility, not behavior or verified evidence.
lessons.action: When no result has been confirmed and the room is quiet, protect the sole publicly declared information-role claimant, as the most likely kill target. Expect that the attack may land elsewhere, and keep the pick tied to who is most visibly valuable rather than switching to guesses about unrevealed players.

lessons.situation: Midgame, after the lone killer (necromancer) was voted out and one or two wolves remain. The healer must choose a protection target. The wolves' pack kills have been landing on other players, and the previous save was either untested or just used. Information landscape: Moderate. One elimination validated an information role's read, but the wolves' kill targets stay hidden, some bodies had concealed roles, and the remaining wolves are unconfirmed. Little evidence says who the wolves will hit next. Stakes: With about six players alive and the wolves as the only night killers, each night's kill moves the board toward wolf parity. A correct save cancels the pack's kill for that night. A wasted save costs one of the few nights the town can use to stay ahead. Target landscape: Living candidates are the town info roles (an investigator whose read was validated by an elimination, a trailseer or sentinel with identity information) plus the sigilist and neutrals. None of the wolves is confirmed. The previous night's saved player is the obvious repeat pick, but the wolves rarely re-hit a target once it has been saved. The choice rests on role value and elimination-validated reads, not on behavior.
lessons.action: After the lone killer is voted out and only the wolves remain as night killers, pick your protection target by who the wolves most need dead, such as the confirmed information holder or the player the pack has been unable to read. Do not simply repeat last night's save. A protected player who was not attacked leaves no trace, so a repeat only pays off if the wolves return to that same target.

lessons.situation: The healer revealed itself after a confirmed save and now faces a likely night kill from the pack or a Necromancer working through a body. The healer must decide whom to protect knowing it cannot cover itself. Information landscape: The healer's claim and the save are on the record. A reanimated-body attack would show a Necromancer is active without naming it. Roles of the remaining players are only partly confirmed. Stakes: The healer is itself a probable victim and nothing it does can prevent that. Its last protections decide whether the remaining Town power roles survive, and one more loss could leave the Town unable to catch up. Target landscape: Candidates are other living Town players, since the healer cannot protect itself. The Investigator, Vigilante and Sentinel are verified or semi-verified, and the other claimants are lower in value and less verified. The healer is the exposed one.
lessons.action: If your Healer role is publicly known and the town just removed a wolf while a killer is still active, assume you are a likely kill target. You cannot protect yourself, so use the night to cover the single most valuable confirmed-Town ally whose death would end the Town's best path to winning. Do not waste the pick on a low-value or unattacked claimant.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game night after a day in which an information role publicly reported a result or helped drive a wolf elimination. The wolves are active (a chanteuse is blocking, and a wolf kill pattern is aimed at information roles). The healer must choose the one other player to protect. Information landscape: Moderate to rich: public claims from the investigator, sentinel and trailseer, at least one confirmed wolf role from a vote, and roleblock evidence of an active chanteuse. Most role claims are unverified, but some are corroborated by eliminations or matching visits. Stakes: Mid-game with several wolves or killers still alive, so one lost information role noticeably slows the town but does not immediately decide the game. Keeping the verified information source alive preserves remaining checks, and an announced save also confirms the wolves' targeting. Target landscape: Several publicly claimed information roles (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) plus unclaimed players. The investigator with a corroborated check record or a wolf exposure is the top-value target. A sentinel who is repeatedly roleblocked, or any claimant the wolves are already blocking, is a less likely kill target. Unclaimed players are lower threat. The basis is public claims, corroboration and the wolves' visible pattern of attacking information roles.
lessons.action: Protect the publicly claimed, corroborated information role (investigator first, otherwise the sentinel or trailseer) that the town is relying on and that just publicly drove a result or an elimination. The wolves have the clearest reason to remove that player, so a protect there is likely to save them or at least keep the wolves from a free kill. If two such roles are claimed, pick the one whose claim has independent corroboration, such as a confirmed wolf death or a matching visit, over one that is merely loud.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an abstained or low-information day vote and a night-1 death. The healer must choose a protection target with no hard evidence on who the killers will attack. Wolves and a lone killer may both want the same visible information role. Information landscape: Info-starved: one revealed or concealed night-1 death, an abstain vote, at most one unverified claim. Everything else is behavioral. Stakes: Early game with several evil attackers alive. One saved information role can produce the next check or trail result and decide whether town finds the first wolf or killer, but a wrong guess costs only a night of protection. Target landscape: Eight to nine living candidates besides the healer: one or two publicly active information sources (a claimed Investigator with a not-suspicious result, or an open player pushing for information), and the rest silent or unclaimed. Roles are unconfirmed apart from dead-player reveals, so the choice rests on behavior and on who is most useful to town.
lessons.action: On night 2 with no confirmed leads, protect the visible information-providing player the wolves or killer would most want gone: a claimed Investigator with a result, or an active player asking for information. Prefer that over repeating an arbitrary night-1 pick or a silent unclaimed player. A save on such a player preserves the town's information flow.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after you publicly claimed Healer and helped push an elimination, either a counterclaiming wolf or a necromancer-led vote. The wolves now have a reason to pick you, and you must still choose someone else to protect. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims and role reveals: an investigator check was validated by an elimination, and a trailseer was partly confirmed. No wolf is fully identified, and a necromancer or reanimated attacker may still be unproven. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. Losing the healer ends all protection, while the wolves and a lone killer can still reach parity. Your own death is probably unavoidable, so your last protection should secure the most useful remaining Town role. Target landscape: Other living players who are not you: a claimed investigator whose read was validated, a claimed trailseer, vigilante and sigilist. Their claims are only partly corroborated and no wolf is confirmed. You are the likely wolf target and cannot be protected by your own action.
lessons.action: When your Healer role is publicly known and you are the likely wolf target, you cannot cover yourself, so protect the most valuable surviving Town player instead. That is usually the investigator or another role whose information is confirmed or corroborated. If your protection pattern is public, switch to the next-most-valuable player, because the protection still stops any other attacker (a necromancer's body, a serial killer) from landing on that player.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a 10-player game with no day-1 vote. The healer must protect one other player blind while the wolf pack and possibly a lone killer may attack. The healer itself is sometimes the opening target, so the night-1 pick may be the only protection Town gets. Information landscape: Information-starved: only one day of undirected discussion, with no claims, accusations, deaths or private results to rank targets by. Stakes: Early game with a full table: no single night-1 outcome decides the game. A lucky save gains a body and credibility, while a miss costs nothing. Since information is zero, a cheap blind protection is the right policy. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no claims, no behavior, no votes and no revealed roles. The pick is a blind guess, and wolves, the serial killer and the neutral are all equally possible. The healer cannot protect itself.
lessons.action: On night 1 with no claims, deaths or reads, protect one other player rather than skipping, and choose any quiet, unclaimed player without agonizing over it. Protection is never used up, and a save is announced if the pick is attacked. The visit also leaves a trace a Sentinel or Trailseer may later cross-check.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an early power-role death (sentinel, trailseer, investigator, or fortune teller) and a no-elimination day. Nobody has claimed, and the healer must choose a protectee from behavior alone. Information landscape: Information-starved: one or two revealed night-1 deaths, a unanimous abstain vote, no claims, and no private leads. Reads are purely behavioral. Stakes: Early game with several town power roles still alive. Losing another power role, such as the vigilante or sentinel, to an unprotected kill hurts, but one bad guess does not decide the game. Protection is never used up, so a guess made on a consistent rule costs little each night. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players besides the healer, none with a public role claim. The candidates are a vocal player driving discussion or demanding claims, and several quiet or generic players. The basis is behavior and table presence only, with no checks, results, or hard leads.
lessons.action: On night 2 of an info-starved board with no claims and an all-abstain vote, protect the visible organizer or most active questioner, since the wolves tend to kill players who drive town reasoning. If a quiet player has not drawn attention, do not pick them on a hunch, because the protection was never tested in the observation that did.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: With 9 alive and 5 eliminations until the leading evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown, the board is not at immediate parity. The game cannot end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this pick is not a one-elimination swing; the end-of-game consequence of choosing now rather than later is unclear from the current record.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved for choosing a winning side: the dead player’s role and will remain concealed, and the claimed night results are not verified. The Sentinel and Trailseer accounts corroborate a visit route, but not either claimant’s role or anyone’s alignment; the Investigator’s Not suspicious claim about you does not distinguish you from most non-wolves.
query_dims.situation: After a concealed night-one death attributed to both wolves and the serial killer, day two ended in a broad abstention; one player’s vote to eliminate the concealed victim’s seat was the sole dissent. The unverified Investigator, Sentinel, and Trailseer claims have not produced a confirmed alignment, leaving your one-time side pick open amid an unresolved board.
query_dims.target_landscape: The side choice is among Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or yourself. Your Speculator role and unmade pick are privately known to you; publicly, the claimed Investigator’s Not suspicious read on you is unverified and compatible with your role. No public evidence clearly favors one side.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after one or two evil eliminations (Chanteuse, Illusionist, or Serial Killer). Town looks ahead and the Speculator must decide whether to lock in its single pick now or wait. Information landscape: Mostly information-rich: role reveals for dead evil players and a validated Sentinel watch. Some gaps remain: one wolf or the lone killer may be hidden behind a cleared read, and the claimed Investigator and Healer are unverified. Stakes: Town holds a clear numerical majority, but one remaining killer, or a double-kill night, could strip key roles and reverse the lead. The pick is permanent and the Speculator has no other ability, so timing matters more than the margin shown. Target landscape: Town, the wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town looks dominant after the Serial Killer and one or two wolves were eliminated. Evidence is mixed: a confirmed Sentinel result and role reveals for the dead, but the remaining evil's identity is only inferred from behavior or from unverified Investigator claims.
lessons.action: Pick Town only once both the wolves and the lone killer are confirmed dead or identified and Town's investigative and protective core is still alive. If a hidden killer is still unaccounted for, or a likely double-kill night is coming, delay the pick one more night, because a Speculator that dies before picking loses.

lessons.situation: A morning after a visible Town success (a lone killer or wolf voted out, or the claimed Investigator saved by the Healer) tempts the Speculator to commit to Town at once. Wolves remain hidden, and Town can still fracture through mis-votes, friendly fire or losing its Healer. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of eliminated players are confirmed and the Investigator's checks are on record. What is missing is the identity of the surviving evil players and whether Town can keep up its voting discipline. Stakes: Town leads comfortably, so an early pick gains little extra. The pick is permanent and announced. Both games showed Town collapsing after the pick through mis-eliminations and the loss of its Healer, which let the wolves win and left the Speculator with a loss. Waiting costs nothing while the Speculator is safe, and the risk is dying unpicked. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or Self. Town leads on numbers, with a living Investigator and Healer. One evil faction is already confirmed dead, but one or two wolves, or a lone killer, are still hidden. The Self pick is unrealistic. Confirmed kills and checks are the evidence; Town's cohesion is only a behavioral read.
lessons.action: When Town looks dominant only because one evil side was just removed, but a wolf or lone killer is still hidden or alive, keep the one pick unspent for another night while the Speculator is not under suspicion. Lock in Town once the remaining evil is down to one hidden wolf with Town's key roles intact. If the Speculator becomes a likely target, pick the leading side right away, because dying unpicked is a loss.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game (nights 2-3) with the speculator alive and unpicked. One wolf has been voted out or a Town save has been announced, but the lone killer and at least one wolf are still hidden. Killers are active every night. Information landscape: Mixed. Some announced facts exist (a revealed wolf death, an announced save, dead power roles), but most night results are unverified claims. The strength of the evil factions is inferred from counts and trend, with no confirmation of the lone killer. Stakes: The board is not at the brink, but each night a hidden killer or wolf can remove the speculator before it picks, and that is a guaranteed loss. The pick is permanent, so a Town pick pays off only if Town survives the lone killer, and Town did lose to a hidden Necromancer or the wolves in some games. Picking by night 2-3 locks in the likeliest winner while the speculator is still alive. Target landscape: Four options: Town, Wolves, the lone killer, or self. Town has the most living members and often a revealed wolf death or verified saves. The wolf pack and lone killer are mostly hidden, and the self pick only wins by being the last player standing. The read rests on public counts and trend more than on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Once Town has a confirmed evil kill or a clear numbers lead (for example a wolf revealed dead and Town power roles still alive), spend your one pick on Town that night. If no side looks clearly ahead, still pick by night 2 or 3, because dying unpicked is an automatic loss and Town is the default side with the most players.

lessons.situation: Midgame, day 3 or later. One evil faction member has just been voted out with a confirmed role, and Town is clearly ahead of what remains. The speculator has not picked and is alive and unexposed. It faces a choice between waiting for more information and locking in a side now. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: a system-confirmed role reveal from the elimination, dead roles revealed, and public vote records showing the village voting together. One or two evil players remain unconfirmed. Stakes: Town's lead over the remaining evil is real but not unbeatable. Evil kills each night, and the speculator is an ordinary kill target. Dying unpicked is a guaranteed loss, so each night of delay costs more than the extra information is worth. Target landscape: Four options: Town, the Wolves, the lone killer, or itself. By now at least one evil faction is eliminated and revealed (a wolf or the lone killer). Town still has a numerical majority over the remaining evil, and the evidence is public reveals and vote records rather than behavior. A self-pick is almost impossible to win.
lessons.action: Once a night arrives in which a lone killer or wolf has been voted out and revealed and the roles left show Town holding a clear majority edge over the remaining evil, spend your single pick that night on Town instead of waiting. The pick is not a visit and cannot be blocked. If you die before picking you lose, and a pick made first still counts after you die.

lessons.situation: Night 1 (or early night 2) of a ten-player game, with the Speculator's single irreversible pick unspent and nothing established yet. Delaying risks an unannounced night kill by the wolves or the serial killer, which would make the Speculator lose automatically. Information landscape: Information-starved: day 1 was discussion only with no vote, no deaths, no verified claims, and no check results. Any read would be behavioral at best. Stakes: The board is far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The Speculator's own survival to the pick is the main risk: dying unpicked is a guaranteed personal loss, while an early Town pick costs little and keeps the win tied to the largest side. Target landscape: Four sides: Town, Wolves, lone killer, or self. No deaths, claims, or votes exist, so the choice rests on prior side sizes: Town has six roles, wolves two, the lone killer one, and a pick of self wins only as last one standing.
lessons.action: On the first night where you still hold your pick and nothing has been confirmed, lock in your pick right away instead of waiting. Choose Town, the largest side (six Town roles against two wolves, one lone killer and you), since a Speculator that dies unpicked loses and any night attack can remove you before you act. If a night-2 report has already confirmed the wolves are dead or clearly outnumbered, pick Town immediately.

query_dims.consensus_text: No public discussion or accusations have been recorded today, so there is no clear village consensus or stated basis for one.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Nine players are alive, and it is five eliminations until the leading remaining evil faction could win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game cannot end within one more elimination, at worst for the town, so a single result is not immediately decisive.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible push or vote today could establish a public position and invite scrutiny of its reasoning; with no public accusations or claims yet, that commitment is still reversible through later discussion, though the vote record will be permanent.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion directed at you is recorded in the available public discussion. Your private pack discussion and block are not public.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the public has a wolf-kill announcement but no identity of the victim's role or will, and no public claims or accusations today. You privately know your block succeeded, but that does not establish the blocked player's role.
query_dims.my_position: No public position relative to a consensus is established; no consensus has formed in the recorded discussion.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know the pack killed a player whose role was concealed, and that your block stopped one player's action last night. Publicly, the village knows only that the wolves killed someone and an illusionist hid the role; the blocked player's experience is private to them.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 begins after the wolves killed a player whose role and will were concealed by an illusionist. The village has no revealed role or will from that death, and today's discussion has not yet produced an accusation or competing public reads.
query_dims.target_landscape: No living candidate has been publicly raised as a target yet. The dead player's role remains unknown to the village, and there is no announced role-based evidence distinguishing any of the nine living players.

lessons.situation: Late game with the wolf partner dead or revealed and the chanteuse as the last wolf. The town is debating announced night events, such as a vigilante shot, a claimed roleblock, or a concealed-role death, and accusing each other. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed role reveals, announced kills and saves, roleblock claims, and several town claims with public vote records. Factual gaps between what was announced and what a speaker says are easy to spot. Stakes: With about five alive and one wolf left, a single wrong vote or a consensus on the wolf ends the game. Keeping the room divided over other players preserves the wolf's path to parity. Consensus: The village is split and nobody has a clear majority target. Accusations run between other players and are driven by claims and roleblock or shot reports. My position: with majority Heat: Low to moderate. Nobody is naming the chanteuse. Any pressure would come from a slip about information the chanteuse should not have. Forward exposure: Citing only announced facts commits the chanteuse to nothing falsifiable and is easy to walk back. Citing an unannounced night event exposes insider knowledge, and the room can test it. Target landscape: Several town-claimed or accused players (speculator, sigilist, vigilante, a suspected serial killer, a quiet player) are under discussion. The case against each rests on claims and night reports, not on proof against the chanteuse. Public vs private: The chanteuse privately knows the pack's real night actions, kills and failed attacks, and which dead player was the partner. The town knows only the announced outcomes and what players claim.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is already dead or revealed and you are the last wolf, speak only from facts the Game Master has publicly announced, such as confirmed shots, announced roleblocks, and revealed roles. Use them to point the room at the open questions about other players' claims, so suspicion spreads over several players instead of settling on you. Before you cite any night event, check that it was actually announced.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a concealed night kill in which the village focuses on your wolf partner and you are unscrutinized. If you say nothing, your partner is voted out and you are left alone. Information landscape: Fairly rich: an announced roleblock, a sigil placement with no effect, and a day-two trail pointing at your partner. That is enough for the town to build a case, so a counter-narrative needs a real hook. Stakes: Losing your partner now leaves a single wolf against a near-parity board, so one more elimination decides the game. Keeping your partner alive is worth a small amount of heat. Consensus: The village is converging fast on your partner, based on earlier tracking evidence and a fresh sigil or block result. My position: Holding out silently while the majority forms against your partner. Heat: Zero to low: nobody has brought you up or examined your earlier positions. Forward exposure: A brief, evidence-based doubt is easy to walk back and commits you to little. Heavy defense of your partner links you to them and is hard to undo. Target landscape: The main candidate is your partner, who has carryover suspicion from earlier tracking evidence. Other candidates are the Sigilist with a charge left and the roleblocked Sentinel, all claimed and unverified. Public vs private: Privately you know your partner is the last other wolf and you know why the night's events happened, for example that your block caused the Sentinel's failed watch. Publicly the village sees only an announced result and a suspect with carryover suspicion, and nobody is looking at you.
lessons.action: When the room converges on your partner and you are unscrutinized, offer at least one alternative suspect or a doubt about the evidence against your partner. Base it on real inconsistencies, such as a claimed result that can't be verified, and keep it short and low-heat. Don't stay completely silent, since silence lets the town unite on your partner and leaves you alone.

lessons.situation: On day 2 after a concealed night kill, several unverifiable night-result claims are in play, including a claim of being roleblocked, and the chanteuse is not under suspicion. Information landscape: Starved: only unverified night-result claims, one hidden-role body, and a roleblock claim that implies a chanteuse exists. Stakes: Nothing forces a move today. Staying hidden protects the pack's blocker and the pack's room to act at night. Consensus: No clear consensus. Attention is on the claimants and on their disputes with each other. My position: Outside the discussion, not driving anything and not attracting attention. Heat: Low: no one has named you, and the roleblock claim attaches to no particular player. Forward exposure: Each new statement is a checkable commitment that others can later compare with your votes. Brevity commits you to nothing and can be changed later. Target landscape: The room has no confirmed roles, only unverified claims from the investigator, sigilist, trailseer and sentinel. Reads are behavioral and no one has been singled out. Public vs private: You know you blocked a player and that your partner may have hidden a body. Publicly the town sees only a roleblock claim that implies a chanteuse exists, not who it is.
lessons.action: When no one has named you and a roleblock claim exists but points at no one, keep your discussion turns brief and generic and make no claim about roleblocks, visits or night results. Anything you say can be cross-checked later, and saying nothing keeps the heat on the claimants.

lessons.situation: After night deaths, claimed information roles present early results and urge suspicion on silent players while the chanteuse has said nothing. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles were revealed by the moderator, and living claimed information roles are publicly reporting night results. Stakes: The pack still has room before parity, but a wolf voted out now removes a killer and the chanteuse's block. Staying off the lurker list matters more than winning any argument. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned behind the claimed information roles' reports and a shared plan to press non-participants. My position: Holding out by staying silent, which is the position drawing the pressure. Heat: Moderate and rising, because the leaders have agreed to scrutinize players who stay silent after morning claims. Forward exposure: A short, non-committal contribution is cheap and reversible and commits to no role claim. Total silence is already public record once the room agrees to interrogate lurkers, and it invites a vote. Target landscape: Claimed investigator and claimed sentinel leading the discussion, the player they have cleared, and other uncommitted town members. The basis is mostly claimed night results plus behavior such as lurking. Public vs private: Publicly the room treats claimed information roles as leaders and flags silent players as suspect. Privately the chanteuse knows its partner's real status and what the pack did overnight, and cannot afford to be the quiet one.
lessons.action: When claimed information roles are reporting results and asking quiet players to engage, speak early with one concrete, town-sounding contribution. For example, ask a claimed role a specific question about its result, or give a short read on an uncommitted player who is not your partner. If your partner is under attack, keep the comment general and do not name or defend them.

lessons.situation: After a night death, a claimed info role lays out a visit chain implicating another player. I appear only incidentally in that chain, and an evasive player asks me to share my information. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead role's revealed will, a claimed multi-night Trailseer record, and other claims that are not yet verified. Stakes: Pack is within a couple of eliminations of parity. Letting the town spend its vote on the accused player, rather than on me or my partner, keeps the wolf bloc intact. Consensus: The room is aligned on testing the claimed visit chain and gathering around the player it implicates, with little attention on me. My position: With the majority, letting the accusation play out. Heat: Low: I was mentioned in passing, and the questioner's prompt did not frame me as an attacker. Forward exposure: Making no claim commits me to nothing and cannot be counter-claimed, and I can still claim later if pressure rises. The risk is that continued silence reads as evasive if another player keeps pressing me. Target landscape: The claimed info role, the player that role accuses, and any unproven claimant such as a Vigilante. The basis is claimed visit records and behavior, not confirmed results. Public vs private: Privately I am a wolf using night blocks, while publicly I read as an unaligned townie who was merely visited or mentioned.
lessons.action: When a player asks you to state your results and you are only a minor name in a claimed info role's visit chain, decline to counter-claim and instead call for the info roles to present testable, cross-checkable results. Let the room's attention settle on the player the visit chain actually accuses.

lessons.situation: On day 2 the wolf partner (illusionist) is caught in a contested claim or placed at a victim's door by a trailseer or sentinel, and the village is arguing about it while the chanteuse is not involved. Information landscape: Sparse hard evidence: one or two visit reports plus rival role claims and rules arguments; no confirmed roles beyond the dead, mostly claim-versus-claim argument. Stakes: The board is early, with plenty of town and neutral players alive, so the wolves are far from parity. Losing a partner hurts, but being exposed alongside them would be worse, so keeping the chanteuse unlinked preserves the wolves' remaining night kills and blocks. Consensus: The village is converging on the accused partner based on the conflicting claims and the visit report, driven by the town information roles rather than by the chanteuse. My position: Holding back as an uncommitted bystander, neither driving nor opposing the forming consensus. Heat: Low: nobody has named, addressed or questioned the chanteuse, who is on the edge of the discussion. Forward exposure: Speaking up for the accused partner would publicly tie the chanteuse to a likely wolf and could not be undone; staying quiet is reversible and leaves no trace on the record. Target landscape: Two conflicting claimants of the same role, one of them the wolf partner, or the partner against a trailseer or sentinel accuser; judged on a single visit report and on timing, with no confirmed roles. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the accused player is its wolf partner and that their claim is a cover story; publicly the partner is just one of two conflicting claimants or an accused player in a claim-versus-claim dispute.
lessons.action: When your wolf partner is under heavy accusation on day 2 and no one has mentioned you, say nothing in the discussion that defends or links you to them. Keep your remarks limited to neutral, non-committal points, or stay silent, so you are not tied to the partner if they are revealed as a wolf. If heat later turns toward you, then answer plainly and briefly.

lessons.situation: Day 3, after a night attack that was saved or that killed a role. An accusation or mechanical theory is aimed at your wolf partner or at a claimant, and you can steer the room by probing the evidence behind it. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are a few claimed night results and one public fact, such as a save or a death, but no verified visitor lists, and the reads are speculative. Stakes: The pack is a few eliminations from parity, so keeping both wolves alive and unsuspected through this vote matters. One misdirected vote can shift the count, but this day does not by itself decide the game. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned and drifting toward whoever has the weakest evidence. No firm consensus exists yet, and the reads rest on inference rather than verified results. My position: With the majority, nudging it by questioning the evidence rather than leading an accusation. Heat: Low. No one has linked you to the night's visits or the roleblock, and your questions read as neutral. Forward exposure: Asking for evidence is a low-commitment, reversible move. Endorsing a specific claim or mechanism, such as a sentinel's watch, commits you to it and is hard to undo once the town trusts that claim. Target landscape: The candidates are the accuser, the accused packmate, and unverified role claimants. No hard evidence exists, so the basis is inference and behavior, and the only new fact is a night result that confirms a wolf attack. Public vs private: You privately know the pack's actions, so the accusation may be accurate in substance, but publicly it is an unverified inference. Asking for the evidence behind it exposes the gap without revealing what you know.
lessons.action: When a day-3 accusation lands on your wolf partner or on a hard-to-verify claim, ask in neutral evidence-seeking terms what separate result backs it, and add mechanical points only where the rules clearly support them. Posing as an arbiter of evidence keeps your heat low, and the accuser has to retract or the room moves to a different target.

lessons.situation: An early day (day 2 or 3) with several role claims on the table, no hard confirmations, and the chanteuse's wolf side unsuspected while the town works through contradictions. Information landscape: Starved: unverified claims, partial cross-confirmation, one or two rules inconsistencies, and little else. Stakes: Wolves are still several eliminations from parity, so there is no pressure to force a vote. Staying unnoticed while the town works through its own claims is worth more than pushing a read. Consensus: The village is cooperatively sorting claims, and in some cases converging on one self-contradicting claimant, on behavioral and rules-based grounds rather than hard evidence. My position: With the majority, adding analysis rather than driving an accusation. Heat: Very low: you have barely spoken, made no accusations, and are not named by anyone. Forward exposure: A neutral rules or procedural remark commits you to no read and no vote, and it can be dropped or reframed at any time. A hard accusation would put your name on a record you would have to defend. Target landscape: Several unverified town claims (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) plus a visitor with no stated purpose, and one claimant already contradicted by their own account. No role is confirmed by the Game Master apart from any dead player, so the basis is behavioral and rules-based. Public vs private: Privately you know your own block result and the pack's kill, while publicly the village is only weighing unverified role claims and nobody connects you to anything.
lessons.action: When you are a low-heat chanteuse in an info-starved early day and the room is sorting through unverified claims, make one short rules-based or procedural point, such as asking a named visitor to explain or noting what a claimed result would imply under the rules. Keep it neutral, tied to public claims, and never reveal your own block or its target. This steers the room toward verification and leaves you with no vote record or read to defend.

lessons.situation: Day 2, before the first vote: the table is converging on the chanteuse's wolf partner after a contested claim or a witness result, and the chanteuse has not been named. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims, with at most one or two night results that cannot be confirmed. No votes have been cast and no role evidence is confirmed. Stakes: Early game with many players alive and parity far off. Losing the partner hurts but is survivable, while exposing the chanteuse as the last wolf is the costlier mistake. Consensus: The village is near-unanimous against the partner, based on a claim contest or a single witness result. My position: On the edge of the discussion, neither driving nor defending, with a light contribution that does not oppose the majority. Heat: None to low on the chanteuse: it is unnamed, has defended no one, and attention is on the partner and their accuser. Forward exposure: Defending the partner would tie the chanteuse to the pack and could not be undone. A neutral procedural point or generic doubt commits to nothing, is cheap, and can be dropped at any time. Target landscape: The partner is the visible target of an accusation backed by claims or a witness result. Other names, such as quiet players, have only silence against them. Everything else is unverified claims or behavior. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows the targeted player is its wolf partner and whether the claims against them are true, while publicly the evidence is unverified claims or a single witness result and the room is piling on the partner.
lessons.action: When the room converges on your wolf partner on Day 2 and you have no heat, stay unclaimed and speak once with a sincere, non-committal point, such as a verification idea or generic doubt about the unverified claims, that flatters neither side. Don't defend the partner or push a new accusation, because a defense links you to a player the table is already set on and cannot be taken back. If the table starts questioning your silence or your link to the partner, pivot to agreeing with the majority.

lessons.situation: Final three at Day 5-6: you are the last wolf, the lone killer is alive, and one other player is Town or neutral. The elimination vote is the last decision, and only removing the lone killer wins it for the wolves. Information landscape: Mostly revealed roles for the dead, public night-kill reports, and the vote history. Nothing is confirmed about the two survivors, so reads rest on elimination logic and behavior. Stakes: One vote decides the game. Removing the lone killer gives the wolves an immediate win at one wolf against one other player. Removing the Town player lets the lone killer win with one other player left. Consensus: The room is split two against one, with the other two accusing each other. The deciding voter is undecided and weighing logic and voting records. My position: Swing voter who can drive the outcome by persuading the undecided player; staying passive hands the framing to the lone killer. Heat: Low to moderate. Others call you quiet or background, or the lone killer tries to frame you with role-count math, but no one has made a decisive case against you. Forward exposure: Naming a target in speech commits your vote and sets the third player's choice. The day ends in an immediate vote with no later discussion, so a wrong pick cannot be undone. Staying silent leaves the room to the lone killer's framing. Target landscape: Two candidates, the third Town-aligned or neutral player and the lone killer, with neither role confirmed. The basis is deduction from dead roles, the trail of reanimated kills or night results, and past votes, with little direct evidence. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the last wolf, and one of the other two is the lone killer; you may or may not know which. Publicly the two others accuse each other and you are the swing voter, with little hard evidence beyond role-count deduction and voting history.
lessons.action: As the last wolf in a three-player endgame with a lone killer still alive, speak early and state a concrete case against whichever player is more likely the lone killer. Build it from role-count elimination, the reanimated-kill or visit trail, and voting records, then ask the third player to commit to that vote. Removing the lone killer leaves you level with the last other player, which ends the game for the wolves, whereas voting out the Town player lets the lone killer reach its own win count.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a night in which the Sentinel and Trailseer report your visit to a player who was blocked, or who sat next to a dead player. The room asks you to explain. Information landscape: Moderate. There are confirmed visits and a dead player or a block claim, but your role is not confirmed and no checks have been shared. Stakes: The board is mid-game, with several eliminations still needed before the wolves can reach parity. Being voted out as a revealed chanteuse costs the pack its blocker and exposes your partner, so avoiding a collision that gets you eliminated matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: The village is converging on you as the one to explain. The basis is the confirmed visit and a victim or reporter saying they were blocked or killed. There is no verified role to anchor on. My position: Holding out against the room's demand, defending under pressure. Heat: High. You are singled out by name as a visitor, with a watch- or follow-confirmed visit and no explanation, and others are demanding one. Forward exposure: A fake role claim commits you to a role whose real holder can counter-claim at once, and a single death can expose it. If you are revealed as a wolf, your partner is put at risk too. A claim cannot be retracted. Withholding a role and attacking the evidence's meaning stays reversible. Target landscape: The choice is between a fake role claim, silence, or reframing the visit. The only hard evidence is the confirmed visit. Every role claim is unverified, and the room judges on timing and demeanor. Public vs private: Privately you are the chanteuse who made the visit, and you know the visit was a block. Publicly, a Sentinel or Trailseer report puts your name on the visit, so you are the only player with an unexplained visit.
lessons.action: When a Sentinel or Trailseer report puts your visit on record, don't invent a role the real holder can contradict. Say that a visit shows only that you went there, never why. Then redirect the room to every other visitor and to the reporters' exact wording, and ask what else the reports show. If an unclaimed role's holder is still alive, any claim to that role invites an instant counter-claim, so claim a role only when the holder is already revealed dead or no counter-claim could come.

lessons.situation: Three players are left and you are accused as the wolf, either by the lone killer using role-count math or by a Town role such as a claimed vigilante or sigilist. The third player is the swing and is weighing you against the other suspect. Information landscape: Info-rich in places: claimed night results, previous-day votes and confirmed deaths allow narrow role-count deduction. Nothing about the survivors is confirmed. Stakes: If the deciding player votes you out, the wolves lose. If the vote splits or lands on the other suspect, you survive and can win that day or at night. Consensus: The room is split and undecided. The deciding player is torn between you and the other player. My position: Driving the discussion to deflect suspicion and shape the deciding player's vote. Heat: High to critical from a direct accusation or a claimed block, but the deciding player is still undecided. Forward exposure: A firm counter-accusation commits you to the vote and to a pro-Town framing that your voting record must support. It is irreversible because the vote follows immediately. Target landscape: The accuser, who may be the lone killer or a claimed Town role, against the quieter third player. Both are judged on behavior, voting history and role-count logic rather than confirmed roles. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the wolf who blocked people, while publicly you must appear as a pro-Town player making an unverified deduction. A claimed roleblock victim or a lone killer may be accusing you.
lessons.action: If the lone killer or the Town player accuses you of being the wolf, rebut with their own logic. Show that the role-count points the other way, that a roleblock claim does not identify who did the blocking, and that your past votes opposed the real killer. Then steer the undecided player toward the other suspect, whose passive or inconsistent record you can point to.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion: you are the main suspect over a coincidence, and you answer your accusers by repeatedly pointing at another player's unverified claim instead of engaging the accusation. Information landscape: Several unverified private claims and one real but non-decisive tension. There are no confirmed roles or caught lies, so the argument rests on claim consistency and timing. Stakes: The board is mid-game with the wolves still needing a few eliminations. Being voted out here costs the pack its blocker and tempo, so surviving the vote matters more than landing a counter-accusation. Consensus: The village is converging on you around a coincidence, such as a block or visit timing that looks suspicious. The claimed tension on someone else is not strong enough to move anyone. My position: Holding out against the consensus and trying to redirect it, with no allies speaking up. Heat: High: multiple accusers are on you, and your repeated deflection reads as a defense with no new content. Forward exposure: A repeated line against another player's claim is easy to repeat but hard to retract. It commits you to that claim being false, and it can look like you know who carried the kill. A single, public-fact-based doubt is cheap to walk back. Target landscape: Only one claimed role is a plausible alternative target, and the room treats its claim with only mild skepticism. Everyone else is aligned on you, and the basis is claim timing and coincidence rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know a claim's inconsistency or truth from the wolf side, such as who carried the kill, but the table only sees unverified claims. Pushing a point that depends on private knowledge risks looking pre-informed.
lessons.action: When several players are accusing you, answer the accusation itself with at least one new, concrete point each turn, such as why your read or action is consistent with public facts. Raise any doubt about another player's claim once, using only publicly checkable tension, and do not repeat the same pivot or lean on what you privately know as a wolf. If your turn adds nothing new, stay brief.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion in which several claims conflict and a night-mechanics dispute is open, and the chanteuse wants to question another player's statement without exposing itself. Information landscape: Mostly claim-based with a few confirmed roles from deaths. Visit and check results are self-reported and unverifiable. Stakes: Board is mid-game with several unconfirmed roles and a lone killer still alive. One careless slip showing wolf-side knowledge could cost the last wolf, but a clean question costs little. Consensus: The village is split among unverified claims and a disputed visit story. There is no firm consensus, and the last vote produced little or nothing. My position: Holding out and probing, not driving any elimination. Heat: Low to moderate. The chanteuse has stayed quiet and has no accusation or claim against it, but a pointed question draws attention. Forward exposure: A pointed mechanical question can show you know night details that a plain villager would not be tracking, and it invites scrutiny of how you know. It is moderately reversible if you concede quickly when the rule is explained. Target landscape: Several living players with no confirmed roles, judged on claims and claimed results rather than hard evidence. The probe targets a claimant whose statement looks inconsistent.
