If the room is split and you hold a private fact such as who must be the immune Serial Killer, vote on that player instead, so your vote stays unlinked from the pack's plan and still passes as an ordinary Town vote.

lessons.situation: First vote day after a night-1 death, with only unverified claims and no leads on any evil faction. Information landscape: Information-starved: self-reported results only, no confirmed roles, no voting history. Stakes: Early game with a wide margin before wolf parity. A wasted or mis-targeted vote gains little, while staying hidden preserves the pack's flexibility. Consensus: The table is quiet and leaning toward abstaining, with no accusations and no evidence-based lead. My position: With the majority, joining the abstain. Heat: Very low: nobody has accused you and you have only made generic comments. Forward exposure: A named vote would be permanent on the record and tie you to a mis-elimination with no evidence behind it. An abstain commits you to nothing and keeps all options open. Target landscape: No strong candidates. Claims are unverified, no roles are confirmed, and any target would be a behavioral guess. Public vs private: You privately know the wolf pack, your own kill and any conceal you used. Publicly the table has only unverified self-reports or a bare death announcement, with no accusations against wolves.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, when no one has accused anyone and no role is confirmed, abstain with the table rather than naming an evidence-free target. If the room is already abstaining, your abstain is invisible, commits you to no read, and keeps both wolves unremarked for another night.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four alive with two eliminations until the leading evil faction can win; one more elimination leaves three alive, and a wolf-side kill tonight would bring the count to three, where a further loss could end the game, so a wrong bet costs a point and a self-bet attempt spent on a non-attacked night is lost for good.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed roles among survivors, one sigilist claim with consistent record support, one investigator Not suspicious read on player_3 from night 2, and only behavioral reads on player_10. Night results for the surviving players are mostly unshared.
query_dims.situation: Night 4 is approaching with four players alive after a necromancer was voted out on day 4. As the fortune teller, you must bet on who dies tonight and decide whether to spend one of your two self-bets, while the remaining wolves and the lone killer are still unidentified among the three survivors and the discussion is split over whether the sigilist's claim is credible.
query_dims.target_landscape: Three living players: player_3 (publicly accused on day 2 by a dead player, admitted no real evidence, checked Not suspicious by a now-dead investigator on night 2), player_9 (claims sigilist, placed a sigil that struck a player on night 3, a claim consistent with the public record), and player_10 (evasive about their night results, the target of the day 4 elimination vote that failed to pass). Role status is unverified claim for player_9 and no public role for the others.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a no-elimination or abstain day. One claimant of a night-info role is the focal point of the discussion and votes, so the wolves and the lone killer both have reason to kill them. Information landscape: Moderately informative. There is a public role claim and a vote record concentrated on one player, plus evidence from the earlier night that killers are active. Nothing is verified, and the read rests on the claimant's visibility and not on confirmed roles. Stakes: Scoring two points here ends the Fortune Teller's win condition outright. A miss costs nothing but a night, though only a few nights remain to score. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players. One stands out as a visible information threat: a self-declared Trailseer or Sentinel who was roleblocked or took the day's votes. Their role is unverified and rests on their own claim. The rest are quiet, with no comparable profile.
lessons.action: When a player has drawn real visibility, such as a self-declared info-role claim (Trailseer, Sentinel) that has also taken votes or a roleblock, bet on that player to die and name the claimed role. Killers have a motive to remove them, and a correct role is worth two points while a wrong role still scores one for the death.

lessons.situation: You reached two points by night 3. Reanimated-wolf kills on consecutive nights show an active Necromancer with few suspects left, and a rival Fortune Teller claim is possible. Information landscape: Information-rich on the threat: consecutive reanimated-wolf kills identified a Necromancer, but nobody knows who it is. Targeting rests on behavior and structure, not confirmed roles. Stakes: With two points banked, further bets have no scoring value and a death in the late game removes you from play, so each self-bet buys a night of survival against a lone killer closing in on a win. Target landscape: Remaining Town players plus yourself. Another bet adds nothing once two points are banked, and your own survival is the live variable. The Necromancer has been killing a Town player every night, and your exposure rests on behavioral and structural evidence, not confirmed roles.
lessons.action: Once you have scored your two points and a killer is picking off players nightly, spend a self-bet each night instead of betting on another player, because scoring is already banked and survival is what remains. A self-bet makes an attack on you fail that night, so use it on the nights the killer is most likely to go after you.

lessons.situation: Night betting after the wolf pack has been eliminated. A hidden lone killer (here the Necromancer, attacking through a dead wolf's body) is the only source of night kills, and you still need one or two points. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: wolf identities and many roles are confirmed from lynches and reveals, and role claims are out. Nothing shows who the lone killer is or whom it will target next, so the pick rests on role-value inference. Stakes: The lone killer needs to whittle the town down by attrition. Your win needs only one or two more deaths guessed correctly, so a well-chosen bet can end your game objectively while play continues. Target landscape: Five to seven living players, both wolves already dead. The candidates are claimed power roles (sentinel, trailseer, investigator, sigilist), the hidden lone killer and yourself. The likeliest victim is the loudest, most credible information source, chosen by role-value reasoning rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone or crippled and a lone killer is the only remaining attacker, bet on the most valuable surviving information or power role (e.g. a vocal claimed sentinel) and name that role. A death scores one point even if the role is hidden, and a correct role guess scores two, so the pair can finish your win condition in one night. Keep both self-bets in reserve unless you are one point short and expect the attack to land on you.

lessons.situation: Late game: wolves are dead or nearly so, a lone killer (the Necromancer) is still killing each night, and the Fortune Teller needs points or must stay alive long enough to score them. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves' roles are revealed, earlier checks are confirmed, and the killer's attack pattern across several nights is visible. The remaining uncertainty is only which player the killer takes next. Stakes: The game is near its end. One more death can decide the outcome, and the Fortune Teller's own survival and point total matter more than anything else it can do at night. Target landscape: Three or four living players, mostly confirmed or claimed roles such as an Investigator, a claimed Sigilist and a rival Fortune Teller claimant. The likeliest victim is the repeatedly attacked information source, chosen from the kill pattern rather than from confirmed knowledge.
lessons.action: Late in the game, with a lone killer still active and few players alive, bet on the player the killer's pattern most likely hits tonight, such as a repeatedly attacked information source, and name their role for the two-point payout. If you are the visible threat and still have self-bets, spend one that night, because it blocks an attack on you and a death before scoring loses the game.

lessons.situation: Early-to-mid game night after a wolf elimination, where multiple killers are active (wolves plus Serial Killer or Necromancer) and exposed claimants are the likelier victims. Earlier bets on a low-profile survivor scored nothing. Information landscape: Starved of confirmed targeting evidence: only public claims, last night's death roles, and killer behavior patterns. The previous bet had no basis beyond having survived. Stakes: Repeated zero-point nights shrink the path to two points. With several killers each night there are often two deaths, so betting on the exposed claimant raises the chance of scoring. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players, including recently claimed information roles (Sentinel, Trailseer, Investigator) who are plausible kill targets for either killer, and low-profile survivors. A pick that survived an earlier night only is weak evidence of a target.
lessons.action: Choose the bet from how the killers have actually behaved: which attacker types have been announced, and whether they hit exposed claimants. Don't bet on a player just because they survived last night. If neither killer has a clear target, bet on the most publicly exposed claimant. If two zero-point nights leave you with few nights left, use a self-bet only if you expect to be attacked.

lessons.situation: Midgame with one point scored and one more needed. The wolves and the Necromancer are killing nightly, a double attack on the sentinel and the investigator's death show their focus, and your earlier bet on a non-targeted player missed. Information landscape: Information-richer: revealed illusionist, trailseer record, necromancer vote-out, and a public attack on the sentinel. The killers' next preference is unstated, so the pick is inference from the kill pattern. Stakes: You need one more point to win and each wasted night costs a bet, while both self-bets remain unused. Missed bets on a player nobody is attacking waste nights that cannot be recovered. Target landscape: Six to seven living players: public-activity roles (sentinel, healer) that the wolves or a reanimating killer are visibly pressing, versus a quiet vote-aligned accuser with no sign of being targeted. The basis is public kill patterns and attack reports, not hidden role knowledge.
lessons.action: When you need a point and the previous night's kill pattern shows whom the killers are pressing (the attacked sentinel, the healer, or a role they just struck at), bet on that visible target to die rather than on a quiet accuser nobody is attacking. If your last bet missed, change the pick to follow the killers' current focus instead of repeating it, and keep your self-bets in hand until you have a reason to use them.

lessons.situation: Four-player endgame where the wolf must attack a high-threat claimed role while a living healer will probably guard that same player. The Fortune Teller has two self-bets left and one point. Information landscape: Information-rich: sigil mechanics are demonstrated, several dead roles are confirmed, and claims define the remaining pool. The healer's choice cannot be seen. Stakes: One save plus one sigil strike can end the game on the spot with the Fortune Teller short of two points. Choosing a bet that can still score when the obvious kill is saved matters more than matching the most likely attack. Target landscape: The claimed sigilist (the obvious wolf target), an unconfirmed healer claimant likely to guard them, and a quiet surviving wolf. The choice is between the heavily protected obvious victim and the less obvious alternatives, based on claims and prior-night events.
lessons.action: If a living healer can plausibly protect the obvious wolf target, bet on a different player who is likely to die by another cause, such as a player a pending sigil or other attack might strike or an alternate victim the pack might choose. Do not stake the bet on a protected player with an active sigil threat that could eliminate the last wolf and end the game before you score.

lessons.situation: Early game, night 2. Wolves and a lone killer are probably all hunting, and the town has just produced a visible claimed power role. You must bet on who dies while the healer may protect the most obvious target. Information landscape: Information-starved. There is one revealed death, an unverified claim or two, and little or no vote record. Nothing shows who the killers will pick beyond how visible the claimant is. Stakes: Early game with no imminent parity. The bet is a modest scoring chance, since a miss costs one night's attempt toward the two points. The two self-bets stay in reserve. Target landscape: Seven to nine living players: one or two public power-role claimants (a trailseer, sigilist or sentinel claimant who stands out as a likely kill target), plus quiet unclaimed players with no behavioral signal. The healer is alive and unrevealed. The only evidence is who died on night 1 and who claimed since.
lessons.action: On an early night with both self-bets still held, when killers are active and one publicly claimed investigative role stands out, bet on that claimant to die and name their claimed role only if you would accept losing the second point. Accept that a healer save can turn an accurate prediction into zero, since only a death scores. Do not move your bet to a quiet unclaimed player, because the evidence points at the claimant.

lessons.situation: Final-night endgame with an evil killer (wolf or Necromancer) one kill from winning and few or no town night-killing abilities left. The Fortune Teller needs points and can be killed itself. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are announced, spent abilities are known, and the remaining pool is nearly fully identified, so the killer's only plausible victim can be deduced. Stakes: The next kill ends the game, so a wasted bet or an unprotected Fortune Teller means a loss. A correct bet on the forced victim with the role named can score the final two points. A self-bet only buys time and scores nothing. Target landscape: Two or three other living players: a claimed or confirmed town role the sole remaining killer must target (the healer already dead or irrelevant), and an unconfirmed player who is the likely killer, with a Necromancer able to attack through a dead Vigilante body. Reads rest on confirmed deaths and claims, not on behavior.
lessons.action: In a 3-4 player endgame with both self-bets left, first identify which enemy can actually kill tonight. If the only living killer is the one who could attack you and you have no other path to a point, spend a self-bet so an attack on you fails; if your bet target is the one certain victim, bet on them and name their role.

lessons.situation: The previous night's wolf kill was stopped by a public heal. A wolf was lynched or lost, and a mixed field of wolves and a lone killer remains. You have one point and need one more. Information landscape: Fairly rich: the save was announced, a role was confirmed by a sigil strike, and one wolf's death was revealed. Which player the wolves will pick next is still a guess from motive. Stakes: With six alive and wolves still active, each night's kill brings them closer to parity. A missed bet wastes a night of scoring while you remain on one point, so choose the bet on motive and not on the last victim. Target landscape: Around six living players: a sigilist who has just survived a save, the healer who made the save, a lone killer, and one or more wolves. The healer is the known obstacle and the likelier next kill. The earlier target is a less likely repeat victim, since it was just protected and the wolves have lost a member.
lessons.action: When the wolves have just failed to kill a target through a heal or block, bet on the player who obstructed them, such as the healer, or on whoever their pack most needs gone. Do not re-bet on the previous target who survived. Only a wolf's kill selection can be predicted this way, so the bet on the obstacle is the better read.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2-3) after a wolf was voted out or a tie vote. Claims are public, and a Necromancer, wolves or a Serial Killer may strike. The Fortune Teller is not under suspicion and needs two points to win. Information landscape: Moderate public signals: claimed roles, announced attacker types (reanimated attack), prior deaths and vote records. Nothing confirms who the killers will choose. Stakes: The game is not at the brink, but each night is a scoring chance and the Fortune Teller needs two points. A night with several possible killers gives more than one death to land on, so a well-chosen bet is worth making every night. Target landscape: Several living claimants (a Healer who revealed whom they protected, a twice-attacked Investigator, a Sentinel or Trailseer) and contested players from a claim clash or tie vote. Roles are public claims, unverified. Picks rest on behavior and exposure, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, bet on the player the killers are most likely to hit, judged from public exposure: a freshly claimed Healer or information role, a player at the center of a claim clash, or one just named by an announced reanimated attack. Add the role guess only when a public claim makes it a strong inference, since a right role is worth two points and a wrong role still scores one for the death.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame night where the killers' obvious priority target, a verified or claimed investigator, has been publicly shielded or saved by the healer, while other prominent claimants are unprotected. The Fortune Teller must choose a bet to reach two points. Information landscape: Information-rich: both wolves or the serial killer are dead or confirmed, healer saves are announced, and protection patterns are visible to every player, including the killers. Stakes: Scoring needs two points, and each zero-point night shrinks the remaining nights in which they can be earned. Repeating a bet the healer can block yields no points and pushes the Fortune Teller toward riskier late bets. Target landscape: A claimed investigator or other focal Town player who is openly or recently healer-protected; an unprotected claimed healer or trailseer; and quieter unverified players. The evidence is public announcements of saves and claims, not behavior.
lessons.action: When the obvious high-profile target was publicly healer-protected or saved last night, bet on a different likely victim instead, such as an unprotected prominent claimant (the claimed healer, or a trailseer or sentinel with no cover). If no protector remains alive, bet on the most prominent unprotected Town claimant.

lessons.situation: Late game with no protective role alive and a single evil killer who must kill the one remaining town power role. The Fortune Teller can predict the casualty and its role. Information landscape: Information-rich: earlier deaths and reveals fix who is alive, who the killer must be, and which role is the logical victim. The claimed role has been corroborated by a visible event. Stakes: The kill decides whether the game ends this night, so the bet is made at the point of highest leverage. Naming the right role can finish the Fortune Teller's win condition alongside the evil side's win. Target landscape: A claimed role whose identity has been established by an earlier reveal (such as a vigilante whose shot exposed the Serial Killer's immunity) and the lone wolf as the only possible killer. The healer is already dead, so nothing can save the victim.
lessons.action: When the killer's victim is forced by elimination, bet on that player to die and name their role, since a correct role scores two points instead of one. Choose the player no remaining protector can cover. Bet only on a death you can explain by who is able to attack, not on a player merely because they are the obvious target.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3, after a vote removed a wolf or resolved a claim conflict. Both the wolves and a lone killer are likely to strike the most threatening public Town claimant. You have 0-1 points, so each night's bet is your main way to score. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: a revealed wolf, claim conflicts and vote records show who threatens the killers. No role is confirmed beyond the reveals, and the healer's protection choice is unknown. Stakes: Scoring two points wins the game for you whatever else happens. Each night's bet is therefore a real chance to progress, and a miss costs only a night, not a use. The Town/wolf balance is not yet critical. Target landscape: Several claimed Town power roles (Investigator, Sentinel, healer, sigilist, trailseer) are alive. One was just validated by a vote or counter-claim win and is the obvious kill target. A healer may be guarding that player. The basis is role-value and behavior reasoning, not confirmed evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack and any lone killer have just lost a member or a public claimant has just been validated, bet on the most visible, freshly validated Town power role (healer, or a claimed Investigator or Sentinel whose report threatens the killers) to die, and name the role if the evidence points to it. Kills tend to aim at that player, so the bet scores if they die; a hidden role still scores, so name the role. If you suspect the healer will guard the obvious target, bet on the next-most-valuable power role the killers could reach instead.

lessons.situation: The night after a failed double attack on a claimed Town role that the healer saved. Both killers have shown interest in that role, and they may pivot or repeat. You have 0 points and unused self-bets. Information landscape: Moderately informed: a saved attack and open claims give real signal about killer priorities, but it is reasoning and not confirmation. You have no cover or confirmed roles. Stakes: You are at 0 points and being voted out before betting would lose you the game, so getting bets placed each night matters. Each unsuccessful night shortens your runway. Target landscape: The previous night's double-attack target was saved by the healer, and the likely next victims are that same player again, another claimed power role such as a sigilist, or the healer. The basis is expected killer behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, place a bet on the likeliest victim instead of holding back, and keep both self-bets in reserve until you are visibly exposed or have been the day's top vote target. If the kill is likely to go onto the same obvious claimant a second time and the healer may repeat the save, pick the second-most-likely target the killers would pivot to, such as a claimed role that bypasses protection.

lessons.situation: After a day in which the Fortune Teller cast an isolated dissenting vote or otherwise stands out, the remaining killers must choose a victim. The obvious saved target is likely covered again, which makes the exposed Fortune Teller the easy kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: the public voting record and announced saves expose who dissented and who the healer protected, and the killers can read both. Stakes: If the Fortune Teller dies with fewer than two points it loses permanently. A self-bet makes an attack on it fail, so it survives to bet again, though it scores nothing that night. Target landscape: The Fortune Teller's own safety, via a self-bet, versus betting on a re-targeted saved claimant or another Town player. The killers may bypass the healer-protected claimant and hit the visible outlier instead.
lessons.action: When your day-3 vote or behavior marks you as an outlier or likely target, and you are not close to the second point, use one of your two self-bets instead of betting on another player. The attack on you fails that night, so you stay alive to score later.

lessons.situation: Night 1, or an opening night with no discussion or only a quiet day. Two or three independent killers may each take someone, and the bet scores if the named player dies by any cause. Information landscape: Completely information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or protection results, and day 1 had no vote. Stakes: Early misses are routine and not decisive, since two points are still reachable later. A blind hit with no role named caps the score at one point instead of two, which is a free loss to avoid. Target landscape: Nine other living players with no claims, votes, behavior or night history. Any pick is a pure guess, and several deaths are possible because there are two or three killers.
lessons.action: When you have no information, still place the bet and always name a role guess. A wrong role costs nothing, since the death still scores one point, and a right role doubles it. If any thin signal exists, such as a power role likely to be a priority kill, use it to pick the target and the role.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer or investigator has publicly accused or outed a player, and both accuser and accused are alive entering the night. The evil faction must decide whether to silence the accuser. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are public claims, a counter-claim dispute, and a visible accusation, but nothing hard confirms the accuser or the accused. Stakes: A correct bet here scores one point toward the two needed. A bet on the accused instead of the accuser yielded zero points when the accuser was killed. Target landscape: An exposer (a claimed trailseer or investigator who caught or outed an evil player), the accused player under suspicion, and other claimants. The basis is public claims and accusations.
lessons.action: When a claimant has publicly accused or exposed a suspected evil player, bet on the exposer as the likely victim, since the wolves are more likely to silence the accuser than to attack their own accused partner. Take that bet only if the exposer is not currently healer-protected.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room is leaning toward eliminating you: the Investigator claimant's result has strong public support from the earlier reveal, and the remaining claimant has explicitly said they would vote for you. The fourth survivor's position is not stated, so unanimity is not established.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Four players remain; the leading evil faction is two eliminations from parity, at worst for the town because a concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so this vote is a swing decision. The end-of-game consequence of this particular vote is unclear from the record; immediately, eliminating you removes one living player.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Your Healer claim is already public and commits you to a role whose protection history cannot be verified from nights with no public save. Continuing to defend that account keeps your Necromancer role and reanimated attacks concealed for now, but leaves you exposed to the corroborated Investigator claim; retracting it would make the deception visible and is not readily reversible.
query_dims.heat_now: High: the player claiming Investigator reports a Suspicious result on you, and their earlier Suspicious result was borne out when the accused was revealed as the Illusionist. The claimed Healer defense has no public save corroborating it.
query_dims.information_landscape: Public information includes revealed roles and town wills, the revealed Illusionist, and the Investigator claimant's previously corroborated result. The current Suspicious result and your claimed protections are private-action reports without independent public confirmation. The concealed roles of two night victims leave some faction composition uncertain.
query_dims.my_position: You are the accused and are defending yourself against the forming vote; you are not driving the consensus.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you are the Necromancer and that your reanimated attacks killed two players; you also know the concealed role of one of those victims was the Chanteuse. Publicly, your role and those actions are unknown. The public sees a player claiming Investigator whose earlier Suspicious result was corroborated by the revealed Illusionist, now reporting you Suspicious, while you claim Healer.
query_dims.situation: A player claiming Investigator, whose earlier Suspicious result was corroborated by an Illusionist reveal, now reports you Suspicious. You answer with a Healer claim and say your protections produced no public save; another survivor favors voting you, so the verified-looking private-result claim is driving an endgame vote against your concealed identity.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate vote centers on you, a claimed Healer now read Suspicious by a player claiming Investigator with a previously corroborated result. The Investigator is a strong-evidence claim, not system-confirmed; the other two survivors have no role status established here. The public basis against you is the result and the lack of a public save, while your own knowledge confirms the result is consistent with your role and actions.

lessons.situation: Late game with three or four alive after a public reanimated attack. The Necromancer pool has been narrowed to a few players, I am one of them, and I must either claim a cover role or accuse the other suspect before the vote. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: announced night attack types, revealed roles, public vote records and a narrowed suspect pool. The remaining evidence is unverified claims. Stakes: With three alive, one vote or one night kill decides the game. If the vote lands on me, Town wins at once; if it lands elsewhere, I am a night kill from winning. Consensus: The room is converging against me. The other suspects' accounts fit the announced night events, and a ballot of two or three players can tie or flip on a single vote. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus and trying to turn the swing voter. Heat: High. I was named the Necromancer by elimination or by a rival claimant, and a public reanimated attack points at whoever has been channeling it. Forward exposure: A fabricated role claim or a flat counter-accusation commits me to a story that the public night record or the real role holder can test. It cannot be withdrawn without confessing, and with three alive the next vote is final. Target landscape: Two or three living suspects, including me. Their roles are claimed but unverified, and the basis is claims plus the public reanimated-attack report, which fits whoever is suspected. Public vs private: I know I am the Necromancer and that my reanimated attack is already public. Publicly I am one of two or three suspects, and my accusers' claims fit the announced night events.
lessons.action: When the Necromancer pool has shrunk to about three and you are named, anchor your defense only in announced facts such as morning reports, public votes and revealed roles. Pick a cover story that no living player can contradict from a private record. If a living player's own record already fits the facts better than your story, shift to showing that their account explains the announced night events no better than yours does. Do not invent a detailed record, such as bets, that a real holder can contradict.

lessons.situation: A claimed Investigator publicly accuses or reads you as Suspicious, around a night where a hidden-role death or a reanimated kill hints at a Necromancer. The village debates how to verify the claim while you are the only one contesting it. Information landscape: Thin hard evidence: an unverified Investigator claim with at most a half-confirmed earlier check, one hidden-role death, and no Trailseer or Sentinel corroboration. Stakes: Being voted out ends the necromancer's only win path, which is to be last standing. This day's vote is therefore existential, and heat must come down before it. Consensus: The village is converging on the claimant's read, and its only open question is how to verify it. The basis is the claim plus any partial confirmation, not hard evidence. My position: Holding out alone against the consensus. Heat: High and rising. A Suspicious read from a plausible Investigator, a public announcement that a Necromancer struck, and your own pushback have put you at the center. Forward exposure: Resisting or denying locks you into an all-in 'fake claim' story that collapses if the claimant is corroborated, and it cannot be taken back. Endorsing verification commits you to little, and you can still shift your stance later. Target landscape: The candidates are the Investigator claimant, who has partial corroboration and no role contest, and you, the accused. No other player is a clear alternative suspect, and Trailseer or Sentinel confirmers are unclaimed or may be dead under a hidden role. Public vs private: You privately know the Investigator's read on you is accurate, or that no one can truly confirm or refute it. Publicly the village sees an unverified claimant versus an accused player and is searching for a way to test it.
lessons.action: When a claimed Investigator names you and the village is looking for a way to verify it, endorse the verification and don't fight it. Offer a cooperative test, such as asking the claimant for the full check history and asking any Trailseer or Sentinel to speak up, and press the village to put its vote on a rival suspect if the evidence stays thin. A flat denial or repeated pushback only reads as fear of proof and leaves you alone against the room.

lessons.situation: Late game with about five players alive. A body-assisted attack has been announced and the town is hunting the lone killer among the few unconfirmed players, while you are one of them. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced role reveals, a will clearing a player, a reanimated-attack announcement, and permanent public votes give the town a lot to cross-check. Stakes: With five alive, one wrongly directed or lost day vote can end your game. Being named the necromancer this round is likely fatal, so avoiding contradictions matters more than pushing a theory. Consensus: The village is converging on a small set of unconfirmed players using announced facts, and it is ready to punish evasive or inconsistent framing. My position: holding out Heat: High. The announced reanimated attack proves a necromancer is alive, so scrutiny falls on every unconfirmed player, and your unexplained votes draw questions. Forward exposure: Claiming to be outside the suspect pool commits you to a facade that cross-examination of your votes can break, and you cannot take it back once challenged. Staying inside the pool and giving consistent reasons commits you to little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: A few unconfirmed players (you, a surviving wolf or neutral, and others) next to cleared or confirmed players such as a healer cleared by an investigator's will. The only hard evidence is announced facts and wills, and the rest is voting-record behavior. Public vs private: You privately know you used a dead wolf's or vigilante's body to attack, while the room knows only that a necromancer is alive and is narrowing down the unconfirmed players.
lessons.action: When a reanimated attack has been announced and you sit in a small unconfirmed pool, put yourself in that pool openly and answer questions about your voting record with reasons that match the public record. Then argue from announced facts such as wills, saves and kill types, and name the other unconfirmed players as candidates alongside yourself instead of presenting yourself as a neutral judge outside the pool.

lessons.situation: Endgame with about four alive and the wolves dead or nearly dead. The town reasons by elimination that you are the Necromancer, and a rival claimant is pushing a vote on you. Information landscape: Info-starved: no hard evidence, role claims cannot be verified, and the discussion rests on elimination logic and vote records. Stakes: With four alive, one wrong vote or kill decides the game. If you survive the vote, your next night kill leaves three alive and brings you close to winning. Consensus: Undecided and fragile: the town knows a lone killer is still alive, but has no evidence separating the remaining players. My position: Holding out against an accusation, countering it rather than driving a wagon. Heat: High: you are the leading suspect through role elimination and the only player without a trusted claim. Forward exposure: A false claim commits you to a consistent fabricated history that can be compared against the real claimant's, and it can only be sustained until the vote closes. It is hard to retract once made. Target landscape: Three or four remaining players: the accuser (a claimant of a neutral role), one other uncommitted claimant, and a possible leftover wolf. Roles are judged on claim-versus-claim and vote tone, not on hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the Necromancer and the accuser's claim may even be true, but publicly it is one unverifiable claim against another, with no hard evidence either way.
lessons.action: When wolves are mostly dead and you are named Necromancer by elimination in a four-player endgame, counter-accuse the accuser and hold a stable story: if the accuser is a claimed neutral, counterclaim that role with a bet or result history that does not line up with deaths the town already knows. Aim to split the remaining voters rather than win every vote, because a split or a wasted vote keeps you alive for your night attack.

lessons.situation: A claimed Investigator names a suspect and states they cleared the necromancer on an earlier night. A counterclaim appears against the accused and the room is leaning toward a vote. Information landscape: Mixed. One Investigator claim that includes a clearance on you, one counterclaim, and no confirmed roles beyond the dead. Stakes: Late-mid game with few players left, so each vote matters. Riding a public clearance keeps you safe while the town eliminates another player. Consensus: The majority is forming behind the Investigator's accusation, based on claims and a counterclaim. My position: With the majority, helping drive the case against the accused. Heat: Low and falling. You were named only as a Not suspicious check and defended yourself by agreeing with it. Forward exposure: Vouching for the Investigator ties you to that claim being genuine. A later check on an attack night would read Suspicious, and reversing would look like a flip. Target landscape: The claimed Investigator, whose check cleared you and who is backed by a counterclaim against the accused, versus the accused player, who is contradicted by another claim. There are no confirmations, only claims and a counterclaim. Public vs private: The Investigator's clearance of you was true only because you were inactive that night. You know you read Suspicious on attack nights, but publicly the clearance looks like solid proof of innocence.
lessons.action: If a claimed Investigator says they cleared you and that claim is gaining support from the room, publicly accept the clearance and side with the Investigator against the counterclaimer. This turns the clearance into cover and aligns you with the likely winning side. Stay aware that checking you on a night you attack would read Suspicious, so keep the endorsement light and avoid vouching for the Investigator beyond what you must.

lessons.situation: With the wolves gone and few players left, a confirmed vigilante is leading the hunt for the lone necromancer and the town is choosing between claimed role players. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves eliminated, a confirmed vigilante kill announced, spent-sigil claims and repeated roleblock claims. A confirmed shooter still holds a bullet. Stakes: A confirmed vigilante with a bullet can kill you at night if you look like the necromancer, so any extra heat can end the game. Consensus: The town is moving toward one elimination on claim-based reasoning, and it is explicitly treating anyone who attacks the protective claimants as suspect. My position: holding out Heat: Moderate to high. A confirmed vigilante has said that players pushing suspicious angles against the claimed healer are prime necromancer suspects. Forward exposure: A loud push against a protective claimant ties you to that accusation and is read as necromancer framing, and you cannot undo it. Agreeing with a forming consensus leaves little public footprint and can be changed. Target landscape: A claimed healer reporting repeated roleblocks, a claimed sigilist with spent sigils, and a confirmed vigilante holding a bullet. Reads on them rest on claims and behavior, not verified evidence. Public vs private: You privately want the confirmed or protective roles weakened, but the room is already moving toward a different elimination and is watching who pushes the claimed healer or other protective claims.
lessons.action: If the town is already drifting toward a target other than you, voice agreement with that drift and support it with the public record, instead of leading a separate push against a claimed protective or confirmed role. If you must dissent, do it with a mild, evidence-based question rather than a sustained campaign against one player.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer reports that an accused player visited a murdered player's home on the night of a concealed kill, and the accused denies it. The necromancer is tempted to dispute the report with an argument about how concealment works. Information landscape: Information-rich: a concealed death, a specific claimed visit report, and several claimed utility roles. Rules arguments are easy to rebut. Stakes: Day votes drive the early elimination pace, and a wolf voted out while the necromancer defended it leaves the necromancer's record tainted. Staying neutral keeps later suspicion on others. Consensus: The village is converging on the accused after the trailseer's report, and the mechanics rebuttal reinforced that. The basis is a specific visit result that fits a concealed night kill. My position: Holding out against the forming push, which is a minority and visible position. Heat: Low. Nobody is accusing me, and I am seen as a neutral voice commenting on mechanics. Forward exposure: A visible mechanics objection commits the necromancer to an anti-investigative stance with no role claim to back it up. If the accused flips evil, the objection ties the necromancer to the defense, and the objection can be rebutted publicly with the exact rule. Target landscape: A claiming trailseer with a specific visit report against an accused player who denies it. Both are judged on claim consistency and on how concealment affects visit visibility. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer has no stake in the wolf's survival and no direct knowledge of the kill. Publicly, raising mechanical doubts to blunt the claimant's report looks like defending the accused.
lessons.action: When a living claimant's result is likely true and the room is converging on a wolf, align with the consensus using only reasoning drawn from public facts. Do not publicly challenge the claimant's mechanics unless you can cite the rules exactly.

lessons.situation: Late game with three or four players left. A night attack through a body, or a corroborated town report, has exposed the necromancer. It must defend a fake role claim before a decisive vote. Information landscape: Information-rich: confirmed roles, consistent night results and exhausted ability kits leave little room for an unverifiable story. Stakes: One vote can eliminate the necromancer and end the game for the town. Any claim that can be contradicted is likely to end the game immediately. Consensus: The village is aligned against the agent. Town claims cross-check each other and the agent's story is the outlier. My position: Holding out alone against a forming town bloc. Heat: Critical: a credible town player has publicly attached a Suspicious result or a corroborated story to the agent. Forward exposure: Claiming a unique town role commits the agent to it for the rest of the game. If a living holder exists, one counterclaim ends the claim, so it cannot be reversed. Target landscape: The agent is under direct accusation. The alternatives are a quiet player or a claimed role holder, but a verified investigator and the other claimed town roles hold the deciding votes. Evidence is mostly mutually consistent night reports. Public vs private: Privately the agent is the lone killer who attacked through a dead role's body; publicly it must present as a town role while a living player holds checkable information against it.
lessons.action: When a living verified investigator or other town player puts heat on you late, claim only a role whose holder is publicly confirmed dead, such as a body whose role was announced. Report only what that role could learn under the rules, and do not name past protections or results that a living player can contradict. If the real holder of the role could still be alive and speak up, a claim of that role is exposed to a single counterclaim and cannot be taken back.

lessons.situation: A final three with the necromancer facing two town players whose reports corroborate each other. The necromancer pivots to an aggressive counter-accusation. Information landscape: Information-rich: both town players' night actions line up and corroborate each other, so any flawed claim from the agent stands out. Stakes: With three players alive, the day's vote decides the game. Failing to split the town bloc means the necromancer is voted out. Consensus: Two town players are united by consistent reports and exhausted kits, and the agent's claim is isolated. My position: Holding out against a two-player town bloc. Heat: Extreme: both remaining players have cross-verified each other and aligned against the agent's claim. Forward exposure: An all-in push on one player in a final three leaves no retreat. If the argument has a mechanical flaw, the town reads it as a necromancer's lie. Target landscape: The choice is between the player whose tracking credibility can be challenged and the player whose lack of remaining utility can be challenged. Both have corroborated each other, so the evidence favours town and only behavioral gaps are available to attack. Public vs private: Privately the agent knows the town reports are probably honest and that its own claimed watch or check is fabricated. Publicly it must make that fabrication look mechanically sound.
lessons.action: When you counter-accuse a town player, build the case on a gap that is real under the rules, for example a claimed result that conflicts with another player's public statement or an announced fact. A watch report names only visitors to the watched player, so it cannot disprove that player's outgoing visits. If the two remaining town players have mutually consistent reports, challenge one claim at a time to split them instead of attacking both.

lessons.situation: Four players are left, a wolf and the necromancer are both suspected, and the wolf accuses you of dodging vote analysis. Information landscape: Fairly rich on eliminated roles, but nothing separates the wolf from the necromancer. Discussion rests on vote records and tone. Stakes: Every vote and kill matters at this count. If the vote falls on the wolf and you live, you can attack the next night to finish. Consensus: Loosely aligned on a two-person suspect pool, based on role elimination and vote records. No decisive evidence. My position: Holding out and countering an accusation, then nudging the vote toward the other suspect. Heat: Moderate: you are named in the suspect pool and directly accused of dodging, but the other suspect carries equal or more suspicion. Forward exposure: Pointing at someone's vote history commits you to a read on a player you may kill later. It is cheap and reversible because no role claim is made. Target landscape: The remaining players are an accuser (a suspected wolf), a neutral claimant or unclaimed player, and a sigilist-type town role supported by confirmed deaths. Suspicion rests on vote behavior and tone, not on evidence. Public vs private: You know you are the lone killer, while the table believes the pool holds a wolf and a necromancer and cannot tell which is which. You can use that doubt to point suspicion at others.
lessons.action: When the table believes the remaining pool is one wolf plus a necromancer and a player accuses you of dodging, answer the accusation point by point in a procedural tone and redirect attention to another player's voting behavior (for example, who cast the first vote on an earlier wagon). Keep the redirect framed as a vote-record observation instead of an outright wolf accusation, so the wagon lands on the player already under suspicion.

lessons.situation: In the endgame at three or four players alive, claimants issue an ultimatum or corner the unclaimed necromancer. The necromancer is one or two eliminations from winning but has no role to claim. Information landscape: Information-rich: successive eliminations and claims have narrowed the roles. Wills, saves and the roles of the dead are public, so a fake claim can be checked against them. Stakes: One mis-elimination of a town claimant at this size would nearly win the game for me, while my own elimination ends it. Credibility is the whole resource. Consensus: The remaining town claimants are aligned on forcing the unclaimed players to reveal, and they judge claims against the record. My position: Holding out against a push to reveal, with the room consolidating against me. Heat: High to extreme: the claimants single out the unclaimed seats for refusing to name a role, and I am the one who cannot account for a night attack. Forward exposure: A claim made now commits me to one role and to its results, so I must check it against the dead roles, the hidden-role bodies and my earlier statements. A claim delayed until the final vote is read as a fabrication. Refusing to claim at all cannot be undone and leaves me with no defence. Target landscape: Three or four players remain: a claimed sentinel or vigilante with spent resources, a confirmed healer or other claimant, an unclaimed player, and me. Roles are mostly known from claims and eliminations, so the unclaimed seats are the natural suspects. Public vs private: Publicly I am one of the unclaimed seats, pressed to give a town identity. Privately I am the necromancer with no real role to claim, and I may have used bodies that make some claims impossible.
lessons.action: Before the endgame ultimatum, pick one town role that is not yet publicly dead, not already claimed by someone else, and whose claimed result is hard to check. Claim it at the first direct challenge, and keep every later statement consistent with the public record. If the role was hidden at death or its owner is accounted for, choose a different one rather than waiting and then claiming it under pressure.

lessons.situation: A town tracker-type claimant has publicly reported that the necromancer made no visits. The room is now sorting out the remaining claimants (Healer, Speculator, Sentinel) in a late-game day where a tie or a bad vote keeps the necromancer alive. Information landscape: Fairly rich in claims: an announced save, a dead-body attack named by its kind, and several competing role claims. None of it is verified except the morning announcements. Stakes: With about five alive, each vote or kill moves the necromancer close to its win condition of at most one other player alive. Keeping a tie or steering the vote off yourself preserves the path to the final three. Consensus: The room is split over several claimants and relies on claimed night results. Nobody has confirmed anything, and votes are scattered or tied. My position: With the majority, using the Trailseer's conclusion to steer rather than lead the push. Heat: Low. A visit-tracking claimant publicly cleared the necromancer, leaving only mild suspicion from one claimant. Forward exposure: Accepting the clearance commits the necromancer to the no-visit narrative and to staying unclaimed. That is reversible only at the cost of looking evasive, and a long-term pattern of non-accountability can be turned against it later. Target landscape: Alternative targets are the claimed Healer and a Speculator claimant, plus a claimed Sentinel pushing the Healer. All are unverified claims, and the case against each rests on behavior and on the claimed visit logic. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer attacked through a dead player's body, which leaves the dead player's name at the door and not its own. Publicly, visit-tracking roles read it as having visited no one and clear it.
lessons.action: When a claimed Trailseer or Sentinel reports no visit from you, confirm the clearance in a sentence or two and then redirect to a concrete alternative suspect, such as a contested claimant, using their stated behavior or claims. Your attack through a dead player's body shows the dead player's name at the door, not yours, so the clearance is real. If pressed to claim a role, answer with brief, consistent reasoning rather than a fabricated claim.

lessons.situation: The necromancer has learned night information through a dead role's body and is tempted to use it in discussion to redirect suspicion onto other players, while the room is actively analyzing who could know what. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are announced role deaths, claimed investigative results, and players closely tracking visits. The sources of knowledge are therefore checkable. Stakes: The necromancer needs the village to shrink, but a mid-sized table still lets one exposure cause a near-unanimous elimination. Surviving the day is worth more than landing one accusation. Consensus: The village is rigorously tracking visit mechanics and is united in cross-checking who could know what. Any claim that cannot be sourced is quickly spotted. My position: Not yet committed, free to stay with the majority. Revealing channeled data would leave me holding out alone against the whole room. Heat: Low to none at the start of the discussion, since nobody suspects the necromancer. It becomes overwhelming once an impossible information source is revealed. Forward exposure: Naming exact visitors or other results from a dead role's body shows knowledge that only the necromancer could have, and once said it cannot be retracted. A vague or announced-facts-only contribution commits to nothing and stays reversible. Target landscape: The living claimed town roles (an investigator, a trailseer, a claimed healer) and unclaimed players. Their standing rests on claims and on visit logic, with no hard confirmation. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer holds results from channeling a dead investigative role, such as the visitors at a door. Publicly that role is dead and no living player has claimed such a result, so citing it would expose the source.
lessons.action: When a night read obtained through a dead player's body would be impossible for any living role to know, hold it back and stay vague, and only restate what the Game Master announced or what living claimants have said. If you push a read, ground it in public voting records and announced facts, so a challenge cannot trace it to your necromancer channel.

lessons.situation: Early-mid game day discussion after a concealed or failed night kill, with clashing role claims and the town deciding how to test them before the vote. I am a hidden lone-killer Necromancer with private body-ability information. Information landscape: Only unverified claims and blocked or missing investigative roles exist; the discussion is information-starved and speculative. Stakes: The board is not at the brink, so one discussion move will not flip the game. The priority is staying off the radar while wolves and town thin each other, not forcing an outcome. Consensus: The room is converging on testing claims or on a pending wolf-versus-claimant dispute, with little hard evidence behind it. My position: Neutral, offering process suggestions while the room converges; neither driving a target nor opposing the majority. Heat: Low to none: I have not been accused or singled out, apart from at most a general call-out of abstainers. Forward exposure: Procedural suggestions commit me to no read and are easy to walk back. Citing movement or results from a body-use ties me to a source nobody can see, invites a 'who watched?' challenge, and cannot be retracted once on the record. Target landscape: Rival claimants (e.g. two Investigators with opposite results) and unconfirmed roles judged only on claims and voting behavior; no role is confirmed, so any side I take would be a guess. Public vs private: I privately know my body-ability plans and results (a concealed victim, a follow or attack through a dead role), while publicly nobody suspects a lone killer and the room is arguing over unverified claims.
lessons.action: When claims clash and you hold private body-derived information, stay unclaimed and offer only procedural, verifiable-in-public suggestions, such as asking claimants to commit to next night's targets so claims can be tested against later visit evidence. Keep every comment to what the room could know openly, and never cite a result that comes only from your own reanimated ability.

lessons.situation: A loud claim-vs-counterclaim dispute, such as dueling Healer claims or an unverified Sentinel or Investigator report, absorbs the day's discussion. The necromancer is not a suspect. Information landscape: One or two unverified claims and a counterclaim. There are few confirmed roles beyond the dead, so the evidence is mostly behavioral and logical. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. Neither evil side is close to winning, so staying unnoticed and letting the room spend its votes on the claim clash is worth more than steering it. Consensus: The room is converging on a claim clash or a single target, based on reports and counterclaims rather than confirmed roles. My position: With the majority, echoing the framing instead of driving it. Heat: Near zero. The necromancer has not been named or accused and has made no risky claim. Forward exposure: Echoing the consensus commits to nothing beyond agreement with a forming read and is easy to walk back. A sharper accusation would create a position and a vote to defend. Target landscape: Two contested claimants, such as a claimed Healer against a counter-claimed Healer or a Sentinel's named visitor. There are no confirmed roles, and the basis is claims plus behavior. Public vs private: Publicly the necromancer reads as an ordinary town voice. Privately it is a lone killer with no stake in which claimant is right, and it is either untouchable or inactive on the nights in question.
lessons.action: When a claim dispute (Investigator or Sentinel report, Healer counterclaims) is dominating the day and nobody is looking at you, speak once and back whichever side the room is already converging on. Frame the dispute as a clean claimant-vs-claimant question to settle, and make no new accusation. That keeps you with the majority, leaves no voting record to defend, and is fully reversible.

lessons.situation: Day 2 discussion after the first night: several Town role claims clash (rival investigators, a rule-inconsistent sentinel result, an unexplained visit), and the necromancer holds private knowledge or an unused usable body while staying unclaimed. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims, one or two second-hand visit reports, and only the dead players' announced roles confirmed. The necromancer's own private information is not publicly known. Stakes: Early-mid game with many players alive: no single vote ends the game, but the necromancer needs to survive daily votes to reach the end, so staying out of the accusation list is the priority. Consensus: The village is split over competing claims and has not formed a firm consensus. Its attention is on whose result is inconsistent, not on the quiet players. My position: On the sidelines or moving with the majority, not driving any accusation. Heat: Low to mild: no accusation or only a passing mention of the necromancer's silence, with the focus on claim conflicts. Forward exposure: A short neutral comment or question commits to little and is reversible, but any reference to unshared results or to how a body works would tie the speaker to private knowledge and cannot be taken back. A reanimated attack would be announced as such, so wording about bodies must not suggest foreknowledge. Target landscape: Rival claimants (two investigators, a contested sentinel result, an unexplained visit) are the natural focus. None has a confirmed role, and the basis for suspicion is claims and rule-consistency rather than behavior; the necromancer is one of several quiet, unaccused players. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows its own role and any night use of a dead player's body (or that the body is available), while publicly it is just one quiet player among several, with Town claims unverified and no one suspecting a lone killer.
lessons.action: While the room is fixated on a role-claim clash and nobody has named you, speak briefly as a Town voice: echo or ask a neutral question about the dispute and steer attention back to the clashing claimants. Cite only publicly announced facts and never reference a body you used or any private result; if a player starts probing your vote or silence, give a short sincere-sounding reason and redirect the question to the claim clash.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after several deaths. Town and wolves are arguing over voting records and a night-timeline theory, and a hidden necromancer is either unmentioned or only theorized about while it stays quiet. Information landscape: Moderately rich: several dead roles are confirmed and some claims are partly corroborated, but wolf identities and the lone killer's identity are unverified. Stakes: Few players remain, so each vote moves the board toward the necromancer's last-two win. Being singled out by a vote or a shot now would end the run, so low visibility with minimal engagement matters. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on a few suspects, driven by wolves and town voices pushing voting-record and behavior cases. It has no hard proof of the lone killer's identity. My position: With the majority and speaking mildly, not driving any accusation; neither holding out nor leading. Heat: Low and not directly accused. At most there is a mild mention of its abstain-heavy votes or of its silence, and a town theory that a necromancer exists. Forward exposure: A generic record-based comment commits the necromancer to nothing and is fully reversible. A role claim or a named wolf would create a checkable statement, and silence plus an abstain leaves a permanent, noticeable pattern. Target landscape: The table is weighing other players, such as a claimed sigilist and quiet town roles, on voting behavior and role inference rather than hard evidence. The necromancer is not among the named suspects; several dead roles are confirmed and living roles are mostly unverified. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it has used or can use dead bodies and that the table's accusation flow does not touch it; publicly it is an unnamed, unsuspected role that the town may only be theorizing about.
lessons.action: When the table is chasing other targets and you are a low-heat necromancer, add one short, sincere, evidence-based observation about the record (e.g. a vote was near-unanimous and so isolates no one) to show engagement. Make no role claim and no wolf accusation, so you stay uncheckable and can drop the point freely. If a town theory starts to name a hidden lone killer, join the discussion before the vote rather than going silent and abstaining.

lessons.situation: A claimed Trailseer reports that followed players made no visits, including an Illusionist on a night it concealed a body. Town players are calling the claim impossible and accusing the Trailseer of being the Necromancer, and the necromancer is deciding how hard to back the accusation. Information landscape: Rich in rules arguments but short on confirmed truth. The Trailseer's record will only be confirmed after elimination, so the mechanical argument cannot be checked until then. Stakes: Removing a tracker who may hold the necromancer's trace is valuable, but the surviving small town can deduce the necromancer from that same record afterward. Any lie told now becomes evidence in the endgame. Consensus: Several players (Fortune Teller, Sigilist, Vigilante) are aligned on the claim that the track is mechanically impossible and are treating the claimant as the Necromancer. My position: With the majority, reinforcing the accusation rather than leading it. Heat: Low to moderate. The necromancer is not accused, but by agreeing with the accusers it is leaving a record that can be checked later. Forward exposure: A flat public claim of impossibility is permanent and gets checked once the accused is eliminated and their record is revealed. It cannot be retracted without exposing the necromancer, and it will stand as a recorded lie. Target landscape: The single target is a claimed Trailseer whose track conflicts with a rule-based reading. The case against it is mechanical and not behavioral, and it is unverified until revealed. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knew the Trailseer's no-visit track could be true, because its attack through the dead Illusionist's body showed the dead player's name and not its own. Publicly it insisted the track was an impossible fabrication.
lessons.action: When others are accusing a claimed tracker or watcher and you join in, argue from behavior or from the claim's unverified status. Make rule statements only if they stay true given your own night attacks, since your attack through a dead Illusionist's body leaves that body's name at the door. Do not assert that a track is impossible if your own actions could later make it true.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown, six eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so a single result or elimination can be decisive despite that worst-case parity distance.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-rich relative to the prior day: the Illusionist's revealed role supports your private Night 1 result, while the Sentinel claim and roleblock claim are unverified. The concealed night-death role remains unknown; no check result on another living player is available yet.
query_dims.situation: After the player you checked was eliminated and revealed as the Illusionist, your Night 1 Suspicious result gained strong public support. You have one check remaining, and the current night presents a choice among the seven other living players for gathering further alignment information.
query_dims.target_landscape: The seven other living players are possible check targets. One claimed Sentinel and reported seeing no visitors at their target; another claimed to have been roleblocked. The other living players have no public role confirmation here. Your previous Suspicious result was supported when its target was eliminated and revealed as the Illusionist; the other night-killed player's role remains concealed.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after an early town-role death and an abstain vote. A key info-role claim, or a result that could steer the next vote, sits unverified, and the investigator has one check left. Information landscape: Mostly information-starved. The only solid information is the investigator's own earlier read, and the other claims are unverified. Stakes: The town needs one trustworthy lead to find the killers. Checking the claimant whose uncorroborated result matters most can turn the best available lead into something the town can act on, without wasting the last check. Target landscape: Eight living players. One player has a claim or result with real consequences for the vote, but no one else can confirm it. The other candidates are silent or unclaimed. Basis is the claim's importance, not evidence against anyone.
lessons.action: If a pivotal claimant, such as a sentinel or trailseer, has an unverified result that the town may act on, use the check on that claimant. A Not suspicious read adds weight to a lead the town would otherwise have to take on faith, and a Suspicious read exposes a false claim. Skip claimants whose visit is already explained by a corroborating watch or follow.

lessons.situation: Night 2. The illusionist is exposed or dead, the first victim's role is known, and the day-2 vote ended in abstain or a thin consensus. Chanteuse, lone killer and possibly necromancer remain unidentified, and the investigator holds one or two checks. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are one or two own check results, perhaps a claim or two with partial corroboration, and no confirmed wolves besides the dead illusionist. Stakes: The wolf pair is partly broken but the chanteuse and a lone killer are still alive. With few checks left, each one that lands on an unexplained player can decide the next day's vote, while one spent on an already-cleared player is lost value. Target landscape: Eight or nine living players, mostly unclaimed or claimed-unverified. A wolf-read on the illusionist may already be confirmed. No hard evidence on any candidate, so the choice rests on behavior and gaps in the room, such as the quiet player, a lone accuser, or an inconsistent statement.
lessons.action: Spend the check on a living player that no claim, watch or follow has yet explained and who shows a behavioral oddity, such as a quiet or low-profile player, a lone accuser, or someone who slipped in describing their own action. If the unverified pool is large, pick the most anomalous player. A hard Suspicious or Not suspicious on an unexplained player is worth more than re-confirming someone already vouched for.

lessons.situation: Late game after key deaths, with the lone killer or a reanimated attack already surfaced and evil still alive. The investigator holds one final check and must decide whether to spend it on an active contributor or a quiet player. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are revealed through deaths, wills and claims, there is evidence of night attacks, and an earlier check result exists. The remaining unknowns are a few players, so the check can sort the pool. Stakes: The pool is small enough that one decisive check can expose the last evil role or confirm a strong ally. A wasted check could let parity close before town finds the wolf. Target landscape: A handful of living, mostly unconfirmed players: role claimants with partial support, one unrevealed player, and an active unclaimed player who steers discussion on night abilities or case analysis. The choice rests on behavior, since no hard evidence ties anyone to the evil roles.
lessons.action: With your last check and a shrinking pool of unverified players, check an active, vocal player whose steering of the discussion is still unexplained, in preference to a quiet player or one whose role is already supported. Either result narrows the pool: Suspicious points to a wolf, or to a Necromancer if it attacked that night, and Not suspicious adds a confirmed non-wolf ally.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended with a near-universal abstain vote and you stand out as the sole non-abstainer or a revealed investigator. You face a night where you may be hit by a wolf kill and must decide whether to spend a check or hold both. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths or role claims, only the day-2 vote tally showing abstentions and one or two outliers. No hard leads on alignment. Stakes: A night death erases that night's check result and the unspent check with it. Spending a check early gives the best chance of a usable Suspicious result before the wolves cut you down. Holding both checks risks dying with them unused. Target landscape: Nine living players: one vocal player you already voted against, and several quiet players blending into the abstain consensus. None has a confirmed role or any evidence against them. Selection is by behavioral standout or blending.
lessons.action: If you have two checks and are likely to be attacked soon (your role is known, or you stood out by voting alone), spend one now on the most behaviorally anomalous player instead of holding both. A check you never use is worth nothing if you die. Pick the target on a concrete behavioral signal such as an outlier vote or a conspicuous silence, not at random.

lessons.situation: After an opening night where several town roles visited or protected the same player and Day 2 ended in abstention, that focal player's alignment is the board's central unknown. Information landscape: Multiple role claims or visit patterns form an activity web around one target, but no alignments are confirmed, so the check can anchor the web. Stakes: Early in the game the town has time but no leads. A check on the hub converts the town's activity into a verified read that can shape later claims and votes. Target landscape: One focal player drawn to by several town-role visits or claimed protections, versus quiet players with no signals. The basis is the converging role activity, not alignment evidence.
lessons.action: When several town roles' claimed visits or protections converge on one player, spend a check on that focal player. If the result is Not suspicious, you have a hub the town can trust, though a lone killer would read the same; if Suspicious, you have exposed a wolf the town was shielding.

lessons.situation: Day 2 ended in near-unanimous abstention or no elimination, with one or two players breaking consensus. The investigator is choosing where to spend a check before a wolf kill or roleblock can stop them. Information landscape: Thin evidence: a night-1 death, perhaps one unverified claim, and a voting record showing only a few non-abstainers. Mostly behavioral reads, with few or no confirmed alignments. Stakes: Wolves are not yet near parity, but the investigator is a prime kill target and may not survive many nights. Each remaining check is scarce, so spending it on the most informative anomaly matters. Target landscape: A handful of living players with no confirmed roles. One or two stand out by breaking the abstain consensus, casting a lone vote, or voting against the investigator. The rest are quiet abstainers with no trail, so the choice rests on voting behavior rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: After a no-elimination Day 2, spend a check on the player whose public behavior stands out, such as the sole proactive voter, a lone dissenter against the room, or a member of a bloc that voted against you. If the result is Suspicious, you have a concrete wolf lead. If it is Not suspicious, you have cleared a likely power-role ally, though that read does not rule out a lone killer.

lessons.situation: A focal player has been tied to suspicious activity by other roles' reports or by a counter-claim against you, and the investigator still holds checks to confirm whether they are evil. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead trailseer reveal, a sentinel report, a roleblock claim, and a counter-claimant who made a claim about you that you know is false. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. A confirmed read on the evidence-flagged player settles the main suspect and protects your standing, so the check is worth spending now. Target landscape: One focal player singled out by a sentinel or trailseer report or by a false counter-claim on the investigator, versus quiet players with no evidence against them. The focal player is chosen on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When other night evidence (a trailseer or sentinel report, a counter-claim on you) has narrowed suspicion to one specific player, spend a check on that player to confirm Suspicious or Not suspicious. A Suspicious read on a player already pointed at by independent evidence gives you a verified evil target and corroborates the other power roles.

lessons.situation: After a day-2 vote where nearly everyone abstained, the investigator is publicly known or stands out. They must spend the final check before the wolves likely silence them. A standout player is available to check. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed evil reads, a concealed or absent role reveal, and a day record of near-universal abstains with one or two outliers. Informational claims exist but none are verified. Stakes: The board is still roughly even, but losing the investigator costs Town its only alignment-check source. One confirmed wolf read could remove half of the wolf pack. A wasted or unreported check leaves Town with only behavioral reads. Target landscape: About eight or nine living players, mostly abstainers with no hard evidence against them. One stands out behaviorally, either by an aggressive outlier vote or by being a silent player others urge scrutiny on. No confirmed evil reads exist yet, so the choice rests on behavior.
lessons.action: With your last check and your role already exposed, check the player whose behavior broke from the room, such as the lone aggressive voter in an all-abstain day or the silent player others are spotlighting. Do it tonight, because you may be killed and an unspent check dies with you. If you survive, the Suspicious or Not suspicious result is hard evidence for the next day.

lessons.situation: The investigator is publicly exposed or being targeted. One or two players cast opposing votes against the investigator or defended a eliminated wolf, so the investigator has a ready suspect and limited time. Information landscape: Moderately rich: a public voting record, possibly a confirmed dead role, and a visible bloc or lone dissenter. Behavior is readable but no alignment is confirmed. Stakes: The investigator is at risk of dying or being roleblocked, so the last check may be the only one that lands. A Suspicious hit could collapse the wolf pack within a day or two, while a miss leaves the town short of leads. Target landscape: The dissenting voters or the sole counter-voter against the investigator, who show the clearest hostile signal, versus passive abstainers or supporters of the investigator's push. The basis is voting records rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: If the investigator's claim is already public, or the investigator is being pushed, spend the check on the player who actively voted against them or defended a confirmed wolf. A Suspicious result then gives the town a wolf lead and exposes the dissenter's partners, whereas a Not suspicious result clears a wolf-adjacent suspect only of wolf status.
