lessons.situation: A rival investigator claim has appeared. The rival says they checked you and found you Not suspicious, but you know you were never checked by a real investigator. Information landscape: Information-rich: you personally know the rival's claim is false, and trailseer and sentinel reports exist that can corroborate the result. Stakes: Your role is contested and the town may side with the rival and lose its only investigator. Resolving the claim fast with a check is high leverage. Target landscape: The single counter-claimant who falsely says they checked you, versus quiet or unconfirmed players. The counter-claimant is the clear target because you hold direct knowledge of their lie.
lessons.action: If another player counter-claims investigator and says they cleared you, use a check on that counter-claimant at night, since you know their claim about you is false. A Suspicious result gives you hard proof that they are lying and evil, and it stays useful even if another night action removes them first.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive, and five eliminations until the leading remaining evil faction can win, at worst for the town because the concealed body's side is unknown. The game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town, so an immediate kill or vote can decide the game even though the stated parity distance is five.
query_dims.information_landscape: Moderate but uneven evidence: your private check found one living player Not suspicious, which excludes a wolf under the rules but not the Serial Killer; a public save confirms protection occurred but not who provided it; the Sentinel's revealed will confirms a visit to the player they watched, supporting but not proving the Trailseer claim. The concealed Night 1 death leaves its role unknown, and the current check would add one private Suspicious/Not suspicious result.
query_dims.situation: Information gain is constrained by the final check: the living field includes a player already privately read Not suspicious who could still be the Serial Killer, a Healer claimant whose account fits the public save, a Trailseer claimant partly corroborated by the revealed Sentinel's will, and players with no confirmed role. The eliminated Illusionist confirms the wolf team has lost one member, while the role and side of the Night 1 concealed death remain unknown.
query_dims.target_landscape: One check remains among living players: the player claiming Healer whose protection account fits the confirmed save but is not independently verified; the player whose Not suspicious result is your own Night 1 finding and who could still be the Serial Killer; a player claiming Trailseer whose Night 1 visit to the revealed Sentinel's target is corroborated by the Sentinel's public will; and three other living players without a publicly confirmed role. The check can distinguish wolves from non-wolves, but the Serial Killer also reads Not suspicious.

Target landscape: One focal player drawn to by several town-role visits or claimed protections, versus quiet players with no signals. The basis is the converging role activity, not alignment evidence.
lessons.action: When several town roles' claimed visits or protections converge on one player, spend a check on that focal player. If the result is Not suspicious, you have a hub the town can trust, though a lone killer would read the same; if Suspicious, you have exposed a wolf the town was shielding.

lessons.situation: A focal player has been tied to suspicious activity by other roles' reports or by a counter-claim against you, and the investigator still holds checks to confirm whether they are evil. Information landscape: Information-rich: a dead trailseer reveal, a sentinel report, a roleblock claim, and a counter-claimant who made a claim about you that you know is false. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive. A confirmed read on the evidence-flagged player settles the main suspect and protects your standing, so the check is worth spending now. Target landscape: One focal player singled out by a sentinel or trailseer report or by a false counter-claim on the investigator, versus quiet players with no evidence against them. The focal player is chosen on evidence rather than behavior alone.
lessons.action: When other night evidence (a trailseer or sentinel report, a counter-claim on you) has narrowed suspicion to one specific player, spend a check on that player to confirm Suspicious or Not suspicious. A Suspicious read on a player already pointed at by independent evidence gives you a verified evil target and corroborates the other power roles.

lessons.situation: The investigator is publicly exposed or being targeted. One or two players cast opposing votes against the investigator or defended a eliminated wolf, so the investigator has a ready suspect and limited time. Information landscape: Moderately rich: a public voting record, possibly a confirmed dead role, and a visible bloc or lone dissenter. Behavior is readable but no alignment is confirmed. Stakes: The investigator is at risk of dying or being roleblocked, so the last check may be the only one that lands. A Suspicious hit could collapse the wolf pack within a day or two, while a miss leaves the town short of leads. Target landscape: The dissenting voters or the sole counter-voter against the investigator, who show the clearest hostile signal, versus passive abstainers or supporters of the investigator's push. The basis is voting records rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: If the investigator's claim is already public, or the investigator is being pushed, spend the check on the player who actively voted against them or defended a confirmed wolf. A Suspicious result then gives the town a wolf lead and exposes the dissenter's partners, whereas a Not suspicious result clears a wolf-adjacent suspect only of wolf status.

lessons.situation: A rival investigator claim has appeared. The rival says they checked you and found you Not suspicious, but you know you were never checked by a real investigator. Information landscape: Information-rich: you personally know the rival's claim is false, and trailseer and sentinel reports exist that can corroborate the result. Stakes: Your role is contested and the town may side with the rival and lose its only investigator. Resolving the claim fast with a check is high leverage. Target landscape: The single counter-claimant who falsely says they checked you, versus quiet or unconfirmed players. The counter-claimant is the clear target because you hold direct knowledge of their lie.
lessons.action: If another player counter-claims investigator and says they cleared you, use a check on that counter-claimant at night, since you know their claim about you is false. A Suspicious result gives you hard proof that they are lying and evil, and it stays useful even if another night action removes them first.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five players are alive; at worst for the town, the leading evil faction is three eliminations from parity and the game can end within one more elimination. A single night outcome can therefore determine whether the game ends immediately, although the concealed body's side is unknown. The end-of-game consequence of any particular body or target choice is unclear from the record.
query_dims.forward_exposure: An attack through the revealed Illusionist body or Vigilante body would be publicly identified as a reanimated attack if it killed someone; an attack also reads Suspicious to any Investigator checking that night. Using the revealed Sentinel body instead produces private information without an attack trace. Staying put avoids those action-specific traces, and these choices can be changed on later nights.
query_dims.information_landscape: Public evidence includes revealed roles and wills, the confirmed elimination of the Illusionist, and the vote record; the Investigator and Trailseer claims remain private-result claims except for the corroborated Suspicious finding. The Necromancer privately knows the concealed role of one night victim, but that is not public evidence. The remaining living players’ roles and tonight’s actions are mostly unknown, so the board is information-starved.
query_dims.situation: After the day’s vote eliminated the revealed Vigilante, the Necromancer has three revealed bodies available for tonight’s ability, while only five players remain. The previous reanimated Illusionist attack established that the Necromancer is active publicly; choosing another attack risks an Investigator reading it as Suspicious, while an information-gathering action or staying put has a different visibility profile.
query_dims.target_landscape: The revealed dead bodies available are the Illusionist, Vigilante, and Sentinel. The Illusionist body can attack but has no conceals left; the Vigilante body can shoot without a miss penalty; the Sentinel body can watch. Living candidates include a player claiming Investigator whose earlier Suspicious result was corroborated by the revealed Illusionist, an unverified Trailseer claimant, an unverified Sigilist claimant, and a player with no role claim stated here. The two other concealed dead bodies have unknown roles and cannot be used.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 3-4) after the wolves' Illusionist died and its role was announced, with the Necromancer unsuspected. The Necromancer can attack through the body at no visible cost to itself, while the town believes the evil is finished or narrowed. Information landscape: Info-rich: dead roles are announced and the town's investigative roles and records are partly known. Nobody has a read on the Necromancer. Stakes: Few players remain, so each kill moves the Necromancer much closer to the at-most-one-other-alive win, and removing the Vigilante or Investigator takes away the town's main ways to stop it. A wasted night costs tempo while the town still has threats. Forward exposure: The morning names a 'reanimated wolf' attack, which publicly confirms a Necromancer is active; this cannot be undone. The kill hides the victim's role and the attacker's identity, and the sigil cannot punish an attack made through a body. If the Investigator is dead or dying that night, no Suspicious read can follow from it. Target landscape: Revealed bodies include the Illusionist, plus other dead roles. Living candidates are the Vigilante (could kill the Necromancer), the Investigator (could read it Suspicious), the Sentinel, the Trailseer and the Sigilist. The Vigilante's and Investigator's threat comes from their role mechanics, not from behavior; the Sentinel's influence on votes is behavioral evidence only.
lessons.action: When a dead wolf's Illusionist body has its role announced and conceals remain, attack through it and aim at the living player who can most threaten you: the Vigilante, who can shoot you, or the Investigator, who would read you Suspicious on an attack night. If that threat is already dying to the wolves or is dead, take the strongest remaining information role instead. The concealed role and the 'reanimated wolf' wording give the town a Necromancer's presence but no suspect.

lessons.situation: A wolf (Illusionist) was voted out and is now the necromancer's body. Town still has the Healer, and surviving information roles are cross-verifying each other, while one wolf may remain. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Illusionist's flip validated certain claims and visit chains exist. The Healer's coverage is unknown, which makes the attack target a guess. Stakes: Each kill moves the necromancer closer to the 'at most one other alive' condition, but a failed or visible kill reveals a Necromancer and draws a vote. A kill that removes a verifier and conceals its role gives the most value per exposure. Forward exposure: The morning report will name a reanimated wolf attack, so the town learns a Necromancer is active and an investigator check on you that night reads Suspicious. This cannot be undone. A hidden-role kill withholds the victim's role, and the Necromancer learns it. Target landscape: The dead Illusionist is the usable body. Candidates are the claimed Sentinel, claimed Trailseer, claimed Investigator, and quiet unconfirmed players. Public claims have been partly validated by the Illusionist's flip, but healer coverage is unknown.
lessons.action: When a dead Illusionist's body is available, attack a key town information role (claimed Sentinel, Trailseer or Investigator) or an unconfirmed player through it, so the victim's role is hidden if they die and the town cannot cross-check it. Prefer a target the Healer is unlikely to be covering (not the most-claimed or most-visible role that the Healer would protect), and check the Illusionist still has conceals left, since the hidden role depends on them.

lessons.situation: Mid-to-late game with three or four players alive; the town already knows a Necromancer exists from an earlier 'reanimated' report, and a further attack would not yet end the game. Information landscape: Info-rich on roles and votes but with no hard evidence about who the Necromancer is. The town deduces your identity from the attack reports and the vote splits. Stakes: An extra announced attack that does not win the game moved the room to a three-player vote where two others could remove you; the kill achieved nothing a vote could not undo. Forward exposure: Each announced reanimated kill confirms a Necromancer exists, and repeated attacks through the same body narrow the pool to the few unknowns. A second announcement makes you the obvious suspect and cannot be reversed, whereas a non-attacking use leaves no announcement. Target landscape: Three other living players, all unconfirmed claims or behavioral reads: a vocal accuser (Fortune Teller), a Sigilist, and a Vigilante or Investigator. None is a verified evil, and some (a Fortune Teller who has already scored two points) gain you nothing if killed.
lessons.action: When four players remain and the kill would not reach your win threshold, use a night action that does not announce a reanimated attack (such as a block or an information-gathering ability through a dead body) rather than a second announced attack, unless the target removes the vote threat. Keep the town from learning that a Necromancer is alive and from narrowing the suspects down to you.

lessons.situation: A town role or wolf has just died with an announced role, giving the necromancer a usable offensive body while town information roles are alive and coordinating the hunt. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced flips and wills, claimed sentinel and trailseer results, confirmed visits, and a public record of earlier night events. Stakes: The board is a few kills from the end of the game. Each town information role removed speeds the collapse toward two survivors, while a failed attack on a protected target gives town a verified pair that will vote me out. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is announced by the body's kind (reanimated vigilante, wolf, or sigil), so town learns a necromancer is active, though not who. I also read Suspicious to any Investigator check that night. The kill cannot be undone, but the dead player's name rather than mine is what a watcher or follower sees at the door. Target landscape: Claimed or confirmed sentinel, trailseer, investigator, and a claimed healer, plus a spent sigilist, an unconfirmed remaining wolf, and quiet unconfirmed players. Town roles are known from claims and flips; the wolf is known only by behavior.
lessons.action: When a freshly dead role with an announced attack body (vigilante, or a wolf's illusionist) is available and the board is crowded with confirmed town information roles, attack through that body at the night's highest-value information or coordination role, such as a sentinel or trailseer that has not been shown to be protected. If a healer is alive and has already been seen protecting that role, shift the target to a different information role, since a save shows the healer is working and ties town together.

lessons.situation: A wolf chanteuse has been eliminated and revealed, giving the necromancer a usable block body from night two onward. The necromancer is under suspicion after a tied or contested vote and must decide whom to roleblock. Information landscape: Information-rich: roles of dead players are confirmed, vote splits are public, and several claims (healer save, investigator results) are on record. The living players' roles remain unverified claims. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive, so a single block rarely flips the game, but the necromancer is being voted against and a wasted night or a visible trace costs tempo it cannot spare. Forward exposure: A block through the dead chanteuse's body shows the dead wolf's name at the door of any watching Sentinel, telling the town a Necromancer is active though not who. It is irreversible once seen, and a block on a player who cannot act yields no gain for that exposure. Target landscape: Living players include a claimed healer, claimed sigilist, claimed investigator with checks reportedly spent, and quiet villagers. Their claims are unverified, and only the chanteuse's role is system-confirmed. Choice rests on remaining ability uses and on who accused the necromancer, not on pure behavior.
lessons.action: When the only usable body is a dead chanteuse, aim the block at a player whose action can still matter that night (a Town role with uses left, or one publicly suspected of protecting a likely wolf target) rather than one whose resources are publicly exhausted. If a Sentinel could be watching your target, treat the dead wolf's name at the door as a visible trace and prefer a target where that trace points suspicion at others.

lessons.situation: Night 3 is your first usable-body night. Town and the wolves are fighting publicly, the Investigator or another info role is active, and no one suspects the necromancer. Information landscape: Moderately rich. A revealed body with its record exists and some public accusations and claims are out, but there is no direct evidence on the necromancer. Stakes: Mid-game with several players alive. You are far from the at-most-one-other-alive win, so staying unseen while Town and the wolves trade kills matters more than rushing a kill, and there is no swing this night. Forward exposure: A passive check or follow through a body is not an attack, so it leaves no morning trace and you read Not suspicious to the Investigator. It commits you to nothing and is fully reversible, whereas an attack through a body would announce a reanimated killer and read Suspicious. Target landscape: Usable bodies are few: a revealed Investigator or Trailseer, while wolf-kill victims with concealed roles cannot be used. Living targets are the publicly contested wolf suspect and the active Town info roles, with mostly unverified claims.
lessons.action: On night 3, when you have only one or two usable bodies and no attack is needed to win the night, use a passive info body (Investigator, Trailseer or Sentinel) on the most contested or highest-threat living player instead of attacking. If the result confirms a public claim, keep staying quiet; if it contradicts one, keep the result as private leverage for a later night.

lessons.situation: Necromancy has just unlocked, an investigator is alive and likely to check, the town has abstained or has few leads, and the necromancer is currently unsuspected. A free attack is available but would immediately mark the necromancer as the lone killer. Information landscape: Information-starved: little public evidence, with wolves and town both searching. The investigator's targeting is unknown. Stakes: Being outed this early is costly: the necromancer can be removed by a daytime vote or, from night 2, by a night attack. Many players remain, so patience costs little, while an early announced kill invited the vote that eliminated the necromancer. Forward exposure: Any attack through a body is announced by the body's kind and reads Suspicious to an investigator that night, so it cannot be hidden afterward. A non-attacking night reads Not suspicious and leaves no announcement. Target landscape: Available bodies include a dead Vigilante (free shot) or dead wolves, with all living players unconfirmed. Attacking a wolf with a Vigilante body removes a threat but reveals a Necromancer to the town and the investigator.
lessons.action: If you are not yet under suspicion and no check or vote is aimed at you, hold the attack and use a non-attacking body ability (follow, watch, check) on the night you fear an investigator may look at you. Attack through a body only when the victim is unlikely to be protected and the gain outweighs the Suspicious read and reanimation headline.

lessons.situation: Five players are alive and you have a usable attacking body, such as a dead Vigilante's. A confirmed Investigator with an unspent check is still alive. Any attack you make this night will read you as Suspicious to that check. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Investigator is confirmed by an earlier wolf flip, and the other claims and visit results are public. Dead roles are revealed, so the usable bodies are known. Stakes: With five alive, one wrong step lets the Investigator's check expose you and you are voted out the next day. Dealing with the Investigator, or not reading Suspicious, matters more than picking off a lesser target. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is announced in the morning by the body's kind (for example a reanimated vigilante), which tells the town a Necromancer struck. It also makes you read Suspicious on that night. A block through a Chanteuse body leaves no announcement and no Suspicious reading. Target landscape: The confirmed Investigator with an unspent check, the other claimed investigative roles such as a Trailseer, an unverified claimant, and an unclaimed player. The Investigator's status is confirmed by a prior flip, so it is the one evidence-backed threat to you. The others are claims or behavior reads.
lessons.action: If a confirmed Investigator with an unspent check is alive, either remove them or keep them from checking you. Use a dead Chanteuse's body to block the Investigator, or attack the Investigator directly, since a player killed at night learns nothing from it. If you can do neither, take a non-attacking action or stay put so you read Not suspicious, rather than attacking a secondary target.

lessons.situation: Night 4 with both wolves dead and you as the lone killer. About four or five players are alive and the town has just lynched a wolf. You must choose whether to attack through a reusable dead-wolf body and whom to hit. Information landscape: Moderately info-rich: both wolves are revealed, several role claims are public, and the Investigator's checks are known to be spent, so your Suspicious reading cannot be exploited. Stakes: Each kill moves you toward the win condition of at most one other player alive. Removing the player who can trace your visits keeps you hidden while the board shrinks. Forward exposure: The attack is announced as made by a reanimated wolf, so the town learns a Necromancer exists, and you read Suspicious to the Investigator that night. With the checks spent, no check can exploit that. The victim's role is hidden if they die, and the announcement itself cannot be undone. Target landscape: Public claimants: a Trailseer who followed the Chanteuse to you, an Investigator with an on-record Not-suspicious read of you, and a counterclaiming Sigilist. They are ranked by how likely each is to reveal your visits, based on their claims and on evidence rather than on behavior alone.
lessons.action: When you are the lone killer with the wolves dead or nearly dead, the Investigator's checks are spent or known, and a usable Illusionist body is available, attack through it against the public claimant most likely to expose your visits (such as a Trailseer who has followed you). If the Investigator still has checks left, switch to a passive use of a dead body instead.

lessons.situation: Night 4 with about six players alive, one wolf left, and you are an unrevealed lone killer. The town still has a voting majority and the wolves are already killing for you. Information landscape: Rich on town roles but incomplete on wolf identities, and nobody else knows your threat status. Stakes: The town could still outvote a revealed Necromancer. Staying hidden while the wolves thin the town sets up the late kills needed to win. Forward exposure: A passive check through a body is fully reversible and leaves no announcement or Suspicious reading. An attack would announce a reanimated killer and give a live Investigator a Suspicious result on that night. Holding back commits you to nothing and keeps the option to strike later. Target landscape: Remaining targets are the Fortune Teller and the Sigilist, plus the last wolf. The usable bodies are a dead Investigator and a wolf. The Fortune Teller has been accurate with reads and bets, so a Not-suspicious check clears it only partially, since many roles read Not suspicious.
lessons.action: If the town still holds a voting majority and a live Investigator could read you Suspicious, hold the attack and use a dead Investigator's body to check a surviving player, which leaves you Not suspicious. Resume killing once the pack is gone or the town is down to the last few players, so the final kills land when the town cannot respond.

lessons.situation: Night 2, your first night able to act. Town and wolves are both intact, you may already have drawn day-2 votes, and no usable body exists to act through. Information landscape: Info-starved: one or two revealed roles, partial and unverified claims, and no hard leads on the quiet players. Stakes: Early game with most players alive, so no single night decides the outcome. Staying alive and unexposed matters more than forcing a low-value action, and you cannot yet win by attrition. Forward exposure: Staying put commits you to nothing, leaves no trace, and is fully reversible because the bodies remain usable on later nights. Any attack through a body would be announced as a reanimated kill and show the town a necromancer exists. Target landscape: Only one or two dead bodies with revealed roles, none with a usable attack or block. Living players are mostly unverified claimants plus quiet unknowns, and you hold no read on who the wolves are.
lessons.action: On your first acting night, if the only revealed bodies give no attack, block, heal or other useful ability (e.g. a fortune teller), stay put. You make no visit and no attack, so you read Not suspicious and the same bodies stay available later. If a dead wolf, vigilante or information role appears on a later night, reassess then.

lessons.situation: Late game, about four players alive, with a Necromancer attack available through a dead Illusionist or another wolf body. One kill now decides who is in the final three and how the last vote splits. Information landscape: Mostly inferred roles with some hard history (a confirmed healer save, public pick or claims, repeated roleblocks). The town has seen only reanimated strikes and has not confirmed the Necromancer's identity. Stakes: Two eliminations from the Necromancer win condition (at most one other player alive). The next kill decides whether the final three-player vote is 2-1 for you or 2-1 against you. A wrong target choice gives the town a guaranteed vote on the final day. Forward exposure: An attack through a body is announced as a reanimated strike, so the town learns a Necromancer is alive, though not who. Hiding the victim's role denies the town a reveal and cannot be undone. It commits you to winning the final three-player vote. Target landscape: Three or four living others: an established town pair (claimed healer and sentinel, one protected or repeatedly blocked), a neutral speculator, and possibly a wolf ally. Roles are mostly inferred, apart from confirmed saves and public claims. Pick the target by who would form a voting bloc against you, not by who is the easiest kill.
lessons.action: With four alive and a body that lets you attack (a dead Illusionist), spend the kill on a member of the town pair or the last visit-reading role, so the final three leaves you with a wolf or neutral who may side with you. If a confirmed pair (for example healer and sentinel) would remain, kill one of them rather than the lone neutral. Use the concealing body while it still has conceals left.

lessons.situation: Late game, about six players alive, the wolves nearly gone. A claimed Vigilante with a bullet left is alive, and your day votes or abstains may have drawn attention. You hold several announced dead bodies, including a Chanteuse's, but you are choosing whether to act or stay put. Information landscape: Information-rich: the Vigilante's claim and remaining-bullet count are public, dead roles are revealed, and the vote record is permanent. Your own night actions stay hidden. Stakes: One Vigilante shot at you ends your game outright, and you cannot be protected from it. Staying put does nothing to stop the shot, so neutralising the shooter this night is the highest-value use of the night. Forward exposure: Blocking through the Chanteuse's body leaves no necromancer trace. A Sentinel or Trailseer would see the dead Chanteuse's name at the door, and the morning report announces nothing. It commits you to nothing publicly and can be repeated on later nights, so it is easy to reverse. Target landscape: The public Vigilante claimant with one bullet left is the main threat. Usable announced bodies are a Chanteuse (block), an Illusionist (attack), and Investigator, Sigilist or Sentinel bodies. The threat is evidence-based, since a public claim plus a spent-or-unspent bullet count is on record.
lessons.action: If a living player has publicly claimed a Vigilante with a bullet left and a dead Chanteuse's role was announced, act through that body and block the claimed Vigilante. A blocked player does nothing and makes no visit, so the shot cannot land, and blocking is not an attack, so you do not read Suspicious. If no Chanteuse body is usable, take the next-best step against the Vigilante, such as a body attack on the claimant, instead of idling.

lessons.situation: Late game, all wolves dead, you are the sole evil role facing a known armed Vigilante and a known Healer. A choice between attacking through the Illusionist's body and blocking through the Chanteuse's body. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves are dead and revealed, the Vigilante is verified by its kill, and the Healer's role is public. The protection target is easy to predict. Stakes: A failed attack leaves you facing a live Vigilante; here the Vigilante's counter-shot killed the necromancer the same night. Two more kills are needed to win, so a wasted or blocked strike costs the game. Forward exposure: An attack through a body announces 'reanimated' and identifies a Necromancer to the town, and it cannot be undone. A block through a dead Chanteuse leaves no such public announcement, so it keeps your identity hidden while removing the protector. Target landscape: Four alive: a confirmed Vigilante with a bullet left, a claimed Healer likely to guard the obvious kill target, and a third player. Dead Illusionist and Chanteuse bodies are both usable. The Healer's identity is publicly known, so the kill target is predictable.
lessons.action: With four players left and a mortal guarded or armed threat alive (a confirmed Vigilante with a bullet, or a Healer free to protect), use a dead Chanteuse's body to block that Healer or the gun instead of attacking into the expected protection. Attack only when the most likely protector is neutralized, since a failed attack announces a reanimated strike and exposes you to a counter-shot.

lessons.situation: A revealed will or confirmed visit trace implicates a specific player as a wolf, and a dead vigilante's body is available to the necromancer. Information landscape: Information-rich but indirect: a sentinel's will names a visitor to the night 1 casualty, and no wolf is confirmed by a flip. Stakes: Two wolves plus a lone killer remain, so removing one wolf lowers the chance of the wolves reaching parity before I reach the final two. A mistaken shot only costs a night and a town power role. Forward exposure: The morning will announce a reanimated vigilante shot, which tells town a necromancer exists but gives no identity. I will read Suspicious to any Investigator check that night. Killing a wolf cannot be reversed, and a miss on a non-wolf spends the night and angers town. Target landscape: The player named in a dead sentinel's will as visiting the first victim, versus town power roles and unrevealed players. The lead is a will-based visit trace rather than a confirmed role.
lessons.action: When a dead player's will or a visit trace points at a suspected wolf and the vigilante body is available, shoot that suspect through the reanimated vigilante, accepting the risk that a wrong read wastes the night. This removes a wolf and cuts the pressure of wolf parity, while the dead body's name, not mine, appears in any watch or follow result.

lessons.situation: Night with exactly three players alive (you and two others), all wolves dead or irrelevant, and a revealed dead wolf or Vigilante body available for an attack. One kill reaches the necromancer win condition. Information landscape: Information-rich: dead roles are revealed, the remaining roles are confirmed or their abilities exhausted, and only your own identity is hidden. Stealth no longer has value. Stakes: One successful kill wins the game outright; if it is skipped or fails, the next day's vote will likely eliminate you since two players can outvote one. This is the highest-leverage night of the game. Forward exposure: The attack is visible (a 'reanimated' kill announcement), but it triggers the win condition at once, so no day or vote remains in which the exposure could be used against you. It cannot be undone, but it does not need to be. Target landscape: Two remaining players, both non-evil and both mortal. Typically a neutral Fortune Teller and a Sigilist with spent sigils, or the Investigator. Either kill ends the game; the choice only matters if a counter-action or protection could stop the attack.
lessons.action: At final three (you plus two others) with a usable dead attacker body (a wolf's or the Vigilante's), attack either remaining player that night. The kill leaves at most one other player alive and ends the game before any vote can expose the reanimated-attack report. Pick the target who could otherwise protect or retaliate, and if neither can, pick the one most likely to sway the vote.

lessons.situation: First night of necromancy (night 2 onward), the day-2 vote ended without a useful elimination or on a town-side vote, and the only usable body is a dead investigative role. The necromancer has no kill-capable body yet and wants intel while staying hidden. Information landscape: Information-starved: few deaths, unverified role claims, and no public record of who the lone killer or neutral is. Only behavioral reads are available. Stakes: Early game with many players alive, so there is no need to force a kill. Spending the first night on safe information costs nothing and builds a picture of the healer, the protected targets and visit traffic for later strikes. Forward exposure: A non-attacking use of an investigative body produces no morning announcement. Any watcher or follower sees the dead player's name, not yours, and an investigator reads you Not suspicious because you did not attack. Fully reversible: nothing is committed, and you can switch to attacking later. Target landscape: One or two announced investigative bodies (dead Sentinel or Trailseer), and nine or so living players with no confirmed roles. Candidates are the claimed investigator, a suspected shooter or healer, and quiet players. Choice rests on behavioral reads and expected traffic rather than evidence.
lessons.action: On the first night a body is usable, if the only body is a non-attacking investigative role (Sentinel, Trailseer, Investigator), use it to watch, follow or check the most likely focal player (for example the likely healer target, or a claimed power role) rather than staying put. Those actions announce nothing, leave only the dead player's name at the door, and read Not suspicious to an investigator on a night with no attack, so you gain information at no exposure cost and can repeat it each night.

lessons.situation: Your first acting night, with several revealed bodies available, including both a sigilist and an information role. Wolves are still active and you must choose which body and target to use. Information landscape: Info-starved for you: few revealed bodies, no attacks yet made through a body, and no read on who carries the wolves' kill. Stakes: Mid-early game with eight alive. A wasted ability night costs tempo toward the two-left-alive condition, while a useful read could direct later attacks without exposing you. Forward exposure: An information-body action is private and unannounced, so it exposes nothing and keeps your options open. A sigil is spent when placed and is wasted if the target does not attack that night. A sigil on a non-attacker such as a watcher gives no information and no kill. Target landscape: Usable bodies are a revealed sigilist (places a sigil) and a revealed investigator (gives a read on a living player). Living candidates include a publicly active sentinel and other claimants, with no confirmed wolf or killer.
lessons.action: When a dead Investigator, Sentinel or Trailseer body with a revealed role is available on a night you act, use it on a plausible living player to gather a read rather than spending a sigil on a player who probably won't attack. Information roles are quiet: they produce no announcement and leave you Not suspicious on nights you don't attack. If you do use a sigilist body, place the sigil on a player likely to attack that night, since a sigil only strikes a target who attacks.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive, and four eliminations separate the leading evil faction from parity; this decision is not a one-elimination swing and the game cannot end within one more elimination, though an unsupported shot would still irreversibly cost a scarce bullet.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible shot would spend one of two remaining bullets irreversibly; if it kills, the morning report identifies a vigilante attack, potentially exposing the shooter. Holding fire spends nothing and preserves both bullets.
query_dims.information_landscape: The Investigator and Trailseer were publicly revealed among the night deaths, but their wills provide no further findings in the available record. The Sentinel claim and its visitor result are unverified; the result is behaviorally compatible with the Trailseer's role. There is no confirmed evidence identifying a living target as a wolf or Serial Killer.
query_dims.situation: After the day ended without an elimination, the village remains information-starved: an unverified Sentinel claim says the revealed Trailseer visited another player, while that visitor is not implicated by the result. A player who drew three elimination votes had no night result to share, but this produced no confirmed contradiction or threat identification.
query_dims.target_landscape: No candidate has evidence-based identification as a threat. The player who received three votes to eliminate them has only a lack of shared night-action information and voting pressure against them; the player visited by the revealed Trailseer was visited in a way consistent with that role's follow action. The remaining living players have no specific public evidence against them.

lessons.situation: A wolf, often the illusionist, was just eliminated on a verified investigator or trailseer read. Evil remains, including a lone killer and possibly the other wolf. The vigilante must decide whether to shoot into an undifferentiated or only behaviorally suspect pool. Information landscape: Information-rich on the eliminated wolf, since the role was confirmed and voting records are visible. Information-starved on the remaining evil roles, because the only leads are vote splits or defense of the dead wolf. Stakes: Town is ahead but several evil players remain, and each night kill erodes the margin. A wasted bullet on a wrong target costs town a villager-side body. Parity is not imminent, so waiting for a solid lead is affordable. Forward exposure: Holding fire shows no visit and does not reveal the vigilante or the bullet count. A shot would spend a bullet that cannot be recovered and would reveal an active vigilante. Holding costs nothing and can be reversed on any later night. Target landscape: Several living players with no public role status. Some voted against the town lead, or the whole room voted together and left no standout suspect. The only basis is voting behavior, not hard evidence, and no candidate is confirmed.
lessons.action: After a wolf is confirmed by a day elimination, with two bullets and no target backed by evidence, hold fire and keep both bullets. Shoot only when a night result, a checked Suspicious read, or a caught lie points at a specific player. If a known investigator or other check-holder is already positioned to test the main suspect, let that check resolve first rather than shooting the same target.

lessons.situation: Late game after the lone killer was voted out and revealed. One hidden wolf remains and the public record has narrowed it to one of two claimants. Town is one wolf kill from losing its margin. Information landscape: Information-rich: a revealed elimination role, an Investigator read, Sentinel and Trailseer visitor lists, and a failed counterclaim all converge on one candidate. Stakes: With seven alive and one wolf left, a correct shot ends the evil faction and wins the game. A wrong shot or a hold gives the wolf another night kill and moves the board toward parity. Forward exposure: The shot is a visit and an attack, and it publicly reveals only a death. It cannot be undone and commits the bullet to one target, while holding stays reversible but leaves a wolf free to kill again. Target landscape: Two or three survivors remain as candidates for the last evil. One has a public clean Investigator read and another is uncleared and was contradicted in a claim duel. Several independent public facts support one of them, not just behavior.
lessons.action: When public evidence (a revealed killer, a clean Investigator read, visitor lists, a failed counterclaim) has narrowed the last evil to one or two candidates, spend a bullet that night on the candidate the most independent facts point to. If two facts disagree, shoot only the candidate with the most corroboration, because a shot is irreversible and a miss still spends a bullet.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a tied day vote with no elimination. Two or more unverified role claims conflict, and the debate is about whether a clean check or a disputed tracking result exposes a wolf or the lone killer. Kills are already on the board. Information landscape: Mostly claims and rhetoric: an investigator clearance and a tracking result, with no verified evidence. Nothing is confirmed, and both claims are consistent with the night report. Stakes: Several players are still alive, so Town can absorb a night but not a wrong shot. A wrongly killed Town role speeds the wolves and the lone killer toward parity, while a held bullet stays available once real evidence appears. Forward exposure: A shot is an attack and a visit that spends a bullet permanently. A wrong target kills a claimed Town player and reveals the vigilante's role through the announced shot, with no way to undo it. Holding reveals nothing and keeps the bullets. Target landscape: The most debated players are a claimed sentinel or trailseer and the player accused against them, plus unclaimed others. Cases rest on competing unverified claims and rule-logic arguments about which roles read clean, with no announced evidence tying anyone to a kill.
lessons.action: On a night after a tied or no-elimination vote, when the only case against a debated player is unverified claims or mechanics arguments, hold fire and keep your bullets. Shoot only when a night report or other announced fact ties a specific player to a kill or a wolf role. If nothing announced backs the target, a shot is a permanent, irreversible bet on rhetoric that kills a Town role if wrong.

lessons.situation: Both wolves are confirmed dead, but a lone killer (the necromancer here) is hidden among the survivors and has not yet been identified. Information landscape: Poor for shooting. Only behavioral clues exist, and the lone killer reads Not suspicious on most nights, so no result or announcement singles out a target yet. Stakes: The lone killer wins when at most one other player is alive, so it is several kills away. There is time to wait for a morning announcement or a night trace to narrow the field before spending a bullet. Forward exposure: Holding makes no visit and reveals nothing, so the move is fully reversible and the bullets stay available. Shooting a guess would out the vigilante and risk a Town death. Target landscape: Six survivors including a claimed trailseer, sigilist, fortune teller, a hidden necromancer, and the vigilante's own seat. No evidence ties any of them to the lone killer.
lessons.action: After both wolves are dead and only a hidden lone killer remains, hold fire while no living player is tied to a lone-killer signal. Keep the bullets for when a reanimated-body kill or other concrete evidence points at a specific suspect.

lessons.situation: The vigilante is in a thin-information endgame with a lone killer still unidentified and a wolf already voted out. A crowd-driven suspect is available, but the vigilante has no result of its own that ties that suspect to a threat. Information landscape: Information-starved: no checks or results of your own, only day accusation behavior and one revealed wolf role. No survivor is confirmed by evidence. Stakes: The board is not yet at a one-kill finish, so a wasted last bullet gives up the vigilante's only offensive tool while the real killer keeps going. A well-chosen later shot is worth more than a shot on a low-threat crowd target. Forward exposure: Firing exposes you as the shooter, forces a role claim, and spends the last bullet for good. A shot at a player the killer already targeted adds no net removal of a threat. Target landscape: Several unconfirmed survivors, including neutrals and a hidden lone killer. The most accused player is accused on behavior and village trust, with no checked result behind it.
lessons.action: When you have a bullet but no personal evidence and the day's accusation only singles out a likely neutral or a player already marked for death, hold the shot unless the board is at parity-critical distance. Fire only at a target backed by evidence or elimination logic that identifies a real threat, such as the lone killer or a surviving wolf.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after one wolf (chanteuse or illusionist) was voted out. The Serial Killer and the other wolf still kill each night, and the vigilante has full bullets and no personal result. Holding fire has so far meant losing a Town player each night, and the vigilante died with every bullet unspent. Information landscape: Mostly unverified claims. Only the voted-out wolf's reveal is confirmed by the system, and the vigilante has no night result of its own. The remaining killers are undetected, so evidence is thin. Stakes: Two killers act every night, so Town loses about two players per night. The board is a few nights from a loss, and unspent bullets are a wasted resource. A single wrong shot costs one Town player, but hoarding costs more over several nights. Forward exposure: A shot is an attack and a visit, and it spends a bullet even on a miss. A Town kill cannot be undone. Holding keeps your identity hidden, but each idle night lets two killers act, and you can die with every bullet unused. Target landscape: Around seven survivors: sigilist, fortune teller, a sentinel or trailseer with unverified claims, a hidden wolf, a hidden lone killer, and you. Nobody is confirmed as an enemy. Any pick rests on unverified claims and behavior, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: With 2-3 bullets, about seven players alive and both a wolf and a lone killer still hidden, spend one bullet each night on the most suspicious living player once you have a concrete lead (a vote record, a visit claim that fits, or a caught inconsistency). Without a lead, still fire at the best behavioral read rather than holding the whole stock: a bullet unused at death is worth nothing, and an 'immune' result from a shot also tells you who the Serial Killer is. Keep the last bullet in reserve for a confirmed target.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a day-2 vote that either exiled a confirmed wolf or tied and exiled no one. The vigilante holds its bullets with no new hard evidence against any specific survivor, while wolves and possibly a lone killer remain active. Information landscape: Starved to moderate. There is perhaps one confirmed role from a vote flip, a sentinel report or a corroborated save, but nothing points at a specific remaining wolf beyond behavioral hunches. Stakes: Several eliminations remain before wolves reach parity, so one night's patience costs little. A mis-shot at a Town player would hurt more than the single night's delay, since the wolves and a lone killer can kill that night anyway. Forward exposure: A shot is an attack and a visit that spends a bullet whether or not it kills. If the target is Town, the miss is irreversible and costs Town a member. Holding fire exposes nothing and keeps every option open. Target landscape: Seven to eight survivors. At most one wolf is confirmed dead, with a wolf and an illusionist still hidden, or none confirmed. The candidates are a quiet or scrutinized player, a vigorous defender of a flipped wolf, and a vote-tied player. All are behavioral reads with no hard evidence, and no confirmed evil remains to shoot.
lessons.action: On the night after Day 2, if no survivor has hard evidence against them (a confirmed role, a caught lie, or a result you hold), keep your bullets and hold fire. Shoot only once one specific survivor passes a stated suspicion threshold, such as a corroborated suspicious result or a clear contradiction; a bare vote lean or a vigorous defense is below it, and a shot spends a bullet and kills a Town player if wrong.

lessons.situation: Day vote deadlocked in a tie or scattered split with no elimination. Multiple killing factions are still alive, and one tied suspect is tied to concrete night evidence. Information landscape: Mixed to rich: tracking results, a dead investigator's checks, or a disputed night-attack narrative point at one candidate, while the rest of the discussion is stalled. Stakes: With two killing factions alive and the day vote stalled, the vigilante's bullet may be the only way to remove a killer this cycle. Each night of delay costs another town death and brings evil closer to parity. Forward exposure: Spends one of two bullets irreversibly and makes you a visitor at the target's door. A kill reveals a vigilante exists. An immune result is private and gives you information to act on. Target landscape: Two or three tied day-vote candidates, none confirmed. One has hard-ish evidence (tracking link to a dead power role, a disputed survived-attack story) and the others are only quiet or behavioral suspects.
lessons.action: When the day vote ended in a tie or no elimination and one candidate has concrete, trackable evidence against them (e.g. the trailseer saw the dead investigator visit them, or they were accused of surviving a night attack), shoot that candidate with a bullet that night. If the target dies, a killer is gone; if the shot is reported as immune, you have learned the target is night-immune and can push the town to vote them out.

lessons.situation: Late midgame after one or two evil roles have died. A wolf or a lone killer is still unidentified among about six survivors, and the vigilante still holds both bullets. Information landscape: Mixed. Roles of the dead are revealed and some Town claims are credible, but there is no direct evidence against any living player, so any shot target rests on behavioral reads. Stakes: The board is thin, so every Town death moves evil closer to parity. A wrong shot on top of the night kill can remove two Town players in one night and leave no margin for error. Forward exposure: A shot spends a bullet irreversibly, and the morning report names the vigilante's attack as a kill. A wrong shot removes a Town player on a thin board, while holding costs nothing and keeps both bullets. Target landscape: Five or six survivors, mostly claimed Town utility roles (sigilist, trailseer, sentinel, confirmed investigator), plus a quiet unclaimed player and sometimes a hidden killer. No hard evidence against any of them, only behavioral impressions.
lessons.action: With 2 bullets and a thin board, hold fire unless a specific living player is tied to evil by hard evidence such as a confirmed Suspicious result, a caught lie, or a recorded vote pattern. Do not shoot a cooperative claimed Town role on behavior alone; a wrong shot costs a Town player and leaves the kill that night free to take a second one.

lessons.situation: You publicly claimed Vigilante with both bullets unspent and drew votes against you. The vote tied with no elimination, and the wolves can see you hold two unused shots. Information landscape: Starved: no private result of your own, scattered votes, and a tie that did not separate wolf from killer. Stakes: With six alive and evil one or two kills from parity, losing the Vigilante unspent costs Town its only attack and a free shot at evil. Firing at least trades the bullet for a chance to remove a wolf or the killer. Forward exposure: Holding fire after an open claim leaves you a known, valuable target. A shot is irreversible and spends a bullet even if it misses, but it converts your threat into board impact before the wolves can remove you. Target landscape: Several unclaimed survivors, among them a lone killer and wolves, with no confirmed roles. The vote split Town and no suspect was separated. A shot would rest on behavior and vote reads alone.
lessons.action: If you have publicly claimed Vigilante and still hold unspent bullets, fire at the best-supported suspect tonight instead of holding again. If votes and reads give no solid lead, shoot the most suspicious non-cleared player at a threshold you accept as a policy, because an unspent claimed bullet makes you the wolves' priority kill and dies with you.

lessons.situation: Early night (night 1 or 2) after a discussion-only day or an abstain-heavy vote. The vigilante holds most of its bullets and faces two or more hidden killers, with no solid lead on any player. Information landscape: Information-starved: no confirmed roles, no caught lies, no voting pattern pointing at a wolf, and only unverified claims and scattered single votes. Stakes: Early in the game, with wolves and a lone killer both alive, Town can afford to wait a night but cannot afford to lose a power role to a wrong shot. A mistaken shot costs more than a one-night delay, and a bullet held until a lead appears keeps its value. Forward exposure: A blind shot would spend a non-renewable bullet and could kill a Town player, and the morning report would show a vigilante shot. Holding fire leaves no visit or attack trace and keeps every option open, and the shot can still be taken on a later night. Target landscape: Eight or nine other living players, all with unconfirmed roles. There are no confirmed wolves and no caught lies, only scattered abstain-day votes and unverified claims, so any target would be a behavioral guess.
lessons.action: With no confirmed wolf, no caught lie and no public evidence naming a specific player, hold fire and keep your bullets, since a blind shot risks killing a Town player and spends a bullet that cannot be recovered. Fire only once a concrete lead singles out one player, such as a confirmed-role record, a caught lie, or a pattern in the public record; if the lead names the Serial Killer, remember a night shot will not kill it.

lessons.situation: Mid-game with no elimination after tied votes. A hidden-role death or a block on you shows that a Chanteuse and the wolves are still alive, and you hold two or three bullets with no hard lead. Information landscape: Starved: a hidden-role death, tied votes, unverified claims, and a roleblock notice as the only firm fact. Stakes: The wolves are still several kills from parity, so there is time. But every night of holding or being blocked lets a Chanteuse live and risks the vigilante dying with unused bullets, so use the bullets at a reasonable confidence threshold. Forward exposure: The shot reveals the vigilante to the wolf pack. Being roleblocked wastes the night without spending a bullet or yielding information, so the plan can be repeated but a block cannot be foreseen. A wrong shot cannot be reversed. Target landscape: Three to five suspects: claimed Investigator, Sigilist or Trailseer (all unverified), plus two unclaimed players tied in the last vote. A known-alive Chanteuse is a priority candidate. The basis is vote patterns and claim accounting, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: When roleblocks, ties and unverified claims leave you with no hard lead, choose your target before the night from the hardest evidence you have: a confirmed Chanteuse (a block you were told of proves one is alive), or the player whose votes aligned with a dead wolf. Shoot that target as soon as the evidence points to one player. Do not keep passing night after night with the bullets unspent, because a vigilante killed with bullets left costs the town every shot.

query_dims.consensus_text: The room has some alignment around scrutinizing you, but it is not a fully grounded consensus: a speaker pointed out that the same public vote and claimed visit apply to the other reported visitor, and no independent evidence distinguishes you.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive, and the leading evil faction needs three eliminations to reach parity; this decision is not immediately decisive, though the current pressure could still affect who faces later votes. The game cannot end within one more elimination.
query_dims.forward_exposure: A visible defense that insists the two visitors are equally suspect commits you to that framing but does not reveal your private attack knowledge. Your last word has already made that argument; it is reversible in later discussion, though the public record of your statement remains.
query_dims.heat_now: High: the opening accusation and subsequent support from two other speakers have focused suspicion on you, based on your Day 2 vote and the claimed visit report. The same visit and vote evidence also implicates the other reported visitor.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved about the killer’s identity: the deaths and revealed roles are system-confirmed, but the Sentinel’s visit report is an unverified claim and a visit does not establish an attack. The public vote record is factual but ambiguous; there is no public mechanical evidence separating the two reported visitors.
query_dims.my_position: You are under pressure rather than driving the discussion; your public stance is that the shared evidence does not justify singling you out, while acknowledging your vote was a judgment call.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, you know you killed the Trailseer on Night 1 and the Sigilist on Night 2. Publicly, the deaths identify those roles, but not their killer; the current discussion centers on the two claimed visitors to the Sigilist’s death, with no public proof of who attacked.
query_dims.situation: After the Sentinel claimant reported that you and another player visited the Sigilist on the night the Serial Killer killed them, the discussion has focused on your earlier vote for that Sigilist and whether the shared visit evidence supports singling you out. The other reported visitor shares both facts, leaving the accusation contested rather than resolved.
query_dims.target_landscape: The immediate scrutiny is between you and the other reported visitor, both of whom voted to eliminate the revealed Sigilist and were placed at that player by the unverified Sentinel claim. The shared evidence does not distinguish the two; the voter accusing you is also behaviorally pressing the case, without role-based evidence.

lessons.situation: Day 3 vote where the town has deduced that you are the serial killer, or are night-immune, from visitor lists and claim contradictions. You are the unanimous target and must choose a vote: abstain, join the vote on yourself, or name someone else. Information landscape: Information-rich. A visitor list, a follow result, a check result, a counter-claim, and your own mechanics slip all point at you, and your rebuttals have been refuted. Stakes: Your elimination ends the lone killer's win chance, and your single vote cannot prevent it. The only remaining lever is removing a threat or leaving a record that muddies the remaining town's reads. A solo vote is not decisive in either direction. Consensus: The village is almost unanimously aligned on eliminating you. The basis is a coherent chain of evidence, such as the sentinel visitor list, the lack of a save announcement, or a failed role claim. My position: Holding out alone against a lopsided majority on you. Heat: Maximum. Seven or eight players are publicly accusing you on mechanical evidence that your counter-arguments did not refute. Forward exposure: The vote is public and permanent, and cannot be reversed once cast. A vote on a claimed role links you to the line that the claim is fake. With the majority settled it cannot change the result, so the main cost is the record it leaves. Target landscape: You are the near-certain elimination target. The alternatives are the claimants who built the case against you, such as an investigator, sentinel, healer, or counter-claimed role, and a suspected wolf. Their status rests on unverified claims and a few private reads, with no confirmed roles. Public vs private: Privately you know your night-immunity or failed claim has been correctly deduced. Publicly the town has converged on you through visitor lists, a missing save announcement, a counter-claim, or a mechanics error, and your counter-theories have been refuted.
lessons.action: When a near-unanimous majority has already locked onto you and your single vote cannot change the tally, still cast it, and spend it on the living player whose survival most threatens a lone-killer win, such as the information role vouching against you or a wolf. If the room is not yet locked and a swing is possible, first try to split the room before using the vote this way.

lessons.situation: First vote of the game after a night-1 death. There are only unverified claims (Trailseer follow, roleblock, Investigator check) and no confirmed roles. The village wants a target but has no hard leads, and you are an unaccused, quiet Serial Killer. Information landscape: Starved: unverifiable claims, one or two corroborations at most, and behavioral reads only. The only confirmed roles are the dead. Stakes: Early in the game with many players alive, no single vote decides the outcome. The priority is to stay unsuspected while the wolves and town thin each other, and to reach the late game with the night kills intact. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned around one claim-fight target or split between a target and abstain, with no hard evidence behind either. My position: With the plurality or the abstain bloc, not driving the push. Heat: Low to very low: no accusations, results or contradictions against you, though a stray vote or two may land on you. Forward exposure: A vote with the plurality or an abstain with the room is public and permanent, but it reveals nothing about your role and is cheap to walk back later. A lone outlier vote would be hard to explain and would invite attention. Target landscape: Candidates are a contested claimant (claimed Trailseer or accused wolf-side player), an unclaimed quiet player, or abstain. Every basis is behavioral or an unverified claim, with no confirmed roles besides the dead. Public vs private: You privately know you are the Serial Killer and that you caused the night-1 death. Publicly it is only an unexplained death with unverified claims and no confirmed roles, and nobody has singled you out.
lessons.action: On the first vote day, when you are an unaccused Serial Killer and the room is info-starved, cast your vote for the same target as the largest bloc, preferring a target the wolves or claim-fight evidence already point at. If the room is heading toward an abstain tie, abstain with it rather than splitting off alone; a visible outlier vote gains nothing and invites scrutiny. This keeps you looking like an ordinary town voter while the town and wolves fight each other.

lessons.situation: Endgame day vote with four players alive, wolves dead or nearly dead, and the serial killer among the survivors. A vote can end with a tie or a counter-wagon on you if it fractures. A decisive elimination reduces the living count to three. Information landscape: Information-rich. Roles are confirmed in the graveyard, full voting histories are on record, and night-visit claims or check results are in play. Stakes: Four alive means one more elimination by vote sets up a night kill that leaves exactly two alive, which is a serial killer win. A fractured vote with no elimination or a wagon on you costs a full cycle and risks your removal. Consensus: The village is split across the three candidates and has no firm majority. Two voters are leaning toward one target on the basis of checks, visit reports, or lack of confirmation. My position: with majority Heat: Moderate to high. Someone voted against you or flagged you as not cleared, and a visit-based or voting-record clue loosely points your way. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and cannot be undone. It aligns you with one other voter and does not reveal your role. It also commits you to the elimination that moves the board toward the final night kill. Target landscape: Three other survivors: an unconfirmed claimant such as a healer, an aggressive accuser such as the speculator, and a claimed investigator or sentinel. Some are backed by evidence, such as a Suspicious check or being named as a victim's visitor, and some only by behavior. Public vs private: You privately know you are the serial killer and that removing any other player by vote sets up the two-alive win. Publicly you are only one of several unconfirmed suspects, and the investigator's note that a serial killer can read Not suspicious is the only thing pointing at you.
lessons.action: With four players left, vote with the plurality forming against a non-you player, joining the most credible accuser or the evidence-backed suspect, so the elimination lands and you are not the focus. Taking the count to three lets your night kill leave two alive, which wins you the game. If the room is split three ways, your vote is the one that makes the plurality decisive, so cast it on the same target as one other voter rather than scattering.

lessons.situation: Day vote with a small group alive, where you (the Serial Killer) are on one of two or more competing elimination wagons and your single ballot can create a tie. Information landscape: Information-rich: claimed investigator, sentinel, sigilist or healer results, prior vote records and a dead wolf's votes all feed the suspicion, though none are verified. Stakes: Few players remain, so one lynch of you ends the lone killer's game while a tie keeps you alive for another night kill. This vote is decisive. Consensus: The village is split among several wagons with no unified focus, so one vote can decide whether the leading wagon is tied. My position: holding out Heat: High. Several players, including claimed information roles or the surviving wolf, have already voted for or accused you over passivity or suspected night immunity. Forward exposure: A tie-forcing vote on a rival wagon or a lone-voted bystander leaves a visible but low-cost record, since votes are public and permanent. A lone vote on an accuser looks like retaliation and cannot be undone once the vote closes. Target landscape: Two to four competing wagons: yourself, a suspected wolf, and a quiet or lightly voted player. Role claims are partly unverified and the votes are driven by behavior and claimed results rather than hard evidence. Public vs private: The room publicly reads you as a suspect through low activity, a night-immunity deduction or a stray vote. Privately you know you are the serial killer and that your own ballot can decide whether you survive.
lessons.action: When you are an SK on a live elimination wagon, count the votes and cast your ballot so it makes the top counts tie, either by joining a rival wagon or by adding a vote to a lone-voted third player. A tie means no elimination, so the SK survives to kill again; a lone retaliatory vote on an accuser leaves your wagon alone in front.

lessons.situation: The first day-2 vote after night-1 deaths. The village is either leadless and abstaining or piling onto a contested claim. You are the unsuspected Serial Killer who needs to survive to keep killing nightly. Information landscape: Information-starved to moderate: a few revealed night-1 dead roles, some unverified claims, and no caught lies or voting history that point to you. Stakes: The board is early, with many players alive and far from the Serial Killer's win threshold. The vote itself is not decisive, so the priority is to stay off the suspect list and alive for the next night kill. Consensus: The village is aligned, either on a unanimous abstain in a leadless day or on a near-unanimous pile-on against a contested claimant. The basis is the room's own discussion, not anything you supplied. My position: With the majority, riding a consensus built without you. Heat: Low to near zero: no one has accused or mentioned you, and you have spoken little or only in support of others. Forward exposure: A vote matching the room commits you to nothing about your role and is indistinguishable from the other votes. Votes are public and permanent, but an abstain can be changed the next day, and joining a shared target is tied to the room, not to you. Target landscape: Around nine or ten living players, with no or only unverified claims. Candidates are a contested claimant or no one, and the basis is behavioral or mechanical speculation rather than hard evidence. You are not among the candidates. Public vs private: You privately know you are the serial killer and caused a night-1 death. Publicly the deaths read as a wolf-side or generic night event, and no one suspects a separate lone killer.
lessons.action: On the first day-2 vote, when you are unsuspected and the room has no lead or has already converged on a target, cast the same vote as the majority (abstain if the room is abstaining, or join the existing pile-on). Don't drive a new accusation or take a lone stance, because a vote identical to the room's carries no tell about your role and keeps your cover for night kills.

lessons.situation: A day vote where the room has converged on eliminating a wolf-side player, accused by claimed town roles. The accused counter-accuses or deflects heat onto quiet players, possibly including you. Information landscape: Mostly claims and behavioral reads, with only partial corroboration (such as a sentinel or trailseer claim) and no hard verification until the reveal. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several players alive. Your vote does not decide the outcome, but sitting in the bloc keeps your profile clean while the wolves thin out ahead of your own kills. Consensus: Most of the village is aligned on one wolf-side target, with a five- to six-vote majority built on corroborating claims and behavioral reads. My position: With the majority. Heat: Low to mild. At most one stray mention, for example being called a quiet player, and nobody else picked it up. Forward exposure: A vote with the bloc reveals nothing and keeps your public record identical to the other voters'. The vote is irreversible, but eliminating a wolf you are not allied with is not something you need to undo. Target landscape: The main candidate is a wolf-side player accused by several players on a mix of claims (a sentinel or trailseer claim, or busing logic) and behavior, and denying it. The alternatives are a claimed town role the wolf accused back, or abstaining. No result is confirmed before the elimination. Public vs private: You privately know you are the lone killer and that the targeted player is a rival wolf-side player. Publicly you are just another quiet, unclaimed voter, so the vote costs you nothing.
lessons.action: When a wolf is the target of a majority-backed vote and you are only mildly mentioned or not accused, vote with the majority to eliminate that wolf. Your vote then matches the bloc's and gives the room nothing to pick at, and a wolf removed by a day vote costs you no night kill. Skip abstaining or voting off-bloc, since that is the only way to stand out.

lessons.situation: Late-game final vote with three to four players alive and the table pointing at you. Survival depends on whether your vote can combine with another player's vote to deadlock the tally. Information landscape: Rich: most roles are revealed or dead, records have been read out, and claims cross-confirm. The vote history and elimination logic point at you. Stakes: At four alive, losing this vote ends your game. A tie keeps you alive for another night, while a lone dissenting vote gives the town the elimination it wants. Consensus: The room is aligned against you by elimination of other roles, cross-confirmed claims, or a coordinated pair. The other living players are mostly voting as one bloc. My position: Holding out alone or with at most one ally against a majority bloc. Heat: High to critical. You are the last unverified or unrevealed player, or two players are openly coordinating against you, and the vote record is the evidence they are using. Forward exposure: Your vote is public and permanent and cannot be reversed. Voting an accuser commits you to open conflict with that player. Voting alone on a neutral or confirmed-looking player adds no pressure and confirms the room's read of you, whereas joining an ally's target can force a tie. Target landscape: The candidates are the lead accuser, the other accusers, and any ally who is also being pushed. Confirmed or cross-confirmed town roles are poor targets. A vote only helps if it matches an ally's vote and leaves the tally level. Public vs private: Privately you know you are the surviving lone killer, immune to night attacks and removable only by a day vote. Publicly, the table has narrowed suspicion onto you by elimination or through coordinated accusations.
lessons.action: When the table is converging on you in a small endgame vote, count the votes before casting yours. If another living player is also under attack or will vote against your accusers, put your vote on the lead accuser they are voting for, so the tally ties and nobody is eliminated. Do not vote for a target nobody else will join, because a lone vote cannot change the result.

lessons.situation: Late-midgame day vote with about five players alive. The room is converging on an unverified suspect and you, the lone killer, are unsuspected. A deviating vote would stand out. Information landscape: Information-rich: multiple revealed roles, a public side pick, and a permanent voting record that later days will be read against. Stakes: With about five alive and a night kill still ahead, your survival matters more than steering this one vote. A stranded outlier vote is the cheapest way to turn a low-heat position into the next day's target. Consensus: The village is forming a majority on one unverified candidate, based on past votes and behavior. The board is information-rich, with several deaths and roles revealed and a public side pick announced. My position: Free to choose between joining the forming majority and holding out alone against it. Heat: Low to negligible. Discussion is focused on other players and no one is accusing you. Forward exposure: Every vote goes on the permanent public ledger and cannot be retracted. A lone vote against a claimed information role marks you as anti-Town if that player is later shown to be Town. Joining the majority commits you to nothing unusual. Target landscape: Two or three unverified candidates, such as an unconfirmed neutral with past-vote suspicion and a claimed information role with disputed results. The room leans toward one of them on behavioral reads, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the lone killer, immune to night attacks and removable only by a vote. Publicly you read as an ordinary unconfirmed player with almost no suspicion, and the room is debating other people.
lessons.action: When little or no suspicion is on you and the room is forming a majority against a plausible, unverified player, cast your vote with that majority. Do not cast an isolated vote against a claimed Town role or any other conspicuous target, because votes are public and permanent and a stranded outlier becomes the evidence later used to vote you out.

lessons.situation: After a night death in an information-rich mid-game, the village has locked onto a majority target. As the serial killer with low heat, I am tempted to cast a contrarian vote on a different player, a claimed information role or a quiet suspect, that cannot swing the result. Information landscape: Information-rich. Role reveals from night deaths, public check or follow claims, and the previous day's voting records are all available to be read against my vote. Stakes: Several players remain, so the vote can be fully survived if I stay unremarkable. The majority outcome is unaffected by my ballot, so a dissent gains almost nothing while adding a visible mark that can cost me the final-day vote. Consensus: Strong and decisive. A clear majority is already committed to one target after a night death or a claim chain, and the vote outcome is effectively fixed. My position: Holding out against a forming majority, which is the position this move corrects. Heat: Low. No one is accusing me, and a claimed check or the discussion has deflected suspicion elsewhere. Forward exposure: A vote against a decided majority is public and permanent, and it cannot be retracted. It invites scrutiny the next day, and opponents can cite it as proof I am the killer. A majority-aligned vote commits me to nothing unusual and can be changed later. Target landscape: A consensus suspect (a suspected wolf or a doubted information-role claimant) who is likely to fall regardless, versus a fringe alternative such as a quiet player or an information-role claimant.
