A killer keeps targeting a known town player, and the sigilist is tempted to put the sigil on that expected victim to counter the next attack. Information landscape: Role information is public, such as confirmed investigator results and verified healer saves. There is still no trace pointing at the remaining killer. Stakes: The remaining killer can keep striking, but the town is not on the brink. Preserving limited sigils for an identified attacker matters more than acting every night. Forward exposure: Holding commits you to nothing and reveals nothing. You keep both charges and can place one on any later night. Target landscape: The remaining candidates are likely victims, such as a claimed investigator who survived an attack or was healer-protected, or unvetted players with no attack evidence. None has been tied to a kill.
lessons.action: If no living suspect has evidence of attacking and the only candidates are likely victims or confirmed-Town players such as a protected investigator, keep your sigils that night. Wait for a suspect with an attack pattern. A sigil on a player who does not attack does nothing, and a likely victim is the one player who will not attack.

lessons.situation: Opening night of a 10-player game; the Sigilist must decide between a speculative sigil placement and keeping both charges, with no discussion or vote having occurred yet. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no public statements, deaths, role claims, votes, or night results exist. Stakes: Early game with full board; no single night decides the game, but only two sigils exist for the whole game. Wasting one on a blind guess has a high cost and almost no expected payoff. Forward exposure: Holding makes no visit and leaves no trace, and it commits nothing; both sigils stay available. Placing one would be an irreversible, secret visit with a spent charge that could be seen by a Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Nine other living players, none claimed, no voting record and no behavior to read. Nothing separates the wolves, the lone killer or a Vigilante from ordinary Town, so any target would be a pure guess.
lessons.action: On opening night with no claims, votes, or night results, keep both sigils instead of placing one on a random guess. A sigil only matters if its target attacks that night, so a blind placement on one of nine players is a low-odds spend of half your lifetime charges; hold them until a death, a result, or voting behavior points to a likely attacker.

lessons.situation: Late game with most roles mapped by deaths, reveals and claims; one evil attacker (wolf or lone killer) is still hidden among very few unverified players, and the sigilist holds its last sigil. Information landscape: Information-rich: revealed dead roles, investigator clears, healer confirmation and visit tracking leave one plausible attacker. Stakes: Few players remain and the next night kill could tip parity or end the game, so one well-aimed sigil can either strike the last attacker and win or confirm immunity evidence that wins the next day vote. Forward exposure: Spends the last sigil irreversibly and leaves no further night tool, so later progress depends on daytime deduction; the placement is a visit but is hidden from the town. Target landscape: One unverified candidate (claimed vigilante or unvetted player) remains against confirmed healer, investigator, trailseer or cleared players; the pick is based on elimination of confirmed roles, not on behavior alone.
lessons.action: When one sigil remains and deduction through confirmed roles and clears leaves a single unverified killer candidate, place the sigil on that candidate. If they attack that night the sigil strikes them (resolved after their attack), so a strike ends the threat. If it has no effect, that is consistent with them not attacking or with night immunity, so weigh it against later visit evidence rather than as a clear.

lessons.situation: Night with a night-immune lone killer possibly still alive. The sigilist has one sigil left and a vote-pressured suspect it believes is the Serial Killer. Information landscape: Moderately thin. There is a public record of votes and confirmed roles for several dead players, but no verified read on the killers. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity, so spending the last sigil on a target that cannot be struck is a costly miss. The sigilist then has no night action left. Forward exposure: A sigil placed on a suspected Serial Killer reveals nothing publicly and is spent. A no-effect result matches both a target who did not attack and an attacker protected by night immunity. Reporting that result by day exposes the sigilist. Target landscape: Two or three suspects narrowed by structural clues, such as who was or was not attacked. One suspect may be a night-immune Serial Killer, and the evidence is behavioral and structural.
lessons.action: Before spending a sigil, list the attackers still possible, such as the wolf carrier, an active lone killer or a possible shooter. Aim the sigil at the suspect who is most likely to attack that night and is not night-immune. If the narrowed suspect may be the Serial Killer, a no-effect result is ambiguous and a strike cannot happen, so choose a different target or hold the sigil.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) after a day with no clear lead. You have publicly claimed Sigilist and hold one sigil. A loud Town power role has survived a double attack because of a healer save, so the wolves and the killer are expected to pivot to other power roles, you among them. Information landscape: Info-starved. There is a death or two and a save, but nothing identifies who the wolves or the killer are, so there is no attacker signal. Stakes: The board is still contested, but a power-role death moves wolves and killer closer to parity. If you die with the sigil unplaced, Town loses both its power role and any chance of a sigil strike. Forward exposure: Placing the sigil is a visit and cannot be undone, and it spends the sigil whether or not the target attacks. Your role and your remaining sigil count are already known, so the move adds little new exposure, and holding the sigil does not stop the pack from targeting you. Target landscape: Candidates are the healer-protected Trailseer who keeps getting attacked, the healer, and quiet or unclaimed players. No evidence points to a specific attacker, so any pick rests on behavior and voting reads. The pack was expected to pivot away from the protected target toward other power roles, including you.
lessons.action: When your role is already public, you are a likely kill target, and you are info-starved, place your remaining sigil on the most plausible attacker instead of holding it. Pick the player whose votes or behavior fit an attacker best, and avoid the healer-protected player the pack keeps hitting, since a victim who is attacked is not the one the sigil punishes. An unplaced sigil is worth nothing if you die that night, while a placed one strikes any wolf carrier or killer who attacks the target.

lessons.situation: An attacked and saved player had two known visitors, and the choice is which one might be the attacker. Visiting a victim is ambiguous because a protector looks the same as an attacker. Information landscape: Information-rich on who visited, but ambiguous on intent. A dead role revealed the door traffic, and the claims conflict. Stakes: A sigil placed on the genuine healer exhausts the sigilist and builds misdirected suspicion against a key protector. Wolves stay free to attack. Forward exposure: Holding keeps the sigil fully in reserve and leaves no visit trace. Placing it on a protector spends the last charge irreversibly, and the miss looks the same as a non-attacker. Target landscape: Two visitors at a saved victim's door, one a plausible healer and one possibly a malicious visitor posing as a protector, with quiet players unvetted. Evidence is the door traffic and competing claims, with no confirmed attacker.
lessons.action: When the unresolved suspects are players whose visit may be protective, such as a possible healer at a saved victim's door, keep the remaining sigil instead of placing it on them. Hold it until a suspect with attack-consistent behavior emerges, because a sigil on a protector is wasted and cannot stop the wolves.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven alive with three eliminations until the wolves can win, so a single kill does not end the game but each town loss narrows the margin; a concealed body costs one of the two remaining conceals and removes a future role reveal from the town, which matters while three more eliminations are needed for a wolf win.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Spending a conceal on tonight's pack victim hides the body's role and blocks the town from learning it, and commits the illusionist to one of only two remaining hides; the carrier's visit to the victim also disappears from watchers, which may protect the pack's trace but cannot be undone once used.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved for the town: the only hard night result is a dead sentinel's untestable watch on a dead trailseer, and two dead town roles' records are already public. The illusionist holds private knowledge of the pack's target and the carrier identity; no living town player has a verified night result.
query_dims.situation: As the illusionist with two conceals left and a wolf partner who is carrying tonight's kill, the pack has chosen a victim among the seven living players, and the illusionist must decide whether that victim's revealed role and record would be worth hiding from the town. Earlier, the sentinel was lynched on a visit claim about the partner, which cannot be tested, and the town is now voting among remaining suspects while the partner has voted for another player.
query_dims.target_landscape: Tonight's pack target is a player whose role is not yet known to the illusionist's side; the illusionist privately knows only the pack's kill and that the carrier is the other wolf. Public role status of the victim is unknown until morning. The wolves' remaining living members are the illusionist and one partner, with no public claims among the town tied to a verified result.

lessons.situation: Late game after the lone killer is gone, with one or two wolves left against a Town that still has an information role able to catch a wolf. The illusionist is choosing whether to commit a limited conceal on tonight's pack kill. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, claims and watch records are public, and voting records exist. The remaining private results are the main danger to the wolves. Stakes: The board is close to wolf parity, so one surviving investigative result can decide whether a wolf is exposed and voted out. Concealing the right victim's role and will removes that risk, but a charge spent on a harmless victim is wasted. Forward exposure: Concealing signals to the village that an illusionist is active and spends a charge that cannot be recovered. Hiding the body leaves no trace at the victim's door when the illusionist carries the kill. It does not erase the victim's earlier public claims or votes. Target landscape: Living Town investigators and watchers (investigator, sentinel, trailseer) and unconfirmed players. Picks rest on who threatens the wolves' cover through private results, rather than on neutral or low-threat players.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a Town role whose private result or will would expose a wolf, such as an Investigator, Sentinel or Trailseer holding a result on you. Otherwise save the charge, since a hidden body does not erase what the victim already said or voted in public. If you carry the kill yourself, the concealed kill leaves no trace at the victim's door, so prefer that route when a watcher or follower is alive.

lessons.situation: Early night 2. Town power roles have claimed and reported night-1 results that threaten the wolves' cover. The pack agrees to kill one claimant, with the Illusionist deciding whether to spend one of its two conceals on that kill. Information landscape: Information-rich. Public claims and night-1 results are on the table, and day-2 vote records already show wolves voting together. A same-night partner death (sigil strike or Serial Killer) can expose the pack no matter what the Illusionist hides. Stakes: Mid-game with several town power roles alive. Removing a threatening claimant matters, but the conceal charges are scarce. Spending one where the role is already known gains little, and a wolf partner's death or vote record can confirm the pack anyway. Forward exposure: A conceal is irreversible and spends one of two charges. The morning report will say 'Their role is hidden by an illusionist', which confirms an Illusionist is in play. It hides the carrier's visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer, but it cannot hide a wolf partner's death or the voting records. Target landscape: Day-2 kill choices among self-claimed power roles (a claimed Trailseer or Sentinel reporting night-1 visits, a claimed Investigator) versus unrevealed players. The claimed roles are accusations based on claims, not verified results. Their roles are already public, so concealing the body adds little uncertainty.
lessons.action: Spend a conceal only when the victim's role is still unclaimed, or when a living Sentinel or Trailseer could otherwise trace the carrier to the victim's door. If the victim has already publicly claimed their role and no tracker threatens the carrier, kill without concealing and keep both charges for a later night. When the Illusionist itself carries the kill, a conceal leaves no trace at that door, so favor it for that night.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, after claims, deaths or votes have created information-bearing town roles. The pack picks a kill, and the illusionist decides whether to conceal the body of a role that matters. Information landscape: Moderately informed: some claims, bodies and records exist but are unverified. Concealing can deny the town role counts and confirmations. Stakes: With fewer players alive, each kill moves the pack closer to parity, and each revealed body feeds town deduction, or a Necromancer's use of the body. Denying role confirmation on a key kill matters more now than on night 1, and unspent conceals are worthless if the illusionist is voted out first. Forward exposure: Irreversible: it spends a use and announces that an illusionist is in play. If you carry the kill and conceal it, you leave no trace at that door. If another wolf carries, your hiding visit can still be seen by a Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Kill candidates are identified by claims or behavior, such as claimed information roles whose role or will would aid the town, rather than by a blind random pick. The pack's reads are partial and unconfirmed.
lessons.action: When the pack targets a town role whose revealed body or record would help the town, such as a claimed Trailseer, Sentinel, Investigator or Healer, carry the kill yourself and conceal it. A carrier who conceals leaves no trace at the victim's door, and the town gets neither a role nor a will. If you are not carrying, accept that your own visit stays visible to watchers and followers, and weigh that before spending the conceal.

lessons.situation: Mid-game, night 2 or 3. The pack has a failed or contested night behind it and agrees to remove a claimed protector or information role. The carrier makes the kill, perhaps while the Chanteuse blocks another claimant, and the Illusionist decides whether to conceal the body. Information landscape: Moderate information: save announcements, conflicting role claims, and Sentinel or Trailseer reports that are claims only. Nothing about the victim's role is confirmed by the Game Master. Stakes: The board is mid-game, with the pack still a few eliminations from parity and a lone killer possibly alive. Removing the protector or the information source without giving the town a confirmed role widens the pack's lead. A failed kill leaves the wolves exposed to the Healer and the Vigilante. Forward exposure: The conceal is spent only if the victim dies; a save keeps it and leaves nothing hidden. Once spent it cannot be recovered. A hidden body gives the town no role or will, but it also tells them the Illusionist exists and that the pack made the kill. Target landscape: Candidates are publicly claimed power roles: a claimed Healer inferred from a save announcement, a claimed Sentinel whose watch tied a partner to a scene, and a rival Investigator claimant leading an accusation. All are unverified, and the pack picks them on behavior and public logic rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When the pack's agreed kill is a claimed power role (Healer, Investigator or Sentinel) whose confirmed role or will would help the town, spend a conceal on it. The conceal costs nothing if the victim is saved, since the use is kept, so commit even without knowing the Healer's target. When the victim dies, the town cannot verify the claim and the pack loses nothing it needed to hide.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a thin day with an abstain or tied vote. The wolves, with the chanteuse, have agreed a kill and the illusionist decides whether to hide the victim's role. A partner may have been told the conceals are for a high-impact target. Information landscape: Information-starved: few or no hard leads, a few unverified role claims, no trace results shared, and the wolves unsure where the serial killer or necromancer is acting. Stakes: Early game with several enemies still alive, so no single kill ends it. The two conceals are the pack's scarce tempo tool, and wasting one on a low-value body costs more than a day of town uncertainty gains. Forward exposure: A hidden-role morning report tells the town an illusionist is in the pack, and the use is spent permanently. The hidden role cannot be reversed, and the count of used conceals lets the town track you. Target landscape: The choice is between quiet unclaimed players, whose roles are unknown and chosen for low profile, and a self-claimed info role such as an investigator with a check left. The kill choice rests on role value and behavior, not hard evidence. A conceal on a quiet victim wasted a use on a sentinel nobody had claimed.
lessons.action: On a night-2-style kill, spend a conceal only when the pack's victim is a claimed or high-impact info role whose confirmed death or role would help the town, such as an investigator-claimant with a check left. If the victim is a quiet, unclaimed player, keep both uses and let the role be revealed. A spent use is permanent, and the count of hidden-role deaths becomes the town's tool for tracking you.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night with the pack choosing a kill while the partner Chanteuse blocks a second threat. The Illusionist decides whether the victim is worth a conceal to deny the town role information and trace. Information landscape: Info-moderate: several dead players have public wills, a few living claimants are unverified, and the town's picture of the remaining roles is incomplete. Stakes: The pack is close to parity, and a hidden role plus a missing trace can keep the town from confirming who is left. Late in the game each conceal is scarce and carries real weight. Forward exposure: Using a conceal makes the morning say an illusionist hid the role, so the town learns an illusionist exists, though not who. Each use is permanent and cannot be undone. Once both are spent, every later kill shows its role and the carrier's visit can be traced. Target landscape: Candidates are an unclaimed voter whose role is unknown, a claimed Trailseer whose follow results threaten the pack, and a claimed Vigilante who can be blocked instead of killed. All roles are unverified, and the choice rests on behavior and threat level, not hard evidence.
lessons.action: While conceals remain, put one on a night kill whose victim is an unverified or high-information-value player, or a tracking threat such as a claimed Trailseer. Hiding the role also removes the carrier's visit to that victim from a Sentinel's watch or a Trailseer's follow, and leaves the town unsure which role is gone. Keep the last conceal for the kill where that traceless result matters most.

lessons.situation: Night 2 or later: the pack picks a claimed power role as the kill and the illusionist plans a conceal. A Healer claim or a previous protective visit to that target makes a save plausible, and the illusionist's own visit may be watched. Information landscape: Info-starved to thin: unverified claims, partial night-1 traces and one or two deaths. Hard facts are sparse, and the Healer's protection target is unknown. Stakes: With the pack down to one or two wolves, every visible visit risks heat and every failed kill wastes a night. A saved victim also leaves the illusionist as a known visitor, which can steer the vote toward the pack. Forward exposure: Your visit at the victim's door is irreversible. If the victim is saved, the conceal is kept but nothing is hidden, and the Sentinel or Trailseer sees you as a visitor. Target landscape: Claimed power roles (Investigator, Trailseer, Vigilante) are the obvious kill picks, but a Healer may have protected the same target before. Choosing is mostly a guess among living players, based on threat to the wolves rather than evidence.
lessons.action: When you are the carrier, or the pack's only wolf, and the kill target is a likely protected role (such as a claimed Investigator or Trailseer with a Healer visit onto them), prefer a target the Healer is less likely to guard, or accept that your visit may be seen. A conceal hides the carrier's visit only if the victim dies; if the Healer saves the victim, every visit to them stays visible to a Sentinel watch or a Trailseer follow, so do not rely on it as cover.

lessons.situation: Night 2-3. The pack has agreed to kill a vocal claimed investigative role, and the serial killer may be attacking the same player. The illusionist must decide whether a conceal is worth spending on this body. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich. Public claims, a tied or abstained day vote, and recorded votes exist, but most roles are unconfirmed. Stakes: Mid-game with parity still a few eliminations away. A wasted conceal costs the pack one of only two uses and gains little, while a well-placed one hides a role the town would otherwise learn. Forward exposure: Spending a conceal is irreversible and uses up a limited ability. On an already-public claim it buys almost no information denial, and the morning report still says an illusionist acted. Target landscape: The pack's candidate is a player who has publicly claimed Trailseer or Sigilist, unverified but already stated. Other candidates are unclaimed players whose roles would be new information if revealed. The pack picked the target on threat and claim rather than confirmed role.
lessons.action: Keep the conceal for a kill whose role the town does not yet know, such as an unclaimed or unverified player, where hiding the role and will denies real information. If the planned victim has already publicly claimed a role and shared results, let the role reveal stand and keep the use for a later night.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a close or tied day vote. The wolves are killing a player who drew vote suspicion. Sentinel and Trailseer have been active or have claimed results. Information landscape: Day talk produced a healer claim, a watch result and a follow result, but nothing hard on the wolves. Watchers are plausibly active and you cannot tell which door they chose. Stakes: Mid-early board where being exposed as the illusionist costs the pack a key wolf. The marginal value of hiding an ordinary victim's role is small next to the risk of a logged visit turning suspicion onto you. Forward exposure: If you are not the carrier, your hide-visit is still seen by a watcher on the victim's door, which can lead to a day accusation against you. The conceal cannot be undone and costs a charge, and the pack's kill visit stays hidden either way. Target landscape: The victim is a quiet or lightly suspected player pulled into a day vote, with no confirmed role. A watcher may be on the same door, and the reason to hide is that the reveal could clear them or point at the voters.
lessons.action: With a Sentinel or Trailseer plausibly active and the day having produced watch or follow claims, conceal only when you are the carrier, or when the secrecy of the victim's role clearly outweighs the risk of your hide-visit being logged. Otherwise keep the charge and let the pack's kill resolve unconcealed, because a visit seen at the victim's door can get you accused and eliminated.

lessons.situation: The pack is about to kill a claimed investigative player. The illusionist is deciding who carries the kill and whether to spend a conceal, with a hidden Sentinel watch or Sigilist sigil possible. Information landscape: Thin on hidden roles. You do not know whether a Sentinel is watching the door or a sigil is on you, though public Trailseer and Sigilist claims exist. Stakes: Losing the illusionist to a sigil or an exposed trace would cripple the pack's late game and speed a vote against it. Careful carrier choice protects the remaining conceals. Forward exposure: A non-carrier's conceal visit is visible to a Sentinel watching the victim. Carrying the kill yourself leaves no trace at that door but makes you an attacker that night, which a sigil on you would punish. Neither can be undone once the night resolves. Target landscape: The pack's victim is an unconfirmed claimant such as the Trailseer, or a self-claimed Sigilist. The serial killer may hit the same victim, and a Sentinel or Sigilist whose position is unknown may be targeting you or the victim's door.
lessons.action: If you conceal, carry the kill yourself, because then you leave no trace at that door and the carrier's visit is hidden from a Sentinel watching the victim or a Trailseer following the carrier. If a Sigilist with sigils left is alive or likely, or it is not your turn to carry, let the pack's kill go unconcealed instead of visiting the body as a non-carrier. A non-carrier's visit to hide the body stays visible to a watcher on that door, and a carrier's attack can be punished by a sigil.

lessons.situation: Opening night, discussion-only day 1. The wolves must choose a first kill and decide whether the illusionist carries it, and whether to spend a conceal on a victim of unknown value. Information landscape: Information-starved. There are no deaths, claims, votes or night results, so the target is a blind pick and any Sentinel or Trailseer who happens to be on the victim or carrier is invisible to the pack. Stakes: Early game with the wolves far from parity, so no single kill decides the game. The cost that matters is a visit trail from the carrier that a watcher or tracker could use on day 2 or 3, which can get a wolf eliminated and cost the pack a member early. That outweighs keeping both charges in reserve. Forward exposure: Concealing makes the morning report say the role is hidden by an illusionist, which confirms an illusionist exists. It spends one of two charges if the victim dies, and the use cannot be undone. In return it removes the carrier's visit trace from any Sentinel or Trailseer. Target landscape: Nine or so living players, none having claimed a role and none read. The pack chooses a quiet, unclaimed target on behavior alone, so the victim's role and any watcher on them are unknown.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the pack picks an unread target and you are the one carrying the kill, spend one conceal on that victim. If the victim dies, your visit leaves no trace for a Sentinel watching them or a Trailseer following you, and if you carried the kill yourself you leave no trace at that door at all. If the victim survives, nothing is hidden and the charge is kept.

lessons.situation: Late game, you are the last wolf and lone carrier after your partner died, with one conceal left and trackers or watchers alive. You decide whether to carry and hide the kill. Information landscape: Moderately information-rich: some town confirmations exist (an Investigator's read on the lone killer), but the town has no read on you. Stakes: You are the only wolf left, so each kill must also keep you hidden. A trace-free kill gives you a night of cover, but the town is still ahead on numbers. Forward exposure: The morning report announces a hidden-role death, which shows town an illusionist exists and the conceal is spent. Afterward every kill is fully revealed, and the victim's true role (for example a Speculator's pick) may become public and either support or contradict your story. Target landscape: Several unclaimed town and neutral players with no hard reads on you. The victim is chosen from an unclaimed pool by behavior, not evidence, and a tracker who followed you only once is still alive.
lessons.action: As the last wolf with a conceal left, carry the kill yourself and conceal the victim, because an illusionist who carries and conceals leaves no trace at that door for a Sentinel or Trailseer. Pick a victim whose role you do not need confirmed, and use the 'no visit' result a follower will report to build a cover story. Spend the conceal on a night when the carrier is you and a tracker or watcher is alive.

lessons.situation: Late game with a tied vote just behind and no conceals left. The pack must stop a claimed Vigilante's remaining shot, and the Illusionist has to judge whether a kill plus a block holds. Information landscape: Info-moderate: the Vigilante claimant said they were blocked and had one bullet left, and the town's other claims are unverified. Stakes: Losing a wolf here leaves a lone wolf against several town players and a vote that can end the game. One failed block or shot can flip which side is ahead. Forward exposure: With no conceals, the victim's role is shown and the carrier's visit can be traced by watchers or followers. Backing a kill on a claimed Vigilante commits the pack to that target for the night, and a failed block cannot be taken back. Target landscape: A claimed Vigilante who may have one bullet left, versus a claimed Investigator whose checks are spent. The pack picks the Vigilante on shot threat alone, with no verified evidence.
lessons.action: Before the last conceal is gone, have the pack kill one player and block the other main threat in the same night. Do not rely on a single block to stop a Vigilante who can still shoot, since a block that fails leaves the shot live and can cost the pack a wolf. If both conceals are spent, favor a kill and block pairing that does not leave your partner exposed to a shot.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game, no day-1 vote, no claims. The illusionist and chanteuse agree on a default kill, and the illusionist weighs spending one of two conceals on a victim of unknown role. Information landscape: Information-starved: no deaths, claims, votes or night results. The only knowledge is the pack's private plan. Stakes: The board is early and far from parity, so a single kill is not decisive. The scarce resource is the two conceals, which are worth more on a later high-value body than on a blind first kill. A spent conceal on a neutral or low-value body is wasted, and an unspent one also stays usable by a Necromancer through a revealed body. Forward exposure: Holding costs nothing and is reversible. Spending a conceal is irreversible, announces that an illusionist exists, and leaves your own visit visible to a Sentinel or Trailseer unless you carried the kill yourself. Not carrying also leaves no trace on you. Target landscape: The pack's night-1 victim is an arbitrary quiet player with no claims or behavioral evidence. Nobody knows their role, including the wolves, so the value of hiding it is only speculative.
lessons.action: On night 1, when the kill is an arbitrary pick with no claims or reads, keep both conceals and let the chanteuse carry the kill so you make no visit at the victim's door. Spend a conceal later, on a victim whose revealed role or will would give town real information, such as a claimed investigator, trailseer, sentinel or healer.

lessons.situation: You are the last wolf with unspent conceals facing a daytime vote that may eliminate you, with confirmed town killers still alive. Information landscape: Partly information-rich: town roles are confirmed and your partner is dead, but a lone killer is only hinted at. Whether the healer will cover the target is unknown. Stakes: Dying with unused conceals wastes your remaining power. A successful hidden kill shrinks the town and obscures the evidence needed to eliminate you, while an idle night gains nothing. Forward exposure: A concealed kill still announces the attack and marks a wolf as alive, but the hidden role and hidden carrier trace give town no role or visit evidence. If the victim survives, the conceal is refunded and nothing is hidden, so the exposure is limited. Target landscape: Choose among players not just saved by the healer; the confirmed vigilante and sentinel are the threats worth removing, while quiet unverified players are the cheaper pick. Role status is mostly public.
lessons.action: As the lone wolf with conceals in hand and town closing in, use a kill on a target the healer is unlikely to cover and conceal that victim's role. This hides your carrier visit from a Sentinel or Trailseer and denies town the role information, rather than skipping the night and giving up all pressure.

lessons.situation: The pack is deciding whether to spend the kill and a conceal on the claimed investigator or sentinel, who is the town's information lead, while the healer's likely protection is predictable. Information landscape: Information-rich: public claims on night-one visits and clearings reveal the town's information lead and its probable guard, and the pack's private knowledge exposes a night-immune player. Stakes: A wasted kill on a protected power role gives the town a free night and keeps its information lead alive. The conceal is refunded, but tempo is lost and the pack is exposed to counterattack, such as from a serial killer. Forward exposure: Authorizing a conceal on a protected target gets no kill, so the charge is refunded. It still commits the pack's kill to a target the town can predict, and a failed attack leaves the claimed power role alive and more trusted. The illusionist's visit to hide the body also shows up to watchers if the attack succeeds. Target landscape: Claimed sentinel or investigator as the obvious priority. Alternatives are unverified quiet players or a known night-immune player (who cannot be killed at night). Evidence is mostly public claims rather than hard reads.
lessons.action: When the most prominent claimed power role (investigator or sentinel) has already been attacked and saved, or a healer claim makes protection of it predictable, steer the pack kill to a different target and hold both conceals. If the town has no healer claim yet, the power role can be killed and concealed, but only if the pack accepts that the healer may be guarding it.

lessons.situation: Your partner carries the kill, or you do, on a role that has already claimed publicly. You have one conceal left and must decide whether to spend it or save it. Information landscape: Information-rich on claims, with several roles claiming results, but nothing verified. Stakes: With no extra conceals after this one, each use should hide something that cannot be inferred from claims. A revealed will carries a limited cost, but spending the last conceal on an already claimed role removes your flexibility for later kills. Forward exposure: Letting the body be revealed publishes the victim's role and any Town will, which may confirm their visit records. This is a one-night choice, and the conceal charge stays available for a later night. Target landscape: A claimed Town power role, such as a Sentinel with a public claim, is the pack's target. Other claimed power roles are active, and the claims are not confirmed.
lessons.action: If you have only one conceal left and the victim's role is already public from a claim, or the victim's will would reveal little, hold the conceal and let the role be announced. Keep it for a later kill of an unclaimed or higher-value role, and use the night's blocks and coordination on other threats.

lessons.situation: Night 1, the pack's first kill, with a conceal on offer and a blind target pick between the illusionist and its wolf partner. Information landscape: No public information at all, only the pack's private chat; nothing is known about anyone's role or night immunity. Stakes: The game is at its start with no pressure on the pack, so the main stake is keeping both conceals for when a role reveal would help the town. Nothing about night 1 forces an early conceal. Forward exposure: A conceal on a victim who survives is kept and shows the town nothing. Holding it back is fully reversible, since both uses stay open for a night when a role reveal would hurt the pack. Target landscape: A single quiet, unclaimed player chosen by default; no claims, reads, votes or deaths. The target's immunity to night kills is unknown, and it could be the lone killer.
lessons.action: With both conceals available and no information on the first-night victim, agree to the pack's kill but hold the conceals for a later night when a power role or a likely-to-die target is the victim. A conceal is only spent if the victim dies, but committing it early to an unscouted quiet player offers no gain, since that target may be night-immune (like a lone killer) and the night-1 kill may fail silently.

lessons.situation: Late game after a tied day vote, you are the last wolf with no conceals left. You must pick a kill among the few remaining town players, who are contesting each other's claims. Information landscape: Info-rich on the town side (a confirmed read on the lone killer, claim conflicts), but the town has not yet worked out your role. Stakes: Two more eliminations bring you to parity. Each night kill decides whether you reach it before the town votes you out. Forward exposure: The kill reveals the victim's role and will, and your carrier visit is visible to any surviving watcher or follower. Because you are the next carrier, a sigil placed on you can strike, and the action cannot be undone. Target landscape: Four living town players (Sigilist, Healer, Investigator, Trailseer) with no hard reads. The Trailseer was chosen because their tracking results threatened your claim, on public behavior rather than evidence.
lessons.action: With no conceals left and you as the carrier, kill the player whose night result most directly threatens your cover, such as a Trailseer or Sentinel who has followed or watched you. Expect the revealed role and will to expose their record, so choose the target whose record does less damage than their living results would.

lessons.situation: Opening night with ten players alive. The wolves must choose a first kill blind and decide whether to commit a conceal charge on the victim. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: no roles are confirmed, no discussion has happened, no deaths or claims exist, and the wolves know only their own partner. Stakes: Early game with a large cushion: one kill cannot decide the game. The value is information, since a hidden early victim denies Town a role reveal, and a night-immune target exposes the lone killer at no cost. Forward exposure: Low exposure: a conceal leaves no public trace, a failed attack is never announced, and a kill on a concealed victim leaves no visit for a Sentinel or Trailseer to see. The only commitment is possibly spending one of two conceals on a low-value role, and a failed attack refunds it. Target landscape: Seven unconfirmed non-wolf players with no claims, no public visits and no voting record. The pack picks a quiet player blindly, and the choice rests on no evidence or behavior.
lessons.action: On night one with both conceals unspent and no information, submit a conceal alongside the pack's kill on an unrevealed, quiet target. If the target dies, their role stays hidden and the Illusionist learns it, and if the attack fails because the target is night-immune, the conceal is kept and the pack learns the lone killer.

lessons.situation: You are the sole surviving wolf after your partner died, choosing the night kill while the healer is known to be active and protecting a publicly attacked player. Information landscape: Information-rich: the game master announced a save on the sentinel, and some town roles are confirmed. The wolves' own stats are known, but the healer's next protection is unknown. Stakes: With one wolf left and a lone killer possibly still alive, each night kill is critical. A wasted kill lets town investigators close in, while one real kill moves the wolves toward parity. Forward exposure: The kill is a lone carry that ties the night's attack to you as the only wolf. Once the target is chosen it is irreversible, and a wasted attack on a healer-covered target gains nothing and removes no town role. Target landscape: Candidates include a claimed sentinel already publicly saved by the healer, a claimed investigator with clears, a confirmed vigilante holding one bullet, and a quiet unverified player. The evidence is public announcements of the saves, not behavior.
lessons.action: As the last wolf, aim the pack kill at a player who was not publicly attacked and saved the previous night, such as a quiet unverified player or a confirmed threat the healer is not visibly guarding. Keep your conceals unspent until a kill is likely to succeed, since a conceal is refunded if the victim survives; if the healer's likely target is unclear, pick the target that was not the previous night's save.

lessons.situation: Night after your wolf partner was voted out and revealed. You are the lone wolf and your public vote pattern made you the likely suspect for a Vigilante. Information landscape: Info-rich about your exposure: a revealed wolf confirms your side, and your vote pattern is public and permanent. Stakes: As the lone wolf and prime suspect you can be killed by a Vigilante shot or sigil strike tonight, so passivity loses the game while a kill buys time. Forward exposure: A kill with a conceal leaves no trace at that door but spends your last conceal. Staying home leaves you exposed to a Vigilante shot or a sigil strike, and a sigil on you only strikes if you attack that night. Target landscape: Remaining town are claimed Sentinel, claimed Healer, Vigilante and Sigilist, with roles known only through claims. The Sigilist who pushed the case on your partner is a high-value target.
lessons.action: As the last wolf when your vote record or partner's reveal makes you a prime suspect, use the night to act instead of staying home. Carry the kill on the player most likely to hold a night killing role or to have deduced you (such as a Vigilante or Sigilist), and use a remaining conceal so the victim's role and your carrier visit stay hidden. If you cannot tell who that is, still make the kill rather than pass.

lessons.situation: Repeated wolf attacks on the claimed investigator were repelled by the healer's protection. The remaining wolf must choose between hitting the investigator again and breaking the protection cycle. Information landscape: Information-rich: investigator, healer and sentinel have publicly claimed roles, targets and results, and morning save announcements show the pattern of protection. Stakes: The wolves are close to parity and the protection cycle is the main obstacle. Removing the healer opens the way to the next power-role kill and to winning. Forward exposure: Spending the last conceal leaves zero charges, so later visits to victims are traceable. The kill itself is irreversible. A conceal on a victim who survives is refunded, and a hidden-role morning report only signals that an illusionist is active. Target landscape: Claimed investigator, who survived repeated attacks, versus the claimed healer, who openly took credit for the saves. Both are public claims backed by morning save announcements rather than by behavior alone.
lessons.action: When a claimed healer has been blocking the pack's kills on the claimed investigator or sentinel, aim the pack kill at the claimed healer and spend a conceal on that body. A hidden role denies the town confirmation and the Necromancer a usable body. If the healer is dead, protection stops and the next kill on the power role should land.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with you as the sole surviving wolf. A sigilist with a sigil left has publicly said they will target you, or has already used a sigil to kill your partner. Any kill you make would reach or approach parity, and the sigil strikes anyone who attacks that night. Information landscape: Information-rich: several roles are confirmed dead, the investigator's record or will clears one living player, and the sigilist's earlier strike or sigil result is public. The sigilist's suspicion of you is explicit. Stakes: One more death reaches or nearly reaches wolf parity, but the sigil can strike you on the same night and end the game for the wolves. A wrong attack loses the game immediately, while holding the kill only postpones the decision to the vote. Forward exposure: Attacking is a visit and an attack. It commits you to a kill that a sigil on you would punish with your own death, and it cannot be undone once the night resolves. Holding the kill reveals nothing and keeps your conceals available. Target landscape: Two or three living players remain: a publicly known or claimed sigilist whose earlier sigil result is confirmed, a player cleared by the investigator who is probably the healer, and possibly one quiet unconfirmed player. Roles come from public evidence and the sigilist's stated intentions, but which target holds an unspent sigil is unknown.
lessons.action: When you are the last evil player and a sigilist has a sigil left and has publicly named or suspected you, hold the kill that night. Your own attack triggers the sigil and the sigil strike still kills you even if the attack succeeds, and a conceal does not help if the healer saves the target. Keep your conceals and let the vote decide, rather than attacking into a possible sigil.

query_dims.consensus_text: No clear direction: the discussion has not formed an accusation or aligned around a candidate. The only shared point is that the Sentinel claimant's reported visit does not by itself implicate the visited player.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight players are alive and four eliminations remain until the leading evil faction can win; a single vote or kill cannot flip which faction is winning, though the early information vacuum makes the next death and any resulting evidence consequential.
query_dims.heat_now: No suspicion or accusation is directed at you in the discussion so far; your Fortune Teller role and zero points are private.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the Night 1 deaths and roles are confirmed, but there are no public wills or verified living-player results. The Sentinel's visit report is an unverified claim, and even if accurate it does not identify the attacker.
query_dims.my_position: Not driving or holding out against a consensus; you have not publicly taken a position.
query_dims.situation: After the wolves killed a revealed Investigator and the Serial Killer killed a revealed Trailseer on Night 1, a player claiming Sentinel said the Trailseer visited another survivor. A second speaker noted that this could have been the Trailseer's follow action and does not establish who attacked them. The room has no current vote target, leaving the next likely death and your own exposure uncertain.
query_dims.target_landscape: No elimination candidates have been publicly advanced. The Sentinel claim is unverified; the dead Investigator and Trailseer were role-revealed by the game master.

lessons.situation: Day discussion after a wolf is revealed dead and further kills were concealed; a lead accuser targets a suspect who defends himself with his vote on the dead wolf. Information landscape: Moderately thin: one confirmed wolf and a voting record, but concealed bodies and otherwise only claims and behavioral inference. Stakes: Midgame with enough players that one vote does not decide the game, but removing a wolf now cuts the wolves' parity threat and the pool of kill sources; the public result may also make me a likelier kill target. Consensus: The room is forming around one suspect, based on the dead wolf's revealed role and voting records rather than hard proof. My position: With the majority, as the second accuser. Heat: Low to moderate: aligned with the lead accuser, nothing exposing said, bets unscored and role undisclosed. Target landscape: A suspect accused of echoing a dead wolf's line who points to his vote on that wolf as proof of innocence, plus quiet players he deflects onto. Only one wolf role is confirmed; the rest is behavioral and voting-record reading.
lessons.action: With a confirmed wolf dead and no night result of your own to share, join the leading accusation against the player whose behavior best fits the dead wolf's. Give a concrete reason, such as a wolf piling onto a doomed partner to blend in, and keep your role and bet history private. If the accusation is led by a player you distrust, state your own independent read instead of echoing it.

lessons.situation: Day 2 after a night-1 death. Conflicting or unverifiable role claims (Investigator, Healer, Trailseer, Sentinel) dominate the discussion, and you are an uncommitted neutral with both self-bets unused. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims, one or two unconfirmed night reports, and a night-1 body, with no caught lies, no votes, and no confirmed wolf identities. Stakes: Early game with many players alive. No single vote or kill decides the game, so staying alive and unexposed to keep betting each night matters more than winning the argument. Consensus: Split or drifting: the room argues over rival claims or abstains, with no hard evidence behind any side. My position: Holding out in the middle or going with the majority, contributing a clarification without driving the vote. Heat: Very low: you have not been named, addressed, or accused, and you have not revealed your role. Target landscape: Two or more rival role claimants (e.g. two Investigators, or two Healers) or one scrutinized claimant, resting on unverified reports and timing. No confirmed wolves, and the night-1 victim's role is either announced or hidden.
lessons.action: When you are an unclaimed, low-heat Fortune Teller on day 2 in an info-starved room of conflicting claims, keep your role hidden and make one short, sincere contribution that shapes the discussion without accusing anyone. Good examples are a procedural point about visit direction, or a note that a hidden-role or dead role means a claim may not be genuine, or a direct question to a player a report ties to a contradiction. This keeps you out of the crossfire while still adding value, since your win depends on night bets rather than on how the vote goes.

lessons.situation: Late-game day discussion after the wolves are revealed dead; a player's claimed night result is being explained away and the Fortune Teller is asked directly whether a self-bet caused it. Information landscape: Fairly rich: public wolf reveals, a healer save and a sigil death are announced, while the claimed immunity result is still a private claim that my answer can corroborate. Stakes: Few players remain, so one correct vote on the lone killer decides the game; clearing the self-bet explanation lets the town converge on the right target. Consensus: The village is mostly aligned on weighing the claimed immunity result; wolves are already confirmed dead, so the debate is about the remaining killer and the unverified claim. My position: With the majority, answering a direct question and removing the main objection. Heat: Moderate and specific: a player floated that I might have bet on myself, making me a possible alternative explanation for the result. Target landscape: A player accused via a claimed night result (e.g. a serial killer said to be immune) versus the credibility of the claimant; the only alternative explanation is the Fortune Teller's own self-bet. Evidence is a private claim plus public deaths and reveals.
lessons.action: When a player directly asks whether your self-bet explains an odd night result (e.g. a claimed immunity), answer plainly and truthfully on whether you self-bet that night; if you didn't, say so and name whom you bet on. This removes the competing explanation, makes the other player's claim the best available evidence, and costs little because a Fortune Teller cannot be blocked and reads Not suspicious.

lessons.situation: Few players remain, the town power roles that could clear anyone are dead, and you are the first to publicly narrow the suspects to two. Information landscape: Information-starved on the key question: dead roles are known and one player is confirmed by an announced fact, but nothing separates the last two unknowns. Stakes: Near parity: every vote and night kill is decisive, and a visible lead on a point-short Fortune Teller invites the killer to remove you before you can score the final point. Consensus: The table accepted the narrowing and then debated voting order; the two suspects deflected onto each other with no firm direction. My position: Driving the framing with no personal lead on which suspect is the killer. Heat: Moderate-low: one earlier vote on a dead player is being cited against you, but no real suspicion. Target landscape: Two unaccounted-for players, with the dead roles known and one player confirmed by an announced sigil strike; no claims or checks separate the two, so any lean rests on voting-order behavior only.
lessons.action: When the pool of evil suspects is down to a few players and the town roles that could clear anyone are dead, state your narrowing and name your lead suspect, but deliver it as a shared conclusion alongside the confirmed player rather than leading it alone. If you are one point short of winning, avoid being the visible driver, since a lone-killer or wolf at the table can eliminate you at night.

lessons.situation: Day 4 with most evil already dead. A claimant's reported results look inconsistent with the rules, and you are the main driver of the case against them. Information landscape: Info-rich on mechanics but conflicted on identity. The contradiction is checkable, but the claimant's honesty is in doubt and a real Town role may be misread. Stakes: Few evil players remain, so one wrong elimination can hand the last evil faction parity or remove Town's last investigative role. A visible driver of the vote is also an obvious night-kill target. Consensus: The room is converging on your rule argument, which makes a fast elimination of the claimant likely. My position: Driving the case as the first and most persistent voice. Heat: Moderate. The accused claimant counter-accused you of pushing too eagerly, though the rest of the room backed your argument. Target landscape: The only claimed role on the table, with unclaimed others. The basis for suspicion is a mechanical inconsistency in the claim, not a past check.
lessons.action: When you spot a rule-based contradiction in a claimant's account, state it once, clearly and as a question. Ask what else could explain it, and compare their answer with any counterclaims. Do not repeatedly assign a specific evil role to them, because other players will pile on and the mislynch can cost Town its last investigative role while exposing you to a night kill.

lessons.situation: A claimed trailseer reports tracking an accused player to the door of a night victim whose role was concealed, creating a confrontation over whether the visit is genuine. Information landscape: Mixed: one concealed night death and a single living claimed trailseer's report, with conflicting readings of the mechanics and no corroboration. Stakes: A wrong elimination would cost Town a body and bring the wolves closer to parity, but no single vote decides the game. The fortune teller benefits from a slower, evidence-driven day that keeps it unexposed. Consensus: The room is leaning toward acting on the trailseer's report, but with open doubt about whether the visit was fabricated or genuine and how concealment mechanics affect traces. My position: holding out Heat: Completely cold; participating neutrally with no suspicion directed at me. Target landscape: An accused player said to have visited a dead player whose role was concealed, versus the claimed trailseer making the accusation; evidence is a single uncorroborated claim.
lessons.action: When a high-stakes accusation rests on an unverifiable visit report and you have no heat, urge caution and ask what corroborating evidence exists. Point out how the stated rules (for example, an illusionist's concealment hiding the attacking trace) limit what such a report can prove. This makes you look measured and analytical and keeps you from being drawn into a rushed elimination.

lessons.situation: Day 4, shortly after a wolf flip and a concealed-role kill. One player voted against the consensus on the previous day, and you can ask them to justify it. Information landscape: A confirmed wolf flip, a concealed-role kill, and a public vote record. Few other facts are verified, so most reads rest on behavior. Stakes: The village is mid-game with evil still alive. A cheap question can surface a claim and a counterclaim fight without committing you to an elimination, and it keeps you alive for the later days. Consensus: The room is loosely aligned after a confirmed flip and a recorded vote pattern, and it is receptive to follow-up questions about odd votes. My position: With the majority, steering the question toward the dissenter without leading an accusation. Heat: Low. You have said little publicly and earlier mild skepticism has not been held against you. Target landscape: Survivors with no confirmed roles except what flips have shown. One player was the lone dissenter in the last vote, and all other reads are behavioral.
lessons.action: When a confirmed flip or kill pattern leaves one player as the lone dissenter in the earlier vote, ask them to explain the deviation instead of accusing them. Their answer, whether a claim, a trace, or a dodge, gives the room something to test and moves attention off you. If they give a claim or trace, hold your read until the room has cross-checked it against other claims.

lessons.situation: Late game with three players left: you and a copycat both claim Fortune Teller, and a single third player's vote decides which of you is eliminated. Information landscape: Information-starved: no verified results, only claims, but a detailed bet history against a thin copy creates an asymmetry the voter can check against the public record. Stakes: With three alive, one vote decides the game: eliminating the false claimant can end it in your favor, while losing the vote likely means your death and a loss. Consensus: Split and starved of hard evidence; the outcome depends on one remaining voter judging whose account is more detailed and consistent. My position: Driving the case against the counterclaimant while holding out against their accusation. Heat: High: under a counterclaim, tied in votes, and your claim cannot be independently verified. Target landscape: Two Fortune Teller claimants (you and a false claimant, likely the necromancer) plus one unconfirmed swing voter whose own claim cannot be verified; the false claimant's bets match only public deaths, while your history has specifics that fit the record.
lessons.action: When a rival claims Fortune Teller (or your claim is otherwise disputed) in a late-game room with few players left, state your claim plainly and give your full bet history: which nights, whom you bet on, the role named, which bets scored, and the self-bets. Point out that a copycat's bets match only publicly known deaths while yours include specifics (wrong early bets, self-bets, role names) that fit the public record, and name the copycat as your top suspect so the swing voter has a concrete reason to side with you.

query_dims.consensus_text: The village is divided on the day 3 sentinel claim and the day 2 abstain pattern, with no clear majority on any living target yet.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Five alive with three eliminations until the leading evil faction can win, and no single result can end the game next; a wrong lynch costs a town player but is recoverable, while your own exposure would remove your ability to strike unseen.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Claiming any role or citing a night result only a dead role could produce would expose you and commit you to a visible position; staying silent and voting with the majority is reversible.
query_dims.heat_now: Low: you have not been named by any active accusation today, though an earlier day 2 vote from one player named you once.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: the only live evidence is a dead sentinel's unverified night-1 watch claim and one investigator check on player_3 (Not suspicious), which is itself a dead player's claim.
query_dims.my_position: With the majority by voting, holding out from any personal accusation.
query_dims.public_private_text: As the necromancer, you privately know you struck player_5 (a chanteuse) through player_6's vigilante body, and that you hold the trailseer and vigilante bodies for later use; publicly no one knows your role and the sentinel's claim against player_5 is the live dispute.
query_dims.situation: Day 4 with five alive after a sentinel was lynched and the chanteuse and investigator were killed at night; the village is debating whether the dead sentinel's claim about a now-dead chanteuse was true, while you, the hidden necromancer, hold two dead bodies whose abilities you can use on future nights.
query_dims.target_landscape: Five players alive: three unclaimed town-aligned or unknown players and two others; the only public claim is a voted-out sentinel's night-1 watch that named player_5, already dead, and no independent evidence confirms it.

lessons.situation: Day 2 discussion after the first night: several Town role claims clash (rival investigators, a rule-inconsistent sentinel result, an unexplained visit), and the necromancer holds private knowledge or an unused usable body while staying unclaimed. Information landscape: Information-starved: unverified claims, one or two second-hand visit reports, and only the dead players' announced roles confirmed. The necromancer's own private information is not publicly known. Stakes: Early-mid game with many players alive: no single vote ends the game, but the necromancer needs to survive daily votes to reach the end, so staying out of the accusation list is the priority. Consensus: The village is split over competing claims and has not formed a firm consensus. Its attention is on whose result is inconsistent, not on the quiet players. My position: On the sidelines or moving with the majority, not driving any accusation. Heat: Low to mild: no accusation or only a passing mention of the necromancer's silence, with the focus on claim conflicts. Forward exposure: A short neutral comment or question commits to little and is reversible, but any reference to unshared results or to how a body works would tie the speaker to private knowledge and cannot be taken back. A reanimated attack would be announced as such, so wording about bodies must not suggest foreknowledge. Target landscape: Rival claimants (two investigators, a contested sentinel result, an unexplained visit) are the natural focus. None has a confirmed role, and the basis for suspicion is claims and rule-consistency rather than behavior; the necromancer is one of several quiet, unaccused players. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows its own role and any night use of a dead player's body (or that the body is available), while publicly it is just one quiet player among several, with Town claims unverified and no one suspecting a lone killer.
lessons.action: While the room is fixated on a role-claim clash and nobody has named you, speak briefly as a Town voice: echo or ask a neutral question about the dispute and steer attention back to the clashing claimants. Cite only publicly announced facts and never reference a body you used or any private result; if a player starts probing your vote or silence, give a short sincere-sounding reason and redirect the question to the claim clash.

lessons.situation: Mid-game day discussion after several deaths. Town and wolves are arguing over voting records and a night-timeline theory, and a hidden necromancer is either unmentioned or only theorized about while it stays quiet. Information landscape: Moderately rich: several dead roles are confirmed and some claims are partly corroborated, but wolf identities and the lone killer's identity are unverified. Stakes: Few players remain, so each vote moves the board toward the necromancer's last-two win. Being singled out by a vote or a shot now would end the run, so low visibility with minimal engagement matters. Consensus: The village is loosely aligned on a few suspects, driven by wolves and town voices pushing voting-record and behavior cases. It has no hard proof of the lone killer's identity. My position: With the majority and speaking mildly, not driving any accusation; neither holding out nor leading. Heat: Low and not directly accused. At most there is a mild mention of its abstain-heavy votes or of its silence, and a town theory that a necromancer exists. Forward exposure: A generic record-based comment commits the necromancer to nothing and is fully reversible. A role claim or a named wolf would create a checkable statement, and silence plus an abstain leaves a permanent, noticeable pattern. Target landscape: The table is weighing other players, such as a claimed sigilist and quiet town roles, on voting behavior and role inference rather than hard evidence. The necromancer is not among the named suspects; several dead roles are confirmed and living roles are mostly unverified. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer knows it has used or can use dead bodies and that the table's accusation flow does not touch it; publicly it is an unnamed, unsuspected role that the town may only be theorizing about.
lessons.action: When the table is chasing other targets and you are a low-heat necromancer, add one short, sincere, evidence-based observation about the record (e.g. a vote was near-unanimous and so isolates no one) to show engagement. Make no role claim and no wolf accusation, so you stay uncheckable and can drop the point freely. If a town theory starts to name a hidden lone killer, join the discussion before the vote rather than going silent and abstaining.

lessons.situation: Late game with about five players alive. A body-assisted attack has been announced and the town is hunting the lone killer among the few unconfirmed players, while you are one of them. Information landscape: Information-rich: announced role reveals, a will clearing a player, a reanimated-attack announcement, and permanent public votes give the town a lot to cross-check. Stakes: With five alive, one wrongly directed or lost day vote can end your game. Being named the necromancer this round is likely fatal, so avoiding contradictions matters more than pushing a theory. Consensus: The village is converging on a small set of unconfirmed players using announced facts, and it is ready to punish evasive or inconsistent framing. My position: holding out Heat: High. The announced reanimated attack proves a necromancer is alive, so scrutiny falls on every unconfirmed player, and your unexplained votes draw questions. Forward exposure: Claiming to be outside the suspect pool commits you to a facade that cross-examination of your votes can break, and you cannot take it back once challenged. Staying inside the pool and giving consistent reasons commits you to little and can be adjusted later. Target landscape: A few unconfirmed players (you, a surviving wolf or neutral, and others) next to cleared or confirmed players such as a healer cleared by an investigator's will. The only hard evidence is announced facts and wills, and the rest is voting-record behavior. Public vs private: You privately know you used a dead wolf's or vigilante's body to attack, while the room knows only that a necromancer is alive and is narrowing down the unconfirmed players.
lessons.action: When a reanimated attack has been announced and you sit in a small unconfirmed pool, put yourself in that pool openly and answer questions about your voting record with reasons that match the public record. Then argue from announced facts such as wills, saves and kill types, and name the other unconfirmed players as candidates alongside yourself instead of presenting yourself as a neutral judge outside the pool.

lessons.situation: Endgame with about four alive and the wolves dead or nearly dead. The town reasons by elimination that you are the Necromancer, and a rival claimant is pushing a vote on you. Information landscape: Info-starved: no hard evidence, role claims cannot be verified, and the discussion rests on elimination logic and vote records. Stakes: With four alive, one wrong vote or kill decides the game. If you survive the vote, your next night kill leaves three alive and brings you close to winning. Consensus: Undecided and fragile: the town knows a lone killer is still alive, but has no evidence separating the remaining players. My position: Holding out against an accusation, countering it rather than driving a wagon. Heat: High: you are the leading suspect through role elimination and the only player without a trusted claim. Forward exposure: A false claim commits you to a consistent fabricated history that can be compared against the real claimant's, and it can only be sustained until the vote closes. It is hard to retract once made. Target landscape: Three or four remaining players: the accuser (a claimant of a neutral role), one other uncommitted claimant, and a possible leftover wolf. Roles are judged on claim-versus-claim and vote tone, not on hard evidence. Public vs private: Privately you are the Necromancer and the accuser's claim may even be true, but publicly it is one unverifiable claim against another, with no hard evidence either way.
lessons.action: When wolves are mostly dead and you are named Necromancer by elimination in a four-player endgame, counter-accuse the accuser and hold a stable story: if the accuser is a claimed neutral, counterclaim that role with a bet or result history that does not line up with deaths the town already knows. Aim to split the remaining voters rather than win every vote, because a split or a wasted vote keeps you alive for your night attack.

lessons.situation: Late game with three or four alive after a public reanimated attack. The Necromancer pool has been narrowed to a few players, I am one of them, and I must either claim a cover role or accuse the other suspect before the vote. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich: announced night attack types, revealed roles, public vote records and a narrowed suspect pool. The remaining evidence is unverified claims. Stakes: With three alive, one vote or one night kill decides the game. If the vote lands on me, Town wins at once; if it lands elsewhere, I am a night kill from winning. Consensus: The room is converging against me. The other suspects' accounts fit the announced night events, and a ballot of two or three players can tie or flip on a single vote. My position: Holding out against a forming consensus and trying to turn the swing voter. Heat: High. I was named the Necromancer by elimination or by a rival claimant, and a public reanimated attack points at whoever has been channeling it. Forward exposure: A fabricated role claim or a flat counter-accusation commits me to a story that the public night record or the real role holder can test. It cannot be withdrawn without confessing, and with three alive the next vote is final. Target landscape: Two or three living suspects, including me. Their roles are claimed but unverified, and the basis is claims plus the public reanimated-attack report, which fits whoever is suspected. Public vs private: I know I am the Necromancer and that my reanimated attack is already public. Publicly I am one of two or three suspects, and my accusers' claims fit the announced night events.
lessons.action: When the Necromancer pool has shrunk to about three and you are named, anchor your defense only in announced facts such as morning reports, public votes and revealed roles. Pick a cover story that no living player can contradict from a private record. If a living player's own record already fits the facts better than your story, shift to showing that their account explains the announced night events no better than yours does. Do not invent a detailed record, such as bets, that a real holder can contradict.

lessons.situation: The necromancer has learned night information through a dead role's body and is tempted to use it in discussion to redirect suspicion onto other players, while the room is actively analyzing who could know what. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are announced role deaths, claimed investigative results, and players closely tracking visits. The sources of knowledge are therefore checkable. Stakes: The necromancer needs the village to shrink, but a mid-sized table still lets one exposure cause a near-unanimous elimination. Surviving the day is worth more than landing one accusation. Consensus: The village is rigorously tracking visit mechanics and is united in cross-checking who could know what. Any claim that cannot be sourced is quickly spotted. My position: Not yet committed, free to stay with the majority. Revealing channeled data would leave me holding out alone against the whole room. Heat: Low to none at the start of the discussion, since nobody suspects the necromancer. It becomes overwhelming once an impossible information source is revealed. Forward exposure: Naming exact visitors or other results from a dead role's body shows knowledge that only the necromancer could have, and once said it cannot be retracted. A vague or announced-facts-only contribution commits to nothing and stays reversible. Target landscape: The living claimed town roles (an investigator, a trailseer, a claimed healer) and unclaimed players. Their standing rests on claims and on visit logic, with no hard confirmation. Public vs private: Privately the necromancer holds results from channeling a dead investigative role, such as the visitors at a door. Publicly that role is dead and no living player has claimed such a result, so citing it would expose the source.
lessons.action: When a night read obtained through a dead player's body would be impossible for any living role to know, hold it back and stay vague, and only restate what the Game Master announced or what living claimants have said. If you push a read, ground it in public voting records and announced facts, so a challenge cannot trace it to your necromancer channel.

lessons.situation: Early-mid game day discussion after a concealed or failed night kill, with clashing role claims and the town deciding how to test them before the vote. I am a hidden lone-killer Necromancer with private body-ability information. Information landscape: Only unverified claims and blocked or missing investigative roles exist; the discussion is information-starved and speculative. Stakes: The board is not at the brink, so one discussion move will not flip the game. The priority is staying off the radar while wolves and town thin each other, not forcing an outcome. Consensus: The room is converging on testing claims or on a pending wolf-versus-claimant dispute, with little hard evidence behind it. My position: Neutral, offering process suggestions while the room converges; neither driving a target nor opposing the majority. Heat: Low to none: I have not been accused or singled out, apart from at most a general call-out of abstainers. Forward exposure: Procedural suggestions commit me to no read and are easy to walk back. Citing movement or results from a body-use ties me to a source nobody can see, invites a 'who watched?' challenge, and cannot be retracted once on the record. Target landscape: Rival claimants (e.g. two Investigators with opposite results) and unconfirmed roles judged only on claims and voting behavior; no role is confirmed, so any side I take would be a guess. Public vs private: I privately know my body-ability plans and results (a concealed victim, a follow or attack through a dead role), while publicly nobody suspects a lone killer and the room is arguing over unverified claims.
lessons.action: When claims clash and you hold private body-derived information, stay unclaimed and offer only procedural, verifiable-in-public suggestions, such as asking claimants to commit to next night's targets so claims can be tested against later visit evidence. Keep every comment to what the room could know openly, and never cite a result that comes only from your own reanimated ability.

lessons.situation: With the wolves gone and few players left, a confirmed vigilante is leading the hunt for the lone necromancer and the town is choosing between claimed role players. Information landscape: Information-rich: wolves eliminated, a confirmed vigilante kill announced, spent-sigil claims and repeated roleblock claims. A confirmed shooter still holds a bullet. Stakes: A confirmed vigilante with a bullet can kill you at night if you look like the necromancer, so any extra heat can end the game. Consensus: The town is moving toward one elimination on claim-based reasoning, and it is explicitly treating anyone who attacks the protective claimants as suspect. My position: holding out Heat: Moderate to high. A confirmed vigilante has said that players pushing suspicious angles against the claimed healer are prime necromancer suspects. Forward exposure: A loud push against a protective claimant ties you to that accusation and is read as necromancer framing, and you cannot undo it. Agreeing with a forming consensus leaves little public footprint and can be changed. Target landscape: A claimed healer reporting repeated roleblocks, a claimed sigilist with spent sigils, and a confirmed vigilante holding a bullet. Reads on them rest on claims and behavior, not verified evidence. Public vs private: You privately want the confirmed or protective roles weakened, but the room is already moving toward a different elimination and is watching who pushes the claimed healer or other protective claims.
lessons.action: If the town is already drifting toward a target other than you, voice agreement with that drift and support it with the public record, instead of leading a separate push against a claimed protective or confirmed role. If you must dissent, do it with a mild, evidence-based question rather than a sustained campaign against one player.
