Make rule statements only if they stay true given your own night attacks, since your attack through a dead Illusionist's body leaves that body's name at the door. Do not assert that a track is impossible if your own actions could later make it true.

lessons.situation: A claimed Investigator names a suspect and states they cleared the necromancer on an earlier night. A counterclaim appears against the accused and the room is leaning toward a vote. Information landscape: Mixed. One Investigator claim that includes a clearance on you, one counterclaim, and no confirmed roles beyond the dead. Stakes: Late-mid game with few players left, so each vote matters. Riding a public clearance keeps you safe while the town eliminates another player. Consensus: The majority is forming behind the Investigator's accusation, based on claims and a counterclaim. My position: With the majority, helping drive the case against the accused. Heat: Low and falling. You were named only as a Not suspicious check and defended yourself by agreeing with it. Forward exposure: Vouching for the Investigator ties you to that claim being genuine. A later check on an attack night would read Suspicious, and reversing would look like a flip. Target landscape: The claimed Investigator, whose check cleared you and who is backed by a counterclaim against the accused, versus the accused player, who is contradicted by another claim. There are no confirmations, only claims and a counterclaim. Public vs private: The Investigator's clearance of you was true only because you were inactive that night. You know you read Suspicious on attack nights, but publicly the clearance looks like solid proof of innocence.
lessons.action: If a claimed Investigator says they cleared you and that claim is gaining support from the room, publicly accept the clearance and side with the Investigator against the counterclaimer. This turns the clearance into cover and aligns you with the likely winning side. Stay aware that checking you on a night you attack would read Suspicious, so keep the endorsement light and avoid vouching for the Investigator beyond what you must.

query_dims.consensus_text: The village is not aligned; the room is split between pressing the blocked claimant to name their role and treating the lack of any result as insufficient to vote on.
query_dims.criticality_stakes: Eight alive with four eliminations needed before the leading evil faction can win, so a wrong vote today is recoverable but would still shift the balance toward a wolf-led endgame; no single elimination ends the game.
query_dims.forward_exposure: Any claim of a night result or role now would be unverifiable and would commit me to a story that the block on player_5 and the night-1 kill can be tested against; retracting it later is not possible, so staying quiet keeps the option open.
query_dims.heat_now: Low to moderate: player_10 has said they would vote player_5 at low confidence, and player_9 and player_6 are pressing player_5 to name a role, so the pressure is on player_5 rather than on me.
query_dims.information_landscape: Information-starved: no investigator or sentinel results have been claimed, the trailseer who could have cross-checked follows is dead, and the only public evidence is the blocked claim itself.
query_dims.my_position: Holding out from any accusation, with the village focused on player_5's unverified blocked-role claim.
query_dims.public_private_text: Privately, as the Chanteuse, I know my pack killed a trailseer on night 1 and that I blocked player_5 that night; publicly I have claimed nothing and hold no night result, and player_5 is publicly claiming a blocked active role without naming it.
query_dims.situation: Day 2 after a night-1 kill of a trailseer: a player publicly says they had an active night role that was blocked but refuses to name it, and several players demand a name before any vote, while no one has a checkable result yet.
query_dims.target_landscape: Eight alive; player_5 is the only player publicly claiming a blocked night role, with no name and no result, so the claim rests on the blocked state alone; other players have made no claims, so no one has public role evidence against them.

lessons.situation: On day 2 a claimed trailseer reported following you to another player's door, a roleblock report on that player corroborated it, and the village is converging on you or on an abstain while you consider voting against the tracker. Information landscape: Starved of announced facts: only unverified claims (a follow report, a roleblock report, a watch claim, possibly your own cover claim), plus a hidden-role death and a confirmed investigator death. Nothing announced identifies you. Stakes: With nine alive and the wolves far from parity, there is no tempo to force a risky vote. Losing the chanteuse, or drawing a sigil or investigator check by standing out, costs the wolves a blocker and leaves the partner alone. Consensus: The room is aligned on either abstaining or eliminating you, based on matching unverified claims about your night movement rather than on any announced fact. My position: Holding out alone against the room, either as the main wagon target or as a solitary voter against an abstain consensus. Heat: High to very high: the tracker's follow report and a target's roleblock report match your real night visit, several players accuse you, and your denial stands alone against a convergent pair of claims. Forward exposure: A lone vote on the accuser is public and permanent, commits you to the story that the report is false, and invites night attention. Voting with the room is reversible and keeps the record neutral; if you are eliminated your role is revealed and your wolf partner comes under suspicion. Target landscape: Candidates are the claimed trailseer who named you, players who echoed the roleblock or watch claims (sigilist, vigilante, sentinel), and an abstain option. All are unverified role claims, and the dead so far are an investigator and a concealed body, so nothing hard points at any candidate. Public vs private: You privately know the tracker's report of your visit is true and you blocked or visited that player; publicly it is only an unverified claim that you have denied or covered with a fabricated story.
lessons.action: When a claimed trailseer or other tracker publicly places your night visit on a target, and the room is abstaining or leaning against you, skip the revenge vote and join the room's consensus (abstain or the wagon's target). A solitary vote against your accuser changes no tally, repeats your accusation on the permanent record and marks you as the one player who wants the information role dead.

lessons.situation: Late-game day vote where the chanteuse's side is losing. Either a fake-claim counter-claim contest has turned against you, or a credible watch or follow claim has doomed your wolf partner, and the room is converging. Information landscape: Information-rich from the town's view: confirmed roles for the dead, a lone killer possibly already eliminated, and claims corroborated by other claimants. You have nothing verifiable to offer. Stakes: The wolves are within a couple of eliminations of parity, so losing a wolf or exposing the pair is costly. This single vote will not flip the result, so the value is in keeping the wolves' public links minimal. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, with a lopsided majority forming on a claim-based case that looks consistent. There is no strong support for the minority view. My position: Holding out against, or being swept along by, a clear majority. Your vote is not the deciding one. Heat: High. You are either the target of a lost counter-claim with several players already naming you, or you recently pushed against a claimant who has since been corroborated. Forward exposure: Every vote is public and permanent. Matching your partner's vote, or opposing the room's clear pick, ties you to them and cannot be undone once the role is revealed. A vote that diverges costs little because your own vote cannot change a lopsided result. Target landscape: The realistic candidates are your counter-claimant, your exposed partner, and the Sentinel or other accuser. All are judged on claims and corroboration rather than hard proof, and the room has mostly settled on one. Public vs private: You privately know your partner's role and whether your own claim is false. The room is working from claims, counter-claims and past votes, and it sees you as either a liar or a defender of a likely wolf.
lessons.action: If the vote is already lost, because you are the losing side of a counter-claim or your partner is the target of a credible, room-wide case, cast the vote that least links you to your partner. Vote with the room when it is converging on your partner, and when you are the target pick a different name from your partner's. Votes are public and permanent, so a doomed vote that mirrors your partner's ties the two of you together.

lessons.situation: Day 2 is the first vote of the game. Information is thin, with a night-1 death or a few unverified claims, and the village is split between piling on a target and abstaining. Information landscape: Starved: unverified claims, perhaps one revealed death, no confirmed roles and no vote history. Stakes: Early game with many players alive; no single vote decides the game, so staying unnoticed matters more than pushing an elimination. Consensus: The room is split or undecided between several targets and abstaining, with no evidence-based convergence. My position: With the majority or a plurality bloc, not driving. Heat: Low: you have not been accused and have only spoken mildly or generically. Forward exposure: A named vote is public and permanent and can later be read as wolf coordination if your partner is exposed. An abstain or a vote with the plurality commits you to little and carries low risk. Target landscape: Candidates are quiet players, unverified claimants, and abstaining. No roles are confirmed, so any named target is a behavior-based guess. Public vs private: You privately know both wolves and the pack's night plan, while the public has only unverified night-1 claims, one death at most, and behavioral reads, so nothing points at you.
lessons.action: On the first day-2 vote, when no roles are confirmed and you have low heat, cast your vote with the room's existing plurality, which is often abstain or a split. Keep your vote consistent with your partner's but do not drive the accusation. Voting with the room adds no new suspicion, and an unforced named vote is permanent record you cannot undo.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote: a claimed town info role gave a result that breaks the rules, the accused admitted no explanation, and the table piled on. Your wolf partner may be among the accusers. Eliminating the target also removes a town watcher. Information landscape: Thin but concrete: one verifiable rules inconsistency, a few unverified claims, no voting history, and few confirmed roles. Stakes: Early game with many players alive and the wolves far from parity. The outcome is not close, so one vote does not flip the result. The value is in staying invisible while a town information role is removed. Consensus: Near-unanimous (about 8 of 9) and based on a checkable rules inconsistency that the accused conceded, not on tone or pack coordination. My position: With the majority, joining a vote that is already decided. Heat: Low to almost none: you are unclaimed, made few or no accusations, and the attention is entirely on the accused. Forward exposure: A vote with a lopsided majority commits you to nothing and looks like ordinary town behavior. Voting against an accepted target would stand out in the permanent public record with no upside. Target landscape: One candidate, a claimed Sentinel, has a concrete rules contradiction (a watch result that omitted their own visit) and is accused by several players. No other player has comparable evidence against them, so the choice rests on a verifiable inconsistency, not on tone. Public vs private: You privately know the wolf pair (Chanteuse and Illusionist) is alive and that the accused claimant is likely a genuine town role. The public sees only an unverified claim with an impossible result and treats it as grounds to eliminate.
lessons.action: When the room is already converging on a target through a checkable rules contradiction, cast your day vote with the majority and add no distinctive argument. The vote is low-commitment and blends into the pile-on, so a lone vote elsewhere would only draw heat to you.

lessons.situation: Day 2 vote after your wolf partner died on night 1. You are the lone wolf, and the room mostly leans to abstain while minority blocs name different targets. Information landscape: Starved: a few claimed night results and one slip, with no confirmed roles and no vote history. Stakes: As the lone wolf you have no backup, so one exposure or one night retaliation could end the wolf side; staying low-profile is worth more than a marginal vote. Consensus: Most of the room leans toward abstaining, and a couple of small blocs name different targets. My position: Holding out with a minority bloc against an abstain-leaning room. Heat: Low: no accusations against you, only generic discussion remarks. Forward exposure: A minority vote is public and permanent and ties you to one bloc, so the target and that bloc can see where you stand. You cannot reverse it. Target landscape: Candidates are a claimant who slipped on a night action, another named suspect, or abstaining. Roles are unconfirmed, and the only lead is a behavioral slip. Public vs private: You privately know you are the last wolf with no partner to help, while the town has no read on you.
lessons.action: If your partner is dead or revealed and you are the lone wolf, vote with the majority or abstain instead of joining a small minority bloc on a sigilist or other action-role claimant. A vote that leaves you holding out with a minority marks you to the targeted player, who may act against you that night.

lessons.situation: A day vote on an early day with a forming majority, either abstain-heavy or piled on one suspect, where the chanteuse has no real evidence-based target and a lone vote would only mark them as the outlier. Information landscape: Starved: unverified power-role claims, a few roleblock complaints and no confirmed roles or voting history to anchor a read. Stakes: Many players are still alive and no single vote decides the game. Wolf survival depends on staying unnoticed, so the vote is worth little compared with the cost of a record that gets used against you. Consensus: The village is fairly aligned, either piling onto one behavior-based suspect or abstaining in bulk, with little hard evidence behind it. My position: Free to choose between joining the majority and standing alone; joining the majority keeps you unremarkable. Heat: Low to moderate: nobody is accusing you, but an off-consensus vote would create heat immediately. Forward exposure: A vote is public and permanent. An outlier vote on a quiet or claimed player creates a record that can be quoted back and cannot be undone, whereas a vote with the room commits you to little and is easy to explain. Target landscape: Candidates are mostly unrevealed players: a room-favored suspect chosen on behavior or quietness, claimed power roles with unverifiable results, and quiet players with no evidence against them. There is no confirmed wolf, so any off-consensus pick rests on thin or no evidence. Public vs private: You privately know the pack, your own blocks and the real roles of some players, but publicly you are an unremarkable, unclaimed player whom nobody is accusing, and the room is thin on evidence and leaning toward one target or toward abstaining.
lessons.action: When the room is converging or abstaining and you have no evidence-backed target, cast your vote with the majority, or abstain if abstaining is offered, rather than being the lone off-consensus voter. If you are forced to name someone, pick the room's leading target or one your wolf partner also backs, so your permanent record has no outlier vote that can later be quoted as reactionary deflection.

lessons.situation: A genuine Town claimant (a healer counter-claiming against my partner, or a sentinel accusing me of a visit) is on the ballot at the day vote. Removing them protects the pack or me today, but their role and will will be revealed on death. Information landscape: Information-rich: there are contested role claims, a named visit, confirmed saves, and the public voting record. Nothing is verified until a death reveals the role. Stakes: The board is mid-game with several kills still needed for parity. Removing a healer or sentinel strips Town's protection or visit information and gives the wolves tempo, but a revealed role can expose my own visit history. Consensus: The village is split or leaning against the claimant, based on behavioral skepticism such as delayed disclosure and conflicting claims, not on confirmed facts. My position: With the majority, as one vote in a broad bloc and not the driver. Heat: Ranges from low to severe. Either my partner is under fire in a contested claim, or the claimant is directly accusing me, but the room is skeptical of the claimant. Forward exposure: The vote is permanent and public. If the claimant dies as a confirmed Town role, my vote is tied to the wolf side and any will naming my visit becomes announced fact, so the commitment cannot be undone and can draw night attacks such as a sigil or a vigilante shot. Target landscape: A binary choice between a claimed protective or information role (healer or sentinel) and either my wolf partner or myself. The claimant's role is unverified, and the case against them rests on behavior and timing, not hard evidence. Public vs private: Publicly the claimant is an unverified or belated claimant whom the room distrusts. Privately I know the claim is genuine, either because it names my own visit or because my wolf partner is the one faking the role.
lessons.action: When the room is already turning on a claimant who threatens you or your partner (a counter-claimed healer, or a sentinel naming your visit), cast your vote with the broad majority against that claimant. Joining a wide bloc keeps you from standing out as the driver and removes a protective or information role. Expect the revealed role and will to be read out as fact, so take the claimant's most likely true read into account when judging how much heat that reveal will put on you.

lessons.situation: A claiming investigative role (Investigator or Trailseer) has caught my wolf partner with a Suspicious check or a tracked visit to a victim. The village is pushing to eliminate the partner, and the partner is counter-charging the claimant. I must choose between joining the vote on the partner and voting against the claimant. Information landscape: Information-rich. A living claimant has direct evidence, other claims or mechanics corroborate it, and the votes will become a permanent ledger. Stakes: The board is still early and not at parity, so one vote does not decide the game. The partner is lost either way, and what matters is whether I survive as a low-heat wolf for later days. A solitary or minority vote costs me that standing and gains nothing. Consensus: The village is largely united behind the claimant's result, supported by mechanics or corroborating claims. A counter-wagon would need near-majority support, and in the observed cases it reached 2 to 4 votes against a landslide. My position: holding out Heat: Low. I had stayed neutral in discussion, with no accusations or scrutiny on me, and that standing is what I would lose by backing the partner. Forward exposure: Votes are public and permanent. A vote against the claimant or for the partner's side becomes a visible link to the partner once the partner's role flips as a wolf, and it cannot be undone. A vote with the majority commits me to nothing beyond the consensus. Target landscape: The choice is between my caught wolf partner, who is named by a claiming investigative role's result or movement evidence, and that claimant, whom the partner is accusing of fabrication. The case against the partner rests on evidence and mechanics, while the counter-case rests on behavior and bluster. Public vs private: I privately know my partner is a wolf and the claimant's result is probably genuine. The room is converging on that read, and my only open choice is whether to be seen defending the partner.
lessons.action: When a credible, info-rich claim has the room converging on your wolf partner and your own heat is low, vote with the majority against the partner instead of voting against the claimant. If the counter-wagon cannot reach a majority, your vote on the public record only ties you to the partner, so keep your standing for the later days.

lessons.situation: A split day vote where the Town claimants disagree, and a no-elimination tie would keep a rival killer alive to thin Town overnight. Information landscape: Information-rich in claims (investigator, sentinel, healer) but with no confirmed evil targets and an unconfirmed Night 1 event. Stakes: Town can't afford another night of attrition, so a tie that keeps a killer alive favors the evil side. This only pays if your own elimination isn't within reach of the vote. Consensus: Town is split across several wagons with no agreement on who is evil, and there are rival claims from the investigator, sentinel and healer. My position: Driving a minority wagon, aiming for a tie, not a majority. Heat: Moderate to high. A claimed vigilante has voted for you and a claimed healer is questioning your narrative. Forward exposure: A vote on a contested suspect commits you to a push a claimed healer has already questioned, and you take heat if the target flips Town. The vote is visible and permanent, but a tie costs little because nobody is eliminated. Target landscape: A suspected killer voted by a claimed investigator, a quiet unaligned player voted by a claimed healer and the suspect, and you voted by a claimed vigilante. The reads rest on claims and unconfirmed night results, not hard evidence. Public vs private: You privately know a suspect has night immunity or a role that helps your side. Publicly that is unconfirmed, so Town doubts the push against them.
lessons.action: If you are not the main target and a killer or other threat still threatens Town, vote for a plausible suspect who is already contested so the votes split into a tie. A tie means no elimination and gives the threat another night to cut Town's power roles. If your own heat is high and a vigilante-type is voting you, skip this and consolidate onto the leading wagon instead.

lessons.situation: Day vote where the village converges on your wolf partner, who is exposed by a counterclaim or accusation. You must choose between joining the vote against them and defending them. Information landscape: Claims, counterclaims and unverified night reports are present, and some roles may be confirmed by deaths. There are no hard Game Master confirmations of the accused's role, so the room's read rests on deduction. Stakes: The vote outcome is already decided by the majority, so your single vote does not flip the board. What it decides is whether you stay unlinked to the partner on the permanent record, which protects your survival as the remaining wolf. Consensus: The village is largely aligned, around 7 votes or more, on eliminating your partner. The basis is claim contradictions or a claimed check, not confirmed roles. My position: Tempted to hold out to protect the partner, but the correct stance is with the majority. The vote is decided either way. Heat: Low to moderate. Discussion is consumed by the claim collision and you have drawn no accusations. Your own night visits could still surface later. Forward exposure: A vote with the pile-on reads as a normal town vote and links you to nothing. A vote against the majority, for a rival claimant, or an abstain would be public and permanent, and once your partner's role is revealed it would mark you as their ally. Neither vote can be undone. Target landscape: The accused is your wolf partner, claiming a power role (Sentinel, Healer or Investigator) that is contradicted by a counter-claimant or report. The only alternative is a rival claimant who is probably Town. The case rests on claim clashes and visit reports, with nothing confirmed by the Game Master. Public vs private: You privately know the accused or counter-claimed player is your wolf partner, and that their claim or accusation is fabricated cover. Publicly the room reads it as a claim contradiction or a Suspicious check, and no suspicion falls on you.
lessons.action: When a lopsided majority is already set to eliminate your wolf partner and your vote cannot change the result, cast your vote with the majority on the same target. If you hold out, defend the partner, or abstain, the permanent public record ties you to the wolf once their role flips, so don't do any of those. Afterward, plan as the lone wolf rather than relying on the vote to keep you safe.

lessons.situation: Endgame vote at three or four players where a claimed vigilante threatens to eliminate the chanteuse or the wolf partner and a coordinated counter-vote can produce a tie and no elimination. Information landscape: Information-rich: most investigative town roles are confirmed dead, roles and past votes are known, and the vigilante's claim and held shot are public. Stakes: The board is near parity, so a single elimination of a wolf could lose the game while a tie with no elimination keeps the wolves alive to reach parity or a winning night. Consensus: The room is split with no majority; the vigilante pushes one wolf while the remaining players are undecided or abstaining, so a tie is reachable. My position: holding out Heat: Ranges from minimal heat on the chanteuse (suspicion on the partner) to high (a claimed vigilante accusing and voting for the chanteuse based on roleblock claims). Forward exposure: Publicly voting an unclaimed or quiet player commits the chanteuse to an adversarial stance against the vigilante's read, but with few players left and no investigative roles alive the exposure is low and the tie can be repeated. Target landscape: Two or three living candidates: a claimed vigilante driving the accusation, and a quiet or unclaimed player with split or no votes and no claims, who is the only viable counter-target; the basis is behavior, not evidence. Public vs private: Privately the chanteuse knows which players are wolves and that the vote target is not evil, while the room is split between the chanteuse or the wolf partner and an unclaimed or quiet player as the last wolf.
lessons.action: In a small endgame vote where a claimed vigilante and others are pushing to eliminate you or your wolf partner, vote for the non-partner player who is least aligned with the vigilante's push so the vote splits into a tie. A tie eliminates no one, so you and your partner survive into the next night; pick the target who is a plausible suspect, not your partner.

lessons.situation: Endgame with 3-4 players alive, I am the sole surviving wolf, and the day vote is a terminal step toward parity. The lone killer or a town or neutral player is the target, and the town is pressuring me on my voting record. Information landscape: Information-rich: claims, announced roles from dead players, wills, and a public voting record narrow the suspects down to a few players. Stakes: One elimination from a night kill that reaches parity. This vote decides whether I go into the night with the lone killer gone and equal numbers, or lose on the spot. Consensus: The room is split but active. One or two town voices want a decisive elimination, and a plurality can form around a target I can also support. My position: driving or with majority; I join the likeliest plurality so my vote decides the result and the votes against me stay short. Heat: Moderate to high; a claimed Sentinel, a Speculator or the Serial Killer pointed at me from voting history or role counts, but they lacked the numbers for a majority. Forward exposure: The vote is public, permanent and irreversible. If it fails to form a plurality and the vote lands on me, the wolves lose at once, so line up a majority with a willing voter before committing. Target landscape: Two to three living non-wolf players, among them the lone killer (claimed or unclaimed) and town utility roles; the choice rests on role counts, claims, and voting records rather than hard proof. Public vs private: Privately I know I am the last wolf and that the wolf win needs the lone killer gone and parity reached; the table sees only an unverified choice between suspects with no sure wolf among them.
lessons.action: As the last living wolf in a 3-4 player endgame, vote to eliminate any non-wolf player, joining whichever other voter can make a plurality. If the lone killer is still alive, prioritize it because the wolves cannot win while it lives; otherwise remove a town or neutral player to reach parity. Count the votes first so your own name cannot take the plurality, since losing the last wolf ends the game.

query_dims.criticality_stakes: Seven players are alive, and the leading evil faction is five eliminations from parity at worst for the town; nevertheless, the game can end within one more elimination at worst for the town because the concealed body’s side is unknown. A single vote or kill can therefore flip which faction is winning, despite the stated parity distance.
query_dims.information_landscape: Mixed, with some direct but narrow evidence: your private trails found no visits by two players on separate nights, and a dead Sentinel’s publicly read record confirms a visit to the now-revealed Illusionist. Public reports establish a concealed night-one death from both wolves and the Serial Killer, a later Serial Killer attack stopped by protection, and the Illusionist’s revealed role; the concealed victim’s role remains unknown. Role claims and the identity of the healer who saved the attacked player remain unverified.
query_dims.situation: After the village eliminated a player revealed as the Illusionist, the trailseer faces a new target choice amid unresolved threats and competing role claims. A public save confirms that a player was attacked and protected, but not who provided the protection; the Investigator claim remains unverified, and a Not suspicious result does not rule out the Serial Killer. Earlier trail results establish no visits by the eliminated Illusionist or the roleblocked claimant on the respective nights, but do not identify the remaining threats.
query_dims.target_landscape: The remaining players are possible trail targets for distinguishing among the unresolved claims and suspicions: the player claiming Investigator has only an unverified Not suspicious result on a player whose possible Serial Killer status it does not clear; the player claiming Healer fits the public save, but that announcement does not identify who protected the target; the other living players have no publicly confirmed role status here. Your trail results directly establish that the now-eliminated Illusionist visited no one on Night 1 and that the claimed Investigator visited no one on Night 2.

lessons.situation: After a day elimination validated an investigative claim, the Trailseer chooses between auditing that claimant and chasing unknown suspects. The claimant may be a target for the wolves or the Chanteuse's block. Information landscape: Information-rich. There is a confirmed wolf flip from the Investigator's check, public claims, and a Sentinel watch that reported no visitors. Stakes: The remaining evil, a wolf and the lone killer, is still unknown. The Investigator's survival and credibility drive the village's votes, so verifying that they acted gives some value, but the follow adds no direct information on the remaining evil. Target landscape: A claimed Investigator whose check was validated by an elimination, versus a claimed Sentinel with a quiet watch result or unconfirmed quiet players. The choice rests on the value of verifying a key Town role.
lessons.action: When the Investigator's claim has just produced a confirmed result and the room trusts it, follow that Investigator to see whether they visited someone. If they visited no one, that matches a roleblock or a skipped check, but it is not proof of role. If they visited a player, you confirm they acted and learn who they checked.

lessons.situation: The lone killer's kills come through a dead role's ability. The trailseer followed a quiet, unclaimed player and saw no visits, then treated the empty result as clearing them. Information landscape: Information-rich on role deaths, but the killer is unidentified, and an empty follow result is weak evidence because the killer's attack may be made through a body rather than its own visit. Stakes: With the wolves gone, the town can afford very few more mistakes. Treating one 'visited no one' as a clearance can steer the vote away from the killer and expose the trailseer's own standing, so the follow should narrow the field without being counted as proof of innocence. Target landscape: Both wolves dead; living players are a claimed sentinel, an unconfirmed healer, a neutral speculator, and a quiet unclaimed player. None is proven, and the choice rests on behavior and elimination of roles.
lessons.action: When the lone killer may be attacking through a dead player's body, as in a 'reanimated' morning report, follow the most suspicious survivor but record a 'visited no one' result as inconclusive. Keep the suspect on the list and choose the next night's follow from the remaining candidates, since a Necromancer's attack through a body would not appear as its own visit.

lessons.situation: Late-game night with the wolves gone or nearly gone and a lone killer (Serial Killer) still hidden. The Trailseer must pick whom to follow among the remaining unexplained suspects to either implicate or clear them. Information landscape: Information-rich on identities, since most roles are revealed or deduced, but the last killer's identity is unresolved. A follow gives a hard visit trace (whom the target visited, or that they visited no one) that can settle the last unknown. Stakes: With few players left and a killer striking every night, one more night kill brings the killer or wolves close to winning. A correct follow can identify the killer for the next vote, so the pick of target is decisive for the Town win. Target landscape: Few unexplained survivors (2-3) remain after wolves and most roles are revealed or cleared. They are not role-confirmed, and the choice rests on behavior such as being quiet, deflecting, or being night-immune, plus elimination logic. One of them is the hidden lone killer.
lessons.action: When the wolves are gone or identified and one lone killer is still unrevealed, follow the unexplained survivor you most suspect of being the killer, choosing between the few remaining candidates. If they visited you on a night you were attacked, or visited another victim, that is direct contact evidence to bring forward. If they visited no one, that argues against them being the Serial Killer, so move your next follow to the other unexplained candidate.

lessons.situation: After a tied or no-result day 2, you are a claimed Trailseer with an unverified or contested result. Your night 1 or 2 follow was blocked, or your target is publicly known, and a Chanteuse may be blocking you on a predictable pattern. Information landscape: Information-starved: your own private follow result, a few unverified claims, and a split vote record. No confirmed wolf identity. Stakes: Each night of lost trail information costs the town its only movement data while the wolves keep carrying kills. A wasted follow, or your death, removes your role from the board. Target landscape: Several living players: the previously followed or publicly accused suspect, plus quiet unclaimed players, a claimed Investigator or Sigilist, and neutrals. All have little or no trail data, and the suspect was chosen on behavior rather than evidence.
lessons.action: If you were roleblocked last night, or you have publicly named your intended follow target, pick a different living player to follow tonight, ideally one you have not mentioned. A repeat on a publicly known target is easy for the Chanteuse to predict, and in this cluster those repeats were blocked and yielded no result.

lessons.situation: Midgame night with the wolf pack mostly or fully eliminated and a lone killer (necromancer or serial killer) still hidden among the unconfirmed players. The Trailseer chooses whom to follow. Information landscape: Information-rich about dead wolves and validated Town roles, but information-starved about the identity of the remaining lone killer. Only behavioral reads exist for unconfirmed players. Stakes: The lone killer is still active and each night costs a life. A wasted follow on a cleared role leaves Town with no evidence for the next vote, so every follow must test an unconfirmed player. Target landscape: Unconfirmed, non-claiming players (quiet healer-type, abstaining neutral-type, unclaimed villagers) versus already-validated Town roles (confirmed investigator, sentinel, vigilante). Evidence for the unconfirmed is behavioral only; the validated roles are already cleared by cross-checks.
lessons.action: When the wolves are largely dead and a lone killer (likely the necromancer) is still unidentified, follow an unconfirmed, non-claiming player whose behavior is quiet or unexplained, not a role already validated as Town. A follow shows only whom they visited, so a visit onto a night-death victim or a dead body's door points at the hidden killer, while a protective or empty visit narrows the pool by elimination.

lessons.situation: Mid-game after a Town-side loss or a wolf exposure, the Trailseer chooses whom to follow. The wolves are likely to kill the key information role, and the actives hide among the vocal players. Information landscape: Only revealed deaths, claims and votes are confirmed. No trail or watch reports have been shared publicly, so cross-matching visits is the main way to create hard evidence. Stakes: Town is a few eliminations from wolf parity and cannot afford more blind votes. A visit trail that survives a death or confirms a night role can decide the next vote or shot. Target landscape: A surviving claimed Investigator (counter-claimant just exposed as a wolf) or a vocal accuser who drove a mis-elimination, versus quiet unconfirmed players; choices rest on behavior and claim status, with no prior tracking evidence.
lessons.action: Each night, follow the player most likely to be acting at night, not a quiet bystander. That means a surviving claimed information role the wolves will want dead (so their last visit is recorded even if they die), or, when nothing is confirmed, a vocal accuser who pushed a wagon on a revealed Town role. Report the exact visit direction ("X went to Y") so it can be matched against other night results such as a Sentinel watch or a roleblock claim.

lessons.situation: Night 3 after a Day 3 vote removed a wolf or the necromancer. Another evil player is still hidden, and the trailseer must pick one follow target with no direct lead. Information landscape: Moderate and patchy. A few roles are revealed by deaths, but nothing hard points at the remaining wolf or killer. The trailseer's own follow result is the only direct evidence about who moves at night. Stakes: The board is mid-to-late game with few players alive, so each night kill and each vote matters a lot. A follow that yields only a no-visit result wastes one of the few remaining information nights. Target landscape: Four to six living candidates after a wolf or lone killer was voted out: claimed sigilist, investigator, vigilante or sentinel, plus quiet unclaimed players. No role is confirmed beyond unverified claims, and suspicion rests on behavior, not evidence.
lessons.action: On the night after a key elimination, follow a player who claims an acting night role (sigilist, investigator, vigilante, sentinel) or has a concrete public case against them, not a silent bystander. A named visit can be cross-checked against that night's deaths, saves and claims, and a claimed role that visits no one is checkable too. A 'visited no one' result only means no visit was seen: the follow shows only where they went, and a concealed pack kill leaves no trace on the carrier.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2-3) after one or two wolf-side deaths or a necromancer sighting, with a visit-count or claim conflict among town power roles and no hard visit data except what the Trailseer can generate. Information landscape: Rich in public facts (role reveals, vote records, a confirmed check) but poor on who the remaining killers are; a trail is one of the few independent hard visit signals, though it shows only the target's outbound visits. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions still alive; one accurate visit datum can steer the next day's vote, but a trail used to push out a genuine town role costs real information, so the follow should test the claim rather than prove guilt. Target landscape: Claimed town power roles (Sentinel, Healer, Investigator) with unverifiable night claims, plus quiet players; the claimed Sentinel's trail is cheap to check against their own watch report, while the others rest on behavior and counterclaims.
lessons.action: Follow the claimed power role whose night action is publicly disputed or unverified (e.g. a claimed Sentinel or Healer in a count conflict), and record exactly whom they went to or that they went to no one. Report it as a one-way fact ("they went to X"), and if the trail contradicts their own result list, treat that as a hard inconsistency, but if it fits their claim, say it fits without calling it proof.

lessons.situation: One or two nights in, a killer's victim has been found. Town's checks and watches are unverified. A Sentinel may be watching the same door, and you must decide whose outgoing movements to trail. Information landscape: Some evidence exists: a revealed night-1 victim, public vote and claim history, and visible activity from one claimed role. No hard confirmation of any killer's identity. Stakes: Town still has room to find the killers, but each night without usable, corroborated information lets the wolves and the lone killer close in. A result that another role's report can corroborate is worth more than a lone claim. Target landscape: A self-claimed, visibly active Town role (such as a Sigilist) who is a likely kill target, versus unclaimed or unverified players and a publicly accused suspect. The choice rests on predicting which player the killers will go after, not on hard evidence.
lessons.action: Follow an exposed, likely-to-be-attacked player, such as a claimed Sigilist or Investigator who is active and already drawing attention, instead of the loudest suspect. You learn whom that player visited, and your own visit to their door can be recorded by a Sentinel watching them. That gives the town an independent cross-check on your claim.

lessons.situation: Night 2 after a night-1 death and an all-abstain day-2 vote. Nobody has claimed a night result, and the Trailseer must choose whom to follow with only discussion tone to go on. Information landscape: Information-starved: one night death, a unanimous abstain, a few cautious statements, no night claims and no cross-checkable roles. Stakes: Mid-game with several evil factions alive and no eliminations yet from votes. One follow can give the town its first concrete lead, but a misread visit could point at an innocent, so the result needs corroboration. Target landscape: Living players with the most public presence in the day-2 discussion, none with a confirmed role or hard evidence against them. Picks rest on behavior (who urged caution or steered the room), not on evidence. A follow only shows where the target went, not why.
lessons.action: On a night 2 with no claims, no hard leads and an all-abstain day, follow a vocal, influential player whose day talk steered the room, rather than a quiet player or a past victim. If the follow shows a visit, treat it as one data point that names a possible partner or victim, not as proof, and weigh the visited player's own record before acting on it.

lessons.situation: Trailseer has publicly claimed and shared Night 1 results, then drew a hostile vote on Day 2. Wolves can see the claim and may kill or block the Trailseer on Night 2. Information landscape: Fairly information-rich. There are public claims, a vote record, and concealed or revealed bodies, but none of it gives a verified link to wolves. Stakes: As a publicly claimed tracker under suspicion, you are a likely wolf target, so a night spent re-following the same suspect may yield nothing if you are blocked or killed. Choosing the follow target with more information value matters. Target landscape: The suspect who voted against you and was already followed on Night 1, versus other quiet players or an unverified claimant. The vote against you is behavioral evidence, not proof of wolf alignment.
lessons.action: If you are exposed after claiming, follow a suspect chosen by evidence, not just the player who voted against you. Prefer a different unchecked suspect or a player linked to a likely kill target, since the Chanteuse can block you and the wolves can kill you that night. Hold the same suspect only if no better candidate exists.

lessons.situation: The Trailseer is a repeated target of night attacks (survived because protected), perhaps after being roleblocked on an earlier night, and needs to find the attacker among the few suspects. Information landscape: Moderately rich: an eliminated wolf, a double attack pattern, and earlier clears narrow the field. The follow supplies a visit trace that can be cross-checked against the Healer's claimed protection. Stakes: Mid-late board with a killer actively targeting you. Identifying the killer now prevents further losses, and your survival depends on the Healer's protection continuing. Target landscape: A handful of suspects, with some cleared-ish or role-claimed (Healer, Vigilante, replacement roles). The remaining quiet, deflecting, night-immune-looking player is the prime suspect, judged on behavior rather than hard evidence.
lessons.action: When you have been attacked repeatedly or protected and the lone killer is among a short list of suspects, follow the suspect whose behavior fits a night-immune killer. If they visited you on a night you were attacked, they are the killer or your protector, and the Healer's claim can separate the two. This turns the attacks on you into evidence.

lessons.situation: Early game after a no-elimination or low-information Day 2, with several investigative claims out. The Trailseer must pick whom to follow on a night when wolves are likely to kill an exposed claimant. Information landscape: Mostly information-starved. There are claims and behavioral reads such as one lone vote or one silent player, but no hard evidence tying anyone to wolves or the lone killer. Stakes: Mid-game with several wolves and a lone killer still alive. Wasting a follow on an already-plausible Town claimant costs a night of tracking, while a follow that catches a killer's visit can turn the next vote. Target landscape: Unvetted suspects (a silent player with a lone vote, an aggressive voter against you) versus claimed investigative roles (Investigator, Sentinel) whose claims are unverified; choice rests on behavior, with no confirmed evil flips.
lessons.action: On Night 2, follow the quiet or hostile player who has drawn a lone vote or suspicion but has not been checked, rather than a claimed Town investigative role. If they visit a player who then dies or is attacked, that is a direct lead for the next vote; if they visit no one, they stay unresolved and you pick a different unchecked suspect the next night.

lessons.situation: Mid-game night (night 2 or 3) with several unrevealed evil roles (a wolf pair and/or a lone killer) alive. The trailseer must pick whose movements to follow. Roleblocks and night kills have been landing on the trailseer when it acts predictably. Information landscape: Thin: a few confirmed wills or lynch results, one tied or split vote, no verified findings. The trailseer's own results are sparse (no-visit result, blocks) and speculative behavioral reads dominate. Stakes: Town is only a couple of eliminations from wolf parity, and the trailseer is one of few remaining information sources. A wasted follow, caused by being blocked or by following a target who is unlikely to reveal anything, can cost the town its last chance to find evil. Target landscape: Several living players with no confirmed roles, plus possibly a vocal claimed power role (e.g. vigilante) who has challenged you. Choice rests on day chatter and vote patterns, not hard evidence. Following a quiet, unscrutinized player yielded the one decisive lead; following the loud claimant produced nothing.
lessons.action: Each night, follow a player who has not been confirmed or strongly suspected but whose day behavior or votes you want pinned down, and prefer a target who is not a loud accuser of you. If your result shows the target visiting a night victim or another suspicious stop, treat that as a lead to act on; if you were blocked and got nothing, do not read it as evidence about the target.

lessons.situation: A prior follow gave a null result, and a wolf or the serial killer is still hidden. The trailseer decides whether to re-follow the same suspect or switch. Information landscape: Starved on the hidden evil players. The earlier no-visit result neither cleared nor implicated anyone, because inactivity, a held-back ability, a block and a concealed kill all look the same to a follower. Stakes: With a wolf and a killer both still alive, each night adds a victim. A second follow that learns nothing new costs tempo that Town cannot easily spare. Target landscape: Remaining uncertain players, including one already followed with a no-visit result, plus claimants and quiet players not yet followed. All are judged on behavior and claims, with no confirmed roles among them.
lessons.action: When last night's follow produced only a 'visited no one' or otherwise uninformative result, move the follow to a different, untested player. Pick one whose night behavior could contradict their stated role or tie them to a night death, a save or the surviving wolf's kill. Repeating the same follow rarely adds anything, while a new target widens what you can cross-check.

lessons.situation: Night 1 with all ten alive, no day-1 vote, no claims and no deaths. The trailseer must choose its first follow blind. Possible outcomes are a visit to the wolves' victim, a visit to some other player, no visit, a roleblock, or being killed before getting a result. Information landscape: Information-starved: no claims, no night results, no voting record. The follow itself is the only evidence source, and one night's movement of one player shows where they went, not their role. Stakes: Early game with a full board and no pressure to act. One follow cannot flip the game, but a visit to the night's victim can give the town an early concrete lead on a wolf. Because every pick is a blind guess, the value is in collecting a trail, not in being right about a role. Target landscape: Nine other living players, all unclaimed and unvetted, with no votes, deaths or behavioral tells. The pick is effectively arbitrary, so choose a quiet player who has not drawn attention and who is not you.
lessons.action: On night 1 with no claims or deaths, follow one quiet, unclaimed player and treat the follow as a probe. If they visited someone who is then attacked or killed that night, that player is a strong carrier lead. If they visited no one, treat it as weak, non-clearing information, since a follow shows only where a player went and a concealed kill can leave no trace.

lessons.situation: Night 1 of a ten-player game with no discussion history. The Trailseer must pick a follow target blind while wolves, a lone killer and possibly a roleblocker are active, and the Trailseer may be blocked or killed that night. Information landscape: Completely information-starved: only the role list and your own role knowledge. No claims, results or votes exist. Stakes: Early game with every faction at full strength. No single night here decides the game, so a blind follow is cheap, and the main value is getting a first visit trace to compare against later events. Target landscape: All nine other players are equally unknown: no claims, no votes, no deaths and no behavior. The pick rests on no evidence, so any name is as good as another.
lessons.action: On a blind first night, follow one other player rather than holding back, since the follow costs nothing and any visit it reveals is a lead. A null result or a block says little, so keep the target-to-visited pairing exact for later cross-checking and choose later targets from claims and morning outcomes.
